INTERVIEW – How is the race for power and profit reshaping space?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:09:42 UTC
22:09:42 KST

For decades, the space race was about getting there first.
The Soviet Union put the first satellite and first human into orbit. The US put the first humans on the moon. Mars then emerged as the distant destination that could define the next generation of exploration.
Today, the competition is becoming much more complicated.
In a wide-ranging conversation with Anadolu, Fabrizio Pinto, an Italian astrophysicist, former NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory navigation specialist and founding director of the EKOSPACE Aerospace Research Center at Izmir University of Economics, explained how space is becoming an increasingly crowded economic frontier.
Where the Cold War space race was an ideological duel between two superpowers, today’s competition involves a growing number of countries and private companies pursuing commercial opportunities alongside scientific and strategic goals.
And as global space leaders prepare to convene at the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Türkiye’s Antalya, the conversation is shifting from how we explore space to how we govern, commercialize and protect it.
The moon, rather than Mars, has become the primary short-term objective of the international space race, according to Pinto.
"A few years ago, the answer would have been colonization of Mars," he told Anadolu. "In more recent years, due to competition with China, that goal has been reset to the moon, which is achievable in the shorter term."
The epicenter of this race is the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are believed to hold vast reservoirs of water ice. If extracted, that ice could provide drinking water and be processed into oxygen and rocket fuel, reducing the supplies that must be shipped from Earth.
NASA’s Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the moon and build the capabilities for a longer-term human presence, with the first crewed lunar landing now targeted for 2028.
China is pursuing a parallel program, targeting a crewed lunar landing before 2030 and developing the Chang’e-7 and Chang’e-8 missions as steps toward its planned International Lunar Research Station, which is expected to take shape in the 2030s.
In 2023, India made history by becoming the first country to land a spacecraft near the lunar south pole with Chandrayaan-3.
Yet, the push to control cislunar space – the region between Earth and the lunar orbit – is as much about terrestrial security as it is about science.
"The states are competing because, politically speaking ... the conquest of cislunar space is basically the strategic height to be conquered in order to dominate the Earth," he said.
"There is a fear on the part of some that the moon will become territory from which the Earth can be controlled, attacked or influenced."
Asked about establishing a sustained human and commercial presence beyond Earth rather than simply visiting the moon or Mars, Pinto called it “the central task.”
"To sustain life on a different planet – even on the International Space Station – is a huge enterprise, because the human body cannot operate above seven or eight miles of altitude from the surface of the Earth."
Keeping a functioning outpost running, he said, means treating it like an industrial supply chain.
Pinto said the current race is being fought simultaneously by governments and private companies, and the two are increasingly impossible to separate.
"When we say the United States, we cannot mean NASA anymore," he said. "Right now, what we mean is SpaceX, maybe Blue Origin, Virgin Galactic."
Modern space architecture relies heavily on commercial subcontracting. NASA, for instance, has contracted SpaceX and Blue Origin to build human landing systems that will carry astronauts from lunar orbit to the moon's surface.
According to analytics firm BryceTech, commercial providers accounted for 87% of the world's orbital launches in 2025.
At the same time, rapid technological growth has outpaced international law.
The foundation of space governance – the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty – banned the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit and declared that no nation could claim sovereignty over celestial bodies.
But the treaty was written for an era when only a few nations had demonstrated independent launcher capabilities.
"The existing laws cannot be enforced," Pinto argued, pointing to modern military discussions surrounding orbital maneuvering, counter-space capabilities and even nuclear-powered space hardware.
"If China lands on the moon and claims an immediate area for exploration, can China actively do anything in order to avoid the Americans landing in the same area or vice versa? Nobody has ever been in that situation."
The issue moved from hypothetical to headline news this week.
On Monday, US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink publicly confirmed for the first time that the US has deployed on-orbit "space control weapons" to protect American satellite architecture from adversary interference.
China subsequently called on Washington to "stop preparing for war in outer space" and avoid triggering a new arms race.
The growing energy and environmental footprint of AI data centers on Earth has sparked proposals to move massive server farms directly into space.
"Clearly here, there is another mechanism to generate revenue," Pinto said.
A US startup called Starcloud has already run an AI model on an Nvidia chip aboard a satellite, Google is building solar-powered satellites for AI processing and SpaceX has proposed a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for orbital computing.
China is developing its own space-based AI computing network, having already launched a cluster of satellites designed to process data in orbit.
Yet, Pinto cautioned, orbital data centers carry hidden environmental costs on Earth.
“If those things are in space, you could argue that the impact is lessened. However, you must not forget that the spacecraft eventually needs to reenter the atmosphere. And when they reenter, we're talking about millions of these vehicles, we are going to have some kind of chemical pollution and thermal effects,” he said.
At the same time, low-Earth orbit is undergoing a quiet traffic crisis. Where space once held a few thousand active payloads, commercial satellite constellations are scaling into the tens of thousands.
As orbits become more crowded, relying on ground teams to guide individual spacecraft becomes harder to manage, he said.
Historically, satellites relied on Earth-based radio dishes, like NASA's Deep Space Network, to determine their position and guide adjustments to their course.
Pinto, who worked on NASA's landmark Deep Space 1 mission, the first probe to test autonomous spacecraft navigation in deep space, explained that traditional manual guidance cannot scale to meet modern orbital density.
Autonomous navigation – allowing spacecraft to make navigation decisions onboard – is becoming essential rather than experimental, he said.
Many of these issues will be on the agenda when the international space community gathers in the Turkish resort city of Antalya next month.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress will take place from Oct. 5 to 9, marking the first time Türkiye has hosted the annual event.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, the congress is expected to bring together 10,000 attendees, including leaders from NASA, the European Space Agency, China’s and India’s space programs and other agencies, under the theme “The World Needs More Space.”
Pinto has watched Türkiye’s space ambitions develop since arriving in the country in 2017, a year before the Turkish Space Agency was established.
He pointed to Türkiye's first astronaut mission to the International Space Station, its communications satellites and its lunar ambitions as milestones in the country's development as a spacefaring nation.
Drawing a parallel to Türkiye’s rapid rise over the last decade into a global exporter of uncrewed aerial vehicles, Pinto sees space as the natural next frontier for developing industrial ecosystems.
"I expect that Türkiye will be able to do the same in space, but it takes time and investment,” he said. “A deal in aerospace has a multiplier effect – it isn't just one spacecraft, everybody benefits."

‘Go and die back home,’ Thai premier says in rebuke to disrespectful foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:07:33 UTC
22:07:33 KST

Saadet Gokce
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul lashed out Thursday at foreigners who break the law or exploit Thai people, urging provincial governors to step up enforcement.
Speaking about Interior Ministry policies, Anutin said foreigners could live alongside Thais if they earned an honest living and did not exploit others, The Nation newspaper reported.
"I have recently learnt that there has even been a request to establish a private cemetery. This is going too far, well beyond the bounds. You should be grateful we have let you come here,” he said.
"If you are going to die, go and die back home. You do not need to die here. And do not exploit us. Nor is it acceptable to apply for permission to open a restaurant but have a place of worship there," he added.
Anutin urged governors to use their legal powers against foreigners who threatened, bullied or exploited Thai people, calling for swift deportation when the relevant criteria were met.
"I do not think you can simply set up a place of worship on your own. These arrangements must also respect Thai society and culture," he said.
The remarks come after hundreds of people demonstrated outside the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok recently, calling on foreign visitors to respect the country's laws and culture amid growing public discontent over the behavior of some Israeli tourists.
He said his concerns involved people from multiple countries across Asia, the Middle East, Central Asia, Europe and Africa.

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The women's basketball competition of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games tipped off on Thursday, with Indonesia, the Philippines, and host Japan all securing comfortable victories in their group-stage openers.
The 11-team tournament features three groups, where the top two teams from each group, along with the two best third-placed sides, will advance to the knockout stage.
In the tournament opener, Indonesia dominated the glass with a 50-36 rebounding advantage to overcome Thailand 61-52 in Group A, which also includes powerhouse China.

In Group B, the Philippines cruised past Kazakhstan 86-58, while host Japan overwhelmed Hong Kong, China 114-37. Japan mounted a fierce 11-0 opening run and held its opponent to just six points in the second quarter and seven in the third, stretching the lead to 65 points by the end of the third period to put the game out of reach. ■

Türkiye diesel prices top 100 liras after second hike in 2 days
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:53 CST
22:06:53 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Diesel prices in Türkiye rose by another 4.68 Turkish liras (about 0.10 U.S. dollars) per liter from Thursday, pushing pump prices above 100 liras for the first time as the country faced its second major diesel price hike in two days.
The latest increase followed a rise of about 6.5 liras per liter on Tuesday, according to fuel retailer Petrol Ofisi.
Following the two consecutive hikes, diesel prices rose to about 100.3 liras per liter in Istanbul, while prices exceeded 101 liras in Ankara and Izmir. In some provinces, prices climbed above 102 liras, according to nationwide pump price data.
The successive increases came as global oil prices remained elevated amid heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns over disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Fuel stations across the country began replacing their price displays with three-digit figures ahead of the latest increase, reflecting the sharp rise in diesel prices.
Diesel prices in Türkiye have risen sharply over the past year. They stood at around 54 liras per liter in September 2025, meaning prices have increased by more than 85 percent over the period.
On Wednesday, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said the government has temporarily given up additional tax revenue through a sliding-scale fuel tax to cushion pump prices against surging global oil prices.
"While diesel exceeds 150 liras per liter in many European countries, it is hovering around 100 liras here. We have truly given up significant tax revenue to achieve this," Simsek said in a televised interview on Wednesday.
Simsek noted that keeping diesel prices temporarily contained is crucial for easing cost pressures on the country's vital agricultural and transportation sectors, which heavily influence inflation. (1 U.S. dollar = 48.68 Turkish liras) ■

WINDHOEK, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has reiterated its call for Cuba's removal from unilateral lists that restrict its access to international financial mechanisms and development assistance.
Speaking Wednesday evening at a state-hosted solidarity gala dinner in Windhoek, Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said no nation should be denied the opportunity to pursue development and prosperity because it has chosen an independent path.
"Constructive dialogue, mutual respect and international cooperation, rather than isolation, must remain our instruments for advancing global peace, justice and shared prosperity," Nandi-Ndaitwah said.
The president reminded the audience that when the Namibian people rose against foreign apartheid occupation, Cuba answered the moral call for justice.
Nandi-Ndaitwah said the bond between Namibia and Cuba is not a matter of recent diplomatic convenience, but a friendship forged through shared sacrifice long before Namibia's independence.
According to the president, consistent with resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly, the African Union Assembly of Heads of State and Government, and the Non-Aligned Movement, Namibia continues to call for the lifting of the economic, commercial and financial blockade against Cuba.
The event sought to raise humanitarian aid and medical supplies for the people of Cuba, which is facing severe economic challenges due to the restrictive commercial, economic and financial blockade imposed by the U.S. government.
It marked the latest milestone in the Namibia National Solidarity Campaign for Cuba, an initiative that has generated more than 700,000 Namibian dollars (about 42,800 U.S. dollars) to procure vital medical supplies and direct relief for the Cuban population. ■

====================================================================================================

EU proposes social media ban for children under 13
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:43 CST
22:06:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Thursday proposed new EU-wide restrictions on children's access to social media, including a ban for those under 13 and a minimum age of 15 for minors to open their own accounts.
Under the proposed EU KIDS Act, children under 13 would be barred from social media, and children aged between 13 and 15 would only be allowed to use limited social media accounts set up through a parent or guardian's account. Such accounts would include restrictions on social contacts and screen time of up to one hour per day.
The proposal would also require social media platforms, video-sharing services, online video games, AI companions and chatbots used by minors to be "safe by design."
Addictive features, including infinite scrolling, certain reward mechanisms and push notifications during sleeping hours, would be restricted. Profiles of minors would have to be private by default, with geolocation, camera and microphone access switched off.
AI companions and chatbots would also be disabled by default for minors and prohibited from simulating interpersonal relationships in ways that could create emotional dependency.
The proposal requires online services and app stores to introduce age-assurance mechanisms. The Commission said its EU age-verification app could be used without retaining identity documents or biometric data.
The act would also reverse the burden of proof for very large online platforms, requiring providers to demonstrate that their services are safe for children. They would have to submit compliance plans for independent auditing before introducing relevant services or features.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the proposal was intended to put parents "back in the driving seat" and require platforms to prove their services are safe by design.
The proposal has been submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for consideration and approval. Enforcement would build on existing mechanisms under the Digital Services Act and the Artificial Intelligence Act, with fines for violations potentially reaching 6 percent of a company's total worldwide annual turnover. ■

China to work with int'l community to further enrich practices in human rights protection: FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:36 CST
22:06:36 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China stands ready to work with the international community to further enrich practices in human rights protection, improve global human rights governance, and together build a community with a shared future for humanity, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Thursday.
Guo made the remarks at a regular press briefing in response to a query about the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council.
On the sidelines of the session, the Chinese side and the United Nations Office at Geneva co-hosted an exhibition themed "Accessibility for All" at the Palais des Nations in Geneva.
"The exhibition brought together more than 300 guests, including UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk, permanent representatives of various countries, heads of international organizations, and media representatives," Guo said.
The exhibition offered a comprehensive look at China's practices in advancing "accessibility for all" in areas such as technology, culture, employment and the rule of law. The event was warmly received with guests trying out cutting-edge smart assistive devices and viewing artworks by persons with disabilities, he said.
Building a barrier-free environment is an important part of human rights protection. In October 2024, the 57th session of the Human Rights Council adopted by consensus a resolution proposed by China, on behalf of 30 countries, titled "Promoting accessibility for the full enjoyment of all human rights by all." Holding this exhibition is an important step in implementing that resolution, Guo noted.
This year marks the first anniversary of the Global Governance Initiative proposed by the Chinese side and the third anniversary of the implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Building of a Barrier-free Environment, Guo noted, adding that China will once again propose a resolution on accessibility to this session of the Human Rights Council. ■

1 killed, 2 injured by falling Houthi drone debris in western Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:06:33 UTC
22:06:33 KST

Mohammad Sio
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
One person was killed and two others were injured Thursday by debris from a drone Saudi authorities said was launched by Yemen’s Houthis and intercepted over the western city of Taif, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
A Civil Defense spokesperson said emergency teams responded after fragments from the intercepted drone fell across parts of the city, the agency reported.
A Yemeni resident was killed, while a Saudi woman and a Pakistani resident were injured, the spokesperson said, adding that the Pakistani national was in critical condition.
The falling debris also caused material damage to several buildings and vehicles.
Saudi authorities said the drone had been launched by Yemen’s Houthi group, according to the report.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the Saudi statement.
Saudi Arabia said Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed a drone allegedly launched by the Houthis toward Mecca before it entered the holy city’s restricted airspace. The Yemeni group denied responsibility.
The Saudi-led coalition said it was the second attempt to target Mecca since 2017.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of missile and drone attacks attributed to the Houthis in recent days amid escalating regional tensions.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has also intensified since early July.
The renewed clashes have ended a period of relative calm that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:28 CST
22:06:28 KST

TEHRAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Iran on Thursday ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave the country within 48 hours in response to Sweden's expulsion of an official at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm, while rejecting Sweden's accusations against Tehran as "baseless."
Iran's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that Alireza Yousefi, director general for Western Europe at the ministry, summoned the Swedish ambassador to Iran on Thursday morning and lodged a strong protest against Sweden's "destructive" policies, particularly its "inappropriate rhetoric about Iran and hosting of anti-Iran terrorist groups and individuals."
During the meeting, the Swedish ambassador was informed that a Swedish diplomat had been ordered to leave Iran within 48 hours "due to reasons that were explained to the ambassador," the statement said.
Sweden's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it had summoned Iran's ambassador and asked an official at the Iranian embassy to leave the country over activities "not compatible with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations."
Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer later told state broadcaster SVT that the decision was made over Iran's alleged activities against "Jewish and Israeli interests" in Sweden.
Iran's Foreign Ministry rejected Sweden's claims, saying Stockholm had, "in an unjustified move that is in violation of international law, compelled a diplomat serving at Iran's embassy in Stockholm to leave the country without any justified reason."
It added that Sweden's action was taken under Israel's influence and constitutes an attempt to disrupt the normal operations of the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.
The ministry said Iran would adopt necessary measures to protect its national rights and interests, including through reciprocal actions. ■

Japan PM Takaichi reshuffles cabinet, retains key ministers, taps first JIP member
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:19 CST
22:06:19 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet on Thursday, retaining most key ministers while bringing in a newcomer from the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), the junior coalition partner of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
It is Takaichi's first cabinet reshuffle since she took office last October.
According to the new lineup, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama all remained in their respective posts.
Among those entering the cabinet for the first time, House of Representatives members Kazuo Yana and Yoshihiro Seki had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal. They were named agriculture minister and education minister, respectively. This marked the first time since the scandal came to light that lawmakers disciplined by the party over the affair had received cabinet positions.
Hiroshi Nakatsuka, formerly secretary general of the JIP, was appointed minister in charge of regulatory reform, making him the first JIP member to serve as a cabinet minister. The move marked a shift from the LDP and JIP cooperating outside the cabinet to cooperation within the cabinet.
Shigeaki Koga, a former official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that on foreign and security policies, the JIP is even more hawkish than Takaichi and could potentially encourage the prime minister to pursue more hawkish policies.
Another focus of the reshuffle is the absence of former Internal Affairs and Communications Minister Yoshimasa Hayashi from the new cabinet. Hayashi was Takaichi's rival in last year's LDP presidential election.
Analysts said the personnel changes indicate, on the one hand, that the Takaichi administration will press ahead with its established military buildup, proactive fiscal policy, and diplomatic agenda.
The Takaichi government is set to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year, potentially including plans to acquire large numbers of unmanned systems and move toward mass production of hypersonic missiles.
On the other hand, Takaichi's latest cabinet reshuffle is also aimed at consolidating her administration's power base and paving the way for her to secure another term as LDP president in next autumn's party leadership race. ■

China's Jingdezhen revitalizes ceramics industry through digitalization, smart manufacturing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:13 CST
22:06:13 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 10, 2026 shows ceramic products made by an intelligent workshop in Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province.
Jingdezhen, known worldwide as China's "porcelain capital," is revitalizing its centuries-old ceramics industry through digitalization and smart manufacturing.
Once reliant on 72 intricate steps and skilled craftsmanship, porcelain production process at the intelligent workshop is now increasingly automated with smart production lines, AGV robots and intelligent kilns, resulting in higher efficiency and precision.
Production steps here have been slashed by one-third, labor efficiency has risen by 40 percent, and the deformation rate in finished products has dropped from 6 percent to 0.8 percent. A fully automated glazing line at the workshop is now capable of processing up to 1,500 pieces an hour. Porcelain products made here are exported to markets including Britain, Russia and Malaysia. U.S. faces global criticism after deploying weapons in space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:13 CST
22:06:13 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The United States faces global doubts and criticism after announcing for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, with countries warning against an "arms race" in space.
U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the United States has fielded "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," but declined to disclose the types of weapons deployed or whether they were designed to target objects in space or on Earth.
Back in March, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman said that the U.S. Space Force was tasked "to contest and control the space domain" to ensure U.S. forces could operate freely while "denying the same to our adversaries."
Established as a separate military branch by U.S. President Donald Trump in 2019, the Space Force was the first new branch of the U.S. military in more than seven decades. It carries out both offensive and defensive operations aimed at affecting adversary capabilities, from disruption to degradation to destruction, including "orbital warfare and electromagnetic warfare," Saltzman said.
Trump is further stepping up the militarization of space in his second term.
Ordering the Pentagon to pursue space-based interceptors during the first week of his presidency, he announced in January 2025 the "Golden Dome" missile defense system with space-based capabilities as a crucial component.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated that space-based components of the Golden Dome system alone could cost as much as 542 billion U.S. dollars over the next 20 years.
Astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has spent decades compiling a list of rocket launches, told The Guardian, a British daily, that it was reasonable to assume Washington had such weapons in space, likely jammers, as it had already deployed several satellites with secret payloads.
McDowell said the United States was moving away from the idea that space should be used solely for peaceful purposes. The United States "sees conflict in space as something that is conceptually normalised, whereas 20 years ago it was 'no, we will never want to do that'," he said.
"I think this is wrong," he added. "I also think it is still not too late to change course on this."
Similarly, Lemmy Nyongesa Mulaku, a scholar of international affairs at the University of Nairobi, said Washington's secret deployment of space weapons has undermined the international legal framework established by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not prohibit conventional weapons in space or ground-based weapons against assets in space, leaving room for interpretation.
"The dangers associated with Washington's actions include triggering an arms race in space, which would pose dangers to civilians in terms of increasing the probability of debris falling; interference with civilian communications networks; and increase an erosion of trust in international treaties," Mulaku said. "An arms race in outer space will make it a contested sphere with consequences for the whole world."
Russia's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that Washington's deployment of orbital weapons ignored the possible consequences of a conflict and threatened long-term stability in space-based activity.
"In pursuit of its narrow self-interests, Washington is ready to completely ignore the catastrophic consequences for humanity of any armed conflict in orbit," Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a commentary on the ministry website.
The country has long argued that the United States and its allies opposed a ban on all weapons in outer space because they planned to deploy weapons there.
Meanwhile, China urged the United States to stop expanding military build-up in outer space and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Tuesday.
Guo added that China stands for peaceful use of outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a war zone. ■

China's Zhao Jiaju becomes first Asian to win Tor des Geants
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:13 CST
22:06:13 KST

GUIYANG, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- After 65 hours, 55 minutes and 22 seconds on his feet, Zhao Jiaju crossed the finish line in Courmayeur in the pre-dawn hours of Wednesday, local time in Italy.
The athlete from southwest China's Guizhou Province claimed the overall championship in the 330-kilometer category of Italy's Tor des Geants (TOR) ultra-trail race. He became the first Chinese and the first Asian runner to win the title since the event's inception, breaking the race record by a full 13 minutes.
Tor des Geants is one of the world's premier ultra-long-distance trail-running events. Its course stretches across the Alps, passing major peaks, including Mont Blanc and Monte Rosa. The course covers 336.1 kilometers in total and features over 24,000 meters of cumulative elevation gain, equivalent to roughly three times the height of Mount Everest.
Over the grueling race, athletes must endure drastic day and night temperature swings, rugged mountain terrain, low temperatures, high-altitude reactions and extreme wind and rain. The event imposes a 150-hour cutoff time with no mandatory rest periods. Sustained high-intensity exertion throughout the race puts extreme demands on competitors' physical reserves, mental fortitude and on-the-spot judgement.
Zhao displayed extraordinary endurance and astute race tactics throughout the arduous contest. He did not stop at his first checkpoint until he had run for 35 hours and 42 minutes, with only around 20 minutes of actual sleep. He adopted a fragmented-sleep strategy, grabbing roughly 10-minute naps at each checkpoint before pressing on. Across the full 336.1-kilometer course, his total sleep time amounted to only about one hour.
After the race, Zhao admitted that the latter half of the competition was so agonizing, it felt "almost unbearable." Suffering from body aches and blurred vision, he had pushed his body to its absolute physical limit and only managed to reach the finish line through sheer willpower.
Born in February 1995 in Guizhou, Zhao was formerly a delivery rider who loved martial arts. In 2014, he learned about trail running from a street advertisement in Hangzhou, developed a keen interest in the sport, and revealed a natural talent for long-distance running.
This championship was no fluke; it was the payoff for years of hard-won progress and breakthroughs. His journey in endurance sports began during his ordinary and sometimes difficult days as a food delivery worker.
While working as a delivery rider, he built up his stamina and speed by running to make deliveries and started taking part in marathons. At 22, he moved on to long-distance trail-running competitions. By the age of 26, he had become the runner with the highest ITRA (International Trail Running Association) points in Asia.
In July this year, he won the 168-kilometer category of the Chongli 168 Super-Trail Race in 19 hours, one minute and 32 seconds, breaking his own track record set six years earlier and earning himself the title of four-time champion of Chongli 168.
In September last year, Zhao took part in Tor des Geants for the first time, but was forced to withdraw at the 203.8-kilometer aid station after running out of energy. At that time, he vowed, "I will be back."
This year's 330-kilometer Tor des Geants marked Zhao's second attempt on this "devil's course." One year later, he kept his promise and made a triumphant return as champion.
Having conquered the "Giant's Journey" and stood atop this ultimate challenge, Zhao has even greater ambitions. Alongside competing in more races, he hopes to inspire more people through the spirit of trail running and encourage more to take up sport.
"I hope my story can motivate more people and give everyone the resolve to forge ahead bravely," he said. ■

DR Congo Ebola cases top 7,400 as transmission shifts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:06:07 CST
22:06:07 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is showing a shifting pattern, with transmission easing in the long-time epicenter of Ituri but rising rapidly in North Kivu, where treatment capacity is nearing saturation, according to the latest government situation report released on Thursday.
As of Tuesday, the country had reported 7,404 confirmed cases, including 3,577 deaths, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.3 percent. A total of 1776 patients have recovered. The outbreak has affected 62 health zones across seven provinces, with Ituri remaining the epicenter of the outbreak, accounting for 77.7 percent of all confirmed cases.
The report pointed to particularly acute pressure on treatment capacity in North Kivu, where 373 patients were hospitalized and the overall bed occupancy rate had reached 94.7 percent.
Jean-Jacques Muyembe, head of the country's National Institute of Biomedical Research, said Tuesday in Kinshasa that Ituri had passed a "peak" and entered a "downward slope," while the epidemic curve in North Kivu was still rising and "has not yet reached the plateau," making it another major hotspot.
World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that the response was beginning to show encouraging signs in some of the worst-affected areas, particularly Ituri.
He nevertheless warned that the epidemic continued to expand and claim lives. In North Kivu, weekly cases had almost doubled over the previous two weeks, rising from about 100 to more than 200.
"The area is so vast that it is hard to speak of a single epidemic. It is many outbreaks, in many places," Tedros told a press briefing in Geneva.
The current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

Türkiye condemns Houthi attacks, welcomes steps against illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:05:15 UTC
22:05:15 KST

Seyit Kurt
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Türkiye on Thursday condemned a drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia last weekend and actions carried out by the Houthis, while welcoming steps by 12 countries to restrict trade and business ties with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Speaking at the National Defense Ministry’s weekly press briefing in Ankara, ministry spokesman Zeki Akturk said Ankara condemns the drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia, as well as actions carried out by the Houthis.
He said such actions threatening regional stability should end as soon as possible, warning that the continued Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait adversely affects not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability.
Turning to Israel’s actions in the region, Akturk said Israel was further deepening instability by continuing simultaneous attacks on Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.
He welcomed steps taken by 12 countries, led by the UK, France, and Canada, to prohibit trade and business relations with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Akturk also called on the international community to go beyond statements and take “concrete and deterrent measures” in response to Israeli attacks targeting camps sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza and residential areas in southern Lebanon.
“We once again emphasize that Israel must immediately end its actions that violate international law in order to ensure peace and stability in the region,” he said.
Mecca Defense Alliance
Responding to questions following the briefing, the ministry said the Mecca Defense Alliance between Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia was based on the countries’ longstanding relations and defense cooperation, as well as the principles of defense and collective deterrence.
“The agreement is not directed against any country, nor does it constitute an alternative to the parties’ existing relations with third countries,” the ministry said.
It added that activities aimed at enhancing military cooperation, increasing interoperability, and strengthening defense capabilities were being carried out in coordination among the three countries, while efforts to institutionalize the alliance were continuing.
Greek premier's Kastellorizo (Meis) visit
The ministry also criticized Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ visit to Kastellorizo, known as Meis in Türkiye, saying Ankara had closely followed his contacts with military personnel stationed on the island.
It said the presence of military personnel and a warship on Kastellorizo, which was transferred to Greece under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty on condition that it remain demilitarized, was incompatible with the island’s status and did not contribute to peace and stability.
Türkiye urged Greece “to comply with its obligations arising from international treaties and refrain from activities incompatible with the demilitarized status of the islands.”
The ministry said Ankara supports developing relations with Greece on the basis of good neighborliness and dialogue, while remaining determined to protect its rights and interests under international law.
US arms embargo decision on Greek Cypriot Administration
On Washington’s decision to extend the lifting of its arms embargo on the Greek Cypriot Administration for another year, until Sept. 30, 2027, the ministry said the move could negatively affect the “sensitive balances and environment of trust” on the island.
The ministry urged third parties to avoid actions that could undermine the delicate balance on the island and to abandon practices that disregard the Turkish Cypriot people.
“Türkiye, as a guarantor country, will continue, as it has in the past, to take the necessary measures in cooperation with the TRNC (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus) authorities for the security, peace and prosperity of the Turkish Cypriots,” it added.

Sakhalin hosts Russian Ethnographic Museum's first branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:04:39 UTC
22:04:39 KST

YUZHNO-SAKHALINSK, September 17. /TASS/. A branch of the Russian Ethnographic Museum opened in Sakhalin. It is the museum's first branch ever, Director Yulia Kupina told TASS.
"It is a special day, we have been working towards it for several years," the museum's director said. "It is for the first time that we are opening our doors not in St. Petersburg, but eight time zones away from our hometown. It is a great honor for us to open a branch in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk in the Year of Unity of the Peoples of Russia."
"Our dream is to have this museum the region's "own" museum," she continued. "So that here, like it is in St. Petersburg, people would say with pride and warmth: "This is our ethnographic museum."
The first exhibition – Here We Live – presents the cultural heritage of Sakhalin's indigenous peoples: the Nivkhs, Wilts, Nanais and Evenks, she said. Many of the items have undergone complicated restoration and now they are back to their place of origin. The region's residents will see exhibits that have not been exposed over recent 100 years. The exposition presents more than 400 items. Most of them were brought from the Sakhalin Island by the famous Russian researcher Viktor Vasiliev in the early 20th century.
"It is a big event in the region's cultural life. Of a historical scale," the Sakhalin Region's Governor Valery Limarenko said at the opening ceremony. "I think it is very symbolic. The year 2026 has been in this country declared the Year of Unity of the Peoples of Russia. Now, we have a platform where unique cultures of this country's different peoples will be presented. I know that the Russian Ethnographic Museum's collection is unique. Sakhalin has been hosting exhibitions almost every year due to the cooperation with the Museum of Local Lore. Now we will have an ongoing opportunity to learn about the exhibits that tell about the life of peoples in this country."
The work on establishment of the Russian Ethnographic Museum's branch on the Sakhalin Island began in 2021, in compliance with instructions from Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Tatyana Golikova. A modern museum complex was built in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The four-story building of more than 3,500 square meters has two exhibition halls, a storage facility, and office space. The Sakhalin Museum Complex will focus on studying and promoting ethnic and cultural heritage and current cultures and traditions of the peoples of the Northern Pacific, the Far East, Eastern Siberia's Arctic Zone, and the Sakhalin Region. Local residents and visitors will learn about Russia's development of the Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands regions.
About the museum
The Russian Ethnographic Museum is one of the largest ethnographic museums in the world. It is located in downtown St. Petersburg. The museum was founded as the Ethnographic Department of the Russian Museum of Emperor Alexander III. The date of its creation is considered to be January 10, 1902, when its staffing table was approved and financing began.
The Russian Ethnographic Museum's collection features more than 500,000 museum items belonging to 157 ethnic groups, including objects and illustrative monuments, photographic documents, books and archival materials on the culture of the peoples of Russia and neighboring countries. The museum collects, studies and presents the multinational traditional culture at exhibitions and permanent expositions, under various publishing and educational projects.

Oil tumbles as supply fears ease, gold and silver rebound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:03:35 UTC
22:03:35 KST

Oil prices fell more than three percent on Thursday as concerns over immediate supply disruptions in the Middle East eased.
International benchmark Brent crude declined 3.5 percent to around $102.10 per barrel as of 1215GMT.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) dropped 3.1 percent to $99.31 per barrel, falling below the $100 threshold.
The declines followed losses of 2.7 percent for Brent and 3.2 percent for WTI in the previous session.
Easing supply fears
Prices came under pressure as developments offering alternative export routes and the prospect of restoring disrupted infrastructure reduced fears of an acute supply shortage.
However, uncertainty surrounding Middle Eastern supplies continues to keep the oil market volatile.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a key source of risk, as the waterway is a critical route for global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Gold, silver rebound
Meanwhile, precious metals rebounded as the recent oil price rally lost momentum, easing concerns over energy-driven inflationary pressures. Gold climbed 1.1 percent to $4,308.80 per ounce as of 0950GMT, recovering from losses recorded in the previous session.
Silver gained 1.2 percent to $63.97 per ounce. The metal was up almost 53 percent from a year earlier, compared with gold’s annual gain of more than 18 percent.
The recovery came as reports that Saudi Arabia was seeking to restore around half of the capacity of its East-West oil pipeline within days and return the route to full operation within six weeks helped cool crude prices.
Fed rate hike caps gains
Sentiment was also supported by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s statement that 18 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products had passed through the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the week.
However, gains in precious metals remained limited after the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates and signaled another increase before the end of the year.
The Fed on Wednesday lifted its federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4 percent, marking its first rate increase in three years.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation remained elevated, while figures released last week showed that core US inflation rose more than expected in August.
Higher interest rates typically weigh on non-yielding assets such as gold and silver by increasing the opportunity cost of holding them.

Sick of sandwiches? Perfect packed lunches – from savoury muffins to bento boxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:02:57 UTC
22:02:57 KST

After an August spent mostly on the road, I’ve found myself unexpectedly enjoying the back-to-school feeling that arrives with September. Usually, I greet it with the sort of enthusiasm reserved for a tax return, but, having been away for so long, it’s actually been rather nice coming home. Of course, there are all the usual inevitable resolutions and to-do lists: go to bed earlier, eat better, take lunch to work. Admirable stuff, although I suspect a summer of one too many honeycomb ice-creams and an irresponsible amount of Irish brown bread and salty butter may also have something to do with it. Taking a packed lunch is, in any case, an all-round win, because eating out is increasingly expensive, and food bought in cafes and restaurants tends to be richer and saltier than a homemade equivalent. Depressingly, school and college canteens don’t fare much better, either.
But a packed lunch needn’t mean a sad sandwich or last night’s tubbed-up leftovers. Nena Foster’s courgette, olive and halloumi muffins are a very good argument for taking your lunch with you: nutrient-dense without being remotely worthy, they work just as well in an adult’s lunchbox as in a child’s, and they freeze brilliantly, too. Add a flask of pumpkin soup or Tom Hunt’s sweetcorn chowder for an excellent autumn lunch.
Shuko Oda’s onigiri bento box is another winner, and pleases pretty much every age group, which is no mean feat. Bento boxes are such a hit, in fact, that I have gone one step farther and bought Japanese egg moulds. There are few things more unnecessary than a hard-boiled egg shaped like a rabbit or bear, but they do make lunchtime more exciting. And, really, that is the point. You can fill those little compartments with whatever you fancy: Caroline Craig and Sophie Missing break it down here, with a little guidance on what to pop in those small compartments. Another option is Jeremy Lee’s ploughman’s, which would be a particularly fine arrangement: thick slices of ham, nuggets of cheese, dollops of chutney, sliced apple. A tiny pub lunch, minus the pub.
On days when I crave something more warming, I’m very happy to dust off the Thermos. There is something deeply pleasing about taking a little pot of hot food to work. Meera Sodha’s pav bhaji is perfect for this. Keep it warm in the flask until lunchtime, then spoon into a pre-toasted, buttered roll. The butter melts into the warm spiced vegetables and you wonder if there has ever been a more perfect use for a flask. I feel the same about Rachel Roddy’s real minestrone and Felicity Cloake’s pasta e fagioli, and I’m sure they could be premade and reheated in a microwave, if you have access to one. But you might not and, besides, I think dishes such as these are best when they’re not too hot, and when that rich broth is starchy and thickened. Which, perhaps, is what I like most about September lunches: they don’t have to be virtuous, elaborate or even particularly organised; they just need to be something you’ll actually look forward to eating at 1pm. And that is a resolution I can get behind.
My week in food
Sweet like chocolate | A road trip from Ireland’s east to west coast this summer was a useful reminder that the country is full of quietly brilliant food-makers. Among them is Grá chocolates, founded by Gráinne Mullins, an award-winning, Michelin-trained chef – and now, finally, shipping to the UK. Her hand-painted chocolates are made with Irish milk, butter and cream, use seasonal ingredients wherever possible, and their fillings are cooked from scratch. As a result, they are, inevitably, rather hard to resist. My family’s current favourite is the pumpkin spice hot chocolate, made with caramelised white chocolate and warming autumnal spices. Forget about the pumpkin spiced latte; this is a much more convincing way to drink the season.
Curry heaven | Emma Basic’s Japanese-style curry cubes are the sort of supermarket shortcut that makes everyone’s life better: loved by all ages, and accommodating all palates and dietaries, you really can have dinner on the table in 20 minutes. Make up the sauce as per the packet instructions, maybe add a few veggies for nutritional purposes, then simply add something crisp – chicken, tofu, aubergine, whatever you like – and serve with rice. No preservatives, no colourings, all good stuff and unapologetically convenient.
Been around the world | Ruby Bhogal’s new book, Around the World in 80 Cakes, is part baking odyssey, part history lesson and part love letter to the humble cake. The former Great British Bake Off finalist has spent three years baking her way around the globe, and I have been following her rollercoaster journey on social media intently. The result? A book filled with thoroughly tested and much-loved bakes: there is everything from Germany’s honey-rich bienenstich to Thailand’s dense, butter khanom badin, and from an Italian torta caprese to a classic British lemon drizzle cake.

Athens, Glasgow and Rome: Here’s where to find the coolest neighbourhoods in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:02:17 UTC
22:02:17 KST

The hottest area in Athens – Neos Kosmos – claimed first in Europe and third place in the overall ranking.
When deciding on where to stay in a new city, an obvious place to start is to narrow it down by neighbourhood. Perhaps you want to stay in a city’s old town, or its creative district. Or maybe you just want to be as close as possible to the nightlife scene.
If you’re looking to stay in the ~coolest~ neighbourhood in town, however, you might just want to check out Time Out’s new ranking.
Based on the expert opinions of the magazine’s editors around the globe, neighbourhoods have been evaluated across their food and drink offering, nightlife, local businesses, liveability and sense of community to create a list of the 40 coolest around the globe.
The top spot overall went to Seoul’s Jongno 3-ga, thanks to its abundance of pojangmachas (the tented street food stalls you’ll no doubt recognise from K-dramas), independent craft workshops and bars.
Second place went to Rabat's beachfront L’Ocean District, which is buzzing with independent businesses and cultural centres.
Where the cool kids are headed in Europe
Of the 40 neighbourhoods in the ranking, 13 are in Europe – including three in the top 10.
The coolest neighbourhood in Europe title goes to Neos Kosmos in Athens, which came out third overall.
Time Out praised the area as one of the city’s “most exciting neighbourhoods without losing its local touch”. Visitors can get their culture fix at Onassis Stegi, and there are tonnes of brilliant bars, restaurants and cafés around to satisfy any and every craving.
The next highest ranked spot in Europe goes to Glasgow’s Govanhill. According to Time Out, the area has a “thriving queer community” as well as a charming blend of restaurants and shops that reflect the diversity of the neighbourhood.
Rounding out the top 10 is Esquilino in Rome, with Time Out noting: “Its appeal lies precisely in that mix: ancient ruins sit beside a Vietnamese pho shop, Rome’s oldest gelateria, contemporary galleries and cool wine bars.”
The coolest neighbourhoods in Europe for 2026
- Neos Kosmos, Athens, Greece
- Govanhill, Glasgow, UK
- Esquilino, Rome, Italy
- Russafa, Valencia, Spain
- São Bento, Lisbon, Portugal
- Slakthusområdet, Stockholm, Sweden
- Rákóczi tér, Budapest, Hungary
- Crooswijk, Rotterdam, Netherlands
- Cathedral Quarter, Belfast, UK
- Oost, Amsterdam, Netherlands
- Quartier d'Aligre, Paris, France
- Newington Green, London, UK
- Boavista, Porto, Lisbon

MAA request for change form
Regulated community should use the Military Aviation Authority request for change form to propose changes to regulatory articles or associated manuals.
Documents
Details
Related information
The regulated community should use the MAA request for change (RFC) form to submit a proposal for change to regulatory articles (RA’s) or associated manuals.
To request clarification of regulation meaning, routine correspondence methods such as email, letter and telephone may be used.
The MAA may still request a completed MAA RFC form, depending on the nature of the enquiry.
Notwithstanding that formal amendment may result from a clarification request, initial requests for clarification should not be submitted on a MAA RFC form.
The MAA RFC form can be submitted via email to the MAA regulatory publications team (MRPT) at dsa-maa-mrp enquires. If clarification is required regarding the need for submission of an MAA RFC form, then the regulated community can contact the MRPT.

Estonia to assess security risks in nuclear plant site selection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

Estonia to assess security risks in nuclear plant site selection
Estonia is commissioning a security threat assessment for six sites in Viru-Nigula and Lüganuse municipalities being considered for the country's first nuclear power plant.
The assessment will be part of the first-stage site selection under the national designated spatial plan for the future plant, being drawn up by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.
The Defense Ministry, Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) and Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI) will assess the shortlisted sites at the tactical, operational and strategic levels using worst-case scenarios.
"The threat profile is the same for all six candidate sites and does not set them apart," the ministry said, adding that where the sites differ is in their vulnerabilities and potential consequences.
The assessment will follow International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) guidelines, scoring the sites on a 0-to-3 scale.
Vulnerability criteria include local and regional threats, proximity to sensitive sites, attack-facilitating conditions, response times and capabilities, security perimeter requirements as well as cooling system vulnerabilities.
Insider threats to be assessed later
Authorities will also assess potential consequences based on people and infrastructure in each site's impact area, including population centers, critical infrastructure, airports and other transport facilities, and the state border. They can also recommend dropping a site from consideration.
According to the ministry, internal security threats will not be assessed at this stage because IAEA guidance defines internal security threats as those posed by people with authorized access to a facility. This means that an insider threat "is not a site characteristic."
Such threats, it noted, depend on personnel background checks, internal control measures and security culture, which would be the same at all six sites. They will instead be addressed at the facility level in the second stage of the planning process.
Construction to begin in 2032
Fermi Energia is planning to build a BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR) in Estonia, which would be the country's first nuclear power plant.
The six sites are being compared based on national defense, environmental protection, socioeconomic impacts, technology and geology. Once a preferred site is selected, a detailed plan and comprehensive environmental impact assessment will be drawn up for the chosen location.
Construction of the plant is planned to begin in 2032, with the operating license application process taking place at the same time.
Construction and commissioning are expected to run through 2035, with the first 300-megawatt (MW) reactor slated to begin generating electricity in early 2036.
A second reactor is planned for 2038.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Aili Vahtla

PM: Estonia ready to immediately close border in case of Russian mobilization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

PM: Estonia ready to immediately close border in case of Russian mobilization
Estonia is preparing for possible security risks if Russia declares a general mobilization, with Prime Minister Kristen Michal saying the country could close its border immediately if the threat assessment warrants it.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Thursday that Estonia is preparing for various scenarios if Russia declares a general mobilization, after a file titled "Cabinet memo: Russian Federation mobilization" appeared in the government's document register.
Tsahkna said the security cabinet regularly discusses potential Russian actions and how Estonia should respond, adding that a general mobilization would significantly increase domestic tensions in Russia.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal stressed at the press conference that it is important to have regular updates on the security situation.
"There is nothing mysterious or extraordinary about this. It is no news to anyone that things are going very badly in Russia. There isn't a single healthy part of their economy and 30,000 to 40,000 men are killed or wounded every month. At some point, they will have to take steps to keep the war going and NATO and European Union countries need to be prepared for those steps and communicate accordingly. That is what we discussed. Dealing with the details and specific measures is the job of the relevant agencies and these will also be presented to the public at the appropriate time," Michal said.
If Russia were to announce a general mobilization, the border could be closed immediately, Michal confirmed.
"Different steps will be taken depending on the threat assessment. The border can also be closed immediately, as we have done on occasion when there have been troublemakers at border crossing points. The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) and the interior minister are aware of this and we have the capability to close border crossing points very quickly. Since mobilization could change the threat assessment, we will take appropriate steps depending on whether it happens and what form it takes. When it comes to measures concerning the border, the principle of reciprocity always applies," the prime minister said, adding that border crossing point opening hours have already been reduced and full customs checks introduced.
Tsahkna said everyone in Europe needs to monitor rising internal tensions in Russia.
"Everyone understands that if, for example, blanket compulsory mobilization is announced for a certain age group, it will significantly increase internal tensions in Russia. This is part of our routine work — we need to anticipate different decisions, assess the threat picture and be prepared. As the prime minister said, for example, closing the border is a decision the government can make very quickly, depending on the threat assessment," Tsahkna said.
The foreign minister said the threat of mobilization is in fact a much broader concern and does not affect Estonia alone.
"Frankly, I think Estonia is much better prepared for potential threats or tensions than the rest of Europe. What we have discussed — and what Estonia is also doing across Europe within the Nordic-Baltic framework — is the fact that last year the Schengen Area issued 650,000 visas to Russian citizens who came here. That pressure could certainly increase. We don't have a problem with this in Estonia because we don't let these people in anyway, but we need to recognize the situation and educate our European partners about the threat that rising internal tensions in Russia pose to European security," Tsahkna said.
Estonia has taken the lead on visa-related issues across Europe. For example, a visa ban on combatants has become part of sanctions decisions at both the European Commission and member-state levels.
"But this practice of continuing to issue visas is completely incomprehensible to us. People in Estonia would find it hard to imagine, but some countries continue to hand out these visas and that pressure will certainly increase. We don't know who these people are who are coming into Europe more broadly," Tsahkna stressed.
The foreign minister added that there are also legal aspects related to visas and that Russian citizens living in Estonia or elsewhere in Europe need to understand that, legally, a mobilization order also applies to them or their children.
"A person in Russia might think that mobilization is coming, so they'll flee to Europe and say that this gives them grounds for international protection. It does not," Tsahkna said.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Marcus Turovski

Norway adds 90 million euro incentive for Ukraine to pass EU reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:00:53 UTC
22:00:53 KST

Norway announced a 90 million euro ($103 million) contribution to Ukraine on Sept. 17 but to be given via an EU mechanism that gives Kyiv cash in return for completing reforms.
Ukraine receives funding from both the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the understanding that the parliament passes reforms intended to align the country with EU norms, improve the business climate, tackle corruption, and improve the rule of law.
"Today, (Norwegian) Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide announced a contribution of 90 million euros to our main instrument for support for Ukraine, the Ukraine Facility," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in Oslo on Sept. 17.
"Building an open, well-functioning, democratic Ukraine is crucial to the country’s future in Europe," Barth Eide said.
Norway is not a member of the European Union, but it is closely integrated with the bloc through the European Economic Area.
For almost a year, reforms have struggled to pass parliament, putting billions of euros of support at risk and holding up Ukraine's EU accession prospects.
But a Sept. 14 push by the European Commission and new Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi seems to have unclogged the legislature, with seven bills advancing two days later, and none being blocked.
An EU official told the Kyiv Independent that the 90 million provided by Norway is expected to be tied to the Ukraine Facility's 11th installment, previously valued at 2.1 billion euros ($2.4 billion).
To receive the 11th installment, Kyiv needs to implement 23 reforms covering public finances, the judiciary, an anti-corruption strategy, and more, all by the end of 2026.
So far, the Ukraine Facility has provided 29.5 billion euros ($33.9 billion) of support to Ukraine since it was agreed upon in 2024.
"The EU and Norway share the same approach in supporting Ukraine. We want to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian aggression today, while supporting the reforms that will make Ukraine stronger and bring it closer to EU membership," Kos said.

====================================================================================================

AI leaders want to slow frontier AI. Who makes sure they really do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging the industry to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” To make such a slowdown verifiable, he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside frontier AI companies. At Anthropic, he wrote, they would get access comparable to the company’s own risk teams and the right to publish their findings.
His idea puts enormous weight on a field whose rules are still being written. More and more, AI auditors are being asked to serve as independent checks on the companies building the most powerful models, even though no standard exists for what a rigorous entails. Amodei’s proposal would add their most high-profile responsibility yet: confirming whether a slowdown is real.
“Amodei has an extremely naive interpretation of what needs to be done there,” says Maurice Chiodo, a mathematician at the University of Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who says he has audited around 30 AI companies. One immediate concern, he says, is what exactly an auditor needs access to. That could include model weights, the numerical parameters shaped during training, as well as internal evaluations, red-team transcripts and incident reports. Chiodo argues that data aren’t enough. “Giving an auditor access to nothing and giving them access to a million documents has exactly the same effect, which is they can't get anything done,” he says. “These auditors need access to people, primarily.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Yet embedding auditors alongside employees, as Amodei suggests, could compromise their impartiality. “The auditors get their badge, and their desk, they go to staff drinks nights on Friday night and they enjoy it,” Chiodo says. “They really become part of the company which makes it difficult to criticize it because the staffers become almost your friends.” Lilian Edwards, professor emerita of law, innovation and society at Newcastle University and director of Pangloss Consulting, calls that setup “an absolute recipe for cultural capture.”
Independence would also depend on auditors’ freedom to speak out afterward. Amodei says Anthropic would retain the right to redact security-sensitive, legally privileged or proprietary information. “If you're writing that in your first proposal, reserve the right to redact and hold stuff back, you've already lost the game in terms of safety,” Chiodo says. Amodei explicitly says Anthropic could not redact a finding simply because it was unfavorable. Edwards is still wary. “Redactions are going to be a political and commercial question, not a technical one,” she says.
Then there is the model being audited. In August, researchers at Transluce, an independent nonprofit AI lab, reported that frontier models behave differently depending on whom they believe they’re talking to. The team varied the identity presented to the model while keeping the underlying tasks the same. “The model actually adapted its behavior based on who it was talking to,” says Jacob Steinhardt, a computer scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, who leads Transluce. The effects were small on average. But with AI lab employees, its answers tended to be more cautious, and its reasoning longer and more critical. Older models sometimes revealed in their reasoning traces, the intermediate steps a system generates before answering, that they recognized the person they were talking to. “For newer models, that's actually no longer visible,” Steinhardt says. That makes the behavior harder to spot. “We don't really know how to solve it as a field.”
“Testing environments cannot be trusted alone,” Chiodo says. “You need to find a way to sample the model when it doesn't think that you're looking.” Steinhardt, though, is not convinced by sampling random AI interactions for human evaluation. “It doesn't let you anticipate new problems before they happen,” he cautions.
There is also the problem of finding enough qualified people to do the work. An audit team, Chiodo argues, needs expertise that mirrors the development team role for role. “If there's a development role that's not reflected in the audit team, then that role can't be audited,” he says. Those experts can make far more working for the AI companies themselves. “I've been shouted at, sworn at, cursed at, and told I can't speak to developers anymore,” Chiodo says. “No one's going to clap for you.”
California is already trying to formalize a broader AI-auditing ecosystem. On September 9, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1405, which directs the state to create an AI Auditor Registry by January 1, 2029; beginning then, only registered auditors may conduct certain audits required for compliance with state law. A companion law, SB 813, tasks the state with deciding who qualifies to independently vet AI systems. Neither law requires frontier developers to submit to an audit to build or deploy a model.
Edwards doubts that voluntary oversight will overcome the commercial incentives to release their latest, most powerful models. “Efforts would be made to fudge it,” she says. “I cannot personally see voluntary certification making a difference between existential AI risk and evading it.”
Anthropic says it intends to bring an embedded external review team inside the company “in the near future.” Chiodo doubts independent auditing can be built fast enough to keep pace with frontier AI development. “Amodei's suggestion of external auditors, that's years into the future,” he says. The next generation of Claude is unlikely to wait that long.

MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova recalled that it was British media outlets and television channels in particular that literally orchestrated global coverage of the fabricated "Bucha" scenario.

"In fact, that is precisely what happened," Zakharova said at a TASS press conference dedicated to the presentation of a report by the International Public Tribunal on the crimes of Ukrainian neo-Nazis, which exposes the falsification of events in Bucha. "And, in fact, Boris Johnson was given the leading role in this spectacle. But something had to be done about the global public opinion, which, indeed, was primarily in favor of these negotiations, because all ordinary people tend to stand for peace."
In this regard, Zakharova stressed that in order to convince ordinary people, political scientists, experts and, of course, journalists, who "in turn were supposed to relay this to the broadest possible audience, that disrupting the negotiations was literally necessary," a small town on the outskirts of Kiev called Bucha was chosen, where "dozens of bodies suddenly appeared."
"They appeared the moment they were broadcast by mass media. Not by locals who failed to see their neighbors, friends and relatives at home or received some sort of messages from them. Nothing of the sort. This never happened. The first time this information emerged was through the media," she said. It was British television channels and, subsequently, media corporations that literally orchestrated the global coverage of this entire "Bucha" scenario.
In addition, the Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman recalled that the information disseminated through Western media "took on an obvious tone of blaming Russia."
On March 30, 2022, Russia pulled back from the town of Bucha and from Kiev’s vicinity as a goodwill gesture during negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul. On March 31, the head of the local administration confirmed this before cameras. A few days later, Western television broadcast footage that showed dead bodies lying in the streets, in contrast to earlier recordings.
