Couples bonding over bad habits may age faster at the cellular level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

A happy marriage usually promotes a longer life, but a new study shows this benefit depends heavily on a couple’s shared daily habits. When partners bond over poor diets and bad sleep, their relationship satisfaction might actually accelerate their biological aging. The findings were published in the journal Brain, Behavior, and Immunity.
Researchers wanted to understand why the health benefits of marital satisfaction vary so wildly from one couple to the next. Stephanie J. Wilson, a psychology researcher at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, led a team of scientists to investigate a concept called symptom-system fit theory. This theory suggests that indulging in unhealthy behaviors together can actually boost a couple’s sense of connection. For example, staying up late to watch television or overeating junk food might make partners feel in sync and satisfied with their relationship.
Over time, however, these shared unhealthy routines could erode physical health. The research team suspected that health behaviors might dictate whether a happy marriage protects against aging or accelerates it. To test this idea, they examined the biological aging of 107 married or cohabiting couples ranging in age from 40 to 87.
The researchers measured marital quality through detailed surveys and by observing the couples in a laboratory setting. During the lab visit, couples engaged in three distinct conversations. They discussed a recent positive event, talked through a personal problem, and tried to resolve a long-standing relationship conflict. Trained coders watched the recorded interactions to evaluate how positively or negatively the partners treated each other.
Participants also provided information about their health behaviors. They answered questions about their physical activity, sleep quality, and adherence to a healthy Mediterranean-style diet. Researchers combined the data from both partners to create average health behavior scores for each couple.
To measure biological aging, the team collected blood samples from the participants at the start of the study and again two years later. They analyzed the blood for three different markers of cellular aging. The first marker was telomere length, which refers to the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes. These caps wear down every time a cell divides, and critically short telomeres cause cells to malfunction.
The second marker involved DNA methylation, which consists of chemical tags on genes that control how they function. Scientists can read these patterns like an internal clock to estimate a person’s biological age. The third marker was a protein called p16INK4a. This protein accumulates when cells enter a state called senescence, meaning they stop dividing but refuse to die, instead releasing harmful inflammatory chemicals into the body.
Looking at the initial data from the first lab visit, the researchers found a link between happy relationships and slower aging. People who reported higher marital satisfaction generally showed lower levels of the senescence protein p16INK4a. However, this youthful cellular profile only appeared among couples who maintained regular physical activity.
A similar pattern emerged during the observed conversations. Couples who showed active, positive support for each other during discussions exhibited slower aging in their DNA and lower levels of the senescence protein. Yet this protective effect was isolated to couples who reported good sleep quality and a healthy diet. When researchers applied strict statistical tests to rule out chance associations, some of these initial healthy patterns were not statistically significant.
The most striking results appeared when the researchers tracked changes over the two-year study period. Couples who started out highly satisfied with their marriages experienced slower increases in the senescence protein over time. But a completely different pattern emerged for the protective telomere caps on their chromosomes.
High marital satisfaction predicted faster shrinking of these telomeres among couples who reported poor sleep and unhealthy diets. In other words, relationship happiness seemed to accelerate cellular aging when paired with bad habits. Similarly, couples who acted highly positive toward each other during the initial lab tests showed accelerated aging in their DNA clocks over the next two years if they shared a poor diet.
These longitudinal results align with the symptom-system fit theory. The data suggest that relationship happiness can become a health risk when it is reinforced by shared negative habits. A happy marriage cannot completely compensate for a lack of sleep, limited exercise, or a diet filled with processed foods.
The participating couples were predominantly white, highly educated, and healthier than average adults. Future research will need to test these ideas in more diverse groups to see if the patterns hold across different socioeconomic backgrounds.
Additionally, while the two-year timeframe shows how habits precede biological changes, the observational design cannot definitively prove that relationship satisfaction directly causes faster or slower aging. The researchers measured an association that they plan to test further with longer-term studies. Identifying how toxic and supportive marital patterns interact with daily health routines will help clarify the physical impacts of a romantic partnership.
The study, “Is a happy marriage a double-edged sword for biological aging? Preliminary evidence for the moderating role of couples’ health behaviors,” was authored by Stephanie J. Wilson, Annelise A. Madison, M. Rosie Shrout, Lisa M. Christian, Elissa S. Epel, Christin E. Burd, Jue Lin, Samuel H. Molli, Rebecca Andridge, Harry T. Reis, and Janice K. Kiecolt-Glaser.

Labor considers smart glasses restrictions, new national AI standards
In short:
The federal government is considering a ban on smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces while advancing a broader suite of AI policies.
New standards for data centres and frontier AI training are out for consultation as ministers focus on workplace protections, investment and online safety.
What's next?
Anthony Albanese travels to the US on Friday, where he will hold talks with tech companies and world leaders.
A ban on smart glasses capable of covertly recording people is being considered for Commonwealth buildings amid concerns about the technology's privacy and security risks.
Restricting the use of wearable devices is among a wide range of technology issues on the federal government's agenda, with ministers progressing plans for Australia's uptake of artificial intelligence and related workplace protections, data centres, investment and online safety.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will travel to the US on Friday for high-level talks with tech executives and world leaders while major employers gather in Canberra for a roundtable and separate consultation begins on national AI standards for data centres and frontier model training.
AI will also feature in the upcoming 2026 Intergenerational Report due to be released next week, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealing he met with an Anthropic official to discuss the technology's economic opportunities and potential risks.
Mr Albanese said AI and online safety would be a major theme of his visit to Apple's headquarters in California and attendance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week.
"We want Australia to be a country that helps shape the AI age rather than simply responding to it," he said.
Labor mulls smart glasses ban
With growing community backlash over the increased availability of more affordable smart glasses capable of secretly recording people, the government has made its first move to rein in the technology.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has asked the Australian Public Service Commission for advice on the use of smart glasses across Commonwealth workplaces, including whether the technology should be "prohibited" and what exemptions might be appropriate.
Ms Gallagher said the Australian Public Service should always set the standard as a "model employer".
"Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information, and we need clear and consistent guidance for public servants," she said.
The government has already asked the nation's Privacy Commissioner to give the use of smart glasses "priority consideration" amid widespread community concerns about their potential impact.
National standards for data centres and training frontier AI
The government has also opened consultation on national AI standards covering large data centres and the training of frontier AI models in Australia.
The proposed rules would set mandatory requirements for data centres covering power supply, energy costs, water use, location, community engagement and skills.
They would also impose safety, security, transparency and local investment conditions on frontier AI training.
Consultation will remain open until October 9 with the government planning to legislate the standards early in the new year.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the standards were about ensuring Australia captured the technology's "enormous opportunities" while maintaining the trust and confidence of the community.
"By setting high standards now, Australia can shape the future of this technology rather than simply adopting standards made overseas," he said.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the government had been "clear" about welcoming AI investment, provided it was on "Australia's terms".
AI will be 'defining influence' on Australia's economy
AI will also feature prominently in next week's 2026 Intergenerational Report, which will examine what the technological shift could mean for productivity, jobs and investment in decades to come.
An excerpt of the report described AI as a "defining influence" on the economy over the next 40 years.
Mr Chalmers said Australia had a "big opportunity" to lift productivity, investment and living standards, but must not be "complacent" about potential downsides.
"The global AI boom is worth hundreds of billions of dollars and we are positioning Australia to capture more of that supply chain," he said.
This week Mr Chalmers met with Anthropic special envoy Jeff Bleich, which the treasurer said was a "really valuable opportunity" to discuss both the economic opportunities of AI and importance of safeguards.
Mr Bleich said Anthropic was committed to realising the "enormous potential" of AI in a "safe, responsible way".
"Working with like-minded countries such as Australia is an important part of that," he said.
Mr Bleich said Australia brought a skilled workforce, strong institutions and a "clear-eyed approach" to new technology.
"We want to invest in those strengths and to keep working with the government so that Australians share in the gains from AI," he said.
Major employers gather to talk AI
Meanwhile, Microsoft, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia are among the major employers will be attending an AI roundtable hosted by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth on Friday.
The meeting is one of five consultations being held this month with unions, employers, small business and academics to help develop Australia's first best practice guidance for AI in the workplace.
Discussions will focus on the lessons from businesses already adopting AI, how to build trust and confidence in the technology and ensuring any benefits reach workers as well as employers.
Ms Rishworth said the consultations would ensure the guide reflected the "realities of modern workplaces".
"Labor believes workers should have confidence that the adoption of AI will improve the way we work, not simply train their replacement," she said.

Romanian shelter offers an alternative to stray dog culls

Unknown Publisher

Romanian shelter offers an alternative to stray dog culls
CATEASCA, Romania, Sept 17 - Every day at dawn, eight veterinary vans pull out of the Smeura animal shelter, deep in a forest in central Romania, and fan out to villages where they sterilize dogs for free.
The pilot programme run by German animal welfare association Tierhilfe Hoffnung has one main aim — to show there is a better alternative to the country's policy of culling unwanted animals.
Romania authorised the capture and euthanasia of strays in 2013 after a child was killed in an attack. Thirteen years on, animal groups say the country still has one of Europe's largest populations of roaming dogs, estimated at 500,000.
The shelter itself has been taking in strays, and sent more than 2,200 of them out for adoption last year alone. But as each one leaves, another arrives.
"The dogs keep coming," Tierhilfe Hoffnung manager Matthias Schmidt said. "If we want to solve the problem, we have to sterilize intensively and en masse in order to achieve this result."
Calls to end euthanasia have increased since an investigation by international animal welfare organization Four Paws earlier this year found evidence of systemic neglect, overcrowding and abuse in publicly funded animal shelters.
"In the next five years we want to solve the problem ... by identifying (dogs), vaccinating against rabies, registering them in a national program, and sterilizing them," Schmidt said.
So far this year, Smeura has carried out nearly 40,000 sterilisations, of both strays and pets, at the mobile units and the unsubsidised shelter, one of the largest in the world, sprawling on the site of a former fox farm.
This week in the village of Cateasca, a steady stream of owners brought their pets to be treated.
The procedure was good for the animals and public safety, said Iulian Stoica, who had come with three dogs. "I think it's better not to over-populate the streets with abandoned puppies," he said. REUTERS

Von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member” left capitals scrambling and seemed to take even Ottawa by surprise.
Carney name-checked the term in his speech on Thursday, praising von der Leyen for “opening the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member,” and adding that he welcomes the ambition.
Pressed by reporters on whether he preferred calling the new EU-Canada relationship an “Alliance for the Future” or “associate membership,” he shrugged off the distinction.
“President von der Leyen used both terms, alliance for the future and associate membership. The nomenclature is a question for Europe; what terms they use,” he said. “What matters is the substance. What are we actually building together.”

Ukrainian forces test four interceptor drone models to counter jet-powered UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

Ukrainian forces test four interceptor drone models to counter jet-powered UAVs
Colonel Vladyslav Voloshyn, head of the department at the Central Directorate for Innovation Activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, reported this to Ukrinform.
“These unmanned interceptors of enemy jet-powered UAVs represent a promising field in which we are currently working quite actively. To date, four promising drone models have been identified and, in collaboration with the manufacturers, have already reached the final stage of readiness,” he said.
According to Voloshyn, these include models with both jet engines and electric powerplants. Prototypes have already been delivered to Ukrainian units on the front lines for testing in combat conditions.
Voloshyn added that, in parallel, they are defining and refining tactics for deploying such UAVs, identifying additional unit requirements, and determining the areas where these drones can be used most effectively. They plan to scale up the experience gained in the future.
“In addition, active efforts are underway to engage new manufacturers in developing solutions to counter jet-powered UAVs,” Voloshin said.
He noted that currently, about ten manufacturers are undergoing testing with their products to verify the claimed specifications. Based on the test results, developers are provided with recommendations on how to improve their products, enhance their flight and operational characteristics, and, in some cases, integrate additional combat automation systems.
Voloshyn is convinced that this should increase the effectiveness of intercepting enemy drones.
“But I’ll say it again: this is no longer just one or two—there are now a dozen such products that are currently at a stage where, before long, the best of these models will also enter service with our units,” he noted.
Voloshyn clarified that the timelines for finalizing the various designs vary and depend on a number of factors. These include the availability of technologies, the technical capabilities of the developer company, the availability of in-house capacity for developing and manufacturing the necessary components, as well as the availability and cost of individual prototypes.
According to him, the need to develop such interceptors as quickly as possible is linked to the improvement of Russian strike UAVs.
“Because right now the Russians… are constantly improving these ‘Shaheds,’ and the fact that they now have jet engines and new guidance systems means we need to develop such interceptors as quickly as possible so they can effectively counter them,” he emphasized.
At the same time, Voloshyn did not disclose detailed specifications of the prospective interceptors, as this work is classified.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 14, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi briefed President Volodymyr Zelensky on the latest developments to counter Russian jet-powered drones.
Earlier, Zelensky stated that there are currently 67 companies operating in Ukraine capable of shooting down jet drones on a large scale. According to him, there are currently 3–5 companies that have already demonstrated results.

Bern museum returns cultural artefacts to Namibia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:54:55 UTC
20:54:55 KST

Bern museum returns cultural artefacts to Namibia
After 120 years in Bern, a collection of cultural artefacts is returning to Namibia. The Bern Historical Museum has transferred ownership to the town of Usakos, where the objects were originally acquired under colonial rule. An exhibition in Bern explores the theme of repatriation.
The exhibition Destination: Usakos will run from September 18, 2026 to July 4, 2027, as the Bern Historical Museum (BHM) announced on Thursday. It features objects which the museum has already transferred to the Namibian town of Usakos.
The collection was assembled in the early 20th century in what was then “German South-West Africa”. In 1906, the Swiss engineer Victor Solioz and his wife Marie acquired around 286 everyday objects, jewellery and weapons from Namibian railway workers. At the time, Solioz was working as chief engineer on a German railway project. The exact circumstances of the acquisition remain unclear to this day. The couple brought the collection to Bern, where the museum purchased it in 1928.
A years-long process of restitution
In June 2026, the BHM transferred ownership of the entire collection to the Usakos Town Museum. Twenty-eight of the artefacts are already in Namibia. The majority are now on loan and on display in Bern, before the objects are also repatriated at the end of 2027.
+ Swiss colonial exploitation highlighted by National Museum
The repatriation was preceded by a process lasting several years. Since 2018, the museum has been strengthening its ties with partners such as the Museums Association of Namibia and the Usakos Town Council. From 2023, a collaborative project was launched in which new knowledge about the objects was gathered in cooperation with the descendants of the railway workers.
Coming to terms with the past and responsibility
“Cultural heritage should be used where it holds significance for people as a source of knowledge and identity,” museum director Thomas Pauli-Gabi was quoted as saying in the press release. The exhibition curator, Samuel Bachmann, added that a collection linked to Namibia’s greatest national trauma could not be retained against the wishes of the descendants. A study from 2024 showed that museums in German-speaking countries hold around 19,000 artefacts from Namibia, while the National Museum of Namibia itself possesses only around 1,600 objects.
A future in Usakos
For the Usakos Town Museum, this is its first collection of its own. The town’s deputy mayor, Kleophas Johannes, expressed the hope that the artefacts would remain at the Usakos Museum for the next 120 years. They must not be locked away again, but must be accessible to the community.
The development of Usakos is closely intertwined with the construction of the Otavi Railway and German colonial history. At the beginning of the 20th century, in what was then German South-West Africa, the railway served as the logistical backbone of the colonial power, Germany. The railway linked the Atlantic port of Swakopmund with lucrative copper mines.
Local labour was exploited for the construction of the railway and the extraction of minerals from the mines. Land and natural resources were seized from the indigenous population without compensation. To this day, the construction of the Otavi Railway is regarded as an example of the interplay between economic exploitation, military oppression and the establishment of colonial structures.

Burnham has to sell Bank rate rises as ‘breathing space’ – good luck with that
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:54:08 UTC
20:54:08 KST

Good luck to Andy Burnham convincing voters he is giving them “breathing space”, if the Bank of England ratchets up interest rates in the coming months.
That was the prospect opened up by Thursday’s minutes of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) meeting, which left rates unchanged at 3.75% – for now – but suggested policymakers may be unlikely to hold out much longer.
“If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case,” the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey said. “It is likely that policy may have to tighten.”
With classic Bank understatement, Bailey said that since hostilities heated up again, there had been, “a seeming loss of urgency to find solutions”.
When Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July, the war had abated, and the UK economy was puttering along nicely.
Since then, the resumption of the Iran conflict has pushed global oil prices back above $100 a barrel, with painful knock-on effects across Europe and Asia.
In the UK, inflation hit 3.1% in August, driven by rising fuel prices. And even without a interest rate rise from the Bank, mortgage rates have already jumped, as markets contemplate a period of higher inflation. The MPC now expects inflation to be above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.
The minutes of its meeting suggested a marked reluctance to raise rates for now. While energy prices have shot up, the jobs market remains weak, helping to contain the risks of the “second-round effects” that allow inflation to become embedded.
And the six-to-three vote for a hold was the same as at their last meeting in July, suggesting no rush to jump immediately. Yet there was also a growing sense of concern about the impact of soaring energy costs.
The widely expected hold decision leaves the Bank an outlier among leading central banks.
Kevin Warsh, the chair of the Federal Reserve, defied Donald Trump’s urgent calls for rate cuts on Wednesday by increasing US borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 – a move that went down well in financial markets, but predictably infuriated the president. The European Central Bank raised its rates last week; the Bank of Japan is expected to follow on Friday.
Burnham kicked off his premiership with modest but tangible cost of living measures, such as capping bus fares and slashing VAT on electricity bills.
But he now faces a double whammy. Higher inflation and energy prices threaten to overwhelm the benefits of such handouts; but higher interest rates on government borrowing has increased the costs of future measures to protect consumers.
All this at a time when – as the MPC acknowledges – weather shocks are likely to push up food prices, and bond markets remain fragile.
The new prime minister has made clear he expects to focus more on domestic affairs and less on striding the global stage than his beleaguered predecessor Keir Starmer.
But if – as currently seems likely – the Iran war goes on and on, the costs of geopolitics will be felt at home regardless.

Killed hostage's father remembers his son

Netanyahu defense asks court to summon former A-G Avichai Mandelblit to testify before election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:53:28 UTC
20:53:28 KST

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit, who authorized the investigations of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and later decided to indict him, could take the witness stand in Netanyahu’s criminal trial weeks before the election. Netanyahu’s defense asked the Jerusalem District Court on Thursday to summon him.
The defense requested seven days of testimony, beginning October 11 and continuing on October 12 and October 18-22. The first proposed date falls four days after the third anniversary of October 7 and just over two weeks before the October 27 election.
It would be Mandelblit’s first appearance as a witness in the trial. Israeli law requires the attorney-general’s consent to open a criminal investigation against a sitting prime minister. Mandelblit gave that consent and, in 2019, decided to charge Netanyahu in Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000.
His testimony is likely to focus on what he authorized investigators to examine, when he authorized it and whether police went beyond those limits. The defense has argued that some investigative steps lacked the required approval and has challenged evidence obtained through them.
Prosecutors say Mandelblit approved the investigations and dispute the defense’s account of what his consent covered.
Wiretap on Netanyahu associate stopped due to lack of proper approval
That disagreement has surfaced again in recent testimony. Former investigator Shmuel Sharvit said a court-authorized wiretap on Netanyahu associate Natan Eshel was stopped after less than a month because it had not received the necessary approval from Mandelblit. A former police legal adviser, Alon Tsarfati, testified that the attorney-general’s consent was required to open an investigation, but not for every step taken within one.
At a hearing this week, Eran Kamin, a former senior Lahav 433 officer, said he had met journalist Ben Caspit at a café to check the reliability of information about gifts to the Netanyahu family; the defense questioned him about an alleged transcript discussing private investigators and airport cameras, whose accuracy Kamin disputed.
The prosecution has pointed to Mandelblit’s approval of inquiries into gifts to Netanyahu. The defense has questioned whether that approval extended to particular lines of inquiry. Mandelblit could now be asked to address the competing accounts directly.
Mandelblit announced his decision to indict Netanyahu in November 2019, and the indictment was filed in January 2020. The trial began that May. Netanyahu took the witness stand in December 2024 and finished testifying in June this year.
The defense has since called other witnesses, including former investigators.

Highlights from Canadian PM Mark Carney's speech in Strasbourg
BRUSSELS, Sept 17 - Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney called for a sweeping strategic alliance with the European Union and proposed joint efforts on critical minerals, AI, defence and trade during a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday.
Carney spoke a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was opening the door for Canada to become an "associate member" in her annual State of the European Union address.
Here are some highlights:
CARNEY ON GEOPOLITICAL BACKDROP
"Today, our societies are being rocked by new storms: the upheavals linked to climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and the use of trade as a weapon."
"The multilateral institutions we relied on have been weakened. Sovereignty and openness are difficult to reconcile today. Economic integration is now being used as a weapon, and tariffs as a means of pressure."
"Technology is transforming the nature of war, the structure of economies, and the ability of states to govern."
"Technology platforms aspire to sovereignty. They want to set the terms of access. They want to dictate the rules of regulation—and even circumvent them. They want to control our data, spread disinformation, and steal our children’s childhoods.
"This is a ferocious storm. A single tree will come down in it. A forest will not."
CARNEY ON ASSOCIATE MEMBERSHIP OFFER
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication."
"We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself but the means to a just society."
"Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together."
"Yesterday, President von der Leyen spoke of moving beyond CETA to an Alliance for the Future - pening the door to Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member. We welcome this ambition - olling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties."
"An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices. Open enough that others can join. Principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than replaces it. "
CARNEY ON ACTIONS A DEEPER ALLIANCE CAN TAKE
"Sovereignty requires resilience—the ability to withstand shocks."
"Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space, and payments."
"We should move towards seamless, digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services. We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic."
"Canada can contribute LNG and hydrogen at large scale to support Europe's energy security including by developing and leveraging new port infrastructure in the high north and on our east coast." REUTERS

Argentina's Milei submits bill to strengthen sanctions on Falklands activities
Sept 17 - Argentina's government has presented a bill to crack down on companies operating in the Falkland Islands, potentially escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the territory that is controlled by Britain but claimed by Argentina.
The proposal introduced on Thursday toughens sanctions on companies and people who unlawfully participate in activities in the Falklands and in Argentina's maritime spaces and continental shelf in "any type of activity aimed at the utilization of renewable or non-renewable natural resources" without authorization from Argentine authorities.
It also creates a National Security Council, led by Argentina's president, to oversee national security policy and safeguard critical infrastructure and national sovereignty.
Its seven members will include the president's cabinet chief, foreign minister, defence minister, economy minister, secretary of national intelligence and the president's legal secretary.
The bill seeks to "punish those who exploit our natural resources illegally, create incentives for them to cease such conduct, and provide the national government with tools to protect itself against external threats," the president's office said in a statement on Thursday.
The new bill aims to revamp 2011 legislation with a tougher regime and stronger sanctions aimed at companies and their shareholders and suppliers, the statement added.
The Argentine government said last week it had opened sanctions proceedings against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas.
Argentina, which invaded the islands in 1982 and fought a 10-week war over them before surrendering to Britain, has accelerated efforts to crack down on companies involved in the Sea Lion oil project since earlier this month U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Washington could reconsider its traditionally neutral position on the Falklands dispute.
Trump's comments came amid his frustration at what he saw as Britain's limited support for U.S.-led military operations in the Middle East.
Centre and left-wing opponents have long accused Milei of not doing enough to defend Argentina's claim over the Malvinas and now say he is acting for political reasons ahead of a likely 2027 re-election bid.
The owners of the Sea Lion offshore project, Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, had said the oilfield project holds valid licenses from the Falkland Islands government and have indicated they do not expect Milei's actions to derail development. REUTERS

Haredi parties plan to remain outside government coalition until draft law is resolved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:53:10 UTC
20:53:10 KST

The haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties are preparing for the possibility of a dramatic shift in their political strategy after the elections, initially refraining from recommending a candidate for prime minister and remaining outside the coalition that is formed, while the new government is forced to deal with the crisis surrounding the draft law, haredi sources involved in internal political discussions told Maariv on Thursday.
Once the issue that has shaken the haredi political establishment is resolved, the haredi parties could then consider joining the sitting government.
Haredi sources familiar with the internal discussions said the emerging direction is currently not to recommend either Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot to the president, based on the assumption that the haredi parties would sit in the opposition during the initial period following the elections.
"The feeling right now is that we won't recommend anyone," a haredi source said. "The haredim are coming in with the intention of sitting in the opposition for the first year."
This is not a formal decision adopted by Shas or United Torah Judaism, nor is it a plan agreed upon by the party leaders. Haredi sources stressed that, at this stage, it reflects a prevailing mood and a commonly expressed view in discussions within the haredi political establishment.
"This still isn't something that people sat down and wrote in a document and had approved by the rabbis," one source said, "but it is a widely held view."
Sources familiar with the haredi discussions said the position has also come up in conversations with senior officials in the haredi parties.
Government will struggle to get past draft law deadlock
At the center of the issue is the deadlock surrounding the draft law. Haredi sources believe that under the current circumstances, it would be extremely difficult for a government dependent on the haredi parties to pass legislation that both meets their demands and survives political and legal obstacles.
That has led to the possibility now being considered: The next government would be required to deal with the issue while the haredi parties are not part of it.
Under the scenario being discussed, the haredi parties would sit in the opposition, oppose the draft law advanced by the government, and even attack it, but they would neither be signatories to the legislation nor bear responsibility for the compromise language.
"Some kind of draft law will pass, we won't be tied to it, and we'll be able to attack it from the opposition," a haredi source explained. "After the law passes, that obstacle will already be behind us."
Even supporting a Netanyahu government from outside the coalition is not necessarily seen as a solution. Some within the haredi political establishment believe the latest term demonstrated the cost of being fully identified with Netanyahu at a time when the haredi community was at the center of the public battle over conscription.
"They realized that being on the grill isn't good," a haredi source said.
In his view, outside support could leave the haredi parties in essentially the same position: They would continue paying the public price associated with being identified with the government, while the problem that led them to remain outside it would still be unresolved.
Once a draft law is passed, another possibility that currently appears more distant could also open up for the haredi parties: joining a government headed by Eisenkot.
Haredis will not rule out joining centrist coalition
Haredi sources estimate that the conscription issue is currently the main obstacle to such a move. If the law were already behind them, they would not rule out joining a centrist coalition that is not based on the Netanyahu bloc.
"After a year, the haredim could enter any government," a haredi source said. "Every government wants to expand and become more stable. The haredim know how to be good coalition partners. Once the draft law is no longer on the table, there is no reason they couldn't be brought in."
That assessment is based on the political experience of the haredi parties and the assumption that a government that has already been formed and weathered the conscription crisis could seek to broaden its coalition and strengthen its stability.
If the government formed after the elections does not want to bring them in after a year, sources in the haredi political establishment said that continuing to sit in the opposition would also be a scenario they could live with.
A draft law passed by a government that is not dependent on the haredi parties would present them with a complicated equation.
Haredi sources estimate that the content of such a law would be tougher for the haredi public and further removed from the parties' demands. At the same time, they believe that a law passed without coalition pressure from the haredi parties could enjoy broader public and political legitimacy.
In their assessment, that could also affect the government's ability to defend the legislation before the High Court of Justice.
The positions Eisenkot himself has presented add further context to the scenario.
In recent months, Eisenkot has made clear that he does not intend to compromise on the principle of service, and has said that if the choice is between forming a government and compromising on the draft law, he would prefer another election.
The framework he has presented is based on mandatory military, national, or civilian service, an end to the blanket exemption, sanctions on those who do not serve, and the possibility of allowing up to 3% of each annual cohort to defer service for one year for Torah study.
Haredi sources assume that a law passed under a government headed by Eisenkot would be far removed from their demands. From the opposition, they could oppose the law without bearing responsibility for passing the legislation, and after its enactment they could reassess their relationship with the government.
Eisenkot's public position fits into that picture. He has made mandatory service one of his fundamental conditions for forming a government.
This could create a situation in which, at least initially, both sides are interested in the same separation: Eisenkot makes mandatory service a basic condition, while some in the haredi political establishment believe they would be better off sitting in the opposition while the legislation is passed.
After the law is enacted, the calculations of both sides could change.
Haredi sources deny having secret deal with Eisenkot
According to the haredi sources, there is no secret deal with Eisenkot behind the scenario.
"There are no talks with Eisenkot," a haredi source said, meaning that, according to the source, there are currently no negotiations or political coordination regarding the future scenario.
Eisenkot has publicly rejected the claim that he is "flirting" with the haredi parties and said he has not held talks with Shas MKs over the past year.
The possibility of eventually sitting in a government headed by Eisenkot is therefore not being presented within the haredi political establishment as the result of any advance agreement with him.
From the perspective of the haredi sources, it could become a practical option if the draft law has already become a fait accompli and the main obstacle from their perspective has been removed.
The major question will be Shas.
At the same time, the party is fighting to win back voters who have shifted toward Itamar Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit, and it is therefore expected to continue presenting a clearly right-wing line during the election campaign.
Nevertheless, haredi sources find it difficult to envision a scenario in which, on the day after the elections, Shas alone joins a government while United Torah Judaism remains outside it.
"When the moment of truth comes," a haredi source assessed, "Shas won't do something different from United Torah Judaism."
Haredi parties enter 2026 elections in weak position
Also in the background is what sources in the sector describe as the relatively weak position in which the haredi parties are entering the elections.
"The haredim are coming into these elections very weak," one source said.
Shas is concerned, among other things, about voters moving to Otzma Yehudit, while the haredi political establishment as a whole is bearing the cost of the ongoing conscription crisis.
That backdrop is also contributing to the view that this time it may be better not to enter the government immediately and once again find themselves at the center of the confrontation over the law.
Once the conscription issue is resolved, the traditional priorities of the haredi parties are expected to return to the center of coalition negotiations: funding for yeshivas and institutions, and arrangements addressing the needs of the haredi public.
Sources in the political establishment estimate the main budgetary cost would be about NIS 1.2 billion to NIS 1.4 billion, and in any case no more than roughly NIS 1.5 billion.
From their perspective, that sum would not constitute a significant obstacle in the context of a state budget worth hundreds of billions of shekels, and a government seeking to broaden its support base could find a way to provide it.
If the move materializes, it could also affect the long-standing relationship between the haredi parties and the Netanyahu bloc.
There is no discussion within the haredi political establishment of severing ties with Netanyahu, but sitting in the opposition during the initial period could restore political room for maneuver that has nearly disappeared in recent years.
From the perspective of the haredi sources, the decision over coalition partnership can wait. First, they want to see how the conscription issue is resolved. Only afterward do they want to examine which government, if any, it would be right for them to join.

“Mosaics in Dialogue” kicks off today in Lisbon, a project that compares the mosaic traditions of Ravenna and the Portuguese region of Coimbra. The initiative will run through September 19 and is part of the European Heritage Days program.
                                    
                                       
				The program connects Ravenna—a center of late antique and Byzantine mosaic art—with the “Universidade de Coimbra – Alta e Sofia” site, the ruins of the Roman city of Conimbriga, and other sites of Portuguese cultural heritage.
                                    
                                       
				The opening day will bring together Italian institutions based in Portugal and representatives from Emilia-Romagna. A student from the Nervi-Severini Art High School in Ravenna will demonstrate the techniques of the Ravenna school by creating a Roman mosaic.
                                    
                                       
				The program will continue on September 18 in Coimbra with presentations by researchers and professionals, as well as a demonstration dedicated to Byzantine mosaics. On September 19, a visit to the ruins of Conimbriga and other sites along the “Rota do Mosaico Romano” is scheduled, led by Vitor Dias, director of the Museu Nacional de Conimbriga.
                                    
                                       
				The initiative is sponsored by the Italian Embassy in Lisbon and organized in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Lisbon and the Nervi-Severini Art High School in Ravenna. The project is promoted by the Association of Emiliano-Romagnoli in the Iberian Peninsula (Aerpi) as part of the “Ordinary Activities 2026” call for proposals issued by the Council of Emiliano-Romagnoli Abroad. The goal is to strengthen cultural and scientific collaboration between Italy and Portugal through the study and promotion of mosaic art.

====================================================================================================

French interior minister accused of drug-smearing pro-Palestinian MEP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:50:52 UTC
20:50:52 KST

French interior minister accused of drug-smearing pro-Palestinian MEP
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez is under fire over allegations that he helped fuel a false drug story about MEP and prominent pro-Palestine activist Rima Hassan.
Hassan’s left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI), or France Unbowed party, has demanded that Nunez resign after a France 2 investigation released Wednesday alleged he leaked a false story to reporters about drugs purportedly found in Hassan’s belongings by police.
The drug was later identified as legal CBD (cannabidiol) and the probe was dropped, prompting LFI to accuse Nunez of media “manipulation” and fueling a false story.
What exactly happened?
The case dates back to April, when Hassan was summoned to Paris police headquarters over a since-deleted social media post quoting Kozo Okamoto. Okamoto, a member of the Japanese Red Army, was convicted over the 1972 Lod Airport attack in Tel Aviv, carried out on behalf of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which killed 26 people.
The French-Palestinian MEP and prominent pro-Palestinian activist was placed in custody on suspicion of online “apology for terrorism,” an offense punishable by up to seven years in prison.
During an inventory of her belongings, police found two containers, one holding a brown substance and another containing white crystals. Hassan said both were CBD products legally bought in Brussels and used for medical reasons.
A preliminary police test indicated the white substance contained synthetic cathinones associated with illegal drugs. Before laboratory results were available – and while Hassan was still in custody – reports that synthetic drugs had been found among her belongings began circulating in the media.
The Paris prosecutor’s office subsequently opened an investigation into her suspected drug use, transport, and possession. However, laboratory tests later established that the substances were CBD, and the investigation was dropped.
Now, according to “Complement d’enquete,” Nunez himself allegedly helped fuel the story.
What did Nunez tell reporters?
The program says Nunez was returning by train from an official trip to Bordeaux when reporters approached him and asked off camera whether drugs had been found in Hassan’s bag.
“He told us: ‘It’s possible that it’s true.’ Then he told us it was a synthetic ‘stuff,’ and that the second product was a cocaine derivative,” one journalist recalled.
Another said Nunez relayed Hassan’s explanation that she had bought the substances in Belgium believing they were legal. Yet another reporter on the train subsequently told his newsroom, based on Nunez’s account, that “synthetic drugs derived from cocaine” had been found among Hassan’s belongings.
Nunez initially agreed to an interview with France 2 before withdrawing and did not answer written questions. His office told AFP that “the reported exchange took place during an off-the-record discussion with the media,” initiated by journalists about information that had already been published.
Meanwhile, Nunez publicly lamented the leaks the following day.
“I also regret that there have been leaks; I understand that there were some leaks before the prosecutor’s office spoke out,” he told BFMTV.
France Unbowed demands Nunez’s resignation
Following the latest revelations, LFI demanded Nunez step down, accusing the government of media “manipulation” against a political opponent.
“The disclosure of information protected by the confidentiality of judicial proceedings and its subsequent exploitation by the media are incompatible with the principles of the rule of law,” the party said in a statement, adding: “La France Insoumise is calling for his resignation.”
LFI founder Jean-Luc Melenchon went further, writing on X: “A manipulative minister manipulates unscrupulous journalists with neither scruples nor professional conscience. Hours of slander.” He accused those involved of acting under the influence of “hatred of Palestinians and support for genocide.”
LFI coordinator Manuel Bompard also attacked Nunez over the apparent contradiction between the alleged private exchange and his subsequent public comments.
“It is not normal for a minister of the interior to violate the law, to contribute to the dissemination of information protected by investigative secrecy, especially when he himself then goes on television to say that he regrets these leaks,” Bompard told France Inter.
Hassan also demanded Nunez resign.
“This crass political manipulation has gone on long enough. He must draw the consequences and resign!” she wrote on X, portraying the episode as part of a wider campaign against her. “Gag procedures, surveillance measures, phone geolocation, false information about an alleged possession of narcotics, spread by the Minister of the Interior in person... How far will this go? What will the next step be?”
The Paris Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation into breaches of investigative confidentiality, while Hassan and her lawyer, Vincent Brengarth, filed a complaint over the disclosure of protected information. Brengarth has also called for Nunez to be questioned by a judge “as soon as possible.”
What’s behind the Nunez-Hassan clash?
The granddaughter of displaced Palestinians, Hassan was born in a refugee camp in Aleppo and came to France as a child. She has since emerged as one of France’s most prominent pro-Palestinian political figures, campaigning to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement, pressing the Palestinian issue in the European Parliament and joining Gaza-bound humanitarian flotillas.
Her activism, however, has put her at the center of repeated legal and police scrutiny in France. By mid-2026, Hassan had faced more than 20 legal proceedings and numerous police summonses, many of which were dropped or dismissed – something her supporters cite as evidence that the cases are being used to intimidate her and damage her reputation.
Tensions with the French authorities escalated over her social media post quoting Okamoto. Investigative reports revealed that police had tracked Hassan’s phone location and obtained detailed rail and air travel records, including movements predating the formal investigation. Hassan challenged the surveillance which she described as “politico-judicial harassment” in a privacy complaint.
Her activism has also brought confrontations abroad. Hassan has accused Israeli forces of physically mistreating her after detaining her during Gaza-bound humanitarian missions, including following the interception of the Madleen at sea in June 2025.
Nunez, meanwhile, defended the French investigation into Hassan, arguing that “apologizing for terrorism is a very serious offense.” He also insisted there was “no witch hunt” against her. Hassan and LFI see it differently, accusing the government of stretching anti-terrorism laws to criminalize political speech and suppress pro-Palestinian activism. They have characterized the string of proceedings as politically motivated “legal warfare.”
Is France anti-Palestine?
President Emmanuel Macron’s government supports a two-state solution and has become increasingly critical of Israeli policies of late, while backing the Palestinian Authority and calling for Hamas, which France classifies as a terrorist organization, to be excluded from governing Gaza and disarmed.
At home, however, French authorities have taken a far tougher approach to pro-Palestinian rhetoric deemed to cross legal boundaries. In 2014, France moved the offense of “apology for terrorism” (apologie du terrorisme) from its press law into the Penal Code, giving prosecutors greater scope to pursue individuals accused of defending or praising terrorist acts. Under this legal framework, French authorities have pursued a range of high-profile figures over controversial speech, including right-wing commentator Eric Zemmour, prominent Islamologist Francois Burgat, and pro-Palestinian activist Mahdieh Esfandiari.
LFI argues those powers are being disproportionately used against opposition politicians and pro-Palestinian activists. Its National Assembly leader, Mathilde Panot, said in April that under Macron, “the criminalization of political opponents has reached a new level.”
Hassan’s trial for alleged “apology for terrorism,” initially scheduled for July, was postponed at her defense’s request and is now due in October.
Update
Nunez rejected his role in the incident involving Hassan on Thursday, telling a National Assembly hearing that he had “not organized any leaks.” He acknowledged discussing Hassan’s case with reporters off the record, but again insisted they already had the information and had approached him for comment.
“I didn’t organize any leaks,” he repeated, saying he had instead “urged caution” during the exchange.
Commenting on X, Bompard seized on the admission, accusing Nunez of confirming information protected by investigative secrecy and calling it a “very serious violation of the law,” while renewing demands for his resignation.

Russia's top-selling dog vaccine linked to spate of pet deaths across the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:49:30 UTC
20:49:30 KST

State veterinary regulator confirmed batch 20 of Multican-8 contained a live Aujeszky's disease virus — typically fatal in dogs — after owners across at least 10 Russian regions reported hundreds of deaths since August.
Russia has ordered a batch of one of its most widely used dog vaccines destroyed after finding a live virus in some of its samples, confirming a link to deaths reported across the country since August.
Russia's veterinary and agricultural inspection agency Rosselkhoznadzor said batch 20 of the Multican-8 vaccine, produced by Moscow-based Vetbiokhim, contained a live Aujeszky's disease virus — a usually fatal illness affecting dogs with no specific treatment.
The regulator ordered the batch withdrawn from circulation and destroyed. Batch 20 contained 60,000 doses, according to independent Russian outlet Meduza.
Dog owners in Moscow, St Petersburg and at least eight regions including Krasnodar, Yaroslavl, Leningrad, Tula, Penza, Saratov and Belgorod had reported severe adverse reactions and deaths in animals vaccinated with Multican-8.
Russia's State Duma said it had received around 300 complaints of pet dog deaths related to the vaccine, according to Russian outlet Baza.
Vetbiokhim initially cited suspected deliberate interference by third parties. The regulator's subsequent finding of a live pathogen and serious production violations does not support the claims of sabotage.
Four other batches of Multican vaccines had already been suspended before Wednesday's order.
Rosselkhoznadzor and the prosecutor's office announced inspections in August, while Vetbiokhim said it was conducting an internal investigation.
In early September, Rosselkhoznadzor said preliminary findings indicated serious production violations and warned the company could face licence revocation.
Vetbiokhim drew up compensation agreements with owners of dogs that died, offering between 200,000 and 300,000 rubles per case, according to Meduza, which cited posts in private chats used by those affected.
The agreements required recipients to waive all further claims and sign non-disclosure agreements barring them from discussing the case with media, on social media or in messaging apps without the company's consent.
The company told Russian business outlet RBC that the confidentiality clause was "standard legal practice".
Multican-8 was the top-selling product in Russia's pet vaccine segment from January to July of this year, accounting for around 20% of the market, according to Kommersant, citing data from RNC Pharma.
Vetbiokhim's products account for approximately 70% of the Russian market for dog and cat vaccines across its range of 15 products.
The company's dominance expanded sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the imposition of sanctions in early 2022, which cut the share of imported veterinary medicines on the Russian market from 50% to between 10% and 15%.
Owners of cats vaccinated with the company's Multifel product have also reported deaths, according to independent outlet Govorit NeMoskva.
Multican-8 is also marketed outside Russia, including in Belarus, Armenia and Kazakhstan. However, there is currently no evidence that any suspicious batches have been exported abroad.

Nearly 1,000 deferment certificates were issued for bribes: in Ternopil region, the entire medical commission has been charged with suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the medical advisory commission, three medical workers and two intermediaries are suspected of selling deferment certificates for $6,000–12,000. The scheme has been exposed.
In the Ternopil region, the head of the medical advisory commission of a district hospital, three members of the commission and two intermediaries were exposed for issuing nearly 1,000 conclusions for deferments in exchange for bribes over three years, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, from 2024 to 2026, the doctors prepared conclusions containing false information about the health conditions of conscripts’ relatives and their need for constant care from another person. These documents were subsequently used to obtain deferments from mobilization.
According to the investigation, the scheme was organized by the head of the medical advisory commission. She recruited three other commission members and two intermediaries, who sought out "clients" among their acquaintances.
The preparation of the documents cost between USD 6,000 and USD 12,000. Over three years, approximately 1,000 commission conclusions were issued stating that conscripts’ relatives needed constant care from another person.
During searches at the residences and workplaces of the medical workers and intermediaries, medical documentation, mobile phones and other materials were seized. They are being examined as part of the criminal proceedings.
Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors from the Ternopil Regional Prosecutor’s Office, four medical workers were notified of suspicion of obstructing the lawful activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and official forgery committed by a group of persons acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy (Part 1 of Article 114-1, Part 2 of Article 28, Part 1 of Article 366 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The head of the medical advisory commission was additionally charged with facilitating the illegal transfer of persons liable for military service across the state border of Ukraine (Part 2 of Article 332 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
One of the intermediaries was notified of suspicion under Part 1 of Article 114-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The other was notified in absentia of suspicion of trading in influence (Part 3 of Article 369-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The court imposed preventive measures on four medical workers and one of the intermediaries.
The investigation is also examining the possible involvement of other individuals in these crimes, including hospital employees and officials of other government institutions.

A fifth of Russian refining sits idle, and the sector’s earnings still grew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:46:55 UTC
20:46:55 KST

Russian oil refineries earned more in the first half of this year than in the same period a year earlier, even as Ukrainian drone strikes kept a fifth of the country's refining capacity out of action, The Moscow Times reported. Record wholesale prices and fast-growing payments from the federal budget have more than covered what the attacks and the repairs cost. Russian consumers are covering the rest at the pump.
Where the profits come from
Russian refineries earned 938 billion rubles ($11.1 billion) in the first half of 2026, 16.2% more than a year earlier, according to the state statistics service Rosstat. Ukrainian drone strikes have put a fifth of the country's refining capacity out of action.
Two things produced that result, according to Promsvyazbank analyst Yekaterina Krylova: high wholesale prices on the SPIMEX commodity exchange, and a sharp increase in state fuel subsidies.
Wholesale prices took off in March, after the war in the Middle East began: light petroleum products have risen 37% since late February and diesel by a third, with July bringing record exchange prices of 82,600 rubles ($982) per tonne of AI-95 gasoline. Crude got cheaper for the refiners over the same stretch, as the ruble price of Urals oil peaked in spring and fell through the summer while the products made from it kept getting dearer.
Ukraine says drones hit Russia’s gas heartland over 3,000 km from its border—a wartime record
The budget pays the difference, the country pays the bill
Russia's damper mechanism compensates oil companies for selling fuel cheaply at home rather than exporting it, and the payments grow as the gap between domestic and world prices widens.
The Finance Ministry paid out close to 350 billion rubles ($4.2 billion) a month in the second quarter, and 500 billion rubles ($5.9 billion) for July and August together. Krylova expects the subsidies and the prices together to widen net margins by 45% in the third quarter, to 35,000 rubles ($416) per tonne of gasoline.
Russia's retail prices tell the other half of the story. Gasoline has risen 21.2% since January and diesel 18.4%, well above Russian inflation. Budget money lets the majors, which own both the refineries and the filling-station chains, hold their own forecourt prices near inflation. Independent chains have no such cushion: they buy at the higher wholesale prices and sell dearer, which is how Russia has been squeezing them out of the market. For drivers, the crisis has been physical as well as financial, with rationing and dry pumps spreading across dozens of regions.
Kazakh refinery deal could ease Russia’s front-line fuel pressure—but it covers just 0.3% of demand
What the strikes have cost
Ukrainian drones have been hitting Russian refineries since 2024, and the campaign escalated sharply from August 2025, when strikes deep inside Russia became systematic. Russian refineries disclose none of their losses from it.
Ukraine's General Staff estimated the total damage to the Russian oil industry since August 2025 at $13.5 billion, in a count published in early July. The insurance broker Mains put direct losses to the oil and gas sector from drone strikes last year at more than 100 billion rubles ($1.2 billion), and above a trillion rubles once lost profit and indirect damage are counted.

- 
							
							
								Russia is squeezing independent gas stations out of its fuel market

Israeli authorities on Thursday reduced the number of patients and wounded Palestinians allowed to leave the Gaza Strip for medical treatment in Egypt from 136 to 61 patients and companions, Gaza’s Health Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said “a group of 136 patients and their companions had received official approval to travel before Israeli authorities reduced the number to 72 patients and companions and sent the remaining cases back.”

It called on the World Health Organization, the UN High Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs and other international institutions to “intervene immediately and pressure Israeli authorities to end the arbitrary restrictions.”
The ministry also called for Israel to fully facilitate the departure of all patients in accordance with the understandings reached in Sharm el-Sheikh in October, and urged that all patients referred for treatment abroad be allowed to leave in future groups without restrictions or exclusions.
Israel’s military campaign in Gaza since October 2023 has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, most of them women and children, according to Palestinian authorities.

Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign - this time targeting opposition voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:45:41 UTC
20:45:41 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign- this time targeting opposition voters
Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign- this time targeting opposition voters
Likud plans to take advantage of a precedent-setting decision by the Elections Committee under which voter-turnout figures will be published for individual polling stations during election day
The Likud party is preparing to revive its controversial “Arabs are flocking to the polls” campaign, this time with a focus on voter turnout among opposition supporters.
Likud plans to take advantage of a precedent-setting decision by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, under which voter-turnout figures will be published for individual polling stations during election day.
The party intends to use the data to mobilize its supporters by highlighting high turnout in opposition strongholds and Arab communities. Likud officials reportedly expect particularly strong turnout among opposition voters and hope that real-time updates will encourage the party’s own supporters to cast their ballots.
Sohlberg’s decision was originally presented as a compromise after Likud was barred from using the Elector voter-management system. The latest developments, however, could allow the party to benefit from both polling-station turnout data and real-time reports from its representatives about who has voted.
Following a lengthy and contentious debate on Sunday, the Central Elections Committee voted 19–11 to allow party representatives to continue reporting in real time which registered voters have cast their ballots and which have not.
Sohlberg had initially prohibited the practice. The High Court of Justice subsequently ruled that the matter fell outside his authority and returned it to the Central Elections Committee for a decision.
The controversy began last month, when Sohlberg ruled that polling-station committee members and party observers could not report voters’ identities to their parties during election day. He determined that sharing information about whether, when and under what circumstances a person voted—including the type of polling station used, such as one in a hospital or one adapted for people with limited mobility—could violate the individual’s privacy under the Privacy Protection Law.
Sohlberg also found that election law does not explicitly authorize party representatives to transfer such information for political activity and that, without clear legal authorization, the practice should be prohibited.
Likud challenged the ruling before the High Court. The court concluded last week that Sohlberg did not have the authority to decide the issue on his own and referred the matter back to the Central Elections Committee.

Finland considers sending convicts abroad as domestic prisons become overcrowded
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
14:45:31 EEST
20:45:31 KST

Finland's Ministry of Justice is examining the possibility of sending people convicted of a crime in Finland to prisons abroad to serve out their sentences.
The practice of renting prison space from another country, otherwise known as prison outsourcing, is outlined in a report commissioned by the ministry and presented to the media on Thursday.
Justice Minister Leena Meri (Finns) noted that renting prison space abroad would be one way of alleviating the overcrowding situation in Finnish prisons, but added that introducing the practice would require overcoming some constitutional obstacles.
"For this reason, these constitutional frameworks should be assessed either as official work or via an external investigation. I hope, of course, that in the next government negotiations a decision will be made to reform Finnish legislation [in this matter]," Meri said.
Tougher legislation means more prisoners
Minister Meri told the press conference on Thursday that Finland's prison population has grown steadily in recent years, noting that prison capacity was exceeded in 2024 and has continued to rise since.
According to figures from the Prison and Probation Service Finland, there are currently about 3,900 people in Finnish prisons, with the agency predicting that number will rise to 4,000 by 2028.
Meri pointed out in particular the sharp rise in the number of foreign-background prisoners currently being held in Finnish prisons.
That number now stands at 950, she said, an increase of about 75 percent over the past decade.
Meri further stated that the growth in Finland's prison population over that same time period (from 2017 to 2026) is being driven by the amount of prison sentences handed down to foreign-background defendants — accounting for some four-fifths of the increase.
The three most common crimes for which foreign-background defendants are sentenced to prison are drug offences, sexual offences and homicides, according to the ministry's report.
This reflects tougher legislation introduced by both the previous government of Sanna Marin as well as the current administration, led by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP), to crack down on such crimes.
Aside from the option of sending prisoners abroad, Meri announced that Finland's own prison capacity will be increased by about 500 places.
"We will get additional prison places fastest in Helsinki, Hämeenlinna, and Kylmäkoski. We are making modular units, and they should be in use by next year," she said, adding that Turku prison will also open an additional wing by 2028.
The Sweden-Estonia agreement
Meri also told reporters at Thursday's press conference that her ministry has not decided to which countries Finland could send prisoners, and that no formal negotiations with any other nation have been started.
The ministry's report, however, did cite as an example the agreement between Sweden and Estonia, made last year, which Swedish authorities initiated as a means of alleviating overcrowding in its prisons.
The agreement sees at least 300 spaces at Tartu prison reserved for transfers from Sweden, and it costs Sweden an estimated 30.6 million euros annually — or about 102,000 euros per prisoner per year.
By comparison, Finland spends about 80,000 euros per prisoner a year.
After serving their sentences, the prisoners who came from Sweden will not be released in Estonia, but will be returned to Sweden.
However, a similar agreement between Finland and Estonia seems unlikely.
"Estonia does not have the willingness, at least according to my information, to make more rental agreements," Meri said.

Black Sea attacks push commercial ships into Marmara anchorages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:44:00 UTC
20:44:00 KST

(İHA Photo)
Hundreds of commercial vessels are crowding anchorages in the Marmara Sea as shipowners increasingly avoid the Black Sea amid a surge in attacks on civilian ships linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
More than 200 commercial vessels bound for the Black Sea have been struck by unmanned aerial vehicles or missiles over the past four months, including Turkish-flagged ships.
The attacks have turned the Marmara Sea into a vast parking area, with hundreds of vessels dropping anchor rather than proceeding into the Black Sea.
Speaking to Turkish media, business representatives called for navigational safety to be restored in the Black Sea.
Yusuf Yalçın Çapoğlu, vice president of the Turkish Shipowners’ and Operators’ Association (KOSDER), said attacks brought commercial activity in the Black Sea to the brink of collapse.
“The number of vessels entering and leaving through the straits has fallen below 30. Under normal circumstances, that figure was above 200,” Çapoğlu said.
“Ukraine is doing everything it can to prevent vessels engaged in trade with Russia from going there. Russia is retaliating. Ships are being hit by missiles and drones. Recently, a vessel bound for Georgia was struck on its way there. The shipowner changed his mind and turned back. It was hit again on the way back,” he added.
Even when the vessels are not operating, shipowners continue to incur substantial costs for every day they remain at anchor.
“Whether you operate the vessel or not, you have to pay these expenses. They start at around $2,500 a day and can rise to $5,000, $6,000 or even $7,000,” Çapoğlu said.
He also warned that if there was no end in sight to the situation, shipowners could take the drastic step of unloading their vessels rather than continuing to operate under such conditions.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sept. 15 said that to the growing number of attacks targeting civilian vessels in the Black Sea is unacceptable in remarks made in Azerbaijan.
Fidan said Türkiye had issued the necessary warnings to the parties, adding that he believed common ground could be found if the required political will was demonstrated and the two sides acted in good faith.

Commander Aktürk, spokesperson for the Defense Ministry (iHA Photo)
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ recent trip to Meis — the closest Greek island to the Turkish mainland— has drawn a sharp reaction from Ankara after he toured military facilities on the legally demilitarized isle.
“The visit of the Greek Prime Minister and his delegation to Meis Island, and his contacts with the military units stationed there, has been closely monitored,” read a statement by the Defense Ministry on Sept. 17.
The ministry statement referred to Mitsotakis’ three-day trip to the island last week, where he inspected local military outposts. The island has a demilitarized status according to 1947-dated Paris Peace Agreement.
The ministry said the deployment of warships and other units to Meis Island and making them public through high-level visits do not comply with the island’s status and do not contribute to stability.
“We emphasize once again that attempts to create a de facto situation in violation of the demilitarized status of Meis Island, which is located extremely close to the Turkish coast, are incompatible with international obligations and will not be accepted by our country,” the ministry said.
Türkiye’s objective is to develop good unneighborly relations with Greece based on dialogue and turn the Aegean Sea and Mediterranean into a basin of peace and stability, it added.
However, the ministry reiterated that Türkiye will not tolerate any actions that undermine its regional rights or attempt to create a fait accompli.
“We call upon Greece to comply with its obligations arising from international treaties and to refrain from violating the demilitarized status of the islands,” the ministry said.
On a question about the relocation of the 51st Commando Unit to Söke district of Aydın province in the Aegean region from eastern Anatolian city of Tunceli, ministry officials said the decision was taken in June and in line with military needs.
US lifting arms embargo on Greek Cyprus unconstructive
The officials also commented on the U.S. decision to prolong the lifting of the arms embargo on Greek Cyprus for one more year, criticizing the move as a step that can disrupt sensitive balances and trust in the island.
“Our expectation from third parties is that they refrain from activities that would damage the delicate balances on the island, abandon practices that disregard the Turkish Cypriot people, and contribute to peace and stability with a fair and impartial approach,” the officials said, referring to the U.S.
They also added that Türkiye, as a guarantor country, will continue to take necessary measures for the safety and welfare of the Turkish Cypriots.

Kanyshai Butun
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday appointed Anton Kovalskyi as acting prosecutor general after parliament approved the dismissal of Ruslan Kravchenko on Sept. 15.
Kovalskyi, who heads the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office, was appointed by presidential decree.
Kravchenko submitted his resignation Sept. 7 amid a National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) investigation into alleged corruption involving officials at the Prosecutor General’s Office.
NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) said on Sept. 5 they had uncovered an alleged criminal organization led by a department head at the Prosecutor General’s Office. Its members are suspected of taking bribes from fraudulent call centers and laundering money.
Kravchenko has denied wrongdoing and accused NABU Director Semen Kryvonos of forging documents.
He also said he signed a second notice of suspicion concerning a person close to the head of SAPO, Oleksandr Klymenko, alleging that the person had influenced judges at Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court, offered them unlawful benefits and helped individuals evade military mobilization.
NABU and SAPO rejected the allegations, saying no notice of suspicion had been served on Kryvonos and describing Kravchenko’s claims as part of an attack on the independence of anti-corruption bodies.
