Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% despite rising inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:00:32 UTC
20:00:32 KST

The Bank of England has kept interest rates on hold as it warned a continuation of the bitter fighting in the Middle East could force it to raise borrowing costs amid mounting fears over inflation.
It also announced a surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in UK government bonds back to the Treasury to avoid fuelling turbulence in the gilt market, a decision that could have significant consequences for the public finances before next month’s budget.
As the fallout from war in the Middle East fuels a rise in energy prices, the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted by a majority of six to three to keep its base rate unchanged at 3.75%.
However, the Bank said the increasingly probable prospect of a lengthy war fanning intense volatility in global markets had dramatically raised the chance of it putting up borrowing costs in future.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said: “So far higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.
“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise [the] Bank rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2% target.”
With Threadneedle Street under pressure to guard against high rates of inflation becoming entrenched, City traders predict a quarter-point rise in borrowing costs from as early as November with three more increases to 4.75% likely to happen next year.
The sharp rise in global energy prices prompted the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023, after a decision last week by the European Central Bank to raise eurozone borrowing costs.
The Bank said inflation was on track to reach 4% by early next year, as the war-driven rise in energy prices hits households.
Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation rose to 3.1% last month from 2.9% in July as the escalating hostilities in the Middle East drove up the average price of petrol and diesel by almost a quarter.
It came after Andy Burnham said he was prepared to take “difficult decisions” to tackle high inflation and keep the economy on track and would take action at next month’s budget on the cost of living.
However, the MPC said the economy was showing signs of resilience and there was not yet a need to take action on borrowing costs because there had been “little evidence so far of material second-round effects” – when inflationary pressures push businesses and workers to demand higher prices and pay settlements.
There were also signs of weaker food price inflation despite the surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war, it added.
Against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets, Threadneedle Street also announced updated proposals for the winding down of its financial crisis-era quantitative easing programme, which had involved the buying of £895bn of UK government bonds at its peak.
In a surprise move, the Bank said it planned to sell £146bn of bonds to the Treasury, at a pace of about £20bn a year until 2034, in a plan that would require signoff from the chancellor, John Healey, next April. The Treasury’s Debt Management Office (DMO) would then sell bonds to cover the government’s financing commitments, including this buyback.
The rationale is that the Bank holds long-term bonds where investor demand is dwindling, whereas the DMO would have the capacity to cover the buyback by issuing shorter-term debt.
The process will be used to complete Threadneedle Street’s “quantitative tightening” programme – which has involved the sale of gilts held on its books since 2022, which has reduced its holdings to about £488bn.
The Bank said it would retain about £120bn of bonds, which were needed to back the issuance of notes and coins circulating in the economy.
Leaving about £222bn of bonds, it said this amount would be disposed of by allowing maturing debts to expire, and through active sales to the state if a deal was agreed. The Bank said it would pause its QT programme until a deal was finalised and that it would resume sales to City investors if an agreement could not be reached.
In a letter to the chancellor, Bailey said the arrangement preserved “the independence of monetary policy” and would “maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime” of the QT programme.
It came as the Office for National Statistics also upgraded its estimates for the UK’s productivity growth, in a boost for Healey as he prepares for the budget.
The UK government’s borrowing costs and the pound fell slightly on Thursday after the decision. The central bank added that it would halt sales of long-dated gilts entirely. The 10-year gilt yield fell by six basis points to 5.243%, the lowest level in a week.

Amid stalemate and assassinations, Gaza awaits Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:00:09 UTC
20:00:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Amid political stalemate and ongoing assassinations, Gaza awaits Israeli elections to be over
Gaza does not appear to be heading towards any significant political or administrative change at this present stage.
Instead, amid all its suffering and tragedy, it appears trapped in a prolonged period of waiting, with the Israeli elections on 27 October dominating the scene, as the outcome will shape the next government and its stance toward the war-battered coastal enclave.
While various parties are discussing post-war arrangements, the administration and reconstruction of Gaza, the future of resistance's weapons and the Israeli military occupation, have been practically postponed until after the political battle in Israel settles.
The current stalemate could continue until the end of this year and perhaps beyond into early 2027.
Neverlesstheless, Israeli bombardment, military attacks and targeted assassinations are ongoing and could bring Gaza back to the forefront of events at any moment.
The difference, however, is that military developments do not necessarily appear to be linked to a parallel political process for a fundamental change in the Strip.
Since the beginning of this week, Israel has assassinated several senior commanders of the Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas, in separate targeting operations in different parts of the Strip.
They include Rafah Brigade commander and head of the brigades' operations system Nail Abu Obeid on Tuesday evening, and, before him, the commander of the brigades' main battalion in Jabalia, Ahmed al-Batsh, along with members of the Islamic Jihad movement.
Israel also conducts daily attacks on several resistance operatives, claiming they are preparing for operations, although the reality on the ground shows otherwise.
As the elections approach, the current Israeli government's ability to make strategic decisions on Gaza becomes more limited, particularly on issues that could be interpreted within Israel as a retreat from the objectives of the war.
This impression is reinforced by the decline in Gaza's presence in international media coverage, after the issue had been a major focus of political and diplomatic reporting during previous periods.
This comes as US President Donald Trump said in a press statement on 13 September that there was less discussion about the issues in Gaza, saying that people no longer heard much about the Strip.
According to the Israeli political timetable, the elections will be held on 27 October, after which consultations to form a new government will begin. There is no fixed date for the new government to take office, as this depends on how quickly a coalition is formed and wins the confidence of the Knesset. This could push the transfer of power to the end of 2026 or the beginning of 2027.
Israeli Security Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday that the army was ready to "eliminate Hamas" to "complete the mission" in Gaza, followed by the implementation of a "migration plan" in the Strip.
"Rafah and 70 per cent of the Gaza Strip have been emptied of their population, and the tunnels and homes have been destroyed," he said, adding that the army "protects the residents of Israeli communities and eliminates many terrorists every week".
Gaza, delayed
In this context, Palestinian expectations do not appear optimistic about the possibility of a near-term change in the current reality.
Any broad political breakthrough may require a new Israeli government, a more decisive US position and an internal Israeli consensus on what happens the day after in Gaza.
Until then, major administrative and political issues may remain unresolved, while the Strip continues to be dealt with through security and military means.
Israeli affairs researcher Mohammad Halsa said there is a growing conviction among observers and even sections of the Israeli public that Israel's political crisis has become directly linked to its inability to take decisive steps on domestic and foreign issues, foremost among them the Palestinian issue and the Gaza Strip.
Halsa told The New Arab that any potential change in the governing coalition or the composition of Israel's political system does not necessarily mean a breakthrough in the situation in the Strip.
He said disagreements among opposition parties do not centre on the substance of their position on the Palestinian issue but often revolve around adopting tougher positions towards Gaza.
"Netanyahu's opponents, even when they disagree with him on some details, do not depart far from his view of the importance of military force, deterrence and security control," he said.
Some of them may, alongside the use of force, propose arrangements or settlements that serve Israeli security without abandoning the principle of Israeli security control, he added.
Halsa added issues such as humanitarian aid and infrastructure could see some movement if there were a political change, but questions surrounding military withdrawal, implementation of commitments and reconstruction of the Strip would require a long time, given the changes that have taken place in public and official positions in Israel.
Similar calculations
The complexity does not end with the possibility of Netanyahu remaining in office or leaving it.
An assessment of the Israeli scene indicates that the internal dispute is not necessarily over the basic principle of dealing with Gaza but rather over the tools, outcomes and timing.
Israel's opposition can criticise Netanyahu for the failure of the war or the way it has been managed, but it faces difficulty in presenting a radically different vision for the future of the Strip.
In this context, changing the government becomes an important factor, but it is not enough to bring about a shift in Israeli policy towards Gaza.
Power may pass from one coalition to another, while core issues, such as security, military control, the disarmament of the resistance and the future administration of the Strip, remain subject to the same constraints.
Israeli affairs expert Adel Shadid said he sees no indications of a genuine political breakthrough in Israel, even with elections being held.
He said the Israeli scene remains governed by a widespread belief that the war on the Gaza Strip has not achieved its stated objectives.
Shadid told The New Arab that despite the military and political measures Israel has taken, it has failed to end the presence of the resistance or achieve the results it was seeking.
This is pushing Israel's political and security establishment to continue dealing with the Palestinian reality from a security and military perspective rather than opening a serious discussion about political solutions, he said.
He pointed out that the continuation of the war and restrictions imposed on Palestinian life are linked, in the Israeli political mindset, to the fact that Gaza still exists and that the battle has not been settled according to the Israeli vision.
He said this reality would affect the shape of the next government in Israel, whether Netanyahu remains in office or leaves it.
Shadid said that if Netanyahu remains, he would not necessarily be in the same position of strength he previously held but would still be forced to adopt tougher positions to maintain his political position amid pressure from rival parties and political forces.
"The Israeli opposition parties are also seeking to adopt a tougher discourse towards Gaza and the Palestinian issue. They criticise Netanyahu over what they consider a failure to achieve the objectives of the war, but they do not necessarily put forward a different political alternative," he added.
Shadid concluded that the Israeli domestic arena faces two possibilities: the continuation of the current political situation or a change in the composition of the government, without either scenario meaning a near-term breakthrough on the Palestinian issue.

In the meantime, Communications Director Burhanettin Duran also reacted on the attacks targeting Mecca.
In a message through his social media account, Duran condemned the attacks.
“Any attempted attack against the Two Holy Mosques, sacred to the Islamic world, wounds our collective conscience. Safeguarding the peace and security of the Holy City of Mecca is a matter of utmost importance to the entire Islamic world,” he stated.
“As our President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has always emphasized, the Islamic world needs not new conflicts, but common sense, dialogue and lasting peace. We stand with our brotherly country, Saudi Arabia and extend our sympathies following this attack,” the director added.
Houthi aggression threatens global stability: Defense
Türkiye’s Defense Ministry also reacted against the continued escalation by the Houthis which target civilian and commercial vessels using the Red Sea and called for the cessation of these attacks.
“The ongoing Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb negatively affects not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability,” the ministry said.
On a question about the Mecca defense pact in the context of the ongoing conflict, the ministry recalled that the trilateral alliance is based on collective deterrence and defense.
“The [alliance] agreement is not against any country, nor does it constitute an alternative to the member states’ existing relations with third countries,” it added.

Soundboks Rider Party Speaker Review: Loud and Durable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Gets very loud for its size. Clear, detailed sound. Very durable build. Swappable battery. IP66 dust and waterproof.
TIRED
Expensive. Overkill for many. Single hand-carry grip. Pricey strap sold separately.
How loud is too loud? That's the question I find myself asking as I turn up the volume dial on the Soundboks Rider portable Bluetooth speaker. By myself, outdoors, a five or six on the dial is plenty loud; anything more starts to get uncomfortable. But this speaker can push out a ridiculous 118-decibel sound pressure level (dB SPL). That's basically a rock concert.
If that's your jam, this may be your perfect speaker. It's distinct, stylish, built to last, and, importantly, sounds great. But it's absolutely overkill for most people, who would be better off with a smaller, more affordable speaker from the likes of Sony, JBL, or Marshall, all of which offer plenty of tamer options below the Rider's $600 price tag.
Bring The Party
Soundboks Rider Specs
The Soundboks Rider looks like no other portable speaker I've tested. It resembles something you'd find on stage at a concert rather than at your next barbecue. Its restrained design is almost the antithesis of the flashy, LED-pulsing party speakers you might find from brands like JBL or Samsung.
The build quality is impressive, confidence-inspiring, and clearly made to last. It's built like a tank, with a steel front grille, silicone rubber ball corners, and a thick plastic cabinet. During a drop test, I was frankly more worried about the speaker breaking my stairs than my stairs breaking the speaker. Another win for longevity is the replaceable battery—it charges via USB-C, and you can swap it in and out in seconds. This feels like a speaker you could have for decades.
While smaller than Soundboks' other speakers, it is still much larger than your average Bluetooth unit, and a bit awkward to carry with its single carry-grip on one corner. I would have loved to see two carry handles, one on each side. That would make the Rider easier and more flexible to carry, similar to the Sony ULT Field 7.
Unlike the larger Soundboks Mix and Soundboks 4, this is meant to be a stand-alone speaker—it does not have Soundboks' wireless multi-speaker connectivity (SKAA TeamUp), a speaker stand mount, or additional inputs (read: XLR).
Loud and Clear
Soundboks speakers can get loud, and despite the Rider being the smallest in the brand's lineup, its audio output is astonishing. I was frankly scared to turn this speaker up to max volume (11 on the dial, IYKYK).
To spare my New York City neighbors, I took this speaker outdoors and cranked it to 11; even then, I could only manage it for a short while before I worried someone would call 311 to file a noise complaint. Which is to say: the Rider is plenty loud for most parties I can think of.
But the Rider isn't just loud—it's clear. Across all volume ranges, it sounds great. While it can produce big bass, it isn't overpowering in the mix. The sound profile matches the speaker's understated, PA-style aesthetic—clear, strong, and detailed.
The speaker can output up to 118 dB SPL. That's well within painful levels, and similar to a rock concert. I'm honestly not sure when or where I'd need to push out that much audio, but if you ever do, the Rider is game.
Fine Tuning
The app is similarly streamlined and unfussy. You can control basically every speaker function remotely, including volume, sound profiles, EQ modes, and even turning it off.
Connecting, however, was a little finicky. I had to pair, unpair, re-pair, power off, and power on a few times before the app and speaker would actually start talking to each other. That was even more irritating because, after a firmware update, the app told me to forget the speaker and re-pair all over again. I've tested hundreds of wireless audio gadgets—Bluetooth connectivity issues with brand-new products are less surprising than you might think and often get sorted out within a month or two of software updates. Still, it made the whole experience feel decidedly less premium than the Rider's $600 price might suggest.
Is It Overkill?
The Soundboks Rider is an excellent speaker. In terms of loudness, durability, and battery life, it runs circles around most of the competition, including larger party-slash-karaoke speakers like the Sony Tower 5 and JBL PartyBox Club 120.
But as a larger, portable Bluetooth speaker meant to stand all on its own, it's a bit niche, especially for $600. I do think it's overkill for a lot of people—I can't think of many folks in my life who need this combination of loud and bombproof in their speaker. You can also get plenty of portable Bluetooth speakers for less (the aforementioned $500 Sony ULT Field 7 and $330 JBL PartyBox Encore Essential 2 come to mind) that might do the job just fine.
Soundboks says this is a portable party speaker built for spontaneity and outdoor adventure. For my spontaneous adventures, the Rider is overkill. But if your adventures include a lot more people (and a lot more space) than mine, it might be the perfect fit—big enough to bring to any party and durable enough that you never have to worry about it.
Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Before that, he was a freelance writer for publications like Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. ... Read More

People Are Pissed Off and Ready to Own Their Shit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The train blasts through right as Louis Rossmann starts to speak. This has happened several times already at the event he’s hosting on a Friday night in San Jose, California. All the speakers before him patiently paused when the train on the nearby tracks roared by, its loud horn blaring, then resumed talking. But Rossmann is mid-sentence in his rapid-fire delivery about the topic he’s fiercely passionate about, and he doesn’t stop. He shouts over the train.
This is the penultimate stop of the Own Your Shit tour, a US-wide odyssey of events this summer put on by ownership advocate and YouTuber Louis Rossmann and his advocacy nonprofit Fulu. Around 80 people have crammed into the narrow side porch of a brewery. The final event will be in Silver Springs, Maryland, on October 1.
Before Rossmann spoke, panels featured an advocate from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, students from San Jose State University’s Fixit workshop, and a leader of the Fisker Owners Association, a group of vehicle owners who refuse to let their cars die. The main call to action is to kill a very specific piece of legislation: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Enacted in 1998, this section of the DMCA prohibits bypassing digital restrictions and locks enabled by a product manufacturer.
Ostensibly, the legislation was meant to ensure device security. Ownership and repair advocates have long criticized it for helping companies put software locks on devices and then charge owners for access to their own hardware. Rossmann, along with fellow advocate Kevin O’Reilly, started Fulu to pay out bounties for people who can disable digital locks on a device, even if there are legal consequences.
“How many people here enjoy it when they get threats of lawsuits?” Rossmann asks during the San Jose event. “Raise your hand.” Maybe four or five hands go up, including a grinning Rohit Chopra, the former director of the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. “I enjoy when people try to sue me,” Rossmann says. “When they send me threats, I literally frame them.”
His presentation bounces through his various ownership- and repair-oriented fights. He calls out companies like Amazon, which removed books from people’s Kindles, and home pipe leak detector company Roost, which discontinued stand-alone Wi-Fi products to the dismay of its users. He criticized Apple, Sony, wheelchair companies, and BMW, which recently ran ads for the new Spider-Man movie on their customers’ dashboard screens. He accuses companies of adding paid subscriptions to their products after customers buy them as a form of “ransomware.”
It’s a righteous screed that feels infectious in the crowd. People cheer and call out their own ownership issues. Rossmann is a preacher at the pulpit of people pissed off by subscription services, the steady decline of physical media, and the inability to fix their stuff.
The Own Your Shit tour comes as people grow increasingly angry with companies like Sony ending physical disc support and deleting digital items in customers’ libraries. (Google has recently done something similar and deleted a user’s copy of The Lord of the Rings.) Amazon just ended support for its perfectly fine older Kindles. People feel squeezed by economic pressures as devices get more expensive and want to hang onto their devices longer.
Katharine Trendacosta, a director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, spoke at the event to call out the way companies have turned just about everything into subscription services users have to pay for. “They get the subscription and our data,” Trendacosta says. “It's a win-win for them and a lose-lose for us.”
The tour may be coming to an end, but right-to-repair legislation has been growing worldwide. This year in the European Union, new regulations require companies to help extend the life of consumer products by making them more repairable and giving them more easily replaceable batteries. John Deere, long criticized for its repair-adverse policies, was hit with a $99 million lawsuit and a US Federal Trade Commission ruling requiring it to make its products more fixable. Repair advocates in the US have shot down anti-repair bills and are calling for federal regulation to ensure better automotive repairs and product longevity.
Chopra, the former director of the CFPB, now heads the newly established California Business and Consumer Services Agency, created in July by California governor Gavin Newsom. In a conversation after the event, he shared a vision for what the BCSA will focus on.
“New technology should not just help out people in the boardroom or in the C-suite,” Chopra says. “It's actually supposed to help all of us, but we are seeing how it can sometimes be designed to scam people, to rip people off, or sometimes create some real harm for them. People who are just trying to get by really feel totally hosed by some of these practices.”
Chopra says his goal in coming to this event was to help spread the word about the new agency and encourage people to reach out to their representatives about unfair consumer practices.
“We are going to be looking hard to make sure that we're cracking down on illegal practices,” Chopra says. “That there's actually some real enforcement, but also when it comes to new technology, that it's really actually helping everybody.”
After the event, I ask Rossmann how he’s feeling about the tour. He says he was initially worried that people were coming for the free pizza but was pleasantly surprised at how engaged and passionate the audiences have been.
“I’m feeling like there’s finally a turning of the tide,” Rossmann says.

How Trump Helped Put a Texas Senate Seat In Play
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If the GOP squanders this fall’s U.S. Senate race in Texas, some Republicans argue privately that President Donald Trump would bear part of the blame.
Trump’s sagging approval ratings, his handling of the GOP primary, and his early hesitance to use his enormous war chest to defend his preferred candidate, the scandal-scarred attorney general Ken Paxton, have boosted Democrats’ chances to win a statewide election in Texas for the first time in more than 30 years. Paxton lags slightly behind his Democratic opponent, state representative James Talarico, in several recent polls. More alarming to party strategists, Talarico has outraised Paxton by enormous margins, giving the Democrat the resources to compete in a huge and expensive state that the GOP did not plan to defend so fiercely.
Mark Jones, a Texas politics expert at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, describes the contest as a “perfect storm” for Democrats. “You have a very unpopular Donald Trump in the White House,” Jones says. “You also have an economy that is viewed negatively by a majority of Texans. The most flawed major statewide candidate that the Republican Party has had in modern memory. And we have a Democratic candidate who, while not ideal, is a very credible politician.”
Trump has the resources to help rescue Paxton: his affiliated super PAC, MAGA Inc., was sitting on more than $400 million this summer as the Republican begged for help. Initially, the President didn’t want to invest heavily in the race. According to three sources familiar with Trump’s thinking, including a senior White House official, Trump harbors doubts about the GOP’s midterm outlook. In private conversations, he has mused about how the money would simply be wasted, citing the history of a President’s party suffering defeats in midterm elections. A senior Trump adviser tells TIME that the President’s political operation has plans to spend tens of millions in the coming election cycle but won’t telegraph their strategy to the press and the opposition. “People are clutching their pearls because we’re not giving away our grand strategy,” the adviser says.
Other aides say there is another reason Trump has been careful to disburse funds: he wants to save as much as cash as he can for 2028 and even 2030, when his presidency would be ending or over, seeing the money as a means of exerting continued influence over the party. “He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now,” one Trump aide says. “He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities.”
Only after weeks of pressure from allies did Trump’s super PAC finally intervene, committing $10 million on Sept 5. to bankroll ad campaigns in Texas to promote Paxton and attack Talarico. When Republicans gathered in Dallas for an extravagant two-night midterm convention this month, Trump’s endorsement of Paxton and praise for his record came wrapped in jabs at his appearance, his sense of fashion, and his shortcomings as a television performer.
The result is a race Republicans once assumed would be easy becoming one of the most competitive and costly in the nation. For Trump, more than a Senate seat hangs in the balance. “I don’t think they fully understand what’s going to happen when we lose the House and Senate,” says Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist. “It’s going to be ‘Fort Apache’ everyday: subpoenas, investigations, impeachments, criminal referrals—the Democrats are perfecting the playbook they ran starting under Pelosi and Biden. Get ready for a near-death experience “
The Texas Senate race occupied an unusual amount of attention inside Trump’s political operation as far back as late 2024. The four-term incumbent, John Cornyn, was a Senate stalwart and close ally of the chamber’s top Republican, John Thune. But he had grown less popular with the party’s base, and Trump wanted him gone. Despite Cornyn’s record of voting with Trump 99% of the time, the President had not forgotten Cornyn’s pointed criticism of Trump’s culpability over the January 6 riots, or his hesitance to endorse Trump during the presidential primary.
But Cornyn only had one serious challenger at the time: Ken Paxton. And Paxton had obvious vulnerabilities.
Indicted on felony securities-fraud charges months after taking office in 2015, Paxton spent nearly nine years fighting the case before prosecutors dropped it in a deal requiring hundreds of thousands of dollars in restitution, as well as community service and legal-ethics courses. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton over separate allegations that he'd abused his office to benefit a wealthy donor—charges he denied and was later acquitted of by the state Senate. In 2025, his wife filed for divorce, accusing him of adultery. Paxton had already admitted to an affair in 2018, after having recommended the woman for a job at one of his top donor's real estate companies.
All that made Wesley Hunt see an opening. The 44-year-old congressman—a West Point graduate, combat veteran, and one of the few Black Republicans in Congress—went to the White House in March 2025 to pitch himself for the job as an alternative who brought MAGA credentials without Paxton’s baggage. Hunt had commissioned polling that showed Cornyn was unpopular with Texas Republicans. He told Trump that the incumbent couldn’t win a GOP primary in Texas but that Paxton would struggle to win a general election. Republicans, Hunt argued, needed a third option—or to find a way to remove one of the two men from the race.
Trump was reluctant. Few voters statewide knew Hunt, and Trump needed Cornyn in the Senate to help enact his domestic agenda and confirm his nominees. While Trump’s advisers saw that Paxton’s political and personal liabilities threatened to make the general election considerably more difficult, the President viewed him as a loyal foot soldier. A source close to Trump encouraged him to offer Cornyn a graceful exit, perhaps a cushy job in the administration or ambassadorship. But Cornyn made clear he intended to seek another term.
With Cornyn in the race, some of Trump’s own political operatives enlisted in the effort to help him stave off Paxton and protect the seat. Chris LaCivita, a senior adviser on Trump’s 2024 campaign and top official at MAGA Inc., signed on with Texans for a Conservative Majority, the super PAC supporting Cornyn. Trump’s longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio joined as well. Their argument was simple: get Cornyn through the primary and avoid Republicans having to spend a fortune defending Texas in November.
It made little impression on Trump. Again Hunt, who launched his campaign in October 2025, pressed his case. A JL Partners poll conducted in January showed Paxton, Cornyn, and Hunt in a statistical tie, with Hunt leading either man in hypothetical head-to-head contests. Another poll from the GOP polling firm Cygnal showed Paxton narrowly ahead of Hunt with Cornyn behind both of them. Hunt’s aides took the numbers to Trump’s and Thune’s teams, arguing that if Cornyn could be persuaded to step aside, Hunt could beat Paxton and spare Republicans the general-election risk they feared. They were dismissed. But Hunt was becoming enough of a threat that Cornyn’s allies began treating him like one, spending nearly $13 million attacking Hunt. A Paxton-aligned PAC spent another $1.4 million.
As the March primary approached, LaCivita pressed Trump to endorse Cornyn. “He was practically begging him,” a senior White House official tells TIME. (LaCivita declined to comment.) Trump still wouldn’t do it. Texas allies warned that rescuing Cornyn could damage his standing with the base.
Cornyn’s allies continued the persuasion campaign after the primary, which advanced the senator and Paxton to a runoff. According to a White House aide, Thune spent hours on the phone with Trump after the primary, trying in vain to persuade him to endorse Cornyn in the runoff. For more than two months, Trump resisted choosing between them. By May, however, Paxton had pulled decisively ahead. Trump’s own pollsters concluded that even his endorsement was unlikely to save Cornyn. Trump finally endorsed Paxton a week before the runoff, and took credit for the victory.
Since then, Paxton has struggled to raise funds necessary for a competitive Senate race in one of the nation’s largest states. Neither the Senate Leadership Fund, aligned with Thune, nor MAGA Inc., run by LaCivita, was eager to fill the gap. Despite its enormous cash reserves, by late August, MAGA Inc. had spent just $800,000 overall; its most conspicuous intervention was to help Darline Graham win the Republican nomination to succeed her late brother, Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina.
That left Paxton’s camp looking to Elon Musk as a possible savior in a race Republican officials believed could cost north of $120 million. Musk had pledged to help Republicans in the midterms, but in Texas his money presented political complications. He is a prominent champion of AI data centers, a political flash point in Texas—the state’s governor, Greg Abbott, recently declared a moratorium on data-center development amid vehement backlash—and of H-1B visas, which are unpopular with parts of the Republican base. “Elon’s money is tainted,” says a Texas Republican operative working on the Paxton campaign. Musk’s super PAC has funneled roughly $1.6 million into the race to help Paxton. A spokesperson for America PAC declined to comment for this story.
It wasn’t until recently that Trump finally opened his wallet with a $10 million Texas ad buy—one of its first general-election expenditures of the cycle. “I’m going to help Ken Paxton,” Trump told reporters, “and I’m going to be spending a lot of time in Texas.”
The Senate Leadership Fund shelled out $54 million to help save Paxton. “The Republican Party is united to elect Ken Paxton and keep Texas red in November,” says the PAC’s executive director Alex Latcham. “Senate Leadership Fund’s investment through Texas PAC affirms our commitment to maintaining the Republican majority.”
When Trump brought his midterm convention to Paxton’s home state, the hope among allies was that it might give one of the party’s most vulnerable candidates the attention and momentum he needed. But the gathering proved less of a windfall than Republicans might have hoped. Some lawmakers balked at the steep price of admission—tickets ran from $5,000 to $250,000. Empty seats were visible inside the arena. When it came time to promote Paxton on stage, Trump urged Texans to elect him—and promised to return to the state “twice or three times” if necessary.
But even his endorsement came packaged as a roast. “He may not dress right. He may not talk perfectly. He may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator.” Trump then looked around for the candidate he had just finished insulting. “I’m sorry, Ken,” he riffed. “Where the hell is he?”

Viru Prison inmates learn to do traditional Estonian handicraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Viru Prison inmates learn to do traditional Estonian handicraft
Inmates at Viru Prison taught themselves to weave traditional Estonian patterned belts. They have become so skilled that their work is now sold at the Estonian National Museum.
Viru Prison was looking for a way for inmates with restricted movement rights to work in their cells. Weaving traditional patterned belts was found to be a suitable option, with the looms also made at the prison. A year ago, one inmate taught himself to weave the belts using a book and a video and now teaches other inmates as well.
"When the first practice belt was finished, I asked him how it was going. His eyes lit up and he said, you know, it's like a jeweler's work: It requires concentration, it requires precision and it requires patience," said Taavi Puusepp, head of Viru Prison's second unit.
The prison asked the Estonian National Museum (ERM) to assess the work and also received valuable advice from the museum's Center for Folk Culture and Information. The patterned belts have now even gone on sale in the ERM store.
"We are very grateful for every contact with someone who makes authentic patterned belts. We don't accept just any patterned belt; we have our own committee that reviews the quality. The belts that were offered to us were of very high quality and we are very happy to have been able to add them to our selection," said Liina Kuzemtšenko, ERM's head of sales and services.
Patterned belts are very popular items at the ERM store. "Especially when a Song or Dance Celebration is approaching, the situation tends to be that we cannot offer as many as there is demand for, so we are always looking for artisans who make authentic patterned belts," Kuzemtšenko said.
Belts made at the prison are not separately labeled at ERM, but Kuzemtšenko said that if a customer specifically wants one made there, staff can find one for them.
Külli Valk, a curator at the Estonian National Museum's Center for Folk Culture and Information, said museum staff were very surprised and excited when the prison contacted them this spring to show them the patterned belts made by inmates and ask them to assess their quality.
"They brought a lot of pieces with them and the quality varied. But the woven belts had complex patterns and were technically of very high quality. We were able to take original items from our collection and compare them with the work made at the prison. We recommended where they could buy yarn in a more authentic warp shade and emphasized that they should pay attention to the colors of the yarn in the original belts," Valk said.
"Looking at the belts now on sale in the store, I can see that they really are top-notch. It's surprising that they've managed to make the belts so authentic. We're very happy about that," Valk added.
In addition to ERM, there are plans to sell patterned belts made by inmates through an online store operated by the prisons' business center, which is due to open soon. The prison sees this as an opportunity to make its own contribution to Estonia's cultural heritage.
"A patterned belt isn't just an object. It carries Estonia's story and at the same time, it represents one person's opportunity to change their own story for the better. You're not only getting a handmade belt; you're also helping someone develop good work habits and return to society, while preserving cultural heritage," Puusepp said.
A total of five inmates at Viru Prison weave patterned belts. According to Puusepp, one inmate makes an average of two belts a month, while the most industrious make four.

Turkish Airlines, Air China expand codeshare partnership to boost connectivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:58:36 UTC
19:58:36 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
- Air China customers can connect to selected destinations in Türkiye, Africa and Latin America through Istanbul
 
Turkish Airlines and Air China have expanded their existing codeshare agreement to offer passengers broader connections through their respective hubs, the Turkish flag carrier announced Thursday.
The agreement was signed during the opening ceremony of the fourth China Air Transport Association Aviation Conference and Exhibition in Beijing, according to a statement from Turkish Airlines.
The two Star Alliance members launched their free-sale codeshare partnership in June 2024, initially covering flights between Istanbul and Beijing.
Under the expanded agreement, the partnership will cover all direct flights between Türkiye and China, as well as selected domestic services beyond Beijing and international connections beyond Istanbul.
Turkish Airlines passengers will be able to travel via Beijing to six additional destinations in mainland China: Shenzhen, Chongqing, Xiamen, Hangzhou, Nanjing and Qingdao.
Air China passengers, meanwhile, will gain access through Istanbul to Ankara, as well as selected destinations across Africa and Latin America.
The African destinations include Accra, Lagos, Marrakech, Dar es Salaam, Algiers and Tunis, while the Latin American connections include Cancun and Mexico City.
The expanded cooperation will allow connecting flights operated by the two airlines to be offered under a single ticket, providing passengers with more travel options between China, Türkiye and onward destinations.
The two carriers said they aim to strengthen connectivity and transfer opportunities between their Beijing and Istanbul hubs.
Turkish Airlines and Air China also plan to add any new direct routes launched between Türkiye and China to the codeshare partnership in the coming period.

Carney seizes Canada-EU associate membership plan despite Trump’s ire
Welcoming the idea that Trump called ‘laughable’, the Canadian PM told the European Parliament, ‘we do not seek power to dominate others’
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed a proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member, but said he did not mean for a closer alliance to create a new bloc that would rival the world’s great powers.
The remarks came after US President Donald Trump suggested the proposed arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly. Trump also called the idea “laughable”.
“We welcome this ambition,” Carney told the European Parliament of European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal, unveiled on Wednesday.
Carney said plainly what he was proposing: deeper Canada-Europe integration across trade, defence, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure.

Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years

Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
- Date:
- September 17, 2026
- Source:
- Johns Hopkins Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.
- Share:
The brain's microscopic wiring may need a different kind of textbook illustration. Instead of the smooth, narrow tubes commonly drawn extending from nerve cells, some axons resemble strings of tiny pearls. These repeating bulges are not simply decorative details. Their shape appears to influence how electrical messages travel.
Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine brought this unexpected architecture into focus in a study published online in Nature Neuroscience on December 2, 2024. Working with mouse neurons, they found evidence that a familiar picture of brain cell anatomy may overlook an important feature of the cells' signal-carrying extensions.
Related research has since documented pearled axons in human brain tissue, extending the observations beyond mice. Together, the findings raise questions about how the physical structure of the brain's wiring helps regulate communication.
"Understanding the structure of axons is important for understanding brain cell signaling," said Shigeki Watanabe, Ph.D., an associate professor of cell biology and neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, in the university's 2024 announcement. "Axons are the cables that connect our brain tissue, enabling learning, memory and other functions."
A Different Picture of Brain Cell Axons
Axons are the long extensions that allow neurons to transmit electrical signals to other cells. The conventional illustration shows a relatively uniform tube interrupted by occasional bulges (synaptic varicosities that hold globs of neurotransmitters, which enable signaling to other brain cells).
Beaded axons themselves are not an unfamiliar sight. Scientists have long observed pronounced swellings in dying neurons and in neurodegenerative conditions, including Parkinson's disease. In those settings, the beading can accompany damage to the cell membrane and the internal framework that helps maintain the axon's structure.
What stood out in the Johns Hopkins study was the presence of much smaller, repeating swellings in axons examined under conditions intended to preserve their normal structure. The researchers called these regions "non-synaptic varicosities." Unlike the familiar bulges associated with communication sites, these swellings were not synapses.
The distinction matters: the study did not suggest that every beaded axon is damaged. Instead, it pointed to a form of nanoscale pearling that may be part of the normal architecture of the axons studied.
A Clue From Worms
Watanabe's interest began with observations of repeating pearls along axons in worms. A conversation with Swiss scientist Graham Knott, Ph.D., prompted him to investigate further. One possible explanation involved the axon's internal skeleton, a supporting network of proteins.
A Harvard University team had reported repeating "skeletal" components within axons in a study published in 2012. Watanabe and Knott wondered whether disrupting that framework would make the pearls disappear. Jacqueline Griswold, a Johns Hopkins graduate student and the study's first author, tested the idea. The pearling remained.
That result redirected their attention toward the axon's physical properties. Watanabe and Griswold joined forces with theoretical biophysicist Padmini Rangamani, Ph.D., a professor of pharmacology at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine, to investigate how the surrounding membrane might shape the axon.
Freezing Brain Cells Reveals Hidden Detail
Studying these extensions of brain cells (neurons) requires imaging structures far narrower than a human hair. Johns Hopkins described them as roughly 100 times smaller than a hair's width. The researchers used high pressure freezing electron microscopy to preserve their delicate shapes before examining them with beams of electrons.
The preparation method was important. Standard electron microscopy commonly involves chemically fixing and dehydrating tissue, steps that can alter the structures scientists are trying to observe. Freezing offers a way to retain a shape closer to the original.
"To see nanoscale structures with standard electron microscopy, we fix and dehydrate the tissues, but freezing them retains their shape -- similar to freezing a grape rather than dehydrating it into a raisin," Watanabe said.
The team examined mouse neurons grown in the laboratory, neurons from adult mice and neurons from mouse embryos. Their axons were nonmyelinated (they were without the myelin insulating cover that surrounds the axon). Across tens of thousands of tissue images, the researchers repeatedly encountered the same pearled appearance.
They also observed pearling with high resolution imaging of living neurons, providing evidence that it was not simply produced by freezing the samples.
"These findings challenge a century of understanding about axon structure," Watanabe said.
How Membrane Physics Shapes Axons
To explain the pattern, the researchers built mathematical models of the membrane surrounding an axon. Relatively simple mechanical models reproduced important features of the pearls, suggesting that physical forces could help determine the shape without requiring a rigid internal mold.
Experiments supported that interpretation. Increasing the sugar concentration in the solution surrounding the axons made the swollen regions smaller. In the model, increasing membrane tension also reduced their size.
Cholesterol provided another way to change the membrane's behavior. Removing it made the membrane less stiff and more fluid. This altered the pearled structure in both the models and mouse neurons and reduced the speed of electrical signaling.
"A wider space in the axons allows ions [chemical particles] to pass through more quickly and avoid traffic jams," Watanabe said.
However, bigger pearls did not invariably mean faster signals. The dimensions of both the swellings and their narrow connecting segments mattered.
Electrical Activity Changes the Pearls
The researchers also tested whether neural activity could reshape the axons. After high frequency electrical stimulation, the pearl-like regions became an average of 8% longer and 17% wider, with enlargement lasting at least 30 minutes.
The published paper reports that electrical signals slowed after this stimulation, with the effect lasting at least an hour. When cholesterol had been removed beforehand, some structural changes still occurred, but the pearls remained smaller than those in untreated cells, and the same significant slowing was not detected.
The findings suggest that axons are not merely fixed cables. Their physical structure can respond to activity and help adjust how messages move through them.
Later Research Finds Pearled Axons in Human Tissue
When the original findings were announced in 2024, the team planned to examine axonal "arms" in human brain tissue obtained with permission from people undergoing brain surgery and from people who had died with neurodegenerative diseases.
A related study subsequently reported pearled axons in human cortical tissue obtained during epilepsy surgery. Led by Chelsy R. Eddings and colleagues, including Watanabe, the work appeared online in Neuron on November 24, 2025, and in its February 4, 2026, issue.
The researchers combined electrical stimulation with rapid freezing to capture tiny membrane changes in mouse and human brain slices. Alongside the pearled axons, they found evidence of ultrafast endocytosis, a process through which nerve endings quickly retrieve membrane after releasing chemical messages.
These observations extend the evidence to human tissue, but they do not establish that every axon has the same shape. Nor do they show that pearling has identical effects on signaling throughout the human brain. The human study primarily investigated membrane recycling at synapses.
The Broader Search for What Controls Axon Shape
The relationship between axon structure and function also became the focus of a National Institute of Mental Health Multiple Principal Investigator grant awarded to Watanabe and Rangamani and highlighted in 2024. The project supports computational models of how a neuron's physical properties and incoming signals affect its axon, followed by tests in mouse tissue and cell cultures.
Separate research is exploring other ways to investigate the dimensions of this microscopic wiring. In a study published in PLOS Biology on July 17, 2026, University of Edinburgh researchers used automated imaging of living zebrafish to screen 880 compounds for effects on axon diameter. They identified 33 initial hits and confirmed that compounds affecting particular chemical signaling pathways could increase axon width. This was not a direct replication of the pearling study, but it provides another tool for investigating how axon size is controlled.
For the Johns Hopkins team, an important question remains how the structure seen in functioning axons relates to the damaging beading associated with neurological disease. Understanding that distinction could help researchers separate normal changes in neural wiring from signs that the system is breaking down.

Two women have filed a federal lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s estate, claiming their photographs were found in his vast collection of child pornography, NBC News reported Thursday.
Identified in court papers only as Jane Doe and Amy, the women allege that “few if any” of the individuals whose photos were in Epstein’s collection had been informed that the photographs are in the hands of federal investigators.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, seeks class-action status and unspecified damages and asks the court to “design and supervise a single, coordinated program for identifying and notifying” other women whose “unlawful sexualized images” were part of Epstein’s collection.
“One of Epstein’s most horrific but often overlooked crimes was his possession, transportation, production, and distribution of child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material (together, ‘CSAM’) of countless children,” the lawsuit says.
“Beginning in the early 1990s until his death in 2019, Epstein, along with his co-conspirators, created and participated in a multi-decade, vast CSAM conspiracy,” it says.
The lawsuit alleges Epstein kept a “modeling book” containing “sexualized images of children” in a locked safe. No CSAM charges were filed against Epstein. According to the lawsuit, Epstein and unnamed co-conspirators said the images “were for the purposes of developing child models for Victoria’s Secret.”
“This lawsuit holds Jeffrey Epstein’s estate accountable for a crime that has never been fully addressed on its own terms,” said Hillary Nappi, a lawyer with AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys.
Named as defendants as co-executors of Epstein’s estate are lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Khan. Their lawyer, Daniel Weiner, declined to comment.
Epstein died by suicide in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Guidance: Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:53:37 BST
19:53:37 KST

Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
The NATO Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement are the international legal agreements that enable UK Defence to operate in Germany.
Documents
Details
The NATO SOFA is a multinational agreement between nations enabling the operation of a nation’s defence task in the territory of another nation.
In Germany, the stationing and operation of UK Defence personnel is governed by the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA. The Supplementary Agreement expands upon the provisions of the NATO SOFA and forms part of German domestic law, providing the detailed legal framework under which UK Defence operates in Germany.
Overview
Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement provides a direct legal entitlement for accompanying spouses or family members to undertake employment in Germany.
The agreements provide a basis for lawful residence and status in Germany for eligible dependants accompanying members of the force or civilian component. Any employment activity undertaken by a dependant must, however, comply with applicable German law.
The UK Ministry of Defence cannot grant authority, permission, or exemptions allowing spouses or dependants to work in Germany. Responsibility for ensuring compliance with host nation legislation rests with the individual and, where applicable, their employer.
There are several routes through which accompanying spouses may lawfully undertake employment within Germany, subject to the relevant legal and regulatory requirements.
Employment within the German Economy
The status of an accompanying spouse is recognised under German immigration arrangements associated with the Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA framework. Consequently, accompanying spouses generally do not require a separate residence permit or work permit to seek employment in the German economy.
Individuals employed by German or other locally established employers will be subject to German legislation and jurisdiction. This may include:
- employment law
- taxation requirements
- social security contributions
- health insurance obligations
- pension arrangements
- other statutory and regulatory requirements
The decision to undertake employment within the German economy is a personal one. Individuals are responsible for ensuring that their employment arrangements comply fully with German law.
Neither the Supplementary Agreement nor the NATO SOFA provides exemptions from German employment, tax, social security, healthcare, or other legal obligations arising from employment.
Operating a Business or Undertaking Self-Employment in Germany
Accompanying spouses may be able to establish and operate a business, trade, profession, or other self-employed activity within the Federal Republic of Germany, subject to the relevant approvals, registrations, and regulatory requirements imposed by the German authorities.
Any business activity undertaken for commercial gain and participating in the German economy will ordinarily be subject to applicable German legislation. This may include taxation, social security obligations, health insurance requirements, licensing provisions, and other regulatory controls.
Individuals considering self-employment or the operation of a business should seek appropriate professional advice from qualified German legal, tax, and financial advisers before commencing any activity.
Care should be taken to maintain a clear distinction between any commercial activity and the rights, privileges, or status derived from dependant status under the NATO SOFA and Supplementary Agreement.
International remote working (IRW)
Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement establishes a legal framework for International Remote Working (IRW).
Remote working arrangements are a matter between the employee and their employer. The UK MOD cannot authorise or validate remote working arrangements undertaken within the territory of another sovereign state. This includes those attracting the term Crown Servant (Civil or Military) not assigned to Germany for the purpose of their employment.
Before commencing any form of remote working from Germany, both the employee and employer should satisfy themselves that the arrangement is lawful and compliant with all relevant German legal requirements.
Consideration should be given to matters including:
- employment legislation
- taxation obligations
- social security requirements
- healthcare obligations
- health and safety legislation
- data protection and privacy regulations
- any other relevant regulatory requirements
Depending on the circumstances, German law may impose obligations on either the employee or employer, even where the employer is established outside Germany and the work is undertaken remotely.
Employees and employers are strongly encouraged to seek independent legal and professional advice from appropriately qualified German advisers before commencing any remote working arrangement.
Where the work involves access to official, government, or sensitive information, additional security considerations may apply. Individuals should ensure compliance with all relevant departmental security policies and seek advice from their employing organisation where necessary.
Key Principles
- The Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA do not provide a right to employment for accompanying spouses.
- Any employment, self-employment, or business activity in Germany must comply with German law.
- The MOD cannot grant permission or exemptions for employment activities in Germany.
- International Remote Working is not covered by the Supplementary Agreement or NATO SOFA.
- Individuals and employers are responsible for ensuring that any employment arrangement is lawful and compliant with applicable host nation requirements.

Credibility concerns: Israeli Film Council demands urgent screening of 'NAZA' after European release
Council members demand a screening of the film, arguing that its absence from Israeli screenings has fueled concerns over its accuracy and political purpose
Israel’s Film Council is pressing for an immediate screening of “NAZA” in Israel as the film prepares to reach a wider European audience.
The council wants the production shown to its members and other Israeli film professionals, saying they should be given an opportunity to evaluate its content and the way it depicts the war.
The demand comes as Dutch cinemas prepare to screen the film beginning October 1. Venues in Rotterdam, Delft and Hilversum have included “NAZA” in their October programs, with advance sales already underway at some theaters.
According to the council, the decision not to make the film available for screening in Israel has created doubts about its reliability.
The council claimed that the lack of access “reinforces the suspicion” that the film was fabricated to advance the interests of Israel’s adversaries, particularly Hamas. It also expressed concern that the film could harm the reputation of IDF soldiers and disrespect Israelis killed in the war.
Filmtheater Hilversum has scheduled screenings for October 1, 3 and 4. KINO Rotterdam has also listed the film from October 1, although tickets were not yet available at the time of publication.
In Delft, Filmhuis Lumen is selling tickets for screenings on October 1, 4, 6 and 7. The final showing is scheduled for 7 p.m. on October 7, marking three years since the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel.
The council is now calling for the film to be screened in Israel as soon as possible, maintaining that independent professional scrutiny is necessary before its European distribution expands.

Such cooperation does not target any third party and shall be free from disruption or coercion from any third party. China opposes long-arm jurisdiction and unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and lack UN Security Council mandate.

Why is inflation rising again around the world?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:50:54 UTC
19:50:54 KST

Counting the Cost
Why is inflation rising again around the world?
Rising energy prices are pushing inflation higher again, forcing major central banks to raise interest rates.
For decades, central banks treated oil shocks as temporary, something to wait out, not hike rates over.
And that’s because raising rates in this case can slow growth without bringing down the price of a single barrel of oil.
But this time might be different.
Oil surged past $100 a barrel last week.
Six months into the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted and Houthi advances threaten Saudi oil supplies, too.
Energy costs are feeding through into household and business bills.
That is forcing policymakers to reconsider the old rulebook even though tighter policy means higher borrowing costs.

from the picturesque to the smartphone: architecture’s obsession with being seen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

before the building, the image
Before the Crystal Palace existed in Hyde Park, it appeared in the newspaper. Joseph Paxton sketched his proposal in June 1850 and sent a view to the Illustrated London News while the scheme was still awaiting approval. It appeared on July 6th. The Royal Commission accepted his design nine days later. Thousands of panes of glass and miles of iron structure still had to follow, but the public had already seen the building in the form of that image.
This sequence still happens now. We regularly meet architecture first as an image, often long before visiting it, and sometimes without ever visiting at all. But this second existence developed over centuries. Buildings occupy sites, and they occupy pictures. Sometimes the picture begins doing so much of the architectural work that it’s hard to separate the two.
Little Island, Heatherwick Studio, New York, 2021 | image by Michael Grimm
before the camera
At Stourhead in Wiltshire, a walk around the English estate frames ever-changing scenes. A Pantheon sits across the water between trees, and an arcaded bridge stretches beyond. Henry Hoare II began to design and build the garden in the 1740s with architect Henry Flitcroft, and drew on classical landscapes and paintings by Baroque-era artists like Claude Lorrain and Nicolas Poussin. Buildings were strategically sited to emerge into view, disappear into nature, and then return beautifully from another angle.
The picturesque had already made the ‘view’ into something that was to be curated by architects and landscape designers. John Macarthur’s writing on the subject follows the way this ‘pictorial’ thinking entered landscape and architectural design, as special importance was given to the viewer in motion. Space could be walked through while certain moments within it behaved almost like finished pictures. Even while the technology of photography would arrive later, architecture already understood the joys of situating someone in exactly the right place to look.
a view of Stour Head in the County of Wiltshire, the Seat of Henry Hoare Esq. (The Temple of Flora) | image courtesy Yale Center for British Art
architecture learns to travel
Of course the picturesque estate was reserved for only a select few. London’s Great Exhibition of 1851, the world’s first international world’s fair, brought this type of experience to mass culture. Millions eventually entered Joseph Paxton’s Crystal Palace, though illustrated newspapers had already given the building another audience.
Paxton understood the usefulness of that audience early. His newspaper image helped build excitement for a proposal still competing for approval. This way, representation became part of the project’s public understanding before it was even built.
World’s fairs were filled with these split existences. Their pavilions were temporary by design, but photographs and printed images gave them an eternal life. The Eiffel Tower remained in Paris, while many structures surrounding it at the 1889 Exposition survive only through their representations. Architecture could vanish from a site and remain alive as a still image.
Crystal Palace, illustration of the transept of the Crystal Palace, designed by Sir Joseph Paxton, at the Great Exhibition of 1851, Hyde Park, London | image courtesy Britannica
modernism finds the page
By the early twentieth century, architecture and mass media were growing together. Le Corbusier selected photographs, edited them and arranged them across books with an understanding that the page could construct its own architectural experience. A house became a sequence in itself as the reader entered through one photograph, turned a page and found another. At this time, experiencing built space in this way was relatively novel.
Historian Beatriz Colomina highlighted this relationship as part of her reading of modernism in Privacy and Publicity. She wrote: ‘modern architecture only becomes modern with its engagement with the media.‘
Her argument places publications and other systems of representation inside architectural production itself. Le Corbusier’s buildings existed on their sites, while another version was being assembled through photographs and printed pages for a much larger public.
‘Le Corbusier: Architect of Books’, Catherine de Smet, archival interior photograph of the L’Esprit Nouveau Pavilion, 1925 | image courtesy Nostos
photography begins changing the building
Claire Zimmerman, Professor of Architecture at the University of Toronto, describes an even more consequential exchange in Photographic Architecture in the Twentieth Century. Architects first turned to photography because it reproduced lines and planes so effectively and helped their work circulate. That relationship soon moved in both directions.
‘Photography altered the material that it represented,‘ Zimmerman writes. Her study follows the overlap between how modern buildings looked and how photographic images made them look.
Once architects spent years seeing architecture flattened onto magazine pages, those pages inevitably entered the visual imagination of architecture itself. Glass became reflection, and white walls became fields of light and shadow. A corner could take up an entire spread. Even though buildings were still rooms and structures, they were being designed inside a culture that was beginning to understand what a camera could extract from them.
Lucia Moholy. Bauhaus Workshop Building from Below. Oblique View. September 1926 | image courtesy MoMA
the pavilion that survived as photographs
Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich’s Barcelona Pavilion makes this exchange especially strange. The original structure stood for only a short time before it was dismantled in 1930. For the decades that followed, architects encountered its marble planes and chrome columns through a limited body of black-and-white photographs. The building became foundational to modern architectural culture while remaining physically absent.
When the pavilion was finally rebuilt in 1986, generations had already spent more than half a century looking at it. Through photography, the project was at once preserved and reinvented. Those images determined the pavilion’s most familiar views, flattened its colors into tones, and established an object that existed outside of built space. The reconstruction eventually gave visitors a building they could walk into, but those photographs had reached them first.
Barcelona Pavilion, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, 1929 | image © Marcin Jezyk
‘a picture of a mood’ becomes the house
Pierre Koenig’s Case Study House #22 offers a more intimate version of the same phenomenon. Julius Shulman arrived to photograph the house in May 1960 while the Stahls were still waiting to move in. Construction dust remained, and was surrounded by incomplete landscaping. During the photoshoot, Shulman noticed two young women sitting in the cantilevered glass corner and rebuilt his composition around them, with Los Angeles glimmering below.
The now-iconic photograph feels effortless because the moment was authentic and temporary. Shulman later described the image as ‘a picture of a mood.’
For millions of people, Shulman’s photograph is their first encounter with Case Study House #22. The image has circulated so widely that Koenig’s architecture and Shulman’s construction of it have become almost inseparable. The house had rooms, changing daylight and years of family life. The photograph compressed all of that into one corner at one hour and somehow gained the greater cultural reach.
Julius Shulman, Case Study House #22, Pierre Koenig, Los Angeles, California | image courtesy Sotheby’s
las vegas reads at highway speed
Denise Scott Brown’s photographs of Las Vegas capture a landscape built to be read in motion. Motel signs hang against huge skies, lettering often larger than the buildings it advertises. In Learning from Las Vegas, Scott Brown, Robert Venturi and Steven Izenour described this as ‘an architecture of communication over space,’ where ‘communication dominates space as an element in the architecture and in the landscape.’ The Strip had to make itself legible before the driver passed it.
Photography was central to how Scott Brown studied that condition. She documented roads, signs and commercial strips. She said: ‘I am not a photographer. I shoot for architecture.‘ The camera became a way to isolate the visual logic of the city. With a vibrant sign floating against the sky, or a parking fronting a low box, architecture is compressed into an image quickly enough to be understood at speed.
Denise Scott Brown, Architettura Minore on The Strip, Las Vegas, 1966 | image courtesy Carriage Trade
from a handful of images to thousands
For much of the twentieth century, a major building entered architectural culture through a small set of photographs. Photographers chose the views, editors repeated them, and certain angles slowly became inseparable from the buildings themselves. Shulman’s Stahl House and the familiar photographs of Mies’s Barcelona Pavilion gained their authority partly through this scarcity.
The smartphone broke open that small circle of image makers. A visitor can photograph a building, edit the image and publish it before leaving. Theorist Lev Manovich calls Instagram ‘the perfect medium of the ‘aesthetic society,’ where image-making has become far more accessible. Architecture now enters a stream of pictures produced almost continuously by the people moving through it.
Corinne Vionnet’s Photo Opportunities combines repeated tourist photographs into a collective image
the visitor enters the frame
MVRDV’s Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen makes this shift especially obvious. Its mirrored facade absorbs Rotterdam and everybody standing around it. Before the building opened, Winy Maas was already watching passersby search for ‘the best place to stand to take a good selfie.’ The visitor becomes part of the architectural image almost automatically.
Case Study House #22 became famous through one highly controlled photograph. A contemporary museum can generate thousands of competing views in its first week. One person photographs the facade while another turns the camera toward themselves. Architecture now often circulates through a constantly feed of images rather than a single iconic frame.
Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen, MVRDV, Rotterdam, The Netherlands, 2020 | image © Ossip van Duivenbode
architecture learns from its own image
This sense of abundance also feeds back into design. Openings frame views, mirrors multiply scenes, and circulation creates new positions between bodies and buildings. Of course these elements physically exist in space, but they also lend themselves to be easily photographed. A building can keep offering images as people move through it.
Claire Zimmerman’s line that ‘Photography altered the material that it represented’ captures the longer exchange. Architects designed buildings, saw them returned as photographs, then designed the next buildings with this image-centric culture in mind. In this way, the camera became part of how architecture understood itself.
Le Corbusier, Beistegui Apartment-external terrace on the 4th and last floor (from Le Corbusier, Oeuvre complète 1929-1934, Paris 1947) | image via Research Gate
the camera moves inside
For most of photography’s history, some distance remained between a building and the production of its public image. Shulman arrived to LA with equipment, Scott Brown photographed Las Vegas as research, publications gradually carried those pictures elsewhere, but the smartphone compresses those stages almost completely.
Buildings now see versions of themselves circulating within hours of their public openings. The smartphone — and social media — accelerated a generations-long exchange between buildings and their representation. Architecture spent the twentieth century learning what it looked like in photographs. Now, the camera walks through the door with everyone else.
Louvre Abu Dhabi, Atelier Jean Nouvel, United Arab Emirates, 2017 | image © Laurian Ghinitoiu
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Sudan gold mine collapse kills 82

Unknown Publisher
