Sudan gold mine collapse kills 82
At least 82 people have been killed after an informal gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, with dozens more still missing, according to several news agencies, citing local officials.
Rescue efforts are continuing at the al-Zara mine near the town of Nuhud, an area controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The collapse began in one shaft on Sunday and spread to interconnected tunnels.
Rescuers recovered 82 bodies by Wednesday afternoon, Suleiman Abu Hmeida, a member of Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, told AP. “But dozens remain unaccounted for,” he said.
The Emergency Response Rooms is a grassroots network that provides assistance to communities and monitors developments during Sudan’s ongoing conflict. A local administration official separately confirmed the same death toll, according to AP.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The Sudan Doctors Network earlier reported 67 recovered bodies and said the death toll could rise as the search continues. The medical group said the informal mine employed unregulated workers and lacked basic safety and protective measures.
“The Network emphasizes that mining activities in areas under RSF control, in the absence of safety standards and adequate protection and rescue equipment, turn mining into a direct threat to the lives of civilians,” they said.
The Kordofan Observatory monitoring group said the mining area extends for more than a kilometer over fragile sandy soil.
Gold is one of Sudan’s most valuable commodities, with official figures showing gold exports generating more than $1.5 billion in the first ten months of 2024, despite the ongoing conflict. The country produced 70 tons of gold in 2025, according to the figures from the state-owned the Sudanese Mineral Resources Company (SMRC).
Deadly mine collapses have occurred elsewhere in Africa. In August, more than 100 people were reported killed when an artisanal gold mine collapsed in Zamboye in the Central African Republic, near the border with Cameroon. Several underground tunnels caved in while miners were working below ground.

Burning tires, empty pumps: $100 oil sparks global unrest as Iran war drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

With no clear end to the war with Iran, most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz still disrupted and escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis placing additional pressure on alternative oil routes, the global energy crisis is increasingly spilling into the streets. Oil has again climbed above $100 a barrel, protesters have burned tires and vehicles, workers have gone on strike and governments from Asia to Europe are scrambling to contain public anger.
The strain is especially acute in developing economies that rely heavily on imported Middle Eastern oil and gas. Many governments already accumulated debt trying to cushion households and businesses from earlier price increases during more than six months of war. They now face the same politically dangerous calculation again: allow higher energy costs to reach consumers and risk accelerating inflation and unrest, or expand subsidies and relief programs at the cost of larger deficits and pressure on local currencies.
“How much fiscal capacity does Asia or the developing world have in general to manage this geopolitical crisis?” Sana Jaffrey, an Asia conflict expert at Australian National University, told The New York Times. She warned that when governments begin exhausting that capacity, the consequences will spread well beyond the countries now struggling with fuel shortages.
Syria erupts after fuel prices jump
Some of the most dramatic protests have unfolded in Syria, where demonstrations broke out across several cities after authorities announced increases of as much as 40% for fuel and gas. The government attributed the move to soaring global prices and work at the country’s largest refinery that has reduced domestic production and increased reliance on imports.
For a country still struggling to recover from more than a decade of devastating civil war, the increase proved explosive. Protesters blocked major roads with burning tires, including routes around Aleppo, and demonstrations continued for several days. In Kurdish-majority Qamishli, protesters carried signs declaring, “No to the policy of starvation.” One demonstrator, 56-year-old Abdel Rahman Khalil, said the public would no longer remain silent and demanded that authorities respond to people’s demands.
Other governments in the region are confronting the same pressure. Lebanon has reported sharp increases in gasoline and diesel prices, while Iraq has seen long lines at filling stations and growing criticism of the government’s ability to secure domestic supplies.
Israel chose another approach. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich temporarily cut the excise tax on gasoline by half a shekel per liter, reducing the regulated price from 8.25 shekels to 7.75. The measure, which runs through Oct. 31, has been criticized by opponents as “election economics” because it comes shortly before Israel’s Oct. 27 election.
Shortages, strikes and blackouts across Asia
The energy shock is particularly severe across Asia, where many economies depend heavily on Middle Eastern supplies.
In Makassar, the capital of Indonesia’s South Sulawesi province, residents have reported shortages of gasoline and cooking gas alongside rolling blackouts. Drivers have been seen pushing motorcycles after running out of fuel or abandoning them in long lines at filling stations. Taxi drivers protested against fuel rationing, while a student demonstration against rising prices in Yogyakarta was broken up.
Line at a gas station in Makassar:
In the Philippines, transport workers launched protests demanding fuel subsidies and lower taxes. Fishermen around Manila Bay, already kept ashore for weeks by monsoon rains, have found that soaring diesel and gasoline costs make returning to sea unaffordable.
“Many were raring to go back to fish, but have no money to buy gas,” fishing association leader Fernando Hicap told The New York Times. Bus drivers have described similarly punishing economics, with some saying shifts of up to 18 hours now barely cover the cost of a meal. The government has offered one-time assistance of about $80 to public transport drivers, but industry representatives say it falls far short of what is needed.
Ride-hailing drivers in Vietnam have also called for protests over fuel costs. Demonstrations have been reported in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, where the energy crunch has compounded an already serious gas shortage. Textile and other industrial plants around Dhaka have been forced to suspend or sharply reduce production, threatening jobs in one of the country’s most important industries.
For Asian governments, the danger is that subsidies meant to prevent immediate unrest may only shift the crisis onto national balance sheets. Public debt in several countries has already risen as governments absorb costs that consumers cannot bear.
French fishermen block fuel depots
Europe is feeling the squeeze as well. In southern France, fishermen have repeatedly blocked oil terminals and fuel depots to protest soaring diesel costs and deteriorating working conditions.
At Fos-sur-Mer, police cleared fishermen from a fuel depot earlier this week. The protests then moved to Frontignan, where around 100 fishermen blocked access Wednesday before police intervened. On Thursday, fishermen returned, burning pallets and tires and preventing fuel trucks from entering or leaving as their representatives prepared to meet the government.
The demonstrations have centered on a simple complaint: at current fuel prices, fishermen say going to sea is becoming economically impossible. The French government has responded by extending targeted fuel assistance through the end of the year and raising aid available to fishermen.
In Portugal, drivers organized through social media have staged slow-moving convoys, deliberately creating traffic jams while sounding their horns. One convoy reportedly blocked access near the major refinery at Sines. The government has announced measures aimed at easing pressure on taxi drivers, transport companies and emergency services as diesel prices reach record levels.
Cars burned in Guatemala
The protests have also reached Latin America.
In Guatemala, truckers, trade groups and other demonstrators have blocked roads over fuel prices, with some protests turning violent. Vehicles and barricades have been set on fire, and two police officers were shot and wounded during clashes on Sept. 11.
President Bernardo Arévalo has accused criminal groups and political rivals of exploiting legitimate public dissatisfaction to provoke violence and destabilize his government. Lawmakers are considering legislation that would cap diesel and gasoline prices and trigger government subsidies once prices cross a specified threshold.
The scenes in Guatemala, Syria and elsewhere illustrate how an oil supply shock that begins thousands of miles away can quickly merge with local grievances over poverty, inequality, taxes and distrust of government.
In the US, no protests but growing political pressure
The United States has so far avoided the street protests seen elsewhere, but fuel prices are becoming an increasingly significant political problem for President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
A New York Times/Siena poll conducted Sept. 8-13 found a sharp deterioration in perceptions of the economy even among Republican voters. In January, 72% of Republicans said the economy was better than it had been a year earlier; by September, that figure had fallen to 29%. The poll also found widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the cost of living and the Iran war.
Fuel prices help explain the anxiety. Diesel has climbed above $6 a gallon and gasoline has hovered above $4 nationally, while economists warn that expensive energy can feed through into transportation, food, electricity and home-heating bills.
Trump has repeatedly insisted that the Iran war will end soon and that fuel prices will fall sharply when it does. At a campaign rally in North Carolina this week, he again sought to reassure voters as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
The president has also argued that temporarily higher energy costs are justified by the objectives of the war, presenting them as a price Americans must bear for the campaign against Iran.
For governments elsewhere, however, there is less room to absorb that price. If disrupted energy supplies persist into winter, when heating demand rises across the Northern Hemisphere, pressure on households, businesses and public finances could intensify further.
The question is increasingly no longer whether the Iran war will raise the cost of energy around the world. It is how much economic and political strain governments can absorb before the anger now visible on streets from Syria to France and Guatemala spreads further.

‘So many loopholes’: Democratic House leader Jeffries flags concerns over Russia sanctions bill – US politics live

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Russia sanctions bill had “so many loopholes” as Congress passed the sweeping bill to give Donald Trump the power to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy.
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.
But Jeffries said the legislation had so many loopholes that sanctions harming Russia might not be applied.
“What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people,” the New York lawmaker said as he announced he would vote no.
He added:
Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?
The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.
It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.
Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.
Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.

Even as the Trump administration seeks to force regime change in Cuba through withering economic isolation, allies of Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, are angling to get rich off the island’s collapse.
Reporting for The Guardian, Lee Schlenker and Ed Augustin found that business interests connected with Trump and Rubio, the architect of current US designs on Cuba, are jostling to fill the void left by companies squeezed out of the island by the latest barrage of US sanctions.
A few key takeaways: A pair of Trump-friendly Texas business magnates are fighting to take over a Canadian company’s stake of Cuba’s mineral wealth. Sources close to the matter say that Trump Organization leaders, operating under a company closely tied to the president’s family, have traveled to Cuba to explore hotel deals after a pair of Spanish hotel chains fled the island. And Franklin Graham, a close ally of Trump on the evangelical right and head of the evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse, recently won a $40m federal contract to oversee the distribution of humanitarian assistance on the island Trump is pushing toward collapse.
One source with decades of background in Cuba policy put it succinctly: “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail.”
The Trump administration has taken an especially severe stance toward Cuba since the start of Trump’s second term. Rubio, the child of Cuban immigrants, has led that campaign, seeking to bring about his long hoped-for goal of collapsing Cuba’s communist leadership and seeing a new US-friendly government in its place.

Carney welcomes proposed special EU-Canada relationship that drew Trump's ire
Speaking to EU officials in Strasbourg on Thursday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seemed open to a proposal to grant his country a new “associate member” status within the bloc – even as details remained thin on what, exactly, that would entail.
“We welcome this ambition,” Carney said of the proposal. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments.”
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, first raised the possibility of making Canada an associate member in an address on Wednesday. Her surprise suggestion to grant Canada – notably not in Europe – a heretofore unheard-of special status within the union appeared to catch member states off-guard.
The same was true for President Trump, who slammed the proposal as “laughable” and as a “hostile act” and went on to threaten sweeping tariffs against Europe if it follows through.
Carney tried to articulate what exactly deepened ties between the EU and Canada might look like, saying he was “not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners.”
“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney continued. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
Ilhan Omar brings bill to make ICE ‘pay the price’ for terrorizing communities
David Smith
The US congresswoman Ilhan Omar is set to introduce a bill that would make federal immigration agencies “pay the price” for terrorising vulnerable communities, blocking nearly $140bn in funding and redirecting it to local recovery efforts, the Guardian has learned.
The Make ICE Pay Act, due to be introduced on Thursday, targets funding previously designated for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) under Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill”.
It would send the money instead to states, local government authorities, nonprofit organisations and small businesses left reeling by Trump’s immigration enforcement crackdowns.
“For over a year, ICE has been tearing through our nation, leading racist terror campaigns that have caused devastating damage to our cities, to our businesses, and to the lives of our constituents,” said Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, covering the city of Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs.
Beginning last December, thousands of federal immigration agents descended on Minneapolis and surrounding areas, resulting in nearly 4,000 total arrests and the fatal shooting of two US citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti. The mood of fear and isolation also had a profound effect on commerce.
Omar added: “In Minneapolis, Operation Metro Surge cost our community nearly $700m. We have a moral responsibility to end this abuse of power. Our bill will force ICE to pay the price for the damage they’ve left in their wake and ensure that these devastating operations can never be repeated.”

A report by Protect Democracy found that 34.8m people - about one in 10 Americans - now live in a different district than they did during the 2024 election cycle.
And about one-fifth of all Americans now live in a district where more than a quarter of voters are new to the district compared with the last election cycle, AP reported.
The findings display the stark overhaul that partisan redistricting fights kicked off by president Donald Trump last year have caused for Americans across the country.
“If this trend continues, it really brings into question whether or not elected officials are really representing their constituents anymore, or if the voters are being randomly picked by mapmakers to squeeze out partisan advantage,” said Ben Raderstorf, a policy advocate at Protect Democracy and one of the paper’s co-authors.

Estonia rejects EU plan for mandatory EV charging stations in parking lots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:48:44 UTC
19:48:44 KST

Estonia will only partially implement the European Union directive requiring that, starting next year, half of the parking spaces at large stores be equipped with electric vehicle charging points, reports ERR News.
The EU updated its Energy Efficiency Directive two and a half years ago, with one of its goals being to promote the widespread use of electric vehicles. For instance, a requirement is set to take effect next year mandating one EV charging station for every ten parking spaces at large non-residential buildings. Additionally, every second parking space must be equipped with the necessary connections to allow for the future installation of a charging station.
Nele Peil, head of the Estonian Traders Association, stated a year and a half ago that the infrastructure investments required to meet the directive’s minimum standards would cost companies between 500 million and 2 billion euros. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also remarked at the time that installing such connections in parking lots was not sensible and that the requirements needed to be discussed with the European Commission.
The Estonian Ministry of Climate has decided not to implement this specific provision of EU legislation; consequently, it was omitted from the draft bill sent to stakeholders for review on Monday. Ivo Jaanisoo, Deputy Secretary General at the Ministry of Climate, stated that Estonia has proposed to the European Commission that requirements regarding charging stations for large parking lots be relaxed. He explained that, following consultations with business associations and an assessment of technological advancements since the directive’s adoption,
it is currently unclear how the new regulation could be implemented in Estonia in its present form.
He emphasized that, for the promotion of sustainable transport, ensuring sufficient grid capacity to support existing practices is far more important.
Jaanisoo noted that all Member States are currently behind schedule in implementing the EU directive, and Estonia hopes that other nations will also reject the implementation of the requirements concerning charging infrastructure. However, these remain mere hopes for now, as the extent to which other countries will implement the directive’s requirements is unknown. Discussions with other nations suggest that the issue is not a priority or a pressing concern elsewhere. Many countries have already made significant strides in developing electric vehicle charging infrastructure and possess large numbers of electric vehicles.
Peil stated that the Estonian Traders Association supports the Ministry of Climate’s plan, noting that some companies have likely already begun actively working to meet the directive’s requirements—for instance, by establishing the necessary connections for charging stations. She pointed out that these companies would benefit even if the requirement were to be scrapped. She argued that, when choosing between making investments for 100% of parking spaces and bearing the full cost, versus addressing 20% now and avoiding additional costs for the remaining 80%, the latter remains the better overall alternative to a 100% investment.
According to data from the Estonian Transport Administration, there are currently nearly 12,300 electric vehicles in Estonia, representing less than 2% of the total vehicle fleet.
The Ministry of Climate will accept feedback from stakeholders regarding the planned changes until the 28th of September.

US Senate blocks bid to expedite AI 'kill switch' bill amid superintelligence risk debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:48:37 UTC
19:48:37 KST

The US Senate on Wednesday blocked an effort by Sen. John Kennedy to fast-track legislation requiring developers of advanced artificial intelligence systems to install an emergency “kill switch,” amid growing debate in Washington over the potential risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI.
Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, sought unanimous consent to advance his AI Emergency Button Act, arguing that humans must retain the ability to shut down an AI system if it becomes uncontrollable, according to The Hill.
“Well, I’ve got a bill, and it basically says that if you’re going to sell an advanced AI model in the United States of America, it has got to have a kill switch,” Kennedy said.
He said the legislation would leave responsibility for activating the switch with the companies developing the systems rather than the federal government.
A “kill switch”
Kennedy warned that advances such as recursive self-improvement could, in a worst-case scenario, allow an AI model to operate beyond effective human control.
“What I would like to see us do is to figure out a way to strike a balance between innovation and public safety,” Kennedy said.
Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, objected to the request, saying Congress should seek a better understanding of the technology before imposing broad requirements.
Paul warned that an open-ended mandate could affect AI systems used throughout the economy, including search engines and medical applications.
“AI is going to be throughout the economy and so many facets. Are doctors going to have to build a kill switch into drug prescription analysis?” Paul said.
Paul proposed establishing a bipartisan committee to study the risks posed by superintelligent AI and possible safeguards. Kennedy rejected the proposal, arguing that another congressional study could further delay action.

‘A really scary place for children’: English hospitals have chronic lack of health play staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:45:29 UTC
19:45:29 KST

Children in English hospitals with serious illnesses are being exposed to avoidable trauma because too few health play professionals are being employed, analysis by a leading charity has found.
These workers help to support children through the trauma and anxiety that can come with receiving medical treatment while in hospital by providing play opportunities through games, toys and activities.
However, the hospitals are facing a shortage of such staff, leaving children without the relief such organised play and games can provide for those having treatment for serious conditions.
Across NHS hospitals, there are only 955 full-time equivalent health play professionals currently supporting 21 million child hospital admissions each year, according to figures obtained by the charity Starlight Children’s Foundation via freedom of information requests. This equates to a ratio of about one professional for every 22,061 admissions, far below the recommended staffing levels of one professional per 2,230 hospital admissions. In England, there are 820 health play professionals supporting almost 17m admissions.
Health play professionals can also help to provide positive healthcare experiences for children, which research has shown can help to reduce distress, improve cooperation and help to prevent lifelong healthcare avoidance and mental health problems associated with traumatic childhood healthcare experiences.
At the age of three, Lyndsey Hookway’s daughter Filly was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She spent 26 months in and out of hospital undergoing treatment including chemotherapy.
Now 13, Filly recalls the positive impact health play had on her when she was younger.
“I definitely did feel less anxious and less nervous, and they definitely did help me overcome stuff like losing my hair, such as playing with a lion teddy called Ollie the Brave who had removable wigs,” Filly said. “I was definitely bored and so having the play specialists really did help with that.
“They really do make a big difference and it really did make a difference on the days that they weren’t there.”
She added: “They should be considered the same priority has other hospital staff because I think especially for children who they’re mostly for, the hospitals can be a really scary place. So it really does help.”
For Hookway, the play professionals also gave parents of seriously ill children relief at a time that was incredibly overwhelming for the whole family.
“Having the health play professionals was a nice break for Filly to have someone who wasn’t me, who was falling apart” Hookway said. “Filly was bored and scared and in pain and unwell, during all of her admissions. But she’s also got a mum who’s probably traumatised and stressed and spinning plates at home as well.”
She added: “We’ve seen the difference between the hospitals that were well-resourced by play specialists and the ones that weren’t.”
Alongside the shortage of specialist staff, Starlight also found that only 23% of NHS trusts and health boards across the UK had dedicated budgets to train health play professionals, resulting in a postcode lottery with inequitable access to therapeutic play support. Furthermore, no integrated care board (ICB) has a dedicated health play budget.
Only 5% of ICBs include health play within their children and young people’s strategies.
Cathy Gilman, the chief executive of Starlight, said: “Every child deserves healthcare that is compassionate as well as clinically excellent. Yet for too many children, hospital is frightening, overwhelming and, ultimately, traumatic. We know those experiences can stay with them for life, affecting their mental health and even whether they seek healthcare as adults.
“Play changes that. It helps children understand what is happening, gives them a sense of control, builds trust with the healthcare team and reduces fear before, during and after treatment. It isn’t entertainment and it certainly isn’t a luxury. It is an essential part of safe, effective children’s healthcare.”
An NHS spokesperson said: “The NHS has worked closely with Starlight to produce the health service’s first guidance aimed at improving health play services across England. This guidance developed with dozens of healthcare professionals is helping local health systems design services which are a welcoming and therapeutic environment for babies and children.”

Canada’s Carney stops short of endorsing von der Leyen’s associate member plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:45:15 UTC
19:45:15 KST

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the members of the Parliament at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, September 17, 2026. | Ronald Wittek/EPA
STRASBOURG — Mark Carney used an address to the European Parliament to sketch out what Ottawa would want from closer ties with the EU but declined to give full-throated approval of Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise “associate member” plan.
Speaking a day after the Commission president floated the unique relationship status, the Canadian prime minister acknowledged the offer and instead of accepting it outright, listed potential individual areas of cooperation, including critical minerals, defense, AI, energy security, and space.
He also called for more seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services, as well as Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU's student exchange program.
Advertisement
"We welcome this ambition," he said, after name-checking the idea of von der Leyen, who was sitting in the audience. "Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties."
Carney's list of potential tie-ups was an early attempt to put substance behind what, for now, remains a largely undefined political proposition.
The “associate member” idea had caused confusion on Wednesday because the Commission hadn't run it past European capitals in advance and no such status currently exists. Later on Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump said he might respond with “serious tariffs” if Canada were to become closer to the EU.
"An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on shared values," Carney said.
In a press conference after the speech, Carney was asked if the Canadian people would have a say on associate membership. He said: “Of course. There will be debates, and there will be a vote in the Canadian parliament, but at this point, this is just the beginning of the process.”
Carney’s admission that there will be eventual votes in parliament on this “Alliance for the Future” with the EU seemed to suggest Canadian lawmakers will get a say in what the prime minister’s team is cooking. The House of Commons returns from summer break on Monday.
Advertisement
Before von der Leyen dropped the “associate member” label, Carney advised Canadian reporters that there would not be a “big reveal” in Strasbourg.
“The real deepening and discussions will be launched with our summit in Montreal … towards the end of October,” he said in Toronto on Tuesday on the sidelines of his global investment summit.“And then go for it from there.”
Europe is a top priority for the Carney government because the EU is viewed as the easiest way for Canada to deepen an existing free-trade relationship, one that was debated in Parliament a decade ago.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly dropped a hint to reporters in Toronto on Wednesday that Ottawa is looking for additional guarantees on trade — which could require new legislation.
When asked about the possibility of “associate” EU membership, Joly observed that countries with free-trade agreements tend to become more insular to protect their own industries when targeted by tariffs.
She singled out the EU specifically.
Advertisement
“We want to make sure that markets are still opened between us and that not only a free trade agreement holds, but that we align our industrial policies, particularly in sectors impacted by the tariffs,” she said. “That’s really important.”
Now there is pressure on officials in Canada and the EU to finish their laundry list of to-dos before they arrive in Montreal to show progress in a range of areas from trade and defense procurement to AI and supercomputing.
Ambassador-designate to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson told POLITICO the goal of the EU-Canada Summit will be to identify “a set of very concrete action items” to achieve during the next year. “The intent is to be very ambitious.”
This article has been updated. Zi-Ann Lum and Sue Allan contributed reporting from Ottawa.

Quadcopters: Israel's weapon for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:44:09 UTC
19:44:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Quadcopters: Israel's weapon of choice for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli military has increased its use of drones known as "quadcopters" in the Gaza Strip, after previously deploying them in eastern and border areas.
This type of drone has been used extensively and on an unprecedented scale, are of multiple types, and their use has are not limited to attacking resistance fighters.
The Israeli military has relied on quadcopters in its field operations. Some emitted disturbing sounds or sent messages to civilians about displacement and movement, while others carried weapons. Particular types were designated for assassinations, either by detonating themselves or dropping explosive munitions.
Quadcopters have played an active and significant role in the context of this war, after previously appearing during the Great March of Return protests along the Gaza Strip border, which Palestinians organised from 2018 to 2023.
60 killed
A report issued by the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor on 12 September this year found that the Israeli army had killed at least 60 civilians with fire from these drones or with munitions they dropped since the ceasefire came into effect on 10 October 2025 until early September 2026.
According to the report, Israel has used small multi-rotor quadcopters and tactical drones in the Gaza Strip, which can be equipped with daylight and thermal cameras and systems for identifying and tracking targets.
It said some models can, depending on the mission, be fitted with 5.56 mm and 7.62 mm weapons or 40 mm explosive munitions.
Palestinians recently documented a video that was widely circulated on social media and described as "terrifying". It showed a quadcopter landing in Gaza City's eastern Tuffah neighbourhood at extremely low altitudes among residents' homes, filming inside homes and taking advantage of the absence of windows.
The footage reflects one of the typical ways this drone operates. The aircraft has become part of Palestinians' daily routine in Gaza, whether through its filming operations, deliberate or random gunfire towards areas where displaced people are staying, or the occasional dropping of inciting leaflets aimed at Palestinian resistance factions.
The Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor said field monitoring had identified three main patterns in the use of these aircraft.
The first involved precise and direct gunfire at individuals whom the operator could see and identify.
The second involved dropping explosive munitions on civilian gatherings and tents housing displaced people.
The third involved imposing fire control over areas adjacent to what is known as the "yellow line" by targeting civilians as they attempted to reach their homes and land or carry out their work there.
Ramy Abdu, head of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said the group had documented a rise in the Israeli army's use of quadcopters as a tool for precise killing in the Gaza Strip.
He stressed that they had not been used only to assassinate activists or people Israel claims are wanted but had also been used to target civilians, including children, directly.
He told The New Arab that the danger of using quadcopters lies in "their technical capabilities, which allow the operator to monitor the targeted person, verify their identity and track their movements before opening fire, greatly narrowing the margin for error in identifying the target and increasing the obligation to refrain from attacking when their civilian status becomes apparent, or there is any doubt about it".
He added that the repeated targeting of children, displaced people, farmers and shepherds with direct fire or munitions dropped from these aircraft, despite the clarity of their civilian status and their lack of any direct participation in hostilities or any imminent threat, collectively provides strong indications that targeting civilians was deliberate and was not the result of an error in identifying the target or an accidental attack.
He noted that these attacks are "prohibited from the outset" and cannot be justified on the grounds of military necessity or subjected to a proportionality assessment.
He further said that direct attacks on civilians are already prohibited and are not permitted by claims of military necessity or the rules of proportionality, and Israel's use of this weapon, according to the group's documentation, violates the principle of distinction under international humanitarian law, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Abdu stressed that the situation differs from weapons that may lack the ability to distinguish, as "the decision to open fire on civilians despite having the full ability to distinguish them is not related to the weapon's inability to distinguish, which means systematic, deliberate and intentional targeting".
On the ground, quadcopters are constantly present in the skies over the Gaza Strip, including areas where displaced people are staying.
Palestinians in displacement areas see these aircraft flying at different hours of the day and descending to extremely low altitudes.
Use of drones
Brigadier General and military affairs expert Naji Melaab said Israel had developed its use of small drones in the Gaza Strip, so they were no longer limited to reconnaissance and intelligence-gathering missions but had become a tool for carrying out precise targeting and killing operations.
Melaab told The New Arab that these drones are distinguished by their small size and ability to move in places that are difficult for soldiers to reach.
He said that they have been used inside tunnels and buildings in Gaza, where they can film the location and transmit information and images directly to the control centre.
He added that the drone can be operated by a single soldier and has advanced capabilities, including capturing sounds and transmitting them to the operator.
It can also create noise or broadcast messages depending on the mission assigned to it.
Melaab also said the most significant development was equipping the drone with a machine gun that allows the operator to control gunfire with precision.
He explained that it can also destroy itself if it crashes or reaches a designated location, and that Israel has used these drones in the Gaza Strip, particularly for reconnaissance operations, as well as for assassinations. The use represents a shift from drones designed for surveillance to systems capable of carrying out direct offensive missions.
This development reflects an advanced use of artificial intelligence and military technology in the war on Gaza, as the drone now combines reconnaissance, target identification and the ability to carry out strikes, thereby allowing killings to be conducted from a distance without soldiers entering the targeted location, according to Melaab.
He warned of the danger of this type of operation, particularly when relying on inaccurate intelligence.
Targeting a building or home with a drone can result in civilian deaths amid the difficulty of verifying information on the ground before carrying out the strike.

PARIS — French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen is open to continue providing defensive military gear to Ukraine but is against sending money to the war-torn country.
“Given the extent of what we've done so far — which is considerable — we're saying we can't do it,” the far-right National Rally leader said on TV channel LCI Wednesday evening.
“This is not an act of hostility toward Ukraine. We can continue to train their soldiers and their armed forces, and we can continue to provide them with equipment so they can defend themselves. But financially, we can’t do it anymore,” she said.
Advertisement
Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of a high-stakes presidential election next spring to replace Emmanuel Macron. One of the campaign's main issues is France's increasingly strained finances, with a public deficit that could exceed 5% this year.
France's direct financial aid to Ukraine is actually quite limited but the National Rally has long been against the EU's €90 billion loan to Kyiv, which is guaranteed by the bloc's budget, fed by national contributions.
National Rally officials privately say that Ukraine will never be able to repay the EU loan and it will ultimately fall on the bloc's capitals to do so.
"You can't say, on the one hand, that there isn't a single euro … to adjust pensions for inflation, but, on the other hand, that there are billions for the net contribution to the European Union," Le Pen said.
While the National Rally is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO, Le Pen's rivals have on multiple occasions accused her party of playing into the Kremlin’s hands in order to undermine the National Rally's credibility. The media has also repeatedly asked top party figures to clarify the party's line on assistance to Kyiv.
In Wednesday evening's interview, Le Pen stressed that France under her presidency would organize a conference for peace that would bring Russia, Ukraine and other European countries such as Germany and Poland to the table. The goal, she said, is to put an end to the war.
She also pushed back against proposals made by her presidential rivals, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, to protect Ukraine's skies with French fighter jets — an option Paris has also so far refused to contemplate. "That would make us co-belligerents," Le Pen told LCI.

Lithuania records EU’s second-highest annual inflation in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

Lithuania recorded the European Union’s second-highest annual inflation rate in August, at 5.6%, according to Eurostat data released Thursday.
Only Romania had a higher rate, at 6.3%.
Annual inflation in neighbouring Latvia was 3%, while Estonia recorded a rate of 1.3%.
Inflation across both the 27-nation EU and the euro area stood at 3.2% in August.
Lithuania recorded monthly deflation of 0.1% in August compared with July. By contrast, prices rose 0.4% on average across both the EU and euro area.
Monthly inflation in Latvia and Estonia was 0.3%.
The figures are based on the harmonised consumer price index, which allows inflation rates to be compared across EU member countries.

The university will connect higher education institutions across eastern Taiwan, Yilan, Keelung, and outlying islands, integrating AI curricula, faculty, teaching materials, and practical training environments.
The initiative aims to break geographical barriers and gradually form a shared national AI education ecosystem. The project runs from July 1 to Dec. 31, 2027.
NTTU said the center is headed by university president Cheng Hsien-tsung (鄭憲宗) and includes nine partner institutions: National Dong Hwa University, Tzu Chi University, National Ilan University, Fo Guang University, National Taiwan Ocean University, National Quemoy University, National Taitung Junior College, and Saint Mary’s Junior College of Medicine, Nursing, and Management.
Cheng said that given the rapid advancement of AI and the transformation of higher education, eastern Taiwan must not be left behind, and NTTU should take proactive responsibility as a regional university. He described the initiative as an “AI garden,” where different disciplines and fields can find their place in the AI era, allowing AI education to “flourish in diversity and coexist in mutual prosperity.”
He added, “We are not just making slogans — we are taking step-by-step action. As long as we accomplish something that benefits the local community, we can truly contribute to society.”

Yemen escalation displaces more than 57,000 children: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:38:41 UTC
19:38:41 KST

Yemen escalation displaces more than 57,000 children: UNICEF
Renewed fighting in Yemen is deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis in a country where more than 12 million children depend on aid, after more than a decade of conflict.
The warning comes from the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) which said that more than 57,000 children have been displaced in just the past two weeks while others have been killed, injured or reported missing.
“Children in Yemen were already living through one of the world’s most grave humanitarian crises, and many have known little but conflict and displacement,” said Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa.
“For children who have already endured years of hunger, displacement and disrupted schooling, this latest violence is eroding what little stability they had left.”
Children killed and injured
Yemeni Government forces, supported by a Saudi-led coalition, and Iran-backed Houthi militia have been at war since 2014, but the country had experienced relative calm following a UN-backed truce in 2022.
The new escalation has forced tens of thousands of families to flee their homes, triggering widespread displacement across several governorates, including Taiz, Hudaydah and Marib.
Since 3 September, at least nine children have been reported killed and 12 injured while three others are missing following an attack on the road from Yemen’s western coast to Aden.
Healthcare and education disrupted
The fighting has also cut children’s access to healthcare and education. UNICEF said services at 26 health facilities that it supports have been disrupted, while 243 schools have closed or suspended classes, affecting more than 137,000 students.
The agency is expanding its emergency response to reach up to 231,000 people. Teams have supported health facilities and distributed hygiene kits and water tanks in Taiz, while providing additional water and hygiene supplies in Marib.
Nine health and nutrition mobile teams have been redeployed to displacement sites and affected communities in Aden, Marib and Taiz. Emergency water and sanitation teams also aim to reach more than 200,000 people with safe water and hygiene supplies and carry out urgent repairs to damaged systems.
Meanwhile, child protection teams are providing psychosocial care and case management, including for unaccompanied and separated children. They are also helping make communities aware of the dangers posed by unexploded ordnance.
Supporting arrivals in Djibouti
UNICEF is also working with authorities in Djibouti to support Yemeni families who have fled there after making the dangerous journey across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. More than 2,000 people, including many children, have now arrived in the country.
The UN agency recalled that even before this latest escalation, roughly 12.2 million children in Yemen needed humanitarian assistance. More than 2.2 million under-fives are acutely malnourished, including over 515,000 suffering severe acute malnutrition.
Across Yemen, around 17.8 million people lack adequate access to healthcare, water and sanitation services, and only 60 per cent of health facilities are fully functional. Some 3.2 million school-age children are out of school.
UNICEF echoed the UN Secretary-General’s call for all parties to protect civilians, including children, respect international humanitarian law, and facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian access to communities in need.

As freshwater reserves shrink, countries must prepare for a new water reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:38:16 UTC
19:38:16 KST

As freshwater reserves shrink, countries must prepare for a new water reality
The world is entering a period in which abnormal water supplies are becoming the norm, with river flows, groundwater and glaciers all showing signs of sustained disruption, the UN weather agency warned on Thursday.
“This is not a single bad year, but a persistent decade-long signal,” said Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), presenting the agency’s latest State of Global Water Resources report.
The assessment shows that 2025 was one of the driest years for river flows worldwide in 35 years, with below-normal discharge across 36 per cent of the world’s river basin area.
It was also the seventh consecutive year in which rivers with historically “normal” flows were in a clear minority, underscoring what WMO describes as an increasingly erratic and unpredictable water cycle.
“Water-related extreme events continue to devastate communities and economies,” Ms. Saulo underscored.
Water ‘savings account’
Groundwater, glaciers, snow, soil moisture, lakes and other freshwater stored on land, act as a buffer during droughts and dry seasons. Ms. Saulo described these slower reserves as the planet’s “savings account”.
Traditionally, she explained, they have absorbed bad years so that a single dry season does not immediately become a water crisis.
“We are depleting that savings account,” she said, noting that terrestrial water storage has been declining since around 2014–2016, while groundwater levels in many regions have fallen over several years.
Nearly two-thirds of monitored groundwater wells were outside their normal range in 2025, with conditions shifting further towards deficit, than recovery.
There were, however, some positive signs. Parts of South America saw a partial recovery in water storage after a severe multi-year deficit, while central and southern Africa maintained much above-normal water levels across several major lakes.
Glacial melt
Every major glacier region on Earth lost ice for the fourth consecutive year.
“All 19 glacier regions around the globe lost ice; in Central Asia, Iceland, the Russian Arctic and western Canada and the United States, it was among the three worst years on record,” said Wayne Jenkinson, WMO’s Director of Hydrology and Cryosphere.
In 2025 alone, glaciers lost around 408 gigatonnes of ice, while cumulative losses between 2023 and 2025 reached roughly 1,400 gigatonnes – equivalent to around one third of the freshwater the world withdraws in a year.
Some regions with smaller glaciers such as Central Europe, the Caucasus, the western Canada and the United States may already have reached “peak water”, Jenkinson warned.
“After this point, the glacier gives less meltwater each year simply because there is less ice left to melt. That matters for every community downstream that relies on water during hot, dry summers,” he said.
Narelle van der Wel, WMO’s Head of Cryosphere Monitoring, Predictions and Services, stressed that while some further glacier loss is unavoidable, the eventual scale of the decline is not predetermined.
“Some glacier loss is inevitable, but total loss of glaciers is not yet inevitable,” she said, pointing to emissions reductions as central to limiting future losses.
Moving the baseline
The report does not attribute every observed change to climate change alone. WMO says pressure on water resources and natural variability also contribute.
Mr. Jenkinson said governments need to prepare for “moving baselines” as historical patterns become less reliable.
“The situation 30 years ago is not where we are today,” he said. Countries, he added, need to prepare “for those changes that have really already arrived”.
Over the past five years, Asia and Africa accounted for at least half of reported water-related extreme events and more than 80 per cent of associated deaths, yet both remain among the regions with the largest gaps in water observations.
Water monitoring has improved significantly since WMO began publishing the report five years ago, with 52 countries now providing data from more than 3,100 river-flow stations, compared with just seven countries and 14 stations in the first edition.
However, WMO says better monitoring, data-sharing and early warnings will be increasingly important as countries adapt to water conditions that are already radically changing.
The recent China-Nepal disaster, which WMO described as a “catastrophic compound crisis” involving a rock and glacier failure, showed how difficult such hazards can be to anticipate.
“Water respects no borders,” Ms. Saulo said. “This is why we need shared data, shared standards and shared early warnings.”

Across China: From village ponds, a Chinese delicacy seeks global markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:37:30 CST
19:37:30 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Across a patchwork of village ponds in central China, rows of floating cages ripple on the water. Beneath the surface, slender, snake-like rice eels twist through the nets -- the fish are a common dish at Chinese meals and a big part of how local farmers make a living.
Also known as the Asian swamp eel, the slippery freshwater fish is still somewhat of a niche delicacy outside of Asia. In China, however, it is widely consumed and has long been prized for its distinctive flavor and nutritional value.
The ponds are in Xiantao, a major hub for rice eel breeding and farming in Hubei Province. The city now accounts for roughly one-quarter of China's rice eel output, according to local industry figures.
The industry began to take shape more than three decades ago, when local farmers started experimenting with raising rice eels in cages.
Getting rice eel farming off the ground wasn't always easy. When people saw how profitable it could be, producers all over China jumped in, creating an oversupply and sending prices tumbling. A lot of farming communities gave up, but Xiantao stuck with it.
"With much of our farmland converted into ponds, rice eel farming had become the only viable way forward," said Zhu Chuanbao, Party secretary of Xianfeng Village in Zhanggou Town and president of the Xiantao rice eel industry association.
The village alone produces about one billion rice eels a year. "That is enough to put Xianfeng's rice eels on the table of nearly every household in China on average," Zhu said. The industry has helped lift villagers out of poverty and onto a path toward prosperity.
Xiantao is now home to China's biggest rice eel processing enterprise and the largest rice eel trading market at the production site. The city's rice eel industry generates an annual output value of over 12 billion yuan (1.77 billion U.S. dollars).
The growth of this industry has been supported by the central government's policies to advance rural revitalization. China aims to basically achieve modernization by 2035, and that cannot happen without the modernization of agriculture and rural areas.
"We are entering a new era of rice eel farming," said Zhu.
Researchers at Huazhong Agricultural University in Wuhan, the provincial capital, and the Institute of Hydrobiology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences have worked with local producers to develop large-scale artificial breeding techniques and controlled-environment aquaculture systems.
These advances have reduced the industry's dependence on seasonal cycles, making year-round production possible.
By allowing precise control of water quality and temperature, the systems help farmers cope with increasingly frequent extreme weather. They also protect rice eels from predators, raising juvenile survival rates in the lab from 50 percent to 90 percent.
The real challenge isn't just raising more rice eels. It's about getting more people to try them, especially outside Asia where many folks are not as familiar with the fish.
That means tapping overseas markets. In the first half of this year, Xiantao exported more than 125 tonnes of frozen rice eels and processed rice eel products to more than 10 countries and regions, including North America, Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea and Southeast Asia.
"There are more than 60 million overseas Chinese, and rice eels are already widely accepted in East Asia and Southeast Asia. We are now seeking to reach more consumers in Europe and North America by developing products suited to their tastes, including grilled rice eel and rice eel steaks," Zhu said.
Rice eel farmers in Xiantao have built a digital platform covering the entire supply chain, from breeding and farming to feeding and processing. Consumers can use it to trace products through every stage of production.
"Traceability gives Xiantao rice eels the confidence to reach consumers across China and around the world," said Lu Huawei, a local government official.
Some farmers are already looking ahead to the next technological upgrade.
Xiao Tiebing is closely following the development of an unmanned boat by a local company in collaboration with leading Chinese universities. Designed to automate repetitive tasks, the vessel can feed the fish and remove uneaten feed.
"I hope new technologies can further improve farming efficiency, just as earlier innovations have done, and help us earn more," Xiao said. ■

Feature: Activists, scholars push to uncover Japan's chemical warfare past
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
18:37:03 CST
19:37:03 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- "Many young people in Japan do not know about the history of the Japanese military's use of chemical weapons. But I think it's something we should learn about." Migita, a 30-year-old visitor, told Xinhua recently at an exhibition on the Japanese military's production and use of poison gas during World War II.
The six-day exhibition, held in Yokohama City, near Tokyo, by a Japanese civic group, invited experts in the field to give lectures almost every day.
At the venue, display panels laid bare a complete and disturbing chain of evidence documenting the Japanese military's poison gas warfare crimes: from producing toxic chemical agents and filling them into shells, to deploying them on the battlefield, and ultimately abandoning large quantities of chemical weapons in China after Japan's defeat, leaving a legacy of harm that continues to this day.
Nobuharu Goi, a member of the exhibition's organizing committee, said that, in addition to the exhibition on poison gas warfare, he had helped organize numerous exhibitions on Japan's wartime aggression, taking part in around 15 such exhibitions in total.
Despite its modest scale, the exhibition still drew a fair number of visitors. Goi said he hopes more people will learn about this history.
Seiya Matsuno, a historian and researcher at the International Peace Research Institute of Meiji Gakuin University in Japan, recently uncovered new evidence about Japan's wartime production of poison gas bombs.
The findings were based on his study of the "Compilation of Reports on the Implementation of Military Mobilization," a production report covering fiscal 1941 operations at the Sone Manufacturing Plant of the Tokyo Second Army Arsenal.
According to Matsuno's research, the Sone plant was responsible for a key link in the Japanese military's poison gas warfare operations: filling artillery shells with toxic chemical agents and assembling poison gas bombs ready for battlefield use.
To meet the Japanese military's needs for overseas aggression and expansion, the facility enlarged its workforce and increased the output of poison gas bombs during fiscal 1941.
"You could say this was one of the origins of Japan's chemical warfare," Matsuno said.
The historian also noted that Japan burned, destroyed, and concealed large quantities of relevant documents at the time of its defeat, leading scholars to believe that no evidence had survived.
Matsuno's research findings have filled in a long-missing link in the chain of evidence documenting Japan's chemical warfare crimes.
However, after Japan's surrender in 1945, this culpability, which should have been fully reckoned with, was not pursued at the Tokyo Trials, and vast stockpiles of chemical weapons abandoned by the Japanese military in China have continued to pose a threat to local residents.
Statistics show that the Japanese military used chemical weapons more than 2,000 times in China during its invasion, causing more than 200,000 casualties among Chinese military personnel and civilians. The chemical weapons left behind in China after Japan's defeat have resulted in more than 2,000 casualties to date.
Under the Chemical Weapons Convention, Japan should have completed the destruction of the abandoned chemical weapons in China by 2007, but due to insufficient attention and inadequate funding, the deadline has been postponed repeatedly, leaving the disposal process seriously behind schedule.
Maiko Sugamoto, a member of a joint Japan-China fund to support the sufferers of chemical weapons, told Xinhua that although some Japanese civic groups have for years called on the Japanese government to help Chinese victims of Japan's abandoned chemical weapons access medical assistance, their efforts have yet to yield meaningful results.
As the war fades further into history, "ordinary Japanese people today have little awareness of the harm caused by Japan's abandoned chemical weapons," Sugamoto said.
She also noted that, precisely for this reason, more than 80 years after the end of the war, it is especially important for more Japanese people to once again learn about the history of aggression and the harm inflicted by the Japanese military through chemical weapons and other means.
Kazuyuki Kawamura, representative of the Association Demanding Investigation on Human Bones Discovered from the Site of the Army Medical College, gave a lecture during the exhibition.
"What we're doing now may seem insignificant, but it's very important to carefully and thoroughly examine how the war happened and bring facts to light," he said.
Kawamura told reporters that, as his father's generation had taken part in the war, he felt obliged to seriously confront that history, take responsibility, and accurately convey to the younger generations what war truly is. ■

Trump threatens EU tariffs over Canada membership plan
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
13:36:34 EEST
19:36:34 KST

US President Donald Trump has threatened new tariffs on the European Union after Canada welcomed a proposal for closer ties with the bloc, including a new form of associate membership.
The dispute emerged as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the European Parliament that Ottawa wanted deeper cooperation with Europe on trade, defence, energy, technology and critical minerals.
Trump described the European Commission proposal as “laughable” and said Washington would respond if he regarded the plan as hostile.
“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” Trump told reporters while travelling to North Carolina. He said the US response would depend on what he regarded as Europe’s intention.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
No such membership category exists under current EU treaties. Any new arrangement would require agreement among EU governments, while its legal structure, rights and obligations have yet to be defined. The EU has previously resisted informal membership structures outside its established accession system.
The Commission rejected the suggestion that the initiative targeted Washington. Its spokesman Olof Gill said von der Leyen had presented the partnership as a measure designed to strengthen Canada and Europe rather than act against another country.
France also rejected any US role in determining European foreign policy.
“It is not up to the United States — or anyone else — to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans,” French Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad told Public Sénat.
Carney used his address to the European Parliament on Thursday to welcome the Commission’s proposal.
“Canada welcomes this ambition,” he said, describing the prospective relationship as “an alliance for the future” that Ottawa and Brussels would define together.
He called for cooperation covering critical minerals, defence production, artificial intelligence, computing capacity, energy, space, payment systems and industrial policy. He also proposed closer digital trade and easier movement for students and young workers, including Canadian participation in the Erasmus+ exchange programme and the EU’s Horizon research programme.
Carney said closer links would reduce strategic dependence at a time when governments face pressure through tariffs, supply chains and financial systems.
“Europe and Canada are stronger together,” he told lawmakers.
His comments came after Canada-US trade negotiations broke down and both governments imposed tariffs on billions of dollars of goods. Ottawa has sought to reduce its economic reliance on the United States while expanding trade and security relations with Europe.
Canada and the EU already operate under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA. Ten EU member states have yet to complete ratification of the agreement, underlining the political hurdles facing any broader institutional arrangement.
Carney said the proposed alliance was not intended to create a new power bloc to compete with the United States, China or other major economies. He said the objective was to give participating countries greater control over their economic and security choices.
Questions also remain inside the EU
Reuters reported that one EU diplomat said “nobody really knows what it means”, while another diplomat described von der Leyen’s announcement as an “unfortunate proposal” that had not been discussed with member states. The comments point to disagreement over both the terminology and the process behind the plan.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the concept could eventually provide a framework for closer relations with other countries, including Australia and New Zealand. She said stronger links with Canada should not be treated as a measure directed against another state.
The next stage will depend on negotiations between Ottawa, the Commission and the EU’s 27 governments over what an associate relationship would contain and whether governments are prepared to create a status that does not exist under the bloc’s present membership system.

President Donald Trump says the United States is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran, claiming that he has directly spoken to officials in Tehran, raising the prospect of renewed diplomacy even as fighting has erupted in Yemen.
However, there is still no confirmation from Tehran that direct negotiations with Washington have resumed. Just a day earlier, a senior Iranian official publicly rejected talks unless Iran’s conditions were met. Tehran, which has, in effect, closed the Strait of Hormuz, has been demanding that the US honour the terms of the deal signed in June.

Trump’s comments come as the conflict has expanded into Yemen, putting increasing pressure on global energy supplies amid an Iran-imposed blockade of the strait through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes. Oil prices crossed $100 per barrel last week and continue to rise as Iran-linked Houthis have damaged Saudi oil installations amid renewed fighting.
So, what is the latest on the diplomatic front, and will the war end soon?
What is Trump saying?
“Well, hopefully we are toward the end of the war,” he told reporters on Wednesday. “They want to make a deal. We’ll see how that works out.”
When asked by a reporter whether he had recently heard from the Iranian side, Trump said he had spoken with them “directly”.
The comments come after Trump on Monday said he was open to talks, and added that Iran “wants to make a deal, quickly and badly” and that he would decide whether Washington would engage with Tehran.
However, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, accused Trump of sending “mixed signals” and said “no talks until Iran’s conditions are met”.
Trump’s claim that he has heard from Iran “directly” is significant because negotiations between Washington and Tehran have repeatedly depended on intermediaries, including Qatar, Pakistan and Oman. This is not the first time that Trump has claimed direct communication with Iran.
Former Iranian diplomat Abbas Khameyar dismissed Trump’s claims. “I don’t think there has been any additional effort beyond what was already under way in recent weeks,” he told Al Jazeera.
There is a US narrative, he stated, “with tweets and statements by President Trump claiming that the Iranians are calling, pleading and asking for a meeting. But nobody believes this, and matters have not unfolded in that way.”
He added that Iran’s diplomatic activity has not moved beyond the framework already in place in recent weeks, centred on securing enforcement of the existing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) rather than opening new negotiations.
What is the latest on the US-Iran diplomacy front?
On Thursday, Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a telephone call with Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who has been leading the high-stakes diplomatic and mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.
Araghchi held the phone call while still in Beijing, during which they discussed and consulted on the latest regional developments and issues of mutual interest, according to Tasnim.
A day earlier, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called on the US and Iran to exercise restraint and “reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date”, following his meeting with Araghchi in Beijing.
Araghchi, in a statement after the meeting, said that Tehran seeks “the restoration of calm to the region and friendly and peaceful relations with our neighbours”.
“In this regard we have begun dialogue with the countries of the region,” he added.
In a post on X, Araghchi described consultations with Chinese officials as “successful”, saying Tehran values the strategic partnership it has built with Beijing.
“Today’s decisions will decide the future strategic balance in the region, with immeasurable knock-on effects,” Araghchi said on Thursday.
China has avoided direct involvement in the war, but President Xi Jinping, at the BRICS summit in New Delhi over the weekend, offered Beijing’s willingness to play a role in peace efforts. He called on BRICS nations to advance peace in the Middle East.
Huiyao Wang, president of the Center For China and Globalization think tank in Beijing, says China’s role in international affairs is increasing in importance during the current geopolitical turmoil.
“China has an enormous role to exercise if needed. So the mere fact that the two fighting parties have no end in sight shows the need for a big guarantor to come in … I think the US wants to end this war and they also need China’s help,” Wang told Al Jazeera.
Meanwhile, US media outlet Axios is reporting that Trump is expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly next week to discuss the conflict, which has hugely affected oil exports from the Middle Eastern countries.
Diplomatic efforts have repeatedly stalled since a Pakistan-brokered MoU signed by Washington and Tehran collapsed last month, as the two sides accused each other of violating their commitments.
The MoU was supposed to kick-start a 60-day period for peace talks between the warring sides and included provisions for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a major flashpoint in the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier this month that Tehran would return to the agreement if Washington did the same.
What do we know about the Houthi meeting with US officials?
US officials met representatives of Yemen’s Houthi movement at the US embassy in Muscat over the weekend, five sources told Reuters news agency. Oman helped organise the meeting.
The Houthis told US officials they did not intend to attack American vessels and remained committed to their 2025 ceasefire with Washington, according to two sources.
One source said they also pledged not to target Israeli or other commercial vessels, with the exception of Saudi ships.
The conflict had largely subsided in recent years after a 2022 ceasefire between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, but reignited in July.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline to cement their grip on the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – a vital maritime route connecting Asia with Europe – while declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping.
The strategic waterway is a critical maritime corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has become an alternative shipping route as the US war against Iran choked the Strait of Hormuz.
