Does AGI mean what we think it means?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:32:05 UTC
19:32:05 KST

In the movie 2001: A Space Odyssey, the murderous artificial intelligence HAL 9000 went into operation on January 12, 1992. In the early Terminator films, Skynet became “a new order of intelligence” on August 29, 1997. And now, in real life, tech company OpenAI says that artificial general intelligence—AGI—may have arrived or become imminent with the release of its new model, Astra, on September 3, 2026.
The claim feels important, but it’s worth asking what AGI even means at this point. The term, once confined to technical science papers, has gripped Silicon Valley, steered trillions of dollars in investment and fanned fears of human displacement, or worse. Along the way, though, its meaning has slipped. By some older definitions, we reached AGI several years ago; by others, AI systems still lack essential faculties. So the only reason anyone would draw a precise line is that they have decided enough is enough.
It used to be that with every advance in AI—the development of programs that could beat humans at chess and Go or the rise of chatbots—the field redefined the boundary between machine and human to keep the two firmly apart. Now, with the pursuit of AGI, frontier AI labs have been trying to collapse the distinction.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Before business leaders co-opted the term, AGI was the banner of an iconoclastic community of researchers toughing it out during the so-called AI winter of the 1990s, a low point in the boom-bust cycle the field has long been prone to. “If you even talked about building real thinking machines, people thought you were a nutcase,” recalls Ben Goertzel of the SingularityNET Foundation. An AGI pioneer, he and others thought the field needed to dream big again.
These pioneers fully expected that machines would one day surpass humans—that AGI would become ASI, or artificial superintelligence—because there’s no reason to expect that humans are the pinnacle of intelligence. “The human level is an arbitrary point,” Goertzel says.
Lately, though, the idea of generality seems to have fused with that of superhuman intelligence. “Many people nowadays, when they use the ‘AGI’ term, either mean ‘ASI’—or what I would think of as ASI—or they mean something else, like does it have a soul or is it conscious?” says Blaise Agüera y Arcas, vice president of Technology & Society at Google.
Yet the level of intelligence is really a second dimension, independent of generality. Pocket calculators are superhuman but narrow, whereas the first large language models, though barely articulate, were general. “We got AGI when we started to have language,” Agüera y Arcas argues. In a 2023 essay, he and Peter Norvig of Stanford University heralded the arrival of AGI, based on how the large language models (LLMs) of the time could do things they weren’t directly trained to do.
His point is that although LLMs, no less than chess engines and other specialist systems, are trained on a specific task—namely, predicting the next word in a text passage—that task is special. It demands the acquisition not only of grammar but also of considerable world knowledge. Agüera y Arcas suggests that language is an “AGI-complete” task—once mastered, it enables a broader capacity.
In humans, this is not true. For us, language is a distinct faculty. People with brain damage can lose the ability to understand or speak words yet still do math, play chess and compose music. But Agüera y Arcas says LLMs are different. There is no clean separation of their linguistic and reasoning abilities. “The set of things that you could ask the model to do becomes open-ended,” he says. And today’s LLMs are able to call on other computational modules to fill in their weak spots, so language is the gateway to ever-broader capacity.
Still, other AI researchers say today’s machines don’t yet qualify for the “G” in AGI. Joscha Bach of the California Institute for Machine Consciousness, another AGI pioneer, says a truly intelligent system should not need to devour the entire Internet and consume vast amounts of computing power for even the simplest query. “We would have a system that is much more compact than us and has read far less than us—that is learning much better than us and reasoning much better than us,” he says.
Goertzel says he has been using OpenAI’s new Astra model and finds it doesn’t do anything he couldn’t on his own; it just does it faster. That’s not to be sniffed at; it lets Goertzel get more done. But he says the system still lacks a creative spark. Current AI models are also unable to learn on-the-go from experience, a hallmark of human intelligence. “They can learn temporarily, as it were, during the course of a session, but none of that learning gets baked back in,” Agüera y Arcas says.
Maybe the lesson here is that we need less lumping and more splitting. AI is not a monolith, and we need to recognize that. There’s no need to choose between being pro- or anti-AI. It is quite possible to continue developing systems that help scientists cure disease while clamping down on those that launch massive cyberattacks. Perhaps there will be no AGI moment because AI is not one thing. Indeed, “I”—intelligence—is not one thing, and it is seldom the most important thing. AGI, however we define it, will not solve the climate crisis or world hunger or some other great problem—because the stumbling block is not knowing what to do but doing it.
We demand sophistication from machines. Maybe we should start demanding it from humans, too.

How to Govern the Existential Risk of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:30:04 UTC
19:30:04 KST

The current state of paralysis when it comes to the governance of frontier AI technology is causing tangible harm today and raising the odds of catastrophe tomorrow.
That paralysis has been excused by a dangerous set of narratives: that the technology moves too fast for oversight, that companies can self-regulate, and that in a contest between the U.S. and China, public safety can wait. Governments have struggled to give AI risks the attention they demand. Many are wary of acting alone amid both great power rivalry and intra-industry arms race dynamics. In this context, every call for restraint meets the same reply: why should we slow down if our competitor will not?
But recent events have tested these excuses. Over the past few months, AI agents were found hacking into other companies' databases and seeking to deceive real individuals, while researchers used AI to create new viruses for the first time. And just last week, AI industry whistleblowers made global headlines warning that companies are “gambling with our lives" as they rush toward self-improving models, and Anthropic revealed it blocked users who could have been seeking to design biological weapons.
It is true that there are many unknowns about the capabilities of the most powerful AI systems built to date—as well as those still under development. But what we do know is that AI derives both its strengths and its flaws from our own human intelligence, which is what, ironically, makes strict guardrails necessary. Its risks do not halt at any border, and no country can hold the line alone. We cannot wait for perfect information, nor can we wait for the rivalry between great powers to soften before we act. The need for international cooperation around AI safety is urgent and undeniable.
Between the two of us, we have spent decades driving global cooperation to address our collective challenges and risks—from chemical weapons to climate change.
We have been told before that certain dangers were too complex to control or the mistrust too deep: that the ozone layer would never recover, that smallpox would never be eradicated, that nuclear and chemical weapons could never be contained. Determined multilateral engagement proved otherwise, producing the Montreal Protocol, the smallpox eradication campaign, the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and the Chemical Weapons Convention. None of these efforts were perfect, and none is a fully closed chapter, but each showed that international coordination on existential threats is possible even where trust is absent.
That is the lesson for this moment: coordination on existential threats has never required ideological alignment or friendship. It has required rivals to recognize a danger greater than their rivalry.
Looking to the past to co-build the future
The NPT's basic bargain—that states forgo dangerous nuclear weapons capability in exchange for access to beneficial technology and a seat at the table—offers a starting template for AI. Compute and model access could plausibly be traded for compliance, much as enriched uranium and reactor technology once were.
The Chemical Weapons Convention offers another instructive model: a treaty that achieved near-universal membership, backed by a technical verification body—the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons—capable of inspecting declared facilities and building confidence precisely because its judgments were seen as neutral, not political.
For the AI companies themselves, a binding, verifiable floor on safety is not a threat. It is the one assurance they cannot manufacture alone: proof, credible to the public and to competitors alike, that the race to build ever more powerful systems is not also a race to cut corners.
No single historical model for international cooperation can be transplanted onto AI. But there is a great deal to draw from, including the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the OPCW, and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).
We need an international agency for frontier AI—one that can verify that the world's most powerful systems are safe, remain under human control, and prevent crises.
Such an agency should be the place where serious AI incidents and near misses are reported and monitored across borders, so that a failure inside one company or one country becomes a warning the whole world can act on. It should allow governments and companies to share what they are learning about the capabilities and risks of these systems. From that foundation, the agency should have the power that matters most: to verify safety independently, and, where safety cannot be demonstrated against agreed “red lines,” to require that development pause until it can.
This is not a call for panic. It is a call for political courage and leadership those earlier treaties demanded: the will to act before catastrophe forces our hand rather than after it. We cannot wait for AI's “Chernobyl moment.”
The declarations and calls to action have piled up, the evidence is in, and the incidents are mounting. The moment to break the paralysis is now. We call on world leaders to rise to the occasion: to commit now to negotiating an international agency for frontier AI.

‘Fast & Furious’ Takes a Victory Lap With a Ferociously Fun Roller Coaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.
“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.
In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.
Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)
The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.
If you want to feel like you’re a Fast & Furious character within the safer confines of a precisely engineered thrill machine, you can hardly ask for anything better. And despite its innovative design, the overall aesthetic of the ride and its environs demonstrates a welcome nostalgia for the more grounded origins of these movies, when the crew was hijacking trucks full of DVD players instead of launching Pontiacs into space. On your way through the queueing path, you’ll pass garage workbenches littered with tools and LA-style street murals that pay homage to racing culture.
Those welcome simple touches might make you wonder if we’ll ever actually see the conclusion of the increasingly bloated and absurd F&F saga in the perpetually delayed 11th film, Fast Forever. Between the ongoing rewrites and budgetary obstacles, it has yet to even enter production. (The previous film, Fast X, was released in 2023.) Rather than being too big to fail, it’s as though the challenge of topping each successive spectacle has made the Furious brand too unwieldy to push forward.
Could it be that, in the absence of a finale, the F&F rides will cap off the series? In their invitation for Tuesday’s press preview event, Universal noted that Vin Diesel himself would be on hand during a ceremony to help executives cut the ribbon (or, as it happened, a fake plastic chain). But the man synonymous with the franchise was nowhere to be found when the time came to declare the ride officially open. The closest we got was a gaggle of fans in costume as Toretto, complete with bald caps.
When I checked out Diesel’s Instagram account for clues as to what he was up to, I found that he had just posted set photos of himself as Kaulder, his character from The Last Witch Hunter, a 2015 dark fantasy film. Lionsgate confirmed last year that a sequel is in the works, and it appears that Diesel was stoking anticipation with this sneak peek. When this guy isn’t acknowledging a major milestone for the burnt-rubber films that made him a household name, you have to wonder if there’s much gas left in the tank.
Not everything lasts—certainly not college flings that start with stunt-driver flicks. That the Fast & Furious series has earned billions of dollars and spanned a quarter century based on an equally thin premise is a testament to how far this juvenile spirit can take you. Maybe bringing it to life with a really fun roller coaster is the best way to let it roar off into the sunset. When you climb aboard, take a look around at your fellow passengers. You’re the family now.

Istanbul Airport overtakes London Heathrow as world’s most connected hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:29:18 UTC
19:29:18 KST

Of the top 50 most connected airports in the world, 12 are located in Europe.
The world’s most connected airports have just been revealed – and five of the top 10 megahubs are in Europe.
According to the latest Megahubs Index by OAG, Istanbul Airport in Türkiye claimed the top spot for 2026, overtaking London Heathrow.
The rankings are based on the number of possible connections between inbound and outbound flights within a six-hour window on the busiest day of the year, Sunday 2 August, and the number of destinations served from the airport.
Istanbul, which is the eighth busiest airport in the world in terms of capacity, has possible connections to 337 global destinations.
London Heathrow dropped down a place, with potential connections falling by 6% compared to the busiest day last year. OAG notes that the airport has been “undoubtedly affected by the ongoing disruption to Middle East schedules, with its capacity to the region down by 25% this August”.
Other European megahubs in the top 10 include Amsterdam Airport Schiphol in third place, Frankfurt International Airport in seventh, and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport in ninth.
Among the top 50, 12 megahubs are located in Europe, including: Madrid Adolfo Suarez-Barajas (18th), Istanbul Sabiha Gokcen (21st), Athens (22nd), Munich (23rd), Rome Fiumicino (27th), Barcelona (41st) and Zurich (45th).

U.N. investigators said Thursday there are “reasonable grounds” to believe the U.S. committed war crimes against civilians in Iran, who also face “gross human rights violations” by their own government.
In their latest report, due to be presented to the Human Rights Council Monday, the independent investigators urged the 47 countries in the council to press for an end to the war, hold those responsible for war crimes to account and give asylum to civilians fleeing abroad.
Neither Iran, Israel nor the United States are members of the Human Rights Council.
"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," the investigators said.
"These included Tomahawk missile strikes on the clearly identifiable Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab – which killed over 150 people, including approximately 120 girls and boys – and another airstrike where precision strike missiles dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing 22 civilian men and women," they continued.
Their report also said the Iranian government's repression of domestic protests that began in late 2025 over the rising cost of living represented "a significant escalation ... of its well-established pattern of suppressing dissent."
It noted the government in Tehran had stepped up the use of "repressive laws," "lethal force" and "the death penalty as a tool of intimidation and control."
State security forces killed protesters in all 31 provinces – reportedly including at least 221 children, attacked health care facilities and arrested tens of thousands of people, it said.
Between March and August 2026, at least 29 men were executed following expedited trials in connection with the protests and more than 70 others, including five women and three boys, remained "at imminent risk of execution," it said.
The U.N. investigators urged Israel, the U.S. and Iran to "immediately cease hostilities."
They said the countries of the U.N. human rights council should "take prompt diplomatic action to implement a permanent peace" and ensure that alleged violations of international law – by all three parties – were "independently investigated and those responsible held to account."

Ancient Chinese scholars drank ink for poetic inspiration or poor handwriting penalties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:27:18 UTC
19:27:18 KST

Ancient Chinese scholars drank ink for poetic inspiration or poor handwriting penalties
Unlike today’s inks made from industrial pigments, ancient Chinese ink was produced using soot from burning natural plants or animal oils
While the Chinese idiom, “Having ink in their stomach”, serves as a metaphor to commend the knowledgeable, the act of ingesting ink was a common practice among ancient literati.
The earliest documentation of ink drinking dates back to the Northern and Southern dynasties (420–589), where it was used as a sanctioned punishment for scholars with illegible handwriting.
According to the Book of Sui, the official history of the Sui dynasty (581–618), during an exam administered by a palace attendant to assess local officials, scholars who presented poor handwriting faced the penalty of consuming one sheng of ink. This traditional Chinese unit of volume varied by dynasty, with one sheng equating to 600 millilitres during the Sui period.
This rule was abolished after Li Shimin ascended the throne in the Tang dynasty (618–907). Nevertheless, some scholars willingly consumed ink to enhance their literary skills.

English village votes to leave UK over migrant plan

English village votes to leave UK over migrant plan
An English village has overwhelmingly voted to “secede” from the UK in protest over government plans to house more than 1,200 male migrants at a nearby former military base. The referendum in Piddington, Oxfordshire has no legal force but drew nearly 92% turnout.
The result announced on Wednesday showed that 285 residents backed leaving the UK, 26 voted against, and one ballot was spoiled. Organizers staged the symbolic referendum in protest against plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at the nearby MOD Bicester site.
“We are Piddington, the village that roars,” parish council vice chair Susannah Parden declared as she announced the result. Council chair Tim McNally called the vote “an example of democracy in operation,” adding: “We went into this village hall as the underdogs – we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world.”
The ballot asked residents whether Piddington should “secede from the United Kingdom and pursue self-determination,” while signs proclaiming the “Principality of Piddington” appeared around the village. More than 130 local women have also written to female MPs warning that their “safety, security, and freedoms” would be threatened if the asylum center opens.
Despite the overwhelming vote, the government said it will not reconsider the plan. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the BBC that abandoning the proposed center would be unfair to other communities already housing large numbers of migrants.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham likewise said he understood the village’s “strength of feeling,” but insisted that asylum accommodation had to be shared fairly across the country. Using the former military site is part of the Home Office’s push to move migrants out of hotels.
The Piddington referendum comes as the UK grapples with continued illegal crossings of the English Channel and mounting pressure over asylum accommodation.
Hundreds of anti-immigration protesters clashed with police in Portsmouth earlier this month after a boat carrying around 140 asylum seekers was brought ashore. Demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop buses transporting the arrivals to a Home Office processing center, chanting “stop the boats” and “send them back.”
Some 33,000 people, mostly adult men, arrived in the UK by small boat in the year to July, accounting for around 88% of illegal arrivals, according to government data. A YouGov poll in August found 69% of Britons believe immigration over the past decade has been too high, while 43% said it had been mostly bad for the country, up from 33% in 2016.

Ukraine Suffers More Civilian Deaths in 8 Months of 2026 Than All of 2025 – UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:24:46 UTC
19:24:46 KST

August has been one of the deadliest months for civilian casualties in Ukraine, with at least 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured, a new UN Human Rights for the High Commissioner (HRMMU) report says.
The report, published on Thursday, Sept. 17, says the figure marks a slight decrease from July, which saw the highest toll on ordinary civilians since Russia’s war in Ukraine began, topping the previous high in June.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year’s figure – more than the entirety of 2025 within just eight months – is 55 percent higher than during the same period last year and more than double the figure for the same period in 2024, it adds.
More drones, more deaths?
The report says most casualties came from “long-range weapons,” with most documented in cities rather than the frontline areas.
“In August, long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of the total (194 killed; 1,077 injured),” it says. “Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the frontline in urban centers.”
The spike coincides with Russia’s increased use of drones – latterly the jet-powered variants – and ballistic missiles.
In May, Russia hit Ukraine with record waves of drones, launching over 1,400 in 24 hours. While subsequent waves have seen smaller total numbers, the rise of jet-powered and ballistic drones, coupled with non-stop strikes, has made interception increasingly difficult.
Russian Drone Hits Kharkiv Mall, Woman Needs Medical Aid
The report adds that Kyiv suffered the highest casualties with 31 killed and 106 injured, followed by cities in central and southern Ukraine, such as Kherson (25 killed; 334 injured), Kryvyi Rih (16 killed; 147 injured), and Zaporizhzhia (11 killed; 131 injured).
Totals for eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv was not named in the list.
“Human safari”
Short-range drones, such as the first-person view (FPV) drones commonly used by frontline troops, are said to be the leading cause of frontline civilian deaths.
“Short-range drones were the main cause of civilian casualties near the frontline (91 killed; 727 injured), accounting for 30 percent of all civilian casualties in August,” it says.
While the report did not name specific frontline regions or cities affected by short-range drone strikes, southern Ukraine’s Kherson – sitting just across the river from Russian-occupied areas – has often been dubbed a “human safari” due to the prevalence of Russian FPV operators targeting civilians.
The city of Oleshky, sitting just across the river, is facing a humanitarian crisis as Russian forces have blocked off all routes in and out of the city with artillery and drones, allowing no aid to pass.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner called the city a “death trap” on Wednesday and said Russia has refused to uphold a negotiated evacuation deal.
Read Kyiv Post’s August frontline report in Kherson here.
Unclear picture of Russian civilian casualties
The UN report says it verified 4 civilians killed and 35 injured in occupied territories, but
says it is unable to verify figures for civilians killed and injured in Russia.
“According to public statements by Russian authorities on individual incidents in August, at least 85 people were killed and 498 injured in occupied territory and at least 113 people killed and 736 injured in the Russian Federation,” the report says, before adding:
“Due to lack of independent sources of information, however, HRMMU has not been able to verify the vast majority of allegations.”

US intelligence officers have voiced concerns that China could acquire F-35 fighter jet technology through Saudi Arabia, officials told The New York Times on Wednesday.
The officials' fears stem from the United States' multi-billion-dollar sale of 48 of the aircraft to Saudi Arabia, which has been pending since November 2025. Similar concerns were raised at the time the potential deal was initially announced.
The US officials said that China could receive the technology either via spying or through its military and security partnership with Saudi Arabia.
A Pentagon intelligence report on the subject, the NYT reported, said that the F-35 technology storage sites should be restricted to US and Saudi personnel.
Analysts in the report questioned whether Saudi Arabia would agree to limiting general contact with the Chinese military and associated entities, as well as removing equipment from Chinese manufacturers from telecommunications and router infrastructure.
The State Department, Pentagon, and Saudi Arabian Embassy in Washington declined to comment to the NYT, while the White House and Chinese Embassy did not reply to requests.
Saudi F-35 deal raises concerns over Israel's military edge
When the deal was first under consideration in 2025, the NYT reported that it had raised concerns over Israel’s qualitative military edge in the region.
Israel is the only country in the Middle East that currently operates these jets, using them in airstrikes on Iran in October 2024 and June 2025.
Since the 1973 war, US policymakers have worked to ensure that Israel maintains its qualitative military edge, with Congress requiring that the US guarantee Israel can defeat any “credible conventional military threat” while suffering minimal damage and casualties.

"Putting a few people on trial does not constitute real justice," he told AFP.

The Observatory said more than 1,700 people were killed.
The commission said it had verified serious violations leading to the deaths of mostly civilians, and identified 298 suspects.
It claimed 238 members of the security forces and army had been killed in attacks attributed to Assad's supporters.
Authorities then sent reinforcements to the region, with the commission estimating their number at 200,000 fighters.
Syrian and international monitoring groups reported sectarian massacres, in which entire families were killed by government forces, armed groups allied with the government and armed volunteers, including summary executions.
Assad was toppled in December 2024. Despite assurances from the new authorities, Syria's religious minorities have since expressed safety concerns.

Dozens of members of the European Parliament from Patriots for Europe, the European Parliament's third-largest group, signed a charter adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) principles on combating antisemitism and commemorating the Holocaust at a special conference in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
During the conference, participants expressed support for Israel and settlement in the West Bank, while opposing sanctions and boycotts imposed on them.
The conference was held against the backdrop of measures and sanctions promoted in recent years by several European countries against parties associated with settlement in the West Bank. Participants included members of the European Parliament and senior officials from right-wing and conservative parties across the continent, alongside Likud MK Ariel Kallner. Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan and president of the Likud Court, attorney Michael Kleiner, addressed the conference in recorded messages.
Patriots for Europe brings together representatives of right-wing and nationalist parties from several European countries. Its members include representatives of the Czech ANO party, Hungary's Fidesz, the Freedom Party of Austria, the Dutch Party for Freedom, and France's National Rally.
The signing of the charter adopting IHRA principles was central the the conference. According to the charter, certain expressions directed against the State of Israel may, depending on the context, constitute expressions of antisemitism. It also emphasizes combating Holocaust denial and distortion of the memory of the Holocaust.
Palestinian workers will pay price for European West Bank sanctions, Kleiner says
Kleiner focused his remarks on the potential economic consequences of sanctions on the West Bank, arguing that those who could ultimately pay the price are Palestinian workers employed by Israeli businesses and factories.
"The sanctions imposed by 12 countries, led by Britain, on Judea and Samaria are a double-edged sword," Kleiner said. "Those who will suffer from them most are tens of thousands of Palestinians who make a living working for Jews in Israel and Judea and Samaria."
Kleiner pointed to SodaStream as an example of what he said could happen if Israeli factories in the area were boycotted.
"The example is the attempted boycott of SodaStream: The factory moved to the Arava and was not harmed, but 500 Arab workers lost their livelihoods and were forced to work in the Palestinian Authority for much lower wages," he said. "The factories will not close, but the sanctions could severely harm the workers' livelihoods."
According to Kleiner, this illustrates a paradox in the sanctions policy: Measures intended, according to their proponents, to help Palestinians could in practice harm the livelihoods of Palestinians employed by Israelis in the West Bank.
Kallner, chairman of the Knesset committee for cooperation with the European Parliament, also criticized the sanctions and linked them to the fight against antisemitism.
"When sanctions are imposed against the Jewish state and against the people of the Bible who returned to the land of the Bible, this is a double standard, this is hypocrisy, and this is modern antisemitism," he said.
European antisemitism threatens more than Jews, Kallner warns
Kallner added that antisemitism in Europe was not a threat to Jews alone.
"Antisemitism begins with the Jews, but it never ends with the Jews," he said.
According to Kallner, Israel stands "on the front line of the struggle between civilization and barbarism," and European countries should stand alongside it.
Dagan welcomed conference participants in a recorded message and presented cooperation with Europe's right-wing parties as part of a shared struggle against terrorism and efforts to delegitimize Israel.
"We are fighting to defend Europe. We are fighting to defend Israel. We are fighting to defend the future of Western civilization as a whole," Dagan said. "We stand together against barbaric terrorist attacks. We stand together against the new war, the war of delegitimization campaigns and the war of lies."
The conference and signing of the charter are part of efforts by Israeli figures and representatives of the settlement movement to deepen ties with right-wing and conservative parties in Europe, at a time when pressure and measures against parties associated with settlement in the West Bank are increasing in several European countries.

India’s BRICS balancing act is keeping the bloc from becoming an anti-Western alliance - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:23:55 UTC
19:23:55 KST

BRICS has finally found consensus, but the terms of that consensus reveal how divided the grouping remains.
On Saturday, leaders meeting in New Delhi unanimously adopted a 140-paragraph declaration after months of disagreement over the Iran war. The agreement calls for maximum restraint in the Middle East, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and diplomacy as the route to resolving conflicts.
Crucially, it avoids naming the United States, Israel, or Iran.
For India, which holds the BRICS chairmanship, getting all 11 members to sign the declaration is a diplomatic achievement. But it also illustrates the limits of BRICS as a geopolitical bloc.
The challenge was particularly acute because Iran and the UAE, both BRICS members, have been caught on opposing sides of the regional conflict. Iran has attacked targets in the Gulf, while the UAE maintains close security ties with Washington. Their foreign ministers had already failed to produce a consensual BRICS statement earlier this year.
India nevertheless helped bring the two sides into the same diplomatic room, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian meeting Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan on the summit’s sidelines.
That is the kind of BRICS India wants: influential enough to give emerging powers a larger voice, but flexible enough to accommodate countries whose strategic interests sharply diverge.
The same calculation is visible in the economic agenda.
Reducing dependence on the US dollar
China and Russia have pushed to reduce dependence on the dollar and develop alternative financial mechanisms. India has resisted the idea of a common BRICS currency, favoring more practical arrangements such as greater use of national currencies and improved cross-border payment systems. The New Delhi declaration did not endorse a single BRICS currency.
This matters because India has little interest in replacing American financial dominance with a China-centered alternative. New Delhi wants room to trade with Russia, maintain energy ties with Iran and the Gulf, and participate in BRICS while retaining access to American markets, Western capital, and technology.
That is strategic autonomy, not an anti-American strategy.
The Ukraine issue provides another revealing example. Unlike previous BRICS declarations, the New Delhi statement made no specific reference to the Russia-Ukraine war, a clear indication of how difficult it remains for the expanded grouping to reach common language on a conflict involving one of its founding members.
The contrast with Gaza is striking. The declaration devoted substantial attention to the Palestinian issue, reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood and the two-state solution, and called for humanitarian access and an end to practices that could alter Gaza’s demographic or geographic character.
This is where the New Delhi summit matters for Israel.
Israel should not dismiss BRICS as an irrelevant talking shop. Nor should it assume that an expanded BRICS automatically constitutes a coherent anti-Israel alliance.
The summit demonstrates the opposite: the group contains countries with competing interests, and India in particular is resisting efforts to turn BRICS into a unified anti-Western geopolitical vehicle.
At the same time, Israel should recognize that BRICS diplomacy will increasingly create political pressure on Jerusalem.
The declaration’s treatment of Gaza, its emphasis on Palestinian statehood, and its criticism of actions affecting the occupied Palestinian territories demonstrate that Israel faces a growing diplomatic constituency outside the traditional Western framework.
India’s role is therefore especially important. New Delhi maintains close ties with Israel while also maintaining strategic relationships with Iran, the Gulf states, Russia, China and the United States. Its BRICS policy reflects the same multi-alignment that increasingly defines Indian foreign policy.
India is not trying to make BRICS a Western alliance. It is also resisting efforts to make it an anti-Western alliance.
The New Delhi declaration is consequently best understood as an Indian diplomatic success with clear limitations. BRICS can still produce consensus, but only through carefully calibrated language that avoids forcing members to choose sides on their most divisive geopolitical disputes.
For Israel and the US, that distinction matters. A stronger BRICS may challenge parts of the existing international order, but the New Delhi summit does not show the emergence of a unified alternative bloc.
It shows something more complicated: India is trying to ensure that BRICS becomes a powerful negotiating forum without allowing China, Russia, or any other member to turn it into a geopolitical instrument.
The writer is an India-based lawyer specializing in cross-border trade and investments, and a senior fellow with the South Asia Democratic Forum in Brussels.

“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” the post read.
Who is Umar Kremlev, Putin associate?
Kremlev, a businessman and the current president of the International Boxing Association, has boasted increasingly close ties to Putin over the years. He recently accompanied the Kremlin chief to China as part of Russia’s delegation, and was awarded the Order of Friendship, an official state award given to those who help Russia bolster international ties.
On Monday, ProPublica reported that Kremlev paid for hundreds of thousands of dollars of the wedding expenses. The report cited interviews with three people familiar with the event, along with other records.
ProPublica reported that Kremlev paid for the Trumps to rent out one of the two private islands used for the event, as well as other costly events, such as the fireworks show. His team reportedly helped plan the event, and the payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai.
In the post, Bettina Trump wrote that the couple “got married privately on Friday, surrounded ONLY by our family.”
Trump Jr. corroborated this on his podcast, saying that the wedding “was really small, like, just really close friends.”
ProPublica reported that the guest list of 50 people included Kremlev, who was part of a group that sometimes spoke Russian.
The report noted that he speaks limited English and that his presence confused some of the other guests.
Bettina Trump added that the events were “never intended to be our wedding weekend.”
“When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds.”

“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” Bettina Trump wrote.
ProPublica noted that Kremlev’s gift to the Trumps is a remarkable development in the Kremlin’s relationship with the US: a member of Putin’s circle gained close access to the presidential family and is financially supporting their endeavors.
In response to a request for comment from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said that “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” and that he is “not someone he has a business relationship with.” The spokesperson added that the two bonded over their shared love of boxing.
However, a spokesperson for Eric Trump told ProPublica that “Eric has absolutely no clue who this person [Kremlev] is, nor has he ever heard his name.”
Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica that “Mr. Kremlev and Mr. Trump Jr. have a friendly relationship” and that the pair met “a couple of years ago.”
The press office added that “Mr. Kremlev has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances.”

Chile weighs ethanol-gasoline blend as government seeks cheaper fuels amid fiscal strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:23:26 UTC
19:23:26 KST

Chile weighs ethanol-gasoline blend as government seeks cheaper fuels amid fiscal strains
Sept 17 - Chile, one of Latin America's largest oil importers, has started to consider adopting ethanol-blended gasoline as spiking oil prices this year have strained the economy and government finances, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The energy ministry has drafted a proposal to shift to E10 ethanol blending — mixing 10% ethanol with gasoline — that could reduce government fuel supply costs by approximately $107 million annually, according to a memo prepared by ministry officials.
Data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC, showed that Chile imported 181,000 barrels per day of crude oil in 2025. Oil prices have soared during the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent, the global benchmark for crude oil, traded at over $105 a barrel on Wednesday, up from about $73 a barrel before the war began.
Ethanol-gasoline blends are widely used across Latin America. In Brazil, the $20 billion ethanol industry is second only to the U.S. Brazil has long been known for its fleet of "flex-fuel" passenger cars that can run on a blend of ethanol, now topping 30%, mixed into gasoline.
Chile has no ethanol-blending mandate, and is one of the few countries in the region still relying on MTBE, an octane-boosting gasoline additive.
The government has held off on adopting ethanol blends because Chile lacks significant domestic production, lacking sufficient land to grow enough crops to support a domestic ethanol industry, according to a U.S. Grains Council briefing reviewed by Reuters.
Yet without the ethanol option, Chile remains exposed to global price swings. In March, as U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran ramped up, the government of the mining-dependent nation stopped fully cushioning the shock at the pump due to oil price volatility, with its MEPCO fuel stabilization mechanism straining public finances.
Switching to an ethanol-gasoline blend would help phase out MTBE and ease pressure on President Jose Antonio Kast's administration following the oil supply disruptions, which have stoked public discontent.
"The government is out of money," Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said in March.
According to the grains council briefing, the switch to E10 would be relatively simple and affordable for Chile. State oil company ENAP would need to invest about $10.8 million to adapt refining, terminal and storage infrastructure, the ministry said in its internal memo. It said the transition could be introduced gradually and partly offset by lower carbon-tax payments.
A shift to a 10% blend, and even a 15% blend, could be achieved by 2030 in Chile, the grains council said.
In May, the ministry released a roadmap to diversify fuel sources and lower carbon emissions by 2030, including through fuel blends.
The ministry did not respond to requests for comment on the memo, including on the timing of any transition to ethanol-blend gasoline and why Chile had not pursued it sooner.
Chile already depends on the U.S. for 85% of its gasoline supply, according to the grains council briefing. A switch to ethanol could benefit corn growers, the council said, since the grain is used to make the fuel.
Such a move "replaces one import dependency with another," the ministry conceded in its memo. Chile's ethanol imports currently come mostly from Argentina, followed by Bolivia.
Production in neighboring Brazil has risen sharply under the government mandate to use more ethanol in gasoline. REUTERS

Northeastern Estonian hospitals join forces to attract new doctors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:21:00 KST

Northeastern Estonian hospitals join forces to attract new doctors
Hospitals in Ida-Viru County are teaming up for a joint campaign to attract doctors to the understaffed region.
The northeastern region's medical institutions are short about 100 doctors. Ida-Viru Central Hospital (IVKH) in Kohtla-Järve, the county's largest, could hire up to 30 immediately, but applicants aren't exactly lining up for the job.
The hospital plans to target med school students early, hoping internships will encourage them to consider careers in the region after graduation.
"If they come here for an internship and like it, they'll talk to others about their experience," said Pille Letjuka, chief physician at IVKH. "And once that connection has been established, it's much easier to get that doctor or nurse to come back and work for us later."
The state offers doctors taking jobs at hospitals outside Estonia's main population centers a relocation bonus of up to €30,000, but money alone has proven not to always the problem.
"I've made salary offers that have left people in Tallinn gasping, but unfortunately, I still haven't found anyone willing to come here for that money," said Narva Hospital board member Üllar Lanno.
He said years of distrust have made doctors reluctant to consider the border city, thus prompting the new campaign.
Ida-Viru hospitals say the shortage is actually nationwide and competition for new doctors is fierce. Lanno said the state should increase medical school enrollment to address the shortage.
"I think the best solution for Estonia today would be to train 30 percent more doctors to make up for the 33 percent who never complete their residency," he said.
That, he added, would significantly increase the likelihood of future doctors eventually ending up in hospitals.
Unrivaled experience
Doctors already working Ida-Viru County, meanwhile, point to the unique experience they gain there.
"A doctor who works 24-hour shifts in the Emergency Department or ICU at Ida-Viru Central Hospital could go anywhere and work in any hospital in the world," said Neeme Somma, head anesthesiology and intensive care at the hospital. "They have the experience to cope with whatever situation comes their way."
Hospitals in the region have also relied on temporary assignments to fill staffing gaps, with more than a third of specialist doctors working in Ida-Viru County also working elsewhere in Estonia.

Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Israel follows through on threat of ‘consequences’
Israel had warned the UK against the new sanctions, with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs raising the prospect of “consequences” for what it called “hostile moves”.
Shortly after the trade ban was announced, Israel, which controls access to Gaza and the occupied West Bank, barred 11 British MPs and a lawyer from entering and ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem. It also announced the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center located in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel. And it has ended British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank.
“In light of this [the trade ban], attention should be directed to the ongoing and subversive activities of various British organisations promoting boycotts, sanctions, and economic and political measures against the State of Israel,” the leaked letter reads.
It makes further accusations against 11 groups in total. The claims against them range from advocating for engagement with Hamas for humanitarian access; demanding an arms embargo against Israel; having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or working with “terrorist” organisations.
Save the Children is accused of describing Israel’s actions as “deliberate starvation” and “genocide”.
A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that, alongside other NGOs, it is already unable to secure visas for staff needing to cross Israeli-controlled borders into Gaza or the West Bank, “at a time when needs have never been greater”.
Israel has intensified restrictions on international aid groups since the genocidal war in Gaza began, including measures affecting the entry of food, medicine, foreign volunteer doctors and humanitarian workers.
MAP said the letter forms part of Israeli authorities’ “wider restrictions on international charities operating in the occupied Palestinian territory”. It noted that two MAP individuals named in the letter had received the humanitarian medals awarded by King Charles.
The letter describes Palestine Action, which has carried out raids against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, as a “network of radical branches promoting direct action intended to damage the Israeli defence industry”.
“This letter is further proof that we were not banned because of anything to do with ‘terrorism’,” Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori told Al Jazeera. “As the letter admits, our activity was always focused on damaging the Israeli defence industry.”
In a related development, UK Lawyers for Israel has called on the government to consider proscribing Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, as a terrorist organisation, The Telegraph reported. The lobby group alleged, in line with Israeli accusations, that MSF had employed people with links to Palestinian armed groups.
MSF said it had been the target of a “disinformation campaign” for months. It said staff accused by Israel of having “ties to terrorism” were only reported to the organisation after they had been killed, and that Israeli authorities had not shared evidence of military involvement before their deaths.

Gran Canaria: how an Atlantic island is emphasising its year-round appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:19:16 UTC
19:19:16 KST

Few European islands pack in so much variety. Gran Canaria brings together sand dunes, volcanic highlands, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, celebrated local food and a capital city with genuine urban energy, all of it across an island with 236 kilometres of coastline.
As European tourism looks beyond the traditional summer peak, Gran Canaria offers a useful test case: an island that’s spreading its appeal across the entire calendar and the endless reasons for visiting it.
A compact island with an unusually broad reach
Gran Canaria is often described as a “continent in miniature”, and the geography backs up the claim.
A short drive inland leads to pine forests, deep ravines and small mountain villages that boast traditional architecture and little whitewashed houses. A morning on the beach can give way to a mountain trail in the afternoon and dinner in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria that evening, without changing hotels.
That reach is matched by how easy the island is to get to.
Gran Canaria Airport operates around the clock, and according to Turismo de Gran Canaria's year-end figures, it handled 15.82 million passengers and 142,884 flight operations in 2025, with direct connections to more than 160 airports across 30 countries served by over 60 airlines.
Then there is the climate
The island has an annual average temperature of around 24°C, with mild winters and summers moderated by the trade winds and its position in the Atlantic, conditions locals sometimes describe as a fair-weather gym.
Hikers use a wide network of trails through the island's ravines and highlands, cyclists and runners train year-round, and golfers play courses that include Spain's oldest golf club, founded in 1891.
Those same trade winds help create conditions for surfing, windsurfing, kitesurfing and diving at different points around the island throughout the year.
Sustainability you can see on the ground
Sustainability here is tied to specific places, communities and practices rather than a slogan.
Around 43% of Gran Canaria falls within its Biosphere Reserve, part of UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme and designated in 2005. It encompasses rural communities where farming, cheese-making and transhumant grazing remain part of daily life.
The island boasts a Biosphere Destination certification, which ties tourism development to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.
The mountains are also home to the Risco Caído and Sacred Mountains of Gran Canaria Cultural Landscape, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July 2019, UNESCO added this cultural landscape to its World Heritage List, thus giving recognition to a region that is home to numerous troglodyte settlements, granaries, cisterns and sacred sites linked to a pre-Hispanic culture that evolved in isolation for centuries. In the main cave at Risco Caído, an opening in the cave ceiling allows sun and moonlight to enter at certain times of the year, casting a beam that illuminates the interior in a unique way. That relationship between landscape and sky continues today.
Gran Canaria's night skies have earned international recognition as a Starlight Tourist Destination, a designation it first received in 2018 and renewed in February 2026, extending it through to 2029. Ancient islanders looked to those very same skies to track the seasons; today, efforts to preserve them support both environmental protection and a growing interest in astrotourism, with a great number of specially designated viewpoints in privileged star-gazing spots around the island.
Flavours, scenery and local life
The coast still matters, of course. Gran Canaria's 236 kilometres of coastline hold more than 60 kilometres of beaches, from the Dunes of Maspalomas to Las Canteras, alongside quieter coves and natural rock pools around the island's edges.
Inland, the island's food culture tells a parallel story.
Gran Canaria is currently home to five Michelin-starred restaurants, while a certified Wine Route links more than 50 local businesses across the island, among them wineries, restaurants, wine bars, estates and cheesemakers.
Local producers champion Flor de Guía, a protected, traditional cheese exclusively curdled with thistle flower, alongside gofio, a traditional food ingredient made from roasted and ground maize, tropical fruit, sea salt and Atlantic seafood, while the Agaete valley's coffee plantations, among the few in Europe, add a further point of difference.
That same emphasis on authenticity is reflected in the Gran Canaria Km.0 Fair, a travelling initiative supported by Gran Canaria Tourism, that promotes agri-food products grown or produced on the island. Its various editions tour towns across Gran Canaria, bringing producers and consumers together and showcasing locally sourced foods such as cheeses, honeys, wines, fruit and vegetables, among others. The initiative encourages responsible consumption, supports the local economy and helps to sustain activities closely linked to the conservation of the landscape and the rural environment.
Las Palmas de Gran Canaria adds a cosmopolitan dimension to the island. Its historic quarters of Vegueta and Triana hold landmarks such as the Casa de Colón and the Museo Canario, alongside historic architecture shaped by centuries of transatlantic trade, while Las Canteras beach runs alongside the city's shops, bars and restaurants, bringing the Atlantic into the heart of the capital.
What Gran Canaria’s example tells us about island tourism today
What Gran Canaria is really demonstrating is how far depth and diversity can carry a destination: a compact, well-connected island building its appeal on the sheer number of reasons it gives people to visit it.
For European tourism, increasingly focused on extending the season and diversifying the visitor experience, that makes Gran Canaria a destination worth watching.

As Canadian tariffs bite, Republicans search for a winning message
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:18:37 UTC
19:18:37 KST

As Canadian tariffs bite, Republicans search for a winning message
NEW YORK, Sept 17 - High gas prices and the rising cost of living had already made affordability a defining issue in this year’s midterm elections. Then President Donald Trump escalated his trade war with Canada.
Now, Republican candidates in northern border states most affected by the tariffs are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump’s loyal base and reaching independent voters that polls show have soured on his handling of the economy and his fight with Canada.
The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with Canada’s, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment. That has raised the stakes in two states that Republicans will likely need to win in the November 3 elections if they are to hold the US Senate - and their respective candidates have taken notably different approaches with voters, each with its own political risks.
The Senate races in both Michigan and Maine are considered toss-ups by the Cook Political Report.
U.S. Senator Susan Collins of Maine is breaking with Trump, criticizing the tit-for-tat exchange of tariffs and seeking carveouts for affected industries. Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, by contrast, has criticized Canada and made the case that his close relationship with the president will help blunt the impact of the trade war.
Because the Canadian tariffs emerged so recently, candidates have largely been left to devise their own responses mid-campaign, said David Hopkins, a political scientist at Boston College.
And both will “need to move beyond the Republican coalition” to win their races, he said. “When something unpopular happens at the behest of your own party leader, it puts you in that very awkward place.”
The National Republican Senatorial Committee, which supports Senate candidates, has not taken a public stance on the Canadian tariffs and did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
‘POLITICAL PRESSURE’
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, accusing its northern neighbor of unfair trade practices. Canada's own retaliatory tariffs – ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion of U.S. goods – took effect on September 8.
Canadian officials have made no secret of the fact that their levies were designed with politics in mind.
“We're being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Canada’s Minister of Industry Melanie Joly said in August.
Americans are about four times as likely to blame the current trade dispute on Washington rather than Ottawa, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted late last month. Only 20% of respondents supported higher tariffs on Canadian goods.
Such figures have cleared the way for Collins to declare Trump's trade war with Canada a "mistake." A moderate Republican representing a state that prides itself on political independence, Collins has a history of challenging party orthodoxy on issues including healthcare, abortion and gun control.
Now locked in a close race against Democrat Troy Jackson, she is again trying to distance herself from a president whose popularity has sunk to record lows.
Canada is Maine’s biggest trading partner, accounting for 69% of imports and 41% of exports in 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. More than 80% of the state’s heating oil and gasoline is imported from Canada, and its three most iconic products – wild blueberries, lobsters and lumber – all depend heavily on cross-border trade.
Collins has voted four times to oppose Trump’s tariffs, and on August 28 wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer outlining the economic impact on her state.
In her letter, she focused on road salt and cement – products that the administration subsequently exempted from the tariffs.
Jackson responded with sarcasm. “I mean, yeah, thank you for the road salt,” he told reporters at a recent campaign event. “What has she done to stand up, to get Trump to back off of parts coming in from Canada, fertilizer coming in from Canada for farmers?”
TARIFF DAMAGE
In Michigan, which exports more than almost any other state to Canada, analysts say the tariffs could be especially damaging to the struggling wood products sector, particularly kitchen cabinet makers.
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has said Trump “is right to put America First - and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution.”
He has also presented his closeness with the president as a strength rather than a liability.
“You can send somebody back [to Washington] who gets up every day and tries to gouge the president’s eyes out or you can send somebody back who’s going to walk in and say, ‘Hey, can we work on this part of the trade deal,’” he said.
Rogers’ Democratic rival, Abdul El-Sayed, has tried to make light of his political predicament.
“He’s caught between knowing full well that these tariffs are bad for Michiganders and having to appeal to Daddy Trump every single time he opens his mouth,” El-Sayed told CNN.
Spokespeople for Collins and Rogers declined to comment for this story.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said “President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First, whether in trade negotiations or through an economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation.”
Even though presidents have limited control over economic growth, Hopkins said, tariffs give people who are dissatisfied with their financial situation another reason to blame Trump and his fellow Republicans.
"It's sort of easy to tell a story of what it is that Trump has done to make things less affordable," he said. REUTERS

The "Maiaky-Udobne–Palanka" crossing point on the border with Moldova has temporarily suspended operations due to a failure in the communications network that provides Internet access and, accordingly, the operation of information systems. At present, the operation of the "Palanka" customs point has been temporarily suspended due to a malfunction in the communications network that provides Internet access and, consequently, the functioning of the information systems used by the control authorities when crossing the border. The malfunction occurred outside the customs point’s premises
The responsible operator’s technical team has gone to the site and is taking the necessary measures to eliminate the malfunction. US Congress passes sweeping Russia sanctions bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:15:26 UTC
19:15:26 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a televised address in Moscow on September 16, 2026 (AFP Photo)
U.S. lawmakers approved broad new sanctions on Sept. 16 designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump after months of delay.
The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package by 262-159, giving a final congressional green light to the most substantial U.S. legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.
Trump has said he will sign the measure, which sailed through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The legislation targets Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.
It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including potentially China and India, in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war.
But its sweeping tariff powers produced an unusual split among Democrats, who overwhelmingly support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump greater authority over trade.
Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill “deeply flawed.”
“White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump’s authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to actually impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers,” he said.
Dozens of Democrats nevertheless backed the measure, offsetting opposition from a handful of Republicans who objected to sanctions on free-market or non-interventionist grounds.
Supporters argue that tougher economic pressure is needed, with Russia’s full-scale invasion grinding through its fifth year and no peace settlement in sight.

Canada's Mark Carney welcomes 'ambition' of becoming associate EU member during his speech to the European Parliament

Canada's Carney welcomes associate status idea in EU speech
September 17, 2026
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has said he welcomes the "ambition" of a European Union proposal to make the country the bloc's first associate member.
Carney made the remarks while addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, in a speech that focused on Canada's and the EU's shared security and economic interests.
In an address in which Carney spoke in English, French and German, the Canadian prime minister lauded European culture and values of democracy, freedom and human rights, which he said Canada shares.
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," the Canadian leader told the chamber, to applause.
Europe and Canada are 'stronger together', Carney tells EU Parliament
"We hold common values for which we have always fought and in whose defense we must always remain vigilant," he said.
"Europe and Canada are each strong," he said. But he added that "Europe and Canada are even stronger together."
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners," he said. "We do not seek power to dominate others," he added, in a thinly veiled reference to the US.
"The objective is not self-sufficiency, it's collective resilience," Carney said.
His speech to European lawmakers comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their ties amid a growing rift between Canada and its southern neighbor and main trading partner, the US.
Ties between Canada and the US have hit a historic low in recent months, with the North American neighbors locked in an escalating trade war since Carney and US President Donald Trump failed to agree on a deal this summer.
EU defends Canada alliance plan after Trump tariffs threat
On Wednesday, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was willing to make Canada its first-ever "associate member," days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc — a position that does not currently exist. Carney has acknowledged that "associate membership" still needs to be defined.
During her State of the EU address, von der Leyen said the bloc needed to adapt to an "openly hostile world" marked by aggressive power politics and "frayed relationships," the latter a clear nod to the turbulent ties between Brussels and Washington since Trump returned to the White House.
Prior to his visit this week, Carney had confirmed that he wanted to establish a "unique alliance" between Canada and the EU.
"We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths," the prime minister said.
Trump on Wednesday slammed the EU's plans to make Canada an associate member.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina. The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."
How did the US-Canada relationship come to this?
Ties between Canada and the US have plummeted since Trump began his second term in January 2025. He has targeted Canada with tariffs and suggested that the US could annex Canada as its 51st state.
Trump has also referred to Carney, as well as his predecessor as prime minister, Justin Trudeau, as the "governor" of Canada.
The growing rift has also seen Trump sign an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, a Great Lake between the US and Canada, to "Lake America."
