Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:05:31 UTC
18:05:31 KST

A UN fact-finding mission has determined there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind military strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in February that killed 120 children, and that these constituted war crimes.
The school strike, which killed 156 civilians including 120 children, involved a US Tomahawk missile that collapsed the roof of the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school, which the UN said was “clearly identifiable”, in Minab, Hormozgan province, on 28 February.
The Pentagon’s own secretive investigation into the incident is understood to have concluded several months ago amid reports that senior US commanders had been warned targeting data used during the war – including for the Minab strike – was dangerously outdated.
The second cited strike, on the same date, targeted a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd with a weapon that scattered tungsten pellets.
The UN fact-finding team said in a statement: “Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.”
The mission also found Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
The UN mission concluded that the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike.
Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”
In June the US president, Donald Trump, said “nobody” had purposely attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident.
The Pentagon has since elevated the inquiry but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over the strike on the sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
The UN mission found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel.
The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.
The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

Zelensky Names Anton Kovalsky Acting Prosecutor General
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Anton Kovalsky acting prosecutor general on Thursday, Sept. 17, following Ruslan Kravchenko’s dismissal amid a major corruption scandal and an escalating conflict with Ukraine’s anti-graft agencies.
According to presidential decree No. 946/2026, Zelensky ordered that Kovalsky assume temporary leadership of the Prosecutor General’s Office.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Appoint Anton Anatoliyovych Kovalsky acting Prosecutor General,” the decree reads.
The appointment came two days after 317 lawmakers voted to authorize Kravchenko’s dismissal and Zelensky formally removed him from office.
Kovalsky, 42, previously headed the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office. He now assumes control of one of Ukraine’s most powerful law enforcement bodies after more than a week of raids, allegations and public accusations between the country’s chief prosecutor and its independent anti-corruption institutions.
Who is Anton Kovalsky?
Kovalsky was born in Vinnytsia on May 12, 1984, according to his official biography published by the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office.
He graduated from the National Academy of the Prosecutor’s Office of Ukraine with a law degree in 2011 and began working in the prosecution service that year.
Kovalsky subsequently held several positions in the Vinnytsia regional prosecutor’s office. From September 2020 until October 2021, he served as deputy head of the Vinnytsia Regional Prosecutor’s Office.
Ukrainian Parliament Passes Key First-Reading Reforms for Parcel Tax and Small Business Bankruptcy
In November 2021, Kovalsky was appointed head of the Chernivtsi Regional Prosecutor’s Office, which he led until the middle of 2025.
He became head of the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office on July 1, 2025. His appointment as acting prosecutor general followed media reports that he and Dnipropetrovsk regional prosecutor Valerii Prykhozhanov were the principal candidates to replace Kravchenko.
Call center investigation reaches prosecutor’s office
The crisis began on Sept. 4, when the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) announced Operation Carthage.
The agencies said they had uncovered an alleged criminal organization operating within the Prosecutor General’s Office that protected fraudulent call centers targeting Ukrainians and foreign nationals.
Investigators alleged that a senior official in the prosecutor’s office helped the centers avoid prosecution, launder their earnings and continue operating in exchange for bribes.
Some call centers allegedly paid approximately $7,000 per month for protection. Hundreds of such operations were believed to employ tens of thousands of people across Ukraine, according to media reports cited by investigators.
NABU officers raided the Prosecutor General’s Office and detained a senior official suspected of involvement in the scheme. Investigators also released images showing bundles of cash reportedly seized during the operation.
Kravchenko denied involvement and said he had never instructed anyone to protect illegal call centers or used his authority as prosecutor general to facilitate their work.
He said the employee implicated in the investigation had been suspended and announced an internal review of the relevant department.
Kravchenko himself was not charged with a crime or officially named as a suspect.
Kravchenko resigns but remains in office
On Sept. 7, Zelensky held separate meetings with Kravchenko and the heads of NABU and SAPO.
Kravchenko subsequently submitted his resignation, describing it as a “conscious political decision” and saying he did not want the Prosecutor General’s Office to become an instrument of political confrontation.
However, he legally remained prosecutor general until parliament authorized his dismissal and the president signed the corresponding decree.
Three other senior prosecutors were dismissed on Sept. 8 as the investigation continued.
The confrontation intensified on Monday, Sept. 14, when Kravchenko announced that he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos.
Kravchenko accused Kryvonos of forging official documents and arranging a fictitious adoption in 2009, allegedly to receive an improper benefit and avoid legal responsibility.
He also claimed to have approved a separate notice against an unnamed person close to SAPO chief Oleksandr Klymenko.
Kravchenko alleged that Operation Carthage was intended to give anti-corruption investigators access to cases concerning their own officials and remove him from office.
NABU and SAPO rejected his allegations, describing them as another stage in a “systematic attack on independent anti-corruption bodies.” They said Kryvonos had not been formally served with a notice of suspicion.
The Prosecutor General’s Office later confirmed that no individual, including the head of an anti-corruption agency, had been formally notified of suspicion under the procedure required by Ukrainian law.
Foreign trip fuels political scandal
Hours after announcing his accusations against NABU and SAPO, Kravchenko left Ukraine in an official vehicle, according to media and Kyiv Post reports.
He said he was traveling abroad on official business for meetings with international partners and planned to raise concerns about the influence of Ukraine’s anti-corruption institutions.
His departure prompted public criticism because parliament had yet to consider his resignation and he remained the country’s serving prosecutor general.
Kyiv Post reported that Kravchenko crossed the Ukrainian-Polish border early on Sept. 14. Because he was still in office and traveled with the necessary authorization, border authorities had no legal basis to prevent him from leaving.
Anti-corruption activists alleged that his departure and accusations against NABU were connected, though no publicly verified evidence has established such an arrangement.
Zelensky and parliament remove Kravchenko
Later on Sept. 14, Zelensky suspended Kravchenko under Ukraine’s martial law legislation and submitted a formal request for parliament to approve his dismissal.
“This prosecutor general has only one path: to leave his post. That is exactly what I told him,” Zelensky said, urging lawmakers to act without delay.
On Tuesday, Sept. 15, the Verkhovna Rada supported Kravchenko’s removal with 317 votes. Zelensky then signed decree No. 932/2026 formally dismissing him.
Kovalsky’s appointment two days later places him at the head of an institution facing scrutiny over its relationship with NABU and SAPO, the handling of politically sensitive investigations and the alleged protection of fraudulent call centers.

Explainer-How Yemen's Houthis went from a small mountain militia to a big regional threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:03:12 UTC
18:03:12 KST

Explainer-How Yemen's Houthis went from a small mountain militia to a big regional threat
LONDON, Sept 17 - A lightning advance by Yemen's Houthi group has brought the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait under its control, making the once ragged highland militia a regional player with global clout.
This is how the group evolved into a formidable fighting force with Iranian support that can disrupt vital shipping and strike critical oil and gas facilities in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
WHO ARE THE HOUTHIS?
Starting out in the late 1990s as a Zaydi Shi'ite Muslim revival movement in north Yemen under the Houthi family, the group waged six wars against the government, building a strong local militia.
When Yemen's central state disintegrated during the 2011 Arab Spring, the Houthis took advantage, gaining more ground and developing a relationship with Iran and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah.
In 2014 they seized the capital Sanaa, ousting the government, and halting a Gulf-backed political transition.
That prompted a Saudi-led military intervention to support the government, leading to years of civil war that ground to a stalemate and a 2022 ceasefire.
The Houthis fired missiles and drones at Israel and international shipping in the Red Sea during Israel's war in Gaza from 2023-25 in what they said was solidarity with Palestinians.
With their closest ally Iran under attack by the United States since February 28, the Houthis have again been firing on Red Sea shipping as well as energy facilities inside Saudi Arabia.
WHAT IS THE MILITARY SITUATION INSIDE YEMEN?
The ceasefire collapsed over recent weeks and fighting resumed along the old front lines: Marib and Jawf governorates in the north, the city of Taiz in the southern highlands, Dhale in central Yemen and the Red Sea coastal strip known as the Tihama.
Last week the Houthis rapidly advanced into the southern Tihama, seizing first the port city of Mocha and then the rest of the Red Sea coastline and islands, putting their guns along the whole shore of the 12-mile-wide (19-km-wide) Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Those territorial gains make it easier to block shipping on the Red Sea, a key route for Saudi oil exports to Asia, and set up a potential launchpad for a new ground thrust towards Aden.
Saudi Arabia has conducted airstrikes in support of government-aligned forces.
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT HOUTHI MISSILES AND DRONES?
The group's ability to strike at distance with growing accuracy is why it now matters far beyond Yemen.
Houthi ballistic missiles have reached as far as Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,800 km) away, and one struck the perimeter of Israel's main airport in 2025. They have struck more frequently in Saudi Arabia, targeting cities and infrastructure. And Houthi missiles have been fired at ships in the Red Sea, halting traffic in the waterway.
Houthi drones have also struck repeatedly at Saudi targets and are now increasingly deployed on the battlefield — a big change from the last bout of civil-war fighting before the 2022 ceasefire.
WHAT EQUIPMENT HAVE THE HOUTHIS BEEN SEEN USING?
The Houthis have posted videos online since the start of September that show some of the military equipment they are using.
Videos show drones dropping different types of mortar and other bombs onto vehicles and opposition fighters, a rocket or missile launching, and precise munition hits on buildings and trucks at a camp, filmed by a high-resolution drone.
Other videos show Houthi forces on the ground including in pick-up trucks, some mounted with weapons, and on foot. Many fighters are shown in Arab robes rather than uniforms and carrying assault rifles. One video also showed a small group of fighters in camouflage uniforms. In some videos, fighters are shown with light and heavy machine guns and scoped rifles.
Videos showed them parading equipment captured from the Saudi-backed forces in the Tihama including armoured and combat vehicles, a tank, an artillery gun, satellite dish, small arms and a drone jamming device. But the videos do not generally show the captured hardware in action.
HOW DO THE HOUTHIS GET THEIR WEAPONS?
A United Nations panel of experts' report in 2025 said the Houthis had developed missile and drone technologies through both technical assistance and domestic manufacturing.
It found there had been widespread arms smuggling despite a U.N. arms embargo, including overland shipments across the Omani border as well as seaborne smuggling.
Items seized included drone control devices, equipment to receive ships' navigational data, drone engines and missile components. A 2023 U.N. report noted seizures of entire drones, ballistic missile components such as chemical precursors and Iranian-made anti-tank missiles.
Iranian sources have said Tehran has supplied its Houthi allies with both weapons and experts. However, Iran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of the U.N. arms embargo.
A 2025 assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies think tank found that while the Houthis had made advances in domestic arms production, they remained dependent on Iran for key technologies and advanced capabilities.
IN WHAT OTHER WAYS HAVE THE HOUTHIS DEVELOPED MILITARILY?
The U.N. panel of experts' report described Houthi military tactics as being focused on infiltration, drone attacks and shelling along front lines, and the laying of mines and other explosive devices.
They assessed that the Houthis had 350,000 fighters, partly through the recruitment of fighters under 18.
Training by Iran and Hezbollah has been critical for the Houthis, according to Yemen analysts. Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London, said such training had begun soon after the Arab Spring and had helped the Houthis transform from a militia to a more organised military force with changes to their structure and movements.
Hezbollah missile and drone operatives were present with the Houthis in 2025, the U.N. experts said. Iranian Qods Force general Abdolreza Shahlaei was also present in Yemen for some time working with the Houthis, the experts said. REUTERS

Fiji declares HIV a national crisis, 1 in 60 adults carry it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:03:00 UTC
18:03:00 KST

Fiji declares HIV a national crisis, 1 in 60 adults carry it
September 17, 2026
Fiji has declared HIV a national health crisis, pledging a "whole-of-government response to address the significant rise in HIV cases and protect communities across the country."
The Pacific island's government announced the move earlier this week, saying it had recorded 2,016 new HIV diagnoses in 2025 — 16 times the number recorded in 2019. The figures point to the virus spreading beyond high-risk groups like drug users and sex workers into the wider population.
Fiji said the known adult prevalence of the virus had almost tripled in five years in the country of a little more than 900,000 people.
What did Fiji's government say about HIV and its response?
"An estimated one in every 60 adults is now living with HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago," the government said.
"Among pregnant women, two in every 100 are living with HIV, while 59 babies were born with HIV in 2025, with 18 dying before their first birthday," it warned.
However, the government also said that expanded testing was helping health services reach more people and identify cases that might have previously gone undetected, noting a period of slower surveillance starting around a decade ago.
Health Minister Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu and four other revlevant Cabinet ministers would form a sub-committe to "help remove barriers to rapid action."
The administration based in the capital and port city Suva said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment — including rapid testing, prevention medecine for people at high risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs and free treatment for diagnosed HIV sufferers.
"The response is focused on protecting lives, improving access to health services and reducing stigma," the government said. "Fiji is also receiving support from international partners, including Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations."
It reminded people that testing was free and confidential across the country, saying "knowing your HIV status allows you to take informed steps to protect your health and others."
UNAIDS welcomes response, estimates less than half of Fiji's HIV sufferers know their status
UNAIDS in Geneva responded to the move on Wednesday, welcoming Fiji's decision to accelerate its response.
"Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," said UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima. "It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently."
The UN organization said that among Fijian cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use.
UNAIDS estimated that new infections increased 12-fold between 2010 and 2025 in Fiji. It also said that of an estimated 9,100 people living with the virus in 2025, "only 39% knew their HIV status and just 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment."
However, given medical advances in recent years and increased efficacy of treatments, it said that there was time to turn the tide.
"The national crisis declaration is a call for action, not fear. HIV is not transmitted through everyday contact, and people on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV," said UNAIDS' Eamonn Murphy. "Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic."
The country director for Fiji at UNAIDS, Renata Ram, told the AFP news agency that transmission rates started rising around 2019 when a group of "very high-risk" injecting drug users emerged, primarily in the sex worker community.
Pacific islands like Fiji have become transit hubs for drugs from Latin America and Asia destined for the lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand. This has also led to increased drug use on the islands themselves, often as a result of foreign crime syndicates paying their local associates with product.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Türkiye’s central bank on Thursday announced a series of measures aimed at strengthening the functioning of financial markets and managing Turkish lira liquidity.
The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) said it reviewed its liquidity facilities in light of recent developments in financial markets.
Under the measures, the bank will increase the amount of funding provided through one-week repo auctions when necessary, taking market liquidity conditions into account.
The CBRT will also revise banks’ borrowing limits at its Interbank Money Market based on the banking system’s existing balance sheet aggregates.
In a further step to facilitate access to liquidity, collateral haircuts applied in the central bank’s markets will be revised downward.
“The CBRT will closely monitor the liquidity conditions and take any additional measure when needed,” the bank said.

Babcock has reported trading in line with expectations across the first five months of its financial year, with demand across its core defence markets remaining robust and full year guidance unchanged, the company stated in a trading update ahead of its annual general meeting.
The update records continued strong performance in nuclear and aviation, the completion of the chief executive transition, a further £200 million share buyback launched in July, and a £250 million six-year sterling bond extending the group’s debt maturity profile.
Harry Holt, who became group chief executive on 31 July, said: “Since becoming CEO, I have focused on maintaining disciplined execution, engagement with customers, shareholders and partners, investing in our people and sharpening the Group’s priorities for sustainable long-term growth.
“We have started FY27 with good momentum and operational delivery, supported by strong demand across our core defence and nuclear markets, while in the near term the UK Government continues to confirm the details of the implementation of their Defence Investment Plan.”
He said: “In this era of global tension and the rapidly changing nature of warfare, our priorities are clear: deliver for our customers, strengthen programme performance, maintain capital allocation discipline and convert our strong market positions into long-term growth.”
David Lockwood, his predecessor, remains with the group supporting the succession until his retirement in January 2027. According to the company, Holt has progressed a number of organisational and leadership changes aligned with his priorities, aimed at driving growth and accelerating transformation delivery.
On submarine support, the update records that a six-month bridging agreement on the Future Maritime Support Programme with the Ministry of Defence has allowed the company to continue delivering increasing levels of critical naval base and nuclear submarine fleet support while the longer-term Gateway support agreement is finalised.
Among the contracts secured, Babcock was awarded a CAD$1.2 billion six-year extension, worth around £600 million, to lead and deliver Victoria-class submarine in-service support for the Royal Canadian Navy, with the potential to extend to the fleet’s expected end of life in the late 2030s. It was also selected as preferred bidder for an eight-year contract supporting operational combat training for the French Air Force, which the company describes as its first combat flight training contract supporting France’s warfighting readiness.
A follow-on contract from the Ministry of Defence covers keeping Ukraine’s gifted military vehicles, including Challenger 2 tanks, frontline-operational. In Australia, a follow-on five-year contract worth around £60 million was awarded in partnership with Saab for through-life engineering and supply chain support to the Royal Australian Navy’s Anzac-class frigates.
The company has announced a collaboration with Supacat to enhance its General Logistics Vehicle offering for the British Army’s Light Mobility Vehicle programme, intended to replace the retiring Land Rover fleet, which it says builds on the delivery of the final British Army Jackal from its production line.
On exports, the update notes that Poland floated off its first Miecznik-class frigate, based on the Arrowhead 140 design, which the company describes as further evidence of the knowledge and technology transfer programme supporting Polish sovereign skills and industrial capability, and a key component of its frigate licence and export proposition.
Babcock welcomed the Defence Investment Plan published in June, noting the £298 billion of spend over four years with further clarity on funding expected at Budget 2026. It also referred to Project Royal Oak, the £26 billion programme announced at Devonport in August covering £7 billion for the naval base and dockyard and £15 billion to regenerate HM Naval Base Clyde, stating that as sole through-life support provider for the nuclear submarine fleet and incumbent site operator at both bases it is well placed to benefit.
On the hybrid navy, supported by around £1.5 billion over four years, the company says it is working with HII and Arondite through ARMOR Force to combine and develop autonomous systems, modular technology and digital innovation.
The group expects to publish its half year results on 19 November, at which Holt said he looks forward to sharing more.

Hanwha and Lockheed Martin unveil new fighting vehicle at DVD 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:01:21 UTC
18:01:21 KST

Hanwha Aerospace and Lockheed Martin UK unveiled a Redback infantry fighting vehicle armed with a British-built 40mm turret at the British Army’s DVD 2026 exhibition, pairing an already fielded vehicle hull with a weapons system developed for a different British Army program.
The turret carries the CTA International 40mm cannon and, for the first time, has Lockheed Martin UK’s SkyKeeper command-and-control system built directly into it. Hanwha said it chose the 40mm cannon because of the range of ammunition types available for it, which the company said gives an infantry fighting vehicle more flexibility to handle different threats. Lockheed Martin UK integrated its turret onto the Redback hull, and the companies described the pairing as a low-risk option that NATO customers could adapt to their own requirements.
The 40mm cannon and its Lockheed Martin UK turret were originally developed for the British Army’s Ajax reconnaissance vehicle and for the Warrior Capability Sustainment Programme, an effort to upgrade 245 Warrior infantry fighting vehicles with the same weapon system. The Ministry of Defence canceled the Warrior program in 2020 and 2021, leaving roughly 245 of the cannons and turrets in storage without a vehicle to mount them on. Fitting the same hardware to the Redback gives Lockheed Martin UK a way to offer that existing stock to a different customer rather than developing a new turret from scratch.
SkyKeeper is a battle management system Lockheed Martin UK designed for ground-based air defense, counter-drone and counter-rocket, artillery and mortar missions. The company holds the system’s intellectual property, meaning its export is governed only by UK regulations rather than requiring separate approval from a foreign supplier. Building SkyKeeper into the turret itself extends the Redback’s role beyond typical infantry fighting vehicle duties into short-range air and drone defense.
The Redback itself is built on Hanwha’s K21 infantry fighting vehicle lineage and has already been adopted outside the UK. Australia selected the Redback in 2023 for its LAND 400 Phase 3 program, ordering 129 vehicles with heavy involvement from Australian suppliers. South Korea has also evaluated the Redback as a possible baseline for its next-generation infantry fighting vehicle, and Hanwha has demonstrated the platform to Poland and Romania as part of separate outreach efforts.
Hanwha and Lockheed Martin UK have not identified a specific program or customer for this turret-and-hull combination, describing it instead as a demonstration of how quickly an in-service platform can be matched with new capabilities.

‘Very messy eaters’: scientists solve the mystery of when black holes ‘burp’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:00:44 UTC
18:00:44 KST

Scientists have solved the mystery of when black holes “burp” – when the astronomical bodies launch jets after feeding on stars, blasting material enormous distances in space.
Black holes are objects so densely compact that beyond a certain point their gravity is too strong for light and matter to escape. This boundary of no return is known as the event horizon – the point at which escaping would require something to travel faster than the speed of light.
Despite their reputation as cosmic sinkholes, black holes are “actually very messy eaters”, said Dr Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University in Western Australia.
“You have to get really, really close to a black hole to get to the event horizon,” Goodwin, also a Forrest Research Foundation fellow, said. “Stars get destroyed further out than that.”
Scientists know from rare observations of stars being torn apart by black holes – a process that involves a stretching effect known as “spaghettification” – that “only about half of the star that gets too close to the back hole will end up eventually being swallowed by that black hole”, Goodwin said.
The other material is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows, sometimes so large they “can influence the entire evolution of a galaxy”, she said. “You can think of it as a black hole burp.”
But the timing of these burps had previously been mysterious to astrophysicists. “Sometimes it would happen a year after the black hole destroyed the star, sometimes it would happen three or five years after.”
In new research published in the journal Nature Astronomy, Goodwin and co-author Dr Andrew Mummery from the Institute for Advanced Study believe they have found the answer, using radio telescopes to study 20 tidal disruption events – instances where stars are eaten by supermassive black holes.
“Radio is the only frequency where we can watch the jets and outflows as they’re moving outwards,” Goodwin said.
They found that supermassive black holes – which range in size from hundreds of thousands to billions of times the mass of our sun – fire off powerful jets in two distinct phases in their feeding cycle.
The first occurs when the black hole is feeding at very high rates. The second occurs hundreds to thousands of days after the star is first torn apart, when the feeding rate drops to about 2% of the maximum rate at which a black hole can swallow material.
That same threshold is already known to trigger burps from stellar-mass black holes, much smaller bodies about 10 to 50 times the mass of our sun.
The research showed that black holes appeared to release jets at the same point in their feeding cycle regardless of size, Goodwin said. She said the finding would enable scientists to precisely predict when such jets would be released, narrowing observation windows and freeing up precious telescope time.
She added: “We can really start to understand not just when the jets are launched, but also how strong they are and if that is then dependent on the black hole properties.”
Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “We are still trying to untangle the very fundamentals of the most extreme objects in the universe – supermassive black holes.”
Webb said the study showed “that supermassive black holes behave rather predictably at two distant periods in their evolution” and the researchers had “tie[d] this back to what we’ve seen previously on the much smaller scale stellar-mass black holes”.

The 'Canaduropean' Union: Canada an associate member of the EU?

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, September 17: Will Canada become an associate member of the EU? Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea in a speech but did not give any details about what it would entail. The press is reacting with scepticism. Also, Le Monde profiles some of the 8,000 people who died during France's summer heatwave. Scientists observe a humpback whale mourning her dead calf for the first time. And Singapore wants to pay citizens to stop scrolling and start reading.
If it goes ahead, Canada could be the first associate member of the European Union. According to Euroactiv, the European media outlet, Ursula von der Leyen put forward the proposal in her State of the Union speech yesterday, specifying that the alliance is not against anyone else but for both parties’ common strengths. The outlet also reminds us that von der Leyen made a similar bid for Ukraine earlier this year, which received a lukewarm response from EU member states. French communist paper l’Humanité, responded wryly: "Ursula von der Leyen doesn’t have oil but she does have ideas."
For the international press, US President Donald Trump clearly has pushed Canada into the EU’s arms. According to the New York Times, it is a sign of the "knock-on effects of Trump’s brand of diplomacy" which often involves threatening countries that were once considered US allies. The paper adds that even if the EU’s gesture ends up being symbolic, it shows how Trump is upending global relationships in ways that will be hard to undo. The editors of Belgian daily Le Soir hails the “new trans-Atlantic union” – noting that it comes at a time where inside the bloc, anti-EU sentiment is rising while, outside the bloc, warmongering is rising. British daily The Guardian wonders if this proposed membership could be a blueprint for future EU-UK relations. In any case, the Guardian says that the bigger the ambitions for relations with the EU, the better. In Canada’s case, the potential alliance offers rich supplies of minerals and rare earths.
Meanwhile, the Canadian press remains very sceptical. Le Devoir wonders what Canada would gain from this alliance. The leader of the opposition already denounced what he calls a threat to Canadian sovereignty. The Globe and Mail note bitterly that Canada already signed a trade deal with the EU ten years ago but 10 of the 27 members have still not ratified it.
The French paper Le Monde is looking back at this summer’s relentless series of deadly heatwaves. According to French public health authorities, this summer’s heatwaves were the hottest in 126 years and caused more than 8,100 deaths. In this interactive article entitled, "The Heatwave Casualties" – Le Monde puts a face to those who died even if, it says, the word heat-related does not appear on their death certificate. Several elderly people died but some as young as 18, including a young man who drowned while swimming in the Seine River.
Scientists say they’ve witnessed the first phenomenon of a humpback whale mother grieving for her stillborn calf. It’s the first detailed scientific study on the subject, according to the Australian academic website The Conversation. It took place last July off the east coast of Australia. For more than an hour, the mother whale returned to the same spot, suggesting she was grieving her dead calf. This sort of behaviour has been observed in the past in toothed whales – like the orca – but never before in untoothed or baleen whales – like the humpback. This is possibly because dead newborn baleen whales often sink quickly, making it difficult to observe such behaviour.
Finally, from you – Singapore is taking some drastic measures to get people off their phones. The Times reports that the country is planning to pay people to read as part of a government initiative aiming to mitigate online content. Readers who read for 15 minutes receive 20 virtual coins. They need 1000 to earn one Singapore dollar which means you need to read 12.5 hours to earn a dollar. The irony is that it is all logged online.

Finland and Sweden plan joint maritime drone surveillance operation in Baltic Sea
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:00:16 EEST
18:00:16 KST

Finland and Sweden are exploring the possibility of jointly procuring maritime drones, or unmanned surveillance vessels, to improve security in the Baltic Sea.
Commander of the Finnish Navy, Tuomas Tiilikainen, announced the plans on Wednesday after meeting with his Swedish counterpart in Suomenlinna.
Unmanned surveillance vessels, also known as Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs), are uncrewed vessels that perform monitoring, intelligence and inspection tasks.
"In practice, a vessel, in this case a surface drone that looks like a sailboat, has a few sensors and a camera radar with which it transmits situational awareness to our operations centres, and accordingly we can identify unknown vessels at sea or initiate identification missions," Tiilikainen explained.
He added that the USVs could begin patrolling Finnish waters before the end of this year.
"At this point, it's probably the case that we will jointly procure this kind of capacity for our use and share that resource with each other temporarily, so that both [nations] benefit from this joint procurement", Tiilikainen said.
Surveillance operation in the Gulf of Finland
In addition to the plans to jointly procure USVs, the Swedish navy will also begin deploying a maritime corvette in the Gulf of Finland to monitor Finland's territorial waters in a short-term operation.
This support from Sweden means Finland's navy can concentrate its efforts on the eastern Gulf of Finland, where drones could potentially stray into Finnish airspace.
"In certain circumstances, it's good that we can concentrate our own capability on the southeastern corner and receive support for maritime surveillance in another direction from our allies," Tiilikainen said.
The Swedish vessel will be placed under the command of the Finnish Defence Forces for the duration of the operation and it will transmit information to Finland's maritime operations centre.

Flock Once Touted Its Cameras as ‘Made in the USA.’ Now It’s Not So Clear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated—product has become more of a mystery.
For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew.
The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes, share footage with immigration authorities, and follow the movements of pedestrians.
But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved.
Flock’s cameras largely rely on suppliers around the world that provide non-custom parts, which are also used in products from other companies. “Our value is in the aggregation and the packaging of all of these things … in a nice waterproof, consumer-friendly device,” Langley said in one marketing video from 2021.
Import records collected by ImportGenius show the company has been increasingly bringing “commodity” cameras, radar systems, and other components over from Primax Electronics in Thailand. Primax is based in Taiwan, but has manufacturing facilities in China, Thailand, and elsewhere.
“My understanding is that these are components, but it looks like Primax manufactures whole security camera solutions,” ImportGenius’ analyst Lynn Hughes says. “Quite a few shipments include ‘Radar’ in the product description which might be related to the radar sensor pods they’re attaching to their cameras.”
Flock didn’t respond to most of the detailed questions WIRED asked for this story, though it did provide some general information. “All products that Flock builds are National Defense Authorization Act compliant,” Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said in an email, referring to a US law that effectively bars government contractors from using parts made by a handful of Chinese tech companies over security concerns.
Cris van Pelt, creator of the anti-Flock advocacy project Have I Been Flocked, says that while where the cameras are made may have relatively minor implications for US communities, the lack of transparency about their origins underscores a broader problem.
“It all speaks to the fact that there is no real oversight, and that tens of thousands of literal and figurative black boxes are being installed on American roads,” van Pelt says. “If any part of the supply chain is compromised, we would never know. That’s a much bigger problem than where the final product is assembled.”
“Aggregation”
The earliest Flock prototypes were made using cameras ripped out of Android phones bought on Alibaba, which were then attached to batteries and soldered onto a solar panel, Langley recalled in one video. The goal was to prove that a useful device could be created from parts collectively costing between $200 to $300. (WIRED reported earlier this week that Flock’s cameras continue to use smartphone-style processors and leave significant data unencrypted.)
As Flock began securing contracts with homeowners associations, it shifted into a corporate office that also doubled as an assembly line. Langley described the setup as fun, but also unprofessional and arduous—pallets of parts shipped in from China had to be dragged a quarter of a mile through the building multiple times a week.
Around 2020, Flock moved its assembly line to a WeWork-style warehouse facility in Atlanta, according to a marketing video produced by the space’s operator. A handful of Flock employees cranked out as many cameras as they could, with engineers assembling the main camera device and less technical staff attaching solar panels and mounts.
Rather than opening up warehouses, Flock stored cameras in self-storage locations across the country for its installation crews to retrieve as needed, according to two former employees. One described the system as “janky,” noting it may have left cameras more vulnerable to tampering than they would have been if kept in more secure locations operated by Flock itself.
In marketing materials from 2019, Flock touted its cameras as “manufactured in the United States.” The following year, it said they were “made in the USA.” In 2021, it got more specific, telling potential customers that assembly was done by “Flock Safety in Atlanta, GA.”
Over the next couple of years, Flock began shifting final assembly to contract facilities in North Carolina and Wisconsin operated by East West Manufacturing and Plexus, according to a person familiar with the matter. It also opened up its own warehouses.
The person says Flock wanted to keep assembly in North America, both to ease security concerns—particularly about potential Chinese surveillance—and to keep factories close enough that it could quickly customize products in response to customer needs.
A Flock marketing brochure from 2023 described its cameras as “designed & manufactured in the U.S.” By 2024, Flock’s manufacturing partners were capable of producing 500 cameras a day, a ten-fold leap from several years prior, one of the people familiar with matter says. Parts still largely came from Asia.
In mid-May, as backlash against the startup swelled, East West removed reference to Flock from a list of case studies on its website, according to archived versions on the Wayback Machine. (A video from East West promoting its work for Flock shared on LinkedIn in late 2021 remains online.)
East West and Plexus didn’t respond to requests for comment.
WIRED was unable to determine where Flock’s cameras are assembled now. A Flock marketing presentation from this year does not mention a location.
In July, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration cited Flock for allegedly failing to promptly report a June incident in which an employee was hospitalized for a leg amputation, according to records from the workplace regulator. The records indicate the injury happened at a Flock “audio and video equipment manufacturing” site in Houston, Texas. It’s possible that the location is actually the site of a camera, and the injury came during an installation or maintenance procedure. Flock and OSHA did not respond to WIRED’s requests asking for clarification about the nature of the site and what work may occur there.
Flock is contesting a proposed penalty of about $9,500, saying it reported the injury quickly after learning about it.
Even if Flock’s manufacturing supply chain remains in the United States, it may do little to calm bipartisan backlash against the company.
“Domestic manufacturing is no substitute for accountability over how these systems are built, sold, and used,” says Matthew Guariglia, senior policy analyst at the civil liberties advocacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation. "The multi-billion dollar industry churning out mass surveillance technology is not safer or more acceptable based on where it is assembled.”
Flock’s top competitors vary in terms of how much they disclose about their manufacturing. Motorola Solutions has described its license plate cameras as being assembled at its own facility in Richardson, Texas. Axon has said little about where its Outpost cameras are produced, but has noted it assembles other products in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Motorola and Axon didn’t respond to requests for comment.
US-Made Drone
Flock has been more upfront about the manufacturing of its new surveillance drone. Last October, it announced the opening of its own facility in Smyrna, Georgia to assemble drones and solar panels, as well as refurbish various other products. US law now largely restricts foreign-made drones, including the models from China-based DJI that Flock has been deploying. No similar US rules apply to license plate cameras.
It’s unclear how well the Smyrna operation is faring. Flock repeatedly postponed the timeline for launching its first so-called Alpha drone, which finally “hit the field” in May, according to a company executive. This year, Flock told Berkeley, California officials it would swap out DJI drones for the US model “within two years.”
Lewbel, the Flock spokesperson, says it continues to “bring more Alpha drones online.”
Additional reporting by Caroline Haskins.

Battle for the Atlantic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:58:50 BST
17:58:50 KST

Battle for the Atlantic
First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff General Sir Gwyn Jenkins delivered a speech at Admiralty House, Department of Naval Research.
Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.
Thank you for joining us, and my thanks to the Department for Naval Research for organising today’s symposium.
As we gather here at Admiralty House, the importance of sea power will not be lost on any of you.
That is because our history has been shaped by the sea.
Because our prosperity, security and influence have for centuries depended on our ability to master it, protect what moves across it, and deny its advantages to those who threaten us.
That’s why my speech today is focused on the Atlantic.
Not simply as a vast body of water, or a theatre of past conflict, but as a foundation of Britain’s security.
Eighty years ago, Britain and her allies fought the longest campaign of the Second World War at sea.
It was fought by sailors, merchant seamen, aircrew, dockyard workers, engineers, scientists and codebreakers…
By men and women who kept Britain alive as Europe fell under Nazi occupation.
Convoys crossed a hostile ocean in atrocious weather, under air attack and constant U-boat threat.
They carried the food, fuel, raw materials, weapons and reinforcements on which our national survival depended.
In 1941, Churchill named this struggle the Battle of the Atlantic.
It was the prospect of losing this Battle – not the Blitz, not the threat to the Empire in the East – that truly frightened him.
As Churchill observed later in his memoirs, Britain’s ability to “carry on the war, or even keep ourselves alive,” rested fundamentally “on our mastery of the ocean routes and the free approach and entry to our ports.”
Churchill attached such significance to the Atlantic because he understood something important.
The sea is not peripheral to Britain – it is existential.
If those maritime arteries had been severed during the War…
Had Britain lost the Atlantic…
Our life support would have been switched off.
We would have struggled to cling on before the Americans joined the fight…
Europe would not have been liberated…
And victory would have been impossible.
That does not diminish the role of our other services, whose contribution to the war was also vital.
Yesterday, we marked the 86th anniversary of the Battle of Britain, a campaign that denied the Luftwaffe air superiority and was also integral to our survival.
And as the son of an RAF crypto mechanic, I know how important air power was and remains to our nation.
But the point I am making is this:
Without the Royal Navy and the RAF, who is to say whether Hitler would have abandoned Operation Sealion and switched his focus to invading Russia instead.
Who is to say whether the Army would have been able to campaign in North Africa, the Med or in mainland Europe.
Sea power not only sustained us during the War.
It arguably saved us.
Lose the war at sea and you lose the war.
That was the warning of Admiral Pound, the First Sea Lord of the day – and it remains true now.
If we are to prevail in the Atlantic again, we must strengthen our warfighting readiness and rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation.
Not because history repeats itself perfectly.
It doesn’t.
But because the factors that made the Atlantic decisive eighty years ago remain decisive today.
The world may have changed beyond recognition – but our dependence on the Atlantic has only grown since.
Almost all our trade moves by sea, and America remains by far our biggest trading partner.
Almost all our energy, food, raw materials and exports flow through maritime routes.
Beneath the waves, our nuclear deterrent protects the nation.
Undersea cables carry almost all data, transactions, and communications on which modern life depends.
In all these areas, the Atlantic is critical.
During the war, the British people understood that a submarine attack on an allied convoy hundreds of miles away had direct consequences at home.
But today, we have reached a dangerous paradox…
The sea, the Atlantic, has arguably never mattered more to Britain.
We are certainly much more reliant on it than we were in the 1930s.
And yet it has become increasingly invisible in the public’s mind.
Supermarket shelves are filled, homes are heated, money moves instantly and the internet turbocharges our modern lives.
We have made this huge progress seem effortless.
But it was not effortless.
It was earned. It was fought for. We have continuously defended it.
And if that defence fails, the consequences will be felt quickly in every household, every business and every department of state.
Our adversaries understand that.
They understand our dependence on the sea and the seabed.
They understand that the Atlantic is not empty space.
It is strategic terrain: the bridge between North America, Europe and with the world.
The route through which NATO reinforcement would move.
The space through which our trade, energy, data and deterrence are sustained.
That is why the lessons of the War remain so important.
In the 1940s, the question was whether Britain could stay connected to the industrial, economic and military strength of North America and its Empire.
Today, in an age of missiles, cyber, space surveillance, and rapid technological change, we also face added challenges, because the seabed has become a new arena of contest.
Uncrewed systems are changing how we fight, advancing at a rate many nations are struggling to keep pace with.
Information is moving faster than it has ever moved before.
And yet, many of the fundamentals remain the same.
The Atlantic is the same body of water…
We are still an island…
We still rely on it to move the goods, fuel and commodities we rely on…
And our most important alliances are still trans-Atlantic.
That is why this issue reaches beyond uniform.
The Atlantic is a military, industrial, diplomatic and economic challenge – and an opportunity.
That is why we need a whole-nation effort if we are to continue to defend it.
History shows us this.
The original Battle of the Atlantic was not won by one decisive action.
It was won by cumulative advantage: better intelligence, faster shipbuilding, improved tactics, effective air cover, convoy discipline and a willingness to learn under pressure.
It was won by leadership, the spirit to fight and the urge to win.
The same approach is required today, but with different tools and in a different context.
We should not allow the complexity of modern technology to muddy what is a simple task.
We must know what is happening in the Atlantic, protect what matters, keep open the sea lanes, and convince any adversary that the cost of coercion or aggression would outweigh any possible gain.
That is the test of warfighting readiness.
Can we fight tonight? Can we sustain the fight tomorrow? And can we adapt faster than our adversaries?
That is the standard by which the Navy must be judged.
The Battle of the Atlantic demonstrated another enduring lesson.
There is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.
No nation secured the Atlantic alone in the 1940s, and no nation will do so now.
Victory depended on Allied integration: navies, merchant fleets, air forces, intelligence, scientists and industry working to a common purpose.
That same principle underpins NATO today.
In any major crisis, NATO’s ability to reinforce Europe depends upon secure access across the Atlantic.
It remains central to collective defence.
That is why the Royal Navy’s role in the Atlantic cannot be separated from NATO’s wider mission.
Our task is to contribute to collective deterrence, support the movement of Allied forces, protect critical infrastructure, maintain awareness and ensure freedom of manoeuvre.
This is also why partnerships matter.
Whether through NATO, bilateral relationships or the Joint Expeditionary Force, our security is strengthened when we operate alongside allies who share our interests and values.
For the United Kingdom, this is both a responsibility and an opportunity.
We are a nuclear power, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a founding member of NATO and the framework nation for the JEF.
We are still one of the most powerful navies in the world.
Our geography, history and alliances give us both a particular stake in the North Atlantic and the ability to act with others at scale.
Which leads me onto the third lesson of the War: our northern flank matters.
The Atlantic cannot be understood without understanding the High North, because control of the ocean has always been closely linked to control of its northern approaches.
The consequences of losing control were painfully evident in 1940, when Norway’s defeat gave the Nazis control of the coastline and deep-water fjords from which they were able to threaten allied shipping lanes in the Atlantic.
Later, the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap became integral in the Cold War.
And today, its relevance remains undiminished.
The Norwegian Sea, the Arctic and the northern approaches are not distant theatres.
They are the gateway to our backyard; they form our open sea border with Russia.
They are where British security, NATO and European stability come together.
And it is also where the JEF makes an increasingly important contribution.
For more than a decade, the UK has led ten like-minded nations that are able to respond quickly to threats in the High North, North Atlantic and Baltic.
It complements NATO, but it also gives us the speed, political alignment and geographic focus to seize the initiative early.
As First Sea Lord, I have been determined to make that partnership stronger.
That is why we have been working with the JEF members on a new Northern Navies agreement, which we will finalise this year.
It will move us beyond episodic activity to a persistent, integrated maritime force.
Navies that train together, exercise together, plan together and, if necessary, fight together.
It requires common systems, shared digital networks, common doctrine, shared logistics and stockpiles…
This isn’t just about fighting together. It’s about building a common British and Norwegian frigate force.
It’s about ensuring a Danish frigate can seamlessly takeover from a British warship in the Atlantic, while also taking control of our flotilla of uncrewed ships and sensors that will remain in position for months on end.
This is how we turn collective strength into credible deterrence.
This is how we create a Vanguard for NATO.
A family of Northern Navies, led by the UK, stronger than the sum of its parts.
Making the Hybrid Navy real, with allies.
The reason why we need this is simple: the greatest threat to our security today is Russia.
That threat is felt most acutely in the maritime domain – in the North Atlantic, in the High North.
Russia retains advanced submarines that are increasingly difficult to track, long-range precision weapons, and specialist systems designed to operate deep underwater.
It is increasingly active in our domain, and we are spending increasing amounts of time and resource monitoring Russian vessels and the shadow fleet.
On average, two Royal Navy warships are now being deployed every week for this purpose.
Russia is probing, testing, and mapping.
It seeks advantage in the grey zone, particularly around the critical undersea infrastructure on which modern societies rely.
And among Ukraine’s western allies, Russia considers us to be one of its greatest foes.
We know that Russia is probing us for weakness.
And we are facing threats…in a way we have not been since the Cold War.
That does not mean we are returning to the days before the Berlin Wall fell.
Nor am I saying that war is inevitable. There are strong parallels, but this is not the 1930s.
The circumstances are different, the technologies have changed, and the context is more complex.
But many of the underlying challenges remain.
That is why the Royal Navy continues to invest in anti-submarine warfare, underwater surveillance, maritime aviation and Allied integration.
This is why we are building the Hybrid Navy.
This is not about seeking confrontation.
It is about preventing it through credible capability, strong alliances, presence and the ability to respond immediately when required.
During the Second World War, German U-boats sought to isolate Britain by attacking the merchant shipping.
Today, the form of the threat is different, but the significance of the underwater domain has grown rather than diminished.
Critical undersea infrastructure is now part of the strategic landscape. Cables, pipelines, sensors and energy networks connect nations, markets and command systems.
They are difficult to monitor, hard to repair at speed and increasingly integral to national resilience.
The day that the UK declared war on Germany, the allies severed its transatlantic telegraph cables.
I pray it does not happen, but were we to go to war again, we know our enemies will try to use the same playbook against us.
That is why protection of the High North, the Atlantic, and of our underwater CNI is not just about naval capability.
It also rests on intelligence, industry, law enforcement, commercial partnerships and close allied coordination.
It is a national endeavour.
The Royal Marines Commandos also play a crucial role in that effort.
The Atlantic campaign was never fought at sea alone.
Its outcome depended upon control of key geography around the wider Atlantic basin, and that lesson remains directly relevant to the northern flank today.
The ability to monitor, secure and influence activity across the maritime domain requires more than ships and submarines.
It requires forces able to operate where sea and land intersect, to work with allies in difficult terrain, and to create advantage before a crisis becomes a conflict.
That is where the Commandos make a uniquely important contribution.
Tough, resilient and resourceful, honed for some of the toughest environments on the planet, they are the tip of the spear when it comes to NATO’s strike forces.
And it is through them that we help create conditions for maritime operations to succeed.
The strategic logic would be familiar to the Commandos of the Second World War.
In May 1940, the Royal Marines led the pre-emptive occupation of Iceland, denying Germany a potential Atlantic base and enabling Allied ships and aircraft to support the convoys.
At St Nazaire, in March 1942, Commandos destroyed the dry dock that could have supported Tirpitz and other German warships raiding those convoys.
And months later, Royal Marines paddled by night into occupied Bordeaux during Operation Frankton, damaging vital Axis shipping and disrupting the blockade runners that sustained Germany’s war effort.
Today, the Commando Force may have undergone a generational transformation – but it remains just as important to our success.
The Royal Marines are part of an integrated fighting system. They have also evolved over the past decade because modern warfare demands adaptation.
The more we integrate, the more we adapt, the greater our advantage over our adversaries.
That logic also sits at the heart of the most radical and far-reaching reform we are undertaking currently: the move to a Hybrid Navy.
The maritime battlespace is becoming increasingly distributed, connected and data-driven.
Our future advantage will come from integrated networks combining ships, submarines, aircraft, autonomous systems, sensors, data and people.
Ukraine has shown how quickly maritime warfare can change.
In the Black Sea, uncrewed systems and long-range strikes have destroyed a Russian fleet that once seemed dominant.
In the Gulf and the Red Sea, drones and missiles have shown how quickly global trade can be disrupted.
The lesson is not that traditional platforms no longer matter.
It is that it is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone.
A ship operating alone is now vulnerable.
But a ship commanding a network of large uncrewed escorts, drones and autonomous sensors…that is a different proposition.
That’s why we must blend old and new. Crewed and uncrewed.
We need a connected fighting force.
This is about changing how we generate combat power.
It will make the Fleet bigger, more lethal, harder to target and knock out of the fight, while also allowing us to adapt faster and impose more dilemma on the enemy.
That is the Hybrid Navy in a nutshell.
Unsurprisingly, we are shaping it around the Atlantic…
Through our Atlantic Series…
Atlantic Bastion is about defending the UK’s continuous at sea deterrent and the critical national infrastructure on which our country, economy and allies depend.
It is the creation of a defensive net across the North Atlantic: crewed and uncrewed ships, drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and weapons working above, on and below the sea to detect, deter and, if necessary, neutralise hostile activity.
Atlantic Shield is about protecting the homeland, the Fleet and our allies from drones, hypersonic weapons and ballistic threats through modern air and missile defence.
And Atlantic Strike is about giving us the ability to hit harder, from greater distance, if an adversary attacks us.
These are the practical building blocks of a new way of fighting.
A new Atlantic Fleet.
The objective is clear: to create a force that can detect threats earlier, respond faster, strike more precisely, survive in the most contested conditions and integrate better with allies.
Yes it is radical, yes we are early adopters, and yes there are sceptics.
But let me be clear: the Hybrid Navy is not opional.
And nor is the need to change our relationship with industry.
During the War we did not just outfight Nazi Germany; we innovated faster and built ships and aircraft at a pace the Reich simply could not match.
The same must be true again now if we are to prevail.
That means we have to move at the speed of the threat.
Software can change a system overnight. Commercial technology can reach the battlefield in days. Our procurement, testing and adoption cycles must reflect that reality.
That means more experimentation, more courage to fail quickly, and the ability to scale what works.
Yes, that creates more risk.
But as First Sea Lord, the only risk that really keeps me up at night is being asked to go to war – and losing.
That is the one risk I will not accept – because my job is not to lose.
My job is to win.
So, as we look to the future, what more must we do?
First, we must not lose focus on the here and now.
We must keep the Atlantic open.
We must continue to protect shipping, reinforcement routes, subsea cables, energy infrastructure and the deterrent.
We are recapitalising the entire nuclear enterprise for the first time since its creation.
We are growing the fleet, with 13 new frigates..
Six command ships for the Hybrid Navy…
Fleet solid support ships…
Four amphibious transport ships for our Commandos…
Two new Astute-class boats, four new Dreadnought-class submarines, and up to 12 next generations SSNs.
We have a Defence Investment Plan, unlocking our uncrewed systems and the Atlantic Series.
But there are plenty of obstacles that risk slowing us down.
We must be relentless in identifying and removing them.
Second, we must invest in people.
Technology changes the character of warfare, but it does not win wars.
Our people remain decisive – and it is leadership, leadership excellence, that wins wars.
War will always remain a contest of human will. That is why we must equip our people with the skills and leadership tools to enable them to win at all levels.
They will have to command distributed forces, fight with uncrewed systems, and make decisions under pressure.
Third, we must act with urgency.
The generation that won the Battle of the Atlantic did so because they learned faster than the enemy.
We are seeing Ukraine do this right now on the front line – and we must do the same.
Perhaps most importantly of all, we must reconnect with the public.
The Battle of the Atlantic still resonates because people understood the connection between events at sea and the war writ large.
We are a maritime nation, an Island Nation – and it’s time we remembered it.
We should make that case with confidence, because many of the qualities that made Britain a maritime power remain.
London is still the global hub of maritime services, insurance, law and finance.
British expertise still shapes the rules and contracts on which global trade depends.
And our ports, shipyards and maritime businesses remain part of an ecosystem that few countries can match.
From the frigates being built on the Clyde and at Rosyth…
To the new Dreadnought submarines at Barrow…
The fleet support at Birkenhead…
Marine engineering at Tyne and Wear and advanced manufacturing in Cumbria…
Investment in the maritime is helping fuel our northern powerhouse.
Across the country, we have a thriving maritime sector worth £224 billion to the UK economy.
It supports 1.7 million jobs and 8,000 businesses….
And that’s before you consider the untapped potential.
That is why we must also reject any idea that the only future for the Royal Navy is one of decline.
Of course, the United States and China operate at a scale others cannot match.
But that does not mean Britain should lower its sights.
We can still be the greatest naval power in Europe, and one of the world’s most powerful navies.
We should not forget just how important our capabilities are, nor the influence and credibility that gives us among our allies.
From aircraft carriers to F35s…
To SSBNs and SSNs…
From frigates and destroyers to the Royal Marines.
Through the Hybrid Navy, we also have a chance to lead the global maritime autonomy race, creating military advantage while generating new economic growth.
We must match this with a serious shipbuilding strategy: ships built in Britain, for us, and exported from Britain, for our allies.
That must surely be the vision: a stronger Navy, a stronger economy, and a stronger maritime nation.
The Battle of the Atlantic was a battle for survival.
It proved that Britain’s ability to determine its own future depended on our naval power, on our ability to remain connected to the wider world.
That lesson endures.
The threat has evolved, the High North has regained strategic prominence, and the seabed has become contested.
New vulnerabilities have emerged, and so have new opportunities.
But one truth remains constant: we depend on the sea.
The Royal Navy’s task is to ensure that, with our allies, with industry, and with the whole maritime nation behind us, Britain is ready.
Ready to lead. Ready to fight. Ready to win.
The Battle of the Atlantic is one of the most important chapters in our history.
And when our own history is written, I am certain the Atlantic will prove decisive once again.
Thank you.

EU adopts KIDS Act restricting social media access for under 13s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:56:28 UTC
17:56:28 KST

The European Commission on Thursday adopted the EU KIDS Act to restrict social media access for children under 13 and set an EU-wide minimum age of 15 for minors to open their own accounts.
 
"The proposal prohibits social media platforms from accessing children under the age of 13 and sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an account of their own at the age of 15," a written statement noted.
 
The act proposes that children can create personal social media accounts only from the age of 15, while allowing parents or guardians of children aged 13 and 14 to set up “mini accounts” that the children can access through their guardians’ accounts.
 
"This would allow them to access age-appropriate social media and video-sharing platforms," the statement added.
 
The proposal also stressed the need for services available on the mini accounts to be designed with safeguards, "such as limited social contacts and limited screen time up to one hour per day."
 
While prohibiting access to social media for children aged between 3 and 13, it allows access to "specially designed child-friendly video-sharing services" through accounts managed by their guardian.
 
Platforms would also be required to provide parents or guardians with easy-to-use tools to limit children’s access to adult devices to child-friendly services and cap their use at one hour per day.
 
The act also imposes obligations on online services, including social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, AI companions, and chatbots, to protect users under 18.
 
It aims to ban addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds "dragging minors into ‘rabbit holes' of harmful content." It also seeks prohibition of infinite scroll, reward tricks, nighttime push notifications, and unsolicited contact from strangers.
 
"In addition, AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default and cannot simulate interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency," the statement further underscored.
 
Minors’ profiles would be private by default, with geolocation, camera, and microphone access disabled.
 
The platforms are also called on to offer easy ways for minors to block and mute users, effective time-management tools, and safe recommender systems.
 
Online services and app stores will also be required to use age assurance tools, while the commission offered the use of an EU age verification app, "which does not retain identity documents or biometric data, thereby meeting the highest privacy-preserving safeguards."
 
"The proposal reverses the ‘burden of proof,' making the providers of very large online platforms responsible for proving that their services are ‘safe by design'," the statement added.
 
The platforms, thus, will be obliged to submit a compliance plan to the commission, and to an independent auditor that has to thoroughly assess the new service, feature, or functionality.
 
'It is time for EU to act'
 
Speaking at a news briefing on the Act, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pointed out how too many children get exposed too early to an online world "they are not ready to navigate."
 
"Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children's well-being and development in mind. Platforms are designed to capture attention," she noted.
 
She described such addictive features as part of business models designed to keep children online and monetize their attention.
 
"Parents cannot compete or keep up against algorithms, and they should not have to. (...) It is time for the European Union to act," von der Leyen underscored.
 
She further cautioned that the proposed age limits would not let the tech companies "off the hook" for the platforms' content.
 
"Platforms have been playing fast and loose with our children's mental health. Now we are reversing the burden of proof. Now they have to prove to us that they are safe," von der Leyen said.
 
She reaffirmed that they are changing the years-long practice of platforms denying their harms and trying to avoid prescriptive rules, instead of setting rules at their own pace.
 
"So instead of authorities proving harm after after the fact, the biggest platforms must submit detailed child safety plans in advance, and that means again that safety will come first," von der Leyen added.
 
She noted that the Act "puts the parents in the driving seat, and the burden of proving safety on the platforms where it belongs."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Awarded a Bib Gourmand in the Michelin Guide Taiwan for two consecutive years, Tableau by Craig Yang is helmed by Chef Craig Yang (楊子毅), a native of a traditional North Coast banquet-catering family.
By marrying Taiwanese banquet culture with refined French techniques, Yang continually reinterprets his local culinary heritage. This season, Tableau continues its “New Chapters of Taiwanese Flavor” series with a tasting menu titled "Memory."
Inspired by the five French mother sauces, the menu creatively re-envisions familiar staples, such as banquet abalone salad and Taiwanese night market steak — through local condiments like mayonnaise, Wu-Wei sauce, and A1 steak sauce.
Yang’s culinary foundation spans traditional banquet catering, Japanese diner chains, and high-end fine dining kitchens. Drawing inspiration from his daily rides to local markets, he uncovered striking parallels between everyday condiments and classical French sauces.
Rather than forcing direct one-to-one pairings, "Memory" explores the intersection of both culinary cultures to evoke shared flavor memories.
The experience begins with an unlisted "five happiness platter," followed by mayonnaise abalone tomato soup, which uses the egg-and-oil emulsion of Hollandaise to elevate traditional banquet seafood. Thick soup and Wensi tofu parallels a French veloute, pairing a rich dried-seafood broth with crabmeat, pickled scallops, delicate tofu threads, and black vinegar pearls.
Wu-wei squid features pan-roasted squid stuffed with pickled cucumber and jicama, finished with a tomato-and-white-wine-vinegar glaze.
For the main course, Taiwanese sauce and lamb rump pairs rich Australian lamb with a sauce blending A1 steak sauce, espagnole, and sea-tangle umami, playfully recreating night market sides with tri-color vegetable puree, crispy angel hair pasta, and a confit quail egg.
To finish, dessert infuses nostalgic fructose syrup into citrus almond tofu, while a bechamel-inspired soy milk and fritters tea dish pairs a soy-infused cheese dip with handmade sesame egg rolls.
The five-course menu is available for NT$1,850 (US$56), plus 10% per person.
