TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — New Taipei is encouraging bird owners to register their pets and take steps to prevent escapes after the city reported a sharp increase in missing birds this year.
The New Taipei Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office said Thursday is National Pet Bird Day. It used this opportunity to offer the first 500 people who complete registration for a non-dog or cat pet to receive a NT$300 (US$9.40) voucher, which can be used at four major convenience store chains, per a press release.
As of the end of August, APHIO received reports of 66 missing parrots, about twice the number recorded during the same period last year. The missing birds included lorikeets, cockatiels, and macaws.
Whenever a pet bird is delivered to the office, information about the bird is posted on its website for 14 days in an effort to locate its owner. Birds that are not reclaimed are placed with Taiwan Bird Rescue Association and are made available for adoption. New Taipei said it monitors the care of birds placed with foster organizations.
New Taipei APHIO veterinarians urged prospective owners to understand the lifespan and care requirements of parrots before acquiring one. Some larger parrots can live for decades, per the press release. The office said parrots are intelligent and capable of learning through observation and imitation.
New Taipei has promoted non-dog and cat pet registration since 2025. The program covers birds and other special pets, with registration intended to improve identification and help reunite lost animals with their owners.
The city said responsible ownership should be viewed as a long-term commitment and urged owners not to abandon their pets. People who find an injured or distressed pet bird can contact the animal protection authorities' 24-hour rescue hotline at 1959 or (02) 2959-6353.

Ministry launches plan to protect recess, traditional games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

(AA Photo)
The Education Ministry published its first action plan prioritizing children’s right to play, mandating the protection of school recess times and integrating traditional games into the national curriculum.
The comprehensive Türkiye Play Policy Document and Action Plan prohibits schools from shortening allocated times for recess and natural play. Authorities will design schoolyards to minimize risks and establish eco-friendly spaces, introducing interactive physical environments such as “talking walls” alongside traditional playground lines.
The ministry will prepare application files to include selected traditional games in the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Local directorates will organize nationwide festivals to revive activities such as five stones, hoop rolling, tug-of-war, drop the handkerchief, jump rope, mangala and sack races.
Play areas will not be limited to a single game type, offering diverse natural elements and catering to different age groups. The plan establishes standards for accessible play areas, allowing children with special needs to play alongside their peers through new space-sharing models.
Officials will prepare a Play Competence Evaluation Guide to assess play opportunities in terms of quality, quantity and accessibility across pilot provinces before expanding nationwide. The ministry will also support domestic digital game developers utilizing Turkish cultural characters, settings and narratives, opening the national inventory for thematic digital game design competitions.
The national curriculum will allocate separate periods for natural play, guided play, educational play and gamified learning. The ministry will train instructor teachers under a play-loving teacher approach and update psychosocial support play contents for crisis and disaster situations.
Authorities will create a value-play matrix matching traditional games with educational values. The initiative also introduces a play module to family training programs, while local municipalities will cooperate to implement neighborhood play streets aligned with a child-friendly city approach.
The ministry will initiate efforts to create a shared play inventory of the Turkic world, expanding the Turkish World Children’s Games Festival to include more participating countries.
The document outlines six goals, 29 policy items and 90 action steps. Officials expect to implement 25 steps in the short term, 53 in the medium term and 12 in the long term. A newly established National Play Coordination Board will meet at least twice a year to publish an annual evaluation report.
The initiative follows a directive sent to all provinces ahead of the new academic year, centering on the theme of play as part of the Century of Türkiye Education Model. The framework covers all educational stages from preschool to high school, adopting a lifelong play approach including adults and senior citizens.

European and Arab military chiefs will meet in Paris on Thursday to assess the Lebanese Armed Forces' needs and discuss the looming end of a United Nations peacekeeping mission, amid fears of a renewed Israeli military offensive in southern Lebanon.
Israel and Lebanon have held several rounds of US-brokered talks aimed at easing tensions along their border. But with elections in Israel and the United States approaching in the coming weeks, diplomats say a breakthrough is unlikely.
Thursday's talks, which will initially be chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron alongside Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Jordan's King Abdullah II bin al Hussein, are not formally part of Washington's efforts.
The US will be represented by a senior military official involved in Middle East security issues.
Europe’s mediation
As part of the US-brokered talks, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a framework deal that envisions Israeli troops gradually withdrawing as Lebanese authorities disarm Hezbollah and deploy across the country's south.
Officials in Paris will seek to assess the precise military and financial requirements ahead of a donor conference likely to be held in late 2026 or early 2027, diplomats said.
The most immediate concern is how to fill the security vacuum that could be left when the UN peacekeeping force UNIFIL, which has about 7,500 personnel, begins drawing down from January.
Despite Lebanon and France both favouring an extension of the UN mandate, neither the United States nor Israel has signalled support for prolonging the mission.
The officials in Paris will discuss options for a new international mission, backed by France and Italy, operating outside a UN mandate, as well as a possible European Union-led mission.
Both concepts would focus on training, equipment, intelligence sharing and mentoring support for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
"The modalities of this international or multinational action remain to be defined — if only because the Lebanese have not voiced requests that align with, in particular, US demands at the Security Council, and because we still need to calibrate the terms of this presence and be absolutely clear about the mandate," a French presidency official told reporters ahead of the meeting.
Highlighting the fragility of the situation, Israeli strikes on a town in southern Lebanon killed at least 13 people, including six children, on Monday, according to Lebanon's Health Ministry, making it one of the deadliest days of Israeli strikes in recent weeks.
Lebanon was drawn into the Middle East war on March 2, following a joint US-Israel strike against Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. In response, the Tehran-aligned group Hezbollah launched missiles targeting Israeli positions.
Israel has killed nearly 4,400 people, wounded 12,500 others and displaced over 1 million in Lebanon since then, according to Lebanese figures.
Fears of a renewed Israeli attacks are growing in Lebanon after days of escalating strikes despite a June ceasefire agreement that was intended to halt fighting.

Sunday’s event will allow participants to make their own handkerchiefs using plant-based dyes and create their own forest maps by incorporating map-inspired images into their artwork.
The name Basianshan was coined by the Japanese after they discovered that the mountain’s peak was nearly 8,000 Japanese feet high (2,439 meters), per the Taiwan Hakka Culture Development Center. Along with the Alishan and Taipingshan stations, the Basianshan Forest Station was recognized as one of three major logging bases during the Japanese colonial era.
The logging industry at Basianshan Forest Station attracted Hakka workers from Taichung, Miaoli County, and Hsinchu County, leading to the formation of immigrant communities near settlements of the local Atayal people. The forest station eventually closed in 1963, after which many Hakka immigrants turned to agriculture.
In related news, Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) announced in late July that he had secured NT$300 million (US$9.41 million) in funding to restore the former Basianshan Forest Station workers’ dormitory in Fengyuan District, per ETtoday. He said restoring the historic site would not only help preserve the district’s roots in the forestry industry but also promote it as a tourism destination.
The National Center of Photography and Images has also launched an online exhibition featuring historical photographs taken when Basianshan Forest Station was still in operation.

Jaguar Land Rover unveiled three variants of a new military vehicle called the Defender Wolf Series II at the British Army’s DVD 2026 exhibition in Bedfordshire on Sept. 16, aiming to replace the Land Rover that has served British forces for more than 70 years.
The event, held at the Millbrook proving ground, is where the Ministry of Defence is expected to evaluate bids for its Light Mobility Vehicle program, a contract to replace the aging fleet of Wolf-spec Land Rovers and Pinzgauer trucks still in service. JLR’s Defender division is competing for that work, and Thomas Mueller, the company’s chief technology officer, said on LinkedIn that the vehicles shown were “the first of many variants of Defender Wolf Series II to come.”
“This is Defender’s first military vehicle launch since the original Wolf, which served the British Armed Forces for more than 70 years,” Mueller said.
Other reporting around the launch describes four planned variants in total, a tactical mobility vehicle, a general mobility vehicle, an ambulance and a utility vehicle, though Mueller’s post confirmed only three were shown on the day. JLR has not said which of the four were unveiled or when the remaining variant might follow.
The new vehicle marks a structural break from its predecessor. Where the original Wolf used a traditional ladder-frame chassis, the Series II is built on Defender’s D7x monocoque platform, the same underlying architecture used in JLR’s civilian Defender models. “Built on Defender’s lightweight D7x monocoque architecture, it delivers exceptional durability, increased payload capability and outstanding strength,” Mueller said. JLR says the vehicle underwent more than 62,000 tests as part of its Extreme Event Test procedure, the company’s standard evaluation for vehicles built to operate in harsh conditions.
The Wolf nameplate dates to 1998, when Land Rover began producing a militarized version of the Defender for British forces. At its peak, more than 8,000 Wolf-spec Land Rovers were in British Army service, and the vehicle has also been used by allied militaries. The replacement effort gained urgency after the original Wolf’s limitations, including insufficient protection against improvised explosive devices, became apparent during operations in Afghanistan.
JLR has also created a new Defender Defense Division to support military and government customers beyond this single program, and the company says the Defender name already serves police, border, fire and mountain rescue agencies in various countries. The Series II’s engine is built in Wolverhampton, though JLR has not disclosed its specifications.

S. Korea's knowledge services deficit widens in H1 on demand for overseas AI, streaming services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:53:14 CST
17:53:14 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's knowledge services deficit widened in the first half amid surging demand for overseas artificial intelligence (AI) software and streaming services, central bank data showed Thursday.
The country posted a deficit of 6.44 billion U.S. dollars in knowledge-intensive services trade during the January-June period, up from a deficit of 5.44 billion dollars in the second half of last year, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It marked the second-largest half-yearly deficit in the country's history, trailing only the deficit of 7.0 billion dollars tallied in the second half of 2010.
The widening deficit was fueled by intellectual property royalties, which saw their shortfall expand from 4.00 billion dollars in the second half of 2025 to 4.90 billion dollars in the first half of 2026.
Notably, the computer and mobile software copyright sector, which includes fees for global AI services, registered a record-high deficit of 2.84 billion dollars in the first half, up from 2.31 billion dollars in the previous half.
Trade in multimedia copyrights, which includes subscriptions to global online video streaming platforms, swung from a surplus of 290 million dollars to a deficit of 40 million dollars in the cited period.
Cultural and leisure services provided a buffer, with its surplus advancing to 720 million dollars in the first half from 530 million dollars in the previous half.
Surplus in the information and communication services slightly shrank from 2.87 billion dollars to 2.42 billion dollars, while the deficit in professional business services moderately narrowed from 4.84 billion dollars to 4.67 billion dollars. ■

S. Koreans face "deficit-surplus-deficit" financial lifecycle, with surplus peaking at 45
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:52:57 CST
17:52:57 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Koreans faced a "deficit-surplus-deficit" financial lifecycle, with their lifetime surplus peaking at age 45, statistical ministry data showed Thursday.
The Ministry of Data and Statistics released the 2024 National Transfer Accounts to analyze the relationship between consumption and labor income across different age groups.
From birth to age 27, individuals spent more than they earned, resulting in a deficit.
The deficit peaked at age 16 and reached 46.04 million won (about 33,330 U.S. dollars), driven by private educational costs for college entrance preparation.
South Koreans transitioned into a financial surplus at age 28, with their labor income outpacing consumption until age 60.
The surplus reached its peak of 19.32 million won at age 45 as per-capita labor income hit a lifetime high of 46.51 million won at that age.
Labor income shrank from age 61, when people entered their retirement years, shifting them back into a deficit.
It was fueled by rising medical and healthcare expenditures in the older generation. ■

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Minister of Information Neth Pheaktra said on Thursday that information integrity is crucial for peace, stability, harmony, and sustainable development across the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC) region.
Speaking in Phnom Penh at a media forum on combating fake news in LMC countries, Pheaktra noted that achieving information integrity requires active collaboration among governments across the region.
"Information integrity strengthens public trust, which in turn fosters social harmony and regional confidence," he told the audience of approximately 200 participants. "Mutual trust provides an essential foundation for peace, stability, and sustainable development."
The minister warned that false or misleading information now crosses borders, languages, and platforms in seconds. Manipulated media can reach millions before it can be verified, while rumors often exploit information gaps during crises.
Consequently, he said, information integrity is no longer just a media-sector issue, but is deeply tied to public trust, social harmony, effective governance, national resilience, regional confidence, peace and sustainable development.
Kan Pharidh, a secretary of state at Cambodia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, noted that while rapid digital transformation and advances in artificial intelligence offer tremendous opportunities, they also amplify the threats of fake news, misinformation, and disinformation.
"If left unaddressed, these challenges can erode public trust, undermine institutional credibility and social cohesion, and adversely affect regional peace, stability, and cooperation," he said.
To safeguard the LMC region's development, he stressed the need for stronger collective action within the LMC framework.
Pharidh emphasized that modern societies require timely, reliable information, professional journalism, and trustworthy media institutions that uphold integrity and foster mutual understanding. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: The "cabbage revolution" -- How China is using science to feed 1.4 billion people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
16:52:51 CST
17:52:51 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- There is nothing remarkable about the tiny cabbage seedlings growing in the fields of Jiayu County in central China.
They are barely more than rows of green tufts against the soil, too young to look anything like the firm heads that will eventually find their way onto dinner tables across the country.
Yet these modest plants tell the story of a decades-long scientific effort to develop better seeds, breed tougher varieties and make one of China's most ordinary vegetables more productive and reliable.
Known as China's "cabbage UN" for its vast collection of varieties, Jiayu in Hubei Province has become a major hub for cabbage breeding, testing and production.
The effort goes back to the 1980s, when China still relied on cabbage seeds imported from countries including Japan and the Netherlands.
"We were determined to build our own capacity and take food production into our own hands," said Qiu Zhengming, chief scientist with the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences, who works at a vegetable science and technology demonstration park in Jiayu.
Led by pioneers, including Fang Zhiyuan of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, generations of researchers set out to find a way to ensure that people in China could have fresh, high-quality cabbage throughout the year.
They started with the seed.
Scientists developed China's first cabbage hybrid, followed by disease-resistant varieties and strains suited to different growing seasons. For winter harvests, they bred varieties that could withstand the cold while producing sweeter heads.
The results have accumulated over decades. Today, more than 70 percent of winter cabbage grown in China's major winter-cabbage producing areas comes from domestic varieties, according to researchers.
"Using science and technology to improve production is important," Qiu said. "Once you have that foundation, farmers' incomes become more stable."
At Jiayu's 460-mu (about 31-hectare) vegetable science and technology demonstration park, researchers test more than 2,000 cabbage varieties each year, continually introducing and screening new ones to find those best suited to local conditions.
The experiments go beyond cabbage. Researchers are also developing new varieties of vegetables that are staples on Chinese dinner tables, including winter melon, pumpkin and Chinese cabbage.
Modern breeding techniques, including hybrid breeding and genetic technologies, are being used to improve resistance to cold and disease and to increase levels of fiber, vitamins and minerals. A nearly 100-mu area has also been established for fully mechanized cabbage production trials.
The fields themselves have become part of the experiment.
At the demonstration park, a network of digital sensors monitors weather, temperature, soil conditions, pests and diseases, as well as water and fertilizer levels.
When something goes wrong, an alert can be sent directly to a farmer's smartphone. Drones fly over the fields to monitor crop health.
The shift is giving farmers more control over their fields. Instead of relying on unpredictable weather, they can make decisions based on data.
Farmers can also order seeds directly from a researcher-managed seed bank, saving them the time and uncertainty of breeding their own varieties and helping them avoid losses caused by bad weather.
Jiayu's vegetables now reach markets across the country, including Hong Kong, Shanghai and Guangzhou. About 75,000 local farmers are involved in vegetable cultivation and their incomes have increased.
For farmer Liu Lianhong, the benefits are measured in more familiar terms. Her household income comes mainly from land-transfer payments and annual dividends from a vegetable farming company, while she also works there. These days, she is busy transplanting cabbage seedlings and clearing weeds.
What is happening in Jiayu is part of a much larger effort in China to use agricultural science to strengthen domestic food supplies.
Perhaps the best-known example is hybrid rice, pioneered by Yuan Longping. The breakthrough dramatically increased rice yields and helped China meet much of its own demand for rice.
Hubei, a major grain-producing province, is now developing high-yield, high-protein corn as an alternative that could help reduce reliance on imported soybeans. Researchers are also breeding fish with improved meat quality.
In neighboring Henan Province, scientists have developed rice varieties less prone to lodging. In Shaanxi Province, researchers have developed drought-tolerant, high-yield wheat.
Some of these agricultural technologies and varieties have also traveled beyond China, helping farmers in Central Asia and Africa increase production and incomes.
These efforts are about more than seeds, technology and yields. They are ultimately about people's lives.
"Of all the things that matter, the well-being of people matters most," Qiu said. ■

UN accuses US military of committing war crimes, Iranian regime of crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:50:36 UTC
17:50:36 KST

A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Iranian and US permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
Minab School strike
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June, US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe, but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports center in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iran abuses also recalled
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes, the US and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests - including violence and killings, cutting off the internet, and the use of the death penalty- marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

Diaspora Ministry launches site collating United Nations bias against Israel in war against Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:49:56 UTC
17:49:56 KST

The Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry on Wednesday launched its first comprehensive international campaign aimed at exposing what it says is the United Nation's mechanism of bias against Israel ahead of the UN General Assembly's general debate, which is set to begin in New York on September 22.
The information presented on the website addresses alleged bias and manipulation, reports of famine in Gaza, UNRWA, accusations of genocide, and publications in which the ministry says the UN amplifies such claims.
The ministry's digital campaign, produced through the Government Advertising Agency, will focus on the United States and target journalists, diplomats, and decision-makers, aiming the direct them to the sources presented on the website.
The campaign will be accompanied by a new website the ministry launched after extensive research and data collection. The website brings together, in an accessible format, the ministry's work examining UN publications and the conduct of UN bodies since the October 7 attack.
According to the ministry, the website presents a broad picture of what it describes as a mechanism of bias against Israel and a system of falsehoods: information presented without sufficient context, claims that gain an authoritative status once they appear in UN publications, and the UN's subsequent amplification of those publications, which the ministry says strengthens misleading narratives.
The website compiles a large volume of information and enables journalists, diplomats, researchers, and decision-makers to follow six interconnected areas and examine the sources behind the findings.
Its launch will be accompanied by a campaign timed to coincide with international attention focused on the UN General Assembly in New York. The campaign videos will present issues examined on the website and direct viewers to the publications and sources cited there.
Site details UN information manipulation, toxic culture, manufactured narratives
The website is divided into six main sections.
The first, "Information manipulation by UN actors," details what the ministry describes as the adoption and dissemination of claims by UN officials, statistical distortions, and the omission of context considered essential to understanding the data. The website alleges that professional definitions were changed and statistical indicators manipulated in order to reach predetermined conclusions before they had been factually examined on the ground, particularly regarding claims of "starvation" and "genocide."
The second section, "Toxic institutional culture," focuses on what the ministry describes as language, statements, and patterns of conduct within the UN that allow one-sided positions against Israel to become embedded in the organization.
A third section, titled "The famine that wasn't," examines the data, forecasts, and messaging through which claims of famine in Gaza received institutional legitimacy and global attention. The ministry claims that this section demonstrates that the UN's presentation of the data is far removed from conditions on the ground.
The fourth section, "UNRWA compromised," compiles findings and allegations concerning Hamas infiltration of the agency and the conduct of UNRWA's leadership following related disclosures. It presents what the ministry describes as intelligence evidence indicating extensive infiltration of UNRWA by Hamas operatives, which it says involves at least 12% of the agency's employees in the Gaza Strip, alongside the discovery of terrorist infrastructure beneath UNRWA headquarters and facilities.
A fifth section, "Manufacturing a genocide narrative," examines how some of the gravest accusations against Israel were formulated and disseminated, as well as what the ministry describes as the false basis presented in support of them.
The final section, "Self-reinforcing ecosystem," tracks the way a claim passes between different actors and publications before returning to international discourse carrying an additional stamp of authority, even when its original source has not been independently verified again.
The website also seeks to expose what it calls a process of "propaganda laundering," described as a three-stage mechanism in which unsubstantiated data originating from Hamas is cited by UN agencies, such as OCHA, stripped of reference to its original source, and then disseminated to the public and international legal bodies as "verified UN facts."
The main findings highlighted in the campaign include allegations of internal silencing and persecution. The ministry says it documented pressure and harassment directed at individuals who sought to maintain what they considered factual accuracy, while those who adopted anti-Israel narratives were allegedly rewarded and promoted.
"For far too long, the world has treated the UN's stamp as a substitute for fact-checking. This website exposes how the poison machine against Israel works: A narrative enters the system, receives institutional authority, is quoted again and again, and influences the positions of governments, media outlets, and the public. Since October 7, the cost of this bias has been particularly high. Anyone can examine what lies behind the headlines," Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli said.
UN officials claim they were pressured to condemn Israel
Testimony and quotations from senior officials and experts who worked within UN mechanisms are presented as evidence of what the campaign describes as a culture of silencing, pressure, and data manipulation.
World Health Organization representative Dr. Michel Thieren is quoted as saying: "The terms 'genocide' and 'famine' were thrown around from the very beginning. The crimes were defined in advance, and then the organizations tried to prove them. For me, this is completely abnormal."
Alice Wairimu Nderitu, the UN's former special adviser on the prevention of genocide, is quoted as saying: "I was bullied and harassed every day... This never happened in any other war. Not in Ukraine, not in Sudan, not in Myanmar. The focus was always on Israel... By taking one side and condemning it every day, you completely lose the purpose for which the UN was established."
The campaign states that Nderitu refused to define the fighting as "genocide" without an authoritative legal determination, and that her UN contract was subsequently not renewed.
UN Special Rapporteur on Torture Dr. Alice Edwards is quoted as describing heavy pressure from UN colleagues aimed at preventing her from publishing an official letter documenting Hamas's crimes on October 7.
"There was a campaign to prevent the letter from being published. It was weeks of bullying and intimidation," she said.
Former UN sanctions coordinator Edmund Fitton-Brown is quoted as saying: "The reverence for the UN allows weak evidence, activists' assumptions, and ideological leanings to launder themselves and become mainstream and accepted opinion."
'The UN rewrites the truth'
The campaign's video series visually depicts what the ministry describes as the manipulation of information and systematic falsification. In the videos, hands working inside what is portrayed as UN headquarters cut up and reassemble headlines from major newspapers. Headlines such as "Humanitarian aid stolen by Hamas," "Stop Hamas terror," and "Hamas harms civilians" are physically altered so that the word "Hamas" is replaced with "Israel."
The campaign concludes with the message: "The UN rewrites the truth."
"The website is an information source that brings everything together, unlike individual publications that do not create the same effect. When you examine where the information came from and how it passes between the different actors, you understand the mechanism," Hadas Maimon, head of the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry's senior public diplomacy division, said.

How to move an ancient mikvah? Inside the IAA's operation to conserve a Second Temple ritual bath
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:49:54 UTC
17:49:54 KST

The Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) recently undertook a complex engineering operation to conserve a Second Temple-era mikvah found during archaeological excavations in the Carmei Gat neighborhood of Kiryat Gat.
Financed by the Israel Lands Authority, the excavations were completed ahead of construction and development works slated to happen in Carmei Gat to preemptively protect the 2,000-year-old structure from harm.
Discovering the mikvah, as well as stone measuring vessels, provides direct evidence of the existence of a Jewish settlement in the area at the time. Stone vessels, which according to Jewish law do not become ritually impure, were widely used among Jews during the Second Temple period.
“The Jewish settlement we discovered here is the first and the only known one in this area,” explained IAA excavation directors Elena Kogan-Zahavi, Maayan Margulis and Shira Lifshitz. “In the Judean Lowlands, many Jewish settlements from the Roman period are known, but in the seam between the Judean Lowlands and the northern Negev, no Jewish settlement was known until now.”
Findings from the site indicate that the ancient settlement was likely abandoned by its Jewish inhabitants during the Bar Kokhba Revolt in the second century CE. The site was revived some 500 years later during the Byzantine period by an entirely different population.
Preparing the mikveh to be moved
As development work progressed, the IAA’s Conservation Administration was faced with a new, even more daunting task: how to temporarily transfer the mikveh, weighing 25 tons, from its current location to the Israel’s National Treasures Department.
Four members of the administration worked for two weeks straight to expose the mikveh in its entirety.
First, they dug around it to expose it on all sides. Then, careful drilling was carried out underneath the structure, and steel beams were then slid through to support the mikveh and allow it to be pulled from the ground.
The ancient plaster on the mikveh’s walls also required special treatment.
The IAA’s team gently covered it in gauze and adhesives to prevent vibrations from the ancient pool’s transportation from causing the plaster to peel off. The entire structure was reinforced with foam to allow it to safely withstand the lifting and the jolts along the journey.
But even after the mikveh was detached from the ground, the challenge was far from over.
Due to the distance between the crane's base and the mikveh, a crane with a lifting capacity of 300 tons was required to lift the 25-ton structure. The mikveh's unusual width, about 4 meters, also required the use of a wide-load transport vehicle.
Transporting the mikveh
Transporting the mikveh to the nearby Beit Guvrin storehouse became an operation in itself.
In order to transport the large, highly sensitive cargo, the road was closed to traffic, and escort vehicles drove in front of and behind the truck.
“Once you lift up a structure like this, there is no going back,” said Eyal Kaho, a senior conservator at the IAA who led the operation. “If it falls apart, we've lost the mikveh.”
“Therefore, every detail must be considered in advance. The day before an operation like this, you don't sleep. You're under pressure, because the responsibility is yours and there’s simply no price that can compensate for mistakes. Even after 36 years at the Israel Antiquities Authority, every time, the adrenaline rises anew.”
Once construction in Carmei Gat is completed, the mikveh will be returned to the site where it was found. It will be integrated into an open public space at the heart of the new neighborhood.
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu (Otzma Yehudit) noted that the discovery of the mikveh in Kiryat Gat adds an “important dimension to our understanding of Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel during the Second Temple period.”
He explained that the IAA’s operation reflects Israel’s national commitment to preserving its heritage amid its rapid development.
“Its future incorporation into the neighborhood’s public space will enable residents and visitors to encounter tangible evidence of Jewish life from 2,000 years ago as part of their daily lives.”

Special education gains popularity, but specialists remain scarce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

Special education gains popularity, but specialists remain scarce
The special education field is attracting more university applicants, but schools across Estonia are still struggling to find the support specialists their students need.
Tallinn University (TLÜ) admits 55 students to its bachelor's program and 42 to its master's program in special education each year, and Tiiu Tammemäe, associate professor of inclusive and special education, said demand is steadily rising.
She said applications for full-time studies outnumbered available enrollment nearly nine times over, while session-based bachelor's studies drew more than 15 applications per spot, making special education one of the most competitive majors in the country.
The university trains as many special education specialists as funding from the Ministry of Education and Research allows.
"At the moment, we aren't looking to increase the size of these study groups either, although there may be public pressure to train more [specialists]," Tammemäe acknowledged.
Still hiring
Yet schools continue to struggle with staffing. Tallinn's Laagna Kindergarten-Basic School, which serves students with special educational needs (SENs), is required to have two speech therapists and two special education teachers, as well as a social pedagogue and school psychologist, said principal Andres Anton.
"There isn't the demand you'd expect among speech therapists, because the University of Tartu (TÜ) simply trains relatively few of them," he said.
His school is currently hiring a special education teacher, speech therapist and school psychologist, and Anton said they have been searching for the support specialists for at least a year already.
"It's not uncommon for someone to apply to several places and then, as always, they go with the highest bidder," he said, adding that candidates will sometimes withdraw at the last minute as a result, sparking competition among schools over pay.
Tammemäe said demand is already reaching university students during their studies, with institutions requesting she share job openings, recruiting during internships and even getting hired before they graduate.
Unqualified staff hired under different roles
A master's degree is required to qualify as a special education teacher or pursue higher-level qualifications as a social pedagogue, speech therapist or school psychologist. Bachelor's graduates, meanwhile, can work as kindergarten teachers or school teaching assistants.
The Education Ministry estimates there are about 2,200 support specialists working in schools. However, 7–12 percent of positions, depending on the specialty, are filled by people who do not meet the formal qualification requirements, said Jürgen Rakaselg, head of the ministry's Inclusive Education Department.
Facing a shortage of specialists, he noted, some schools have formally placed under- or unqualified staff in other roles.
"We know some schools have never had a school psychologist at all, despite the law requiring them to provide that service," Rakaselg admitted.
Schools are best staffed in terms of social pedagogues and special education teachers, the ministry official said. School psychologists and speech therapists, meanwhile, are harder to find; the latter two are currently available at just over half of the country's schools.

The work that cannot wait
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:49:00 EEST
17:49:00 KST

The work that cannot wait
Social cohesion is not built through statements of unity. It is built through the systems, skills and institutions that enable societies to manage disagreements, address tensions and make fair decisions together.
In Ukraine, the word "dialogue" requires careful explanation. It is sometimes understood as a euphemism for concessions to the aggressor state, and Ukrainian society reacts strongly to that framing, understandably so.
But an important distinction must be made. Dialogue as an instrument of foreign policy is one question; dialogue as domestic infrastructure, the capacity of communities to address disputes, rebuild trust and solve problems together, is another. It is this second form that deserves greater attention as Ukraine advances recovery and reconstruction.
Cohesion is built through practice
Conflict exists in every society. What determines resilience is whether people have trusted, constructive ways to address it: where such mechanisms exist, disagreements can inform decisions; where they do not, grievances deepen over time.
Ukrainian society has shown extraordinary solidarity since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Recognising emerging internal tensions does not weaken that unity, it helps communities address them before they harden into deeper divisions.
Some tensions are already visible: differing wartime experiences, displacement, military service, caregiving, loss of homes and loved ones, years under bombardment. There is pressure on housing and services in host communities, veterans navigating civilian life, and questions of language, identity and belonging. These are not signs of fragility but consequences of an experience of extraordinary scale, and the task is to give people safe, fair, credible ways to address them.
My work, including visits to frontline, war-affected and host communities, has surfaced three patterns.
First, the visible issue is often not the underlying one: a dispute over assistance or resources may reflect deeper questions of recognition or fairness, and once acknowledged, solutions become easier to find.
Second, many tensions exist within communities rather than between clearly defined groups, and are rarely visible from the capital, understanding them takes direct engagement and sustained local presence.
Third, impartial facilitators create space for difficult conversations: members who raise sensitive issues themselves risk being seen as representing one side, while a trusted third party helps all perspectives be heard.
Beyond individual disputes, dialogue serves a broader purpose: war and recovery are reshaping expectations between the state and citizens, and among citizens themselves, through thousands of practical conversations about compensation, services, veterans' reintegration and local decisions. Acknowledging these differences is the first step; the second is treating them not as fault lines but as realities institutions and communities must navigate. Difference recognised and given a constructive channel becomes a resource; difference denied becomes a division.
Why dialogue capacity matters now
A common argument is that dialogue mechanisms can wait until after the war. Experience suggests otherwise: trust takes time to build, and local facilitation and mediation capacity cannot be created overnight.
Ukraine has already laid a legislative foundation through the 2021 Law on Mediation, which establishes mediation as a voluntary, confidential procedure. The next stage is to translate that framework into practice, trained professionals, trusted institutions, quality standards and local referral mechanisms, to meet substantial potential need: compensation for damaged homes; property, inheritance and land disputes; return and reintegration in de-occupied areas; access to services; and employment challenges linked to veterans' transition to civilian life.
Not every disagreement requires mediation, and dialogue should never replace legal remedies or accountability. But addressing disputes early and fairly saves people time, eases pressure on administrative and judicial systems and gives communities a better chance of preserving relationships.
Learning from others while respecting Ukraine's context
International experience offers valuable lessons and tools, but global dialogue and mediation models cannot simply be transferred to Ukraine; some need adaptation, others need their assumptions reconsidered. Programmes that prioritise formal models or qualifications over local legitimacy risk building mechanisms communities do not trust or use. Ukraine's social dynamics also cannot be reduced to a framework of "two sides": the fundamental cause of the war is Russia's external aggression, and any approach must recognise that.
Practical solutions are usually more effective when dialogue is tied to concrete issues, housing, compensation, services, employment, local decision-making. The objective is not dialogue platforms for their own sake, but embedding dialogue and mediation in recovery processes where people already face real questions requiring workable solutions.
Impartiality, not neutrality
For international organisations, one distinction matters: impartiality is not synonymous with neutrality. The UN's Guidance for Effective Mediation defines impartiality as running a balanced process that treats all participants fairly, while a UN mediator stays bound by universal principles and international law — a position grounded in the UN Charter and General Assembly resolutions reaffirming Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and calling for a just and lasting peace. That is fully compatible with fair, inclusive domestic processes: when communities address tensions between displaced people and host communities, veterans and employers, or residents and local authorities, participants must have a meaningful opportunity to be heard.
International support adds value by convening actors and contributing comparative experience and long-term investment, but it cannot create local legitimacy. That belongs
to Ukrainian institutions, professionals and communities; the role of partners is to strengthen their capacity, not replace it.
A shared responsibility for recovery
Building social cohesion is a collective effort. The state provides legal safeguards and institutional frameworks; international partners contribute resources and continuity; civil society and mediation professionals bring local knowledge and trust; local governments are where these elements come together in practice. The strongest results emerge when institutions create space, partners provide sustained support and local actors lead — with real safeguards: voluntary, inclusive participation, recognised power imbalances, and dialogue that never substitutes for rights, accountability or access to justice.
Investing in the foundations of recovery
Recovery is often measured in visible achievements: roads rebuilt, energy restored, homes reconstructed. But rebuilding a country also means rebuilding relationships between people. A community may have new infrastructure and still struggle if residents cannot influence decisions or resolve disagreements fairly. Reconstruction restores buildings; social cohesion restores the relationships that let communities and institutions function.
The scale of investment ahead is immense: the Fifth Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA5) estimates Ukraine's ten-year recovery needs at almost $588 billion, including more than $96 billion for transport and nearly $91 billion for energy. Social cohesion is not costed as a standalone RDNA5 sector, but that should not be mistaken for marginal importance, it is an enabling condition for effective recovery: when people can take part in decisions, challenge them fairly and address disputes early, reconstruction is more likely to strengthen public trust than generate new grievances.
The foundations already exist, in Ukrainian communities, legislation and professional networks. The priority now is integrating dialogue and mediation into recovery planning, strengthening trusted local capacity, and ensuring these mechanisms are available wherever reconstruction creates difficult choices or competing claims.
Ukraine does not need dialogue as an abstract slogan. It needs it as practical infrastructure for recovery, and that infrastructure must be built now.

A corresponding motion has been submitted to a panel of judges at Shevchenkivsky District Court of Kyiv.

ETH researcher among favourites for Nobel Prize in physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:48:50 UTC
17:48:50 KST

ETH researcher among favourites for Nobel Prize in physics
In just over two weeks’ time, the 2026 Nobel Prizes will be announced in Stockholm. The identities of the winners remain a closely guarded secret right up until the last moment. Nevertheless, there is already a flurry of speculation. A Swiss-British researcher is also being tipped as a possible laureate.
Nicola Spaldin, a professor at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich, features on the list of researchers of Nobel Prize calibre published on Thursday by the British-American data firm Clarivate.
The names of those nominated for a Nobel Prize are, as a rule, kept secret for 50 years. No information about the committees’ deliberations are made public. The laureates are only informed immediately before the official announcements. It is therefore difficult to predict who might win a prize.
+ British researcher wins top Swiss science award
The list of Nobel Prize contenders compiled annually by Clarivate is based on the impact their work has had within the scientific community – in other words, on how often their academic articles have been cited by other scientists.
Novel materials
Clarivate considers ETH researcher Spaldin to be a potential Nobel Prize candidate in the field of physics. This is due to her theoretical work on so-called magnetoelectric multiferroics.
These are materials that can be influenced by both magnetic and electric fields. This makes them of interest for applications such as energy-efficient data storage or high-precision magnetic field sensors. Spaldin laid the theoretical foundations for this class of materials.
In total, Clarivate has included 22 researchers on its list this year. Alongside Spaldin, those named come from the US, Canada, Denmark, Israel, Japan and China.
Success rate
Since 2002, Clarivate has honoured a total of 487 researchers as so-called “Citation Laureates”. Some 89 of them went on to win a Nobel Prize. This corresponds to a success rate of around 18%. Often, several years elapsed between inclusion on the list and the award of the Nobel Prize.
Clarivate, for example, predicted the Nobel Prize for the Swiss physicists Didier Queloz and Michel Mayor – albeit six years before they received it.
More
The Basel researcher whose work triggered a longevity revolution
Other researchers working at Swiss universities who have not yet received a Nobel Prize were also honoured as Citation Laureates in previous years. These include the chemist Michele Parrinello (Università della Svizzera italiana and ETH Zurich), the biochemist Michael N. Hall (University of Basel), the chemist Michael Grätzel (Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne – EPFL), the economist Ernst Fehr (University of Zurich), the physicist Daniel Loss (University of Basel) and the immunologist Andrea Ablasser (EPFL).
The Nobel Prizes in the sciences will kick off on October 5 with the Nobel Prize in Medicine. This will be followed on October 6 by the announcement of the Nobel laureates in Physics, and on October 7 by those in Chemistry.

An overnight Ukrainian drone attack sparked a fire at one of Russia’s largest oil refineries in the city of Yaroslavl northeast of Moscow, Yaroslavl region Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said Thursday.
“There’s damage to the oil refinery,” Yevrayev wrote in a post on Telegram, referring to the Slavneft-Yanos refinery, which is jointly controlled by Rosneft and Gazprom.
Ukraine’s military has previously claimed attacks on Slavneft-Yanos, saying it provides fuel and lubricants for the Russian military. Slavneft-Yanos has a crude processing capacity of 300,000 barrels per day, or 15 million metric tons per year.
Governor Yevrayev reported no casualties and said the refinery fire was fully extinguished by Thursday morning.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the strike on Slavneft-Yanos and reported damage to three Russian transport aircraft and three helicopters in a separate attack on a military airfield in the southern Rostov region.
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said an overnight air barrage cut power to four districts in the regional capital Rostov-on-Don, where around two-fifths of the city’s residents live. No one was hurt in the strikes, he added.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 641 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
Russia’s Central Election Commission, which is running parliamentary and regional elections this weekend, said one of its members was killed in a drone attack in the occupied Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia earlier on Tuesday.
In Kyiv, officials said a large-scale Russian attack on the city overnight wounded at least 16 people. Several others were reported injured in separate attacks across Ukraine.
Authorities in Ukraine also reported that a Russian drone strike on a Tanzanian-flagged civilian ship in the Black Sea killed its captain. They did not disclose the nationality of the captain.
Ukraine’s latest attacks targeting Russian oil refineries came despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump earlier in the week that Moscow and Kyiv allegedly agreed to pause such attacks. The Russian military has also continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump has sought to blame the surging cost of diesel in the United States on Ukrainian strikes against Russian fuel production facilities and supply lines. While Ukraine’s attacks have put pressure on gasoline and diesel prices both inside Russia and globally, analysts broadly agree that the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is the leading cause of current disruptions in energy markets.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to pass a law that would revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames Israel’s soldiers, including the directors of NAZA, a documentary about Israeli soldiers’ killings of civilians in Gaza.
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA documents allegations that mass civilian deaths were built into Israel’s target decisions in its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza – something Netanyahu and the army reject.

The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last week. During his acceptance speech, Abraham said “our country is doing these crimes” and highlighted that Israel is systematically and deliberately targeting Palestinians in Gaza.
“NAZA” takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected “collateral casualties” and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers.
It has been harshly criticised in Israel, with the military examining potential legal action against those involved in it.
But it has also played into the charged domestic political atmosphere before Israel’s October 27 election, as public opinion polls suggest Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition could fall short of a majority in parliament.

On Wednesday, he pledged to advance two bills that he said would address the “immense damage” done to Israeli soldiers in the film.
“The first [order]: To revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames [Israeli] soldiers, and the second: To hit them in their pockets and increase the statutory damages for defamation they can be sued for by 20 times,” Netanyahu said in a social media video. “We will hit them both in their pockets and in their citizenship, as their place is not with us.”
Netanyahu cited three examples in proposing the bills: “The recent film NAZA which portrayed [Israeli] officers and soldiers as war criminals”, 2025 remarks by left-wing ex-general-turned-politician Yair Golan that “a sane country does not kill children as a hobby”, and a military legal officer’s 2024 leak of a video showing soldiers abusing a Gaza detainee.
In 2022, Israel’s Supreme Court passed a law that permits stripping citizenship from Israelis who carry out actions that constitute a breach of trust against the state. Any new legislation would likely face similar court challenges.

Israeli charged with plotting drone bomb attack on Amdocs server farm

08:47:53 UTC
17:47:53 KST

The State Attorney’s Office filed an indictment Thursday against Mustafa Issa, a 20-year-old resident of Kafr Qasim, accusing him of planning a nationalist-motivated terror attack against a strategic site in Israel.
Issa was charged at the Central District Court in Lod with offenses including preparing to commit a terror act involving malicious damage with explosives, weapons activity for terrorist purposes and training or instruction for terrorist purposes.
According to the indictment, filed by prosecutor Assaf Harlopsky of the Central District Attorney’s Office, Issa decided against the backdrop of the war to carry out an attack against a strategic Israeli target.
Prosecutors allege that for about a year and a half he explored ways to carry out the attack, including planting an explosive device or dropping one from a drone.
During that period, according to the indictment, Issa volunteered with Israel’s Fire and Rescue Services and exploited the position to travel through different areas and collect information about potential targets.
Prosecutors say he eventually decided to focus on an Amdocs server farm in Ra’anana, believing that damaging the facility would cause serious economic and national harm to Israel.
As part of the alleged preparations, Issa downloaded guides, files and videos dealing with the manufacture of weapons and explosive devices as well as methods used by lone attackers, which prosecutors say he used as training material.
The indictment further alleges that Issa attempted to assemble an explosive device by mixing flammable substances with the contents of fireworks and firecrackers he had purchased. In another experiment, he prepared a mixture containing sulfur, charcoal and other materials, but destroyed it after the attempt failed.
Prosecutors say he also bought a drone and equipment that could be used to attach an explosive device to it, while watching instructional material on mounting explosives to drones.
The State Attorney’s Office asked the court to keep Issa in custody until the end of legal proceedings.
In its detention request, prosecutors argued that he posed a high risk because he had allegedly begun taking practical steps to carry out his plans. They also cited what they described as his nationalist motive, linked to the war and IDF operations, as well as his claim that he had been taught at school to hate the State of Israel.

Dutch asylum numbers a third lower than a year ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:47:42 UTC
17:47:42 KST

Dutch asylum numbers a third lower than a year ago
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of people registering for asylum in the Netherlands has fallen below 600 a week for the first time this year, according to weekly figures from the asylum ministry.
The drop is heavy compared to last year, when for most of autumn 2025 the weekly total was around 1,000, Volkskrant reported on Thursday.
The drop in numbers is mostly down to a reduction in family reunification requests. The number of relatives arriving to join people who already have refugee status has dropped from around 300 a week before the summer to between 110 and 120 a week over the past fortnight.
Syrians
 The Netherlands has recorded more than 40,000 asylum-related arrivals every year since 2022. New applications fell sharply after the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, but the total stayed roughly level because Syrians who already had refugee status were still bringing over their families.
A record 16,500 family members arrived in 2025, up 39% on the year before, and three-quarters of them were Syrian, according to statistics agency CBS.
Tighter EU rules on family reunification came into force in June under the European migration pact. The ministry has not yet said what is behind the drop.
Senate
 The ministry has only published a breakdown of the weekly figures since late June. Until then its weekly press release was a single line giving one total for new applications, repeat applications, resettlement and family members combined.
Applications are reportedly falling across Europe. The EU asylum agency EUAA said last week that the 27 member states plus Norway and Switzerland received 332,000 applications in the first half of 2026, 17% fewer than a year earlier and the lowest first-half total since 2021.
The agency attributed much of the drop to fewer applications from Venezuelans and Syrians.

On Rescuer’s Day, the State Emergency Service honored 130 colleagues who died during the full-scale war
Kyiv • UNN
On Rescuer’s Day, 130 emergency responders who died after the start of the full-scale invasion were honored. Nearly 1,000 rescuers received awards.
On Rescuer’s Day in Ukraine, emergency responders who died after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion were honored. Volodymyr Zelenskyy also reported that since the beginning of the full-scale war, nearly 1,000 employees of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine had received state awards, UNN reports.
Details
"Today, on Rescuer’s Day, we bow our heads in a minute of silence and honor those whose feat is forever etched in our history. On this professional holiday, with deep sorrow and boundless gratitude, we remember our emergency responders whose lives were cynically cut short by the Russian invasion," the post by the State Emergency Service of Ukraine says.
The State Emergency Service also published archival family footage of the rescue workers who died.
"In these archival family videos, our male and female rescuers are still simply living and rejoicing in each day. They hug and kiss their loved ones — mothers, wives, husbands, and children. They joke. They laugh. They love. They dream. They had plans for the future. Wishes they wanted to fulfill. A cozy home where they were always awaited after a difficult shift. Every day, they risked their lives to give others a chance at life. But because of the brutal Russian invasion, each of their lives was cut short... Our large State Emergency Service family was orphaned of 130 courageous hearts. Now only memories, the voices of loved ones in recordings, photographs, and these short clips remain, in which they are still smiling and alive. We remember every male and female rescuer who gave the most precious thing for the sake of saving others. Forever in our memory. Forever in our hearts. May their memory be eternal and may they be eternally honored," the post by the State Emergency Service says.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy also highlighted the work of the emergency responders.
"The State Emergency Service of Ukraine is truly a strong, courageous, and professional system that works, is well organized, and guarantees reliable protection to Ukrainians. Fifty-six thousand specialists, more than ten thousand of them women — these are all people who care about what will happen to others, and this is all extraordinary service to goodness and humanity," the president said.
He emphasized that since the beginning of the full-scale war, nearly 1,000 rescuers had received state awards of Ukraine. Another six rescuers were awarded the Gold Star of the Hero of Ukraine, two of them posthumously.
"Please remember each and every one — all the rescuers who, while protecting people and protecting lives, gave their own lives. Thank you for saving lives and people! Glory to Ukraine!" Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized.
We remind you
On September 17, Ukraine celebrates Rescuer’s Day and Adoption Day; under the auspices of the WHO, World Patient Safety Day is observed around the world, while the United States celebrates Constitution Day. According to the church calendar under the new style, Saints Martyrs Faith, Hope, and Charity and their mother Sophia are commemorated, while under the old style, the day of the Icon of the Mother of God "The Unburnt Bush" and the memory of the Prophet Moses are observed.

‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:46:11 UTC
17:46:11 KST

‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
India is one of the world’s largest sugar consumers, but usually produces even more. A crisis has flipped that equation — hitting sugarcane farmers and low-income consumers alike.
Jai Krishan, a 43-year-old labourer from Bihar in northern India, has saved 15,000 rupees ($160) to travel home from Indian-administered Kashmir, where he works, to celebrate Diwali with his family in November.
Each year, he buys boxes of sweets — laddu, barfi and kaju katli — to take home as gifts for his family and friends. He spends about $35 just on sweets for Diwali, he says, as he prepares afternoon tea for himself and his roommates in their rented accommodation in the Hawal area of Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir’s largest city.
“For someone from a lower-middle-class family, this is a lot of money. But Diwali is one of the most important festivals for Hindus and you cannot skip celebrating it,” he says.
This year, though, Krishan fears he may have to cut back on other purchases — such as toys and clothes — to keep his limited budget under control. The price of sugar has risen sharply in recent months, with retail prices reaching as high as 75 rupees ($0.79) per kilogramme (2.2 pounds) — up from 40 rupees in September 2025 — in some markets, raising concerns that the cost of sweets could also increase.
“I can reduce my spending on clothes or other things, but I cannot return home without bringing sweets for my family,” Krishan said.
The price rise comes as India enters its festival season. Celebrations begin in late August with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi and Onam, before gathering pace in October and November with Navratri, Durga Puja, Dussehra and Diwali, popularly known as the festival of lights.
India’s sweets sector is worth more than $1.1bn, with peak festive sales accounting for more than 40 percent of annual revenue. Traditional sweets can contain 30 to 60 percent sugar by weight, making sugar a major ingredient. India is the world’s largest consumer and second-largest producer of sugar.
The country consumes between 29 million and 32 million metric tonnes of sugar each year, roughly 15 percent of global consumption. But it produces about 20 percent of the world’s sugar, second only to Brazil — an amount that means that the country usually has enough supplies of sugar for its needs, with some to spare for exports.
Not this year.
A rare sugar shortage
Sugar production, according to government data, is expected to be about 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026. This is 11 percent lower than the government’s earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.
The government attributes the lower production mainly to a decline in sugarcane cultivation and lower rainfall during the El Nino weather pattern. It has also accused hoarders of storing extra sugar once the effects of El Nino became clear, to further tighten supplies in a bid to earn extra profits.
But Mukesh Chandra, a sugarcane farmer from Punjab, says several other factors have contributed to the fall in production and the rise in sugar prices.
He points to a shift by some farmers from sugarcane to other crops, high labour costs coupled with low returns from sugarcane farming, and the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production as among those reasons.
“These factors have led to a decline in the amount of sugarcane available for processing, putting pressure on sugar supplies and pushing up prices,” Chandra told Al Jazeera. “Why would a farmer cultivate a product that is going to give him less returns?”
The Indian government, however, has rejected the claim that diverting sugarcane to ethanol production under its ethanol blending programme has contributed to the surge in sugar prices. It pointed to figures showing that the share of sugar diverted to ethanol has fallen from about 12 percent in 2022-23 to about 9 percent in 2025-26, with nearly three-quarters of India’s ethanol now made from grains such as maize.
India introduced ethanol blending to reduce its dependence on expensive crude oil imports, strengthen energy security and increase farmers’ incomes by creating a market for surplus crops. The initiative is also intended to reduce vehicle emissions and support the country’s broader decarbonisation goals.
Moving away from sugarcane
Regardless of the Indian government’s assertions, Chandra argues that the economic logic of sugarcane farming works against cultivators.
He estimates that producing 100kg of sugar costs about 470 rupees ($4.90), including expenses for labour, irrigation, cultivation and transportation, as well as the extraction of sugarcane juice and its processing into sugar. But the return is only about 416 rupees, leaving farmers with a loss of approximately 54 rupees per 100kg. He said sugarcane farmers also do not receive the same level of support available to farmers growing crops such as paddy — particularly with fertilisers, diesel and electricity.
The United States-Israeli war on Iran has also complicated economic equations for farmers, with fuel prices — and so, electricity costs — rising. The inflation due to the war “has added a further burden on our shoulders,” Chandra said. “The rise in fuel prices has increased the cost of running water pumps used to irrigate sugarcane fields, adding to farmers’ expenses at a time when their margins are already low.”
Suresh Pal, another sugarcane farmer from the state of Uttar Pradesh, agrees that sugarcane production is declining. He attributes the current shortage and price rise to a combination of agricultural and climate-related challenges faced by farmers in the state.
Farmers in Uttar Pradesh remain heavily dependent on the Co-0238 variety of sugarcane, which, Pal said, has become increasingly vulnerable to diseases such as red rot fungus and pest attacks. He added that continuous cultivation and the heavy use of chemicals have also contributed to soil degradation, while the crop’s high water requirements have put further pressure on the state’s groundwater resources.
“We are facing problems from many sides. The varieties we depend on are becoming vulnerable to diseases, the soil is losing its strength and water is becoming harder to manage,” Pal told Al Jazeera. “And at the same time, the cost of farming is increasing. Fertiliser, pesticides, labour and irrigation are all becoming expensive,” he added.
For small farmers, Pal believes, the financial strain is made worse by delayed payments from sugar mills, leaving them with little money to invest in better seeds, modern farming methods and new technologies. “When the mills delay our payments, how can a small farmer invest more in his fields?” Pal said. “Our costs keep rising, but the money we earn from farming is not increasing at the same pace. This is making it difficult for people like me to continue cultivating sugarcane.”
A Diwali that’s less sweet
To manage domestic supply, the government has authorised the duty-free import of one million tonnes of raw sugar, with a cap on rates, until October 31, 2026. The move is aimed at easing supply pressures ahead of the festival season.
“The measure is best understood as a price ceiling rather than a price cut,” said Sanjay Kumar, professor of economics at Delhi University. The government waived heavy import duties to allow the import of sugar at about $0.55 per kg. “That price now limits how high domestic sugar can go, because once imported sugar is cheaper, no mill can hold its own price above the landed cost for long,” Kumar added.
But so far, that strategy doesn’t seem to be working.
That, Kumar said, is because the imports are of raw sugar; the domestic Indian market demand is primarily for refined sugar.
Aman Jaswal, a resident of Patna in Bihar, said sweets were costing 15 to 20 percent more this year. “Sweets are closely tied to happiness in Indian culture. Whether it is Diwali, a wedding or a religious occasion, we rarely celebrate without them,” Jaswal said. “Even prasad [the sweets offered during religious rituals] is shared among people. Gifting sweets is a way of sharing happiness and it has become part of our celebrations and relationships.”
Back in Srinagar, Krishan, the labourer, has already started thinking about what he can sacrifice this year to be able to afford sweets for his family back home.
He has taken to walking to work, instead of taking public transport.
“My workplace is about eight kilometres from my room but I walk to save 50 rupees ($0.52) a day for the happiness of my family,” he said. “What difference does it make to the rich? They will celebrate the festival with great pomp and show anyway. It is poor people like me who will bear the impact.”

India says will take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:44:57 UTC
17:44:57 KST

Ahmad Adil
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
India on Thursday said it would take “all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” after the US Congress passed a major Russia sanctions bill.
 
India’s Ministry of External Affairs acknowledged the passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US Congress, saying “we are monitoring further developments on this matter.”
 
The House approved the bill on Wednesday by a 262-159 vote, with dozens of Democrats joining Republicans. The measure now goes to US President Donald Trump for his signature. The legislation would allow the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, including China and India.
 
New Delhi on Thursday also said India remains “firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” and “will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.”
 
“This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side,” the ministry said.
 
The ministry stated that the Indian side “has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.”
 
“Government will work closely with Indian trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of these developments,” it said.
 
The US and India announced in February that they had reached an interim framework deal to end a bilateral trade dispute.
 
Last year, tensions escalated between the two countries over the 50% tariffs imposed on Indian goods by the Trump administration, partly because India purchased Russian oil amid the ongoing Moscow-Kyiv war.
 
Trade between India and Russia reached a record $68.7 billion last year.
