EU defence chief says a ‘painful response’ to Russian hybrid threats is needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:44:02 UTC
17:44:02 KST

Senior Baltic European Commissioners tell Euronews they are supportive of Ursula von der Leyen’s bold plans to turbocharge European defence, from a "painful" anti-hybrid warfare playbook to a new political security group.
European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius said Europe can respond to Russia in a “painful way” through the development of an anti-hybrid warfare playbook.
“We can find ways for how Russia will pay quite a painful price for their provocations,” he said in exclusive comments to Euronews’ flagship current affairs news programme, Europe Today.
“This is what the Commission president spoke about.”
He was responding to comments made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at her agenda-setting State of the European Union speech on Wednesday, in which she proposed that Europe must develop a mechanism to be able to respond to hybrid warfare incidents.
Recent drone incursions have rattled Europe’s Eastern flank, as have many other incidents inhabiting the grey zone of warfare, such as cable-cuts and weaponised migration.
The steady drumbeat of incidents last month prompted five Baltic European Commissioners to demand a stronger response from the EU executive to support the region.
Von der Leyen used her State of the European Union address on Wednesday to outline a new European response to threats “which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security”.
Among the proposals the Commission president unveiled was a mechanism to complement NATO's Article 4, which would be referred to as the Emergency Security Protocol.
“When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response," von der Leyen explained, "to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact.”
Coming together
Kubilius told Euronews that the European Commission is working on plans for how it can assist countries particularly impacted by hybrid threats.
“The European Union is a solidarity union,” he said.
But the security effort does not stop there, with von der Leyen also touting a potential new leader’s format, titled the European Security Council.
According to her, the group would include not just EU member states but also like-minded countries such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada, banded together to address the biggest geopolitical issues facing Europe — among them an increasingly brazen Russia and the retreat of the United States from Europe's security architecture.
"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent," von der Leyen said. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play."
In practice, leaders like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are already frequently invited to European Council meetings. The new format would institutionalise this relationship, giving it a dedicated framework to discuss security matters.
The big question is how the group would not duplicate the efforts of the 77-year-old NATO, of which 23 EU countries are members.
European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said the European Security Council would “complement NATO” and not “compete with NATO”.
“We see the war in Ukraine has been turned into a drone war and Russia is producing millions of drones a year,” he said on Europe Today. “We need to strengthen our drone defence capabilities.”
Asked whether duplication could occur through the proposed Emergency Security Protocol or the European Security Council, a NATO official told Euronews they welcome European Allies and partners stepping up to do more in support of shared security.
“As again underlined at the Ankara Summit, NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda — including to ramp up defence industrial production and to ensure continued support to Ukraine,” the official said.

Up to 25,000 North Koreans work in Russian drone production
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:40:00 EEST
17:40:00 KST

Up to 25,000 North Koreans work in Russian drone production
Russia is recruiting North Korean workers to manufacture drones used in the war against Ukraine by bringing them into the country on student visas. Up to 25,000 North Korean workers are currently employed in drone production at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Russia's Tatarstan.
Source: a report by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT); a joint statement on the report
Quote: "North Korean overseas labourers are reportedly employed in Russia's manufacturing industry including as many as 25,000 North Korean labourers at a widely-sanctioned Russian drone factory in Alabuga, Tatarstan…
The DPRK has promoted the deployment of labourers to Russian Geran-2 drone factories in the Alabuga SEZ in Tatarstan, Russia since 2025."
Details: According to the MSMT report on North Korea's overseas labour programme, Russia currently hosts between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean workers, linked to 70-80 DPRK companies.
Most are employed in construction, agriculture and similar sectors. However, up to 1,000 workers are employed at strategically important businesses, including weapons manufacturing plants, steel processing facilities or shipbuilding complexes.
Russia currently ranks second worldwide in terms of the number of North Korean overseas workers, behind only China. The number of North Korean workers in Russia has risen particularly sharply since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia sends some of them to work in roles supporting its military-industrial complex.
North Koreans work within the Alabuga special economic zone, which is involved in supplying Russian forces with drones used in the war against Ukraine. In 2025, for instance, Russia completed construction of a large residential complex at Alabuga to house foreign workers, including North Korean citizens.
On average, a North Korean worker earns around US$7,500 a year in Russia, although almost all of this income is seized for the benefit of the North Korean regime.
Over recent years, Russia and North Korea have built up an extensive system combining state-level sanctions evasion with corrupt practices. For example, instead of work permits, Russia uses student and tourist visas to bring in North Koreans. In 2025, almost all North Korean workers entered Russia on student visas, posing as international students.
According to the report, intermediaries from third countries may also be involved in recruiting and dispatching North Korean workers to Russia. At least one such case is known to have occurred in Belarus.
Background: The BBC reported earlier that North Korean workers who have fled the country told the BBC about slave-like working conditions in Russia, where they are sent to fill the labour shortage exacerbated by Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.

One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:39:30 BST

One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
- Published
North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.
Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.
Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.
The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".
Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.
Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.
Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.
In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.
Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET.
"Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.
Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption.
In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.
The downpour comes as Spain emerges from its hottest summer on record and an exceptionally warm start to September.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn.
The Mediterranean Sea absorbs heat during summer, increasing evaporation and contributing to heavier rainfall when storms develop.
The flooding comes less than two years after devastating flooding in Valencia killed more than 230 people.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine, Slovenia working on preparing Drone Deal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
11:39:13 EEST
17:39:13 KST

Ukraine and Slovenia are currently working on preparing a Drone Deal, President Volodymyr Zelensky has reported following a meeting with Slovenian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Tone Kajzer and Minister of Defense Valentin Hajdinjak, who are visiting Kyiv.
"Today in Kyiv, a government delegation from Slovenia together with representatives of leading companies. Met with Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Tone Kajzer together with Minister of Defense Valentin Hajdinjak. Our countries are working on preparing a Drone Deal, and we discussed the initial results and joint defense projects that we can implement," Zelensky wrote on his Telegram channel on Thursday.
According to him, during the meeting they discussed at length Ukraine's future in a united Europe, regional security, and constant Russian attacks.
"I thanked for Slovenia's contribution to PURL of $50 million and all support. And we are very grateful for such respect for all our people and for our soldiers who gave their lives defending Ukraine and all of Europe. Today we together honored their memory with a minute of silence," Zelensky wrote.
The Drone Deal is a multi-year international cooperation program initiated by Ukraine, aimed at comprehensive interaction in the security and defense sphere. It unites Ukrainian combat expertise, supply chains, and defense-industrial cooperation.
The Drone Deal can include a range of projects depending on specific partner requests, such as air defense development, scaling of drone technologies, training programs, and defense-industrial production. The entire system is built on Ukrainian combat experience.
The 10-year format of agreements allows for building a more flexible yet stable partnership. These arrangements are designed for a long-term period and create the basis for stable financing of cooperation.
The program is aimed at large-scale export of Ukrainian defense technologies, attracting foreign investment, and joint production of unmanned and anti-drone systems tested in real combat conditions. The National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) serves as the coordinator of this program.
Prior to the full-scale war, Ukraine prohibited the export of its own weapons, but the Drone Deal format officially opened this possibility during martial law. The main idea is that Ukraine offers Western partners and other states its unique combat experience and technologies, receiving in exchange financing and access to foreign production capacities. Each agreement is adapted to the specific needs of the partner country.

Pakistan army chief urges Iran to persuade Houthis not to target Saudi energy facilities: Sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:38:46 UTC
17:38:46 KST

Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has urged Iran to persuade Yemen's Houthi group not to target Saudi Arabia's energy facilities, Pakistani government sources told Anadolu on Thursday.
In Islamabad's latest attempt to bring a negotiated settlement to the raging Middle East conflict, Munir spoke to Iran's top diplomat Abbas Araghchi over the phone, urging Tehran to "use its influence" on Houthis to halt their strikes on Saudi oil and economic infrastructure, the sources added.
The two spoke during Araghchi's visit to China on Wednesday, Iranian state media confirmed.
"The army chief discussed the overall regional situation, with special focus on Houthis' attacks and revival of stalled direct talks between the US and Iran," a source familiar with the developments said.
Islamabad has already warned that the recent escalations would further complicate the already complex regional scenario.
Describing Araghchi's response as "hopeful," the sources did not provide further details.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei recently stated that Tehran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs and described the Houthis as independent actors "pursuing their own interests."
The latest conversation comes a day after a Houthi drone was intercepted near the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia, which invited ire from the international community, including Muslim countries. Houthis denied they launched the drone.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia last year inked a bilateral defense pact, which subsequently led to the signing of a trilateral Mecca defense agreement last month involving Türkiye.
Yemen has been gripped by war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
The group has been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since July, when it declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh, and has recently claimed advances along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, which has further raised oil prices in the international market.
 
Committed to defense pacts, says Islamabad
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry Thursday reiterated its committment to “implementing” its bilateral defense agreement, as well as the trilateral Mecca pact.
“However, when, how, where and what force will be used against what objectives, in which modes and matters ... — operational confidentiality requires us to be discreet at this stage,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan told reporters in Islamabad.
He was responding to a question on whether “any mechanism had been devised as to how Pakistan will ensure that recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia are thwarted."
"Pakistan has for a long time ... shared the perspective that we would like to have peace and stability because this is not only in the interest of Pakistan and Iran, but also the entire region and beyond," said Khan, according to Dawn newspaper.
The situation in Bab al-Mandeb, he said, is “exceptionally serious," urging Houthis to “stop their activities.”
“In this regard, our discussions basically revolve around bringing peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy and not through coercive measures,” he added.
 
Revival of stalled talks
Sources said that the Pakistani army chief and Iran's top diplomat also discussed ways to revive stalled direct talks with the US to end their months-long war.
Aragchi, for his part, said Iran is ready to return to negotiations as the US halts hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and "abides by the Islamabad memorandum," the sources further said.
China is also assisting Pakistan's efforts to revive the US-Iran talks and stop the conflict from spilling over, they added.
"Beijing is equally worried about the raging hostilities because it's getting its oil bill heavier," a source said, without offering further details about China's assistance.
In his meeting with Araghchi in Beijing on Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi encouraged Iran and the US to remain rational, exercise restraint, return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, and "engage in substantive consultations."
China "does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea," Wang added.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington, DC, next week, where the two sides are likely to discuss ways to resolve the lingering Middle East conflict, in addition to other pending issues between the world's two largest economies.
Pakistan has remained the main mediator between Iran and the US throughout the war that began on Feb. 28, and has maintained close contact with both sides.
The US and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding on June 17 and launched negotiations toward a final agreement. However, the talks later stalled over disagreements on security guarantees and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategic routes for global energy supplies and trade.
Between July 8 and July 24, the US and Iran exchanged military strikes, with Washington launching attacks on targets inside Iran, and Tehran responding by striking US military facilities and equipment in several Arab countries, including Jordan, Bahrain, and Kuwait.
After securing a ceasefire on April 8, Pakistan hosted the highest-level direct talks between the US and Iran since they broke diplomatic ties in 1979. The talks, held in Islamabad on April 11-12, ended inconclusively.
Since the war began on Feb. 28, more than 3,500 people, both civilians and soldiers, have been killed in Iran.
Tehran has hit US bases and assets in the Middle East, and the Pentagon has confirmed over a dozen fatalities, besides dozens of injuries to its personnel.

‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:37:15 UTC
17:37:15 KST

Abandoning their homes and cramming into cars, Yemeni families have fled in their thousands from a lightning advance along the Red Sea coastal plains and up the rugged hills towards the mountaintop city of Taiz as the war returned in dramatic form this month.
“We fled a large, comfortable home, and here we are struggling to find a plastic sheet and wooden poles,” said one of the displaced, Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who fled her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren.
“This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day and are all struggling now to find shelter.”
The family fled the Maqbanah district in the wide Taiz region and headed toward Al-Shimayateen District, arriving at a camp for displaced families where she has relatives. More than 100,000 people have fled their homes in the last month.
“The fighting was fierce in our village, and some of our civilian neighbours were killed or injured, so we fled home and left everything behind,” she told the Guardian. “Amid the fierce battles you forget everything. We left our home belongings, and one neighbour even left his livestock behind.”
As soon as Taleb arrived in the camp, she found three or four families living in every tent because newly displaced people were constantly arriving. Left with no other option, she moved in with a relative’s family and three others.
“On the first day, we were happy just to reach safety, but then we felt the suffering the next day. Displaced families kept arriving, and there was no space in the camp and not enough tents,” she added.
Some humanitarian organisations intervened, providing displaced families with canned food and hygiene kits.
Taleb said she had never left her village in her life except for brief emergencies, always returning in a day or two. This is the first time she has been forced to flee long-term, and she feels returning will be difficult.
“I dream of returning to my village today, before tomorrow, but it isn’t in my hands. The fighting is still ongoing, and more families are arriving every day.”
Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people (about 18,000 households) since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha).
The International Organization for Migration said more than 2,000 people fleeing the hostilities have reached Djibouti’s northern shores so far, landing at scattered points along the coast near Obock.
Hatem Qasem, a farmer in his 40s from Al-Wazeyah district west of Taiz city, grew up in a village where residents rely on farming and raising livestock. He stated that when battles approached their village, they thought of nothing but their safety.
“We are farmers and rarely leave our village except for emergencies, but three days ago, the shelling and clashes were all around us, and we found ourselves in a position where we had to flee,” Qasem told the Guardian.
He explained that they sold their livestock at low prices simply to cover the cost of fleeing, as they could not take the livestock with them to an unknown destination.
“We took the children and left – around five families in one car. We couldn’t believe we managed to escape the fighting, but praise be to God, we made it,” he added.
They arrived in Al-Shimayateen district in Taiz. Although they do not have shelter there, it is a safe area where many displaced families have sought refuge.
“I am happy that we are safe now and that no one in the family was killed or injured, but we have started to realise that it will be difficult to stay here for long. We have no work here and no one to help us,” Qasem said.
According to Save the Children, at least 19 children were killed and a further 49 injured between 1 August and 9 September, bringing the total number of civilians killed in the escalating violence in Yemen to 117 and of those injured to 206. At least 175 were killed or injured in a single week (3-9 September), including 43 children, the highest weekly child casualty toll in the past 12 months.
With fierce fighting ongoing in Qasem’s village, returning home is not an option. To remain displaced, however, he needs a source of income to provide for his family.
“We will wait this month out here and see. If the fighting moves away from our village, we will return; if it continues, we will look for another solution.”
Qasem’s family of eight lives with three other displaced families in the same house – each family occupying a single room to share the cost of rent.
In Al-Safia makeshift camp, displaced people have no work and depend entirely on humanitarian organisations for their basic needs.
In 2026, an estimated 22.3 million people in Yemen – more than half the population – require humanitarian assistance and protection services, including 5.2 million displaced people, according to Ocha.
Ali Qaid, manager of the executive unit for Internationally Displaced People Camps Management in Taiz governorate, confirmed that some humanitarian organisations have begun providing aid to newly displaced families arriving in areas like Al-Shimayateen. However, he noted that many civilians remain trapped in active combat zones.
“Displacement from the western districts of Taiz governorate is still ongoing, and many people are trapped in the middle of the fighting, preventing humanitarian organisations from reaching them with assistance,” he told the Guardian.

Australia to restrict student, backpacker visas in migration clampdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Australia to cut student, backpacker visas in migration curb
September 17, 2026
Australia will cut migration by toughening visa rules for foreign students, backpackers, and working holiday-makers, the Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Thursday.
Under the new rules, foreign students will no longer be allowed to bring partners and children to join them while they study in Australia, while people who overstay their working holiday visas will face tougher enforcement.
The government is also cracking down on so-called "visa hopping," where foreign migrants who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.
"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa. If you want to come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa. And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia," Burke said.
What else did the Home Affairs Minister say about the migration reforms?
In remarks to the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday, Burke insisted that immigration remains "fundamentally a strength" for Australia, but acknowledged that rules needed adjusting to ease pressure on housing.
"We need immigration to soften enough that housing has a chance to catch up," he said, while stressing the housing shortage was not caused by migrants.
Burke said it was "simply demonstrably wrong" that his ruling center-left Labor party was beefing up its visa rules as a response to a surge in the polls by the far-right One Nation.
This year, the group has become one of the country's most popular parties, campaigning on pledges to slash migration to the country as part of its "Australia First" approach, which has drawn similarities to US President Donald Trump.
The hard-right party said this week that it would cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over the next three years to give Australians "breathing space."
The cost of living and immigration have ranked as some of voters' most pressing concerns in recent polls.
What is the migration situation in Australia?
The changes are set to see net annual migration fall from the current 300,000 to around 225,000 by 2028. That would see numbers return to the levels before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Annual migration surged to its highest level of 538,000 in 2022, after borders reopened.
Data on Thursday showed that migration numbers had declined to 292,100 in the year to March, 47% below the peak following the pandemic, Burke said.
Students make up the biggest immigrant group: some 753,000 foreign students live in Australia, most of whom come from China and India.
The reforms will see Australia return to its policy of a decade earlier when those who overstayed were given two weeks to leave the country or face detention and deportation, the minister said.
People seeking to extend their working holiday visas in rural areas will enter a ballot for a second or third year.
Applicants with skills in construction and housing will be prioritized for visas, Burke said.
Relatives of visa holders wanting to visit the country will have "no further stay" conditions applied to their visas.

Türkiye expands measures to contain fund market strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:31:43 UTC
17:31:43 KST

Türkiye has expanded measures to address payment problems in the fund market, suspending trading in funds run by seven asset managers on its electronic fund platform while the Central Bank increased liquidity support following a sharp stock market sell-off.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered a halt to purchases and sales on TEFAS, Türkiye’s electronic fund trading platform, for all funds established by Tera Portföy, Pusula Portföy, Hedef Portföy, Atlas Portföy, A1 Portföy, Pardus Portföy and Bulls Portföy that trade on the platform.
The board also ordered the liquidation of specified funds established by these companies, under procedures it would determine.
In a separate measure, the SPK allowed brokers to lower the minimum maintenance margin for securities bought on credit from 35 percent to 20 percent. Brokers may apply the lower requirement in line with their risk policies, taking client requests into account.
The temporary arrangement runs through the close of trading on Oct. 2, subject to further announcements by the board.
The measures followed a Sept. 17 meeting of the Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek. The committee described the fund market problems as “temporary and manageable” and pledged swift action to ease the liquidity squeeze and prevent contagion.
In a statement released by the Treasury and Finance Ministry, it attributed market volatility to credit and liquidity problems at some funds managed by a limited number of portfolio management companies.
It said there was no fundamental or structural risk to the functioning of Borsa Istanbul or the capital markets, with the difficulties concentrated in a particular segment of the fund market.
The Central Bank announced that it would increase funding through one-week repo auctions, taking liquidity conditions into account. It subsequently opened a 300 billion Turkish Lira auction on Sept. 17, up from 1 billion liras the previous day, Bloomberg HT reported.
The bank also said it would update banks’ borrowing limits in its Interbank Money Market to reflect the banking system’s current balance-sheet size. Bloomberg HT, citing sources, reported that those limits had been increased tenfold to 510 billion liras.
The Central Bank will also reduce collateral haircuts in its markets, allowing banks to borrow more against eligible assets.
The benchmark BIST 100 index fell 5.54 percent to 13,122.58 on Sept. 16. It opened 1.32 percent lower the following day but reversed those losses, trading more than 2 percent higher by 10:28 a.m., according to Bloomberg HT.
Fund disclosures had outlined the payment difficulties. Pusula Portföy announced on Sept. 15 that some funds it managed had defaulted on payments to investors seeking to redeem their holdings.
Tera Portföy subsequently reported redemption payment defaults in its lira money market fund and an equity fund. Tera Holding Chairman Emre Tezmen described the difficulties at certain funds as a temporary liquidity shortage and said group companies continued to operate.
Atlas Portföy said on Sept. 17 that redemption payments at its PSE money market fund were delayed while it worked to strengthen the fund’s liquidity.
The Financial Stability Committee said regulators would continue to act against those found to have engaged in market-disrupting activity. The Central Bank said it would monitor liquidity conditions closely and take further measures if needed.

Russia’s Su-57 skips external fuel tanks for Egypt flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:29:06 UTC
17:29:06 KST

Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said its Su-57 stealth fighter flew to an air show in Egypt this month using fuel tanks built into its internal weapons bays instead of the external drop tanks fighters typically carry on long ferry flights.
UAC said the aircraft made the trip to the El Alamein International Airshow with one intermediate stop, and still had enough fuel for another 1,000 km (620 miles) after landing. That reserve let the jet fly a demonstration flight the following day, which UAC and Rostec, the state conglomerate that owns UAC, described as comparable in fuel use to a full air combat sortie.
External tanks are standard on most fighters for long ferry flights, but they add drag and increase an aircraft’s radar signature, working against the low-observable shaping that defines a stealth design. Using internal tanks instead lets the Su-57 stretch its range without that tradeoff.
“The ability to use insert fuel tanks inside the weapons bays instead of external suspensions fully corresponds to the fifth-generation aircraft concept,” Rostec said in a statement. “This solution preserves the aircraft’s aerodynamics and provides a significant ferry range reserve. The flight showed that among tactical aircraft, the Su-57E is unmatched in combat radius and time aloft.”
The Su-57E is the export version of Russia’s Su-57 fighter, built with low observability, high maneuverability and a wide range of compatible weapons, according to UAC. The company says deliveries to foreign customers are already underway, though it has not named which countries have received aircraft or in what numbers.
The jet has appeared at a string of international air shows over the past two years, including Zhuhai in China in November 2024, Aero India in February 2025, and the Dubai Airshow that November, where a Su-57E carrying the tail number 509 was on static display. This year’s El Alamein show, running Sept. 8-10 at El Alamein International Airport on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, was the aircraft’s second appearance in the country after the inaugural edition in 2024.
The Russian jet shared the ramp at El Alamein with U.S. Air Force and Texas Air National Guard aircraft, including C-130J and C-130H transports, A-10 attack jets, F-16s and F-15Es, along with a Chinese contingent of fighters, tankers and airborne early warning aircraft. Organizers billed the event as trade-only, open to approved business and government visitors rather than the public, with Egypt’s Ministry of Defense, Air Force and Ministry of Civil Aviation backing the show.

Independent Journalism Is Critical For European Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:29:00 UTC
17:29:00 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered the EU’s annual state of the union address on Wednesday, calling for the robust defense of European values and warning of the dangers of cognitive warfare, foreign propaganda, and disinformation powered by viral deepfakes.
Shaped by social media algorithms and surging AI, the integrity of Europe’s information space has become a core security and economic concern as foreign adversaries and extremists seek to paralyze democracies. Von der Leyen promised to respond by toughening sanctions enforcement and putting more funds towards promoting the rule of law.
Europe is right to treat these issues as a high-stakes, generation-defining challenge. But there was a key omission in her speech: Independent journalism is a precondition for democratic resilience, and supporting it must remain a priority for the EU. Journalism exposes the inner workings of the threats facing our institutions, and populates our public spaces with reliable, factual, nuanced information. It is the most durable answer Europe has to the disinformation and foreign interference the President warned against. Only an informed public can make free choices.
While media freedom is folded into the EU’s broader Democracy Shield and rule of law frameworks, journalism lacks protection as the distinct, load-bearing pillar of democratic resilience that it is. In the face of rising attacks, Europe needs more explicit prioritization of financial support and protections for journalists.
It’s not hard to find real-world examples of why this is so important. OCCRP’s cross-border reporting often generates valuable findings for over-stretched enforcement agencies that struggle to work across borders. Our recent investigations have exposed scam networks with tens of thousands of European victims, and revealed cognitive warfare operations deployed by the Kremlin in European capitals. We have also helped identify war criminals torturing Ukrainian prisoners, and mapped the trade routes through which European materials continue to strengthen the Russian war machine. We don’t have numbers for the whole industry, but our reporting alone has triggered 477 government investigations and 842 arrests or indictments since 2009.
President von der Leyen rightly lauded the recent Hungarian elections as a sign of hope. In that contest, Hungarians reacted in part to the long record of corruption racked up by Viktor Orban and his cronies. How did they know about that? In large part thanks to the intrepid reporting of independent journalists, including OCCRP partners Direkt36 and Átlátszó. In Lithuania, investigative reporting led to a powerful demonstration of democratic accountability this year, with a prime minister stepping down amid an integrity scandal. In the EU’s neighbors, the students who mobilized nationwide protests in Serbia were also empowered by journalists’ findings, while journalists in Ukraine have held the government to account and prompted it to act on corruption allegations.
We know that the European Commission values journalism, as evidenced by initiatives like the European Media Freedom Act and enhanced anti-SLAPP rules.
But its support must outpace the rising threats in their physical, legal, digital and reputational forms. OCCRP alone faces 80+ lawsuits, and is fending off unprecedented DDoS attacks on its web infrastructure and AI-enabled takedown requests by PR firms hired by wealthy targets of our reporting. Our partners in Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan face false charges and prison terms. Within EU institutions and beyond, extremist groups are villainizing the media, leading to smear attacks and online hate. The recent verdict in the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial in Malta is a grim reminder of the pushback journalists can face when they report on politicians, crime bosses, tech oligarchs, and other power brokers.
Funding, meanwhile, is in short supply. Last year, President von der Leyen called for stepping up where others have stepped back. The funding crisis is especially urgent for nonprofit media. OCCRP and our network of 40+ European news outlets have been badly affected by the changing landscape in media funding, including the loss of an estimated $1.7 billion in U.S. funding for freedom-of-expression programs. While the EU funds journalism through several channels, what outlets still lack is sustained support for reporting on big, complex threats to democracy.
Now is the time for the EU to take a stand: prioritize journalism as a pillar of democratic resilience; bolster multi-year support for investigative reporting; and fortify the conditions in which these journalists work.
Journalists have proven their ability to counter the leading threats to Europe’s security. Their role in achieving President von der Leyen’s “strong and independent Europe” is more than symbolic. You cannot win a battle of narratives when the infrastructure that provides citizens with reliable information is crumbling beneath your feet.

Italy’s Contributions to Space Exploration on Display in Osaka
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:27:23 CEST
17:27:23 KST

From September 19 to October 25, 2026, the Osaka Science Museum will host the exhibition “From the Moon to Mars. Italy in Space Exploration’ will be on display at the Osaka Science Museum. The exhibition, sponsored by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and curated by Viviana Panaccia, is part of the celebrations marking the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan and the 45th anniversary of the sister-city relationship between Milan and Osaka. The exhibition traces the long history of space exploration through photographs that have captured some of its most significant moments, while also presenting the evolution of the Italian space industry to the public. The exhibition also includes a special section dedicated to Giovanni Schiaparelli’s observations of the “canals” of Mars.
                                    
                                       
				Among the highlights of the exhibition—on display in Japan for the first time—is a faithful replica of the new Axiom Extravehicular Unit (AxEMU) spacesuit, jointly developed by Prada and Axiom Space. The suit is intended for the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface after more than fifty years.

UN says US strikes in Iran were war crimes, Tehran crackdown crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:26:58 UTC
17:26:58 KST

A United Nations fact-finding mission said Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for deadly strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in February, concluding that the attacks amounted to war crimes.
In the same report, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on nationwide anti-government protests that began in late December.
The mission, whose mandate includes investigating serious human rights violations in Iran and preserving evidence for potential legal proceedings, is due to present its findings to the UN Human Rights Council during its September-October session.
Deadly strike on Minab school
The investigators said they had reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces carried out the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, where Iranian authorities said more than 150 people were killed, including about 120 schoolchildren.
UN investigators had opened an inquiry into the strike in March after U.S. military investigators concluded preliminarily that American forces were likely responsible, although the Pentagon had not reached a final determination.
The fact-finding mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate, caused civilian deaths and damaged civilian infrastructure, and therefore amounted to a war crime.
According to the report, the U.S. relied on intelligence indicating that a senior Iranian military commander was at the site but failed to sufficiently verify that information before launching the strike.
Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm that the building remained a military objective went beyond simple negligence.
“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen,” the report said.
UN experts had previously described the Minab school as a protected civilian object and called for an independent investigation, saying attacks on civilian schools can constitute war crimes unless the facilities have become military objectives.
President Donald Trump said in June that “nobody” had intentionally attacked a girls’ school in Iran, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon later elevated its inquiry but has not publicly released preliminary findings.
The UN mission said it found no evidence that the school was being used for military purposes.
Second strike in Lamerd
Investigators reached a similar conclusion about a U.S. strike on a sports center in Lamerd.
According to the report, the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school, killing and wounding 22 civilians. The mission concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore also constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in March that American forces had not carried out any strikes in Lamerd that day.
The findings come as the UN mission continues to warn about civilian casualties from the ongoing conflict. Earlier this week, it called on all sides to comply with international law after additional U.S. strikes in southern Iran reportedly killed civilians, stressing that parties must distinguish between military and civilian targets and take precautions to minimize civilian harm.
Iran accused of crimes against humanity
The report also examined Tehran’s response to the mass protests that erupted in late December.
Investigators concluded that Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack on civilians involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
The mission said it could not independently establish the full number of casualties but believed the toll was substantially higher than official Iranian figures of 3,038 people killed and 25,000 injured.
Iran has blamed the unrest on “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and foreign powers, including the United States and Israel, and has repeatedly rejected allegations of systematic human rights abuses.
The UN investigators said the crackdown represented a significant escalation from previous patterns of repression, citing the scale of violence, killings, internet restrictions and use of the death penalty.
The Human Rights Council expanded the mission’s mandate in January to urgently investigate alleged violations linked to the protests that began on Dec. 28, 2025, including for possible use in future legal proceedings.

Electric cars’ market share in Europe tops 30% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:26:46 UTC
17:26:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Battery-electric vehicles accounted for more than 30% of new car registrations across key European markets in August, according to an industry report released Thursday.
A total of 202,833 new battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) were registered across 16 European markets during the month, marking an annual increase of 54.2%, according to a monthly bulletin prepared by Brussels-based E-Mobility Europe and independent transport research organization New AutoMotive.
BEVs represented 30.5% of all new car registrations in the markets covered, while their estimated share across the EU reached 31.2%.
During the January-August period, BEV registrations increased 33.1% year-on-year to 1.67 million. Their market share over the eight-month period stood at 22.5%.
Germany and France led the expansion in Europe’s electric vehicle market.
France registered 36,159 fully electric cars in August, with their market share reaching 38.3%. Registrations rose 72.2% from a year earlier.
Germany recorded 68,980 BEV registrations, giving fully electric cars a market share of 32.5%. Registrations increased 34.5% year-on-year.
BEVs accounted for 98.7% of new car registrations in Norway, 85.9% in Denmark, 52.3% in Finland and 48.9% in the Netherlands.
Belgium followed with a 46.2% share, while electric cars accounted for 36.1% of registrations in Portugal.
The report covers Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland.
Together, these markets represent approximately 90% of the combined EU and European Free Trade Association car market.

King’s College London (KCL) will reinstate an Egyptian student who was suspended after his participation in pro-Palestinian protests, CNN has reported.
Usama Ghanem, 22, will return to KCL this fall, nearly 18 months after university officials suspended him indefinitely and moved to withdraw his visa sponsorship over allegations concerning his involvement in student-led pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
Ghanem reportedly received an email from the university in late August stating that it continued to uphold its finding of non-academic misconduct against him, while also informing him that he had committed “no breaches” of the terms of his exclusion.
“The conditions set have been met, and there is no reason for your suspension or exclusion to remain in place,” the email said. “Accordingly, you will be invited to re-enrol for the 2026/27 academic year and will be permitted access to King’s College London.”
The university also reaffirmed that it would begin the process of reinstating Ghanem’s visa sponsorship in a separate memo sent in early September.
Ghanem’s case reportedly drew public criticism from some academics, who raised concerns over a crackdown by US and UK universities that disproportionately affects Muslim students and students of colour for lawful expressions of Palestinian solidarity and criticism of Israel.
Ghanem told CNN he “unequivocally” denied the misconduct allegations, saying the outcome of the review set “a huge precedent.”
He added that he would continue to advocate for “Palestinian rights, and the fight for divestment from all weapons and from all complicit actors with the genocide in Gaza.”
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza
Meanwhile, a KCL spokesperson told CNN that a review of Ghanem’s suspension had always been scheduled to take place one year after it was imposed as part of the university’s standard procedures.
“Following that review, a panel determined that he had met the conditions agreed for suspension, and that re-enrolment was now the appropriate outcome,” the spokesperson said, and added: "We will always apply a fair approach to misconduct proceedings, and have a duty to act where behaviour breaches safeguarding and security regulations, or puts others at risk.”

As Ghanem prepares to return to the university, a legal case he filed against KCL remains ongoing. The case claims breaches of human rights, assault, personal injury, discrimination and harassment on the part of the university.

New county bus contracts to deliver drivers hefty pay rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:26:00 UTC
17:26:00 KST

New county bus contracts to deliver drivers hefty pay rise
New regional bus contracts will require drivers to be paid Estonia's average wage, increasing the amount of state funding needed to subsidize bus services.
Regional bus routes have for years operated under a sector-wide collective agreement between employers and employees that sets bus drivers' pay rates.
In 2025, the Association of Estonian Road Carriers and the Transport Workers' Union agreed that bus drivers would in future have to be paid Estonia's average wage. Contracts for regional bus routes are awarded for eight years and this year public transport centers will begin conducting the first procurements under the new terms.
"Over the next five years, all of our contracts will be renewed. Some have already been renewed, so to speak, while some are still being processed. Next year there will be two contracts and after that two contracts a year through 2031. The requirement to pay the average wage is now fully included in the new contracts," said Andrus Nilisk, executive director of the North Estonia Public Transport Center.
The calculation would be based on the previous year's average wage, or around €2,100, while bus drivers working under existing contracts that still have several years to run are being paid €1,500 this year. Their wages are increased through indexation.
"With the old contracts, wages also rise by €100 each year, so they will eventually reach roughly the same level, but under the new contracts the increase is steep," Nilisk said.
However, the wage increase would mean raising the state's annual taxpayer-funded subsidy.
"Labor costs account for about half of the price per route kilometer, so naturally this will have an impact on the subsidy. During the transition period, it will require around €1.5 million a year in additional subsidies. For the past five years, every year when the state budget has been adopted, there has not been enough funding to last through the end of the year and then additional money has been found midway through the year," said Kersten Kattai, director of the Association of Estonian Road Carriers.
The minimum salary for teachers is €1,970 this year. Estonia's median wage has been €1,750 this year. Minister of Regional Affairs Hendrik Johannes Terras would now have to seek additional funding for subsidies in order to pay bus drivers €2,100.
"I know that this agreement has been reached. It may have an impact on the bids submitted in terms of the price per kilometer. But given that relatively few of our contracts will be renewed next year, I don't expect it to have an impact on the budget," Terras said.

EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
09:25:26 BST
17:25:26 KST

EU announces plan to restrict social media access for under-15s
- Published
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.
Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.
Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.
The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove platforms were safe by design or face fines of up to 6% of their global sales. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".
She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".
The restrictions would not just affect well-known apps such as TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat but also YouTube and other video sharing platforms as well as AI chatbots and online games.
"Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.
Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".
She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans.
"For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principle of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.
Some individual EU countries have already announced their own plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.
The proposed EU-wide legislation would supersede those, and member states will not be able to opt out from what would be a legally binding regulation.
It is understood the Commission has warned some member states they would need to repeal any national laws passed before the EU Kids Act comes into effect.
The new plans need to be agreed by EU member states and approved by the European Parliament.
Already there are questions about how this EU-wide legislation would be enforced and the plans are likely to face opposition in the months to come.
France provides an indication of how the path ahead could be bumpy as individual member states may try to strengthen or weaken the proposals.
The Macron government drew up legislation for a ban on social media for under-15s but last month the country's top court blocked it, ruling that it infringed upon freedom of expression.
French ministers have now amended their original plans.
Some critics of social media bans for children cite privacy concerns.
They worry about teenagers being forced to submit personal information as they go through an age verification process to prove they are old enough to access platforms.
The Commission has said age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app, and no personal data would be collected or shared.
Social media companies will also make their position on the restrictions clear as the act is debated in the months to come.
Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".
The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.
In July, the EU said Meta must change the "addictive" design of Facebook and Instagram or face a heavy fine.
In preliminary findings, the European Commission said features such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos and personalised recommendations could encourage "compulsive use", particularly among children and teens.
A spokesperson for the tech giant told the BBC it disagreed with the findings "which don't accurately take into account the significant steps we've taken to protect teens".
In a separate case, Meta agreed in August to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. It denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement.
The European Commission said its proposed legislation built on findings, external from its special panel on child safety online, which recommended age-appropriate regulation for children, with different guidance for each age group.
It also cited recent EU survey data, external, which found 92% of respondents considered the need to strengthen children's protection online as a top policy priority.
Von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" - which banned social media platforms for under-16s last year - when putting together the proposal.
The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.
A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.

Amid an ongoing political battle over which party's at fault for a lack of housing and migration numbers, an unlikely target has emerged: yoga teachers.
Labor has been accused by the Opposition of prioritising bringing in instructors of the flexible exercise to Australia, over construction workers sorely needed to address a critical housing shortage.
The Coalition since 2024 has levelled claims against Labor of putting instructors for martial arts and yoga ahead of tradies like bricklayers, painters, roof tilers and stonemasons in the visa queue.
The origins of the political line of attack appeared to come from a Nine Newspaper report which said in 2024 that a federal agency, Jobs and Skills Australia, listed yoga teachers as a skill in demand. Former coalition MP Michael Sukkar highlighted the report on social media, saying: "Under Labor they'll be more Yoga teachers and less tradies!".
On Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke sought to put the claims to bed, once and for all.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It is absurd," he told the National Press Club, saying it was among the "silliest of all" arguments.
Burke outlined that rather than deprioritising construction workers, the government had tripled the number it was bringing in, from 4,500 to 15,000.
"In the life of this government, the number of yoga teachers we have brought in is zero," he said.
"Zero. And yet this claim is constantly made about yoga teachers."
According to a fact check from Australian Associated Press (AAP) newswire, the opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg and colleagues made the claim a number of times in the past year, saying the government was bringing in more yoga teachers than construction workers.
AAP checked the claim against figures from the Department of Home Affairs, finding that only four yoga instructors have arrived since July 1, 2022, compared to thousands of construction workers that have come to Australia on skilled visas.
"While this figure may include yoga teachers, it could also cover coaches of other sports such as basketball or cricket," it said in an August finding.
Yoga teachers came under the temporary skilled visa program in 2022 after the Morrison government signed a trade agreement with India. The places are reserved for Indian nationals under that deal.
"It's a tiny argument, but it is so constantly out there and so demonstrably wrong, it gives an indication as to how a debate like this can just run out of control," Burke said.

Ukrainian officials stole $3 million from Polish gift to Kiev – investigators (PHOTOS)
Officials in Kiev embezzled more than $3 million by exploiting the delivery of old Soviet Russian-made metro cars donated by Poland, according to Western-backed anti-corruption investigators.
The 60 cars were donated by Warsaw in late 2022, allowing the Polish capital’s Metro to dispose of older railstock while demonstrating solidarity with Ukraine following the escalation of the conflict with Russia. Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko described the donation slated to be cannibalized for spare parts as “meaningful help” for the city when the first batch of six cars arrived in May 2023.
However, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) alleged on Wednesday that a group of officials in Kiev skimmed funds allocated for transporting the cars from Poland by manipulating a tender through which the cost was dramatically inflated.
NABU surveillance records show that a preliminary quote provided by a Ukrainian company to one of the suspects was ten times lower than the final contract price. The actual transportation services cost around a quarter of the sum, and the remaining $3 million was stolen and laundered in the EU, the agency said.
Investigators have issued formal suspicion notices to a former Kiev Metro official, three serving officials in the city’s municipal utilities, two alleged accomplices, and the owner of the company that won the tender.
The businessman apparently clashed with the alleged masterminds of the scheme after the unrealistic terms of the contract attracted scrutiny from financial monitors. In one surveillance recording, he told an associate who knew about his dealings that he threatened to testify against the officials because he did not want to be left taking the blame.
“I am the worst criminal here, I am Mindich,” he said, referring to fugitive businessman Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of Vladimir Zelensky who NABU accused of running a $100 million kickback scheme in the energy sector.
“Nah, you are higher,” the other man replied. “You are f**king Yermak.”
Andrey Yermak served as Zelensky’s chief of staff until he was forced to resign last year after becoming embroiled in the Mindich scandal. NABU has since accused him of money laundering in a parallel investigation into Mindich’s alleged criminal activities.
Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court ordered the removal of an electronic tracking anklet from Yermak this week after his defense argued that the device posed a health risk.

Türkiye sees over 127,000 home sales in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:18:59 UTC
17:18:59 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Türkiye recorded 127,410 home sales in August, down 14.7% from the same month last year, official data showed Thursday.
According to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat), sales of new homes declined 4.5% year-on-year to 44,378, accounting for 34.8% of total transactions.
Istanbul recorded the highest number of house sales among Türkiye’s provinces with 20,426, followed by the capital Ankara with 10,851 and the western province of Izmir with 6,532.
Sales of existing homes dropped 19.4% to 83,032, representing 65.2% of the total.
Mortgaged-financed home sales, however, rose 7.2% from a year earlier to 22,131, making up 17.4% of all sales. Other home sales fell 18.3% to 105,279.
In seasonally and calendar-adjusted terms, sales of new homes increased 3.5% and sales of existing homes rose 0.7% from July.
During the January-August period, total home sales decreased 6.8% year-on-year to 950,529.
Mortgage-financed sales increased 27.6% to 188,813 during the eight-month period, while other sales declined 12.7% to 761,716.
Sales to foreign buyers edged up 0.1% year-on-year to 1,938 in August, accounting for 1.5% of total home sales.
Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 343 transactions, followed by Ukrainians with 147 and Iranians with 140.
In January-August, house sales to foreigners fell 6.3% from a year earlier to 13,141.

Germany news: Mysterious explosions reported in Frankfurt

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 17, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
RTL and Sky Deutschland cutting roughly 500 jobs amid takeover
The private broadcasters RTL and Sky in Germany plan to cut about 500 jobs as part of their merger.
The RTL group, which bought out Sky Deutschland this year, confirmed the plans after they was first reported in the Bild newspaper on Thursday.
It said that most of the downsizing and restructuring was already complete and had been carried out in close coordination with works councils and unions. It said many of the cuts were achieved by not renewing expiring contracts or not hiring to fill open positions, in a bid to minimize layoffs or redundancies.
It did not say how the losses were split between the two companies.
The German arm of the RTL Group — a Luxembourg-based company that broadcasts in a string of other European countries like Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands — acquired Sky Deutschland in a bid to strengthen its position in the streaming and sports markets in Germany.
It was already effectively competing with Sky in broadcasting sports like Formula 1 and football.
It said it hoped the takeover would create "synergies" worth some €250 million (roughly $290 million), albeit primarily thanks to "optimization of content and of material costs" rather than personnel savings.
"Beyond that, duplicate structures will be dismantled, responsibilities will be bundled, and more efficient and forward-looking decision-making processes will be established," RTL said when announcing the takeover.
According to company data, RTL Germany currently employs 5,326 people and Sky has 2,170 employees.
Iraqi man arrested over alleged church attack plot
A 24-year-old Iraqi man has been arrested in Germany on suspicion of planning attacks on a church in the northern city of Bremen, among other targets, federal prosecutors have said.
The man was arrested in the Barnim region of Brandenburg state, just outside Germany's capital city, Berlin.
The man is believed to adhere to the radical, militant ideology promoted by the Islamic State (IS) terror group.
Prosecutors say the man allegedly procured a firearm and was scouting out the church in Bremen as the first of several potential targets.
The federal prosecutors, headquartered in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe, also say the man tried to recruit at least one other person for the plot. That person remains unknown, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (Bundeskriminalamt or BKA) said in a statement.
The suspect has been placed in pre-trial detention, accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state, trying to form a terrorist organization and violating the weapons act, the BKA said.
IS has claimed responsibility for some of the worst terror attacks in Germany's history, including the attack on the Berlin Christmas market in 2016 and a knife attack in the western city of Solingen in 2024.
Bavarian nurse accused of sexually abusing disabled patients
A nurse in Bavaria is charged with sexually abusing disabled patients, including many young children, in his care over the course of several years.
Prosecutors in Bamberg said on Thursday that a 33-year-old man was in investigative detention, accused of abusing 24 different people in three institutions in the southern state since October 2018. Some were under the age of 14.
He's alleged to have taken photographs and videos of the victims and to have touched several of them inappropriately.
Investigators believe that "as a result of their severe physical and mental impairments, [the victims] were unable to recognize and understand the offenses committed against them as such."
The investgiation was launched after German investigators received a tip-off from the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) about several sexually explicit videos of children that had been uploaded to a cloud online.
On searching the man's flat earlier this year, investigators secured more than 38,000 child pornography images and more than 600 videos.
The nurse is accused of the production and possession of child pornography, the sexual abuse of children, patients and vulnerable individuals in his care, and infringement of privacy and personal rights by taking photos and recording people without their understanding or consent.
Bamberg's regional court must now decided if it believes the case should go to trial. The nurse could face a jail term of between 1 and 15 years.
Klingbeil visits struggling VW, calls for tougher EU line on Chinese cars
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has called on the EU to expand tariffs on Chinese imports to include hybrid cars, saying Chinese manufacturing subsidies endanger Volkswagen and other companies.
KIingbeil made the call on a visit to VW's Wolfsburg HQ in Lower Saxony; it coincided with a joint appeal from the heads of Germany's three major carmaking states, Bavaria (BMW, Audi), Baden-Württemberg (Porsche, Mercedes) and Lower Saxony (VW).
"I am in favor of us standing up against unfair trade practices, and for Germany to adopt a different level of self-confidence and assertiveness towards countries that threaten our industry," Klingbeil, who leads the Social Democrats and is also deputy chancellor, said in Wolfsburg.
The VW Group is just embarking on a major restructuring and cost-cutting drive amid falling sales figures, planning to cut or otherwise phase out as may as 100,000 jobs in the coming years across its various marques — almost a sixth of its workforce.
The unpopular restructuring was approved earlier this month despite resistance from trade unions and from Lower Saxony's state government, which is led by Klingbeil's center-left Social Democrats (SPD). Klingbeil said it should be just the beginning of an ongoing transformation.
He said the EU would have to tighten local content rules and introduce tariffs on Chinese-made plug-in hybrid cars.
In what seemed a coordinated appeal, the state premiers of Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg and Lower Saxony, each representing a different German political party, appealed to the federal government in Berlin and authorities in Brussels to act with haste to protect the car industry.
"Without a combination of competitive conditions in the domestic market, effective protective instruments and fair trade within the bounds of the WTO, the car industry is threatened with irreversible damage," state premiers Markus Söder (Bavaria), Olaf Lies (Lower Saxony) and Cem Özdemir (Baden-Württemberg) wrote.
Söder belongs to the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), Lies is in the SPD and Özdemir belongs to the environmentalist Greens.
The three premiers called for tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrids, to be modeled on existing fees imposted on all-electric cars from China.
In 2025 alone, the German car industry shed more than 50,000 jobs.
German court holds Meta held liable for fake ads
A German court on Thursday ruled that Facebook parent company Meta is liable for fake advertising on its social media platforms.
The case involved ads using the logo of a financial advice website, alongside photos of the website's founder, to promote fraudulent investment schemes.
The Frankfurt regional court found that Meta was liable, citing a European Court of Justice (ECJ) decision ruling a service provider is liable for content that it exercises control over.
Meta was ordered to cease the publication and distribution of the fake ads, compensate the claimant for any damages, and disclose the revenue generated.
Meta had argued that it had no knowledge of the fake ads, but the Frankfurt court said it was up to the social media giant to decide how ads are published on its platforms.
The decision can be appealed, and a spokesperson for Meta said the company was considering further legal steps. Meta said it had taken several measures in the case, including removing the content after it was reported.
IN DEPTH: Klopp wants Germany team to 'reclaim the flag'
In an apparent reference to a recent electoral victory by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, newly-minted Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp said he wants his team to reflect "positive patriotism."
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself— or for us," Klopp said.

Heat and drought set to wither Germany's 2026 potato harvest
Extreme heat and drought this summer will lead to a weak potato harvest in northwestern Europe this year, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the UK-based Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).
In Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, a combined shortage of 3,1 million tons compared to the five-year average harvest is expected.
The data shows the weak harvest will hit Germany particularly hard, with the country's share of the total expected potato harvest shortage coming in at 1,13 million tons.
These figures do not yet represent a final harvest report, but are an estimate.
"As fall begins, the effects of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and agriculture are becoming clear," said ECIU analyst Tom Lancaster.
Potatoes are among the crops in Europe that require the most water.
The analysis also reports a significant increase in prices. In Germany, spuds served at dinner are set to cost up to €280 per metric ton, compared to around €150 last year.
The expected 2026 harvest shortfall comes after oversupply in 2025 flooded the market.
Germany backs social media ban for under-13s
Karin Prien,Germany's education minister, backed plans to restrict social media use among young people and children. "Any system will have to comply with data protection rules and minimize the amount of information that is collected about the user, without age-verification data being transmitted online. However, the primary responsibility for protecting minors lies with the social media platforms themselves," Prien told German public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday.
In addition to requesting age checks, Prien said media education and providing more information on the issue to parents are key. On Wednesday, the president of the European Commission,Ursula von der Leyen, proposed that children under the age of 13 be banned from accessing social media platforms such asTikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram. They would be able to use "mini-accounts" controlled and supervised by parents, with a maximum usage of one hour per day, and open a separate account from the age of 15.
Changes to social media platforms
Prien said the restrictions should be part of a broader, more comprehensive strategy. She also called for a rule under which children under the age of three have no screen time or access to digital services. The education minister announced plans as early as October for a German interim solution while rules are consolidated at the EU level. Under the EU proposals, social media platforms would be required to introduce safer designs, including measures to prevent endless scrolling and videos from playing automatically. The plans also include limits on screen time and other measures aimed at protecting young people.
