Houthi gains at Bab el-Mandeb expose Israel's unresolved Eilat shipping crisis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:19:55 UTC
16:19:55 KST

The Houthis' takeover of key points along Yemen's western coast and of Perim Island, in the heart of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, has brought renewed attention to a threat Israel knows well and has been paying a price for nearly three years, as the group's latest advances turn the Red Sea shipping threat into an increasingly urgent strategic problem for Saudi Arabia as well.
Even before the threat to Saudi oil routes prompted Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to seek US assistance, the Houthis had already registered a significant strategic achievement against Israel by almost completely disrupting regular commercial shipping to the Port of Eilat.
Nearly three years have passed since the problem emerged, and no solution remains. The IDF has repeatedly struck Houthi targets in Yemen, the state has provided assistance to the port, and an alternative import route has been established through Aqaba. None of this has brought international shipping companies back to regular, direct sailings from the East to Eilat.
Based on publicly available information, no cabinet decision has defined the restoration of commercial freedom of navigation to Eilat as a security and diplomatic objective, nor has the government presented an approved plan to bring ships back to the port.
Recent developments have changed the circumstances in which Israel is confronting the problem. The Houthi threat to Bab al-Mandab has become an urgent strategic issue for Saudi Arabia as well, and the Saudi crown prince has already requested military assistance from the US.
Israel and Saudi Arabia now have parallel diplomatic and strategic interests concerning the same maritime route. From Israel's perspective, Saudi Arabia's predicament creates an opportunity that did not previously exist to the same extent: to harness a regional effort around Bab al-Mandab to restore shipping to Eilat as well.
The Houthis captured Mocha, advanced along the coast, and took control of Perim, the island located inside the Bab al-Mandab Strait. They also seized Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish islands, strengthening their hold around one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.
Traffic through the strait continues, and the Houthis do not currently control the passage in a way that would allow them to halt all shipping. Their new positions do, however, improve their ability to monitor maritime traffic and selectively threaten vessels they choose to target.
Bab al-Mandab is a passage only about 18 miles wide, connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and from there to the Suez Canal. In normal periods, oil equivalent to roughly 7% of global production passes through it.
Control of Mocha, Dhubab, Perim, and the Hanish islands improves the Houthis' ability to monitor and threaten traffic in the strait. Shipping companies and insurers price that risk into insurance premiums, and in some cases simply forgo the voyage when the destination or vessel is perceived as a potential target.
Eilat port shipping interrupted by Houthi attacks since 2023
For Israel, the problem has persisted since November 2023, when the Houthis began attacking and threatening vessels linked to Israel. Major shipping companies stopped calling at Eilat along the previously standard route. The port continued to operate on a limited basis, but the commercial activity it relied on was severely damaged.
In 2023, the Port of Eilat recorded 132 ship calls and unloaded approximately 150,000 vehicles. In 2024, the port recorded only 16 ship calls, and it unloaded no vehicles. Port revenue, which stood at approximately NIS 212 million in 2023, fell by about 80% the following year.
The figures demonstrate how effective the Houthi threat was without requiring physical control of the shipping route. The threat to ships alone was enough for shipowners, insurers, financiers, and line operators to conclude that sailing to the Israeli port was not worthwhile.
The strikes carried out by the IDF in Yemen have also failed so far to bring the shipping companies back. Ultimately, the decision on whether to return to Eilat lies with shipping companies and insurers, and depends in part on their assessment of the risk along the route.
This year, a solution was found that allowed some vehicle-import activity to return to Eilat without the large car carriers themselves returning to the port. Ships arriving from the East docked in Aqaba, Jordan, where the vehicles were unloaded and then transferred to Eilat on smaller vessels.
In March alone, 5,905 vehicles were unloaded in Eilat, followed by another 3,142 in April.
The arrangement through Aqaba restored activity to the port and eased its predicament, but the direct shipping route from the East has not resumed. International shipping lines still do not call directly at Eilat as they did before the war. The large car carriers stop in Aqaba, and the cargo continues from there to Eilat.
Since 2023, Israel has addressed the problem through several channels. The IDF has struck Houthi targets in Yemen, and the defense establishment deals with the threat from Yemen on an ongoing basis. Israeli strikes have focused on damaging Houthi capabilities and responding to attacks against Israel.
Publicly available information does not indicate the existence of an approved plan in which restoring regular commercial shipping to Eilat was defined as an objective in its own right.
MK Forer pushes for action to fully reopen shipping route to Eilat
The issue was raised unusually prominently during a Knesset Economic Affairs Committee hearing in June. MK Oded Forer argued that the shipping route to Eilat was effectively closed because of the Houthis and that the government had not made reopening it a diplomatic and security objective.
"It doesn't matter who the operator is. If ships don't enter the port, there will be no port," he said.
Eilat Mayor Eli Lankri said the port was almost completely shut down.
For more than two years, a significant share of government efforts has focused on the port's economic distress. The state allowed payment deferrals, provided a loan guarantee, and approved direct assistance.
It also formulated a plan to subsidize the arrival of car carriers, under which it approved about half a million dollars per ship, aiming the bring four ships a month for three months, at a total cost of up to NIS 21 million.
The plan was not implemented. During Knesset discussions in early 2026, the situation was described as a "dead end." According to figures presented by the port management, its debts had reached approximately NIS 30 million, while the monthly gap between expenses and revenue stood at around NIS 5 million.
Most government efforts focused on financing the port's continued operation and trying to restore cargo traffic. Publicly available information does not indicate that any specific government body was given overall responsibility for restoring the direct shipping route to Eilat.
At the same time, the port tried to promote additional solutions. Its management examined the possibility of US assistance, approached Egypt, and attempted to advance mechanisms that would make it easier for ships to arrive through a safer or more heavily subsidized route.
None of those efforts have brought international shipping lines back to regular, direct operations in Eilat so far.
Port of Eilat's future remains undecided
The port's future also remains undecided. The current operator's concession is due to expire in 2028, and the state has yet to decide what the operating model will look like afterward.
The debate over the identity of the next operator is taking place while the issue that determines whether the port can function at all - the return of ships - remains unresolved.
This also has implications for the role of the Port of Eilat in Israel's national security doctrine. Eilat cannot replace Ashdod and Haifa in every scenario. It is not a major container port, and its infrastructure is limited.
Its importance derives largely from geography: It is Israel's only commercial port facing the Red Sea. If activity at the Mediterranean ports is disrupted or restricted, an operational southern maritime gateway could provide Israel with an additional route.
For it to be usable in an emergency, Israel must also maintain infrastructure, workers, equipment, and a functioning logistics system during routine periods.
Israel has already been paying a direct price at the Port of Eilat for nearly three years because of the Houthi threat. The Houthis' latest advance now makes the threat to Red Sea shipping routes a far more urgent problem for Saudi Arabia as well.
In the background lies a fact that has almost disappeared from Israel's public agenda: An Iran-backed organization, operating from roughly 2,000 kilometers away, succeeded in prompting international shipping companies to stop calling regularly at Eilat.
Even after a long series of Israeli strikes in Yemen, the ships have not returned. Nearly three years after regular shipping to Eilat was disrupted, the government has invested money and effort to preserve the port and prevent its collapse.
It succeeded in keeping the port alive. It has still not brought the ships back.

Former MoD permanent secretary: Datasel contract followed 10 months of preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:19:00 UTC
16:19:00 KST

Former MoD permanent secretary: Datasel contract followed 10 months of preparations
Former Defense Ministry Secretary General Kusti Salm told ERR about how the contract with Datasel was signed. He stressed that the defense minister bears responsibility for decisions made in procuring ammunition for Ukraine.
Salm said providing military support to Ukraine has been important to Estonia and that the decisions related to it were made by politicians.
"These have all been decisions made by politicians and they are all decisions that the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), the Ministry of Defense, the foreign ministry's dedicated diplomats and the Government Office have faithfully carried out. And it has not been purely altruistic. The politicians who made these decisions have also reaped the political benefits," he said.
According to the former permanent secretary, the level of risk involved in sourcing ammunition for Ukraine was so high that procuring such items with Estonia's own money would have been out of the question.
"Now one of those risks has materialized. And we are in a situation where the very same people who did their jobs successfully in dozens or hundreds of other cases are now being lined up one by one and essentially portrayed as criminals in front of the Estonian public," Salm said.
According to Salm, there is no one in Estonia other than the defense minister — Reform's Hanno Pevkur held the post at the time — who can bear responsibility for such decisions.
"There are no other people who have a mandate from the public to spend €2.4 billion every year. The minister decides. The permanent secretary's role in this respect is to implement the minister's decisions," he said.
"As for these specific transactions, I was involved in them and I absolutely take full responsibility for the proposals I made, just as I take responsibility for the things that were done during that period and for some of the things that were left undone," Salm said.
The former permanent secretary pointed out that it took 10 months to enter into a contract with Datasel.
"People traveled to Italy, people traveled to India. The entire process took 10 months at a time when, in reality, there was a great deal of urgency," he said.
Salm explained that at the time, major ammunition manufacturers were charging several times the usual price, while producing the ammunition would have taken years. Ukraine also had many Soviet-origin weapons and Russia was also seeking ammunition compatible with them. Such ammunition was available from countries including India, Pakistan and countries in North Africa.
Asked whether the bar for following standard procedures had been deliberately lowered, Salm said: "This was not some general agreement, but a detailed instruction from the defense minister that this was exactly how these matters were to be handled because the risks were known."
"My task was to put the necessary processes in place and make sure that RKIK carried out its duties," he added.
According to Salm, the contact with Datasel came from the defense minister, Hanno Pevkur, who recently left office.
"Today, there is no question about that whatsoever. It came through the defense minister, which is completely normal," he said.
The former permanent secretary stressed that Pevkur led the process of procuring ammunition for Ukraine.
"The minister managed the process of assisting Ukraine in detail and in a very hands-on way. He had his own instructions and views on matters. People who know Hanno Pevkur know that he is a proactive person. He gets into the details, he keeps himself informed and that is exactly how he operated in this case. He was also generally very firm in his instructions," Salm said.
Background
In 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed four procurement contracts with Datasel S.R.L., an Italian company acquired earlier that year by Indian-owned Neco Defence Munitions. Despite neither Datasel nor its parent firm having any prior track record of manufacturing or selling artillery shells, RKIK wired roughly €70 million in advance payments.
The contracts meant to deliver desperately needed ammunition to Ukraine using EU European Peace Facility funding suffered severe delivery delays. Ammunition that did arrive was flagged as incomplete and of substandard quality, leading RKIK to terminate the agreements and launch legal efforts to recoup the money. Datasel has denied wrongdoing, claiming it delivered tens of millions of euros' worth of goods and was left with financial losses.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office has since launched an investigation into the use of European Peace Facility funds by Estonia.
The scandal was part of Minister of Defense Hanno Pevkur's recent decision to resign, alongside wider accounting and oversight issues at the Estonian Defense Forces and other parts of the ministry's administrative area.

Trump threatens EU over Canada 'associate membership' proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:18:52 UTC
16:18:52 KST

US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose heavy tariffs on the European Union or halt some trade with the bloc after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada its first associate member.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Trump said his response would depend on whether he viewed the proposal as a hostile act.
"I think it's laughable," he said. "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things."
He added: "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
The proposal comes as Brussels and Ottawa seek to reduce their reliance on the United States amid trade tensions under Trump's leadership.
Von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address in Strasbourg, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the first non-European head of government to join the event.
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," she told Carney, drawing a standing ovation in the European Parliament.
She said Brussels and Ottawa needed to draw closer as democracies faced a "fracture in the international rules-based system".
A broader alliance
Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday, with his visit intended to build momentum ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.
He has pursued closer ties with the bloc as Canada becomes increasingly embroiled in a trade war with the United States.
Von der Leyen called for the relationship to move beyond trade cooperation towards a broader "alliance for the future", with closer ties in technology, defence and energy.
"We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project," she said.
She also identified critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, cyber security and economic security as areas for cooperation.
"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she said.
Both Canada and the EU have faced US tariffs and territorial threats, alongside competition from China.
"In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is forging stronger relationships with trusted partners," Carney's office said in a statement.
What would associate membership mean?
EU treaties make no provision for "associate membership", leaving the scope of von der Leyen's proposal unclear.
"We don't really know yet what it means," said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left German member of the European Parliament and the main sponsor of a resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz first floated the idea for Ukraine earlier this year, but it received a cool reception from Kiev, which is seeking full membership.
Under that proposal, Ukraine would have been able to attend EU summits, have a representative in the European Commission and access parts of the bloc's budget, without full voting rights.
Any partnership with a non-EU country requires approval from member states, and it remains unclear how much support von der Leyen's proposal would receive from their governments.
Brussels and Ottawa already have close ties. Their CETA free-trade agreement, which abolished almost all tariffs, has been credited with helping boost trade in goods and services by more than 80 percent since 2016.
Canada also became the first non-EU country to join the bloc's flagship defence loan programme this year.
Following von der Leyen's address, Carney travelled to Britain for his first meeting with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The two attended a football match between Everton and Wolverhampton before Carney's return to Strasbourg for his speech on Thursday.

Cuts, punishment powers and a notable exception: Key changes in Labor's migration shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:14:56 UTC
16:14:56 KST

In brief
- The federal government has announced a suite of changes to Australia's immigration policy settings.
- Working holidaymakers, visa overstayers and students are among those most affected.
The federal government has announced a shake-up of Australia's migration system, with visa-hoppers, overstayers, students, and backpackers targeted in the crackdown.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled the changes during a National Press Club address on Thursday, following weeks of delay, heated debate and speculation.
Burke began his speech by highlighting the contribution of migration to Australia, but acknowledging there were problems with the current policy settings.
Here's what you need to know:
What's changing?
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Burke said the reforms are split into three parts: who arrives, who stays and who leaves.
Among the most consequential changes are those affecting students, backpackers, visa overstayers and visa hoppers.
International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia, with some exceptions for PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students.
The changes are not retrospective and apply only to future students.
"We're not going to be breaking up families on shore," he said.
As part of a so-called "visa-hopping" crackdown, Burke said the government will introduce a qualification scale, meaning only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's for example) will be able to extend their visas.
A ballot system and cap will be introduced for backpackers wishing to extend their visit to a second or third year.
Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively. This will not affect United Kingdom citizens under the rules of a free trade agreement.
The government has already slowed down the processing of working holiday visas, with applications now taking months to be approved. Burke said processing of second-and third-year visas will be restored to the previous, faster pace — with the exception of UK citizens, who are exempt from regional work requirements to secure a visa extension.
The number of UK backpackers has risen sharply since the free trade agreement came into effect in 2023, from about 17,000 in 2021 to just under 80,000 now.
People who overstay their visas, of whom there are about 77,000, will face tougher sanctions, including detention. The government is now looking for more facilities, compliance officers and beds.
Burke said this was a return to a pre-2015 model, when visa overstayers would be taken into detention, and within a few weeks, organise their own flight and leave.
"That didn't just affect them. It had a behavioural impact," he said.
However, he said it would not involve "the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries", an apparent reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, which have involved mass deportation operations, arrests, and third-country removals.
Powers to punish dodgy migration agents who help with applications they know have no merit will be expanded, including deregistration.
The points test, which determines which skilled migrants are admitted to Australia, will be revamped to treat construction-related qualifications as equivalent to university degrees.
Tweaks to ministerial directions will also prioritise visa applicants with in-demand skills, including in healthcare, construction, education and law enforcement.
Why the changes?
The government is trying to bring Australia's Net Overseas Migration, which represents population growth due to migration, down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027 and 225,000 each year thereafter, and to curb visa-hopping, "rorting" and "gaming" the system.
That figure has stubbornly exceeded Labor's forecasts since the party came to power in 2022, but Burke said migration was now tracking in line with its targets.
The Coalition wants the target to be about 170,000, in line with housing construction, and One Nation wants a 130,000-person-a-year cap.
Burke said immigrants were not to blame for Australia's housing crisis, but said immigration needed to slow down so that housing had a chance to catch up.
How are the changes being implemented?
Some of the changes will come under improved ministerial powers, but others may not become law because negotiations between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition leader Angus Taylor broke down in the week before Burke's address, dooming hope of getting reforms through the Senate.
Without parliament's approval, the government cannot proceed with restrictions on phoney asylum-seekers' claims.
But Burke insisted negotiations with the Coalition were ongoing and productive, and said: "We have put nothing forward that is a wedge to them."
What has the reaction been?
Kon Karapanagiotidis, CEO and founder of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, said the announced changes marked "a dark day for multicultural Australia".
"Today our government chose to turn on migrants, international students and people seeking asylum who have built lives here, contributed to this country and asked for nothing more than the chance to belong," he said in a statement.
The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) said changes to backpacker visas risked Australia's food security, farm safety and regional economies which rely heavily on working holidaymakers.
"This is not how serious policy is made. You do not switch off, slow down or redesign an important workforce pathway on the eve of harvest and expect farmers, contractors, processors and regional communities to absorb the damage," NFF president Hamish McIntyre said.
His comments were echoed by the NFF Horticulture Council executive officer Richard Shannon, who warned of a spike in food prices if the agricultural sector faced a worker shortfall.
"Backpackers doing harvest work in regional Australia are not the cause of housing shortages in our capital cities. They are the reason fruit gets picked, packed and onto supermarket shelves," he said.
Earlier this week, Universities Australia chief Luke Sheehy said political parties competing to cut international student numbers needed to be honest about what Australia would lose.
"A vote for dramatically fewer international students is a vote for a poorer, less skilled Australia," he said.
"You can't take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences."
— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press

Russia damages railway station in Berestyn: trains delayed by up to six hours – photos
A Russian attack has severely damaged a railway station in Berestyn, Kharkiv Oblast, and infrastructure used by Kyiv's circular commuter rail service. Some passenger trains will take an alternative route and are expected to be delayed by about six hours.
Source: the state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways)
Details: At the moment of the strike, passengers and station staff in Berestyn were in a shelter, so no one was injured. The company is assessing the damage, and there are no plans to cancel trains to the city.
In Kyiv, infrastructure at Mykilska Slobidka station was damaged. The Kyiv City Express is running on a limited loop, bypassing the Darnytsia-Pochaina section. Repairs are expected to take around a day.
Glass and doors of an electric-powered train, a depot and several other railway facilities were also damaged.
Trains No. 7/8 Odesa-Kharkiv and No. 53/54 Dnipro-Odesa will take an alternative route. Estimated journey times will increase by six hours.
Background:
- On 27 August, Russian attacks caused Ukrainian Railways trains to run more than 10 hours late. For example, the Kharkiv-Chełm train was running 11 hours and 30 minutes late.
- On 13 September, trains in various regions of Ukraine were running one to ten hours late due to evacuations and rerouting following Russian attacks.

Vishwakarma Puja: The Day Nobody Touched the Tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

Idols of Lord Vishwakarma are on display for sale in Kolkata
On Vishwakarma Puja, remembering a leather factory that honoured a Hindu god with Muslim hands participating and biryani from Park Street. Nobody thought it needed explaining.Few Hindu festivals can be entered in an office calendar years ahead without consulting a panjika, and Vishwakarma Puja, which falls today, is the most dependable of them, because it is pegged to Kanya Sankranti, the last day of Bhadra, a solar date rather than a lunar one, which is why it generally lands on September 17 every year.It seems only right that the god of engineers should keep better time than most gods.He is, by his résumé, the most accomplished contractor in the Hindu universe. Tradition credits him with Lord Krishna's Dwarka, the golden Lanka that Hanuman ji later set alight, the Pandava capital at Indraprastha and the chariots in which the gods flew. What is less remarked upon is how differently India has chosen to picture him. In the west and north-west he is an old, four-armed man with a white beard and a swan for a mount, which scholars read as a nod to Brahma; in the east he is a young, muscular man with a black moustache, no sons in attendance, and an elephant as his vahana, which suggests God Indra instead.
West Bengal, a state with no shortage of bearded elders, decided that its engineer should look like a foreman in his prime, which tells you something about who was doing the worshipping.The flying chariots are how Bengal explains its kites, which dot Kolkata's skies on this day. Hindu mythology is full of gods travelling by air, and Vishwakarma is held to have built the vehicles. The skies over Kolkata on this day used to (and perhaps still do to a lesser extent) fill with petkati and chandiyal, and the morning began with the cry of bhokatta from some rooftop where a boy had just cut a rival's string.
Kites being bought
Held on the last day of Bhadra, the puja also opens the long Sharodiya season, so the kites were, in effect, the city's first announcement that Maa Durga was on her way. In many Bengali homes the day carries a second observance that has nothing to do with machines. Arandhan, tied to Manasa Puja at Bhadra Sankranti, requires that food be cooked the night before and eaten stale the next day, with cooking itself forbidden; the custom has loosened with modern life but survives in Bengal's villages and in Kolkata's suburbs. The folk phrase for it, Bhadre rendhe, Ashwine khaoa — cook in Bhadra and eat in Ashwin — is as good a summary as any.
Ranna Puja ( File Image)
The puja's real home, though, was never the household. It is observed mostly on factory floors, where workers pray for safe conditions and for their machines to run well, and shrines go up among the tools themselves. Historians studying Kolkata's working class have argued that this was something the workers made their own; Dipesh Chakrabarty wrote about festivals as a source of solidarity inside hostile workplaces, and Leela Fernandes's ethnography of the jute mills treated the building of Vishwakarma pandals as a space of the workers' cultural autonomy.The leather factory: My family's business was a leather factory on Tiljala Road, right behind Don Bosco School, and on this day the more than four hundred men who worked there, nearly all of them Muslim, did not touch their tools. The work that honoured the god had been done the day before, when the craftsmen who spent the rest of the year shaping leather goods turned to sheets of coloured paper instead, cutting out decorations with a skill that matched their day jobs and a gusto that suggested they found paper the more forgiving material. Everything the day required was prepared on the eve, and on the day itself the hands rested.By the time the priest arrived, the god of craftsmen was presiding over a room that craftsmen, most of whom did not pray to him, had dressed for him. I have never been sure how much of the abstention was reverence and how much was the ordinary pleasure of a working day on which no work was expected, and I suspect the men themselves would have found the question tiresome, which is perhaps the point.
File Image
Then there was lunch. Many factory feasts on the day were vegetarian, a mutton curry being the mark of the more generous units, and ours had apparently decided that gastronomy in this feast was a competitive sport and opted for biryani. The biryani came from Shiraz on Park Street, which opened in 1941 at the Park Street and Mullick Bazar crossing, specialising in Awadhi food, founded by Mohammed Arshad Ali and Ali Hussain, who had come to Calcutta from Bihar. Calcutta's biryani, as every Calcuttan will tell you at length, came down from Awadh with Wajid Ali Shah's exile, and Shiraz's cook Shamsuddin, who joined in the 1970s and reworked its biryani, is said to have had an ancestor who cooked for the nawab.
Nadia: An artisan works on an idol of Lord Vishwakarma ahead of 'Vishwakarma Puja', at a workshop, in Nadia, West Bengal. (PTI Photo)(PTI09_16_2026_000049B)
Consider the arrangement then. A feast for the Hindu god of craft, cooked to a deposed Muslim king's recipe by a kitchen that claims descent from his, eaten by four hundred Muslim leatherworkers and one Bengali Hindu family, on a day when the stoves in half of Bengal's kitchens were not supposed to be lit. The factory had solved Arandhan by outsourcing it to a Park Street restaurant, and nobody, as far as I remember, felt the need to hold a seminar about it. (We'd hold a good many seminars or news channel debates now.)The next morning the god went into the waters of the Hooghly, and the men went back to their benches. The tools, having been worshipped for a day, went back to being worked, which is, if you think about it, the only form of worship a tool has ever asked for.
Sources/Reading:Dipesh Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (Princeton University Press, 1989)Leela Fernandes, Producing Workers: The Politics of Gender, Class, and Culture in the Calcutta Jute Mills (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997)
As a Group Business Head at Times Internet Limited, I spend my days growing a newsroom I once belonged to. My journalist friends insist I’ve crossed over to the dark side; I maintain I’ve merely changed seating arrangements. I live at the edge of the newsroom now; close enough to hear the first draft of history, far enough to question it. I write occasionally on experiences and things that stay with me. Distance, after all, has its uses. It sharpens perspectives; and sometimes, if you’re lucky, it restores curiosity.

10 Maoist rebels sentenced to death in India over 2013 attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:08:26 UTC
16:08:26 KST

A special Indian court has sentenced 10 Maoist rebels to death over their role in a 2013 ambush on a convoy that killed 27 people, including members of the Congress party.
The Maoists were convicted of multiple offences, including "conspiracy" and "waging war against the state", before being handed the death penalty, India's National Investigation Agency (NIA) said on Wednesday.
The nearly six-decade-long Maoist rebellion, which began in the 1960s and killed more than 12,000 people, was once described by a former prime minister as the "biggest internal security threat" India faced.
But the insurgency has been effectively defeated after a sustained military offensive across the "Red Corridor", areas where the guerrillas shut out the government and established their own parallel administration.
The landmine and gun attack in May 2013 took place in a remote forested area of the central state of Chhattisgarh, effectively wiping out the top state leadership of the Congress party.
The attackers detonated an explosive device, opened "indiscriminate firing" and threw grenades at the convoy, the NIA said in a statement.
The agency said its investigation had established that the 10 Maoist members were involved in a "criminal conspiracy to attack and kill senior Congress leaders and security personnel".
India imposes the death penalty by hanging.
The last executions in India were in March 2020, when four men convicted of the 2012 gang rape and murder of a woman on a Delhi bus were hanged, in a case that sparked huge nationwide protests.

Morocco's political parties battle youth disenchantment ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:08:15 UTC
16:08:15 KST

Morocco's political parties battle youth disenchantment ahead of election
RABAT/CAIRO, Sept 17 - Morocco’s political parties are trying to entice young voters to the polls next week with promises of jobs and affordable housing after violent protests last year and a border rush on the Spanish enclave of Ceuta highlighted widespread discontent.
Uneven development and continuing economic hardship among young people were seen as drivers of both events, against a backdrop of recent progress in sectors such as manufacturing, ports and railways lifting living standards in major cities.
The vote, due on September 23, is the country’s fourth since the 2011 Arab Spring protests led the monarchy to share more power with parliament before moving to reinforce its position.
A moderate Islamist party ran the government for about a decade but suffered a crushing defeat in the last vote five years ago, ceding its place to two parties founded by men close to the palace.
Those parties, the National Rally of Independents (RNI) and the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), have both put youth employment at the centre of their campaigns, pledging to create about one million jobs over the next parliamentary term.
They have also touted roughly $20 billion of infrastructure investment ahead of the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal, and streamed rallies on social media to draw the attention of young voters.
"We reject the idea that young people simply want an easy life," the PAM's campaign manifesto says, listing housing, regular income and "dignified work" as policy priorities.
Analysts say the challenge of engaging young voters was illustrated by deadly, Gen-Z-led protests last year, and by the massive border rush on Ceuta in July.
"The Ceuta mass migration attempt was a new form of social protest in which many citizens demonstrated a physical exit from Moroccan politics altogether," said Mohamed Masbah, head of the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, a think tank.
YOUNG VOTERS 'NO LONGER BELIEVE' PROMISES
While 18- to 24-year-olds make up some 12% of the population, they account for only about 3% of registered voters, official figures show.
Just one third of Moroccans between 18 and 35 years old say they trust parliament, the prime minister or political parties, according to a survey published in March by Afrobarometer, a research nonprofit.
Young voters say they have been discouraged by an impression that elections shift the balance between parties with little ideological space between them without producing major policy changes.
"We keep seeing the same faces return with promises that many young voters no longer believe," said university student Mohamed Azzaoui, who said he does not intend to vote.
Under Morocco’s system, the monarchy retains control of the country’s overarching policy direction. In recent years the palace has also consolidated power over key portfolios, including the foreign and interior ministries.
That means parties are competing less over the overall development model, and more over how to achieve the palace's objectives, according to economist Rachid Aourraz.
In practice, Masbah said, that means that "if everything goes well, the monarchy takes credit. If things go wrong, the government gets the blame."
AMBITIOUS ECONOMIC GOALS
In recent years, authorities have leant heavily on their economic strategy. Already one of Africa’s most diversified and industrialised economies, Morocco’s growth targets are ambitious.
The country’s “New Development Model”, a national economic plan launched about five years ago, aims to double gross domestic product per capita by 2035. The country has seen billions pour into sectors such as deepwater ports, phosphates, green energy and rail lines.
But this has often not translated into popular satisfaction.
Youth unemployment is around 27% — the highest rate of any age group — and one in three young Moroccans is neither working, studying nor training, according to official statistics.
As the country’s central bank wrote in a recent report, stubborn unemployment and other factors have opened "a gap … between objectively measured economic performance and citizens' perceptions." REUTERS

"Canada and Europe are stronger together," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in his address to the European Parliament.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the invitation for his country to become the European Union's first-ever "associate member" in a speech delivered before the European Parliament on Thursday.
He later stressed that the outcome of the negotiations would respect Canadian sovereignty and be put to a final vote in Ottawa. Notably, he said the "nomenclature" would be for Brussels to discuss and decide.
"Canada welcomes this ambition. And I will tell you, polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe," he said in Strasbourg.
Carney portrayed an ever-closer EU-Canada alliance as a "beacon for other democracies" based on shared values and "open enough that others can join".
He cited energy security, critical minerals, defence capabilities, artificial intelligence and finance as areas for deeper integration. He also said the two sides should work to allow young people to "live, work and study" on either side of the Atlantic Ocean.
Carney's speech came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first-ever "associate member", a novel concept that lacks legal precedent and raises more questions than answers.
Overnight, US President Donald Trump threatened to slap "very serious tariffs" on Europeans if the idea of "associate membership" were carried out as a "hostile act".

Carney says Canada not seeking full EU membership
Canada's PM Mark Carney welcomed the invitation to become the first "associate member" of the European Union, but emphasised that the intent is not to become a full member nor to cede sovereignty.
"Canada is not in a position nor seeking to become a full member of the European Union," he said. "Therefore, it's a different framework. It's a framework that is relevant for a country that shares deep bonds with Europe."
Carney also emphasised that the exact name of the arrangement was for Europe to define, as what mattered was the substance of a new, positive framework between the EU and Canada.
The Canadian leader also made clear Ottawa does not intend to cede sovereignty to Brussels, as "we are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty".

‘We should not be scared of something new,’ Metsola says
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the EU should not “be scared of something new” in relation to the unprecedented associated membership status offered to Canada.
“Europe has never been afraid of forging new paths and creating new frontiers,” she said, underlining the role of the European Parliament in the ratification of the CETA trade agreement with Canada.
Metsola also said that “opportunities can only get bigger with Canada”, referring to flagship EU programmes such as Erasmus and Horizon.
New EU-Canada alliance is not 'reaction' to Trump, Carney says
During the press conference, Mark Carney was asked about Donald Trump's threat to slap tariffs if the EU's "associate membership" for Canada was done as a "hostile act".
"This is a positive initiative. It's ambitious, and it's positive. It's about building for people, creating opportunity. Just think of the opportunity for young people in Europe (and) in Canada to study, to live and work in those jurisdictions, to learn from each other, build the bonds that will strengthen our ties," Carney said.
"This is a fundamental point. This is for a better future for our citizens. It's not a reaction to something else. It's moving to the future."
New alliance will respect Canada's sovereignty, Carney insists
The new alliance between the EU and Canada will respect Canadian sovereignty, Mark Carney has said, pushing back against critics.
"It will make Europe stronger. It will make Canada stronger. It will make -- I'll speak for Canada -- Canada a better partner with the United States," the premier said when asked about red lines.
"And with respect to sovereignty, as I detailed in my remarks and as has been our strategy from the start, we are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty, and that's what is on offer here," he added.
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike international agreements."
Carney says 'associate member' status is up for EU to determine
Mark Carney has stressed that Canada is not seeking to become a full-time member state of the EU and the final name that defines the relationship will be for Brussels to determine.
"President von der Leyen used both terms: alliance for the future and associate membership. The nomenclature, the precise nomenclature, is a question for Europe," he said.
"What matters is the substance. What are we actually building together? How do we combine our strengths in a way that serve our people better, protect our fundamental rights, and create prosperity?"
"Canada is not in a position nor seeking to become a full member of the European Union. Therefore, it's a different framework," he went on. "It's a framework that is relevant for a country that shares the deep bonds, histories and the ambitions for people that the European Parliament has for Europeans and the Canadian government has for Canadians."
Greens leader listened to Carney’s address wearing a Canada hockey team T-shirt
MEP Terry Reintke, leader of the Greens/EFA group, listened to Carney’s address wearing a Sidney Crosby Canada hockey team T-shirt, which brought a smile to Carney’s face when he greeted her before the start of the session.
Several other MEPs wore red in the hemicycle.
Associated membership could affect trade, defence and foreign policy, according to MEPs
EU lawmakers are still trying to figure out what Canada’s “associate membership” would mean in practice, a day after Ursula von der Leyen announced it in her State of the Union speech.
As the details remain unclear, senior MEP Sandro Gozi of Renew Europe believes it could entail greater cooperation in three main areas: trade, defence and foreign policy.
“Maybe Carney would join EU leaders’ summits and his ministers would meet with EU ministers regularly,” he told Euronews. “But it is difficult to know what von der Leyen really has in mind.”
According to European People’s Party MEP Siegfried Mureșan, the proposed associate membership would enable the EU and Canada to deepen cooperation on the economy, security and investment, while also strengthening people-to-people ties.
“The vision is that we want closer ties with friendly countries, with liberal democracies outside Europe,” he told Euronews.
Carney calls for integrated EU-Canada capital markets
In his speech, Carney said that “Canada and Europe should also explore creating an integrated market for financial services", arguing that integrated capital markets would “broaden choice and reduce costs for our citizens, improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience”.
The European Union is currently undertaking a legislative reform of capital markets aimed at overcoming fragmentation, a major obstacle for companies and investors alike.
The reforms are a main component of the bloc's competitiveness agenda, which was inspired by a landmark competitiveness report by former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has advocated for capital markets reform as a prerequisite for EU to advance.
The legislative files on capital markets are currently under negotiation. The EU has the aim to finalise the agreement by the end of the year, but disagreement still persists.
New alliance will be put to a vote in Canadian parliament, Carney vows
The new alliance between Canada and the EU, which could involve "associate member" status, will be "ultimately" put to a vote in the Canadian parliament, Mark Carney has said.
"We will have a series of debates, I'm sure, in parliament (and) relevant committees. And ultimately, there will be a vote in the Canadian parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we're working on," he said, next to Metsola.
"I observe that there has been a fair bit of preparation for this," he added, noting the discussions were the "start of a process" that needed to be further fleshed out. The next key moment will be the EU-Canada summit in Montreal at the end of October.
"It will all roll out transparently," he said. "It's an exciting time because this is an opportunity to speak for Canada to make Canada stronger, more sovereign, more independent, more prosperous, more sustainable."

Let's flourish as free people together, Carney says, concluding among applause
Mark Carney concludes his speech by bridging the past and the future of EU-Canada relations.
"My country, it's often said that Canada became a nation during the Battle of Vimy Ridge, and certainly the thousands of Canadians who didn't return from that battle sacrificed their lives for something much bigger than themselves," he tells lawmakers.
"One who did come home stopped first to pick up some acorns. And today, the same Vimy Oaks grow in Canada as in France," he adds.
"Living proof that what we cultivate together can survive the darkest winter to thrive again. So let us now deepen those roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day."
The speech concludes with loud applause from MEPs.
Carney offers energy supplies as well as critical raw materials to the EU
Carney proposed on Wednesday that the Europeans meet their needs for critical raw materials and energy.
The statement comes as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada on Wednesday to join a new alliance designed to deepen economic relations between the EU and Canada.
“Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals, and we are among the top producers of the ten most essential for the world’s energy transition,” Carney said. “Our alliance can help fill Europe’s need for reliable supply.”
The proposal will fit into the EU’s strategy to diversify, as it still relies on China, which holds a monopoly over the production and processing of some key materials.
Carney also said that his country can contribute LNG and hydrogen “at large scale” to support “Europe’s energy security.” The proposal includes the development of new port infrastructure in the high north and on Canada’s east coast.
“We, in turn, can benefit from your leadership in many clean energy technologies,” Carney added.
Canada-EU alliance should be open for others to join, Carney says
Mark Carney has framed the nascent Canada-EU alliance as a "beacon for democracies" that can be "open enough" for other nations to join.
"A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies. An alliance not defined by what we oppose but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability," he said.
"An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens and our citizens to do for themselves. An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices. An alliance open enough that others can join. An alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeks to replace it."
I'm not proposing a 'great-power rival', Carney says
Mark Carney says his vision of a closer EU-Canada partnership does not seek to create a "great-power rival", in another apparent dig at Donald Trump.
"I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners," he says, prompting laughter in the room.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience. So no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," he adds.
"It's these motivations, these fundamental motivations, combined with our latent hard power, that mean that we can help to create the next just, stable and prosperous world order."
‘We will definte it together,’ Carney welcomes associated membership
The Canadian leader has hailed the invitation of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to become the first EU associate member.
“We welcome this ambition - polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties. An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on shared values,” he said.
Carney went on to detail what he sees as the potential advantages of such an arrangement, notably in terms of critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments.
Sovereigny requires collectively addressing strategic gaps
Canadian PM considers Europe and Canada can collectively stand stronger together by filling in strategic capability gaps that would allow both to better withstand shocks.
“Sovereignty goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves. It now requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines and space-based communications,” he said.
For Carney, the need to fill these gaps are even more important as ‘global’ companies appear to be aligned with a national government, falling short of mentioning the US.
“Closing these gaps is not possible alone, but it is very achievable collectively,” he added.
Carney mentions Canadian participation in landmark EU defence programme, SAFE
Mark Carney highlights that Canada is participating in the European Union’s €150 billion Safe Action For Europe (SAFE) defence loan programme, as “the first non-European member”.
"But the ecosystem we have built is not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate,” he said to the hemicycle, in reference to the loan as well as other initiatives such as CETA, the EU and Canada’s free trade agreement.
Carney did concede, however that “we should recognise that the ecosystem we built is not yet equal in ferocity of the changing climate, and nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of upheaval.”

CETA was concluded in 2016. It removed tariff barriers between both sides of the Atlantic, while SAFE was created by the Europeans in 2025 to boost the EU’s defence industrial base through joint procurements.

Did it all start in Davos?
Ursula von der Leyen's invitation for Canada to join the EU as associate member has seized the political spotlight this week -- but the seeds of the idea may have been planted months ago.
In his address to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney called for a coalition of "middle powers" to join forces to revive the rules-based world order, just as Trump ramped up his tariff war and threatened to annex Canada.
"The question for middle powers like Canada is not whether to adapt to the new reality – we must. The question is whether we adapt by simply building higher walls, or whether we can do something more ambitious," Carney told the audience in Davos.
He also said that "when we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness", adding that middle powers had a choice between "competing with each othe for favour" or combining to "create a third path with impact".
That speech -- read in Washington as an affront to the world's greates economic powers -- also drew a rebuke from US President Donald Trump.
The speech also led to months of closer political collaboration. Carney became the first non-European leader to attend a summit of the European Political Community (EPC) in May, and Canadian minsiters have become a regular feature of EU ministerial meetings.

Could Article 217 pave the way for Canada's 'associated membership'?
There's no precedent for the "associate membership" that Ursula von der Leyen has offered to Canada. The concept doesn't exist. It's basically invented. So what's next?
Amid the confusion and speculation, a possible legal path has emerged: Article 217 of the EU treaties.
"The Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure," the article says.
This provision, which is broadly worded and therefore subject to interpretation, underpins the European Economic Area that brings Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein into the single market and extends the four freedoms (goods, services, capital and people) to their territories.
Since both von der Leyen and Mark Carney are aiming for closer economic ties, Article 217 could pave the way for bringing the relationship to the next level while stopping short of actual membership.

Poll ahead of Carney's speech shows 49% of Canadians support EU membership
Just how much do Canadians support EU membership?
Ahead of Mark Carney's speech in Strasbourg, Abacus Data published a new poll showing the sentiment among Canadian citizens. Here are some of the findings, which are truly remarkable considering the country lies on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.
- 49% support Canada becoming an EU member state, 30% oppose, and 21% are unsure
- 71% of Canadians have a positive impression of the EU, while 16% have a negative perception
- 80% support deepening strategic cooperation with the EU on foreing policy, defence and economic priorities, while 10% oppose and another 10% are unsure
- 81% support closer integration between Canada and the EU, while 10% oppose it and 9% are unsure
- 56% feel they have more in common with the EU than with the US, 20% say they have about equally in common with both, and 16% say they have more in common with the US than with the EU
- 61% think a closer EU-Canada relation would increase Canada's economic independence, while 9% think it will decrease it and 16% think it will have no real impact

The EU-Canada trade relationship: from the CETA trade deal to von der Leyen’s “Alliance” offer
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Wednesday for an “Alliance for the Future” with Canada to move beyond CETA – the trade deal clinched by the EU and Canada in 2016.
Von der Leyen’s offer comes as Ottawa has been trapped in a trade war with the US since late August, pushing Canada to seek a closer relationship with the EU.
“We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space,” von der Leyen said.
She added that the Alliance will include work on “intelligent” manufacturing, on “a tech alliance” and “defence industrial bases.” She also cited “a flagship joint project” in the Arctic and work “on energy, critical minerals and batteries,” as well as “AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.”
The Alliance should push further cooperation beyond CETA, which has already removed tariff barriers on most goods, except for sensitive farm products. However, it has not yet been ratified by all EU countries and had to be provisionally applied to come into force.
An EU-Canada summit is due to take place at the end of October in Montreal, where economic and security cooperation will be discussed.
Canada might offer better access to its critical raw materials to the EU, which seeks to move away from China for its supply. Energy could also be on the list of the Canadian proposals. A digital agreement would also be in the making.

What is the EU-Canada defence relationship?
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand told Euronews in May that Ottawa was “very enthusiastic” to continue working with Europe and other “like-minded countries”.
“What I believe we should be looking at is how we can work together pragmatically for our respective countries to deliver economic benefits and defence and security benefits,” she said.
From a defence perspective, this is already exemplified through the EU and Canada Security and Defence Partnership, finalised in 2025. This was seen as one of the first steps by Canada to shift its reliance away from the United States, and an increasingly bellicose Donald Trump, towards like-minded allies.
Most importantly, this partnership paved the way for Ottawa to participate in the EU’s €150 billion SAFE loan programme. As part of the European Commission’s push to ensure that the 27 EU member states have enough financing and capabilities to ward off aggression, it means that the Canadian defence industry can supply a portion of capabilities as part of these orders.
Hypothetically, this could span the production of anti-drone technology to weapons supporting a land army, for example.
How that could be expanded upon with potential EU associate membership is yet to be seen, but the new relationship could also forge deeper collaboration in regions that occupy the focus of both Brussels and Ottawa, such as the Arctic.
As the US trade war escalates, Canada looks to diversify its trade ties
Yesterday’s surprise invitation from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become an “associate” member of the EU came as Ottawa’s relationship with its closest ally, the United States, continues to deteriorate amid a trade war that has been ongoing since late August.
Two weeks ago, trade talks broke down after Canada left the negotiating table, accusing Washington of seeking concessions on French-language protections, with French being one of Canada’s two official languages.
US President Donald Trump responded by announcing tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian cars and trucks. On Tuesday, the measures were extended to additional products, including certain steel goods. Canada has also imposed tariffs on $20 billion (around €17.5 billion) worth of US imports.
In the days that followed, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for stronger ties with the EU.
Ottawa faces mounting pressure to diversify its trade relationships, given its heavy dependence on the US: more than 70% of Canadian exports were destined for its southern neighbour in 2025.
While Canada will need to broaden its economic focus towards Europe and Asia, the two North American economies remain deeply integrated, making any rapid shift away from the US market difficult.

With eight words, Tony Burke may have handed his opponents a campaign ad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:07:23 UTC
16:07:23 KST

analysis
Tony Burke announces migration changes and commits a cardinal sin of politics
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Tony Burke was most of the way through his long-awaited appearance at the National Press Club when he made one of politics' most cardinal sins: he committed to an absolute.
"I won't say that because that won't happen," he said on the possibility of the government not reaching its migration targets.
The government has been under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation to act on migration. It's possible that with those eight words, he's handed them a campaign ad — and another reason not to reach a legislative compromise.
It recalled previous rolled gold promises of Labor's: such as shaving $275 off power bills or Prime Minister Anthony Albanese declaring his word was his bond on not touching the stage three tax cuts (which he famously did).
The home affairs minister was at the Press Club on Thursday to outline a raft of changes that Labor hopes will put a squeeze on net overseas migration. While it's fallen from its peak in mid-2023, when international borders reopened after COVID, it's still well above the government's targets.
An hour before Burke stood up, the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirmed that figure was currently sitting at 292,000 in the year to March. The government's target is 225,000.
Back in 2001, the Liberal prime minister John Howard declared "we will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come". Burke's speech had echoes of that sentiment in its title: The Work of Managing the Migration Program: Who Arrives, Who Stays, Who Leaves.
Asked about that comparison, Burke responded that he wasn't afraid of the word "sovereignty". He also did not shy away from a desire to increase the government's ability to detain and remove people who remain in Australia after their visas have expired.
The plan is to target overstayers and temporary visa holders, including international students and their families. A ballot system will be introduced for working holiday visa holders who want to stay in Australia longer than a year.
All of it will have to be enacted through ministerial direction or regulation, not legislation, after hopes of an agreement between the Coalition were dashed. Burke indicated he would've gone further if he had the opposition's support.
Six weeks ago, the ABC broke the story that Burke had abruptly cancelled his planned address. At the time my colleague Tom Crowley reported the home affairs minister was due to unveil an expansion in the use of ballots for working holiday makers.
Cabinet disagreements were downplayed as the weeks passed without a settled agreement. Then, on Wednesday, came confirmation the policy was to be dropped (conveniently the day before the PM jets off to the United States — more on that shortly).
One Nation has its own migration plan
Burke wasn't the only one selling migration policy this week. One Nation beat the government to the punch in revealing its own plan.
The minor party promised to cut Australia's stock of 3 million temporary visas by 750,000 and place a hard cap on student visas and stop much needed skilled migrants from bringing their partners and kids with them.
Business groups warned it would cause a COVID-like shock to the economy. Hanson argued it was worth it. Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce doesn't think voters give a toss about what economists think.
Burke was keen to distance his plan from One Nation's, most importantly on family visas for skills migrants — 50 per cent of doctors bring their families, 66 per cent of nurses.
But it's interesting to note they do have one thing in common: removing the option for people on student visas to access the family reunion program (although Labor is offering some exemptions).
So where does the Coalition stand? TBC. Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam is likely counting the weeks until he bids farewell to the federal parliament but wants the policy settled before he does so.
But wherever the opposition lands, Duniam vowed it would be modelled.
Hanson's apology of sorts
Pauline Hanson may have had the jump on the government and Coalition when it comes to migration, but she spent much of the week dealing with the issue of resurfaced podcast interviews.
First, it was remarks about Albanese's dead mother, Maryanne, who had chronic rheumatoid arthritis and spent much of her life in social housing. Hanson declared on Karl Stefanovic's podcast back in February that was "not on". When the remarks were published over the weekend, a tearful Albanese told reporters he was "stunned".
Hanson was also widely condemned after a podcast interview in which she called Indigenous Australians "the most primitive race on earth" came to light.
Politicians from across the divide swiftly rebuked the comments. Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said they were "derogatory" and "completely racist" and urged her to apologise.
A day later, the One Nation leader walked into the News24 studios to express regrets. She claimed "[I] put my foot in my mouth" and that the comments about First Nations people were referring to the past, when Australia was colonised.
Later, she told reporters she was sorry if her remarks offended people. Hanson also apologised if the PM was offended by what she said about his mother.
Hanson blames two Liberal frontbenchers, James Paterson and Tim Wilson, for the podcast interviews resurfacing. Paterson rubbished that claim as "baseless".
"You don't need a private investigator to find a YouTube video of a podcast that Senator Hanson or Malcolm Roberts or her other colleagues have recorded," he said.
Both sides have ramped up its focus on Hanson in recent months. So, it's true that you don't need a private investigator. But a dirt unit helps.
Loading
Albanese is bound for Silicon Valley
The prime minister will be trading Canberra for California on Friday as he jets off to the United States. He'll be meeting with former Apple chief executive Tim Cook. The pair spoke back in June after the tech giant released an update on safety controls for children.
Don't be too surprised if there is an AI flavour to the prime minister's visit to Silicon Valley. Deputy PM Richard Marles met with the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic when he was on a trip there two weeks ago. The trip comes at a time the government is actively courting tech giants to bring their data centres down under.

Albanese told the chamber on Thursday it was important to keep up a dialogue.
"If we don't get this right in the next few years, it can get away from us, and we need to make sure that doesn't occur," he said.
The prime minister's AI focus comes as leaked policy documents seen by the ABC reveal Labor is looking at imposing an opt-out model, where artists' work would automatically be available to AI companies unless creators take steps to block or remove them.
From California, the prime minister will travel to the United Nations General Assembly in New York. While he's there, he'll be honoured at the Atlantic Council Global Citizen Awards.

U.S. DFC to fund Vodafone Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:06:55 EEST
16:06:55 KST

The Board of Directors of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) on Tuesday approved financing for Vodafone Ukraine (VF Ukraine, VFU), Ukraine's second-largest mobile operator, which is wholly owned by the NEQSOL holding company.
"To strengthen and modernize critical telecommunications infrastructure during the ongoing war," the DFC said in a press release on its website, without specifying the amount.
According to the corporation, U.S. companies operating and investing in Ukraine will also benefit from access to secure and reliable 5G infrastructure.
Overall, the DFC Board of Directors approved more than $8 billion in investments on Tuesday, with another project in Ukraine also included. It's financing for DTEK's 200 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage systems at six sites in Ukraine.
As reported, VF Ukraine increased consolidated net profit by 14.2% year-on-year in January-June 2026, to UAH 1.9 billion, while revenue rose 10.6%, to UAH 14.9 billion.
The mobile operator had 15.1 million customers in the second quarter of 2026, including 3.3 million contract subscribers.
The company said that in the first half of 2026 it invested more than UAH 3.5 billion in the restoration and development of telecommunications infrastructure, matching the level of investment in the first half of 2025. Among other results, the operator highlighted the continuation of 5G testing, with the first zones available in Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv and Borodianka, while it was recently announced that open 5G testing had also begun in Odesa.

"After they fill in the necessary details on the app, foreigners will be free to travel across Nepal without carrying their passports," Dhakal said. "They would not need to produce a physical passport to travel on domestic flights, exchange currency at money exchange counters, or show their passports to trekking agencies for travel arrangements."
He said police would also not require foreign nationals to produce a physical passport if an inquiry is necessary after their details have already been submitted through the app.
The department aims to achieve two objectives through the initiative: helping tourists enjoy their holidays in Nepal in a more relaxed manner while allowing authorities to track foreign nationals in the country. ■

Economic Watch: Britain looks to Autumn Budget for cost-of-living relief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:05:59 CST
16:05:59 KST

LONDON, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- British businesses and households are counting on effective measures in October's Autumn Budget to offer some "breathing space" amid rising inflation and a subdued labor market that are intensifying cost-of-living pressures, experts said.
The country's consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.1 percent year-on-year in August, up from 2.9 percent in July, data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed on Wednesday.
On a monthly basis, the CPI rose 0.5 percent in August, up from 0.3 percent a year earlier, the ONS said, noting that transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution.
"Higher fuel prices caused inflation to accelerate further in August. With tensions escalating across the Middle East, we expect that increased energy costs and some pass-through to domestic prices will further push up inflation over the months ahead," said Martin Sartorius, lead economist at the Confederation of British Industry.
"Inflation has now topped 3 percent just five months after it last breached that mark (3.3 percent in March) -- once again heading in the wrong direction," the Resolution Foundation said, adding this is bad news for families struggling with the cost of living.
Stuart Morrison, research manager at the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said the BCC forecasts a further CPI increase will result in higher domestic food costs.
Morrison also highlighted the price pressure for businesses, noting the BCC's latest survey of almost 5,000 firms shows inflation is now the main concern, cited by 66 percent of firms.
"High domestic costs and geopolitical headwinds are combining to create choppy inflationary waters for businesses to navigate," he noted.
In terms of everyday essentials, August CPI figures highlight the challenging environment retailers face, with headline inflation going up and goods such as clothing and accessories seeing marked increases, said Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium.
Although retailers continue to do all they can to hold prices down, "they will be fighting with one hand tied behind their back" until fiscal conditions improve, he added.
Businesses' confidence in hiring was accordingly dragged by cost pressure. Tuesday's ONS data showed Britain's unemployment rate for people aged 16 and over persisted at a high level of 4.9 percent in the three months to July.
Notably, total pay growth has eased in recent months and was last lower nearly six years ago, marking an impressive difference between the public and private sector. In the June-August period, job vacancies remained at their lowest level outside the pandemic period for more than a decade.
Slower pay growth and fewer job posts, together with hiking prices are making it harder for low-income households to make ends meet.
In particular, the Resolution Foundation mentioned the energy bill, which is still 26 percent higher in real terms than five years ago, with the price cap set to rise in October and again in January 2027, possibly by a significant amount.
"With money tight and living costs rising, the government should resist throwing money at costly blanket support. It would get far more bang for its buck by targeting help at lower-income families feeling the squeeze most -- through targeted energy discounts -- if bills rise sharply in January as now looks increasingly likely," said James Smith, chief economist at the foundation.
"The cost of doing business and the cost of living are two sides of the same coin," Morrison said, adding that it's crucial the chancellor of the exchequer looks to ease business cost burdens at next month's Autumn Budget. He called for a targeted tax reduction package to ease energy and business rate pressures for all firms.
Taking the Autumn Budget as a chance to reset and reduce the cost pressures for retailers, Dhillon said the chancellor can take meaningful action to halt the rise in costs, including business rates, energy bills, employment costs and packaging fees in order to support retailers, and by extension, the households who depend on them. ■
