====================================================================================================

Across China: A 3,000-year-old glimpse into China's Bronze Age technological prowess
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
15:05:57 CST
16:05:57 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- China is famous for its ancient inventions: papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the compass. But there is far more to its technological legacy than these.
One notable achievement is the Tonglushan ancient copper mining site. More than 3,000 years ago, people in China were already mining and refining high-purity copper on a large scale at this site, a feat that put them some 2,000 years ahead of the rest of the world.
Located in Daye, Hubei Province in central China, this site has welcomed more than 20 million visitors since it opened in the 1980s, including tourists from Japan, the Republic of Korea, Europe and Africa.
It received official designation as a National Archaeological Site Park in 2025 and is now working toward UNESCO World Heritage status.
To further showcase China's ancient industrial achievements to international visitors, a large-screen presentation launched last year features English subtitles alongside Chinese ones, while the park has also opened an educational workshop for visitors from China and abroad.
"The site shows that China has long had the capacity to develop advanced technologies independently. It also strengthens our cultural confidence," said Chen Jiayi, a staff member at the site park.
In the 21st century, China has once again emerged as a major industrial and technological power -- home to the world's most comprehensive industrial systems and making rapid advances in areas ranging from new-energy vehicles and artificial intelligence to robotics, quantum technology, space exploration and marine science.
The Tonglushan site was discovered by chance during mining operations in 1973, and archaeological excavations found that mining and smelting activity there dates back at least to the early years of the Spring and Autumn Period (770 B.C.-476 B.C.).
"It confirms that China's Bronze Age civilization followed a complete and independent course of development," Chen said. "Archaeological comparisons show that the copper used in the Bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng, a famous set of bronze chime bells, as well as many other bronze artifacts, came from Tonglushan."
Excavations have found that the ancient mine shafts and tunnels at the site total more than 8,000 meters in length, and over 400,000 tonnes of smelting slag have been unearthed so far.
Researchers estimate that between 80,000 and 120,000 tonnes of crude copper were produced there over the centuries, enough to cast about 48,000 sets of bronze bells comparable in scale to those of Marquis Yi of Zeng, or a far larger number of ritual vessels and weapons.
"Bronze gave physical form to China's long-standing ritual and musical traditions, its social hierarchy, its way of life, and indeed its pluralistic yet unified civilization," Chen said.
Ancient craftsmen at this location had already mastered sophisticated mining and smelting techniques.
They used bellows-equipped shaft furnaces and two procedures, namely "oxidized ore to copper" and "sulphide ore to matte to copper," thereby precisely controlling furnace temperatures at around 1,200 degrees Celsius.
At the time, crude copper reached a purity of 93 percent, while the copper content in slag was just 0.7 percent, which is a level far ahead of the rest of the ancient world, with some techniques approaching near-modern standards.
Mining and metallurgical activity at Tonglushan never really stopped, and by the late 19th century it was home to what was then Asia's largest integrated iron and steel enterprise, while production further expanded after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
"Today, copper production here has moved into higher-value processing, serving fields such as new-energy vehicles, 5G communications and semiconductor chips," said Pan Xiaojin, mayor of Daye.
Daye has also expanded into a range of other industries, including intelligent connected new-energy vehicles, optoelectronic information, hydrogen energy, intelligent robotics, the low-altitude economy and green building materials.
"The spirit of craftsmanship, fueled by a drive to grow stronger and tempered through countless trials, continues to inspire us to create new wonders," Pan noted. ■

Lithuanian households brace for painful heating season as energy costs soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

With winter approaching, Lithuanian households are preparing for significantly higher heating bills as rising natural gas and biofuel prices put pressure on the country’s energy system.
The Energy Agency estimates that heating prices could increase by about 20% this season. If winter temperatures are as cold as last year, household heating bills could rise by as much as 30%, according to the Lithuanian District Heating Association.
For some residents, the increase is already a financial reality.
Justina, who sells fruit and berries, said she has resigned herself to spending more on heating this winter.
Juozas, meanwhile, prepared well in advance and says he has little reason to worry.
“I live in my own house. I bought three tons of briquettes, and I’m not afraid of anything,” he said. “I have enough firewood to get through two more winters easily.”
But the wider energy market is facing a more difficult season.
“Everything is 25% to 30% more expensive,” said Antanas Budraitis, a data analyst at Lithuania’s Energy Agency. “Given the current situation, there is certainly no reason to expect prices to remain unchanged. The only question is how much they will rise. In our assessment, the price of heat should increase by about 20% this heating season.”
Natural gas is at least twice as expensive as it was a year ago, while biofuel prices have also risen sharply. Biofuel is particularly important for Lithuania’s district heating system, which relies heavily on it.
The energy market is also being affected by continued uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.
Valdas Lukoševičius, chairman of the Lithuanian District Heating Association, said biofuel prices are already about 50% to 60% higher than last year.
“Biofuel producers are, of course, trying to take advantage of the situation to make money, and some are even holding back supplies for the winter because they expect prices to rise further, even though they are already about 50% to 60% higher than last year,” Lukoševičius said.
The government has instructed the state-owned State Forest Enterprise to maximise the supply of biofuel feedstock from state forests.
“The State Forest Enterprise plans to provide additional biofuel supplies for this season, increasing supply and thus helping control the price surge that we are seeing,” Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said.
The additional supply is expected to help stabilise prices rather than reverse the increases.
Higher fuel costs could also affect households that heat their homes with electricity. Žygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor Bank, said electricity prices could become the second-highest on record.
There had been hopes that the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz would soon end, allowing energy companies to replenish gas supplies at lower prices. But that has not happened, leaving storage facilities less than fully stocked, Mauricas said.
During winter, when solar generation falls and wind production may not be sufficient, power producers rely more heavily on natural gas, he said. Higher gas prices therefore feed directly into electricity prices.
While temperatures remain relatively mild, many Lithuanians have already begun applying for heating subsidies.
About 30,000 people applied during the first two weeks, 4,000 more than during the same period last year, according to the Social Security and Labour Ministry. The government plans to allocate about 80 million euros for heating compensation.
The system is designed to ensure that households do not have to spend more than 10% of their income on home heating, regardless of how much heating prices rise, ministry spokeswoman Svetlana Kulpina said.
“People can apply for compensation throughout the entire heating season,” she said. “Compensation is granted regardless of the type of fuel used for heating.”
This year also brings a change to the start of the heating season. Across Lithuania, it will officially begin October 1.
That does not mean radiators will automatically begin heating homes if outdoor temperatures remain comfortable. Heating systems will be ready to operate, while residents will continue to have control over how much heat they use.

====================================================================================================

Polish foreign minister: Ukraine should choose its heroes carefully or don’t be surprised
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
10:05:00 EEST
16:05:00 KST

Polish foreign minister: Ukraine should choose its heroes carefully. If not, there will be a reaction
Radosław Sikorski, Poland’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister, visited Kyiv at the end of last week.
Relations between Kyiv and Warsaw are not in the best shape. But if we had to pick out the Polish politicians who are trying to repair them, Radosław Sikorski would certainly deserve a prominent place on that list. That is why we met with him to hear his views and ideas, as well as the objections he voices towards Ukraine.
Not all of his remarks on historical issues are pleasant to hear. But this also means that even from the broadly pro-Ukrainian camp of the Polish political establishment, softer positions simply cannot be expected at the moment.
We spoke on the sidelines of the annual Yalta European Strategy meeting organised by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation – the event that brought Sikorski to Ukraine. The conversation took place before the minister made his widely-reported remarks about Poland’s readiness to defend itself against Russia, and also before Russia began striking targets near the Polish border. Therefore, the interview does not include questions on these issues.
We began by discussing recent anti-Ukrainian provocations in Poland.
"He risks going to jail, which is where he belongs"
Radek, it’s good to see you again. We did an interview two years ago, and back then, you were quite optimistic about the development of our relations. Have they developed in the way you expected?
Well, Ukraine is now a candidate to join the European Union, and I hope one day we will be members of the same family.
I’m pretty sure I know what you’re going to say, and we’ll talk about that later, but I have to start with the most recent incident involving Grzegorz Braun, who desecrated a memorial dedicated to Ukrainians. How on earth could this happen? When are you going to stop him?
I'd like your listeners and viewers to know that Grzegorz Braun is the outer right-wing fringe of Polish politics.
He's a fascist, an antisemite and a criminal.
He has already been charged with several offences of using violence to destroy a menorah displayed in the Polish parliament, and he has also been charged for denying the Holocaust.
He is so toxic that nobody wants to even speculate about doing a coalition with him.
And I only hope that Polish courts work faster in order to eliminate him from public life.
Is there a legal way to do that?
He risks going to jail, which is where he belongs.
Okay. But I also believe that to some degree, the kind of views he expresses are contributing to what is unfortunately one of the most visible problems in our relations. These days we are seeing reports almost daily about Ukrainians being beaten up or harassed simply because of their origin. Do you think this is happening more often than before?
We do unfortunately have crimes of ethnic prejudice and even violence. Those are very quickly and very firmly dealt with by the police.
And we also have controversies to do with historical facts that are encouraged by those who wish ill to both Ukraine and Poland. Let me remind you that when the latest controversy flared up, the leaders of our countries were congratulated by Dmitry Medvedev.
Is there a way not just to deal with the offenders, but to prevent these incidents from happening in the first place?
Well, there needs to be responsibility on behalf of the politicians of both countries not to use issues of the past to stoke up hatred today.
I think we have had some success.
[Ukrainian Foreign Minister] Andrii Sybiha and I were able to announce two years ago that the exhumations of the victims of the Volhynia massacre would resume, and they have resumed. [Sikorski is referring to the massacres of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia known as the Volyn (Volhynia) tragedy, a series of events that led to the ethnic cleansing of the Polish and Ukrainian populations in 1943 – ed.]
Equally, there are exhumations of Ukrainian victims in Poland.
On my previous visit here, I requested the Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Church to appeal, the way I appealed to both sides, to give Christian burial to the victims of those events. And that seems to be working.
That is the spirit that we need to overcome historical issues. You know, neighbours always have some historical issues. And the question is how you deal with them. And I propose that the role of politicians is to make sure that the bad stuff doesn't repeat itself.
Reconciliation is not necessarily between brothers and friends.
Reconciliation is usually between former enemies.
But if Germany and France could create the European integration process five years after the Second World War, in which they were massacring each other, so can we.
"Be careful how you choose your heroes. Don’t be surprised if there’s a reaction abroad"
What else can we do – not just as journalists or politicians, but as ordinary citizens? What can ordinary people do to prevent these incidents from happening?
Well, I have one suggestion for Ukrainian politicians.
Of course, every country decides who their heroes are. But tell me who your heroes are and I'll tell you who you are.
You have plenty of genuine heroes in Ukraine, for example, heroes of your heroic resistance against Russia. So be careful how you choose your heroes from the past, because some of them have a mixed record, shall we say. And we don't need more historical controversies.
I don’t remember Ukrainians ever complaining about Poland honouring Piłsudski, Dmowski, the Home Army or the Peasant Battalions – because they are your heroes.
Piłsudski was trying to save your statehood together with Petliura in 1919.
Sure, we have some controversial heroes too.
I was recently in South Africa, and they have a national pantheon. And do you know who is in the national pantheon? Mugabe and Castro!
I received a collection of medals from Mongolia struck on the 800th anniversary of Genghis Khan, who is, I think, a controversial figure both in Poland and in Ukraine.
Every country has its historical narrative, but those historical narratives will be judged by others.
You referred to the Pantheon. Do you mean that we need to reconsider the decision made by parliament, or…?
No, I'm saying most countries have such an institution, but just be careful who you put in there, because that will produce reactions abroad.
And if you put in there people who have stained their reputation by conducting war crimes, then don’t be surprised.
You met with Petro Poroshenko here. Was that meeting also about this issue?
No, it's about me meeting with the opposition in countries that I visit.
When I visited Russia, I met the opposition.
When I visit Germany, I meet not only the government, I meet the opposition. Because the nature of opposition is that it can become the government.
Okay, let’s move on to the EU. You said that one day we will end up in the same family...
And by the way, when Croatia was a candidate to join the European Union, Croatia was told: if you continue to praise your fascists from the wartime period, then you're denying yourself the right to belong to our family, because in our family we do not put fascists on monument plates.
The key difference is that the UPA is not the same thing as fascism.
It has a fascist ideology.
Well, Dmowski also did. But he is still honoured in Poland.
Which is why he's such a controversial figure.
"Poland will not block any negotiating chapters"
Regarding our European future, what do you see as the key obstacles that we still have to overcome?
I helped to finish the negotiations on Ukraine's Association Agreement, which includes a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area, but that was back in 2011. It was 15 years ago, and you still have not fully implemented the Association Agreement.
My advice would be – do that!
Because you can have access to the single market even before you become a full member. And that's a big benefit. Poland will not block any negotiating chapters, but that's not to say that we will not have a difficult negotiation on some matters. And we know what they are!
Agriculture will be difficult for existing members,
not just for Poland, because you have a different structure of your agriculture.
Because of the collectivisation and Holodomor carried out by the Soviet authorities, thousands of your small farms were destroyed, and you have these huge holdings of tens of thousands of hectares. That's a completely different pattern of land-holding than in the European Union.
You also have the best land in Europe. You are very, very competitive in agriculture.
We have a similar relationship that Poland had with Western Europe in terms of wage competitiveness, for example, in transportation.
Your long-distance truckers are more competitive than Polish truckers, and there will be vigorous debate here.
The nature of the relationship is that overall it is beneficial to both sides, but there will be some sectors where the costs will fall disproportionately. And you have politics and we have politics.
Did I understand you correctly – do you support the idea that we should open all the negotiating clusters as soon as possible?
No, it's more complicated than that. The Commission first has to say that Ukraine fulfils the criteria for opening clusters. And then it's a political decision to open them, and we have no objections against opening clusters, but others do.
The European Commission has said multiple times that Ukraine has met the conditions for opening the clusters. Meanwhile, Hungary’s Foreign Ministry recently stated publicly in parliament that it was Poland that asked Hungary to block them…
That's not true. We're not blocking a single chapter.
That Poland asked Hungary to block the process.
No. No. This is not a matter of speculation. You either raise your hand for blocking or you don't. We don't.
Okay. When do you expect the clusters to be opened?
There is a vigorous debate between Ukraine and the new Hungarian government on the minority issues, and I hope it produces a positive result.
Is it possible that our European friends, including Poland, could tell, ask or at least hint to the Hungarian government that it’s time to move forward?
No… Yes, we do.
We need all member states to fulfil the criteria for treating minorities according to the Council of Europe Convention on Minorities, which means that if in any district there are 20% people or more from a national minority, there should be double signs on the names of streets and roads, there should be education of at least some subjects in the language of the minority, and that the language of the minority should be available in public spaces.
I understand there is now a constructive debate between Ukraine and Hungary on this.
"You have to calculate what your national interest really is"
You mentioned that there are some sectors where we will have difficult debates or issues to resolve during the negotiations. Unfortunately, in Ukraine there is a perception that Poland could potentially block our path towards EU membership because of some of these issues.
I think I've said it clearly enough that we will not block!
We will negotiate.
Opening a chapter is not the same as closing the chapter. Opening means that you start negotiating, and we will have issues, just like Western Europe had issues with us.
Let me give you an example. I live in the countryside, and you know, Poland used to have a very big milk industry. And we had to close down some of our milk processing plants because of the quotas we received from the European Union.
Were we happy about it? No we weren't!
Have we benefited from EU membership since then? Yes we have!
You will have some painful decisions to make too.
What makes you confident that compromises will be possible? Let me explain why I’m insisting on asking this. People remember the border blockade in 2023. So we need to give them more reason to believe that compromise is actually possible.
Now let's remember what actually happened.
When the Russians blocked your export capacity through the Black Sea, just as they're doing now, Poland out of friendship allowed the transit of Ukrainian grain through Poland to your traditional markets, to Egypt and to China.
And then what happened was that two-thirds of the Ukrainian grain, instead of getting to Egypt, stayed in Poland and depressed prices in Poland, which was not supposed to happen.
And Polish farmers protested.
See, these are difficult issues.
Can you see a way to convince hauliers, farmers and all the other groups that could be affected that Ukraine’s accession to the European Union would also be beneficial to them?
We have creative solutions.
So when our truckers became too competitive with Western European truckers, the European Union devised a scheme whereby if you cross the border of your country, you have to be paid as a trucker the wage of that country, which benefits the truckers, but doesn't benefit the trucking companies.
And so you have to weigh those interests, and you have to calculate what your national interest really is. Do you back the truckers, or do you back the owners of their companies?
And you will have to make such calculations yourself.
Is it possible to convince them? Might Poland hold a referendum on Ukraine’s EU accession, as some countries have done?
It's not obliged in Poland, but in some countries it is, you are right.
And would you consider that possibility, or…?
It's unnecessary.
As the British have learned, you have to be careful with the referendum.
"The Russians have proven that they are a threat to all of Europe"
Let’s talk about security and NATO. You personally support NATO membership for Ukraine, I know.
I supported it in Bucharest back in 2008, when it didn't happen.
Does the Polish public support it? And what about the Polish political establishment?
I'm not sure. I don't recall a recent opinion poll on this.
But it's a hard issue, because NATO membership is essentially a security guarantee. Unfortunately, Ukraine already has Western security guarantees under the Budapest Memorandum. And you also have a security guarantee from Russia, both under the Budapest Memorandum and in your border treaty, signed and ratified by Putin.
What I'm saying to you is that guarantees are useful if they're credible.
There is nothing more dangerous in international affairs than a non-credible security guarantee.
What is a feasible way of integrating Ukraine into Europe’s security and defence architecture? Because I believe Europe also needs Ukraine.
Sure. You are resisting Russian imperialism, which is a threat to all of Europe, and not just Eastern Europe.
With their attacks on Germany, the Russians have proven that they are a threat to all of Europe.
So what would be the way to include us?
The best way is for you to win.
You will be a huge exporter of military technology, and we will be learning about how to conduct a modern war in your military academies.
And perhaps one final topic: our peace negotiations. We’ve heard concerns – or perhaps I should call them demands – that Poland should be involved in these negotiations.
Well, Poland is the only country in Europe that borders both Russia and Ukraine.
We also carry 95% of all assistance to Ukraine as a transit country.
And we provide security for that hub, without which you wouldn't get the stuff. And Poland will be directly affected by the outcome of these negotiations.
We are also now a G20 economy.
We spend $50 billion per annum on defence, on hard defence – even more if you include dual-use stuff. We have more tanks and more brigades than Germany, France and Britain combined that we could deploy.
So we think yes, that we should be consulted.
Do you feel that Poland’s interests and concerns are being taken into account?
We have meetings in various formats. The one that we prefer is the E5, which includes countries of the Southern tier, Northern tier and Eastern tier.
The times when Western Europe was deciding about our Eastern European security should be confined to bad history.
Interview by Sergiy Sydorenko

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The National Science and Technology Council co-organized a three-day semiconductor forum in Munich with Germany’s Ministry for Research, Technology and Space, reports said Thursday.
The Tuesday to Thursday event was designed to boost cooperation in chip design and advanced packaging, per UDN. The forum also formed part of a collaboration project now in its third year.
The cooperation project covers domains such as quantum computing, wireless communications, design automation, and edge computing AI chips. Research into batteries was the first field Taiwan and Germany covered with a project starting in 2017. The cooperation resulted in the signing of a Science and Technology Arrangement in 2023, leading to subsidies for 23 projects.
In an address at the forum, ministry representative Fabian Kohler said cooperation in semiconductors to train chip design talent and enhance global market resilience was of utmost importance. He expressed Germany’s interest in continuing to provide resources and advance research into microelectronics to the next stage, UDN reported.
The National Science and Technology Council delegation had discussions with academics and researchers from prominent German universities and corporate representatives, including Infineon Technologies, BMW, and Siemens. More than 100 people attended the event, per UDN.

PHOTO BTA
Font size
Traffic is normal at all border checkpoints and border crossings in the country, the Border Police reported.
The European network of traffic police services ROADPOL has designated September 17 as a Day Without Road Deaths, Bulgaria’s Ministry of the Interior said. The initiative is part of the annual ROADPOL Safety Days (RSD) campaign, which this year runs from September 16 to 22.
In 2026, the campaign focuses on pedestrian safety, with pedestrians being among the most vulnerable road users. Police urges drivers to exercise increased caution in built-up areas, in places with heavy pedestrian traffic and when approaching pedestrian crossings. Observing speed limits is crucial, as speed is one of the key factors determining the severity of the consequences in a collision with a pedestrian.
Unfortunately, two people were killed and 30 injured in 24 serious road accidents across the country over the past 24 hours, Traffic Police reported. Since the beginning of September, 362 serious road accidents have occurred in Bulgaria, claiming 17 lives and leaving 447 people injured. Since the beginning of the year, 330 people have lost their lives on the country’s roads, while 6,024 have been injured.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The European Parliament plenary voted on Tuesday to adopt the “Findings and Recommendations of the Special Committee on the European Democracy Shield,” which recognized Taiwan as an important partner in situational awareness.
The resolution said Taiwan regularly conducts large-scale civil defense and resilience exercises to counter China’s increasingly intensified gray-zone operations, according to the foreign ministry. The resolution also suggested that the country's whole-of-society resilience experience can help the EU enhance the overall effectiveness of the European Democracy Shield.
The resolution called on the EU to deepen cooperation with like-minded East Asian partners such as Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea on countering foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) and on submarine cable security. The foreign ministry thanked the European Parliament for recognizing and supporting Taiwan’s experience in democratic resilience. It pledged to continue cooperation with the EU to resist hybrid threats and contribute to regional and global peace.

Taiwan's Yang Ming christens new dual-fuel container ship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:04:23 UTC
16:04:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Yang Ming Marine on Thursday christened its fourth LNG dual-fuel container ship, YM Weight, at the HD Hyundai Heavy Industries shipyard in Ulsan, South Korea.
The vessel is the fourth of five dual-fuel container ships ordered by Yang Ming. After delivery, it will operate on the company's MS2 service, linking major markets in Asia, the Western Mediterranean, and North America.
The 365-meter-long vessel can carry about 15,600 20-foot-equivalent units (TEUs). It is powered by a high-pressure dual-fuel engine capable of using liquefied natural gas and low-sulfur fuel oil, per a press release.
The ship is also equipped with an integrated navigation information system, equipment-condition monitoring, and global satellite broadband. It also has energy-saving equipment designed to improve operational efficiency and navigational safety.
YM Weight underwent verification by the China Classification Society and the American Bureau of Shipping and completed underwater noise measurements. Yang Ming said the vessel received both the CR Underwater Radiated Noise and ABS Underwater Noise class notations, making it the first container ship to receive both certifications, per CTEE.
The company said the certifications are intended to reduce the potential impact of vessel operations on marine life and support safety standards for LNG dual-fuel vessels. It added that YM Weight will be managed and operated by the company itself, allowing it to build experience in LNG dual-fuel vessel operations as it expands its fleet of new-energy vessels.
Yang Ming is also expanding training for crews who will operate LNG and other alternative-fuel vessels. Senior Captain Pan Ming-yong (潘銘勇) will serve as captain for YM Weight. Yang Ming said Pan was the first Taiwanese seafarer to receive the Maritime and Port Bureau's IGF Code Advanced Training Certificate, certificate No. 0001.
As of Thursday, 148 Yang Ming Class A seafarers had completed advanced IGF training. The company plans to arrange onboard apprenticeships on LNG vessels and practical training in alternative-fuel bunkering. The company said the training program is intended to develop the personnel and safety-management capabilities needed to operate an LNG and alternative-fuel fleet.
YM Weight's port rotation is Busan, Shanghai, Ningbo, Kaohsiung, Shekou, Singapore, Cape of Good Hope, Tangier, Valencia, Barcelona, Genoa, La Spezia and Fos-sur-Mer. It will return to Asia via the Cape of Good Hope with port calls at Langkabang, Cai Mep, Yantian, Busan, Long Beach, Auckland, and Busan.

Breadcrumb
Lebanon returns 37 artefacts smuggled out of Egypt
Lebanon on Wednesday returned to Egypt dozens of pharaonic artefacts that had been seized from the Beirut port years earlier.
"Thirty-seven antiquities... were seized from Beirut port in 2020, having arrived from an Arab port," Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salameh said during a handover ceremony at the Beirut national museum.
"After investigating the identity and ownership of these items, it was determined that they belonged to Egypt," he added.
Five of the items were on display at the ceremony, including masks made of fabric, wood and clay.
"Cooperation between states... contributes to preserving humanity's heritage," Egyptian ambassador Alaa Moussa said at the ceremony.
Laura Salloum, an official with Lebanon's directorate of antiquities, told AFP that at the time of their seizure, the items were stored in a single container.
They "had been purchased by a Lebanese national without any official documentation regarding their source -- namely, Egypt," she said.
Antiquities smuggling is common in Egypt. Over the past decade, Cairo has recovered nearly 30,000 archaeological artefacts, according to officials.

====================================================================================================

Israeli Air Force pilot rejects NAZA claim: ‘No strike risking 500 civilians was approved’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:03:28 UTC
16:03:28 KST

He does not want his name published, but he wants his argument heard. Reserve Col. A., a fighter pilot with the Israeli Air Force’s 101 Squadron who says he has taken part in thousands of strikes across multiple fronts and until about a year ago commanded Ramat David Air Base, rarely speaks publicly. But after the documentary NAZA won at the Venice Film Festival and reignited debate over Israel’s conduct in Gaza, he decided to respond.
A. says he has not seen the film itself or heard the testimony in full, and is responding to descriptions and headlines about it. “I haven’t seen the film or heard the testimonies. I’ve seen paraphrases by people who have, and I’ve seen the headlines,” he said. “But whoever took a process whose entire purpose is to put the truth, transparency, dilemmas and morality directly in front of you, as clearly and precisely as possible, and turned it into a claim that we deliberately tried to harm civilians, has done something astonishingly cynical. They have turned the entire process on its head.”
At the center of the controversy is nezek agavi, Hebrew for collateral damage and the phrase behind the acronym NAZA. A. describes it not as a single calculation but as part of an extensive system of intelligence, target verification, risk assessment and operational approvals developed by the IDF and Air Force over decades. He argues that the system was built to confront armed groups operating from within civilian areas. “The enemy does not separate the civilian population from terrorist infrastructure,” he said. “The missile is in the bedroom, the weapons depot is in the children’s room, the headquarters is on one floor of a densely populated civilian building and the hospital is used as a command center. That is not an accident. It is deliberate planning.”
A. argues that Gaza’s density alone does not explain that deployment. “Gaza is crowded, but it also has open and agricultural areas. If the enemy wanted to separate itself from the population, it could have done so. It deliberately chose otherwise,” he said.
‘You ask yourself what the operational gain is compared with the risk’
Describing the planning of an airstrike, A. said a proposed target begins with intelligence and must be verified as being used for terrorist activity under what he described as highly stringent standards. If there is uncertainty, he said, the target is rejected. Once verified, it passes through additional approvals before the final strike configuration is generally authorized by a senior officer.
“As a pilot, I’m the fourth stage in that process,” he said. “There are conditions that have to be met: weather, visibility, precise identification.” He said drones, helicopters or surveillance aircraft may scan the area before a strike to determine whether people are nearby, while aircrews can delay an attack or change the munition if conditions change. “If something doesn’t add up, I have discretion. Sometimes you change the size of the bomb. Sometimes you use a ‘roof knock’ to get people out of the building before the strike. An enormous amount of time is invested in trying to make sure nobody gets hurt.”
The final moments before releasing a weapon, he said, can involve what he called an extremely difficult judgment. “You ask yourself what the operational achievement is compared with the risk. It’s a multistory building. The risk to civilians is this or that, and the operational gain is eliminating a Hamas brigade commander. They give you as much information as possible to help you decide what is right.”
He recalled one operation in which an aircrew asked to wait because the conditions were not right. “I once saw an operational crew say, ‘I’m not carrying this out under these conditions. Let’s wait another two minutes,’” he said. “And during those exact two minutes, a barrage was fired from the launcher they were supposed to destroy.”
One allegation surrounding NAZA has drawn particular attention: testimony that a strike was approved despite the possibility of causing hundreds of civilian deaths, reportedly as many as 500. A. emphatically disputes that account. “I was responsible for planning and carrying out thousands of strikes,” he said. “I never encountered a number like that, or anything close to it. I can say with a high degree of confidence: There was no such approved strike.”
At the same time, he does not deny the civilian toll inherent in war. “Every strike carries a risk of harming uninvolved people, and on a human level that is terrible. War is genuinely hell,” he said. “Even five or 10 dead is unacceptable. I would want the number to be zero in every strike. But the alternative, raising a white flag and leaving the rockets where they are, is not an alternative.”
For A., that calculation is also personal. “I know my brothers in Golani are on the ground below me, and my family is in Hamas’ sights in Sderot,” he said. “I know I am the solution. I am what stands between that rocket and the home or the force it is aimed at, and I am very proud to be the person who meets that threat before it reaches our civilians and our soldiers.”
‘What would you have done in my place?’
Despite his criticism, A. said he is not angry with filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. “They were, at the very least, wrong in their perspective. Maybe they even lost their moral compass,” he said. “But if I met them, I wouldn’t throw accusations at them.”
He said he sees scrutiny of the military as an essential part of a democratic society. “I love investigations, criticism and transparency. That is what makes me proud to serve in the military of a democratic and liberal country, one that allows difficult questions to be asked even about itself,” he said. Instead, he would ask the filmmakers one question: “What would you have done in my place?”
“I think anyone with a head on their shoulders and a heart in their chest would answer that they would have done exactly the same thing,” he said. “I sleep peacefully with regard to my duty to the paratrooper maneuvering below me, to my family in Sderot and to the Israeli public in whose name I fight.”
“We don’t have a millimeter to be ashamed of,” he added. “But there is not the slightest bit of joy in us over what we were forced to do.”

Zelensky Hails ‘Powerful’ US Sanctions Bill After Overnight Russian Missile, Drone Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:02:59 UTC
16:02:59 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed the US House of Representatives’ passage of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill, calling it a powerful tool to pressure Moscow toward peace after another overnight Russian attack damaged civilian and energy infrastructure across Ukraine.
The House passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by a 262-159 vote on Wednesday, sending the legislation to US President Donald Trump for his signature. The bill had already passed the Senate in August.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In a Telegram post following the vote, Zelensky wrote that the legislation passed on the same night as another major Russian attack involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones.
“It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives’ passage of Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones,” Zelensky wrote.
According to him, Russian forces damaged civilian infrastructure in eight regions, including energy facilities in the Sumy and Odesa regions, along with residential buildings in Kyiv and Odesa.
According to the latest reports, 20 people have been injured in Kyiv and seven in Odesa, with young children among the casualties.
“Lindsey Graham’s bill – along with other robust sanctions measures taken by our partners against the source of this war, Russia – represents an incredibly powerful tool capable of halting this terrorist war and compelling Russia to establish peace,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky Names Anton Kovalsky Acting Prosecutor General
He said strong sanctions were necessary to support diplomatic efforts being conducted with the US, Europe, and other partners.
Zelensky thanked members of the House and Senate, as well as congressional leaders, for supporting the legislation.
What the sanctions bill does
The legislation gives the US president expanded powers to impose sanctions on Russia and entities supporting its war effort.
The bipartisan sanctions and tariff package passed on Wednesday gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
The legislation targets Russia’s energy sector, defense suppliers, major financial institutions, and sanctions-evasion networks, while also authorizing sanctions against individuals involved in the abduction of Ukrainian children.
Its central provision allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying large volumes of Russian oil and gas or helping Moscow evade sanctions, potentially affecting major buyers such as China and India.
The package also targets Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers, foreign suppliers supporting its defense sector, and networks helping Moscow circumvent existing restrictions. It would further restrict new US investment in Russia and exports that could support the Russian military.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who worked on the legislation with Graham, described the measures as “scorching sanctions” intended to “throttle Putin’s war machine.”
The bill is named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, a prominent supporter of Ukraine who spent more than a year building support for the legislation before his death in July. Its passage marks a major congressional effort to increase economic pressure on Moscow as Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues.

The ins and outs of postal voting in Switzerland
Are you comfortable putting your vote in the letter-box? From the US to Germany, some politicians say you shouldn’t be. In Switzerland, where postal voting is second nature, such debates remain marginal.
“We are now the only country in the world that uses mail-in voting,” US President Donald Trump complained in 2025. The statement was untrue: more than 30 countries use it, either for all or for some voters. But the claim was symbolic of a wider backlash, especially in the US. In Switzerland, by contrast, where postal ballots are the norm, authorities have even cited them as a potential boost to democratic security.
How does postal voting work in Switzerland?
It’s a well-oiled system. Up to four times a year, without having asked for it, voting age citizens in Switzerland get a thick envelope delivered to their letter boxes. Inside is information about an upcoming vote or elections, a ballot paper, and a voter ID card. After considering their options, they can fill out their choice and return the vote – by mail or into a dedicated municipal letter box – or wait to vote in-person on ballot day. They can also bin the lot.
Because it’s so embedded in political life, and so widely used, it’s easy to forget that postal voting in Switzerland is not so old. Analogue to the US, it is managed by cantons: the first ones rolled it out in the 1970s, around the same time California became the first US state to get on board. In 1994, the Swiss federal parliament ruled that mail-in ballots should be available nationwide; by 2005, all 26 cantons had complied. Minor local differences still remain: for example, some places offer free return postage, some don’t.
According to International IDEA, an intergovernmental organisation that promotes democracy worldwide, Switzerland is one of 11 countries offering mail-in ballots to all voters; 21 countries offer it to some citizens, like the elderly or voters abroad. In the US, rules vary by state, which helps explain some of the tension around mail ballots: for years, Trump has engaged in back-and-forth legal and political battles to restrict them, including ahead ofExternal link the November 2026 mid-term elections.
How extensively do Swiss citizens vote by post?
The short answer: very. “Almost everyone votes in advance,” says Alina Zumbrunn from the University of Bern. There are no exact figures, but postal ballots are estimated to account for over 90% of votes nationally; in June 2026, canton Aargau logged a rate of 98%. Neither is it a rural or urban affair: cities like Geneva or Basel have similar rates to rural Obwalden. Those who actually do vote in person are a motley bunch, Zumbrunn adds: those who like the social side of it, or first-time voters, or those who simply forgot to do it by post beforehand.
Internationally, these numbers are high. Some US states with all-mail-in ballots, like Oregon or Washington, have seen Swiss-style rates over 90%, according to the US Election Assistance CommissionExternal link. But nationally, with the exception of Liechtenstein, it’s hard to find any country with a higher overall mail-in ballot rate than Switzerland – even if some countries have made big jumps, not least due to the impetus of the Covid-19 pandemic; Germany logged just under half of votes by post in the 2021 elections.
The speed of adoption in the Alpine nation was also striking, jumping from an estimated half or two-thirdsExternal link of voters in the late 1990s to today’s near-universality. What makes the country so well-suited? One factor is the world-leadingExternal link postal system. There’s also the frequency of votes, Zumbrunn adds – for many, mail-in ballots are easier than trooping down to the polling station four times a year. And there’s the trust factor: Swiss citizens have high faith in their institutions – in this case, their electoral system.
Is there any opposition to it à la Trump?
The thing about trust, says Therese Pearce Laanela from International IDEA, is that it can be “less about the workings of a system itself, and more about people and their relationship to the system”. As such, postal voting can be loved in one place and hated in another, depending on culture, habit, or efforts to undermine trust. In the past years, for example, Trump has periodically sought to restrict mail-in ballots. The far-right Alternative for Germany party wants to do the same.
In Switzerland, however, the issue is “much less politicised”, Zumbrunn says. This is not only due to trust. It’s also because political parties don’t stand to win or lose hugely by attacking it. In the US, Democrats vote by mail more than Republicans. As a result, there is clear political capital, and potentially votes, to be gained or lost. In Switzerland, why criticise a system that everyone – young, old, conservative, liberal – is generally happy with?
That said, it’s not immune to criticism. In late 2025, for instance, Jean-Luc Addor from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party called on parliamentExternal link to boost in-person voting at polling stations, what he called an “act of citizen participation with societal significance”. It’s about “restoring trust and reducing the effect of potential fraud”, Addor said. The Swiss government, however, was not impressed. Postal voting is popular and convenient, it answered, citing usual advantages: accessibility, flexibility and voting from abroad.
>> One group which depends on postal voting is electors abroad – including US citizens based in Switzerland:
More
US midterms: Democrats target voters on Swiss trams and buses
Is it as foolproof as all that?
In Switzerland, there is no major evidence to the contrary. Every few months, a couple of million citizens vote by post, and cases of fraud are rare. But as the government acknowledged in its response to Addor, abuse cannot be fully ruled out. For example, an appeal after local elections in November 2025 in Vernier, Geneva, led to the discovery by graphologists that 189 voter ID cards had been filled out by 79 people. The election results were not impacted, but investigations are ongoingExternal link, according to the Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
The Geneva case highlighted an issue with mail-in ballots which is sometimes mentioned but seldom quantified: family members or friends filling out – and deciding – for others. Other potential risks are theft: in canton Valais in 2017, a man was suspected of stealing and filling out 150 votes. Beyond such fraud, meanwhile, there’s the possibility of votes going missing before they’re counted – something that almost never happened in Switzerland.
Zumbrunn says that with concrete cases of abuse rare, trust in the Swiss system remains largely intact. Internationally, however, it can be a balance between what Pearce Laanela from International IDEA calls the “benefits of convenience and concerns about security”. For transitional or new democracies, the “controlled setting” of the polling station is still the “gold standard” for ensuring a safe vote, Pearce Laanela says. Elsewhere, its success depends on various factors – the obvious one being a dependable postal service.
Are there any other democratic advantages to it?
While it can make life easier, postal voting doesn’t necessarily turbo-charge turnout. The convenience of it can help foreign-based and elderly voters, or during a pandemic. But “people also vote for various other reasons, including whether it’s meaningful or a habit,” Pearce Laanela says. In Switzerland, where turnout is generally low, postal voting is estimated to have raised it by around four percentage points since being introduced, Zumbrunn says. Paid postage for mail-in ballots boosts this again by three percentage points, she found in a 2025 studyExternal link.
Other democratic aspects are more intangible. Whether postal voting cheapens the idea of democracy as a “social event” depends on your vision of a social event. Zumbrunn adds that it’s difficult to force such jollity, especially in Switzerland, where democracy is rather a part of everyday life. Meanwhile institutions like municipal assemblies or the Landsgemeinde open-air votes, which are based on the premise of people gathering physically, often have turnout rates lower than the already-low Swiss average.
Finally, in an age of hybrid threats and disinformation, some see new upsides in what is now a well-established system. For the government, the country’s mail-in voting practices could even help democratic stability. They allow “voter participation over several weeks (and not just on a single election day, as in many other Western democracies)”, it wroteExternal link in 2025. Along with voters’ “familiarity” with electoral procedures, and a decentralised organisation, they help “make the system robust and protect against foreign interference”, it said in response to a parliamentary question about potential meddling in the 2027 elections.

Why ocean warming matters for landlocked countries such as Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Why ocean warming matters for landlocked countries such as Switzerland
The seas have never been this warm since records began. Rising ocean temperatures also affect life in land-locked countries.
A refreshing dip in the sea? For swimmers who spent their August holidays in Mallorca, that was probably not the case. A buoy off the Balearic island logged a record temperature of 33°C, only a few degrees below a hot bath at home.
“For the Mediterranean, this is truly an extraordinary temperature record,” Thomas Frölicher, professor of climate and environmental physics at the University of Bern, told Swissinfo.
The anomaly is not limited to the Mediterranean, where in some areas water temperatures reached up to 6°C above the seasonal average. Globally, the average sea surface temperature reached 21.1°C this summer, surpassing the record set in 2024, the hottest year since measurements began, according to CopernicusExternal link, the European Earth observation programme.
However, ocean warming, which has now reached 1.1-1.2°C above pre-industrial levels, goes far beyond uncomfortable swimming conditions. Its consequences extend to marine ecosystems and to the climate of land areas, including countries far from the coast, such as Switzerland.
“What worries me most is that today’s exceptionally high ocean temperatures will become the norm within ten or 20 years,” Frölicher says. The most fragile ecosystems risk exceeding their capacity to adapt, triggering cascading effects on biodiversity, fisheries, food security and coastal communities.
The chart below shows how average ocean surface temperatures have now reached record levels.
>> The following graph shows how the average ocean surface temperature has now reached record levels:
Why are seas and oceans getting warmer?
The main cause of warmer seas is greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane, and other gases trap heat in the Earth’s atmosphere. The oceans absorb more than90%External link of this excess heat generated by human activities.
As on land, marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent, more intense and longer lasting. The share of European ocean waters affected by these events has increased from an average of 40% in the 1980s to 98% during the period 2023-2025External link. About a decade ago, a marine heatwave in the northeastern Pacific lasted nearly a year, Frölicher notes.
Warming is not limited to the ocean surface. As Frölicher explains, heat is accumulating throughout the ocean, particularly in the upper 2,000 metres. Measurements around Antarctica and in the North Atlantic indicate, however, that deep waters are also gradually warming.
Climate change, and in particular the burning of fossil fuels such as coal and oil, is the primary driver of rising temperatures in European seas, according to a new studyExternal link by World Weather Attribution (WWA), an international group of experts that analyses the role of climate change in extreme weather events.
“Every additional tonne of carbon we emit [into the atmosphere] pushes European coastal waters and ecosystems toward conditions that have never been experienced before,” says Frölicher, one of the study’s co-authors.
More
Ailing oceans ‘pose greatest threat to planet’
What impact does El Niño have on ocean temperatures?
El Niño is a natural, cyclical climate phenomenon that causes an abnormal warming of surface waters in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. This year’s event is particularly intense, possibly the strongest ever recorded.
El Niño plays an important role because it redistributes heat between the tropical Pacific and the atmosphere, Frölicher explains. “As a result, global sea surface temperatures temporarily rise even more than they would from the effects of global warming alone.” According to a recent studyExternal link, El Niño events are now more extreme than in the past 1,000 years.
How do warmer oceans influence climate and weather in Europe?
What happens in the ocean does not stay in the ocean, the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS) remindsExternal link us.
The oceans surrounding Europe play a crucial role in shaping the continent’s climate and weather patterns. The North Atlantic influences atmospheric circulation through the prevailing westerly winds, while variations in sea surface temperatures directly affect rainfall patterns.
Warmer seas provide more energy and water vapour to storms, increase evaporation, and can lead to heavier and more intense rainfall over land. They can also influence monsoons and increase the destructive potential of tropical cyclones.
In Europe, unusually warm Mediterranean waters have been linked to extreme rainfall events. One example is the floods that struck the Spanish city of Valencia in 2024External link.
Why do rising ocean temperatures matter to a landlocked country such as Switzerland?
High Mediterranean temperatures increase evaporation and enrich the atmosphere with heat and moisture. When these air masses reach southern Switzerland, they can encourage episodes of intense rainfall, Frölicher explains. A similar process can also occur in the North Atlantic: if particularly warm, moisture-laden air is transported toward Switzerland and encounters the Alps, it can trigger heavy precipitation.
“This does not mean that every storm and every episode of intense rainfall in Switzerland is caused by high sea surface temperatures,” the professor stresses. However, warmer seas do increase the risk of extreme rainfall events in Switzerland as well.
Research is currently underway to better understand the relationship between sea surface temperatures and episodes of extreme precipitation in Switzerland.
>>In Switzerland, global warming is proceeding at twice the global average rate:
More
Why Switzerland is among the ten fastest-warming countries in the world
What effects do rising ocean temperatures have on marine ecosystems?
Exceptionally high sea surface temperatures and marine heatwaves have “devastating consequences for marine ecosystems”, WWA warns. They are responsible for mass mortality events among key species such as corals, sponges, and macroalgae (seaweed).
In the Mediterranean, exotic and sometimes invasive species such as lionfish are spreading and may disrupt ecological balances, Guido Gnone, scientific coordinator of the Genoa Aquarium, told Swiss public broadcaster RSIExternal link. While some species may gain new opportunities for expansion, such as the Mediterranean’s most common sea turtle (Caretta caretta), climate change overall risks causing a significant loss of biodiversity, according to Gnone.
Thomas Frölicher agrees.“Some fishing sectors in northern regions could benefit from the migration of species,” he says. “However, if we look at the situation on a global scale, the balance is negative.” The highest price will be paid by countries in the Global South, which depend heavily on fisheries both as a source of income and as a vital food resource.
What are the impacts of ocean warming on human health?
According to WWA, rising marine temperatures encourage the spread of waterborne diseases such as vibriosis. In addition, jellyfish blooms, favoured by the new environmental conditions, can negatively affect beach tourism and lead to the temporary closure of some beaches.
How can we adapt to ever-warmer seas?
Phasing out fossil fuels and reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the most effective way to limit ocean warming and reduce future impacts.
At the same time, adaptation measures are also needed. According to UNU-EHS, establishing marine protected areas, managing fisheries sustainably, and restoring coastal ecosystems such as mangroves are among the solutions that can strengthen ocean resilience.
“People often underestimate the fact that ocean warming is not simply a short-term phenomenon or one confined to the surface,” says Frölicher. “The heat that is accumulating in the oceans will remain there for centuries.”
The oceans remain one of our greatest allies in regulating Earth’s climate and mitigating global warming. How effectively they can continue to play that role will also depend on the choices we make today.

Republicans fear Russia sanctions bill will give Trump too much power on tariffs

Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
The US Congress has delivered President Donald Trump a major Russia sanctions bill ahead of the midterms, but Republican concerns over its tariff provisions have exposed divisions within the party.
The House approved the bill Wednesday by a 262-159 vote, with dozens of Democrats joining Republicans. The measure now goes to Trump for his signature.
Most Republicans support the legislation, which imposes mandatory sanctions on senior Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, as well as oligarchs, state-owned companies and foreign businesses supporting Russia’s defense industry.
However, nearly a dozen Republicans privately urged party leaders to remove provisions granting the administration new tariff powers, fearing they could increase prices before the midterms, according to CNN.
The legislation would allow the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, including China and India.
Although US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer would determine the final tariff level, some Republicans remain concerned that the measure could ultimately give Trump too much authority over tariffs and create wider economic consequences.
Democrats have also criticized the tariff provisions. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposed the bill, questioning why Congress would give Trump additional authority to impose economic harm.
“Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” he asked.
Three senior House Democrats — Gregory Meeks, Richard Neal and Don Beyer — likewise argued the bill would “do more harm than good.”
“This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable,” they said.
Supporters from both parties maintain that the tariff authority is limited and carefully structured, arguing concerns about expanded presidential trade power are unfounded.
The bill was introduced in April 2025 after more than a year of negotiations led by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who secured Trump’s backing shortly before his death.

Global: Women Human Rights Defenders take their fight to the UN during week-long advocacy meeting

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:56:05 UTC
15:56:05 KST

Women Human Right Defenders (WHRDs) from around the world will be gathering in Geneva from 21 to 25 September, to learn about the UN Human Rights Council, advocate for their rights and amplify their own stories.
The week-long training, known as the Women Human Rights Advocacy Week, is co-organized by nine human rights organizations including Amnesty International (see below for full list). It is aimed at providing participants with practical tools to understand the Human Rights Council, while offering guidance on how to engage with it strategically and advocate for change in their communities.
“The women attending are risking their lives every day to protect their communities from climate change, greedy corporations and land theft,” said Lisa Maracani, Amnesty International’s researcher on human rights defenders. “Their knowledge is crucial to ensuring bodies such as the Human Rights Council remain effective, while the WHRD Advocacy Week is designed to provide these women with the tools and strategies to advance their advocacy on this global stage.”
The women attending [this meeting] are risking their lives every day to protect their communities from climate change, greedy corporations and land theft.
Lisa Maracani, Amnesty International’s researcher on human rights defenders
Participants attending are WHRDs working at the nexus of gender, climate and conflict, and includes activists protecting the environment, the rights of women migrant workers, Indigenous land rights, as well as the rights of communities impacted by businesses activities.
The training aims to facilitate participation for activists who face multiple barriers to accessing the UN, to equip participants with a broad knowledge of the human rights system, to foster networks among them as well as between them and human rights experts, and to amplify their voices and calls for international accountability.
Participants will be able to speak before the Human Rights Council, and meet with, lobby and inform UN officials, diplomats and Council-mandated independent experts. Several participating defenders will also speak at a public event at the UN headquarters on Thursday 24 September alongside the UN Special Rapporteur on the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.
“The UN human rights system must be open to and informed by those who have most to contribute to it: human rights defenders,” said Fabiana Leibl, programme manager for the International Service for Human Rights. “With this training, we seek to make sure the perspectives of women human rights defenders are effectively represented at the Human Rights Council’s and across its key mechanisms.”

"Once again, civilian infrastructure was under fire, with damage reported in eight regions. The Russians shelled energy facilities in the Sumy and Odesa regions. In Kyiv and Odesa, there were direct hits on ordinary residential buildings. More than ten people were injured, including children. Some have been hospitalized. Fires broke out in many communities," Zelensky stated.
As reported, the U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday approved the late Senator Lindsey Graham's 2026 bill "On Imposing Sanctions against Russia and Iran," which provides for the introduction of sanctions and potential tariffs against Russia in connection with the war in Ukraine. The document is now to be submitted to President Donald Trump for signature.

Nagel noted that the German economy is in a good position to grow by around 1 percent this year. ■

Column: Development as common aspiration: enduring bond between China and India
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:59:10 CST
22:59:10 KST

by Mohammed Saqib
When President Xi Jinping visited New Delhi for the BRICS Summit 2026, the first such visit in seven years, it was more than a diplomatic event. It was a symbol of renewal, a reminder that China and India, two civilizational giants and largest developing countries, share a responsibility to cooperate for development. In this uncertain world, development stands out as the greatest common denominator binding our nations together.
From the spread of Buddhism across the Himalayas to centuries of trade along the Silk Road, histories of the two countries are deeply connected. These ties are not just relics of the past; they remind us that cooperation is part of our shared heritage. Today, as both nations modernize, these connections gain new significance. Development serves as a bridge linking our past to our future.
The meeting between Xi and Narendra Modi in New Delhi represented a commitment to stabilizing their relationship and focusing on shared interests.
Economic engagement could be a major aspect of bilateral cooperation. China's strength in manufacturing and infrastructure aligns well with India's dynamic services sector and innovation ecosystem. Collaborations in renewable energy, digital platforms and green finance could unlock significant potential and accelerate shared prosperity. However, development goes beyond economics; it also involves investing in people. Expanding student exchanges, cultural festivals and joint research programs can help deepen trust between the two nations.
Beyond bilateral relations, the Global South views China and India as pillars of hope. In forums like the BRICS, SCO, the G20 and the United Nations, China and India can amplify the voices of developing countries. The Global South looks to China and India to demonstrate that cooperation among major developing nations is not only possible but also essential.
The vision for shared prosperity is clear. China and India must embrace development as the greatest common denominator. By cooperating in trade, technology, infrastructure and cultural exchanges, they can inspire the Global South, strengthen multipolarity and shape a fairer international order.
Xi Jinping's visit to New Delhi reminded us that civilizational ties and modern aspirations converge on one point: development. It is the bridge that connects our histories, the mission that unites our peoples, and the hope that inspires the Global South. By embracing development as the foundation of cooperation, China and India can move beyond differences, strengthen exchanges and work together to build a brighter and more inclusive future for the world.
We must recognize that what unites us is far stronger than what divides us.
Editor's note: Mohammed Saqib is the founder and secretary general of India China Economic and Cultural Council, a think tank on India-China's economic and cultural issues.

====================================================================================================

Global freshwater storage declines, glaciers continue to retreat: WMO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
21:59:08 CST
22:59:08 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Rivers around the world had one of the driest years in more than three decades in 2025, according to a new report released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Thursday. The report warns of a continuation of the long-term decline in freshwater storage and glacier retreat, trends with serious implications for the future of the planet, its people and economies.
The WMO State of Global Water Resources Report shows that the water cycle has become more erratic and unpredictable, swinging between too little and too much. The past seven years have seen the fewest rivers with "normal" flows since 1991.
For the seventh year in a row, the number of river basins with "normal" conditions was in a clear minority: ranging between 34 percent and 38 percent, compared to an average of 46 percent between 1991 and 2020.
Terrestrial water storage -- the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation and ice and snow -- has been in decline since the mid-2010s.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said that the planet's water reserves used to act as a "savings account" that absorbed the occasional dry season, thereby avoiding a water crisis. "One of the central stories of the 2025 report is what is happening to that savings account. And the simple answer is that we are depleting it," she told journalists at the launch of the report in Geneva.
The year 2025 marked the fourth consecutive year with widespread glacier loss across all regions, leading to short-term hazards such as flooding, and water insecurity in the long term. Between 2023 and 2025, glaciers lost mass in each reporting year with cumulative global glacier mass loss at 1400 gigatons of water. This is roughly equal to about one third of annual freshwater withdrawals.
"All 19 glacier regions around the globe lost ice; in Central Asia, Iceland, the Russian Arctic, and western Canada and the United States. It was among the three worst years on record," said Wayne Jenkinson, the WMO's Director of Hydrology and Cryosphere, at the conference.
In each of the last five years, National Meteorological and Hydrological Services around the globe have reported record-breaking floods and droughts. Some places have had no recovery time between one event and the next, the report noted.
"Water respects no borders. A river basin's water balance depends on what happens in another country. A glacier's retreat in one country reshapes water availability for populations hundreds of kilometers downstream. This is precisely why we need shared data, shared standards, and shared early warning, the exact function WMO exists to perform," said Saulo. ■

Shortly after 4 pm, for reasons as yet unknown, the aircraft collided with the northern slope in the Fluhalp area near Leukerbad. Members of the public subsequently reported heavy smoke in the region.

The emergency services from the Valais Cantonal Rescue Organisation (KWRO 144), which had been mobilised, immediately made their way to the scene of the accident with three helicopters and two rescue specialists. Ten aircraft crashes in ten years

Sust has launched an investigation to determine the cause of the accident. The Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland (OAG) is conducting the criminal investigation in cooperation with the Valais Cantonal Police. The investigations by the OAG and Sust are being carried out in parallel and in close coordination.
Over the past ten years, there have been nine aviation accidents in Switzerland involving three or more fatalities, excluding the incident in Leukerbad.

Fiji declares HIV emergency as one in 60 adults affected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:50:48 UTC
15:50:48 KST

Fiji has declared a national HIV crisis as sexual transmission and illicit drug use help to spread the virus, now infecting an estimated one in 60 adults in the Pacific nation.
New HIV diagnoses surged to 2,016 cases in 2025 — 16 times the level recorded in 2019, authorities said, vowing a "whole of government" response.
"I am formally declaring a national HIV emergency in Fiji," Health Minister Atonio Lalabalavu told reporters on Wednesday.
"This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent, coordinated response our country now needs."
An estimated one in 60 adults in Fiji have HIV — up from one in 167 five years earlier, the government said.
Two in every 100 pregnant women have the virus. Of the 59 babies born with HIV in 2025, 18 died before reaching their first birthday.
The government said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment, including rapid testing, preventive medication for people at higher risk and harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs.
Fiji is receiving support from Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations.
Among cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and over 42 percent to injecting drug use, according to UNAIDS.
The UN agency welcomed Fiji’s plans to introduce legislation allowing a needle-and-syringe programme.
“Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic,” said Eamonn Murphy, UNAIDS director for Asia and the Pacific.
“Stronger cooperation across the Pacific and sustained international solidarity can reinforce the national effort and help accelerate action.”
HIV transmission began rising around 2019 with the emergence of a group of high-risk injecting drug users, UNAIDS country director Renata Ram told AFP earlier this year.
Fiji and other Pacific islands have served as transit hubs for drugs moving from Latin America and Asia to lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand.
The flow of highly addictive drugs, increased sharply after a lull during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime.
The drugs have increasingly entered domestic Pacific markets, partly because foreign criminal organisations sometimes pay local facilitators with drugs.
