TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Labor on Thursday proposed extending marriage leave for workers from eight days to 14 days, giving newlyweds six additional days of paid leave.
The proposed amendment is part of the government's "New Strategic Approach to Taiwan's Population Policy — Family Support" initiative. The ministry said the measure is intended to give young people more time to prepare for weddings and establish families, per a ministry press release.
The proposal would bring marriage leave for private-sector workers in line with the 14 days available to military personnel, civil servants, and teachers, according to the ministry. The amendment is scheduled to take effect Oct. 1 after the required legal procedures are completed.
The draft amendment has been published on the government's Public Policy Online Participation Platform and is available for public comment. Members of the public can submit opinions during the notice period. The ministry's toll-free 1955 labor consultation hotline is available for questions.
Under the proposed transition rules, workers who registered their marriage before the new system takes effect could still qualify for 14 days of leave if they have not used all eight days under the existing system and remain within the applicable leave period. Under current rules, workers can take marriage leave beginning 10 days before their marriage registration date and within three months afterward, per the press release.
The ministry said employers are required to pay workers their regular wages during marriage leave. To offset the additional cost to companies, employers would be able to apply for a government wage subsidy after paying workers for the six additional days, covering days nine through 14 under the proposed system.
Details of the subsidy and application procedures will be announced when the amended regulations are formally issued.
The ministry said the measure is intended to encourage companies to create workplaces that better support employees who marry and start families. It is also promoting workplace policies covering pregnancy, childbirth, and child-rearing as part of its broader family-support initiative.

She also ordered the Ministry of Economic Affairs to strengthen monitoring of petrochemical products, industrial paper, and steel, and instructed joint price inspection teams to intervene promptly if irregularities emerge.
Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude oil prices remained above NT$3,190 (US$100) per barrel Wednesday. Domestic gasoline and diesel prices rose NT$0.70 and NT$0.60 per liter this week after remaining frozen for six consecutive weeks.
The sustained rise in international oil prices could add to inflationary pressure, with the consumer price index increasing by more than 2% year on year for four consecutive months from May through August, UDN reported. The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics forecasts a 2.07% increase in the CPI this year.
The tax reductions, the 18th round of such measures, will remain in effect through March 2027, per Newtalk. They include exemptions from business tax on imported soybeans, wheat, and corn.
The government will exempt wheat from import tariffs and cut tariffs on butter, baking milk powder, and beef by 50%. It will also reduce the commodity tax on gasoline by NT$3.415 per liter and diesel by NT$1.995 per liter.
Commodity taxes on cement and liquefied petroleum gas will be halved, Newtalk reported. The measures aim to lower operating costs for businesses and limit the impact of global commodity price fluctuations on domestic prices.
The Cabinet said its response to the situation in the Middle East is organized around seven priorities, including stabilizing energy supplies, oil and gas prices, and essential goods, per SET News. Other measures include cutting industrial costs, strengthening price monitoring, maintaining market order, and assisting affected industries.
Cheng said the government will maintain domestic fuel prices at the lowest level among neighboring Asian countries, with CPC absorbing part of international crude oil price increases under a special stabilization mechanism. Household natural gas and LPG sold in cylinders will remain frozen through the end of the year to limit the impact of energy price volatility on households and businesses.

Srinivasan said falling production costs could create opportunities for smaller language communities, allowing them to produce content tailored to their cultures.

Reza Pahlavi accepts Coalition invitation to visit Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:07:18 UTC
15:07:18 KST

Exiled Iranian prince accepts invitation to visit but Coalition says there is no endorsement
In short:
The exiled former crown prince of Iran has accepted a Coalition invitation to visit Australia, telling the ABC he is a "bridge" to democratic elections, not a candidate for leader.
Iran expert Kylie Moore-Gilbert says the Coalition strayed into "choppy territory" by appearing to treat him as Iran's opposition leader.
What's next?
Ted O'Brien says he expects the government to engage with Mr Pahlavi in good faith. No date has been set for the trip.
The exiled former crown prince of Iran, Reza Pahlavi, has accepted a Coalition invitation to visit Australia, insisting he would be a transitional leader if the regime falls rather than a long-term candidate.
This morning, Mr Pahlavi joined a virtual meeting attended by 10 Coalition MPs and senators, including Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien.
Following the meeting, Mr Pahlavi told Radio National Breakfast he did not have personal ambition to lead Iran in the long term.
"My only focus is to be able to be a transitional leader and provide them with a road map to that end," Mr Pahlavi said.
"I'm not here as a candidate. I'm here as a bridge to that destination."
No date has been set for his visit to Australia. Asked when it would happen, Mr Pahlavi said he hoped it would happen soon.
Loading...
Who is Reza Pahlavi?
Mr Pahlavi labelled Iran's rulers a "corrupt, mafia-like dictatorship" that he said was now controlled by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The former crown prince has not lived in Iran for 48 years, having left in 1978 for pilot training in the United States shortly before the Islamic Revolution that ended the rule of his father, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Historians have frequently criticised the shah's monarchy for political repression, corruption and human rights abuses.
Mr Pahlavi has previously said his legitimacy comes from his fellow Iranians.
Speaking to the ABC, the former crown prince said he had "overwhelming support in Iran and within the diaspora" and that being forced into exile had not disconnected him from his compatriots.
"When I called for action inside Iran, millions of people came on the streets chanting my name. This doesn't occur by coincidence," he said.
He has previously advocated for US military intervention and said that regime change in Iran was inevitable.
Warning against treating Pahlavi as main opposition leader
In an earlier statement, Mr O'Brien said the invitation to visit Australia was extended following "significant calls" from Australia's Iranian community.
But Kylie Moore-Gilbert, a research fellow in security studies at Macquarie University, said the Coalition had strayed into "choppy territory" by appearing to treat Mr Pahlavi as the Iranian opposition leader.
Dr Moore-Gilbert said Iranian politics was "extremely complex" given the country's disparate ethnic groupings and the difficulty of talking to people on the ground.
"It did seem as though they were endorsing him as the opposition leader, which I think is problematic given there's a plurality of voices, all of which are opposing the regime," she said.
"If they are wanting to endorse Reza Pahlavi — and I'm not sure that they are — I think it's misguided.
"I think they should be engaging with all opposition groups."
Threats and a 'cult of personality'
Dr Moore-Gilbert, who was detained in Iran for more than two years, said she had previously received death threats, rape threats and other online abuse over her criticism of Mr Pahlavi.
She distinguished between his supporters generally and what she described as a "fanatical" minority, saying the many supporters she knew in Australia were "moderate" people.
But she said a section of Mr Pahlavi's support base had developed what she described as a "cult of personality", with some wanting to restore him as an absolute monarch despite his own stated commitment to democracy.
"Some of his more fanatical supporters … cannot accept anybody critiquing this, cannot accept any discussion or debate, which is obviously not a democratic ethos at all," she said.
"Any attempt at coalition-building between various opposition figures has been thwarted by these extreme individuals who've been targeting and attacking anyone who might look like a competitor to Pahlavi. Or anybody, like myself, who wonders or questions whether it is a truly democratic movement as it says it is."
Mr Pahlavi told Reuters in July he condemned violence by his supporters and that those responsible should face prosecution. Reuters found no evidence he was involved in the incidents it documented.
Responding to Dr Moore-Gilbert's "cult of personality" characterisation, Mr Pahlavi said there were "some extremists here and there" among his supporters, which he said was nothing new.
He said anyone who did not accept the democratic process, or who wanted a system of absolute rule, was "by definition" undemocratic.
Coalition says meeting not an endorsement
Mr O'Brien denied the meeting with Mr Pahlavi amounted to an endorsement and said the Coalition had engaged with other Iranian opposition groups.
"At the moment, because of a very brutal regime, the people of Iran are not empowered. And therefore, voices like Mr Pahlavi's are vitally important for us to listen to and engage," he said.
"Mr Pahlavi himself spoke about the importance of democracy in our meeting today and I'm sure he'll have more to say as time goes on."
Mr O'Brien said the issue "should be a bipartisan matter" and that he expected the government to engage with Mr Pahlavi in good faith if the former crown prince visits Australia.
"We need to be speaking to all voices that have a positive vision for a free Iran," he said.

====================================================================================================

Cuts to income tax: experts back the measures but warn situation in Portugal may worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:06:48 UTC
15:06:48 KST

A cut in income tax and pension bonuses bring some relief amid inflation and clawback measures, but global conditions may yet make matters worse.
This Thursday, the Portuguese government will formally decide, in the Council of Ministers, to grant the bonus for pensioners and a cut in IRS income tax brackets for workers.
Pensioners with pensions of up to 1,611 euros will receive an extraordinary top-up in December, between 100 and 200 euros, totalling 400 million euros.
IRS will be reduced up to the sixth bracket, in an amount of up to 400 million euros. But because of the progressive scale, the higher brackets will also be affected. The measure will be applied from November.
In parliament, Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said the IRS cut is intended to "support the middle class".
"Families can't take any more"
The Portuguese government (the centre-right AD coalition) made these announcements last week, during a debate on a motion of no confidence, which was rejected. Before that, the prime minister defended the cabinet's social and economic policy, including measures in response to rising fuel prices.
The previous day, diesel in Portugal had reached its highest price ever and petrol its highest level since the invasion of Ukraine. This time, the rise was met with protests. In a go-slow march towards Galp's refinery in Sines, placards read "families can't take any more".
Economist João Rodrigues dos Santos regards these measures as legitimate, as a "give-back to those who need it most", but disagrees with the method.
"I consider these to be budgetary policy measures and that they should be more structural in nature, reflected in the State Budget," says the professor who coordinates the academic area of Economics and Management at the European University.
**"**The government surely has good intentions, but I think this may not be the best way to conduct budgetary policy. Public policy cannot depend every year on whether there is money in the coffers or not, can it?" he asks.
Rebate mechanism
And, in fact, there is money. Tax lawyer Tiago Caiado Guerreiro points out that, with prices rising, the state has collected more tax.
**"**The VAT take on fuel goes up as fuel prices rise. Why? The taxable base on which it is levied increases in size," says the tax expert, referring to the consumption tax.
**"**This is just one more reimbursement mechanism, in this case via IRS, with which I could not agree more," argues Tiago Caiado Guerreiro.
"And then the bonus for pensioners is a somewhat political measure, but it is not something that shocks me, given the low pensions that exist in Portugal," the tax lawyer concludes.
João Rodrigues dos Santos also agrees that the state has taken in more VAT revenue from the rise in fuel prices, an amount that, "according to the government, could come to around 700 million euros". But he also recalls the reduction in the Tax on Petroleum Products (ISP).
"It is true that this revenue should be neutralised through cutting ISP, precisely to prevent the state from benefiting fiscally from higher fuel prices," he explains.
Even so, the increase in VAT receipts covers other products beyond fuel.
"Ultimately, if the state collects more revenue because prices have gone up and families are paying more for the same goods and services, it seems legitimate to me that part of that extraordinary fiscal windfall can be returned to taxpayers."
High taxes and many brackets
Both experts agree that taxes are too high in Portugal.
"Anything that serves to lower taxes or put money into people's pockets, I usually agree with," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro.
The tax lawyer argues that IRS "is extremely high in Portugal. In other words, people who work are heavily penalised by taxation".
João Rodrigues dos Santos, for his part, advocates a simplification of the IRS system.
"There could be fewer brackets, with less steep progressivity, because the current setup is absolutely stifling," he argues.
And cutting VAT?
The opposition has been advocating another path: VAT cuts. The Socialist Party (PS, centre-left) is calling for zero VAT on essential goods, and Chega (far right) also says it intends to put forward a proposal along these lines.
But Tiago Caiado Guerreiro warns that such a measure could be difficult to implement.
**"**Technically, cutting VAT is very difficult, because it would be reduced to a lower band, which would mean a loss of revenue that the government would not be able to manage. You cannot bring the rate down from 23% to 22% or 21%, as I saw suggested in some reports; that is not possible," says the tax lawyer, adding that in future this budgetary room for manoeuvre may not exist.
"I think that, given the international circumstances and the rise in the price of oil, economies in Europe and elsewhere in the world will probably start to slow. And the tax take will probably not stay on a permanently upward trajectory."
European Union countries set their VAT rates, but these have to be framed within the EU directive on the tax (source in Portuguese).
"A cut in VAT, for example from the maximum rate to the intermediate rate or even the minimum rate, would depend on authorisation from the European Union," explains João Rodrigues dos Santos, adding that one of the disadvantages of VAT is that it is a non-differentiated tax.
"VAT is a tax that affects everyone in the same way. Those who need more support and those who do not need support."
Nevertheless, this economics professor believes that such a measure could end up being "an inevitability", an exception in a scenario of rising fuel prices that "will necessarily spread to the rest of the economy".
"I would say that a generalised VAT reduction, above all on basic necessities, is not a measure I consider unreasonable. On the contrary, it may well be the most effective measure, because it is across the board and the vast majority of Portuguese people have very low wages," he explains.
"I think this will take years"
Right now, the international climate is not the most promising. Last Thursday, in Frankfurt, the European Central Bank (ECB) once again raised interest rates. At the time, ECB president Christine Lagarde warned of inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East.
The two experts, interviewed by Euronews, are equally pessimistic about the future.
"I do not know whether fuel prices will ever fall back to the levels they were at before the war, given all the instability that exists in the Middle East and other parts of the world," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro, referring to the war in Ukraine and to blockages in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.
"We are in a period of great instability; I do not think this will be resolved quickly. And I never believed this war would end quickly, I think this will take years," he adds.
In fact, the crisis is dragging on. And not only is it dragging on, it is deepening," argues João Rodrigues dos Santos.
The European University professor thinks the government also has this scenario in mind.
"With a budget surplus of more than 2 billion euros, the fact is that this government has remained uncompromising in relation to its strategy. And, from my point of view, it has remained uncompromising because it has always understood that this crisis, which we have now been living through for more than six months, was here to stay."
The economy is growing, but wages are low
In parliament, the Portuguese prime minister said these measures "are only possible thanks to the economic performance of Portugal and the government's sound financial and budgetary management".
Luís Montenegro also described the growth of the Portuguese economy as having "the best economic performance in Europe and the biggest employment growth in Europe".This despite the fact that, according to Eurostat, it was not the country with the strongest growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter, but rather the seventh, together with Cyprus (up 0.8%).
"I think we are in a good phase; we are among the six or seven best in the European Union and that usually does not happen, as you know, we are normally closer to the bottom," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro, highlighting the contribution of some areas, such as tourism.
But the tax lawyer also says this is no reason for excessive optimism.
"We are indeed in a very reasonable period of growth, compared with the European economy, which is rather sluggish. It is one of the slowest-growing economies in the world. So there is no reason to get euphoric about it."
João Rodrigues dos Santos points to the low wages paid in Portugal, which means that tinkering with IRS will not solve families' income problems.
"We must not forget. In Portugal, 75% of those registered with social security have wages of up to 1,000 euros," the professor says.

Iran calls for international engagement with Afghan officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:01:17 UTC
15:01:17 KST

Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Afghanistan on Wednesday (local time), Darzi said that the significant reduction in armed conflict and violence across vast areas of Afghanistan, along with the relative improvement in the security situation—achieved five years after the current authorities came to power—are important gains that must be preserved.
The full text of the letter by the Iranian envoy to the UN is as follows:
In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful
Statement by
H.E. Mr. Gholamhossein Darzi
Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative
of the Islamic Republic of Iran to the United Nations
Before UNSC Briefing on “Situation in Afghanistan
New York, 16 September 2026
Thank you, Mr. President, for convening this meeting.
At the outset, we congratulate Ms. Rabab Fatimah on her appointment as the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of UNAMA
and wish her every success in discharging this important responsibility.
We look forward to further constructive and close cooperation with her.
UNAMA plays a vital and indispensable role in assisting the Afghan people, facilitating dialogue, coordinating international assistance, and promoting a coherent and coordinated international approach to Afghanistan.
We thank the Secretariat and UNAMA for their continued efforts to support the people of Afghanistan.
We thank the briefers for their insightful briefings.
We take note of the Secretary-General’s latest report (S/2026/724), which notes some economic stabilization and efforts by the de facto authorities to maintain governance and economic activity.
At the same time, the report indicates that Afghanistan continues to face serious challenges, including acute humanitarian and economic needs, restrictions affecting women and girls, and the persistent threat of terrorism.
Against this backdrop, I would like to make the following points:
First: Five years after the de facto authorities assumed power, the significant reduction in armed conflict and violence across much of Afghanistan and the relative improvement in the security situation are important gains that must be preserved. However, the terrorist threat remains.
ISIL-K and other extremist groups operating in Afghanistan and the region continue to pose a serious threat to Afghanistan and neighbouring countries.
Addressing this threat requires sustained and strengthened regional cooperation.
The Afghan authorities have a responsibility to prevent their territory from being used to plan or carry out terrorist acts against neighbouring countries, while the international community and countries of the region should support Afghanistan in strengthening its counter-terrorism capacities.
Second: The significant reduction in opium poppy cultivation is also an important achievement with positive global implications.
However, as highlighted in the report, its economic impact on rural communities remains severe.
Sustained investment in alternative livelihoods, rural development, and market access is therefore essential to ensure that these gains are durable.
Third: The humanitarian and economic situation remains deeply concerning.
Declining external assistance, financial and banking constraints, limited investment, and the return of Afghan nationals have placed additional pressure on the country’s economy and public services.
As noted in the report, the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan remained severely underfunded, with only 29.9 per cent ($513 million of the $1.7 billion required) funded.
Humanitarian assistance must therefore be provided on the basis of need and without politicization. Access to food, medicines, health care and other necessities must not be affected by political considerations.
Practical arrangements should also be pursued to facilitate Afghanistan’s access to its financial resources and assets, so that these resources can support the Afghan people and essential economic and public services.
In the meantime, sustainable recovery requires greater focus on trade, investment, employment and economic infrastructure.
Fourth: As a neighbouring country, the Islamic Republic of Iran closely follows developments in Afghanistan.
Our longstanding historical, cultural and human ties, and the direct implications for regional peace and stability, underscore the importance of sustained engagement and cooperation.
Iran has consistently pursued a practical and neighbourly approach.
Despite decades of sanctions and economic pressures, and having recently suffered from the US acts of aggression and maritime blockade, Iran has hosted millions of Afghan nationals and provided them with access to education, health care and employment opportunities.
Iran has also continued to expand economic cooperation with Afghanistan in trade, transit, energy, railways and agriculture.
The further development of trade and transit, including through the capacities of the Port of Chabahar and facilitation for Afghan traders, can provide Afghanistan with greater access to regional and international markets.
Fifth: Continued international engagement with the de facto authorities remains indispensable to advancing stability and addressing Afghanistan’s challenges.
Constructive and principled engagement is also the most effective means of encouraging progress in the protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls and members of ethnic and religious communities.
The Secretary-General’s report underscores the importance of a comprehensive approach based on principled and pragmatic engagement. Constructive dialogue remains essential to addressing humanitarian, economic, counter-narcotics and governance-related challenges.
Finally: The Islamic Republic of Iran reiterates its support for continued dialogue and cooperation among Afghanistan, the countries of the region and the international community, and stands ready to further contribute to regional and bilateral efforts in support of Afghanistan’s stability and sustainable development.
I thank you.
MNA/IRN

Ferry strike called off as Kihnu Veeteed and union reach deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

Ferry strike called off as Kihnu Veeteed and union reach deal
A ferry strike that threatened connections to Estonia's small islands has been called off at the last minute after the Estonian Seamen's Independent Union (EMSA) and ferry operator Kihnu Veeteed reached a collective agreement.
The deal, reached following negotiations EMSA chair Jüri Lember described as "tense," means the strike planned for Friday, September 18, is off and there will be no service disruptions for passengers.
As recently as last week, crews working for Kihnu Veeteed, which connects the islands of Kihnu, Manilaid and Vormsi to the mainland, along with a Saaremaa–Hiiumaa link and a freshwater route to Priisaar on Lake Peipus, were preparing for a strike that would have disrupted services indefinitely. Talks had been stalled since March, and a one-hour warning strike was held on July 26.
EMSA had been seeking 20–30 percent pay rises, while Kihnu Veeteed said its margins were too narrow to meet that. Under the new agreement, employees get an agreed pay scale, options for an additional performance bonus of up to 5 percent, and a rise in the food allowance. From 2028, basic pay should rise in line with growth in Estonia's average gross monthly wage.
"We managed to get a pay scale included, meaning that new employees cannot be hired for a particular position at a rate below the monthly pay level we have agreed on," Lember said. "The most important figure here is certainly the pay for deckhands, which is around €1,650."
Lember said the strike had not been called for its own sake, but was the result of the other party being "not constructive, when specific figures are not discussed at the negotiating table or when the negotiations are simply not conducted in a serious manner."
The new collective agreement will remain in force for three years or until Kihnu Veeteed stops operating its current ferry routes. If a new operator takes over — the state has selected Tuule Liinid OÜ to take over the small-island routes from 2027 — Lember said most of the current vessels and staff will switch over in any case, which he said would be an easier move for employer and employee alike.
EMSA has also proposed concluding a sectoral collective agreement with the national shipowners' association, which, according to Lember, would apply to shipping companies operating ferry routes and regulate working hours and minimum permitted pay levels.
The protracted dispute even led to the formation of a breakaway union, which had been talking to Kihnu Veeteed. Just over half of the line's crew are EMSA members.

Peers call for UK to enact tobacco-style ban on gambling advertising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:00:42 UTC
15:00:42 KST

The UK should introduce a ban on almost all gambling advertising to protect public health, a cross-party group of peers has urged, prompting fury from the lobby group for bookmakers and casinos.
In a 173-page report, the House of Lords liaison committee said the government had been “too passive” in response to an explosion of digital advertising and social media influencers promoting the gambling sector.
British bookmakers, slot machine venues and casinos won £12.6bn from customers in Great Britain last year, while up to 1.4 million people have a gambling problem, according to official statistics.
The report found that a tobacco-style blanket ban on advertising, with carve-outs for the lottery and racecourses, would be the “most effective” way to reduce harms such as financial ruin, relationship breakdown and even suicide.
A ban would likely result in the UK’s gambling sector shrinking, the report acknowledged, but would lead to longer-term economic benefit as money previously spent on gambling is diverted to other parts of the economy.
The report was dismissed as “deeply misguided” by the industry’s lobby group, the Betting & Gaming Council (BGC), which said any such policy could increase harm because it would benefit the illicit market, which would continue to advertise.
Lord Foster, one of the report’s authors, said the illicit market, whose exploitative activities have been documented in Guardian investigations, was a “legitimate concern” and pointed to ongoing efforts by regulators to crack down on rogue sites.
“That should not deflect us from the need to address the harm that is being created by the legal market,” he said, insisting there was a wealth of evidence linking gambling advertising to harm.
Gambling advertising in the UK was liberalised via the 2005 Gambling Act introduced by Tony Blair’s government, a landmark piece of legislation that aimed to regulate the sector but also promote its growth as a legitimate leisure activity that could create jobs and boost the economy.
Before the act, only bingo, the football pools and lotteries, including the National Lottery, were allowed to advertise on television.
The volume of gambling advertising has ballooned since then, with annual spend by the industry reaching £2bn in 2024, according to estimates.
In contrast to Blair, Andy Burnham has been a vocal critic of the gambling industry and recently moved to give councils more power to block new betting shops and “slot farms” opening up on high streets.
As mayor of Greater Manchester, he expressed a desire to “relegate gambling sponsorship of sport to the history books”.
The BGC pointed to voluntary measures already taken by the industry, including “whistle to whistle” ban that saw its members agree not to advertise during the course of a televised sports fixture.
The trade body has also estimated that half of the money spent on advertising by gambling firms now comes from a fast-growing illicit market not subject to the same controls as licensed operators.
Grainne Hurst, the BGC chief executive, said:“A blanket advertising ban would remove a key competitive advantage of being licensed and regulated while doing nothing to stop illegal operators targeting British consumers.”
The Guardian ceased accepting advertising from gambling companies, excluding the National Lottery, in 2024.

====================================================================================================

Access-to-nature crisis ‘on par with that of Victorian Britain’s filthy air’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:00:41 UTC
15:00:41 KST

Nearly half of all parliamentary constituencies in England have low access to nature despite a government target to ensure everyone is within a 15-minute walk from a green or blue space, new research reveals.
The analysis by the Wildlife Trusts comes as the charity presents a green paper to ministers in an attempt to speed up Labour’s manifesto promise to improve access to nature and promote biodiversity.
The research from the Wildlife Trusts and Liberal and Democrats for Nature and Climate (LDNC) has found that 238 English parliamentary constituencies (44% of the total) have 20% or more local properties situated more than 15 minutes’ walk from green or blue space (the latter an area with water, such as a river, canal, lake, pond, sea or other waterfront). Seven of the 10 most economically deprived constituencies had low access to nature.
After a spring and summer of extreme heat across England, when some cities and towns saw temperatures of 38C, the Wildlife Trusts said there was increased need for cool, shady and nature-rich spaces. It is seeking a meeting with ministers to present its green paper.
Matthew Browne, the head of public affairs at the Wildlife Trusts, said: “This research reveals stark inequalities in access to nature across England, with direct parallels between economic and nature deprivation.
“Coupled with the extreme heat we’re experiencing in urban areas, this access crisis is on a par with that of Victorian Britain, when filthy air and water led to a programme of public park-building for the benefit of all. In facing today’s challenges, we need to embrace this same level of urgency once more, utilising existing legislation so that real change can be felt quickly in local communities.”
Despite promises by ministers, the government has yet to publish its access to nature green paper. Critics say ministers need to act with more urgency.
The Wildlife Trusts is calling for the government to:
- 
  Make it more affordable for local authorities to use compulsory purchase powers for land purchase.
- 
  Establish a community right to buy land for nature access.
- 
  Treat nature as essential infrastructure, and free up capital funds to pay for the ongoing maintenance of natural spaces.
- 
  Make it mandatory for developers to create climate- and nature-friendly housing estates.
- 
  Make access to major rivers, especially those in urban areas, a statutory right.
The trusts published the results of a public consultation with 5,000 people, in which they described how they sought out cool spaces in nature during the summer heatwaves.
One contributor said: “Walking in my local woods in heatwaves is cooling. The physical benefits of a brisk, daily walk are well known, and I feel them.”
Another said: “I have a long-term health condition which affects my mobility and mental health, particularly during periods of extreme heat. Access to natural spaces is incredibly important to me.”
Dom Higgins, the head of health and education at the Wildlife Trusts, said there was a mountain of research and evidence from the public that showed the impact of nature on our physical and mental health. He said in an age of climate-driven extreme weather events and the growing health implications, access to nearby healthy natural spaces should be the right of every citizen.
“Natural spaces in our cities can literally save lives, by keeping the air cooler and cleaner and reducing the strain on our hearts and lungs,” he said. “The blood pressure of pregnant women is lower when they live near an accessible park or garden, and young children who spend longer in nature-rich spaces have healthier lives.
“Yet, despite the growing body of scientific evidence, having access to the natural world in whatever form that takes – from a river walk to a pocket park in an urban neighbourhood – is still not equal across the UK.”
In the spring of last year, the Department for Environment Food and Rural affairs held workshops with experts to inform proposals to increase access to nature, in advance of a promised green paper last autumn. But a year on, the government has failed to deliver the paper.
“The Wildlife Trusts don’t want the public to have to wait any longer,” the report said. “Access to nature is not a ‘nice to have’, it is a necessity. The time is ripe for action.”
A government spokesperson said: “This government is focused on the things that matter most to the British public, including restoring nature so that we have pride in local communities and access to green spaces.
“We are increasing access to nature and the countryside, delivering nine new National River Walks, a Coast-to-Coast route in the North of England and the 2,700 mile King Charles III England Coast Path.”

The "Canada effect": Which European companies could benefit from closer ties?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

The US trade war is pushing Canada towards Europe. Defence, aerospace and industrial technology are where European companies may gain first.
The US-Canada trade war is pushing Ottawa closer to the European Union. For European companies, that shift is already creating opportunities in defence, aerospace and industrial technology.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got a standing ovation in Strasbourg on Wednesday, not something that happens often to a foreign prime minister in the European Parliament.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen later gave that welcome a political meaning.
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” she said during the annual State of the Union address.
Von der Leyen described the broader relationship as an “Alliance for the Future”, covering defence, energy, technology, critical minerals and the Arctic.
What does an "associate member" mean?
There is no established “associate member” category in the EU treaties and no template Canada can simply join.
Creating one would require agreement among member states and complex legal negotiations.
Ten, including France and Italy, have yet to ratify Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) fully, almost a decade after the trade agreement between Canada and the European Union was signed.
Carney has also said Canada is not seeking full EU membership. Ottawa instead wants a “unique alliance” that extends beyond a conventional free-trade deal.
For now, the proposal is more political signal than legal blueprint.
However, recent contracts show that the commercial relationship is already moving ahead.
EU–Canada trade already has a head start
Trade in goods and services between the two sides has grown by more than 81% since 2016, the year before the CETA took provisional effect, reaching just over €130 billion in 2025, according to the Council of the EU.
EU goods exports to Canada amounted to €48.9 billion. Services exports added another €29.4 billion.
Germany shipped roughly €12 billion of goods to Canada last year. Italy followed at €6.3 billion, ahead of France at €4.4 billion.
Machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and transport equipment dominate European sales to Canada.
European machinery sales to Canada hit a record €9.5 billion last year. Electrical equipment climbed from €2 billion in 2022 to €3.3 billion, and cars rose from €2.9 billion to €4.4 billion over the same period.
Aerospace moved hardest of all. Sales of powered aircraft went from €449 million in 2022 to €1.2 billion last year.
European defence companies stand to gain
Defence provides the clearest evidence that Canada is looking beyond its traditional American suppliers.
In July, Ottawa selected Germany's TKMS AG & Co. KGaA, the naval shipbuilder spun off from Thyssenkrupp AG last October, as preferred supplier for up to 12 new submarines.
While the final contract has not been signed yet, the decision places a European company at the centre of one of Canada's largest military procurement programmes.
Sweden’s Saab has also gained ground. Ottawa selected the company as its preferred supplier for six GlobalEye surveillance aircraft, ahead of alternatives from Boeing and L3Harris.
The GlobalEye is built on business jets made by Canada's Bombardier Inc. and Saab has offered to carry out much of the work in Canada, combining European sensors and mission systems with Canadian airframes.
The aircraft use jets produced by Canada’s Bombardier. Saab has offered to complete much of the work in Canada, combining European technology with Canadian manufacturing.
Canada also became the first non-European country admitted to procurement under the EU's SAFE defence programme in June.
That gives Canadian manufacturers access to joint European purchasing, and it makes it easier for European defence groups to build supply chains that include Canadian firms.
Airbus and Siemens already have a strong foothold
The opportunity extends beyond military equipment. Air Canada has placed a firm order with Airbus for eight A350-1000 aircraft.
The government has also contracted Airbus for four new A330 tankers plus five conversions, part of a C$3.6 billion (€2.2bn) programme whose first new-build aircraft flew in July.
Ottawa has committed a further C$1.5 billion (€930mn) to keeping the fleet in the air.
Germany’s Siemens is investing C$150 million (€97 million) over five years in a Canadian research centre for AI-powered battery manufacturing.
French groups Keolis, Systra and SNCF Voyageurs are also part of the Cadence consortium selected in 2025 to develop Alto, the planned high-speed railway between Toronto and Quebec City. Canada has allocated about €2.4 billion to the project’s development phase.
Critical minerals could become the next opportunity
Canada’s reserves of nickel, lithium, copper and other critical minerals offer another potential area of cooperation.
Europe wants to reduce its dependence on concentrated and politically risky suppliers.
Canada wants more investment, processing capacity and customers outside the United States.
In March, the European Investment Bank and the Canadian government signed a letter of intent to explore financing for Canadian critical-minerals projects.
The agreement does not yet contain financial commitments.
However, it could eventually support European companies involved in mining technology, processing, recycling and battery production.
The price of deeper European access
CETA had eliminated 99% of tariff lines by 2024. A new alliance would therefore need to offer more than another reduction in customs duties.
The next gains would probably come from government procurement, investment, digital trade, professional mobility and the mutual recognition of standards.
Greater access could also require Canada to align some of its rules with the EU in the sectors covered by any future agreement.
However, it is too early to assume that Canada would adopt European rules on everything from agriculture to data protection. That will depend on what “associate membership” eventually means.
Angelo Katsoras, a geopolitical analyst at National Bank of Canada, said in an August note that Brussels is “increasingly using procurement rules, subsidies, tariffs and local content requirements to encourage more manufacturing within Europe”.
That could create difficulties for Canadian companies trying to enter the European market.
“Diversifying trade beyond the United States to regions such as the EU will likely be more challenging than many people anticipate,” Katsoras said.
The same logic applies in the opposite direction. European companies are more likely to succeed in Canada when they invest locally rather than rely entirely on exports.
Can Europe replace the United States?
The short answer is no.
The US absorbed 71.7% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025. The EU, by comparison, represented 8.7% of Canada’s total trade in goods.
Canada cannot quickly replace the pipelines, railways, factories and cross-border supply chains built around its southern neighbour.
The more realistic outcome is a gradual redistribution of investment and government contracts.
Defence and rail can move first because governments choose the suppliers. Critical minerals, battery technology and energy infrastructure could follow as financing and supply chains develop.
Canada’s European pivot is therefore less an economic divorce from the United States than a decision to stop relying on a single partner.
For European companies, the biggest winners will not necessarily be those exporting the most.
They will be the groups prepared to turn European technology into Canadian production, investment and jobs.

OpenAI discloses new 'concerning' behavior

OpenAI discloses new 'concerning' behavior
September 17, 2026
OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, revealed on Wednesday that it has detected new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) has behaved in "unexpected or concerning" ways.
The developer has conducted several behavioral tests on AI models, and according to them, some models made significant efforts to "cheat." In one specific case, it attempted to upload files to the internet that it had created itself, only to cite them later and present them as reliable sources in its responses. In another case, a model, after failing to find the requested information, fabricated it and attempted to conceal the fact that it had done so.
OpenAI also identified a problem related to instructions concerning "roles and identities" that its software occasionally left for itself.
These disclosures are part of a new approach by OpenAI, where it claims it is now focused on making such findings transparent, especially in cases where AI behaves in unexpected ways or pursues objectives different from those of human users.
Is AI a threat?
The ChatGPT developer pledged to provide greater transparency regarding its testing procedures after its software independently escaped a secure sandbox and hacked into systems belonging to the artificial intelligence company Hugging Face. The reason the software moved to bypass Hugging Face's security during the cyberattack was that it believed it would find answers to a test it had been assigned.
During the attack, AI agents exploited software vulnerabilities and coordinated with one another. The hacking incident and other similar events have fueled concerns that AI systems are becoming increasingly advanced and could eventually escape human control.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also recently supported proposals to slow down the development of the technology and introduce greater regulation.
While noting that these concerns may be justified, researchers have also questioned whether this is part of a diversion tactic to drum up investment and distract from the environmental damage AI data centers are currently causing.

World’s water cycle ‘becoming more unpredictable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:57:08 UTC
14:57:08 KST

(AFP Photo)
The planet’s water cycle is becoming increasingly erratic, swinging between too little and too much, the United Nations warned on Sept. 17, with an unprecedented El Nino expected to exacerbate the long-term trend.
Last year was among the driest for the world’s rivers in over three decades, the U.N.’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in a report.
In 2025, one of the warmest years on record, glaciers also shrank across all regions, even as groundwater levels in many parts of the world are in multi-year decline, it found.
Overall, the WMO’s annual State of Global Water Resources report showed that the Earth’s freshwater storage, the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation and ice and snow, continued a decade-long decline.
Some elements of the water cycle change rapidly, like precipitation, river flow and soil moisture, responding to weather within days or weeks.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo voiced particular concern about the decline in “slow reserves,” like groundwater and glaciers, which she said had traditionally served as the planet’s “savings account.”
They have served as “a buffer that absorbs bad years so that a single drought or a single dry season does not translate directly into a water crisis,” she told reporters.
Now, “we are depleting that savings account,” she warned. “We are spending our reserves.”
Glaciers have also been shrinking at a precipitous rate, with 2025 marking the fourth consecutive year where they shed significant ice mass across all regions.
Between 2023 and 2025, the report estimated that glaciers lost a cumulative global glacier mass of 1,400 giga tons of water, roughly equal to the water required to fill 560 million Olympic-sized swimming pools, or about a third of the world’s annual freshwater withdrawals.
“Groundwater tells a similar story: Nearly two-thirds of monitored wells worldwide showed conditions outside the historical norm in 2025,” Saulo said.
She highlighted that this was happening in parallel with “more water-related disasters.”
In particular, she pointed to the current El Nino pattern, which is expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
“The strengthening El Nino will increase the risk of drought in some areas, and flooding in others,” Saulo cautioned.
Already before El Nino hit, rivers worldwide were showing “abnormal” flows, WMO said, with 2025 among the three driest years for rivers in 35 years.
For a seventh year in a row, the number of river basins globally experiencing “normal” conditions were in a clear minority in 2025.
Only around 36 percent saw normal flows, while an equal percentage saw below-normal discharge conditions and 21 percent were above normal, the report found.

What are the world’s biggest AI companies and how much are they worth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:55:22 UTC
14:55:22 KST

What are the world’s biggest AI companies and how much are they worth?
From Nvidia and OpenAI to Anthropic and xAI, we break down the companies driving the AI boom and how much they are worth.
A renewed debate has emerged over who should control the development of artificial intelligence (AI).
The latest dispute follows an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has argued that the development of increasingly powerful AI systems needs to slow down, calling for greater regulation.
US President Donald Trump pushed back, writing on Truth Social that the US already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies, framing safety concerns as a conspiracy that only benefits China. He went on to say that whoever wins the AI race wins outright.
As states grapple with how to regulate an industry developing at an unprecedented pace, Al Jazeera unpacks the companies driving the AI race and the trillions of dollars behind them.
Who is who in AI?
Chatbots and large language models are only the visible tip of the AI industry. Beneath them sits a much larger ecosystem of hardware, infrastructure, and software.
These companies can be broadly grouped into three categories:
Hardware
At the foundation of the AI industry are the companies that design and manufacture the physical chips AI runs on, along with the equipment that keeps data centres powered and cooled.
These include:
- Chip designers such as Nvidia, Marvell, AMD, Broadcom, and Intel.
- Chip makers like TSMC, which physically manufacture the designs.
- Infrastructure firms such as Arista Networks, Vertiv, and Eaton, which supply the power, cooling, and networking equipment data centres depend on.
Cloud and compute
These are the companies that turn raw chips into usable computing power, delivering the storage and processing capacity that AI systems run on.
These include:
- Hyperscalers, including Alphabet (Google Cloud), Microsoft (Azure), Amazon (AWS) and Oracle, which operate large-scale cloud infrastructure, storing data and delivering networking globally.
- Neoclouds, such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius, and Nscale, a newer wave of specialised providers built to supply the enormous computing power needed to train AI models.
Software and applications
These are the companies that create the AI products people and businesses actually use.
These include:
- Frontier AI labs, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google DeepMind and Meta AI develop large language models, with many also building their own compute infrastructure.
- Enterprise AI companies, such as Palantir, ServiceNow, Salesforce, and Snowflake, apply AI to automate business operations.
How much are AI companies worth?
The 10 largest public companies operating in the AI space – spanning AI chips, cloud infrastructure, and AI-driven software and services – have a combined market capitalisation of at least $25 trillion.
That’s bigger than the gross domestic product (GDP) of every country except the United States, and larger than the entire Chinese economy.
The graphic below shows the 20 most valuable public companies with direct exposure to AI, ranked by market capitalisation.
Nvidia is the largest AI-focused public company, with a market capitalisation of roughly $5.1 trillion as of mid-September 2026. It designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and AI accelerators – hardware components in a chip that speed up AI workloads – that power leading AI models. It makes its money by selling these chips to hyperscalers and AI companies.
Apple, while primarily a hardware company, has invested heavily in on-device AI features and its market cap of $4.86 trillion makes it one of the most valuable companies with any AI exposure. Its main AI product, Siri AI, launched in 2026 and runs on Google’s Gemini models under a licensing deal.
Taiwan Semiconductor (TSMC) is the world’s largest chip manufacturer, with a market cap of $1.9 trillion. It makes the most advanced chips, designed by the likes of Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD. It makes its money by manufacturing these chips at enormous scale, and currently controls over 70 percent of the global foundry market.
Additionally, several private AI companies are valued in the billions of dollars, with some expected to go public in the coming months.
Anthropic, valued at about $965bn (May 2026), develops the Claude family of AI models. The company filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June 2026 to sell stocks publicly, and is reportedly targeting a listing as early as October 2026.
OpenAI, valued at about $852bn, develops the GPT models behind ChatGPT. OpenAI filed for an IPO in June 2026, but is now reportedly leaning toward a 2027 listing.
xAI, now merged into SpaceX, develops the Grok family of AI models. At the time of the February 2026 merger, xAI alone was valued at about $250bn.

Labor unveils migration cuts targeting students, backpackers and overstayers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:49:10 UTC
14:49:10 KST

Labor tightens visa rules as Tony Burke vows migration targets will be met
In short:
Labor is tightening visa rules for international students and backpackers, while increasing efforts to remove overstayers as it seeks greater control over migration.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said housing pressures mean net overseas migration forecasts are now considered a target that must be met.
What’s next?
Labor will implement changes that can be made under existing powers but still wants a parliamentary path for further reforms targeting student arrivals and weak protection visa claims.
Australia will crack down on visa overstayers, stop international students from bringing family and limit the stay of backpackers under a series of changes to drive down migration.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has outlined a raft of changes he said would restore the "integrity" of the migration program and give the federal government more "control" over the demand-driven components of the system.
In a speech at the National Press Club (NPC) in Canberra on Thursday Mr Burke described the overhaul as the "next stage" of policies designed to deliver the net overseas migration (NOM) figures in the budget of 245,000 this year and 225,000 next financial year.
He confirmed the government now considered these forecasts a target to meet due to the "challenges" Australia was having with housing.
Net overseas migration fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released today.
Mr Burke declared claims that Australia was a country of mass migration were "absurd" and warned deeper cuts to the NOM — as flagged by opposition parties — would destroy the economy.
He said Labor's changes amounted to a "relatively simple proposition".
"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa," he said.
"If you want to come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa.
"And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia."
Labor's announcement comes as One Nation unveiled plans to push the country into negative NOM for three years and then 130,000 after that, while the Coalition is finalising plans for a policy expected to target between 150,000 to 170,000 people.
Asked how he would win the case with the public that the government's higher target was the right thing to do, Mr Burke said because the "lower levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy".
In addition to immediate visa rule changes, Mr Burke flagged further areas Labor would like to legislate but could not do without the support of the parliament, including limiting unrealistic applications for asylum.
But he said he would not blame this limitation for any failure to achieve the government's NOM target because overshooting the number "won't happen".
Mr Burke also criticised One Nation's policy of preventing skilled migrants from bringing their spouses and children to Australia, arguing about half of all doctors and construction workers and two thirds of nurses came to the country with family.
"Imagine half of the construction workers who we have to build the houses that we need, not coming," he said.
"Imagine two-thirds of the people who we rely on in aged care or nursing not coming."
Housing and lack of control among problems with current system
Mr Burke said a key problem with Australia's current migration program was that too much of it was demand driven.
He said Australians wanted the government to be able to take a "higher level of control" over different parts of the system.
Mr Burke also identified "visa hopping" as an issue related to individuals who would "never" meet the qualifications to become a permanent resident.
"(They) effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.
Mr Burke said migration needed to slow enough for housing supply to "catch up", but blamed falling household sizes and other issues for the shortage of homes in Australia.
"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.
"But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."
Changes to skilled work visas
Among the changes flagged in Mr Burke's speech was a redesign of the points test to increase the economic value of skilled permanent migration, with housing construction trades to receive the same recognition as a university qualification.
Mr Burke also announced Ministerial Direction 119 would be changed to give processing priority to construction, healthcare, agriculture, fisheries and teaching after business backlash to an earlier decision.
In July, he had issued a sweeping directive pushing skilled visa applications, lodged offshore, to the back of the queue.
The change meant visa processing times for visas blew out from a few days to more than a year in some cases.
Backpacker ballot for second and third year stays
Mr Burke unveiled a dramatic overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker program, also known as backpackers.
After a months-long go slow on applications, processing will return to the previous faster pace for countries whose schemes require regional work to qualify for a second or third year of stay.
However, a ballot system would be introduced to limit the number of backpackers who are able to stay in Australia beyond one year.
Eligibility for a second year stay will be capped at 45,000 places and applicants would still need to complete 88 days of regional work before entering the ballot.
For the third year, the ballot would be restricted to just 5,000 places with a six-month regional work requirement to qualify.
Last year about 57,000 backpackers stayed in Australia for a second year and about 31,000 did a third year.
Mr Burke said not everybody would get to stay in Australia beyond the first-year because the government needed to have "some control and certainty of what those numbers are".
UK applications would be excluded from the faster processing because the scheme does not have a regional work requirement and is part of the UK, Australia free trade agreement.
The number of UK backpackers in Australia has risen sharply since the FTA took effect during the pandemic when there were about 17,000 people to now just under 80,000.
"It's a level of growth that means we are just, at the moment, going to continue to be processing that one slowly," Mr Burke said.
Labor to tackle international student 'visa hopping'
Another major change impacts international students, who would largely no longer be able to attach family members to their visas.
Existing families already in Australia would not be separated, and exceptions would continue for Pacific and ASEAN nationals and certain courses, such as PhDs.
To tackle "visa hopping" students who wanted to transfer courses would have to apply for a new visa.
Meanwhile international students who complete from a course would only be able to move into a new course of a higher qualification level.
For example, Mr Burke said a bachelor's degree graduate could apply for a master's course.
"To hop around, up and down, to different institutions, and claim that what is actually just seeking a migration outcome as part of Australia's export of international education will come to an end as a model," he said.
Mr Burke also flagged changes to visitor visas so they would all generally carry a "no further stay" condition.
He said this would prevent people from arriving as visitors and then applying onshore for another visa and moving onto a bridging visa.
Crackdown on visa overstayers
In a section of his speech about who would be required to leave Australia, Mr Burke announced a crackdown on migration agents encouraging baseless claims.
The code governing this sector would be changed so agents could be sanctioned or deregistered for encouraging clients to lodge "non-meritorious" claims.
"We cannot have people with some sort of official, formal status, using that official formal status to encourage people to make something which, by any definition, is an unacceptable abuse of the system,"
He also announced the government would increase its capacity to detain and remove people who remain in Australia after their visas expired.
The extra resources included 100 additional compliance officers and 250 new detention beds.
The government is also examining if the former quarantine facility in Melbourne could also be repurposed.
Mr Burke said he wanted to restore a pre-2015 deterrent where detention was used to influence behaviour and encourage visa overstayers to leave.
"When people had overstayed a visa, we would bring people into detention centres, give them a bridging visa, tell them to leave," he said.
"If they hadn't left, you'd bring them into the detention centre, and within a few weeks they'd organise their own flight and leave."
Mr Burke said the "behavioural change" was "actually the biggest outcome".
Burke flags legislation wish list
Mr Burke outlined two gaps in the migration package he said would require legislation to implement, noting Labor at this stage did not have a likely pathway through the parliament for new laws.
The first would be the creation of an expression of interest mechanism that would allow government to control student arrivals rather than simply processing demand.
Mr Burke said this would directly address the broader "demand driven" problem but could not happen without legislation.
The second area to tackle would be disingenuous protection visa claims.
Mr Burke said he wanted changes aimed at people who lodge weak asylum claims after exhausting other visa pathways in order to remain in Australia during lengthy review and court processes.
"That's not a legitimate reason for the protection system," he said.
"It actually holds up the processing of the legitimate claims."
He revealed applicants from countries where more than 85 per cent of protection applications fail accounted for about 80 per cent of the processing caseload.
Mr Burke said the reason Labor would not simply introduce its preferred migration legislation and try to negotiate Coalition or crossbench support was because it would immediately cause people to exploit migration pathways before the laws passed.
"If people see something you're doing that you're closing down a visa-hopping process, and the legislation is then before, you'll get a behavioural change completely against the national interest that would happen immediately," he said.
Burke hits out at 'absurd' migration arguments
Mr Burke made the case against what he said were a series of "absurd" claims, including that Australia was a country of "mass migration".
He said the country was instead on track to have 700,000 fewer people in 2030-31 than had been forecast prior to the pandemic.
Mr Burke described Australia's migration peak post-COVID as "too high" but argued the country was now 47 per cent lower.
Mr Burke said migration was "critical" to the economies of the regions and cities, defending foreign students as an important job creator.
"For all the talk about student visas, it is also the case that there are people who work and have jobs in Australia as a result of international education being an incredibly important export," he said.
"Drastic cuts, wherever you make them, hurt the economy in every part, in every area."
On Australia's need for extra housing, Mr Burke said in both Sydney and Melbourne almost two-thirds of plasterers were born overseas.
"It's pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved," he said.
"We need immigration."
Mr Burke said the "silliest of all" the arguments made about migration was the "endless refrain" that Australia was "bringing in yoga teachers and not construction workers".
He said under Labor there had been 15,000 construction workers enter Australia and "zero" yoga teachers.
Mr Burke said yoga teaching had been added on the migration skills list under the former Coalition government in a deal with India.

Russia’s first parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine begins tomorrow, with its only anti-war party barred and genuine competition all but eliminated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:40:12 UTC
14:40:12 KST

Russia’s first parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine begins tomorrow, with its only anti-war party barred and genuine competition all but eliminated
Voting for a new Russian parliament begins tomorrow. The State Duma elections will run for three days, from September 18 to 20. This will be the first Duma election since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine. But the candidates are largely the same: More than 70% of current lawmakers are seeking another term. Voters will elect 450 State Duma members: 225 through party-list voting and 225 from single-member districts, where they choose a specific candidate. As Meduza reported several months ago, the authorities intend to ensure there is no genuine competition in these elections.
Pro-government pollsters claim United Russia’s support is higher than it was in 2021. A week before voting begins, FOM and VTsIOM put the party’s support at 33–37%, compared with 29% before the last election, and predicted that it would win 47–53% of the vote. In 2021, pollsters predicted 41–42% for United Russia, but its official result was 50%. If United Russia improves on that result now — amid the war, escalating repression, and economic problems — it will show that the authorities have “complete control over the vote” in Russia, according to Faridaily.
Yabloko, the only anti-war party, was barred from the elections. The Central Election Commission initially registered Yabloko’s party list, but two weeks later — amid a surge of interest in the party — the Supreme Court disqualified it on absurd grounds. Courts also began removing Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts from the ballot. In some regions, however, other strong challengers to United Russia candidates were also disqualified. There is some good news: The pressure on Yabloko has shown that the party has support among young people.
With no better option, voters have begun taking a closer look at New People. The party is a Kremlin project designed to appeal to liberal voters. It has cultivated a reputation for opposing government bans but does not cross the authorities’ red lines on crucial issues such as support for the war. As political competition has been increasingly eliminated, some young and protest-minded voters have come to see New People as an acceptable alternative to United Russia and the old parties of the Kremlin-tolerated “systemic opposition.” VTsIOM predicts that New People will compete with the Liberal Democratic Party for third place in the elections.
“Undesirable” candidates were disqualified en masse over posts about Navalny. The scheme works like this: Old posts mentioning Alexey Navalny or his organizations suddenly surface on a candidate’s social media accounts. The candidate is fined for displaying “extremist symbols” and barred from running in elections for another year. The first person targeted under this scheme was Boris Nadezhdin, the only anti-war candidate in the 2024 presidential election. He left Russia because of pressure that began ahead of the State Duma elections.
The election debates became a farce. Television channels are required to give candidates free airtime for debates. But Russia has long lacked a culture of political debate — Vladimir Putin has not participated in a single debate during his 26 years in power — and this was particularly evident ahead of the current elections. Candidates from United Russia and other Kremlin-tolerated parties either skipped the debates entirely or attended but remained silent. The channels sometimes cut away from the debates to show Putin or Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
The opposition has proposed several protest-voting strategies. In today’s Russia, elections remain one of the few legal ways to express dissent. The disqualification of candidates the authorities deem unacceptable and vote rigging have narrowed the space for such protest, but it still exists. Here is how different groups within the Russian opposition recommend using it:
- Spoil the ballot. Yabloko is promoting this approach. The party is urging its supporters to spoil their ballots in the party-list vote. In single-member districts, they should vote for Yabloko candidates where any remain. Where there are none, they should spoil those ballots too.
- Vote against United Russia. This is the strategy proposed by Maxim Katz and Yulia Navalnaya. In the party-list vote, they recommend choosing any party except United Russia. In single-member districts, they suggest voting for the strongest challenger to the United Russia candidate. Yabloko has openly criticized this approach.
- Go to polling stations at noon. Ilya Yashin and Maxim Reznik argue that this will allow people to protest the war and the current government legally. Yashin is urging people to come at noon and vote against United Russia, while Reznik offers no guidance on how to vote.
- Do not vote for anyone who supports the war. This is the Russian Anti-War Committee’s only recommendation. Beyond that, the committee considers it unnecessary to prescribe a specific tactic, such as spoiling the ballot, supporting United Russia’s opponents, or going to the polls at noon.
- Stay home and do not vote for anyone. Garry Kasparov, among others, is calling for a boycott. “Calling on people to participate in these ‘elections,’ or going to vote in them yourself, means voluntarily taking part in a political spectacle,” the opposition politician said.
Should we expect street protests? It’s unclear. The most visible protest action may be “Noon for Peace,” proposed by Ilya Yashin and several other opposition figures. The action requires people to show up at polling stations and could provide a measure of the extent of public discontent in Russia. But it is too early to judge how many people will heed Yashin’s call. Meanwhile, the Russian authorities are preparing for possible protests outside polling stations abroad: they have already asked that rallies near Russian embassies in various countries be banned during the State Duma elections.

Associate Membership – Appreciated in Canada; a Non-Starter in Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:40:00 UTC
14:40:00 KST

On Wednesday, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pitched the idea of working towards welcoming Canada as a first “associate member” of the European Union.
The announcement – presented to great fanfare – will ring a bell in Kyiv, where German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently proposed the “associate membership” label as a special membership track for Ukraine. Among other provisions, this would allow Ukraine to participate in EU Council formations and would bring it under the EU’s security umbrella (Article 42.7 TEU).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Both offers show the EU is increasingly seeking concepts below the level of fully fledged Union membership and reflect a normative discussion about the closer integration of non-EU members – bearing in mind that the bloc has not really been a champion in this respect over the past decade. After the negative referendum in Iceland, the EU is in desperate need of a more positive integration narrative. Although actual membership for Canada is, for various reasons, out of the question.
For Canadians, admission to the European Union is out of the question. It would require implementing the entirety of the EU rulebook, becoming part of its structures and entering the Internal Market. And since it is clearly not a European country, full membership is prevented by the EU Treaties.
At Least 10 Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russian Attack Injures 16, Including Two Children
Associate membership should rather be seen as a normative idea to bind the European Union and Canada closer together. It implies building upon the CETA trade agreement but also increasing the security partnership and people-to-people contact below administration level – including participation in EU programmes like Erasmus+ and Horizon.
This would go some way in fulfilling Carney’s now-trademark vision for cooperation between middle powers and, crucially, would paint the EU as an attractive partner. This latter objective is critical, in light of Iceland’s rejection and an enlargement process that seems intractably hamstrung by the reluctance of a few EU countries to open up the fold. Hence von der Leyen presented yet another variation on membership-lite – a PR win, if only they could pull it off.
Yet it is precisely this added value conferred by “associate membership” that Ukraine takes issue with. Because while Ottawa might read opportunity, Kyiv sees a rebuff. Ukraine is not seeking an added-value partnership; it wants credible security guarantees that can finally wrench it away from Russia’s sphere of political influence.
As such, associate membership is only a half-baked proposition compared to full integration into the European Union. Kyiv will take great interest in Canada’s case, given the security provisions it receives from its North American partner. But there is no question that it will accept a similar arrangement.
Nothing short of full membership – including full access to the Single Market and credible security guarantees within the EU framework – will suffice. Von der Leyen’s SOTEU surprise has only muddied the waters.
Linn Selle is head of the Europe Center at the German Council of Foreign Relations (DGAP), a think tank that is currently undertaking the series “The Future Shape of Europe” to inform and inspire the debate about EU enlargement and structural reform to the EU’s inner workings.
