Rachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:00:39 UTC
14:00:39 KST

Yesterday’s lunch and this week’s recipe is thanks to my friend, the designer Jake Tilson, who gave me a pristine 1977 edition of The Talisman Italian Cook Book. With a cover of red, white and green stripes cover that makes me think as much of seaside rock as Italy’s national colours, the edition was part of the 24th printing of the US translation of Il Talismano della Felicità (The Talisman of Happiness), by Ada Boni. First published in 1950, the abridged translation was sold as a complete guide to Italian cookery, covering all notable dishes. Well, on the cover at least; inside, the introduction is more realistic, warning the reader that, “to criticise the writer [Boni] or translator [Mrs Matilde La Rosa] for failing to include certain dishes is useless”, because no living man or woman can be acquainted with all the variety of dishes of a such variegated country.
The introduction, by a man called Mario A Pei, goes on to explain that the variety of dishes mirrors the wide dialectical array in Italy at the time (1950); its diversity of speech, customs, costumes, psychology and general world outlook. In the next sentence, he notes that this variety was undoubtedly a very bad thing from the standpoint of national unity and progress (the professor and polyglot was an ardent supporter of European fascism and uniting humans under one language). Not that you would guess that from his following sentence: “Variety is the spice of life.” I regretted reading his introduction, and also telling an Italian friend, who said, laughing: “You don’t know the half of it”, in reference to my romanticism about the original Talismano, which may be great, but also (in her opinion) endorses a Stepford Wives fantasy of womanhood; a journey with Boni as patient guide.
I don’t regret making the recipe from page 161 for rice with aubergine, however, which I have adapted for variety’s sake. This bake is good when made with tinned tomatoes, but fresh ones bring a brighter burst of flavour. Ideally, try to get a mix of varieties – a few sweet cherries, a couple of plums, a big fleshy one – that have been peeled and cooked into a sweet-savoury sauce; if necessary, add a pinch of sugar.
A reason for eating this pretty much straight out of the oven and while it’s still steaming hot is the mozzarella, because the cheese is molten and pulls into those long strings that make serving it and eating it so entertaining. The benefit of waiting half an hour or longer is that the flavours develop, while the bake itself (and the mozzarella inside and on top) firms up. Or serve at whatever stage or temperature you like, with whatever variety of salad or vegetable.
Rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake
Serves 4-6
2 medium aubergines
  Olive oil
  Salt
  500g fresh, ripe tomatoes – tinned as a last resort
1 onion, peeled and thinly sliced
A few red chilli flakes
  1 handful basil leaves
  Sugar (optional)
  400g long-grain rice
  80g grana padano, parmesan, or cheddar
  400g mozzarella, well-drained
Using a peeler, pare strips of skin from the aubergines so they are striped, then cut into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange these on an oiled baking tray, zigzag with more oil, sprinkle with salt, then bake at 180C (160C)/350F/gas 4 for 30-40 minutes, until tender and a little golden.
Peel the tomatoes by plunging them first into boiling water for four minutes, then cold water, then pulling away the skins. Roughly chop the flesh.
In a pan on a medium-low heat, soften the onion in olive oil, then add the tomatoes, some salt, chilli, most of the basil leaves (reserve a few for constructing the bake) and some sugar, if necessary, and simmer until rich and saucy, mashing as you go to break up any lumps; you can also pass the sauce through a food mill.
Boil the rice in salted water until al dente and a minute shy of the recommended cooking time. Drain and mix the rice with two tablespoons of olive oil, four tablespoons of the tomato sauce, 30g grated parmesan and salt, if needed; it should be well seasoned.
Thinly slice or tear the mozzarella, then construct the bake. Spoon half the rice mix in the base of a round 22cm metal tin or 20cm x 30cm ceramic lasagne-type dish, then use half the aubergine to make a layer on top. Top that with half the sauce, followed by half the mozzarella and a few basil leaves, then repeat this process with the remaining ingredients, ending with a layer of the remaining 50g parmesan. Bake for 20 minutes at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, until bubbling.

Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:00:36 BST
14:00:36 KST

Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
- Published
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).
That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.
"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.
That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?
Far from it.
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.
As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.
I said no surprises. But there have been some.
"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.
The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.
"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."
In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:
"The Communist Party, onwards we go!
"We're with the people, don't you know?"
More X Factor than exit poll.
Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:
"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"
It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.
"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.
"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."
I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.
But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.
And if a party doesn't support the war?
One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.
Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.
"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.
"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.
"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."
For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.
"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."
Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.
The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.
Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.
In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.
The war is front and centre of people's minds here.
"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."
"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."
Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.
"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."
Expectations are low that this election will change much.
"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.
"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

Anthropic priced above $2 trillion as markets eagerly await IPO filing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

Traders are pricing Anthropic above $2 trillion (€1.73tn) in pre-IPO markets, more than double the company's valuation in its last private funding round, as investors wait for the public release of the S-1 filing that could open the way to the largest flotation in history.
Crypto traders are assigning Anthropic an implied valuation more than $1 trillion (€866bn) above its last funding-round price, before public investors have even seen its accounts.
The company behind Claude has filed its IPO paperwork confidentially and chosen Nasdaq for its initial public offering.
What remains is the public release of its S-1 filing, the official registration package that a US company submits to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Until it arrives, the only live price on Anthropic comes from a corner of the crypto market where pre-IPO speculation runs rampant, and it currently sits far above anything the company has ever agreed with an investor.
The last agreed valuation was $965 billion (€836bn), set when a $65 billion (€56bn) Series H round closed at the end of May, led by Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia.
That was already an extraordinary figure for a company founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei, and it followed a valuation of $61.5 billion (€53.3bn) barely a year earlier, representing a nearly sixteenfold increase in roughly 12 months.
Revenue has moved almost as fast.
Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate passed $65 billion (€56bn) by the end of July, driven by enterprise adoption of Claude.
The losses are also enormous, reportedly reaching close to $42 billion (€36.4bn) in 2025, reflecting the cost of training frontier models. Amazon has committed to investing as much as $33 billion (€28.6bn) in the company, while Anthropic has committed to spending more than $100 billion (€86.6bn) on AWS technologies over the coming decade.
Given these figures, investors are already aiming considerably higher than the valuation in the last round.
Reports have put the target IPO valuation at $2 trillion (€1.73tn), with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley leading an offering expected to raise more than $60 billion (€52bn).
The market that is already trading
Perpetual futures contracts tracking Anthropic's pre-IPO valuation are currently trading on Hyperliquid, the largest decentralised derivatives venue, where the implied market capitalisation reached an all-time high of roughly $2.36 trillion (€2.05tn) and sits near $2.15 trillion (€1.86tn) at the time of writing.
That is about 2.2 times the Series H valuation.
Heng Yu Lee, partner at market maker DWF Labs, which is active in these instruments, rejects the suggestion that leverage rather than conviction is driving the premium.
"Whether it's leveraged or not, everyone trading the pre-IPO market is genuine demand at the price that's reflected," he told Euronews, adding that "the premium is pricing in public information that's available, such as expected revenue numbers and expected market demand for the stock."
These contracts will also be the first instruments to react when the filing lands, trading around the clock while equity markets are shut.
"At a moment like the S-1 dropping, you typically see volume spike and prices fluctuate heavily as the market digests the information," Lee explained.
However, the market remains small relative to what it is valuing.
"Currently, the market isn't super deep, with just $6M in 24-hour volume and $31M in open interest on Hyperliquid," Lee said, adding that liquidity should improve as the listing approaches, given that more investors are likely to pile in.
Lee is also candid about how much weight the number deserves.
"As of now, I wouldn't rely too heavily on the absolute pricing as we have yet to have a public S-1," he stated while clarifying that "the direction of how the prices move typically still accurately reflects the shifting sentiment towards the company as things develop."
A crowded year for AI listings
Once Anthropic files publicly, it will cement 2026 as the year of AI IPOs.
It started with chipmaker Cerebras Systems, which designs wafer-scale processors pitched as an alternative to Nvidia's. The firm listed on Nasdaq in May after two false starts, raising $5.55 billion (€4.76bn) at $185 a share, above its revised price range.
The stock opened 89% higher and closed its first day near $311, valuing the company at roughly $67 billion (€58bn) compared with the $23 billion (€20bn) it had been worth three months earlier.
Investor appetite for a credible Nvidia challenger proved fierce, though the enthusiasm cooled quickly after a disappointing first earnings report. Cerebras is currently trading at a valuation of around $43.7 billion (€37.8bn).
Then came SpaceX, which listed in June, raising more than $85 billion (€73.6bn) at a valuation that briefly touched $2.8 trillion (€2.4tn) before falling back to around $1.95 trillion (€1.69tn).
OpenAI was also slated to hold an IPO this year and had already filed confidentially, but has now stepped back entirely. The company has a private valuation of $852 billion (€738bn), set during a $122 billion (€105bn) round in March.
CEO Sam Altman told Fortune on Saturday that listing this year would be "ill-advised", ruling out 2026 and declining to commit to 2027. He said the company had "a lot of stuff to do" on safety and alignment and that being private made that easier.
Altman's comments arrived the same day that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier", arguing that AI companies should deliberately slow the rate at which they improve their most capable models.
Amodei proposed three steps: independent evaluators with employee-level access to frontier systems, coordination on safety standards among labs in democratic countries, and international agreements on the most dangerous categories of use.
Anthropic has already committed unilaterally to the first, and the endorsements came quickly, with Sam Altman saying he agreed on the need to pace the frontier and Elon Musk replying simply: "Dario is right".
However, US President Donald Trump did not.
In his first public response to the three CEOs, Trump, speaking in Ireland on Sunday, dismissed the argument.
"We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins," Trump said, describing some warnings as things "that won't happen".
Trump has since reiterated that argument in several social media posts.
Likewise, China's foreign ministry called the warnings "fearmongering".
Markets registered the exchange, with shares in SoftBank, Kioxia and SK Hynix falling sharply on Monday. Shares in the Japanese and South Korean companies fell more than 6% and 4.3%, respectively.
This leaves Anthropic in an awkward position as it approaches what could be the largest listing ever attempted in public markets.
The company is asking public investors to fund frontier AI development while its founder argues publicly that such development should proceed more slowly.
That is not necessarily a contradiction, since pacing is not stopping, and Anthropic has always argued that safety-focused labs should be at the frontier rather than ceding it.
However, it is a story the S-1 filing will have to tell convincingly, and the risk factors section will be read unusually closely.

Hong Kong to support rocket, satellite IPOs as SpaceX-led sector takes off
Exchange will examine listing-rule changes to attract space IPOs in alignment with Beijing’s prioritisation of space technology
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Hong Kong aims to adjust listing rules to grab a share of initial public offerings by mainland China’s space companies, in line with Beijing’s priorities and heightened activity in the sector following the blockbuster June listing by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
That could lead to more head-to-head competition between the Hong Kong stock exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which is now drawing a majority of applications, including commercial space launch providers and reusable rocket makers CAS Space and Landspace Technology.
The objective was revealed on Wednesday in the annual policy address by Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, who said that bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) would, in the first half of next year, launch a consultation on revising Chapter 18C of the city’s listing rules to court space-related IPOs.

Inside von der Leyen's pitch for a new EU security architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

The State of the Union speech saw the Commission president outline what sound like grand plans for European security, but big questions remain unanswered.
A new European Security Council, an emergency protocol and a new strategic enabler initiative: in her State of the Union speech on Wednesday, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen laid out a new security architecture for Europe. But several question marks still hang over it.
With the war in Ukraine increasingly spilling over into Europe's eastern flank and Russia intensifying its campaign of sabotage attacks and drone incursions, security and defence took centre stage in von der Leyen's annual address.
"We already have many tools. And we are strengthening our work with NATO. But our doctrine, our institutions and our decision-making have not kept pace with the new reality," she said.
The speech previewed several of the main elements expected in the EU's new security strategy, due next month, which is meant to redefine Europe's security architecture.
European Security Council
Among the most significant proposals von der Leyen teased is a new security-focused political format dubbed the European Security Council, a special configuration of the EU leaders' summit that will include partners such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada.
In practice, leaders like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are already frequently invited to European Council meetings. The new format would institutionalise this relationship, giving it a dedicated framework to discuss security matters.
"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent," von der Leyen said. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."
The idea itself is not new. French President Emmanuel Macron floated it during his 2017 presidential campaign, and it received formal backing the following year in the Franco-German Meseberg Declaration.
"We cannot allow ourselves to stay with the status quo. Doctrines and institutions, which were created during peacetime, are not fit any more for the purpose," said European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius.
Still, how this moves from proposal to reality remains unclear: von der Leyen set no start date and offered no tangible deliverables beyond future-proofing Europe's security. How far the new initiative will overlap with NATO and the so-called Coalition of the Willing is also an open question.
"A European Security Council is no panacea. Consensus would presumably still be necessary, but compared to the European Council, a shared threat perception would presumably instil a greater sense of trust and shared destiny amongst its members," wrote Nathalie Tocci, director of Rome's Istituto Affari Internazionali, in a policy brief.
Emergency security protocol
Hybrid warfare was another major flashpoint, after weeks marked by a flurry of Russia-suspected sabotage acts, attempted attacks and drone incursions intended to destabilise EU countries.
"Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook," von der Leyen said on Wednesday. "We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents: those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security. In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO's Article 4."
Article 4 allows NATO members to formally request emergency consultations when they believe their security, territorial integrity or political independence is under threat.
For von der Leyen, the bloc needs its own version of Article 4, dubbed an Emergency Security Protocol, built on the EU treaty's mutual defence clause, which states that "when an EU member state is the target of armed aggression on its territory, the other member states must assist it by all the means in their power".
The mutual defence clause resurfaced earlier this year when an Iranian-made drone, suspected of being launched by the Lebanese militia Hezbollah, targeted a British airbase in Cyprus – a member of the EU, but not of NATO.
Discussions around the clause prompted a "war gaming" exercise conducted by EU ambassadors to map out what triggering it would mean in practice, and von der Leyen's security protocol appears to take the preparation one step farther.
"When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response [and] to deter further escalation and mitigate the impact," she said.
At the same time, EU officials have previously warned that invoking the mutual defence clause could further incentivise the US to disengage from NATO – even though "assistance" doesn't automatically mean joining an armed conflict, and could instead take the form of financial support or civilian protection.
As hybrid threats across Europe grow increasingly kinetic, the advantage of a European defence clause is that it can be activated even for lower-intensity activity, without necessarily requiring a military response, Euronews understands.
Oana Lungescu, NATO's former spokesperson, said that while it's welcome that the Commission President wants closer EU-NATO cooperation, it's hard to see how this would actually deter Russia.
"Protocols and playbooks already exist in both organisations," she said.
Strategic enablers
With the US signalling its intention to reduce its military presence in Europe, subject to a posture review due later this year, the EU is now scrambling to fill key defence capability gaps known as strategic enablers.
Strategic enablers are the logistical backbone of modern warfare: satellites, airlift, refuelling and intelligence capabilities that allow military forces to operate effectively.
"The war in Ukraine has shown us the importance of strategic enablers," von der Leyen said. "These systems are essential, and we need more of them. Only together does Europe have the scale to deliver them."
To that end, she announced a new European Instrument for Strategic Enablers, meant to channel the long-term investment needed to build up these capabilities in alignment with NATO.
In June, Commissioner Kubilius warned that replacing US military assets in Europe would require an eye-watering €500bn investment.
How exactly the new instrument will close this gap remains unclear, as Brussels tries to work out how to incentivise national investment in the area.
"We welcome our European allies and partners stepping up to do more in support of our shared security," a NATO official told Euronews. "NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence, and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda."

Pig’s head at Kaunas mosque fuels debate over religious hatred
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A protest by motorcycle clubs outside a mosque in Lithuania’s second-largest city, where bikers disrupted Muslim prayers and displayed a pig’s head, has prompted a criminal investigation into possible incitement against a religious group and interference with religious rites.
Kaunas police said they opened a pretrial investigation into possible incitement against a group based on nationality, race, ethnicity, religion or other characteristics, as well as interference with religious ceremonies. Authorities are also conducting administrative proceedings because organisers had not obtained permission for the public gathering.
The protest involved members of several motorcycle clubs, including Roadhogs MC, Vilkai MC and Vorai MC. Club representatives were reluctant to discuss the incident, but one, who asked not to be identified, said the bikers were protesting what they described as disorder around the mosque.
“Cars, public order, when they pray in the yard. Many things that are unacceptable,” the biker told LRT.lt. “The main thing is complete disorder, complete disregard and disrespect for Lithuanian citizens and those around them.”
He said the protest was not directed against Islam itself, but was intended to show that the bikers considered public prayers and the disruption they said they caused to local residents unacceptable.
The protest has nevertheless been widely viewed as an act of hostility toward Muslims. Legal scholar Skirmantas Bikelis said Lithuania’s political leaders missed an opportunity to respond quickly and condemn what he described as a hate crime.
A symbol with a long history of abuse
Arūnas Kučikas, director of Kaunas Archdiocese Caritas and chairman of the Lithuanian Caritas Council, said attempts to intimidate a religious community while it is praying, particularly through historically loaded symbols, can have serious consequences.
“We Christians do not advocate merely for abstract tolerance,” Kučikas said. “We may not agree with religious content, but we should not prevent a religious community from praying, especially during prayer, or frighten and intimidate them.”
He said the use of a pig’s head recalled historical episodes of persecution, including pogroms and attacks against Jews.
Lithuanian courts have previously dealt with incidents involving pig parts being used to target Jewish people. In 2013, a court in Šilutė district found a man guilty after he nailed two fresh pig ears to the door of a former synagogue in Švėkšna. The court concluded that the act publicly mocked and incited hatred against Jews.
In 2015, a Kaunas court convicted Jevgenijus Pleganovas after he placed a pig’s head wearing a hat and sidelocks outside a Kaunas synagogue in 2010.
Both Judaism and Islam prohibit the consumption of pork, and the animal has consequently been used as an offensive symbol against members of both religions.
Egdūnas Račius, a professor at Vytautas Magnus University who specialises in Islam and Muslim communities, said the pig is widely understood in Western societies as a symbol intended to offend Muslims.
“Symbolically, in the eyes of non-Muslims, the pig represents what Muslims are supposed to dislike most,” Račius said.
But he cautioned that the meaning may not be as straightforward for Muslims themselves.
“The pig’s head is a classic example of everyday orientalism: ‘Here, we have brought you a pig’s head,’” Račius said. Some Muslims, particularly those from countries where pork is uncommon, might not immediately interpret the gesture in the intended way, he said.
Milda Ališauskienė, a sociology and religious studies professor at Vytautas Magnus University, said the incident also reflected a change in how such acts are carried out.
“In the past, pig’s heads were placed while people tried to conceal their identities,” she said. “Now we see people proudly standing there holding a pig’s head and seeking to humiliate and demean people of another race and faith.”
She said the incident raised questions about whether Lithuanian society has become more tolerant of religious and racial hostility.
Calls for interfaith dialogue
Kučikas said the incident showed the need for a stronger platform for dialogue among religious communities, with greater involvement from Kaunas municipal authorities.
He acknowledged tensions between Kaunas’ historic Tatar Muslim community and the newer Muslim community that has grown in recent years, but said those tensions should be addressed through discussion rather than confrontation.
“We do not have normal interfaith communication practices either in Kaunas or throughout Lithuania,” Kučikas said. He called for religious leaders to meet regularly to discuss common issues, including the right to practice one’s faith.
Kaunas Archdiocese also condemned the protest, saying it opposed the disruption of Muslim prayers and the disrespect shown toward Islam.
“Religious freedom and respect for human dignity are inseparable from a mature democratic society,” Archbishop Kęstutis Kėvalas said. “We may disagree, we may have different views, we may criticise, but we cannot humiliate a person because of their faith.”
The archdiocese urged people to respect one another despite disagreements and reject actions that encourage hatred or hostility.
Legal questions over hate speech and religious rites
Bikelis said previous Lithuanian court rulings showed that acts such as displaying a pig’s head or attaching pig parts to a synagogue could be interpreted as humiliation, mockery and incitement to hatred based on religion.
But he noted that a recent appellate court ruling in a case involving former lawmaker Petras Gražulis could complicate the legal assessment. Gražulis had publicly described homosexual people in derogatory terms and accused them of spreading sexually transmitted diseases. A lower court found his statements constituted mockery, humiliation and incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation, but an appeals court overturned that finding, ruling that public mockery and humiliation alone were insufficient to establish incitement to hatred.
The case is pending before Lithuania’s Supreme Court.
Bikelis said the appellate ruling could make a hate-crime conviction in the Kaunas mosque case less certain, although he argued that the incident involved a particularly aggressive and intimidating expression of hostility toward Muslims.
He said prosecutors could also pursue the separate offense of interfering with religious rites.
Lithuanian courts have previously convicted people under that provision. In one case, filmmaker Emilis Vėlyvis and three actors were convicted after entering a church dressed as clergy during a religious service and promoting a stage production. Their actions disrupted confessions and private prayer.
Bikelis said the Kaunas protest similarly appeared intended to disrupt worship, although the bikers remained outside the mosque.
“Prayer is a sacred act that requires concentration,” he said. “It was disrupted by noise, heavy metal music and psychological intimidation intended to offend.”
The fact that the prayers continued did not necessarily rule out criminal liability, he said, because an attempt to disrupt religious services can itself be legally significant.
Political response
Bikelis also criticised what he described as a slow response from Lithuania’s political leadership, saying public condemnation by senior officials can help prevent divisive incidents from escalating.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius on Monday called on all sides to refrain from further escalation. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said disagreements over migration, religion or other sensitive issues should not be expressed by humiliating people or interfering with religious rites.
Bikelis said he was particularly concerned by comments from the defence minister, who he said appeared to suggest that the Muslims targeted by the protest had somehow contributed to the situation.
Claims about parking and public-order problems around the mosque, Bikelis said, should not be turned into broader accusations about Muslims’ willingness to break laws or disregard social norms.
“Those are everyday details,” he said, noting that parking problems occur regularly around apartment buildings and other public spaces.

Australia's population grows by more than 390,000 people in 12 months

Australia's population grows 1.4 per cent in one year, ABS says
Australia's population has grown by more than 392,000 people in 12 months, according to the Australia Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
ABS head of population statistics Bjorn Jarvis said almost 75 per cent of the increase came from overseas migration.
It marked a total annual increase of 1.4 per cent in the year leading up to March 2026.
"Our population was 27.9 million people at 31 March 2026, that's 392,700 more than the same time in 2025," Mr Jarvis said.
"Natural increase, that is the number of people born minus those who died, added 100,600 people to the population.
"Births and deaths were both up, 0.3 per cent and 3.1 per cent respectively.
"We saw 292,100 people added to our population from net overseas migration from March 2025 to March 2026."
This was compared to 309,500 people in the previous 12 months.
Population data for the past two decades showed the annual change plummeted in early 2020 with the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
It peaked again in September 2023 before beginning a slow return to pre-pandemic levels in the following years.
In the past year, 557,500 people immigrated to Australia from overseas, a decrease of 4 per cent compared with the previous year.
A further 265,400 emigrated from Australia in the same time period, a decrease of 2.2 per cent.
The net overseas migration figure noted by Mr Jarvis came from subtracting the number of people migrating away from Australia from the number of people immigrating to Australia.
All states and territories had some population growth in the year ending March 2026.
Western Australia had the fastest growth rate, with an increase of 2.1 per cent or 64,200 people compared with the previous year.
Tasmania was the slowest, with an increase of 0.6 per cent or 3,400 people.
The majority of those immigrating to Australia moved to New South Wales, while Tasmania and the Northern Territory had the lowest numbers of overseas migration.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:54:00 UTC
13:54:00 KST

On September 15, PNS Hunain, a Pakistan Navy corvette, collided with an Indian Navy warship, INS Kolkata, in the north Arabian Sea, 220 kilometers east of Oman. The following day, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) summoned Pakistan’s top-most diplomat in New Delhi, Chargé d’Affaires Saad Ahmad Warraich, to the foreign ministry to protest the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of Pakistani naval units.
“While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991,” the MEA said in a statement.
Article 10 of the 1991 Agreement, which Pakistan reportedly flouted, states that naval ships and submarines belonging to the two countries should not come within three nautical miles of each other while operating in international waters. The agreement was signed as a confidence-building measure to put in place mechanisms for India and Pakistan to inform each other about military exercises or troop movements to prevent a crisis from arising due to the misreading of the other side’s intentions. It came following heightened tension when India conducted Brass Tacks, a massive military exercise in the states of Punjab and Rajasthan along the India-Pakistan border, in January 1987.
Meanwhile, across the border in Pakistan, the response mirrored that of India, with Islamabad blaming India for the incident. “While the Pakistan Navy was undertaking its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, the Indian vessel carried out aggressive maneuvers in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels, ” the Pakistan Foreign Office said in a statement.
While the MEA described the incident as a collision, unnamed officials “aware of the matter” said that “it involved a close-in maneuvering by the Pakistani vessel, which approached the Indian warship at high speed and in an unsafe manner,” Hindustan Times reported. Another report in First Post, citing “sources within India’s defense establishment” claimed that “the Pakistani vessel shadowed the Indian ship, ignored multiple warnings and then made a high-speed crossing directly in front of the bow, resulting in the crash.”
A report in The Hindu, which cited sources in the defense ministry, said that INS Godavari was “on a routine surveillance mission,” when PNS Hunain “approached the Indian vessel while attempting to intercept or follow it. The close-range maneuver caused the two vessels to graze each other.” The Pakistani vessel “sustained damage in the collision and returned to the harbor. As for INS Godavari it “suffered minor damage and continued on its mission.”
Indian and Pakistani naval vessels last collided in 2011, when Pakistan’s PNS Babur “brushed past” INS Godavari in the Gulf of Aden, causing minor damage to the Indian warship’s helicopter safety net and triggering diplomatic tension.
Following the latest collision, both India and Pakistan summoned the charge d’affaires of the other side to lodge strong protests and have also asked their own charge d’affaires in the other country to register complaints with the government.
“Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” the MEA statement said.
Collisions involving naval warships are rare. This is the first instance of military tension between India and Pakistan erupting into the open since the four-day military clashes in May of last year.

Finland faces prospect of biting cold winter, FMI meteorologist says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:51:09 EEST
13:51:09 KST

Finland could be in for an especially cold and overcast winter, according to Ari-Juhani Punkka, a meteorologist with the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
Punkka bases his warning on the C3S (Copernicus Climate Change Service) forecast, a climate prediction system that combines data from international meteorological centres to look six months ahead.
The C3S forecast indicates air pressure anomalies, which allows meteorologists to assess where high and low-pressure systems will most likely move.
The outlook for mid-winter, around January and February, suggests Finland will remain on the colder side of a low-pressure front — and at the mercy of chilly northerly, northeasterly or easterly winds.
"If low-pressure systems pass south of us in February, then mild air masses will also remain far south of Finland," Punkka said, adding that it is rare for the six-month forecast to show such "strong signals" of air pressure movements.
This could mean biting cold temperatures or very heavy snowfall, although Punkka further noted that wintry weather can manifest in different ways. For example, conditions could be very cloudy but with little snow cover.
"When we have clouds overhead, the temperatures can also be quite mild," he said.
However, another possible scenario, according to Punkka, would see a low pressure system moving into Finland from Siberia — in which case the temperatures would drop significantly.
Another factor that will affect winter temperatures is the El Niño phenomenon, a weather pattern that occurs every two to seven years and usually lasts for about a year.
"When we have a strong El Niño underway, it is somewhat more likely than usual in the European region that wintry weather patterns occur in January–February," Punkka said.
However, despite the icy outlook, Punkka also noted that weather forecasts — especially six months ahead of time — are not particularly reliable and subject to change.

For cancer survivors, tai chi can ease sleep problems, fatigue and pain, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:50:56 UTC
13:50:56 KST

Mind-body therapies can help people living with the lingering effects of cancer treatment manage fatigue, pain and sleep problems, according to a new analysis.
Breathing exercises, meditation and tai-chi and qigong practices reduced fatigue and pain in people with cancer who had completed their primary treatment but continued to experience at least moderate psychological distress, a new study found.
Tai-chi and qigong — an ancient Chinese mind-body practice that combines gentle, flowing movements with heightened attention to body sensations and breathing — also improved sleep quality, something most cancer patients struggle with.
Mind-body therapy “has been a tremendous help navigating this most unpleasant journey,” said cancer survivor Ken Taub, who took part in the trial, adding that now he “can start the day feeling fresh and limber.”
There is a growing number of cancer survivors like Taub. “More and more people with cancer are surviving longer term but often, they are struggling with long-term side effects that can be difficult to manage,“ Linda E. Carlson, a professor at the University of Calgary and lead investigator on the study, said in a press release.
This clinical trial included nearly 600 participants with a variety of prior cancer diagnoses, including breast, prostate, gastrointestinal, lung and many other types of cancer. Approximately half of the participants had early-stage cancer.
Participants either chose one of two programmes — mindfulness-based cancer recovery or tai chi and qigong — or were randomly assigned to one. A waitlist group served as a control.
Mindfulness-based cancer recovery included yoga, meditation and in-person group discussions for nine weeks. The tai chi and qigong group practised flowing rhythmic movements, along with breath awareness and a variety of cognitive skills, including focused attention, heightened body awareness, and imagery, for 11 weeks.
“Both mindfulness-based cancer recovery and tai chi/qigong helped participants manage some of the most common and burdensome challenges faced after cancer treatment, including fatigue, pain and, in the case of tai chi/qigong, sleep difficulties,” said senior author Peter Wayne, director of the Osher Center for Integrative Health at Mass General Brigham, adding that the findings "reinforce the value of a whole-person approach to cancer survivorship care."
Pain was measured in two ways: intensity and interference with daily activities. Although there were minimal effects on intensity and pain interference, the more psychological aspect of pain improved over time with both practices. Researchers also found that symptoms of pain interference, sleep disturbance and fatigue tended to cluster together, so when one symptom improved, the other two did as well.
“If this kind of practice could be incorporated from the beginning, that could help a lot of people,” Cynthia Good, who participated in the tai-chi and qigong practices 11-week program, said.

Turkish sailors sue Ukraine over deadly drone attack
The crew of a Turkish cargo ship hit by Ukrainian drones has filed a complaint against Kiev with the International Criminal Court (ICC) over the attack, which killed one sailor and injured two others, lawyers said on Wednesday. The plaintiffs include 12 crew members, the family of the deceased sailor, and the ship’s owner.
The ICC filing says the vessel was carrying wheat meal from the Russian Black Sea port of Tuapse to Trabzon when it was attacked on July 22, although Turkish media reported at the time that it was carrying coal from Taman, another Russian Black Sea port.
Photos and videos taken after the attack show “extensive internal damage” to the ship’s compartments and apparent traces of shrapnel, according to the complaint. The plaintiffs have asked the Hague-based court to investigate the attack as a possible crime against humanity.
Ukraine ratified the ICC’s Rome Statute in 2024, becoming a full member of the court on January 1, 2025.
“There is concrete information and footage showing that the attack originated from Ukraine,” Nuri Koray Kurun, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said. He added that the strike was consistent with Ukraine’s stated campaign of targeting shipping in the area.
“Videos of this operation, as well as footage showing the moment our ship was hit, were openly shared on official social media accounts. Our technical analysis of the vessel shown being struck in the video established that it was the Reyhan Sari,” Kurun said.
Türkiye summoned the Ukrainian ambassador last month, formally lodging a protest over strikes on its commercial shipping in the Black Sea. In July, India also summoned Kiev’s envoy after drones targeted the cargo vessel Omorfi, killing an Indian sailor.
Ukraine stepped up attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov over the summer in an effort to disrupt Russian logistics and target Russia’s supposed ‘shadow fleet’, which Kiev alleges helps Moscow circumvent Western sanctions.
Russia has denied that it operates a shadow fleet and accused Ukraine of striking purely civilian targets. Moscow has also accused Kiev of routinely targeting civilian trucks, energy facilities, and apartment buildings as part of its long-range drone campaign.
Russia responded by intensifying strikes on Ukraine’s energy and port infrastructure, as well as vessels it says are carrying military equipment. The Kremlin has described the operations as retaliatory, arguing that Kiev has “opened Pandora’s box.”

ADHD is linked to almost 50% increase in gut problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:45:08 UTC
13:45:08 KST

People with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are significantly more likely to experience a range of gastrointestinal symptoms, according to a new systematic review covering more than 1.9 million people.
A new review suggests that ADHD is associated with a substantial burden of functional gastrointestinal symptoms — problems affecting how the digestive system works without necessarily reflecting an identifiable structural disease.
Researchers screened over 9,000 records and included 23 studies, and found that ADHD was associated with higher odds of every gastrointestinal symptom examined — including irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, indigestion and encopresis.
"Almost every gut symptom we looked at … appeared to be associated with ADHD,” said co-lead author Sarah Blake, a Medical Student at Warwick Medical School. “These symptoms can have a real impact on daily life, but they could easily be overlooked if the focus is on ADHD itself.”
The researchers found a 48% increase in the odds of experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms overall among people with ADHD. The association was particularly strong for constipation, where the odds were almost twice as high, and encopresis — loss of bowel control — where they were more than four times as high.
Why the link?
The researchers say there are several possible explanations, but the study does not establish that ADHD itself causes gastrointestinal problems.
One possibility is behaviour. Emotional dysregulation and increased sensitivity to stress, both associated with ADHD, may affect gut sensitivity and contribute to functional abdominal pain. Irregular eating patterns, skipped meals and binge eating may also influence symptoms such as indigestion, bloating, constipation and abdominal pain.
Food-related sensory sensitivities could play a role, too. People with ADHD may experience differences in sensitivity to food textures and smells, potentially contributing to selective diets that are lower in fibre and could affect bowel habits.
The researchers also point to differences in interoception — the ability to recognise internal bodily signals — as a possible factor. Reduced awareness of the need to have a bowel movement could potentially contribute to constipation or encopresis.
Medication may be another contributor. Stimulants such as methylphenidate are known to cause side effects including appetite suppression, abdominal pain, nausea and constipation. Sleep disturbances, which are common among people with ADHD, may also affect gastrointestinal motility and sensitivity.
The gut-brain connection
The researchers also highlight the gut microbiome as a possible biological pathway.
Previous research has identified differences in gut microbial composition between adults with ADHD and neurotypical controls. Other studies have linked changes in the gut microbiome with gastrointestinal symptoms.
One hypothesis is that these differences could influence inflammation and communication between the gut and brain. Genetic factors may also contribute.
"We can't yet say ADHD causes these gut problems, or exactly what is driving the link, but the pattern is striking enough to warrant attention,” Saran Shantikumar, associate clinical professor at Warwick Medical School, said. “Clinicians caring for people with ADHD may want to consider asking about gastrointestinal symptoms, particularly if they may be affecting quality of life."

Latvian companies to gain support from German chambers of commerce in more than 90 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:38:32 UTC
13:38:32 KST

The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) and the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK) signed a memorandum of understanding on Wednesday, 16 September, to help Latvian companies develop exports in foreign markets. Businesses will gain access to the knowledge, contacts and services of the German Chambers of Commerce Abroad network, which operates through 150 offices in more than 90 countries.
The memorandum was signed at the Latvian stand during the international Big Bang AI Festival in Berlin. The signing ceremony was attended by Latvia’s Minister for Economics, Viktors Valainis, and representatives of the Latvian business delegation visiting Germany as part of a trade mission organised by LIAA and the Embassy of the Republic of Latvia in the Federal Republic of Germany.
“Latvian companies need local contacts and accurate information about market requirements when entering foreign markets. Through this memorandum, we are giving them the opportunity to use the knowledge and contacts of the German Chambers of Commerce Abroad network in more than 90 countries. Businesses will be able to find customers and cooperation partners more quickly, while Latvia will gain broader export opportunities and new markets for our goods, services and technologies,” Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis said.
On behalf of DIHK, the memorandum was signed by Dr Volker Treier, Chief Executive of Foreign Trade and member of the Executive Board, and Benjamin Leipold, Head of the AHK Network and Managing Director of DIHK DEinternational GmbH. On behalf of the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce, it was signed by Reinhold Schneider and the organisation’s Chief Executive Officer, Florian Schröder. LIAA was represented by Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of its Export and Innovation Services Department.
Support for Latvian companies in more than 90 countries
The German Chambers of Commerce Abroad network brings together bilateral chambers of commerce, delegations of German industry and commerce, and representative offices worldwide. Under the memorandum, Latvian companies will be able to access AHK services abroad on the same terms as German companies and businesses from the respective country.
AHK provides tailored market and product advice, information about the business environment and prospective partners, as well as guidance on legal matters, public procurement and human resources. These services will be available to companies for a fee, according to the price list of the relevant chamber.
“Europe needs to cooperate more closely in these challenging times. Through this agreement, Latvian companies will gain full access to AHK’s international business network, its expertise and contacts in 93 countries around the world, where 150 AHK offices operate. Together with Estonia and Lithuania, this cooperation model now covers all three Baltic states, creating a strong link between the Baltics, Germany and almost 100 global markets,” emphasised Florian Schröder, Chief Executive Officer of the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK).
Dedicated contact point for Latvian exporters
The memorandum provides for the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce to establish a dedicated contact point to support Latvian exporters. It will advise Latvian companies and connect them with AHK offices in their markets of interest. LIAA, meanwhile, will inform Latvian businesses about the available services and, together with AHK, organise one or two events annually focusing on specific countries or regions.
Each year, LIAA and AHK will select two countries and two sectors in each of them in which to provide targeted support for Latvian exports. The parties will also establish a joint steering group to agree on priorities and the necessary support measures, as well as evaluate the results achieved during the previous year.
“Each year, together with our German partners, we will select two countries and two sectors on which to place particular emphasis. LIAA will invite Latvian companies that are ready to begin or expand their operations in the selected markets to participate. Representatives of the German Chambers of Commerce Abroad in the respective countries will provide information about market requirements and help identify prospective customers and cooperation partners. Latvian companies will therefore receive practical support for operating in the selected markets,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
The memorandum of understanding has been concluded for one year and will be renewed automatically unless one of the parties decides to terminate the cooperation. It also provides for the possibility of developing dedicated support programmes in the future for Latvian companies seeking to enter selected foreign markets.
One of the outcomes of the Latvian business trade mission
The signing of the memorandum is one of the outcomes of the Latvian business trade mission to Germany. The mission is taking place in Berlin from 14 to 17 September and includes companies operating in information and communications technology, financial technology, life sciences, smart energy, defence and dual-use technologies. The programme features visits to companies and innovation centres, participation in industry events, and individual business meetings with prospective German partners and investors.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvia’s exports of goods and services to Germany have increased by more than 40%, from €1.47 billion to approximately €2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France and China combined. Growth has continued this year: during the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, compared with a 6% rise in Latvia’s total exports. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for service exports, which reached €779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 companies with German capital operate in Latvia, with their combined investment in share capital exceeding €800 million.
LIAA organises participation in international trade missions under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with support from the European Regional Development Fund and national funding. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving financial support to cover eligible costs.

World’s water cycle becoming more unpredictable, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
04:35:00 UTC
13:35:00 KST

World’s water cycle becoming more unpredictable, UN warns
- The UN warns the planet’s water cycle is becoming more erratic, with 2025 among the driest years for rivers and glaciers shrinking worldwide.
- Groundwater and glaciers, acting as vital water reserves, are rapidly depleting, increasing risks of water crises and disasters.
- The strong El Nino in 2025 will worsen droughts and floods, highlighting the need for shared data and cooperation across borders.
AI generated
GENEVA – The planet’s water cycle is becoming increasingly erratic, swinging between too little and too much, the United Nations warned on Sept 17, with an unprecedented El Nino expected to exacerbate the long-term trend.
The UN’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in a report that 2025 was among the driest for the world’s rivers in over three decades.
In 2025 – one of the warmest years on record – glaciers also shrank across all regions, even as groundwater levels in many parts of the world are in multi-year decline, it found.
Overall, the WMO’s annual State of Global Water Resources report showed that the Earth’s freshwater storage – the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation and ice and snow – continued a decade-long decline.
Some elements of the water cycle change rapidly – like precipitation, river flow and soil moisture, responding to weather within days or weeks.
WMO secretary-general Celeste Saulo voiced particular concern about the decline in “slow reserves”, like groundwater and glaciers, which she said had traditionally served as the planet’s “savings account”.
They have served as “a buffer that absorbs bad years so that a single drought or a single dry season does not translate directly into a water crisis”, she told reporters.
‘Spending our reserves’
Now, “we are depleting that savings account”, she warned. “We are spending our reserves.”
Glaciers have also been shrinking at a precipitous rate, with 2025 marking the fourth consecutive year where they shed significant ice mass across all regions.
Between 2023 and 2025, the report estimated that glaciers lost a cumulative global glacier mass of 1,400 gigatonnes of water – roughly equal to the water required to fill 560 million Olympic-sized swimming pools, or about a third of the world’s annual freshwater withdrawals.
“Groundwater tells a similar story: nearly two-thirds of monitored wells worldwide showed conditions outside the historical norm in 2025,” Saulo said.
She highlighted that this was happening in parallel with “more water-related disasters”.
In particular, she pointed to the current El Nino pattern, which is expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
El Nino is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle that occurs every two to seven years and is characterised by above average ocean temperatures across the Pacific, and brings worldwide changes in winds and rainfall patterns and erratic weather.
“The strengthening El Nino will increase the risk of drought in some areas, and flooding in others,” Saulo cautioned.
‘Abnormal’
Already before El Nino hit, rivers worldwide were showing “abnormal” flows, WMO said, with 2025 among the three driest years for rivers in 35 years.
For a seventh year in a row, the number of river basins globally experiencing “normal” conditions were in a clear minority in 2025.
Only around 36 per cent saw normal flows, while an equal percentage saw below-normal discharge conditions and 21 per cent were above normal, the report found.
The WMO stressed the importance of good data to map the developments in the water cycle, warning that significants gaps remained in hard-hit areas.
“Weather respects no borders, and this is especially true for water,” Saulo said, arguing for the importance of “shared data, shared standards and shared early warnings”.
“A river basin is fed by water upstream, often in another country,” she pointed out.
And “a glacier disaster in one country can lead to devastation in another as we saw with the recent tragedy of China and Nepal”. AFP

S. Korea's interbank forex trading grows in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
12:31:16 CST
13:31:16 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's interbank foreign exchange trading grew in August due to an expansion in spot and forward trading, central bank data showed Thursday.
The daily average transactions of foreign currencies and derivatives in the domestic interbank market increased 2.68 billion U.S. dollars from a month earlier to 57.23 billion dollars in August, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The growth was driven by robust activity in the spot exchange market, which rose 3.43 billion dollars to reach a daily average of 25.31 billion dollars.
The daily average trading of the U.S. currency gained 2.04 billion dollars to 20.42 billion dollars, and the transaction of the Chinese currency surged 1.38 billion dollars to 4.90 billion dollars.
The forward contracts also showed a notable uptick, with the daily average trading volume rising 1.04 billion dollars to 3.18 billion dollars in August compared to the previous month.
Trading in the FX swap market fell 1.48 billion dollars to 25.36 billion dollars, and the transaction of other derivatives, including currency swaps and options, was down 310 million dollars to 3.39 billion dollars.
The daily average volatility in the South Korean won versus U.S. dollar exchange rate sank to 0.31 percent in August from 0.53 percent in July.
The won versus dollar exchange rate dipped to 1,368.6 won per dollar at the end of August from 1,424.0 won tallied a month earlier.
Premium on credit default swap, which gauges credit risk for five-year government bonds, averaged 22 basis points in August, down from 23 basis points in the previous month. ■

Moderates ministers want to scrap Aula in Danish schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17

13:31:15 KST

Three Danish government ministers from Moderaterne, the Moderates, want schools to stop using Aula, the digital platform used for communication between schools, daycare facilities and families.
Ministers Monika Rubin, Christina Egelund and Jakob Engel-Schmidt made the proposal in a joint interview with Berlingske. They have not proposed an alternative to Aula.
“An IT system has been created that sucks so much oxygen out of the school and the classroom that it is harmful to our children’s well-being and learning,” Engel-Schmidt said.
Aula was introduced in 2019 to replace Skoleintra. Danish public schools and public and self-governing daycare facilities have access to the platform, where students, parents and employees can receive and share information.
Rubin told DR that the amount of communication on the platform had become excessive.
“More communication is not always better communication. 10,000 messages are sent on Aula per minute between half past seven and nine in the morning. It has gotten out of hand,” she said.
According to Berlingske, Egelund said answering parents’ questions is not a core task of Denmark’s public schools.
The proposal follows the latest PISA study, an international assessment of 15-year-old students’ performance in reading, mathematics and science, which showed a decline among Danish students.
Other government parties have expressed skepticism about removing Aula.
Nanna Bonde, education spokesperson for SF, the Socialist People’s Party, one of Denmark’s governing parties, suggested guidelines for the platform could be introduced instead, according to DR.

Apartment sales in Copenhagen fell sharply in August, while several other parts of Denmark saw more houses change hands than a year earlier, new figures from Boligsiden show.
A total of 390 owner-occupied apartments were sold in Copenhagen Municipality in August, 36 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
It was also the third-lowest number of apartment sales recorded in Copenhagen for an August since Boligsiden began collecting the data in 2011.
“Significantly fewer owner-occupied apartments are being traded in Copenhagen, and there has been a clear shift in the otherwise hectic pace that we have seen for a long time in Copenhagen,” said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Across Denmark, apartment sales were 20 percent lower than in August 2025.
Overall housing sales also fell slightly during the first eight months of the year compared with the same period last year, after seasonal changes are taken into account.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal economist at AL Sydbank, said the apartment market was largely responsible for the decline, while sales of houses and holiday homes remained strong.
Boligsiden recorded more sales of detached and terraced houses than a year earlier in South Jutland, West and South Zealand, North Jutland and Funen.
House sales fell in Copenhagen, the Copenhagen suburbs and North Zealand.
“Now, we see the activity spreading to other parts of the country to a greater extent,” Daetz said.
A Lego model of the Danish royal yacht Dannebrog has been sold at auction for 60,000 DKK after spending 28 years at Legoland in Billund.
The model was sold Wednesday by auction house Bruun Rasmussen for twice its estimated price of between 20,000 and 30,000 DKK.
Legoland said the proceeds will be donated to the Mary Foundation, which works to combat social isolation.
“We think it could be nice to donate the money to the Mary Foundation, now that it is the royal yacht ‘Dannebrog’ that we have had up for auction,” said Jan Mouritzen, head of Legoland’s model department.
Bruun Rasmussen specialist Line Hjorth Langkjær said the model’s history at Legoland and the royal yacht’s place in Danish history had helped increase interest.
It is the first time Legoland has auctioned an original model from Miniland, where landmarks are recreated in miniature using Lego bricks.
The original Dannebrog model contains about 25,000 bricks. It was replaced after a new Copenhagen Harbour area opened in Miniland in July with an updated version made from 225,000 bricks.
The real Dannebrog serves as the official and private residence of the Danish royal couple and other members of the royal family during summer cruises and official visits overseas.
The Mary Foundation was established by then-Crown Princess Mary in 2007. The foundation said the donation will support efforts to combat bullying among children and loneliness among young people.
A patient at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn underwent surgery for an inguinal hernia on Wednesday while the surgeon performing the procedure was in Aabenraa, southern Denmark.
The operation used robot-assisted telesurgery, with the surgeon controlling a robot in the Faroe Islands from an office in Aabenraa.
It was the first time the technology had been used for an operation in Denmark and between two public hospitals in the Nordic region, Sygehus Sønderjylland, the Southern Jutland hospital, said in a press release.
Chief physician Jan Krzak said the operation had a “highly satisfactory result.”
“We have started out with a few selected patients with an uncomplicated inguinal hernia. The first step was to document whether the technology, safety, communication, and cooperation functioned stably in practice,” Krzak said.
The operation is part of a project examining whether telesurgery could eventually provide treatment to patients who live far from major medical facilities.
Elinborg Mortensen, chief physician at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn, said the technology could be particularly useful in the Faroe Islands, where many patients currently have to travel long distances for hospital treatment.
“Therefore, it is interesting for us to investigate whether new technology can bring some of the expertise closer to the patients in a safe and controlled manner,” Mortensen said.
A full surgical and anesthesia team was present with the patient in Tórshavn throughout Wednesday’s operation. The team was ready to take over if the technology or connection failed.
Robot-assisted telesurgery has previously been used internationally, including for operations performed remotely between London and Gibraltar.

The commander of a Russian warship that fired two signal flares at a Danish military helicopter Monday has received an award for his actions, according to the Russian Ministry of Defense.
The ministry said Wednesday that two flares were fired to prevent what it described as a “provocation,” Reuters reported.
Russia identified the vessel as the Soobrazitelny and described it as a corvette, a relatively small and lightly armed warship. The Danish Armed Forces have described it as a frigate. According to TV 2, Russia and NATO countries use different classifications and standards for warships.
The Russian ministry said the vessel was carrying out “operations in neutral waters,” according to Russian media outlet Tass. It did not specify what those operations involved.
The ship’s commander was praised for his response during the incident, which the ministry said caused the Danish helicopter to leave the area shortly afterward.

Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin has previously described the helicopter’s actions before the flares were fired as “provocative.”
He said the helicopter had carried out “dangerous manoeuvres” and that the Russian vessel had been unable to establish contact with it. He also said the communication problem was on the Danish side.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, rejected that account.
“I trust the Armed Forces. The fact is that there are plenty of ways to contact such a helicopter via radio and other things,” Bruus said.
“There was no contact before these flares were fired, and that should have been done.”

Passengers can choose between a ticket for a new journey on the same route or a cash payment.
Applications for compensation can be submitted through DSB’s travel time guarantee scheme.

According to a press release from the Danish Finance Ministry, Naalakkersuisut (the Government of Greenland) and the Danish government signed a partial agreement on Tuesday worth 1.2 billion DKK for investments in Greenland from 2026 to 2029.
“The agreement means, among other things, that there will be a relief package for the Greenlandic citizens who are the most vulnerable economically,” the ministry said.
The governments have also agreed to provide funding for Greenland’s utility sector. This includes water supply projects in Ilulissat and support for Nukissiorfiit, Greenland’s self-rule-owned utility company, to help develop the country’s energy infrastructure.
Funding will also go toward operating Greenland’s new international airports, with the agreement including money for feasibility studies in 2027 for a new regional airstrip in Ittoqqortoormiit and a new deep-water port in Qaqortoq.
“We are investing in initiatives that can be felt in the everyday lives of the Greenlandic people, and which at the same time support Naalakkersuisut’s work to develop a strong and sustainable Greenlandic society,” Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said.
The agreement follows another deal between Greenland and Denmark reached in February, which provided funding for Greenlandic patients to receive treatment in the Danish healthcare system.
Both agreements stem from a framework agreement reached in September last year between Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Under that framework, the two sides agreed on a package worth 1.6 billion DKK for Greenland’s healthcare system, the deep-water port and a new airstrip.
Around 100,000 AL Sydbank customers will no longer have to pay up to 600 DKK a year for an account, online banking access and a debit card.
The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.
“When we did the merger, we promised that you would be able to get an account, access to online banking, and a debit card without it costing anything,” said Svend Randers, AL Sydbank’s director responsible for private customers.
“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.
The bank has not yet decided which debit card will be included.
