Large genetic study links GLP-1 receptor activation to improved mental well-being
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:27 UTC
11:00:27 KST

A new study provides evidence that activating the GLP-1 receptor, the biological target of popular weight-loss and diabetes medications, is associated with better mental health and a lower risk of conditions like depression and bipolar disorder. The research also suggests a potential protective effect against substance use disorders, hinting at psychiatric benefits that go beyond simple weight loss. These findings were published in Translational Psychiatry.
The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor is a protein found on the surface of cells in various parts of the body, including the pancreas and the brain. When activated, it helps regulate blood sugar and sends fullness signals to the brain, reducing appetite. Medications that activate this receptor, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, have become widely used for managing type 2 diabetes and obesity. Because these drugs act on the central nervous system, scientists have been investigating whether they might also influence mental health.
Early clinical research hinted at potential psychiatric benefits. For instance, an early 2016 clinical study found that the GLP-1 medication liraglutide improved cognitive problems in patients with mood disorders. Following up on that, a 2017 experimental study showed that GLP-1 treatment produced physical changes in brain areas that regulate mood in people with mood disorders. More recently, a 2023 review of clinical trials showed that GLP-1 drugs can reliably reduce symptoms of depression.
These observations prompted researchers to ask whether activating the GLP-1 receptor genuinely protects against psychiatric and substance use disorders, or if the mood improvements were simply a side effect of patients feeling better about losing weight. To answer this, a research team led by Guoyi Yang conducted a large-scale genetic study to isolate the biological effects of GLP-1 receptor activation.
“GLP-1R agonists, such as semaglutide, have transformed how we treat obesity and type 2 diabetes,” said Yang, a postdoctoral researcher at the Division of Translational Medicine and Human Genetics, Department of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. “Concerns were raised about the risk of suicidal ideation and self-injury in people using GLP-1R agonists. In contrast, clinical trials suggested that these medications reduced depressive symptoms. To better understand the psychiatric effects of GLP-1R agonists, we used genetic variants as proxies for GLP-1R activation, the intended target of these drugs, to evaluate whether activating this receptor influences mental health outcomes,” he told PsyPost.
The researchers used a technique called Mendelian randomization. This method acts like a natural clinical trial by looking at genetic variations that people are born with. Because genes are assigned randomly at birth and are not influenced by lifestyle choices or environmental factors, they can help establish whether a specific biological mechanism directly influences an outcome. The team focused on specific genetic variants near the GLP1R gene that mimic the effects of taking a GLP-1 drug.
This approach uses genetics to predict what happens when you intervene on a specific biological target. “Our research uses genetics as a tool to predict the impact of GLP-1R activation – we aren’t saying that GLP-1R activation is only relevant to people with a certain genetic background,” Yang explained. “We hypothesize that the genetic variants that we consider in this paper affect the same mechanism that the drug affects – and so the genetic variants tell us what happens if you intervene on this target using the drug.”
Yang and colleagues identified two sets of these natural genetic proxies. The first set lowers body mass index, which is a common measure of body fat based on a person’s height and weight. The second set lowers glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), which is a measure of average blood sugar levels over several months. They analyzed data from massive genetic databases, including the UK Biobank, which contained information from hundreds of thousands of people of European ancestry. The researchers examined how these GLP-1-activating genetic variants related to a broad spectrum of mental health outcomes.
The mental health outcomes included general well-being, comprising life satisfaction, positive affect, neuroticism, and depressive symptoms. The researchers also looked at diagnosed mental health disorders like major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Finally, they examined the risk of substance use disorders, such as alcohol dependence and cannabis use disorder. To ensure their results were robust, they compared the effects of the specific GLP-1 variants against general genetic variants from across the entire genome that simply lower body weight or blood sugar.
The findings indicate that genetically predicted GLP-1 receptor activation through the body mass index pathway is associated with widespread mental health benefits. Specifically, for every 1-kilogram per square meter decrease in body mass index driven by GLP-1 receptor activation, individuals experienced a 0.06 standard deviation improvement in overall mental well-being. This included higher life satisfaction and lower levels of neuroticism and depressive symptoms.
The researchers also found a reduced risk for severe psychiatric conditions. A 1-kilogram per square meter decrease in body mass index via the GLP-1 pathway was associated with an odds ratio of 0.82 for major depressive disorder, meaning a roughly 18% lower risk. The association with bipolar disorder was even stronger, showing an odds ratio of 0.61, or a 39% reduction in risk. There was also suggestive evidence that this specific biological pathway lowers the risk of ADHD and postpartum depression.
“We were surprised by just how broadly GLP-1R activation seems to benefit mental health, extending to depression, bipolar disorder, and potentially substance use disorders,” Yang said. “The effect on bipolar disorder was striking, showing almost a 40% lower risk (odds ratio of 0.61). These results highlight GLP-1R agonists as promising candidates for future psychiatric therapies.”
Notably, these mental health benefits were much stronger than the effects seen from general, genome-wide genetic variants that just lower body mass index. This suggests that the psychiatric advantages of GLP-1 receptor activation are not entirely explained by weight loss alone. The receptor’s direct activity in the brain, potentially regulating stress responses and neuroinflammation, likely plays an independent role in improving mood. Interestingly, genetic variants that mimicked the blood-sugar-lowering effects of GLP-1 activation did not show these same broad mental health benefits.
The study also provided suggestive evidence that GLP-1 receptor activation is associated with a lower risk of substance use disorders and fewer reported alcohol problems. These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which examined actual prescription records and hospitalizations rather than genetic proxies, and similarly found evidence linking GLP-1 pathway activity to a lower risk of substance use disorders.
The new results are also consistent with another study covered by PsyPost in 2026. That study, which also used Mendelian randomization to analyze genetic proxies for GLP-1 receptor activation, found no evidence of increased risk for major psychiatric conditions like depression and bipolar disorder, alleviating early concerns that the medications might provoke psychiatric distress.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. The Mendelian randomization approach relies on the assumption that the selected genetic variants only affect the outcomes through the GLP-1 receptor. It is possible that these specific genes also influence neighboring biological pathways, which could independently affect mental health. The researchers used statistical tests to check for this, but the possibility cannot be completely ruled out.
“A key limitation of this method (Mendelian randomization) is that it relies on rigorous assumptions that cannot be verified,” Yang pointed out. “While we carefully selected genetic variants in or near GLP1R to mimic the drug target, we cannot rule out the possibility that nearby genes might also play a role. Clinical trials are needed to determine whether these psychiatric benefits directly translate to patients.”
Additionally, looking at genetic variants measures the effect of lifelong exposure to slightly altered GLP-1 receptor activity. This is quite different from an adult taking a concentrated, high-dose medication over a few months or years. While the genetic data suggests that activating this pathway is safe and potentially beneficial for mental health over a lifetime, clinical trials are needed to confirm whether GLP-1 medications produce these exact psychiatric benefits in real-world patients.
“The effect size reflects the lifelong genetic effect of GLP-1R activation in the general population,” Yang noted. “In contrast, patients in the real world usually take GLP-1R agonists for shorter periods. Therefore, our numbers should not be viewed as the exact risk reduction patients will experience when taking these medications.”
Looking ahead, the research team aims to dive deeper into how these medications work in the body. “Our immediate next step is to understand the biological mechanisms underlying these psychiatric effects of GLP-1R activation,” Yang said. “In the long term, our goal is to define the multifaceted effects of GLP-1R agonists across organs and to identify novel, genetically validated drug targets for cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic diseases.”
You can follow Yang’s work on X (formerly Twitter) at @yanggy_hku.
The study, “Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor activation and mental health: a drug-target Mendelian randomization study,” was authored by Guoyi Yang, Stephen Burgess, and C. Mary Schooling.

Feijóo: In Ceuta, it’s up to Europe to clean up the Spanish government’s mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Police officers control a large group of migrants crowding outside the entrance of the Loma del Colmenar reception center, waiting for admission, in Ceuta on September 1, 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images
Alberto Núñez Feijóo is Spain’s leader of the opposition and the president of the People’s Party.
On July 30, at least 80,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco, the largest violation of territorial integrity we have experienced in recent decades. That challenge tested the resilience of Spain’s southern border and, therefore, of Europe’s southern border. It continues 50 days later. With no clear prospect of when it might be resolved. It is therefore time to ask ourselves whether our response matches the scale of what is at stake.
Advertisement
A border is not just a line on a map. It is the expression of a political community that decides which values to protect and which responsibilities to share. When a European border is breached, Europe as a whole becomes weaker. When a border is not properly defended, Europe as a whole is left unprotected. That is what is happening.
The response of the current Spanish government, incapable of acknowledging the true nature of the problem and implementing the correct solution, obliges me to reiterate, first and foremost, the obvious, as the President of Ceuta did last week during his visit to Brussels. We are not witnessing a conventional migration crisis, but rather the consequences of an invasion originating from Morocco, which must therefore be held responsible for having condoned or instigated it.
Normality has disappeared from Ceuta for more than six weeks, and the scenes of chaos, overcrowding and insecurity should both shame us and compel us to act. To think that the prolongation of this situation will have no consequences is a mistake we cannot afford to make: it affects our sovereignty, our collective capacity to defend the rule of law, the safety of our citizens, and the credibility of the European project in ensuring its own stability.
El briefing imprescindible para quienes deciden, negocian y marcan la agenda política.
Undoubtedly, the national authorities are the first to bear the responsibility for resolving this crisis, in accordance with a non-negotiable principle shared by all EU member states under the Pact on Migration and Asylum: those who have entered irregularly must be returned. All of them. The Spanish government’s obligation is not to find accommodation for them, but to expedite their departure.
That said, given the time that has elapsed and the escalation of violent incidents in Ceuta, Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again. Just as Europe has responded when faced with other hybrid threats — on energy, trade or disinformation — the attack on our southern border now demands the same determination.
Firstly, the European Union must ensure that Spain implements, with due rigor and efficiency, all the European instruments available to facilitate returns. Secondly, it must clarify why the Kingdom of Morocco itself has reiterated in an official statement its willingness to take back all those who entered on July 30, while Spanish ministers maintain that no such cooperation exists.
Advertisement
Thirdly, it must make full use of all its diplomatic resources to ensure that the relationship with Morocco, a strategic partner for Spain and for the rest of Europe, continues to develop on the basis of transparency and mutual respect. While I advocate the need to establish a loyal and stable relationship with our neighboring country, I believe it is in the interests of the entire European Union to ensure that this relationship is not undermined by the exploitation of migration flows or by the questioning of the Spanish identity of Ceuta and Melilla, territories that are just as European as Berlin, Paris or Brussels.
Finally, I would like to stress that humanity cannot be used as an excuse for inaction in response to what has happened. It is true that the attack on Ceuta did not involve soldiers, that many of those who crossed Europe’s southern border were themselves victims and that, in fact, more than a hundred people died. But contrary to what some cynically claim, it is precisely humanity that compels us to discourage people from risking their lives at sea: this must cease to be a valid means of reaching Europe.
As many know, I aspire to become the next prime minister of Spain. Consequently, it is my duty to seek the support of the European Union and all of its member states for my country at this crucial moment. The first duty of a leader is to guarantee the safety of citizens, defend national sovereignty and uphold the credibility of institutions. But this also reflects a commitment to a certain way of understanding Europe, one that I personally share with all our allies: the responsibility to safeguard its territorial integrity and its values is a shared one. Now it is our turn to defend Ceuta, Spain and Europe.
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

Don’t get ‘locked in’ by EU rules, top nuclear adviser warns Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LONDON — Britain should not feel “locked into” pre-Brexit EU environmental rules as it tries to rapidly boost its nuclear power capacity, a top adviser to the government has warned.
John Fingleton, author of an influential government-commissioned review into how red tape is blocking new U.K. nuclear projects, said in an interview that Whitehall should not dampen efforts to boost domestic capacity through “risk aversion.”
“I think on some of the environmental things there’s a risk that people in the system legally think we’re locked into EU regulation circa 2022 when we left [the EU],” he said.
Advertisement
“When the reality is that member states within the European Union have a lot of freedom to be flexible within the EU framework. And I don’t think the U.K. should, in its discussions with the European Union, accept less flexibility than a member state has in terms of our ability to comply with that.”
The Labour government has promised to bring forward a “golden age of nuclear,” signing off on both Sizewell C and Rolls-Royce’s small modular reactors since entering office in July 2024.
But it still faces four of the U.K.’s five existing power stations closing down by 2030. Hinkley Point C will be the first new nuclear power station in the U.K. since Sizewell B opened in 1995.
Fingleton’s 2025 review urged ministers to bring forward a “radical reset” of the U.K.’s nuclear regulations, including scrapping duplication across existing environmental laws.
The U.K. is currently negotiating a post-Brexit “reset” in relations with the European Union. As part of those talks, both parties are seeking so-called “dynamic alignment” across electricity markets. This would mean the U.K. potentially following EU rules on electricity, while making it easier to trade electricity in and out of the trading bloc.
Fingleton stressed that the U.K. should not impose more stringent interpretations of these regulations than rival nuclear markets in the EU. This follows supplier EDF paying out up to £700 million to protect marine life at Hinkley Point C — including an infamous “fish disco.”
“We don’t always have a trade-off between the environment and building things, but we often create an artificial one by making it very site-specific,” Fingleton warned.
He argued that with a reformed nuclear framework developers could have instead spent “a fraction of that on other measures to improve fish in the river,” this would “have a better environmental outcome and less delay … and lower costs for nuclear.”
Message to Burnham
Fingleton also said that ministers should not rush to implement all the recommendations of his 2025 review, saying Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new crop of ministers have time to make future legislation as effective as possible — and should use it.
“I think it’s really important to get the legislation right rather than to rush it,” Fingleton said. “So probably, if I was asked: ‘Should you take an extra few months to get this right rather than rush it through?’ I would ease the time limit in order to get the right answer — because it’s important rather than urgent.”
Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s response to Fingleton’s report committed to “implementing everything [in the recommendations] by the end of 2027, subject to legislative timelines.” Governments have historically been “too cautious and too slow” on nuclear reform, Starmer wrote back in March.
“We are taking forward the recommendations of the Nuclear Regulatory Review and have published our implementation plan, with all reforms expected to be completed by the end of 2027,” a DESNZ spokesperson said.

In Germany’s east, a rare center-left star looks to stem the far right’s rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

In Germany’s east, a rare center-left star looks to stem the far right’s rise
State premier Manuela Schwesig is close to stopping the AfD’s advance ahead of Sunday’s regional elections — but at a great cost to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Manuela Schwesig, Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and German Social Democrat stands at the harbour in Rostock on September 14, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
ROSTOCK, Germany — Manuela Schwesig, a popular center-left politician, is within striking distance of stopping the far-right’s advance in the former East Germany.
Her success is coming, however, at a steep price for embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the ailing national coalition her party helps sustain.
Ahead of an election in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, Schwesig, the sitting premier of the state and the lead candidate for the left-leaning Social Democratic Party (SPD), has narrowed the far-right Alternative for Germany’s lead to just a few percentage points in some polls.
Advertisement
It’s emblematic of just how far mainstream parties have fallen across large swaths of Germany that Schwesig is considered a rare and remarkable success for simply managing to keep her SPD — a sinking party that has suffered a string of historic defeats — within range of beating the far right on Sunday in what would amount to a major upset. “Manuela Schwesig could be Germany’s savior,” ran the headline of one column in Der Spiegel magazine.
Schwesig, a former tax inspector who has risen to become one of Germany’s most well-liked politicians, has thrived by casting herself as a bulwark against the far right — employing the slogan “Frau gegen Blau” — “Woman against Blue,” a reference to the AfD’s party color.
To help her cause, she has also frequently attacked the deeply unpopular Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and their financial struggles — exhibiting a populist streak that both distances her from a historically unpopular federal coalition while blunting the AfD’s ability to capitalize on the widespread anti-Merz sentiment that propelled itsregional election victory in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.
Schwesig’s approach has effectively turned the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. Her strategy was clear during a “citizen dialogue” with a few hundred supporters held in a tent on the waterside in the port city of Rostock one evening this week.
When someone from the crowd asked what she would do to halt rising gasoline prices, Schwesig, dressed in the bright red of her SPD, called it “fully unacceptable” that Merz had failed to implement a price cap to lower costs for consumers in her rural state, where people often need to drive long distances to get to work.
“I’m pretty angry at Chancellor Merz,” she said.
Advertisement
Schwesig’s success is creating an unprecedented challenge for Merz’s conservatives — and may hasten the demise of the coalition he shares with the SPD. Recent polls show Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union has crashed to around 7% support in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in recent days, as the race increasingly morphs into a contest between the strongest mainstream candidate and the far right.
That level of support for the CDU would already constitute the worst result for the party in any state or federal election in Germany’s postwar history. A further decline would put the party at risk of failing to meet the 5% vote threshold required to enter the state parliament. A CDU collapse on this scale will almost certainly intensify internal debate that has been roiling since the summer over replacing Merz in a so-called Kanzlertausch.
Conservative leaders are blaming Schwesig’s “Frau gegen Blau” campaign for effectively taking them out of the running in the state as centrist voters rally around the SPD candidate to prevent an AfD victory.
A woman walks past an election campaign billboard that shows Manuela Schwesig, Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and German Social Democrat, prior to state elections in Rostock September 14, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
“Her attempt to keep the CDU in check with a personalized campaign weakens the political center and ultimately helps the AfD,” the party’s general secretary, Franziska Hoppermann, told the German Press Agency.
From Schwesig’s perspective, however, the CDU and Merz have no one to blame but themselves. A vote for her and the SPD, she said during her campaign event in Rostock, “is the only real chance to prevent the AfD from becoming the strongest party.”
‘Heart for the vulnerable’
Schwesig is by no means simply a local politician. Having served as Germany’s family minister for a three-and-a-half-year stint under former Chancellor Angela Merkel, she has a national profile and a high degree of influence within the SPD. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Schwesig was a strenuous advocate of importing natural gas from Russia via the Nord Stream pipelines, though she has since argued her state’s future lies with renewable energy.
Advertisement
If she’s able to defeat the AfD on Sunday, it will raise her national stature immensely — and likely lead to calls for her to run for chancellor.
But her popularity in her home state and beyond stems mainly from her ability to project herself as an empathetic, relatable politician at a time when many in Germany view their government as out of touch with the concerns of regular citizens.
“She’s close to the people,” 64-year-old Simone Kroh, a former elder caregiver, said outside of Schwesig’s campaign event in Rostock. “She’s one of us.”
Schwesig, by contrast, projects herself as a politician who understands the struggles of everyday people. Born and raised in the former East Germany, she often tells the story of how her family struggled after her father lost his job in construction around the time of the fall of the Berlin Wall — an experience many families from the region can identify with.
As premier of her state, she has pushed through measures to make pre-schools free for all families and to give young people in vocational training and seniors a €20 discount on monthly train passes — a measure she says makes a big difference in the lives of retirees who often survive on small state pensions.
Advertisement
She has also criticized Merz’s federal reform drive as punishing hard-working people, even though her own party has enabled it nationally, pushing back against one proposal in particular from the coalition to curtail early retirement for people who have worked 45 years.
“Reforms, yes, but they must be fair, and they must also be reasonable,” Schwesig told the crowd at her campaign event in Rostock. “What we currently have on the table regarding pensions, long-term care, and health care — we are not satisfied with this, and it is our duty to represent the interests of the people here.”
The message clearly resonated with many people in the crowd, particularly in a time of rising prices and slow growth. Following her talk in Rostock, supporters approached Schwesig to ask her about their financial worries. A school social worker asked whether funding for her job would be guaranteed. A university student asked whether state money to cover living costs during his studies would be cut.
For Kroh, the former elder caregiver, Schwesig’s criticisms of Merz and the government were absolutely justified.
Schwesig, she said, recognized people’s struggles.
“Merz,” she added, “just doesn’t have a heart for the vulnerable.”

Europa tiene que solucionar ahora el desastre provocado por el Gobierno español en Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Agentes de policía vigilan a un grupo de migrantes frente a la entrada del centro de acogida de Loma del Colmenar, en Ceuta, el 1 de septiembre de 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP vía Getty Images
Alberto Núñez Feijóo es el líder de la oposición en España y presidente del Partido Popular.
El pasado 30 de julio al menos 80.000 personas cruzaron a Ceuta desde Marruecos, la mayor violación de la integridad territorial que hemos vivido en las últimas décadas. Aquel desafío puso a prueba la frontera sur de España y, por tanto, la frontera sur de Europa. Continúa 50 días después. Y es imposible atisbar un horizonte cierto en que pueda resolverse. En consecuencia, es hora de preguntarnos si la respuesta está a la altura de lo que tenemos en juego.
Advertisement
Una frontera no es solo una línea sobre un mapa. Es la expresión de una comunidad política que decide qué valores protege y qué responsabilidades comparte. Cuando una frontera europea es violada, toda Europa es más débil. Cuando una frontera no se defiende adecuadamente, toda Europa se desprotege. Es lo que está ocurriendo.
La reacción del actual Gobierno español, incapaz de asumir el verdadero diagnóstico y aplicar el correcto tratamiento, me obliga a reiterar antes de nada la evidencia, tal y como ya hizo la semana pasada el presidente de Ceuta en su visita a Bruselas. No asistimos a una crisis migratoria al uso, sino a las consecuencias de una invasión procedente de Marruecos, que por ello debe hacerse responsable de haberla consentido o instigado.
En Ceuta se ha esfumado la normalidad desde hace más de seis semanas, y las escenas de caos, masificación e inseguridad deben avergonzarnos e interpelarnos. Pensar que la prolongación en el tiempo de esta situación no tendrá consecuencias es un error que no podemos permitirnos: afecta a nuestra soberanía, a nuestra capacidad colectiva para defender el Estado de Derecho, a la seguridad de los ciudadanos y a la credibilidad del proyecto europeo para garantizar su propia estabilidad.
El briefing imprescindible para quienes deciden, negocian y marcan la agenda política.
Sin duda, las autoridades estatales son las primeras que tienen que asumir el compromiso de resolver esta crisis bajo un principio irrenunciable, compartido por todos los miembros de la Unión Europea en el Pacto de Migración y Asilo: aquellos que han entrado irregularmente deben retornar. Todos. La obligación del Gobierno de España no es buscarles acomodo, sino agilizar su salida.
Dicho esto, a tenor del tiempo transcurrido y del agravamiento de los episodios de violencia en Ceuta, el conjunto de Europa debe reconocer el fracaso del Gobierno de España y ejercer la presión adecuada para que esta crisis no se enquiste, no se extienda y no se repita. Del mismo modo que ha sabido responder cuando se ha visto afectada por otras amenazas híbridas (como la energía, el comercio o la información), el ataque a nuestra frontera sur exige ahora la misma determinación.
En primer lugar, la Unión Europea debe tener interés en que España aplique, con la intensidad y agilidad debidas, todos los instrumentos europeos que permitirían el retorno. En segundo lugar, debe dilucidar por qué el propio Reino de Marruecos ha reiterado en comunicado oficial su disposición a recibir a todas las personas que accedieron el 30 de julio, mientras que hay ministros españoles sosteniendo que no existe dicha colaboración.
Advertisement
Y, en tercer lugar, debe aprovechar todos sus recursos diplomáticos para garantizar que la relación con Marruecos, socio estratégico para España y para el resto de Europa, siga desarrollándose sobre la base de la transparencia y el respeto mutuo. Del mismo que defiendo la necesidad de establecer una relación leal y estable con nuestro país vecino, creo que es de interés para toda la Unión Europea defender que no se vea debilitada por la instrumentalización de flujos migratorios o por el cuestionamiento de la españolidad de Ceuta y Melilla, territorios tan europeos como Berlín, París o Bruselas
Por último, deseo subrayar que la humanidad no puede utilizarse como excusa para la inacción tras lo ocurrido. Es cierto que el ataque sufrido en Ceuta no ocurrió con soldados, que muchas de las personas que superaron la frontera sur europea fueron víctimas y que, de hecho, más de un centenar murieron. Pero al contrario de lo que cínicamente a veces algunos proclaman, es precisamente la humanidad lo que nos obliga a disuadir a las personas de jugarse la vida en el mar: esa tiene que dejar de ser una forma válida para llegar a Europa.
Como saben, aspiro a ser el próximo presidente del Gobierno de España. En consecuencia, pedir el apoyo de la Unión Europa y de todos sus Estados miembro para mi Nación en este momento clave es mi deber. La primera obligación de un gobernante es garantizar la seguridad de sus ciudadanos, la defensa de su soberanía y la credibilidad de sus instituciones. Pero también responde a un compromiso con una forma de entender Europa, que asumo en primera persona con todos los aliados: la responsabilidad de velar por su integridad territorial y sus valores es compartida. Ahora, nos toca defender Ceuta, España, Europa.

Friedrich Merz’s endgame: All the scenarios, rated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces the threat of being ousted as soon as this weekend, just 16 months after entering office promising an ambitious reform agenda and vowing to bring back German leadership in Europe.
Ahead of two key state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin this Sunday, where Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union risks painful defeats, senior party members are privately discussing whether Germany needs a so-called Kanzlertausch — a change of chancellor — to arrest a rapidly accelerating decline in support for the government.
That same poll shows the far-right Alternative for Germany leading with 29%. The AfD also finished first in a recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, coming close to winning an absolute majority, while Merz’s CDU lost more than half of its voter support.
European and international allies are watching with bewilderment as Germany — once a bastion of stability during the 16 years of Angela Merkel’s leadership — potentially faces its second quick-fire change of leadership (Merz’s predecessor Olaf Scholz saw his ruling coalition collapse in November 2024).
Merz canceling his trip to the U.N. General Assembly next week threw the scale of his domestic crisis into sharp focus. “His presence is required in Berlin,” said a senior German official, as the chancellor fights for his political survival.
POLITICO analyzed five scenarios for how the German leadership tumult could unfold — and rated their likelihood.
1. Merz resigns lacking party support
The chancellor has convened a high-stakes meeting of his party’s leadership on Sunday at 5 p.m., which will coincide with the state election exit polls at 6 p.m. At that meeting, Merz reportedly wants to ask his party allies whether they still back him and his reform plans. If not, he wants to urge them to put forward the name of a potential successor.
By seeking the confrontation, Merz will try to exploit a weakness of his critics: There is no clear consensus on who should take over.
Advertisement
North Rhine-Westphalia’s Minister-President Hendrik Wüst (CDU) is frequently mentioned, but he has elections in his populous home state coming up in April — so the timing isn’t great for him. An alternative would be Markus Söder of the Christian-Social Union, the CDU’s Bavarian sister party, but he isn’t short of critics. Other, less probable potential candidates are Hesse’s Minister President Boris Rhein (CDU) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU).
However, should the elections Sunday be a total disaster for Merz’ conservatives — the party could even miss the 5% hurdle to enter parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, for the first time in any state election — frustration within the CDU/CSU could boil over and lead to broad calls for Merz to resign.
The showdown does not necessarily have to happen Sunday but could follow within the next days or weeks. Should Merz accept that fate, he could inform German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier of his intention to step down. Steinmeier would then most likely ask him to remain in office in a caretaker function until a new chancellor is elected by parliament.
However, this ain’t easy: Any successor for Merz would need the votes of the CDU/CSU’s coalition partner, the Social Democrats, who would likely ask concessions in return — triggering a time-consuming renegotiation of the coalition treaty. It also means Merz could still remain in power for months and represent Germany on the international stage, for example in EU budget talks.
Adding to the complications, the coalition’s majority in the Bundestag is thin: There’s always a risk of defectors during the secret ballot, as happened to Merz himself during the first election round last year.
Likelihood:
Advertisement
2. No-confidence vote forces Merz out
Pressure from within the party cannot actually force Merz to resign. For historical reasons, the German constitution provides elected chancellors with a very stable position.
Given that, the only possibility to forcibly oust him would be through a no-confidence vote. However, the German constitution requires that such a vote must be “constructive,” meaning an opposing candidate must at the same time receive a majority to replace Merz.
This makes such a scenario very unlikely. Apart from the negative public image that the CDU/CSU would display by openly seeking to topple their chancellor in parliament, it seems unlikely that any candidate could immediately get the required votes amid the thin majority of the coalition and the negotiations that would likely have to happen first with the SPD.
Likelihood:
3. Merz seeks a confidence vote
Merz could also call for a vote of confidence himself, seeking to show that he still has sufficient support within the coalition — or otherwise open the door to snap elections. It’s a scenario that has happened in the past, most recently with Scholz in December 2024.
Should Merz lose the vote, Steinmeier could decide to dissolve the Bundestag within 21 days — but only if Merz proposes it to him. However, given the strong position of the AfD in current polls, neither the CDU nor SPD has an interest in new elections at this stage.
Advertisement
It would also be possible to elect a new chancellor within those 21 days, if there is a quick majority for a successor.
All in all, not too likely.
Likelihood:
4. Far-right support against Merz
Theoretically, it would be possible for a Merz successor to get the necessary majority in parliament by receiving indirect backing from the AfD (minority government) or even form a coalition with the far-right party.
CDU/CSU and AfD would enjoy a comfortable majority in parliament, but it would mean breaking with Germany’s anti-far-right “firewall.”
However, it’s an idea that is unacceptable for many in the party leadership. Merz himself has also ruled out staying in power with far-right support.
Advertisement
Likelihood:
5. Merz clings to power
Contrary to the Saxony-Anhalt election aftermath, where the chancellor seemed discouraged and delivered an unconvincing speech in the Bundestag, he now appears to want to fight for his leadership.
Merz’s position was bolstered by a letter Wednesday from eight center-right state premiers — including Wüst and Rhein, but not Söder — in which they wrote that “Germany needs reliability and action” instead of “discussions about personnel.” The letter also refers to elections in France, Italy, Poland, Spain and Greece next year, noting that “a stable and strong Germany” is now needed in Europe.
The letter is far from an unwavering support for Merz; in fact, it doesn’t even mention his name and may also be an attempt to quell internal debates ahead of the important elections on Sunday. However, it may also mean that there isn’t sufficient appetite among senior party leaders to oust Merz at this point. Instead, the party may seek to close ranks and regain popularity by urging the SPD to pursue even more vigorous social reforms.

Farage aide caught in donor sting attended Egypt retreat with JL Partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage is handed a sign by Dan Jukes ahead of the local elections in May, in central London on April 10, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — Former senior Nigel Farage aide Dan Jukes went on an all-expenses-paid trip to Egypt with the polling company JL Partners in December 2025, according to an internal email seen by POLITICO.
Jukes joined a JL Partners staff retreat at a resort in El Quseir on the Red Sea in December 2025 and gave a talk for the company, which subsequently released opinion polls publicly without disclosing that they were financed by supposed donors to Reform.
The trip provides a window into the extent of the business relationship between Jukes and JL Partners, which provided him with travel, meals and accommodation. One person with knowledge of the trip said he also dined with the company and took a limousine from the airport to the hotel, also at JL Partners’ expense.
Advertisement
During the trip, Jukes was asked what a Reform government would want from a polling company and replied: “Showing that we’re winning,” according to the same person.
JL Partners director James Johnson shared several pictures of the Egypt excursion on social media, but Jukes did not appear in any of them. A spokesperson for JL Partners said that Jukes had been invited in a personal capacity and, like other guest speakers, had expenses covered, adding: “Anyone familiar with these sorts of events will know that no inference can reasonably be drawn from the participation of any individual speaker.”
A Reform UK spokesman acknowledged that Jukes, who resigned from his official role earlier this month, was at the gathering but also said it was not on behalf of the party, saying: “Mr Jukes attended the event in question in his capacity as a political consultant and not as part of any political activities in connection with his membership of Reform UK. Reform UK had no involvement and no breach of electoral law has taken place.”
A representative for Jukes said: “There is an active police investigation which has just been announced and as such our client is not commenting further until that is concluded. For the record, he denies any allegations of wrongdoing.”
Caught on camera
Jukes served as Farage’s closest aide and communications director until earlier this month, when he stepped down in the wake of an undercover sting. He was filmed making arrangements for a fictitious wealthy American benefactor and his son to pay for a set of polls by JL Partners on behalf of Reform that were published in British national newspapers.
The polls were released without disclosing the ties to Reform, prompting an inquiry by the British Polling Council, the industry watchdog, which specifies that all research carried out by pollsters which enters the public domain “must include reference to the … client commissioning the survey” as well as dates, methodology and sample size.
Advertisement
Johnson, who founded JL Partners after working as an adviser to Theresa May in No. 10, was shown in the undercover footage broadcast by Channel 4 News as saying Jukes was his “main contact” at Reform and had given him instructions on the kind of polling he wanted, while Jukes was recorded saying he had a “really, really discreet” relationship with Johnson.
Under electoral law, members of political parties in Great Britain are required to register any overseas visits with the Electoral Commission if they are connected to their political activities as party members. POLITICO could not find a record of any such declaration.
“There are clearly major transparency gaps that must be addressed if the public are to have confidence in what the polls tell us,” said Tim Picton of the campaign group Spotlight on Corruption. “The Electoral Commission should now clarify whether this trip was subject to declaration requirements, otherwise the rules will need tightening to close this loophole.”
Steve Goodrich from Transparency International added: “There is a clear public interest in knowing that a pollster who provided off-the-books services to a political party also gave them other freebies.”
More polls
POLITICO reported last week on other instances in which JL Partners had carried out polling which gained press coverage without disclosing who had paid for it.
In response to the original report by Channel 4 News, JL Partners said it was undertaking an internal review to “eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.”
Advertisement
A Reform UK Spokesman said the party “denies any wrongdoing” in relation to the undercover sting, while Farage has said he faces a “complainants’ society” in which his party is “under investigation every day for virtually everything we do”.
Reform UK has been embroiled in a series of financial scandals in recent months which are currently under investigation by the police and parliamentary standards commissioner.

Taiwan's China Airlines expects strong cargo revenue in Q4
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:55:33 UTC
10:55:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's China Airlines expects monthly cargo revenue to remain at high levels in the fourth quarter as strong demand for air freight continues.
The carrier’s cargo revenue reached NT$7.52 billion (US$236 million) in August, up 36% from the same period a year earlier. It expects monthly revenue to reach around NT$8 billion in the fourth quarter, according to LTN and CNA.
President Chen Han-ming (陳漢銘) said the fourth quarter is traditionally the peak season for air cargo. The company is focusing its freighter capacity on cargo markets with the strongest demand, particularly fresh produce, drones, and heavy cargo, he said.
The carrier also handles temperature-controlled shipments, live animals, and smart cargo operations. It plans to increase the amount of freight carried in the belly compartments of passenger aircraft.
Liu An-chih (劉安琪), general manager of China Airlines’ cargo operations in Amsterdam, said Taiwan’s electronics industry generates significant air freight traffic. This includes shipments of semiconductor components, AI servers, and consumer electronics.
About 30% of Taiwan’s air cargo consists of semiconductor components and other goods shipped from the country. Another 60-70% is cargo from other parts of Asia that is consolidated in Taiwan before being sent to Europe and the US, Liu said.
Liu added that cargo traffic rights are generally easier to obtain internationally than passenger traffic rights. Unlike passenger flights, which typically operate as round trips, cargo flights can operate in a single direction, while air freight can also contribute to economic growth, he said.

Epstein survivors sue his estate over child pornography collection
NEW YORK – Two women whose images as girls were found in pornography seized from Jeffrey Epstein filed a class action lawsuit on Sept 16 seeking damages from the late sex offender’s estate for individuals featured in his collection of thousands of pictures and videos of child sexual abuse material.
The lawsuit seeks at least US$6 million (S$7.66 million) on behalf of more than 40 people, some of whom were in Epstein’s so-called “modelling book”, a collection of sexualised images of children seized by federal investigators in 2019 from his New York home, according to the filing in Manhattan federal district court.
Others were shown in thousands of downloaded videos and images of child sexual abuse material and other pornography taken from the late financier’s properties, according to the action.
The lawsuit aims to broaden legal reckoning against Epstein beyond women who have sued his estate over sexual assaults, to those he exploited as children through pictures he and his associates took of them or obtained.
In some cases, the images were then distributed to others.
The lawsuit was filed against Epstein’s former attorney Darren Indyke and his former accountant Richard Kahn, the co-executors of the Epstein estate.
Daniel Weiner, a lawyer representing Indyke, declined to comment. An attorney for Kahn did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
One of the plaintiffs, identified as Jane Doe, alleges Epstein stole partially nude photographs of her taken when she was 12.
The other, using the pseudonym Amy, says she is featured in child sexual abuse material seized from Epstein’s properties in 2019 that is still being traded today.
Hillary Nappi, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said the lawsuit could potentially involve thousands of class members.
She said in an interview that most people pictured in Epstein’s collection had never been identified.
The lawsuit calls for Epstein’s estate and federal authorities to work with the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children to identify individuals in the collection and inform them.
It asks for the estate to pay class action members US$150,000 each, as well as other penalties.
Epstein was convicted of soliciting sex from a minor in 2008 and charged with sex trafficking of minors in 2019, months before he was found dead in a New York jail cell, his death ruled a suicide.
He was never prosecuted for creating, obtaining or distributing child sexual abuse material. REUTERS

In Yaroslavl, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries is on fire after a drone attack — OSINT
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out at the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery after a drone attack, OSINT analyst ASTRA claims. The plant processes 15 million tonnes of oil annually.
In Yaroslavl, Russia, a fire broke out at the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery during the night of September 17 following a drone attack. The facility is among Russia’s five largest oil refineries. OSINT analyst ASTRA located the site of the fire using photographs taken by eyewitnesses, UNN reports.
Details
Mikhail Yevrayev, governor of the Yaroslavl region, announced a UAV threat overnight and said that a Ukrainian attack had been repelled. Part of the M-8 highway on the outskirts of Yaroslavl toward Moscow was closed, and public transport routes were changed.
At the same time, Russian authorities did not officially report the consequences of the attack. Based on the geolocation of footage published by eyewitnesses, ASTRA claims that the fire broke out specifically on the premises of the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery.
One of Russia’s largest oil refineries
The facility processes approximately 15 million tonnes of oil per year. The plant produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene and jet fuel, as well as lubricants, bitumen, liquefied gases and fuel oil.
In 2026, fires were recorded at the facility at least 8 times following attacks — on March 28, April 26, May 8 and 22, July 6 and 16, and August 6 and 28.
During the massive attack on Yaroslavl on August 28, according to the regional governor, 1 person was killed and another 27 were injured.

WARSAW, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's run at the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup ended in the round of 16 on Wednesday after a 5-4 penalty shootout defeat to Italy following a 1-1 draw after extra time in Sosnowiec, Poland.
Italy enjoyed more possession early and took the lead in the 34th minute through Karen Appiah. China looked to respond on the counterattack but went into halftime a goal down.
China increased the pressure after the restart and leveled in the 73rd minute when Wang Dantong sent a looping effort from outside the area that goalkeeper Elena Belli failed to hold. The goal was officially recorded as an own goal.
Neither side found a winner in the remainder of normal time or during the 30 minutes of extra time, sending the match to penalties. Italy converted all five of its kicks, while China missed its fifth attempt, allowing the European side to advance to the quarterfinals.
China captain and goalkeeper Liu Chen said the team should be encouraged by its fighting spirit.
"We need to go back and look at where we fell short," Liu said. "To equalize and take the match to a penalty shootout, we already did very well. There is still plenty of room for us to improve."
Head coach Wang Jun said the performance showed progress for Chinese women's football, contrasting it with the senior team's 2-0 round-of-16 defeat to Italy at the 2019 World Cup.
"After 40 days of player selection and training, followed by the tournament, I think these players have given everything," Wang said. "By facing teams from different continents, we showed the positive and enterprising side of Chinese women's football. There may still be a gap in quality, but we can take things step by step. This tournament is a sign that we are starting to fight back."
In other round-of-16 action on Wednesday, Brazil beat the United States 5-4 on penalties after a 1-1 draw following extra time, Spain defeated Portugal 2-0, and South Korea edged Argentina 1-0.
Brazil will face Spain in the quarterfinals, while Italy meets South Korea. ■

Fiji declares national HIV emergency as Pacific nation grapples with surge in cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:43:49 UTC
10:43:49 KST

Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency amid a spike in infections as the Pacific nation grapples with a correlating rise in methamphetamine use.
The country’s health and medical services minister, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu, said in a statement on social media that an outbreak-level response was no longer sufficient to address what he described an “epidemic”.
“Today I am formally declaring a national health emergency in Fiji,” he said. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent coordinated response our country now needs.”
The health minister said the government estimates that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is now living with HIV.
“Five years ago, the estimate was one in 167. In 2025, we recorded 2,060 new HIV diagnoses,” he said, adding that one in 50 pregnant women has HIV.
The emergency declaration followed on from a cabinet decision on 9 September and would require a coordinated response, he added.
Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally, according to UNAIDS, which said that new infections spiked 12-fold between 2010 and 2025.
Fiji’s location as a drug-running hub coupled with the escalating use of methamphetamine locally has fuelled the rapid spread of HIV, a situation worsened by unsafe injecting and a lack of access to clean needles. Low health awareness, cultural stigma and inadequate testing and treatment have exacerbated the crisis.
Among HIV cases in Fiji with a known mode of transmission, over half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, according to UNAIDS.
Of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in Fiji in 2025, only 39% were aware of their HIV status and only 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment, the UN said.
Responding to the emergency declaration, UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyima said in a statement on Wednesday that the situation was a “a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over”.
“HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” said Byanyima. “Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response.”
The UN agency said it welcomed plans to introduce a needle and syringe programme, with legislative amendments expected to go before parliament, as well as efforts to expand prevention, testing and access to treatment.

From 'cashies' to convictions: The ATO's $2.7 million warning shot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:41:25 UTC
10:41:25 KST

Key Points
- More than 350 individuals or businesses have been successfully prosecuted as part of a shadow economy crackdown.
- The prosecutions related to tax avoidance and underpayment of entitlements.
Hundreds of people and businesses have been prosecuted for tax offences, with millions of dollars in fines handed down as authorities crack down on the shadow economy.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) on Thursday revealed non-lodgment prosecutions against "dodgy shadow economy operators" had risen by 80 per cent over the past two years, as it warned those who broke the rules would be held accountable.
The shadow economy involves both legal and illegal economic activity, including demanding cash payments for work, known as "cashies", to avoid tax, and underpayment of entitlements such as superannuation.
The ATO said more than 350 individuals or businesses had been successfully prosecuted in the past two years, resulting in more than $2.7 million in fines.
In the 2025-26 financial year, Queensland accounted for 28 per cent of non-lodgment prosecutions, followed by Western Australia (26 per cent) and NSW (20 per cent).
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
ATO assistant commissioner Tony Goding said avoiding tax and super obligations was seen by some as a victimless crime, but came at a cost to the community.
"The shadow economy undermines legitimate businesses and reduces revenue that would otherwise fund essential public services that support all Australians," he said.
"It doesn't matter what profession you're in, if you're a tradie, hairdresser or cafe owner, and you deliberately avoid paying the right amount of tax, you risk more than financial penalties."
Of the prosecutions, more than 305 resulted in convictions, representing a nearly 60 per cent increase from 2024–25 and 2025–26 financial years.
Goding said the figures demonstrated the ATO was holding those who break the rules to account.
"People who deliberately break the law risk their reputation and future, and the impact of a criminal conviction extends beyond the courtroom," he said.
"The cost of deliberately not lodging isn't measured in fines alone.
"We've seen business owners receive criminal convictions, lose the trust of their customers and community, and in some cases, lose the very business they were trying to keep afloat. For more serious offending, time in prison is even a possibility.
"Our message to the community is clear: deliberately ignoring your obligations comes at a significant cost."
A 2016 government task force estimated Australia's shadow economy could be worth as much as 3 per cent of GDP, or approximately $50 billion in 2016 figures.
More recent ATO estimates show the shadow economy has continued to grow, reaching up to 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2023.

Why Israel wants more heavy bombs from the US and why the sale is controversial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:40:00 UTC
10:40:00 KST

Why Israel wants more heavy bombs from the US and why the sale is controversial
David M. Halbfinger and John Ismay
JERUSALEM – The Trump administration’s decision to send 60,000 powerful one-ton bombs to Israel as part of a US$2.8 billion (S$3.58 billion) deal – one of the largest arms agreements ever – will allow Israel to replenish its supply of a munition it considers vital.
The weapons became the focus of great tension between the Biden administration and Israel after one-ton bombs were widely used in densely populated areas of the Gaza Strip where Israel had steered civilians for their safety.
With opposition to military assistance to Israel growing in Washington, such a huge sale of heavy bombs, paid for by the US government, could be an effort by the administration to stock up the Israeli arsenal before political shifts in the United States make such shipments impossible, analysts said.
The Israeli military pivoted towards the use of the one-ton bombs after the Hamas-led attack against southern Israel on Oct 7, 2023, drastically changing its shopping list, US government data show. In 2025, Israel bought nearly eight times as many one-ton bombs from the United States as it did from 2012 to 2015.
Israel’s emphasis on buying and using some of the largest bombs currently made runs counter to that of most other modern militaries, which have been making their aerial munitions smaller and even more accurate in the hopes of limiting civilian casualties during combat.
Israel has used a vast amount of the one-ton bombs in large part to target the tunnel network Hamas developed in Gaza for its fighters, weapons and command centres. Israeli officials have said that Hamas fighters intentionally embed themselves among civilians, forcing the Israeli military to risk killing civilians.
A New York Times investigation in December 2023 found that the Israeli military routinely used one-ton bombs in the weeks immediately after the 2023 attack and identified more than 200 instances of Israel dropping the powerful munitions, including in densely populated areas.
Here is a closer look at the transaction and its significance.
What bombs are being sold?
According to a US official, Israel will receive 20,000 Mk-84 bombs and another 20,000 BLU-117 bombs. The two types of one-ton bombs are nearly identical.
The bombs are highly versatile, experts say. They can be set to detonate above ground, sending shrapnel 300m in any direction, or, with delayed fuses, set to explode underground. They can be fitted with kits that allow them to hit targets with precision and from a long range. The craters from one-ton bombs can be up to 15m deep.
In addition to the 40,000 Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs, Israel will also receive 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads, which explode on delay after busting through a surface like soil, rock or concrete, the US official said. They also weigh a ton each, but because their casings are thicker and far heavier, they carry far less explosive power than the Mk-84 and BLU-117 bombs.
According to the US Army office that oversees bomb procurement, “ideal targets” for one-ton bombs “are buildings, rail yards and lines of communication”. The 110kg and 220kg bombs more typically used by the US military are designed for “soft, fragment sensitive targets” such as troops, fuel storage tanks and radars, the office said.
The US$2.8 billion purchase is being funded from the Pentagon’s budget for foreign military sales. That means the money effectively flows from US taxpayers to Israel’s military and then to US munitions manufacturers.
Can Congress block the sale?
Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Sept 16 that he had placed a hold on the proposed sale, citing concerns about the bombs’ potential use in densely populated areas in Gaza and Lebanon. Such holds are part of an informal congressional review process and are not necessarily binding.
To stop a weapons transfer at this stage, a resolution of disapproval would have to pass both the House and Senate and then overcome a certain veto by the president. That would require a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers, which has never happened.
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have bypassed congressional review of weapons sales to Israel by invoking emergency authority. The Biden administration used it twice in December 2023, while the Trump administration invoked it in 2025 to expedite additional arms sales to Israel.
In addition, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has repeatedly exercised emergency powers to proceed with such transactions. In March, he bypassed Congress to send US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) in weaponry to Israel, including more than 35,000 of the same kinds of one-ton bombs.
Some congressional Democrats have called for ending US military aid, or even all aid, to Israel in response to the huge civilian toll of Israel’s war in Gaza.
Anger toward Israel is also growing on the right.
Former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, an outspoken critic of Israel, wrote in a social media post on Sept 15 that there was no justification for supplying Israel with so many of the bombs it had used in killing Palestinians in Gaza. He said it would only embolden Israel elsewhere.
“The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region,” he wrote. “If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.”
Why does Israel need these bombs?
Experts describe one-ton bombs as a workhorse of the Israeli air force, which has operated in seven theatres of conflict over the past few years: Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Iran, Syria, Yemen and Iraq.
Those campaigns have severely depleted the air force’s munitions. One former air force commander, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information, said that Israel had learnt it was necessary to amass a multiyear supply, in case of delays in replenishing stocks, and that 40,000 one-ton bombs were considered a full supply.
“The traditional concept of Israel’s defence doctrine was short wars,” said a retired major general, Amos Yadlin, a former deputy air force commander and former head of Israeli military intelligence. “What we saw in the last three years was Israel was dragged – and maybe even with some contributions of Israeli decisions – to a long war. And if you’re in a strategy of long wars, you need more ammunition.”
Why are these bombs controversial?
The New York Times reported in December 2023 that in the first six weeks of the war in Gaza, Israel routinely used one-ton bombs in parts of the enclave that it had designated as safe for civilians, including densely populated areas. The Times identified 208 craters of at least 12m across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel had ordered civilians to move to for their own safety.
Munitions experts say that bombs of that size are almost never dropped by US forces in densely populated areas, and US military officers have said such bombs are unsuitable for urban combat. Since the Vietnam War, US forces have used one-ton bombs sparingly.
Israel reaches for them far more often. It says that the heavy bombs are necessary to strike enemy forces hiding in large buildings or in underground tunnels, and that its military always seeks to avoid or minimise civilian casualties.
The one-ton bombs became a source of friction between former US president Joe Biden and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May 2024, when Biden held up a shipment of 1,800 bombs in an effort to deter Israel from attacking the city of Rafah, where many displaced Palestinians were sheltering.
Israel attacked and destroyed much of Rafah anyway. The Trump White House released the shipment of bombs days after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
What does the transaction say about US-Israel relations?
At a time when the relationship between Trump and Netanyahu has been on a roller-coaster ride, the political dimensions of proceeding with such a large deal for heavy bombs cannot be ignored.
Chuck Freilich, a former Israeli deputy national security adviser, said the deal should not be seen as an attempt to aid Netanyahu’s campaign for a new term in October’s election, in which he is behind in the polls. “If it was a new deal for F-35s, it would be worth a headline,” he said.
Still, Yadlin said, the arms deal sends an important signal to Israel’s enemies that the United States still has its back. “This is a way to show that, even if there are some differences, on the basic security of Israel, the US is still a very strong ally,” he said.
But Israel’s defenders are also mindful that the political winds have shifted and that it is not likely to become any easier to obtain such munitions from the United States in the foreseeable future, especially with the 2028 election nearing.
Jesse Weinberg, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said that officials in Israel and many of Israel’s supporters in Washington were looking to “front-load” military aid to Israel “because we don’t know what the construction of the next Congress is going to be – and then there’s the eye to 2028”.
“The view at the Kirya,” he said of Israel’s military headquarters, “in the prime minister’s office and also among Israel’s supporters on the Hill, is that if you want to move things, now is the time.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Crew-13 mission comprising Russian cosmonaut Teteryatnikov due in early October — NASA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:38:43 UTC
10:38:43 KST

NEW YORK, September 17. /TASS/. The start of the Crew 13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS), which comprises Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, is scheduled for early October, NASA said.
"NASA and SpaceX are now targeting as soon as early October for the launch of the Crew-13 mission," the US space agency said on its website.
The launch was initially scheduled for September 12 but was postponed to address an oxidizer leak in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system, which was detected during standard pre-launch spacecraft processing.
Teteryatnikov will travel to the ISS with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk. Teteryatnikov and Kutryk will serve as mission specialists, Watkins as commander and Delaney as pilot.

ICE agent charged with assault, lying about shooting, arrested in Minnesota
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:38:06 UTC
10:38:06 KST

ICE agent charged with assault, lying about shooting, arrested in Minnesota
- ICE agent Christian Castro was arrested in Minneapolis on assault and false reporting charges for shooting Venezuelan Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during a 2023 immigration operation.
- Castro allegedly lied about the shooting, claiming an attack disproved by video, and faced extradition issues between Texas and Minnesota governors.
- He is suspended by DHS, faces state and federal court appearances, and a civil rights investigation is ongoing into the incident.
AI generated
MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota – A federal immigration officer wanted on assault charges for shooting and wounding a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis was arrested there on Sept 16, eight months after a confrontation that became a flashpoint over US President Donald Trump’s deportation sweeps.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro was taken into custody by agents of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in downtown Minneapolis and was booked into the Hennepin County jail on his outstanding arrest warrant, the agency said.
Castro had been released on bond from federal custody earlier in September, after an initial appearance in US District Court in McAllen, Texas, on charges of lying to investigators about the circumstances of the Jan 14 shooting.
Under an agreement with Minnesota law enforcement, Castro voluntarily drove to Minneapolis from Texas to turn himself in to the state authorities at his attorney’s office but ended up being arrested minutes before he was due to arrive, the lawyer Daniel Gerdts told Reuters.
Another lawyer representing the ICE agent, Rolando Cantu, said his client always had intended to answer to the charges in Minneapolis.
He disputed Hennepin County prosecutors’ assertions that Castro might flee to Mexico, saying: “He wants his day in court.”
The federal indictment charging him with making false statements marked the first US Justice Department prosecution of a federal law enforcement officer accused of wrongdoing arising from the massive Minneapolis ICE deployment dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
That operation, part of President Donald Trump’s wider immigration crackdown, drew weeks of protests and clashes between ICE and demonstrators, leading to the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal agents.
Castro already faced state assault charges in Minnesota stemming from the confrontation in which he shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, in the leg through the door of the man’s apartment while children were present inside the home.
The state charges also include false reporting of a crime after Castro allegedly told superiors at the US Department of Homeland Security that Sosa-Celis and others attacked him with a snow shovel and broom, which was disproved by video evidence.
Initial efforts to arrest Castro were thwarted when the ICE agent returned to his home state of Texas, leading Minnesota officials to issue a warrant for his arrest.
Castro was apprehended by Texas Rangers, but Texas governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and supporter of Trump’s mass deportation sweeps, refused to sign extradition papers sent by Minnesota governor Tim Walz, a Democrat.
Abbott questioned whether Castro could be considered a fugitive from justice, and thus subject to extradition,because DHS had reassigned him to his home state of Texas after the Minneapolis shooting.
The ICE agent ultimately spent 90 days in a Texas county jail and was released on Aug 27 after a federal judge in Texas denied a request from Minnesota to immediately order his extradition.
Castro, who Minnesota officials branded a flight risk. He was re-arrested in Texas following his federal grand jury indictment in early September.
DHS has suspended Castro from ICE, and a person familiar with the case has said a civil rights investigation into the Sosa-Celis shooting had been opened.
Castro was expected to make his first state court appearance in Minneapolis on Sept 17.
He will then make an initial appearance in US District Court in neighbouring St. Paul, the state capital, on the morning of Sept 18 to face charges in the federal indictment.
“Governor Abbott’s attempt to shield Mr Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who brought the state case, said in a statement. REUTERS

Trump threatens EU with further sanctions over Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:35:00 UTC

Trump threatens EU with further sanctions over Canada
September 17, 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday responded to the European Union's plans to add Canada as an associate member with threats and ridicule.
During her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was opening the door for Canada to become its first associate member.
Such a relationship to the bloc does not currently exist and would have to be created from scratch.
How did Trump respond to Canada's EU associate membership idea?
In comments to reporters on Wednesday, Trump said the idea could become a "hostile act." He threatened to impose sanctions on the EU in response.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina.
The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."
Why is Canada turning to the EU?
The potential Canadian EU associate membership comes as Trump, during his second term in office, has shaken Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor to the core.
Canada was among the first victims of Trump's tariff policy.
Tensions escalated between Ottawa and Washington after trade talks broke down last month, with Trump imposing further sanctions on Canada and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowing to respond in kind.
Washington's transatlantic ties have also suffered under Trump, most notably after the US president's push to take control of the Arctic island of Greenland, which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The EU was also hit by Trump's wide tariffs, as were most countries worldwide, but the two sides reached a trade agreement to bring them down.
