Malaysian PM Offers to Host Myanmar’s President in Refugee Repatriation Push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:35:00 UTC
10:35:00 KST

Malaysia is set to welcome Myanmar’s military-appointed president for an official visit, in a bid to expedite the return of thousands of Rohingya Muslim refugees.
Speaking on a podcast yesterday, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he had invited Min Aung Hlaing to the country, on the condition that Myanmar agrees to take back citizens currently in Malaysia.
“I invited him to say we can be friends, we can trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them [the refugees] back,” Reuters reported.
If the trip eventuates, Malaysia will become the fifth member state of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It will also become the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to take such a step.
The six maritime ASEAN states – Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, and Timor-Leste – have generally been more critical of Myanmar’s military than the nations of the mainland, since the coup of 2021.
Malaysia in particular has been one of the most outspoken, repeatedly expressing frustration at the Myanmar military’s refusal to cease hostilities and counseling a harder ASEAN line.
Anwar said yesterday that Malaysia was not ready to recognize Myanmar’s new government, but needed an authority to negotiate with on returning refugees.
“To me, that’s better diplomacy than just shouting angrily at Myanmar. Who’s going to take them? Where do we send them? They don’t even have Myanmar citizenship,” he said. “We, following ASEAN, don’t want direct relations with Myanmar. So who are we supposed to negotiate with?”
While Malaysia’s hard line on Myanmar has softened somewhat over the past year, Anwar is under pressure to respond to the growing public hostility toward the Rohingya in Malaysia.
Large numbers of Rohingya have come to the country since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya asylum seekers are currently registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, around half of the agency’s total, although Malaysia does not recognize them as refugees.
While the Rohingya were initially welcomed by their co-religionists, public opinion has soured in recent years as the population has continued to grow. During the course of 2026, in particular, Rohingya have faced an upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric and public hostility, particularly online.
This has put pressure on Malaysia’s government to advance long-stalled talks aimed at the refugees’ repatriation. The country’s immigration authorities have already reached a deal with Naypyidaw for the “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 refugees, which make up around half of the 10,388 Myanmar nationals currently being held at immigration detention depots.
The first 1,476 of this group is scheduled to return to Myanmar on September 29 aboard two Myanmar Navy warships and a hospital ship. In announcing the repatriation, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the refugees’ presence had become a “major financial burden, caused serious social problems, and created a real security threat to the country.”
Anwar said yesterday that the government was ultimately planning to send back 200,000 people, and that this could be carried out in stages if Myanmar was unable to receive all of them at once.
“If they cannot take 200,000 at one go, take them back in stages and we will help resolve it,” he said.
While the Malaysian side is narrowly focused on reaching a deal on refugees, Myanmar likely has wider diplomatic goals in mind. Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing has been on a regional charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of foreign investment to revive Myanmar’s war-damaged economy. This has involved state visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, and also to the four mainland ASEAN member states.
In particular, he has prioritized the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Since late 2021, the bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
While Myanmar will no doubt seek to milk the Malaysia invitation for maximum legitimacy – a presidential spokesperson said this week that these countries “fully support Myanmar’s resumption of its active engagement in ASEAN as before” – the success of refugee repatriations remains very much in doubt.
The first question is whether the returns will be in any way “voluntary.” The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has already expressed concerns about the September 29 repatriation, saying that the ongoing conflict and repression made it difficult to guarantee refugees’ safe return.
“Under customary international law – a binding obligation on all states – no one should be sent to a country where their rights or freedoms may be at risk,” UNHCR told Reuters last month. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, and take place in conditions of safety and dignity.”
The second issue is whether the Naypyidaw government even has the authority to negotiate the return of Rohingya to Rakhine State. Most of the state is now under the control of the Arakan Army (AA), an ethnic Rakhine nationalist organization that is fighting for – and, since late 2023, has largely achieved – autonomy from the central state. This includes the northern townships of Maungdaw and Buthidaung, where a large proportion of Rohingya formerly lived.
How these refugees are to be returned remains very much an open question. A recent Myanmar military offensive aimed at seizing back territory from the AA around the state capital of Sittwe appears to have ground to a halt, leaving the central state with precarious footholds in Rakhine.

Reading a text that describes the beauty of a summer day, we automatically begin to imagine it. The…

Reading a text that describes the beauty of a summer day, we automatically begin to imagine it. The warm breeze, the sound of a fountain running, the air rich with the scent of growth, the blinding sunlight, the taste of ice cream — through words, these things can come to life as though we were actually experiencing them. But if we were then asked if our imagined experience was real, we would likely respond that it was not.
Without prompting, the distance between an imagined experience and a real one might go unnoticed. The day described might feel so close to one from memory that we relive that past reality as part of our imagined experience. This is the power of language, to transport us through the representation of old experiences into new versions of those experiences, while drawing our attention to some particular aspect of them.

Good El Nino? How a bad monsoon left Delhi drenched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:08:43 UTC
10:08:43 KST

Delhi had a season’s rainfall surplus of 8% in a meteorological subdivision (Haryana)
NEW DELHI: The capital defied the odds this monsoon. As of Sept 16, Delhi had a season's rainfall surplus of 8% in a meteorological subdivision (Haryana) that's reeling under a 23% deficit and a region (northwest India) that has logged a 10% shortfall. The season's peculiar rainfall pattern indicates that a strengthening El Nino as well as climate change may have played a role in giving the capital an unlikely monsoon bounty.A look at the season's district-level rainfall map of the region shows Delhi literally at the edge of the good monsoon zone this year (see graphic). Just north of the capital lies a swathe of deficient districts starting with neighbouring Sonipat (-32%) and Rohtak (-47%) and all the way up to Hoshiarpur (-53%) and Kapurthala (-69%) in Punjab - a cluster of over 30 rain-starved districts in Haryana and Punjab as well as adjoining Rajasthan, Himachal and west UP.
So how did Delhi turn into a wet pocket next to a rain-deficient region? The answer lies in the way low-pressure systems coming from Bay of Bengal shifted direction this season, probably under the influence of El Nino, and how their interactions with westerly disturbances uniquely aided rains in Delhi-NCR.
Wet capital
A majority of monsoon rainfall in northwest and central India happens under the influence of moisture-laden low-pressure systems (LPSs), including depressions, travelling inland from Bay of Bengal.
Contrary to what one would expect, the number of such systems does not decrease in an El Nino year. In fact, a 2024 study in Climate Dynamics showed that the number of Bay of Bengal depressions increased in El Nino years in the 1979-2020 period, averaging 3.9 during July-Aug versus 2.4 in normal years.This year there were 10 LPSs, including four depressions in July-Aug, against a normal of less than nine.What generally changes in an El Nino year is the direction of the LPSs. "In El Nino years, there is subsidence of air over south India and its adjoining northern parts. This prevents formation of LPSs in the southern latitudes, say in central Bay of Bengal, which would normally move towards the north Andhra-south Odisha coast," said IMD director general Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.Here's where Delhi benefited, particularly in Aug, when as many as six LPSs, including two depressions, impacted India. With a northward shift, most of these systems entered inland over north Odisha-Bengal and tracked north-northwest, affecting Odisha, Bengal, Jharkhand, UP, Uttarakhand and the Delhi region, with lesser impact in Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab.
There was another factor in play, likely linked to climate change. WDs are moist wind systems moving east from the Mediterranean region that usually bring wet weather to north India in winter through early summer. Historically, WDs are rare during the monsoons as the jet stream, which causes the disturbance, typically migrates north of the Himalayas by April-May. However, in recent years, the jet stream has persistently been retreating late, a trend scientists attribute to global warming. This year, there were 16 WDs in the June-Aug period - eight in Aug alone, as per IMD.There were several instances of the easterly monsoon system interacting with a WD, intensifying rainfall over parts of north India, including Delhi. For instance, monsoon's onset over the capital on July 2 happened during an active WD spell. The heaviest rain spells in Delhi (July 8-9, July 29, Aug 7-8, Aug 25) occurred when both a monsoon system and a WD were simultaneously active in the region. These interactions also brought heavy rains in west UP and left a catastrophic footprint in the hills - the Bandipora (J&K) cloudburst, fatal flash floods in Chamba (HP) and forced closure of around 290 roads across HP and Uttarakhand - but don't appear to have majorly impacted Haryana and Punjab.

Israel and Morocco agree to open embassies after New York talks
Israel and Morocco agreed on Wednesday to open embassies in each other’s countries following talks between their foreign ministers and the US ambassador to the United Nations in New York. The two countries established diplomatic ties in 2020 under the US-brokered Abraham Accords, which normalised Israel’s relations with several Arab states.
Israel and Morocco have agreed to open embassies in their respective countries following a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations in New York on Wednesday.
The two countries established ties in 2020 as part of the US-led Abraham Accords, under which several Arab states normalised relations with Israel.
At the meeting, Israel and Morocco reaffirmed their commitment to measures including "upgrading diplomatic relations between the two countries, elevating their respective diplomatic missions to the level of embassies, and the appointment of ambassadors", an Israeli foreign ministry statement said.
A joint statement released by the US mission to the UN on behalf of all three countries said they believed that the "establishment of full diplomatic, peaceful and friendly relations between Morocco and Israel is in the common interest of both countries and will advance the cause of peace".
The statements did not offer a timeline for the establishment of the embassies, and Israel had previously made a similar announcement in June 2022 during a visit to Morocco by then-foreign minister Yair Lapid.
The two countries also said after Wednesday's meeting that a series of economic agreements would be concluded between them by year's end, while the Israeli statement added that "high-level reciprocal visits between the two countries will take place in the coming months".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

At Least 10 Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russian Attack Injures 16, Including Two Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:05:51 UTC
10:05:51 KST

At least 10 explosions were heard across Kyiv within several minutes early Thursday as Russia launched a massive missile and drone attack on the Ukrainian capital, a Kyiv Post journalist reported from the city.
At least 12 people were injured, including two children aged 10 and 12, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said initially. Nine of the injured were hospitalized.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Later, after 8 a.m., Klitschko clarified that the number of casualties in the capital had risen to 16, including two children.
At 9:33 a.m., the mayor reported that the number of casualties in Kyiv had risen to 18.
“The enemy continues to attack the capital. Pay attention to air-raid alerts! Stay safe!” he added.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Post correspondents in various districts of the capital reported hearing a loud explosion shortly after a drone threat was announced at 9:30 a.m.
At 12:11 p.m., Klitschko clarified that the number of wounded in the capital had risen to 20. Five of the injured are currently hospitalized in city hospitals.
The blasts followed warnings of an incoming missile threat as Russia struck multiple areas of the capital overnight.
Damage was reported across the Dniprovskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts.
In the Dniprovskyi district, debris fell at several locations, damaging residential and office buildings. Windows were blown out in several homes, while warehouse premises and an area near a gas station were also damaged.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 16, 2026
In the Sviatoshynskyi district, a non-residential building was hit, while a warehouse building was destroyed in the Solomianskyi district.
Authorities said the combined attack damaged residential buildings, warehouses, offices and other non-residential premises across Kyiv.
A separate Russian attack also damaged a higher education facility in the Holosiivskyi district, where the facade and windows of a four-story building were hit and a small fire broke out before being extinguished.
Russian forces also attacked Kyivvodokanal in the capital overnight. The company is currently operating normally and supplying water to residents across the city.
The shelling partially disrupted water supplies on the Left Bank and reduced water pressure in some areas of the Right Bank. Specialists promptly restored the facilities’ operations and water services.
Emergency crews continued working at the affected sites as authorities assessed the full extent of the damage.
According to the Air Force, Russia launched the following weapons against Ukraine starting at 6 p.m. on Sept. 16:
- Oniks anti-ship missiles
- Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles
- four Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles
- 10 “Banderol”/“Dan-T” drones
- 157 strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), mostly Shahed-type drones, with more than half being jet-powered, as well as Parodiya decoy drones
The primary targets were in the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian Defense Forces aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
“According to preliminary data, as of 8 a.m., air defense forces had shot down or neutralized 131 targets: seven ‘Banderol’/‘Dan-T’ drones and 124 UAVs, including Shahed- and Gerbera-type drones, as well as other models,” the Air Force said.
At the same time, Russian missile and strike UAV impacts were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at five locations.

Canada formally applies to join northern Europe’s military initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:05:48 UTC
10:05:48 KST

WASHINGTON, September 17. /TASS/. Canada has officially applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which comprises northern European countries, the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said after talks with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham in Liverpool.
"They [the two premiers] noted the deep and growing defense and security partnership between the two countries and discussed opportunities to further strengthen these efforts," Carney’s office said in a statement. "To that end, Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the UK’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative."
According to the report, the premiers "also discussed opportunities for defense industrial cooperation" through a joint UK-Italy-Japan program of creating a sixth generation stealth fighter-bomber. Canada joined this project as an observer in July 2026.
Also, Carney and Burnham "emphasized the importance of strengthening economic cooperation" between Canada and the United Kingdom, and agreed to deepen cooperation on frontier technologies, including development and use of artificial intelligence.
Established in 2014, the UK-led security coalition comprises Denmark, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, Sweden, and Estonia. Its participants hold regular joint military exercises. Commander of the UK Royal Navy, General Gwyn Jenkins said in late August that the JEF can de-facto replace NATO in the region.

What is celebrated on September 17 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:56:33 EEST
09:56:33 KST

What is celebrated on September 17 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Rescuer's Day and Adoption Day are observed, while around the world, Patient Safety Day and U.S. Constitution Day are observed. The church calendar commemorates Saints Faith, Hope, Love, and Sophia.
On September 17, Ukraine observes Rescuer’s Day and Adoption Day; globally, under the auspices of the WHO, World Patient Safety Day is held, while the United States celebrates Constitution Day. According to the new church calendar, the holy martyrs Faith, Hope, Love, and their mother Sophia are commemorated, while according to the old calendar, the day of the icon of the Mother of God "The Unburnt Bush" and the memory of the prophet Moses are observed, UNN writes.
Rescuer’s Day in Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 2008. The occasion is dedicated to employees of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU), fire protection services, emergency and rescue services, sappers, divers, and civilian volunteers. The holiday honors the courage and self-sacrifice of rescuers, who daily deal with the consequences of man-made and natural disasters, enemy missile and artillery shelling, clear territories of mines, and pull people from under the rubble during the war.
Adoption Day in Ukraine
An official date moved by Decree No. 455/2023 of the President of Ukraine from September 30 to September 17 due to the transition of Christian churches to the Revised Julian calendar, as the holiday has traditionally been timed to coincide with the commemoration day of the holy martyrs Faith, Hope, Love, and their mother Sophia. The day honors foster parents, guardians, adoptive parents, and employees of family-type children’s homes, calling on society to support orphans and children deprived of parental care and to ensure their fundamental right to be raised in a caring family.
World Patient Safety Day (World Patient Safety Day)
An official global date held under the auspices of the WHO, established in May 2019 at the 72nd session of the World Health Assembly. The day aims to raise international awareness of patient safety issues, prevent medical errors, adverse treatment outcomes, and medication side effects, and stimulate concerted action by governments, healthcare workers, and patient organizations to create safe and high-quality healthcare systems.
U.S. Constitution Day (Constitution Day and Citizenship Day)
An official national holiday established to commemorate the signing on September 17, 1787, in Philadelphia, by delegates to the Constitutional Convention chaired by George Washington, of the fundamental law of the United States—the world’s oldest written constitution still in force. The day is dedicated to studying the history of American constitutionalism and the rights and duties of citizens, and is also accompanied by solemn ceremonies for the swearing-in and naturalization of new immigrants.
International Country Music Day (International Country Music Day)
An unofficial global observance established in the 1950s in honor of the birthday of Hank Williams (1923–1953), one of the most influential American performers, songwriters, and pioneers of the country genre. The event brings together millions of folk and country music fans, celebrating the cultural contribution of this traditional genre to the development of the modern popular music industry.
The Commemoration Day of the Holy Martyrs Faith, Hope, Love, and Their Mother Sophia
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the holy martyrs Faith, Hope, Love, and their mother Sophia—Christian saints who suffered in Rome during the reign of Emperor Hadrian in the 2nd century. The young girls endured brutal torture for refusing to sacrifice to pagan gods, while their mother Sophia died of grief at their grave three days later. The martyr Theodotia is also commemorated on this day.
According to the old calendar, believers observe the day of the icon of the Mother of God "The Unburnt Bush"—one of the best-known Christian holy icons, symbolizing protection from fire, lightning, and conflagrations. Its image was inspired by the burning bush that was not consumed, in which God appeared to Moses. The memory of the holy prophet Moses the God-Seer and the hieromartyr Babylas, Bishop of Great Antioch, is also honored on this day.

Protesters attack EU office over Kosovo leader’s war crimes conviction (VIDEOS)

Protesters attack EU office over Kosovo leader’s war crimes conviction (VIDEOS)
Violent protests have erupted in Serbia’s breakaway region of Kosovo and abroad after a Hague-based special tribunal convicted former politician and paramilitary commander Hashim Thaci of war crimes.
In its ruling on Wednesday, the tribunal sentenced Thaci, a commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to 25 years in prison for the murder of 96 people and the torture of around 300 others during the group’s fight for the region’s independence from Serbia in the late 1990s.
Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo in 1999 after NATO accused Belgrade of ethnic cleansing and launched a bombing campaign against Yugoslavia. After the war, Thaci went on to serve as the first prime minister of the self-proclaimed Republic of Kosovo and later as its president.
Ethnic Albanians, who make up the majority of Kosovo’s population, took to the streets to protest the verdict.
In footage circulating on social media, hundreds of demonstrators are seen facing off against riot police in the breakaway republic, with dozens kicking at officers’ riot shields.
Protesters gathered outside the European Union Rule of Law Mission (EULEX) building in Pristina, launching fireworks and throwing bottles and stones.

Congress passes sweeping US sanctions bill targeting Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:55:13 UTC
09:55:13 KST

Congress passes sweeping US sanctions bill targeting Russia
The bill marks the first time in more than two years the US Congress has passed legislation assisting Ukraine.
The United States House of Representatives has passed a bipartisan sanctions bill targeting Russia over its continued war in Ukraine.
Lawmakers on Wednesday voted to send the sweeping legislation, championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, to US President Donald Trump’s desk, ending more than a year of delays and obstacles. The final vote was 262 to 159. It had already passed in the US Senate.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland
- list 2 of 3At least five killed in Russian drone strike near Ukraine front line
- list 3 of 3Efforts underway for Zelenskyy-Trump meeting at UN next week
The much-anticipated bill would give the president new abilities to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries, like China and India, that import energy supplies from Russia, allowing Washington to further restrict funds sent to Moscow. The measure would also impose sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been pushing for the bill’s passage and made a direct appeal to senators shortly before they passed it last month.
Fifty-eight Democrats bucked their party’s leadership and joined with a majority of Republicans to pass it.
The Democratic Party has overwhelmingly supported Ukraine in the war. However, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposed the bill, citing new tariff authorities given to the White House that could be used to exploit US allies.
“The manner in which this bill has been written doesn’t require the president of the United States to impose sanctions on Russia,” Jeffries said on the House floor Wednesday. “In fact, there are so many loopholes written into the bill, I believe, that it’s very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day.”
The bill marks the first time in more than two years the US Congress has passed legislation supporting Ukraine. Graham, after whom the bill was named following his sudden death in July, had helped negotiate Trump’s support for it.
House Speaker Mike Johnson heralded the bill’s passage, saying it places “maximum pressure on … the Russian war machine”, including the country’s President Vladimir Putin.
“For too long, Putin has bankrolled this devastating war with money and resources from countries willing to look the other way, and today, that ends,” Johnson said in a post on social media. “This bill sends a powerful message of American unity and gives the Administration every tool in the toolbox to help bring this war to a just end, and we are proud to send it to the President’s desk.”
After the vote, a group of Republicans and Democrats from the House and Senate celebrated the vote at a rare bipartisan news conference.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who wrote the bill with Graham, said he hopes the sanctions will help force Putin to the negotiating table and end the war.
“To Vladimir Putin – we have your number,” Blumenthal said. “And to Ukraine – you are not alone.”
Trump is expected to sign the bill into law.

A defense company producing shells for Ukraine has caught fire for the second time in a week in Europe
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
03:51:20 EEST
09:51:20 KST

A defense company producing shells for Ukraine has caught fire for the second time in a week in Europe
Kyiv • UNN
A fire at the ZVS Holding plant in Snina halted production. The employees were evacuated, there were no casualties, and the causes of the fire are being investigated.
A fire broke out at the ZVS Holding production site in the Slovak city of Snina, which manufactures artillery shell casings, including for 155 mm ammunition supplied to Ukraine. This is already the second similar incident in a week at European facilities whose products are supplied to Ukraine, The Moscow Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
The fire broke out on September 16. Local authorities urged residents not to approach the facility and to limit the time spent outdoors while the fire was being extinguished.
According to CSG Holding representative Andrei Chirtek, the fire started on the roof of the building during repair work carried out by an outside company. The employees were evacuated, there were no injuries, and the fire was brought under control in approximately two hours.
Production temporarily halted
Due to the incident, production at the affected facility was temporarily suspended. The extent of the damage and the cause of the fire will be assessed and determined later
ZVS Holding is part of MSM Group, which is a division of the Czech industrial holding company Czechoslovak Group. The company manufactures ammunition for tanks, artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, mortar shells and ammunition components. The plant in Snina specializes, among other things, in casings for 155 mm artillery shells.
The fire occurred several days after a blaze on September 11 at an ammunition warehouse belonging to the Bulgarian defense company EMCO, whose products are also supplied to Ukraine. Bulgarian law enforcement authorities are considering various theories regarding that incident, including possible arson.

Feature: From candies to football, a Russian coach's love story with Dalian
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
08:50:10 CST
09:50:10 KST

DALIAN, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- For Artyom Apukhtin, football has taken on many meanings over the years.
As a boy, it meant the candy his father brought home to Russia from China's eastern coastal city of Dalian. As an adult, it was the roar of the Northeast Super League that drew him across the border to a city he had previously known only through stories. Now, he hopes football can become a bridge between Vladivostok and Dalian.
"I saw your posts about the Northeast Super League. I'm coming to Dalian in a few days. I want to look for cooperation with the local football association. Could you help me get in touch?"
That message arrived in the inbox of "Romantic Dalian," a social media account run by the Dalian Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism. The sender was Apukhtin, chairman of the Vladivostok Amateur Football League and a football coach.
From home, he had watched videos of Dalian's matches in the Northeast Super League. The pitch was green, with the sea on three sides. The stands were packed and the cheers rolled through the stadium.
China's first cross-provincial urban football league, the Northeast Super League brings together eight city teams and 390 amateur players from Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces and Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Since kicking off in May, it has attracted growing attention.
Last weekend, Dalian hosted Yanbian in the semifinal. In the days leading up to the match, the local culture and tourism bureau coordinated with the sports bureau to help arrange Apukhtin's visit and meetings with local football officials.
For Apukhtin, however, the trip was about more than football cooperation. It also brought him closer to a family story that began three decades ago.
In a photograph from 30 years ago, a Russian footballer has his arm around a Chinese teammate's shoulder as they smile at the camera.
"He always talked about Dalian, about the green pitch that summer, about the wind by the sea, and about the people of this city," Apukhtin said of his father.
Around 1995, his father, Alexander Apukhtin, played football in Vladivostok before joining a club in Dalian. "That year, I was only five or six," he recalled.
At that age, Apukhtin barely understood football. What he did know was that whenever his father returned from Dalian, there was candy in his bag. The memory of that sweetness stayed with him long afterward.
A knee injury forced Alexander to leave Dalian after only half a year and return home. He later played for several clubs and remained involved in football until his death two years ago.
Inspired by his father, Apukhtin began formal football training at the age of eight. He progressed from player to coach and event organizer, and now leads the Vladivostok Amateur Football League. He also organizes football, table tennis and volleyball events for people with hearing impairments and promotes sporting exchanges for people with disabilities.
Another aim of his trip was to find his father's old friends in Dalian and continue the cross-border friendship begun by the previous generation.
During a visit to the Dalian Football Youth Training Base, Apukhtin was impressed by its natural turf, rehabilitation and physiotherapy rooms, fitness areas and locker rooms. As he watched young players train, he got a closer look at the foundations of Dalian's reputation as a football city.
Dalian has a long football tradition and has produced many prominent players. Dongbei Road Primary School and Experimental Primary School are well-known for their youth development programs. As one of Liaoning's two representative teams, Dalian topped the Northeast Super League regular-season standings.
"Very professional, very standardized, full of hope," Apukhtin said.
Apukhtin has long worked to promote football exchanges between China and Russia, with his teams taking part in exchange activities with Harbin for many years. During his visit to Dalian, he established contact with the Dalian Football Association and hopes to organize annual friendly matches and exchanges between youth teams, extending the football ties between the two cities.
He had previously experienced the atmosphere of Dalian's Suoyuwan Football Stadium only through a screen. Now in the city, he hopes to attend a Dalian Yingbo home game and watch a Northeast Super League match in person.
"This city is warm, comfortable and beautiful," he said. "Football is a bridge. I hope more Russians will get to know Dalian and fall in love with it." ■

New Zealand economy grows 0.2 pct in Q2
China
Unknown Publisher

WELLINGTON, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.2 percent in the June 2026 quarter, slowing from a 0.9-percent increase in the previous quarter, official figures showed Thursday.
The growth reflected mixed results, with activity increasing in nine of 16 industries, Stats NZ general manager and macroeconomic spokesperson Jason Attewell said in a statement.
Construction was the largest contributor, rising 2.7 percent, its largest increase since the June 2023 quarter, which was driven by higher residential building activity, Attewell said.
Public administration and safety, up 2 percent, also contributed to the GDP growth, the statistics department said.
The largest downward contributors to GDP in the June 2026 quarter were transport, postal and warehousing, which fell 1.7 percent, and retail trade and accommodation, down 1 percent, Stats NZ said, adding that GDP per capita rose 0.1 percent during the quarter.
The expenditure measure of GDP increased 0.4 percent in the June quarter, following a 1.1-percent rise in the March quarter, statistics showed.
Export volumes rose 3.3 percent, driven mainly by higher goods exports, including meat, other foods, beverages, tobacco and dairy products, Stats NZ said, noting that U.S. demand for New Zealand beef contributed to the increase in meat exports.
Import volumes fell 0.8 percent, while gross fixed capital formation, or investments in fixed assets, rose 1.5 percent in the June quarter, led by a 4.4-percent increase in spending on residential building work, the department said. ■

CGHS 'family' expands, but contribution stays unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:40:57 UTC
09:40:57 KST

On Sept 1, the eligibility criteria for CGHS was expanded to include married sons and brothers of scheme card holders who are critically or terminally ill
On Sept 7, the health ministry extended coverage of Central Govt Health Scheme (CGHS) to adopted sisters of scheme beneficiaries. On Sept 1, the eligibility criteria for CGHS was expanded to include married sons and brothers of scheme card holders who are critically or terminally ill. Over the years, the criteria for beneficiaries have been steadily expanded. Yet the contribution by the cardholder remains the same, unlike in health insurance where the addition of a beneficiary, especially an elderly or ill beneficiary, could entail a steep increase in the premium paid.According to the Sept 7 office memorandum, the ministry received references "regarding the eligibility of adopted sisters (i.e. sisters adopted by parents of a CGHS beneficiary) for inclusion as dependent family members under CGHS". The 'sisters' have to be legally adopted by the parents of CGHS beneficiary and have to satisfy the existing criteria of dependency (staying in the same house as the cardholder), income ceiling (not be earning more than Rs 9,000 per month plus the applicable dearness allowance) and marital status (i.e. be unmarried, divorced, abandoned or separated), as applicable to biological sisters.
The coverage of sons and brothers of beneficiaries was earlier available only to unmarried dependents. There were also age limits of 25 for sons and 18 for brothers, except for those permanently disabled, who were covered for life. The office memorandum issued by the health ministry on Sept 1 spelt out that "marriage shall not constitute a ground for cessation of CHS/medical attendance facilities in respect of dependent son or brother covered under these provisions whether on account of critical/terminal illness or permanent disability..."Also, the lifetime coverage would now also apply for "chronic, severe, critical or terminal illnesses resulting in substantial and continuing functional impairment or inability to earn a livelihood/self-sufficiency".The addition of critically terminally ill beneficiaries could have a major financial implication for the exchequer as there is no ceiling on the amount spent on CGHS beneficiaries. Since no health insurance would normally cover a critically or terminally ill person, this expansion is fortuitous for an ill person, but only if s/he has a parent or sibling who is a CGHS cardholder.
For dependent daughters and sisters there has never been any age limit but the coverage stops once they get married or get a job with salary above the stipulated limit. Similarly, unmarried/divorced/abandoned/separated daughters and sisters have been eligible for coverage for life, provided they fulfilled the condition of dependency and income. Children and siblings are required to "normally reside" with the primary cardholder to qualify for benefits.

US House advances first Bill addressing economic impact of data centre boom
- The US House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act to address rising electricity costs from data centre expansion, requiring states to charge large users for related power infrastructure.
- President Trump supports data centres as key to AI leadership, calling them the "oil of the next 20, 25 years," despite public concerns over electricity price hikes.
- Some lawmakers say the bill is insufficient to protect consumers, with only 11% of Americans supporting new AI data centres in their communities, reflecting widespread opposition.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The United States House of Representatives on Sept 16 passed a Bill aimed at protecting households from electricity cost increases tied to the expansion of data centres, the first time the chamber has advanced legislation directly addressing economic concerns linked to the industry’s growth.
The Republican-majority House voted 417 to three in favour of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require state utility regulators to consider whether large electricity users, including data centres, should bear the incremental costs of power infrastructure built to serve them.
The vote underscores the complicated politics surrounding the US data centre boom.
US President Donald Trump strongly backs data centre development as critical to leadership in artificial intelligence (AI).
Earlier this week, he said data centres make people and states wealthy, calling them the “oil of the next 20, 25 years”.
At the same time, lawmakers from both parties have faced growing constituent concerns over rising electricity costs associated with the industry’s surging power demand.
Just 11 per cent of Americans would support construction of an AI data centre in their community, according to a poll by the University of Massachusetts Amherst published this week.
House Republican leaders moved the Bill before lawmakers leave Washington ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
US representative Derrick Van Orden, a Wisconsin Republican seeking re-election in a competitive district, said the Bill’s passage bolsters his record as he heads into the final stretch of his campaign.
Van Orden said he has worked with the Department of Defence for months to build data centres on military bases while his Democratic opponent, Rebecca Cooke, has called for a moratorium.
“The Chinese Communist Party understands that whoever wins the AI war either wins or prevents the next war,” he said. “The Chinese are not going to quit. And so we have to do this responsibly, and that ameliorates all these very, very valid concerns.”
Consumer rights non-profit Public Citizen said the legislation did not go far enough to protect Americans.
“The Ratepayer Protection Act has very limited ability to actually protect consumers from higher utility rates, as it simply asks states to ‘consider’ requiring data centres to pay for certain grid interconnection costs,” Tyson Slocum, director of the group’s energy programme, said in a statement.
“While a federal mandate forcing states to consider such a step provides opportunities for advocates to press for consumer protections, there are a myriad of other consumer and community impacts from data centres unaddressed in this Bill.”
US Representative Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, said in advance of the vote the measure does not go far enough, but would garner significant support from members who are hopeful more reforms will follow.
“Clearly, they’re trying to get in front of the data centre issue, but the reality is they’ve done nothing, really, on that,” he said of House Republicans.
“I think a lot of their base voters are really angry. There has to be actual real protections put in place for people, and this is not it.” REUTERS

India sees no growth in power sector CO2 emissions as clean energy rises: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:30:00 UTC
09:30:00 KST

A surge in clean energy in India has kept carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in check across the country
NEW DELHI: A surge in clean energy in India has kept carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in check across the country’s power sector, with no growth from the first half of 2024 to the same period in 2026, and this is the first time in more than 50 years that there has been no growth in coal power over a two-year period, found an analysis published by the UK-based Carbon Brief on Thursday.The analysis, done by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) for Carbon Brief, underlined that coal power has not recorded growth during the period, even as overall electricity demand grew.It also noted that both oil and gas consumption, at the same time, have fallen across the nation for two years in a row, helping alleviate the shock of the Hormuz crisis. Emissions from oil and gas, in fact, fell by 7% year-on-year, extending a reduction that began in 2025, despite higher demand for road transport fuels.Nevertheless, the new six-monthly analysis shows that India’s emissions grew by 3.7% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, due to increases from steel, cement and other sectors. The analysis found that the carbon-intensive steel and cement emissions grew by 8% year-on-year, reaching a 23% share of India’s total CO2 in the first half of 2026.Flagging India’s performance, the report noted that clean energy met all of the 7% rise in the country’s electricity demand over the two years, adding 63 terawatt hours (TWh), equivalent to the total demand of Switzerland.
India has added 77 gigawatts (GW) of solar in this two-year period, helping meet 60% of the rise in electricity demand overall, it added.Looking at the state-wise contribution that led to the clean-power shift in India, the report said Gujarat saw both the largest reduction in fossil-fuel generation and the largest expansion in clean power. After Gujarat, the largest increases in clean-power generation were seen in Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, which also saw reductions in power generation from fossil fuels.
The report suggested that if the pace of India’s clean-energy expansion is to continue, it will need to upgrade its electricity grid, rapidly build out energy storage and boost the flexibility of coal power.The analysis, based on official monthly data for fuel consumption, industrial production and power generation from different ministries and govt institutes, shows that though clean-energy expansion is covering most or all of India’s power-demand growth, the fossil-fuel industry continues to pursue major capital investments.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

‘Harrowing reading’: what the inquiry into NZ fugitive father Tom Phillips revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:28:15 UTC
09:28:15 KST

1. Agencies overlooked harm Phillips was causingOver “significant periods”, police and Oranga Tamariki (OT), the ministry for children, “underplayed or overlooked” the harm Phillips was causing before and after he vanished, the inquiry found. They were too slow to identify important information, and the search was launched too late. Police intentionally adopted “a low-key approach”, the inquiry said. “This strategy appears to have been predicated on the misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children’s welfare.” The inquiry found OT was dismissive of multiple concerns raised by the maternal family after Phillips’ first disappearance, telling the family court the children were “completely fine” and further OT involvement was perhaps not needed.
 2. Significant family concerns minimisedHad OT taken into consideration the significant concerns of the children’s mother and two other sisters, they “may have prevented or made more difficult” his second disappearance, the inquiry found. The sisters, who had lived with their stepfather Phillips for some years, repeatedly raised concerns over his pattern of isolation and harm he caused. The sisters were “uniquely placed” to comment on family dynamics and it was “regrettable the agency did not meet with them.” The children’s mother, named as Ms Smith, had told OT of Phillips’ controlling behaviour towards her. The inquiry found OT failed to hear her concerns before Phillips disappeared the second time. She also notified police that Phillips stashed multiple firearms “all over the place” six months before he disappeared. Police questioned her credibility because of a “custody dispute in the background” and did not respond to her allegations.
 3. Phillips’ state of mind and beliefs not treated seriously enough  Police built a comprehensive profile of Phillips while investigating his first disappearance. His alcohol consumption concerned them, and his home was “very dirty”. They formed the view he was controlling and difficult to live with. A person close to Phillips was concerned that, if cornered, he would turn “violent”. Another told police he had a dislike of government agencies, “meaning anyone that might try to remove his children from him”. Phillips held anti-vaccination views and had told family he and the children would “just disappear” if there was another Covid lockdown. A 2021 police report, before his second disappearance, said Phillips was “prepared to put the children’s wellbeing at risk by hiding them” to deny Ms Smith access. His firearms licence was suspended and police wanted him to access mental health support. But the inquiry saw no evidence that support was explored or provided by police. The inquiry found police did not adequately share information with OT, and OT should have more carefully considered mental health concerns. Better communication between the two “may have prevented, and would likely have made more difficult” Phillips’ second disappearance.
 4. Public sighting a missed opportunityIn May 2023, a woman living near Marokopa, close to the Phillips’ family farm told police a man had approached her house asking to jump start his car. She described a man fitting Phillips’ profile and said “he smelled … like someone who had not had a shower in a very long time”. She saw children in his car and later called police. A police unit was dispatched but, before it arrived, it was diverted to another incident. The inquiry found no evidence the police attempted to visit the location of the sighting, or the woman’s home. Police followed up the tip 10 days later.
 5. Authorities accept all recommendationsThe inquiry made nine recommendations, including urging agencies to better communicate, particularly in cases related to a child’s safety and ensuring gun safety concerns raised by former spouses are “actioned promptly”. The minister for social development, Louise Upston, apologised to Phillips’ children saying  “our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you”. The government accepted the 41 findings and nine recommendations. The police commissioner, Richard Chambers, said it was “clear there were gaps” in communication and police should have put more resources into their investigation earlier.  Oranga Tamariki chief executive, Amanda Malu, said the report made for “harrowing reading”. She said the agency was immediately strengthening its checks and procedures.

Government bows to pressure to scrap allied health cap for veterans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:25:38 UTC
09:25:38 KST

Government bows to pressure to scrap allied health cap for veterans
In short:
The federal government has scrapped a plan to cap allied health care for veterans at $5,000 a year.
The proposal had been criticised by veteran advocacy groups and the Coalition, who said it would create barriers for ex-servicemen and women.
What's next?
Minister for Veterans' Affairs Matt Keogh said he would continue to engage with veterans to create a fairer system.
The Albanese government has bowed to pressure, scrapping a plan to cap allied health services for veterans at $5,000 a year.
The proposal would have imposed an "annual monetary limit" on services such as physiotherapy and dentistry, with veterans able to access more funding if they "demonstrated clinical need".
The May budget showed the measure would have saved the government roughly $750 million over three years but was rubbished by both the Coalition and veteran advocacy groups for making health services harder to access.
Minister for Veterans' Affairs Matt Keogh released a statement today confirming the threshold measure was "off the table".
"We have been consulting on this measure, and we have heard from veterans there are concerns about this approach," he said.
Mr Keogh had initially been under pressure after the Coalition accused him of declining to meet with veterans or properly understand their needs.
He later told the parliament he "got it wrong," with some government sources confirming the issue was being considered at the highest levels, including the prime minister's office.
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie, who is herself a veteran, made an emotional speech in the Senate last month about healthcare access following recent surgery for vaginal prolapse.
She turned to the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) to pay for the surgery, but eventually footed the bill herself after facing serious administrative hurdles.
Senator Lambie linked her personal experience to the concerns being expressed by other veterans about looming changes to the way the DVA manages access to allied healthcare.
Today, she said scrapping the cap was a win that belonged to "every veteran".
"They knew what would happen to our most vulnerable veterans if this cap went ahead and they fought like hell to make sure it didn't," she said.
"This cap was cruel, it was dangerous and it should never have been announced in the first place. I'm relieved that the government has finally listened and scrapped it and I thank them for doing it."
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government had taken "too long" to drop the policy and called on Mr Keogh to step down.
"It has taken too long to scrap this cap. It should never have happened, and frankly, it's time for this minister to go," he said.
But advocacy group Fair Care for Veterans, which had pushed the government to drop the changes, said the minister had "made it right".
"This is what happens when a government listens to veterans," spokesman John Armfield, a former navy clearance diver, said.
"Veterans, families and doctors came from all over the country to say one thing: this cap would only ever hurt the most badly injured.
"The minister made the right call, and he deserves credit for it."
Government still wants to find a fix
The government had said it wanted to introduce the limit to stamp out "over-servicing" of veterans who were being charged for support they did not need.
Department figures suggest about 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.
A Senate estimates hearing in June heard examples of overcharging, including one case where a single patient was charged $101,000 in a single year by a dietitian, equivalent to 19 appointments a week.
The policy also aimed to reduce the administrative burden on veterans under the current system, which requires them to go back to a GP every 12 allied health visits for a new referral.
Mr Keogh said he would continue to engage the veteran and provider community to address those goals and "deliver on the objective of achieving better veteran wellbeing outcomes while ensuring integrity of the system".
"We will not change our commitment to improving access to allied health care through the fee increase to allied health providers," he said.
Mr Armfield said Fair Care for Veterans was open to further conversations.
"We welcome that, and we'll be there," he said.
"We'll also make sure whatever comes next doesn't bring the cap back under another name."
Senator Lambie introduced a bill in to the Senate on Thursday that would ensure there would not be a monetary cap placed on veterans' health in the future.
It was sponsored by crossbench senators David Pocock, Lidia Thorpe and Fatima Payman, and Greens senator David Shoebridge.
The bill passed 33 votes to 19, but will now need to go to the House, where it is unlikely to pass as the government controls the numbers.

The issue has been flagged multiple times over last 15 years but a fresh push by Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revived a question that has remained unresolved for years: who ultimately sets price of a medical device - the manufacturer, the hospital or the regulator?
NEW DELHI: An IV infusion set priced in the wholesale market for Rs 11 carries an MRP of Rs 325, while a disposable syringe available for under Rs 7 has a price tag of around Rs 60, putting a spotlight on one of the least visible components of hospital bills: the price of widely used consumables during treatment. The gap becomes even more stark for high-value devices such as pacemakers, heart valves and intraocular lenses, where the final MRP may be 10-30 fold higher than the import landed price.Such huge mark-ups ultimately inflate the patient's hospital bill and may add significantly to the out-of-pocket treatment cost.
How the prices are changed
The issue has been flagged multiple times over last 15 years but a fresh push by Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revived a question that has remained unresolved for years: who ultimately sets price of a medical device - the manufacturer, the hospital or the regulator?Several earlier analyses by National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) of hospital bills had shown how certain private hospitals procured consumables at rock-bottom prices but charged patients the high printed MRP, sources told TOI.Flagging mark-ups as high as 2,841% on commonly used hospital consumables, Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra FDA commissioner, posted on X on Tuesday, "The regulatory gap is structural: scheduled medicines are capped under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. Most medical devices and consumables are not, leaving both the pricing and the information around it almost entirely unmonitored.'' He urged the Centre to frame guidelines to address the "permissible gap between trade procurement price and declared MRP".
Nearly a decade ago, prices for cardiac stents and orthopaedic knee implants were capped by NPPA. And, in 2020, govt capped trade margins on certain critical items, including pulse oximeters, blood pressure monitors and glucometers, during the Coronavirus pandemic.
Historically, the industry - domestic and MNCs - have been split over the capping of trade margins. The domestic industry represented by AiMeD cautioned that the current regulatory framework under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, is inadequate to address the pricing of medical devices and has proposed capping trade margins at 75% for widely used consumables such as syringes and IV sets, and at 50% for high-value devices such as pacemakers and heart valves."Genuine device manufacturers and importers are at a clear disadvantage under the current system of unchecked hospital mark-ups. Ethical suppliers price their products transparently, based on ex-factory or landed import price, but when hospitals inflate MRPs by 10-30 times, the market rewards those willing to play the distortion game. Responsible companies that refuse to indulge in excessive margins are forced out of competition or in order to survive, have to comply with these unfair demands,'' said Rajiv Nath, forum coordinator, AiMeD, saidAs against this, Medical Technology Association of India, which represents MNCs, said it concurred with Maharashtra FDA Commissioner's "three asks of margin rationalisation, an inter-agency review and clear guidelines governing the permissible gap between trade procurement costs and declared MRPs", which is the "essence of Trade Margin Rationalisation".

SC pulls up govt for 'denying' disabled soldiers their benefits

SC junked over 270 appeals filed by govt against such soldiers
NEW DELHI: Quoting Raksha Mantri 2015 Report, which admitted that "many disabled soldiers in India are still denied disability benefits on hyper-technical reasons", Supreme Court has pulled up Centre and the defence ministry for litigating against them in all forums of the judiciary - from tribunals to HCs and SC. It also highlighted that govt filed appeals after a long time in most of the cases.A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe noted that Raksha Mantri Report had recommended the immediate withdrawal of appeals pertaining to disability and pensionary benefits pending against soldiers with disabilities but said the recommendation had not been faithfully implemented. "Appeals such as these are filed and continue to be filed, even after the ministry of defence accepted the committee's recommendation for withdrawal of this class of litigation," the bench said, junking over 270 appeals filed by govt.The bench also examined the outcome of such cases in different judicial forums."The sad part of this litigation is that, out of around 271 civil appeals and special leave petitions, most of them are barred by limitation. Many similar appeals that were barred by limitation have already been dismissed in the past; the present batch is only a small number that survive. Moreover, it is significant to note that the number of appeals rejected at the first appellate stage, after a dismissal by the release medical board, far exceeds those accepted," SC said.
According to information obtained under RTI Act, of the 2,997 appeals before the first appellate authority, 2,855 were rejected and only 142 appeals were accepted, the bench added. Before the second appellate authority, out of 456 appeals, 439 were rejected and only 17 accepted.
The court examined Entitlement Rules 2008, passed in 2010 to replace the 1982 rules, and did not find any error in them. The 1982 Rules clearly create a presumption that if a member of the service is in sound physical and mental health at the time of entrance, then any disability at the time of discharge would be attributable to military service. The 2008 Rules, however, withdraw this presumption by adding a causal connection requirement. They say, "Mere fact that a disease has manifested during military service does not per se establish attributability to or aggravation by military service."The bench upheld the new rules, saying, "The mere addition of a causal requirement and a removal of the presumption that when a member joins service healthy, and, if, he leaves with a disability, it ought to be attributable to the military service, does not, by itself, change the core scheme of the Entitlement Rules 2008 because the other beneficial provisions broadly remain untouched. The onus to prove that the member's disability is not attributable to service still lies on the employer. The relevant rules regarding attributability and aggravation continue to hold that if cause of disability is unknown,... then the disability is attributable to service."

Missing pages of priceless missing Henry VIII–era manuscript finally found
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:03:47 UTC
09:03:47 KST

A 600-year-old book that once belonged to a personal attendant of King Henry VIII is helping to reveal the shifting allegiances and religious ferment that captured the Tudor court, shaping world history along the way.
The book in question is a copy of Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ, a religious tract that was translated and adapted from Latin early in the 15th century by a monk named Nicholas Love. It was a “medieval bestseller,” says James Wade of the University of Cambridge: owning a copy signaled you were a pious Catholic. The book stresses the importance of the sacraments and other orthodoxy, such as oral confession to a priest and the transubstantiation of Christ’s body and blood when taking communion.
“It was a hugely popular work of English prose in the 15th century, and the reason it’s so important is because it’s right on the fulcrum of orthodox and heterodox belief,” Wade says. “It becomes a lightning rod for judging whether someone is a heretic or not.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Enter John Gage, an aristocrat who served Henry VIII. Among Gage’s jobs at Henry’s court was taking stock of monasteries and either turning their possessions over to the Crown or destroying them, as the king sought to both increase his wealth and assert himself as leader of the Church of England.
Gage himself was a devout Catholic. So when he came across a copy of Mirror, he didn’t destroy it. At the time, owners would sign their books—they were pricey pieces of property—and as evidenced by his signature, Gage decided to keep this one for himself. It remained in his family’s possession until 1976, when a distant descendant sold the book at auction to Japanese professor and rare book collector Toshiyuki Takamiya. When Takamiya gave his book collection to Yale University’s Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Mirrors was included, and it was later digitized.
But the manuscript was incomplete. Now six missing pages, which touched on Jesus raising Lazarus from the dead, have been found.
It’s not entirely clear how the lost pages got separated from the rest of the book. What is known is that the stitches that bound the pages came loose at some point and that the pages were left out when the book was mended.
The loose leaves ended up in a collection of Gage family estate records and passed through several sets of hands before they ended up at an archive called the Keep based in Brighton, England. No one there realized exactly what they had in their possession—a missing piece of important British history essentially hiding in plain sight—until Wade and Katie Walter of the University of Sussex started to suspect the two texts had originally been one.
In a new study published in Notes and Queries, Walter and Wade describe how they compared the dimensions of both documents, as well as the style and color of the annotations and headers on the pages, and found the two were identical.
“It was known that these pages existed, but they weren’t cataloged accurately,” Wade says. “We identified what the six pages were. And then, once we realized what they were and the book that they came from..., we started looking to extant manuscripts of the mirror to match it up, and we found the match.”
While the missing pages have been found, it is unclear if they will ever join the rest of the manuscript. This is not a matter of repairing a library book that the dog got into because the pages themselves are an invaluable historical artifact.
“All those decisions are above my pay grade, but I’m pretty sure that, no, they won’t be reconnected,” Wade. “But it’s useful to reconstruct medieval objects. Yes, this book is incomplete, but now you know where to find what’s missing.”

Coast Guard and FBI boarded tankers due to cyberattacks. How big is the risk?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:03:46 UTC
09:03:46 KST

Coast Guard and FBI boarded 2 energy tankers due to cyberattacks. How big is the risk?
U.S. Coast Guard personnel and FBI agents boarded two Texas-bound energy tankers last month after cyberattacks struck the vessels while they were traveling toward the United States, according to U.S. officials.
One of the vessels was the VL Prosperity, a 1,093-foot Liberian-flagged crude oil tanker headed to Galveston, Texas. Iranian state media identified the ship shortly after the incident and claimed hackers had gained access to its propulsion, navigation and cargo systems, knocking out communications for 30 hours.
The Coast Guard has not publicly pinned the attacks on Iran. But Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of U.S. Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News in a network exclusive interview that investigators did find evidence of a malicious cyber actor.
"They started out by doing an assessment of the information technology and the other systems on board the vessel, and they did find malicious cyber activity," Grable said.
The U.S. is investigating whether the two cyberattacks are connected and whether Iran or another foreign adversary was behind the attacks.
What happened?
The VL Prosperity is what's known as a supertanker — more than three football fields long and capable of carrying roughly 2.3 million barrels of oil.
Public vessel data shows the ship departed Egypt's Sidi Kerir oil terminal on Aug. 1 headed for Galveston. U.S. officials say it slowed near the Strait of Gibraltar around the time of the cyberattack before continuing across the Atlantic and toward the U.S.
Iran's Mehr News Agency reported on Aug. 20 that the VL Prosperity had been attacked on Aug. 7 while transiting through the Strait of Gibraltar. Citing an unnamed crew member, Mehr alleged hackers breached the engine room, reducing engine cooling flow, increasing engine speed and interfering with fuel systems.
Rob Lee, CEO of Dragos, an industrial cybersecurity firm specializing in operational technology, said the Iranian report's details were technically plausible, but warned that authorities have not yet revealed who was behind the incident.
"The details that they published, from what we understand of these types of vehicles and ships and similar, is spot on," Lee said. "Everything they're saying is very realistic."
The next day, Aug. 21, Coast Guard cyber personnel, law enforcement officers, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the ship for four days.
Grable said Coast Guard teams had been alerted by interagency partners and went offshore with the FBI to climb aboard — one of roughly 40 to 50 missions the Coast Guard's Cyber Protection Team has undergone in the past year.
She said investigators were hunting for malware and combing through information technology systems to root out malicious activity.
"The real thing we're concerned about is those IT systems being connected to other systems on the ship that control propulsion, navigation and other systems that are critical to the safety of that vessel," Grable added.
Typically, investigators collect data that is later analyzed, and Grable told CBS News that the Coast Guard plans to provide the vessel owner with recommendations for patching vulnerabilities. She stressed that response teams did not find any evidence indicating the ship had become unsafe to navigate when they boarded it.
How difficult is it to attack a ship?
The concern surrounding large cargo vessels and maritime critical infrastructure transcends stolen files or disrupted communications.
More and more, modern commercial vessels run on internet-connected systems, relying on them for navigation, propulsion, steering, ballast and additional critical machinery. A cyberattack that penetrates those operational systems could potentially be weaponized or manipulated.
"When these vessels are highly connected, they're susceptible to cyber threats," Grable said, warning that an attack could lead to "a vessel blocking a waterway or a pollution incident or any other number of safety and security hazards to our ports and waterways."
The danger that a large vessel could be compromised near an American port is something that authorities fear.
"Of course we're worried about a collision, an explosion, anything that blocks the channel for other vessels to safely enter and exit the port, pollution incidents — we're kind of worried about the whole gamut," Grable said.
The potential economic impact is also colossal. Grable said $5.4 trillion in commerce flows through U.S. ports annually — which could mean high economic stakes for even a relatively small disruption.
"Any small delay, because of a cyber breach, like, for example, if a port has to shift to manual operations, it causes a big delay with tankers and cargo vessels coming in and out of the port," she said.
Perhaps most concerning, Grable said the technical barrier may not be as high as the public assumes.
How sophisticated would an attacker have to be to move beyond breaking into a computer network to manipulating machinery aboard a modern tanker?
"Not necessarily that sophisticated," Grable told CBS News. "There is malicious source code that people can get their hands on."
Grable said that code is available right now, and added that "artificial intelligence is accelerating the rate at which we need to take action."
She urged operators to zero in on network segmentation, phishing attacks and basic cyber hygiene. "Just taking basic precautions would prevent most of these occurrences."
Just one firewall away
On many ships, the barrier between a satellite internet connection and critical onboard systems can be as fragile as a single firewall.
Behind that firewall, Lee said, can be a shared network containing "navigation, propulsion, ballast, steering, ship command — everything on one shared network."
Lee explained that artificial intelligence could make that problem worse because it can assist attackers in picking out weakly protected systems, speeding up attempts to breach internet-facing systems on energy carriers.
"The very thing that we think is our one protection — not that you should have one protection — is the very thing that AI is actually really good at," Lee said.
Still, experts concede that while older vessels may not have the same digitally connected control systems, even on modern ships, reaching critical machinery still requires some knowledge of the onboard environment.
Is 'remote hijacking' a real threat?
Asked whether cyber access to a ship could amount to a form of remote hijacking, Grable called it a fair description of the broader risk.
"That's a good way to characterize it, and yes, it is a concern," she said.
Lee agreed that the scenario is realistic if an attacker gains a foothold.
"I do think there's a realistic concern," Lee said, describing the possibility of remotely messing with a maritime asset, even running it aground.
But former Coast Guard cyber official Quinton DuBose seemed skeptical of the notion that hackers could simply take over an entire supertanker like a remote-controlled vehicle.
"I'd be kind of cautious about saying that somebody can just take control of the ship," DuBose said. "Ships are incredibly complicated systems."
The more realistic threat, he said, may be an attacker disrupting one or more critical subsystems enough to make the vessel unsafe.
"Rather than looking at it as, 'okay, I'm going to take full control of this thing,' it's, 'what systems can I disrupt to the point where it affects the safe handling and makes the ship less safe to operate,'" DuBose said.
Iranian state media claims under scrutiny
The U.S. has not publicly stated who is behind either cyberattack. But Iranian state media began pushing out content around the VL Prosperity incident before U.S. authorities even publicly acknowledged the boarding.
Four days after Mehr's initial report, Iran's Tasnim News Agency published an article with the headline, "No American Vessel Is Safe Anymore: Will Cannons Give Way to Codes?"
DuBose stressed that the Iranian narrative remains unverified, cautioning that Iranian-linked actors are often quick to oversell their cyber influence.
Attribution in cyberspace can take weeks or months, DuBose added.
According to Grable, investigators typically compare the attacker's tactics, techniques and procedures — effectively their digital fingerprints — against known threat actors.
"We look at things called TTPs, which are tactics, techniques and protocols that certain adversaries use — kind of like their trademark fingerprints on how they gain access to systems and what they do and what their payloads are," she said.
A warning to the maritime industry
For Coast Guard Cyber Command, the growing concern is that increasingly connected vessels create more porous entry points for attackers, as ships adopt satellite communications and connect IT networks with their onboard control systems.
"Because they're facing the internet, that is a vector for attackers to gain access and deploy malicious activity on the vessels," she said.
DuBose said the industry should take the threat seriously, while resisting the notion that all vessels are suddenly vulnerable to remote takeover.
He added that maritime infrastructure is so critical that the federal government "has increasingly imposed baseline cyber requirements across the sector."
Grable's warning to vessel owners and operators was blunt: "We need everybody to pay attention to this."

The United States adopts Ukraine’s experience — military HMMWV and HEMTT vehicles receive protection against drones
Kyiv • UNN
During Exercise Thunderstruck 3.0, U.S. troops equipped HMMWV and HEMTT vehicles with metal anti-drone structures. The protection replicates Ukrainian solutions.
The US military has begun testing anti-drone screens on HMMWV vehicles and HEMTT trucks, similar to structures used by the Ukrainian Defense Forces. The new protection was spotted during Exercise Thunderstruck 3.0, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
During the exercise, US troops practiced convoy movement and evacuation under conditions of active drone use. In the released footage, the HMMWVs and HEMTTs are equipped with additional metal structures to protect against drone attacks.
On the HMMWVs, rigid grilles form a kind of rectangular "dome" that covers the vehicle almost down to the wheel level. Similar structures are already being used in Ukraine, in particular on American HMMWVs operated by Ukrainian units.
The US is adapting Ukraine’s experience
On the HEMTT trucks, the anti-drone screens primarily cover the upper part of the armored cab, which should provide the crew with additional protection against attacks from above. At the same time, the sides and front of the vehicle remain less protected.
As the publication notes, the appearance of such structures indicates that the US military is adapting the experience gained by Ukraine amid the widespread use of UAVs.
Anti-drone screens cannot protect equipment from all types of unmanned aerial vehicles, but they can reduce its vulnerability to some attacks and increase the crew’s chances of survival.
