New study disentangles the concepts of beauty and attractiveness in art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
00:00:26 UTC
09:00:26 KST

A study that asked participants to rate 192 art portraits found that beauty and attractiveness ratings are highly associated but depend on somewhat different factors. While both characteristics were associated with the artistic style of a portrait, beauty ratings also depended on self-similarity and symmetry. The paper was published in i-Perception.
Human faces have been among the most enduring subjects of art, appearing in portraits across cultures and historical periods. Even when artists use highly distinctive styles, they usually preserve enough facial structure for viewers to recognize the person being depicted. This makes portraits unusual aesthetic objects because they can be appreciated both for the beauty of the artwork itself and for the attractiveness of the person shown.
These two forms of appeal are often closely related, but they are not necessarily based on the same psychological processes. Facial attractiveness depends strongly on the visible characteristics of the face, whereas the beauty of a portrait can also be shaped by composition, color, lighting, technique, and artistic style.
A portrait can be visually beautiful even when the depicted person is not especially attractive. Conversely, an attractive face may appear in an artwork that viewers find aesthetically unremarkable or even unpleasant. Judgments of artistic beauty also seem to be more strongly influenced by interpretation, context, and other cognitive effects than judgments of facial attractiveness.
Study author Gregor U. Hayn-Leichsenring wanted to find a way to distinguish between beauty and attractiveness based on their relationship to objective properties. He conducted an online experiment using art portraits as stimuli.
Study participants were 300 adults aged 18 to 71. Their average age was 33.6 years. 101 of them were women.
The study author created a database of 192 digital copies of art portraits. It included portraits from different artistic styles (Baroque, Impressionism, and Expressionism) and their numbers were balanced.
In the experiment, each participant viewed 70 randomly selected images from this database and rated them for attractiveness and beauty. The ratings were made on a 9-point Likert scale (a rating format ranging from 1 to 9). There were no time restrictions for giving the ratings. The author used the QIPs toolbox to analyze the characteristics of art pieces in the dataset. The QIPs toolbox is an open-access tool for calculating standardized quantitative image properties such as color, complexity, symmetry, balance, fractal structure, or entropy. It is used in empirical aesthetics research.
Results showed that attractiveness and beauty ratings were highly correlated within a style. However, they were not identical. Overall, Impressionistic art pieces tended to be rated as more attractive, while Baroque pieces tended to be seen as more beautiful. Most Expressionistic pieces were seen as less beautiful and attractive than the other two styles, with notable exceptions.
The author created a statistical model that aimed to examine the associations between attractiveness and beauty ratings and characteristics of pictures. He found that beauty and attractiveness ratings both depend on style, but that beauty ratings also depend on self-similarity and mirror symmetry of the image. Attractiveness ratings were not predicted by any specific image properties that the QIPs toolbox could identify.
Mirror symmetry is the degree to which an image is similar to its mirror reflection along major axes. Self-similarity, on the other hand, is a measure of how similar edge and gradient patterns are across different spatial scales of an image. Higher self-similarity indicates that there are repeated structural patterns at multiple levels.
“In this study, two closely related hedonic values were examined, only one of which showed systematic relationships with self-similarity and mirror symmetry. Overall, beauty evaluations are not only more influenced by cognitive processes than attractiveness evaluations, but are also more strongly associated with specific QIPs [quantitative image properties], which was not observed for attractiveness ratings,” the study author concluded.
The study sheds light on how humans perceive beauty and attractiveness. However, the author emphasized that the link between image properties and beauty ratings was likely driven primarily by Baroque portraits, which were on average less self-similar and more symmetrical than the other styles. It should also be noted that the study focused exclusively on artistic portraits, and findings evaluating beauty and attractiveness of other types of stimuli might differ.
The study, “Disentangling beauty and attractiveness in art portraits: Differential links to quantitative image properties“, was authored by Gregor U. Hayn-Leichsenring.

Fiji declares a national emergency as HIV cases skyrocket
Unknown

2026-09-17

Fiji declares a national emergency as HIV cases skyrocket
Zane Irwin
- Fiji declared a national emergency after HIV cases surged 16 times since 2019, with over 2,000 new cases in 2025 and one in 60 adults infected.
- The rise is linked to increased injectable drug use, including a dangerous practice called "bluetoothing," and Fiji's role as a drug transit hub during the pandemic.
- The government plans a full response with free testing, treatment, harm reduction, and calls for community support to fight stigma and control the epidemic.
AI generated
SUVA – Fiji has declared a national crisis amid an extraordinary rise in HIV cases, with health officials raising the alarm about an epidemic that has emerged alongside an increase in injectable drug use.
Fiji, a Pacific island nation of less than one million people, recorded more than 2,000 new HIV cases in 2025 – 16 times as many as in 2019, the government said in an official statement on Sept 15.
One in 60 adults on the archipelago is living with the virus that causes AIDS, the government estimated.
UNAIDS, a United Nations programme, said in a statement on Sept 16 that it was “one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally”.
Winnie Byanyima, the executive director of UNAIDS, added that Fiji’s epidemic was “a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over”.
The outbreak is not limited to particular areas or populations, health officials warned.
And because the nation serves as a regional hub for business, tourism and transport, the surge in cases could affect other countries in the South Pacific if left unchecked.
That inter-connectedness may have contributed to the soaring rates of infection, said Eamonn Murphy, director of regional support teams in the Asia-Pacific, Central Asia and Eastern Europe for UNAIDS.
An influx of drugs on the islands during the Covid-19 pandemic added “fuel on the flame” to a long-standing but low-level HIV presence in Fiji, Murphy said.
The country is a key example in a growing trend of Pacific island nations “caught in the middle of illicit smuggling routes”, according to a 2024 UN report.
As substances like methamphetamine and cocaine pass through Fiji and other island nations on their way to Australia and New Zealand, the report said, those nations have emerged as drug markets, not just way stations.
Fiji is also one of several global hot spots where a dangerous trend called “bluetoothing”, in which people inject themselves with the blood of other drug users to get a cheap high, is contributing to spikes in HIV rates.
Health officials say they believe that drug use is a key driver of Fiji’s epidemic.
A December report by the World Health Organization and UN Development Programme found that nearly half of the HIV patients with available information about their exposure had injected drugs, primarily crystal methamphetamine.
“Fiji was off the map in terms of HIV,” Murphy said.
But in recent years, the virus has spread throughout the country, heavily affecting young men but also raising mortality rates among children and babies born to infected women.
In its statement on Sept 15, the government said that 59 infants were born with HIV in 2025, with 18 of them dying before their first birthday.
Fiji’s government has ramped up testing and treatment efforts since January 2025, when the nation declared an HIV outbreak.
But “an outbreak-level response is no longer sufficient”, Atonio Lalabalavu, the nation’s health minister, said in a video statement posted on Sept 15.
Fiji pledged a “whole-of-government response”, including expanded access to free testing, prevention services and treatment, as well as harm-reduction measures such as programmes that allow people who inject drugs to exchange used needles for clean ones.
Murphy praised the government’s efforts, but said community leaders and the religious authorities would have to help combat the stigma around drug use and misunderstandings about HIV and its treatments.
“They really need to move fast,” he said. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Zelensky’s Former Comedy Studio Hit in Russian Strike – But It’s the Symbolism Moscow Is After
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:55:04 UTC
08:55:04 KST

When a Russian jet-powered drone strike destroyed a Kyiv warehouse used by the Kvartal 95 comedy studio on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 20 years of costumes, sets and props went up in flames.
No studio employees were injured, but the symbolism is striking: Russia destroyed part of the physical archive of the career that took Volodymyr Zelensky from comedian to president.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The illusion of control
Totalitarian rulers have long tried to weaken rivals by attacking their leaders and symbols – an impulse known since ancient Rome as damnatio memoriae.
During World War II, Stalingrad showed the power of symbolism: the city had strategic value, but its name – honoring Joseph Stalin – gave its capture enormous propaganda importance for Hitler and its defense equal significance for Stalin.
Compensation for military failure
When Russia cannot achieve decisive victories on the battlefield, symbolic attacks become another way to project power at home.
Kryvyi Rih, Zelensky’s hometown and the city where his parents lived, has repeatedly been hit by Russian missile and drone strikes.
This week, Zelensky told CBS News that Russian drones twice targeted his presidential aircraft during recent trips through Moldovan airspace.
Hitting a leader’s hometown, threatening his aircraft, or destroying the physical remnants of his past allows Moscow to project its reach where it has failed to impose its will, despite staggering battlefield losses.
At Least 10 Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russian Attack Injures 12, Including Two Children
When Russia cannot break Ukraine on the battlefield, it goes after its symbols.
Moscow’s changing narrative on Zelensky
For years, Russian state media and officials dismissed him as a former comedian who would crumble within days of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
But as Russia’s so-called “special military operation” dragged into its fifth year, that narrative became harder to sustain.
The irony is striking.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov now speaks of Zelensky not as a political footnote, but as a central figure in the West’s support for Ukraine.
The man Moscow once dismissed has become the wartime leader of a country the Kremlin has failed to subdue – and one of its most persistent obsessions.
Misunderstanding where Ukraine’s power resides
The strength of Kvartal 95 never lived in a warehouse of props, just as Ukraine’s resilience does not depend on a single building, aircraft, or city.
Hours after the attack, the studio issued a statement that captured the country’s unyielding spirit:
“Russian weapons can destroy property. But they cannot stop us,” the Kvartal 95 statement read.
“We continue to work, write new jokes, and help Ukrainian defenders. All scheduled concerts will take place. With props or without them...
“Because laughter today is also about life. About life that continues despite everything.”
By trying to burn Zelensky’s past or obliterate historic archives such as those at the Dovzhenko Studios, Putin resorts to a classic form of Soviet-style revisionism. Yet the Kremlin miscalculates: destroying the symbols cannot erase what they represent.
Ukraine has long since torn up Moscow’s script.

Around this time of year, new products launch left and right. I wrote similar words just yesterday ahead of Boox launching its latest devices. And now, Dyson, one of the big names in vacuum cleaners, just launched three innovative products.
Dyson already announced several new products earlier in September, from vacuums to an electric toothbrush with a built-in camera. Some of those vacuums are now available to buy, specifically the three robot vacuums in the new Dyson Nurovi line: the Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry ($550), the Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash + Dry ($700), and the Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV ($1,200).
This robot vacuum line has a new look, but the technology has changed too. All three Nurovi models share a light gray color scheme that makes the base station and vacuum easy to distinguish from the Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai, but the base stations keep the canister-style compartments that make these vacuums look and feel distinctly Dyson. They also feature lidar laser-precision navigation—Dyson's last robot vacuum relied on an HD camera—and the most expensive model now uses a UV light to help find stains on your floors. Finally, they have what Dyson calls a Twin-Capture System to pick up dust and debris on both hard floors and carpets. The cheapest R1 model is a vacuum only, while the R2 and R3 are both vacuum-mop hybrids. But the R2 will only be available at Costco, while the R1 and R3 will be available on Dyson's website (and presumably at other retailers).
Here's a look at the three new robot vacuums. I'll be testing these soon to see how they measure up against similar vacuums, but a few features already intrigue me.
Dyson’s Nurovi Robot Vacuum Lineup
The Nurovi R1 is a vacuum-only robot, but like its siblings, it uses lidar to navigate and features the Twin-Capture tech. It promises a much better experience than what we had with the Dyson Vis Nav from a few years ago. It's an interesting option if you have mostly carpet and soft flooring that doesn't need a mop job, but I'm curious to see how it compares, since you can find other vacuums for this price that do both.
Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry for $700
This is the vacuum I'm most intrigued about. It's a great price point—nearly half the price of the Spot+Scrub model—but has lidar navigation and the new Twin-Capture technology. It has triangle-style pads for mopping, which is unique and something I hope works as well as I imagine, as someone who loves to corner-test a robot vacuum. It promises 21,000 Pa of suction, which is a nice amount of power. The only downside is that you need a Costco membership to purchase one, as it's a Costco exclusive.
Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200
This is the new top-of-the-line model of Dyson's robot vacuums. I wasn't super impressed by the previous Spot+Scrub Ai, since it didn't really seem to find stains. My favorite robot vacuum uses UV successfully to spot stains on floors, so I'm curious whether this Dyson model will deliver a similarly great experience. This vacuum still incorporates AI, which Dyson says can identify up to 200 types of household substances and clean them until they're gone. It packs a higher suction power than the R2 (30,000 Pa), though I don't always find the highest suction makes for the best results. Keep an eye out for my review of all three Dyson models once we test.

CikLeak claimed to have gained access to data from Russia’s Central Election Commission and contractors of the GAS “Elections” 2.0 system. There is currently no independent confirmation of the scale of the attack.
The anonymous hacker group CikLeak claimed to have hacked the infrastructure of Russia’s Central Election Commission and its contractors working on the GAS “Elections” 2.0 system. The obtained materials were handed over to the “Vazhnye Istorii” outlet, which reported that it had confirmed their authenticity, UNN writes.
Details

Journalists contacted “Tsifrotekh” Director Oleksii Husiev. Asked to comment on the information about the hack, he replied that this was the first he had heard of it.
The CEC had claimed a high level of protection
The report about the hack appeared on the eve of the State Duma elections, with voting scheduled for September 18–20. This is the first federal election campaign in Russia that is to be held using the new GAS “Elections” 2.0, which was put into operation at the beginning of 2026.
Shortly before the hackers’ reports, the head of Russia’s Central Election Commission, ella pamfilova, stated that GAS “Elections” was “as protected as possible” because it operates autonomously and is separated from the global network. After an analysis was conducted, the CEC identified the video surveillance and uninterrupted broadcasting systems as the most vulnerable elements of the electoral infrastructure.
There is currently no independent technical confirmation of the scale of the alleged hack or its possible impact on the operation of the electoral systems.

Snap tries to bring AR glasses to enterprise market, partnering with Nvidia, AWS and Salesforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:40:05 UTC
08:40:05 KST

Snap is partnering with Nvidia, Amazon Web Services and Salesforce as part of an effort to bring its $2,000 Specs augmented reality glasses to the enterprise market. 
Evan Spiegel, Snap's CEO, characterized the initiative as tied to the company's broader effort to help people "understand that Specs is a computer, not a pair of smart glasses for taking photos."
When Snap revealed the Specs AR glasses in June, with a $2,195 price tag and $200 refundable deposit, the company pitched the device as catering to the public instead of developers. Although AR and related virtual reality technologies have improved over the years, devices like Microsoft's HoloLens and Meta's Quest-branded VR headsets have failed to become breakout hits.
Spiegel said the bulkiness of those older devices were a major hindrance, and said his company's Specs AR glasses will be better suited for tasks like helping field technicians troubleshoot equipment problems by viewing digital instructions, and interacting with workers.
To date, Snap's success has been in the consumer market. The company is hoping that a partnership with the likes of Nvidia can change that.
"They've got an open-source XR AI platform that a number of businesses are already building on top of," Spiegel said. "The goal with both Salesforce and Nvidia is to make it really easy for businesses to get the benefits of those agentic platforms."
Snap is also debuting a consumer-oriented AI service dubbed Specs Intelligence that's like a digital assistant that can do tasks across the AR glasses as well as iPhones and Mac computers. Spiegel said the company hasn't determined specific pricing details yet, but it will include a free tier and "different price points" depending on usage.
The company's latest AI-related foray comes as debate heats up in the broader technology market about safety, and whether foundation model leaders like Anthropic and OpenAI should slow the pace of development.
Spiegel said, "these are concerns that have been raised for a long time."
"It's really important that we coordinate an international and thoughtful response," Spiegel said. "It's really important that regulators and policymakers consider actual potential harms rather than imagined harms, and so that's why I think it's going to be really important for a thoughtful and international group to really get together on this."

Here’s What Snap’s Expensive Specs Can Actually Do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:40:00 UTC
08:40:00 KST

Snap, the company behind Snapchat and a new pair of $2,195 augmented-reality smart glasses, is finally sharing more about what its glasses can actually do. Details came at a launch event in Los Angeles, where the company also announced a new AI service that anticipates what you want to do while wearing the glasses—or even just using your phone or laptop.
Snap announced its latest Specs in June at the Augmented World Expo tech conference. It says it will begin shipping them to buyers sometime this fall. They are expensive and look huge and heavy to wear, uncomfortable even on Snap CEO Evan Spiegel’s ears when he wore them at the AWE reveal, something he was widely mocked for online and that left people worried about how comfortably these glasses would fit. (Spiegel later posted on X with a picture of his unburdened ear, writing, “that's just what my ear looks like.”)
Despite that, Spiegel and the company repeatedly reiterated that Snap’s goal with the glasses is to make “computing more human.”
Here are some things you can do with the Specs glasses:
- Take calls via Bluetooth;
- Listen to music on Spotify;
- Capture photos and videos;
- Stream video from services like YouTube and HBO Max (the glasses feature a display);
- Buy stuff on Shopify, where you can view 3D product models, position them in a room, then pay for them;
- Mark up a digital whiteboard so you can brainstorm in the park;
- Translate spoken languages in real time. The glasses can listen to someone speaking to you in a different language and offer the translation through the speakers and as transcribed text on the display. Snap also has a partnership with Tripadvisor that lets you translate reviews, local phrases, and currency. Keep in mind that these kinds of real-time language translators can be hit or miss;
- Shoot hoops. Snap is partnering with the NBA and WNBA to build an interactive basketball experience that works with real-world basketball hoops and balls. The Specs can overlay visual guides and drill cues on real equipment. Similar experiences are available for sports like soccer and golf.
- Wave a magic wand. Thanks to an HBO Max collaboration, Specs can augment the room you're in to conjure up some virtual Harry Potter paraphernalia, letting you do things like receive a Hogwarts acceptance letter;
- With another person wearing Specs, you can play digital games like chess, ping pong, battleship, and dominoes;
- As you read a real, physical book, you can use the Specs to highlight and save passages or bookmark where you stop;
- Meditate;
- Become a digital DJ.
Snap is also pitching Specs as an enterprise product. It has partnerships with Salesforce, Amazon, and Nvidia to build out features that bring up codes or specs in the wearer’s field of view. They could also be used to find parts on a product or check backstock for an item. (Google similarly had an enterprise version of its Google Glass project but shut it down in 2023.)
Snap seems keen to separate its glasses from the ongoing criticism surrounding camera-equipped smart glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which have been called “pervert glasses.” (Ironic, considering Snap popularized the category with its original Spectacles, designed to record hands-free video for Snapchat Stories.) An LED indicator lights up when the cameras are actively capturing video or taking a photo.
Snap representatives have said the Specs “do not record the world to understand it,” noting that the glasses do not use facial recognition to identify people. WIRED found code in Meta’s apps earlier this year indicating the company was experimenting with a facial recognition feature on its smart glasses, but Meta subsequently removed it.
Are We Human?
Snap also wants in on the AI chatbot game. At its event, the company announced a brand-new AI service called Specs Intelligence. The app releases today and will work on iPhone, Mac, and the Specs glasses. You don’t need the glasses to use the app.
Snap calls Specs Intelligence an “anticipatory AI,” meaning it collects data about your day-to-day life and tries to envision what you want to do. The features will sound familiar if you’ve interacted with any AI chatbot that syncs with your calendar, email, or location info. It can help find a hotel, book travel plans, or answer questions.
Snap says its AI service organizes information based on “corners” like work, family, and goals. The AI “builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect.” That sounds like a whole lot of data collection will be necessary to build out a holistic picture of what you want in life.
Starting on October 1, people can go to a Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles to try before they buy.
But Spiegel routinely drums the “making computing more human” line without really reckoning with what its Specs are. Snap wants them to be a social gadget that lets people play games together, but one pair would cost you more than buying a PlayStation 5 for three of your friends. The company wants people to wear them while playing sports, but the glasses are huge and heavy. Will that be comfortable? How do you look down at a soccer ball and keep the glasses on your face?
I guess it's up to the humans who want to wear them to figure that out.

Fed’s Warsh heeds own advice with record short press conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

Fed’s Warsh heeds own advice with record short press conference
WASHINGTON – US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh has said he thinks policymakers should do a lot less talking.
He followed his own advice on Sept 16 when he held the shortest press conference on record for a Fed chair speaking after a regularly scheduled policy meeting.
Warsh’s customary news conference following the Fed’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time in more than three years clocked in at right around 30 minutes.
That was the shortest session since Fed chairs began holding regular press conferences in 2011.
The chairman stuck to his commitment not to foreshadow the Fed’s future actions, instead focusing on this week’s meeting and how Fed officials currently see the economy.
The Fed also changed the seating arrangement in the briefing room.
While journalists from major newspapers and wire services used to populate the front row, the seating was switched to alphabetical order by outlet name.
That meant Agence France-Presse got a spot in the front row. Reporters for The Wall Street Journal and Reuters were moved to the back of the room.
The future of the press conference, meanwhile, remains up in the air.
One of five task forces created by Warsh will examine communications.
It is charged with reviewing how the Fed “conveys policy deliberations and decisions amid uncertainty”, an umbrella that could put the press conference, among other communications tools, on the chopping block.
The Fed chief has said he does not want the central bank’s decisions to be front-page news.
At his first meeting as head of the Fed in June, he drastically shortened the post-meeting statement issued by policymakers.
He has also previously expressed scepticism about the benefits of news conferences, saying in June that the sessions are most useful when there is “something important to say”.
In July, he committed to continuing the regular press conferences – but only until the end of the year. BLOOMBERG

Live updates: Tony Burke set to unveil migration overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:27:13 UTC
08:27:13 KST

Thanks for joining us
Thanks for joining Miles Proust and me today as we covered the government's long-awaited unveiling of its migration shake-up.
Today:
- Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled a suite of migration changes, including tighter rules on visa-hopping, tougher action against visa overstayers, and a crackdown on rogue migration agents
- The government said the measures will reduce net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 by 2027-28, while continuing to prioritise workers in key sectors
- Construction workers, healthcare staff and educators will be prioritised under the migration system, with Burke arguing migration remains critical to housing construction and essential services
- Burke rejected claims Australia is experiencing "mass migration", arguing the debate has been distorted and warning that deep migration cuts would damage the economy
You can find out more about the migration changes on SBS World News at 6.30pm AEST and via OnDemand, including analysis by SBS News' chief political correspondent Anna Henderson.
SBS News will also publish more stories in the coming days to help you understand how these changes may affect you and your community.
You can also download our app and subscribe to our newsletter. It's the best way to stay across our updates, explainers and analysis as we continue covering these changes.
Until next time.
— Alexandra Koster
A 'dark day for multicultural Australia', asylum seeker advocate says
Kon Karapanagiotidis, CEO and founder of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, says the changes announced today mark "a dark day for multicultural Australia".
"Today our government chose to turn on migrants, international students and people seeking asylum who have built lives here, contributed to this country and asked for nothing more than the chance to belong," Karapanagiotidis said in a statement.
He was particularly concerned about how the changes would affect those seeking asylum, as well as plans to ramp up detention centre use for those overstaying their visas, saying they were reminiscent of US President Donald Trump's ICE immigration raids.
"Minister Burke went to great lengths to reassure Australians this would not look like Donald Trump's immigration raids.
"But look at what is actually being planned: 500 more compliance officers tasked with finding people, 1,250 more detention beds including plans to turn former COVID quarantine facilities in Victoria into detention centres, and billions more for removals."
He said the changes would double Australia's immigration detention regime and argued they would make Australia "smaller, meaner and more divided".
"We will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags," he added.
"We will fight any attempt to take away the right to work or shut people out of seeking protection."
— Alexandra Koster
What you might have missed
Here's a look back at some bits you may have missed from today's eagerly awaited migration plan.
Working holidays
A ballot system will be introduced for second and third-year working holiday-makers, who are required to work regionally.
Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and just 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively.
British citizens will remain exempt from having to work regionally in their second and third years, with the government honouring a free trade agreement between Australia and the UK.
Overstayers crackdown
People who overstay their visas will be taken into detention, reviving a policy that was in place before 2015.
The government will also seek more facilities, compliance officers and beds to prepare for the crackdown.
The Department of Home Affairs estimates there are around 77,000 unlawful overstayers.
International students targeted
A suite of changes will target international students.
International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring their family members to Australia, though there are some exceptions, including for PhD students.
The only way foreign students will be able to extend their visas is by transferring to higher-level courses, like a bachelor's to a master's.
— Alexandra Koster, with additional reporting by Australian Associated Press.
Chalmers asked how the government can be trusted
Nationals MP Kevin Hogan asked Treasurer Jim Chalmers how Australians can trust the government after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the refugee intake would remain at 20,000.
His question was in reference to Albanese confirming the intake would not change, despite reports the government was planning to slash the figure by a third.
Chalmers said migration was a force for good, reiterating some of the points Tony Burke made during his National Press Club address.
"The difference between this side of the House and that side of the House is our migration policy is determined by cabinet ministers in the cabinet room. The Liberal Party's migration policy is determined by One Nation in the cockpit of a plane donated by a billionaire [a reference to mining magnate Gina Rinehart] ," he said.
— Miles Proust
Question Time kicks off in parliament
Question Time in parliament has begun with Opposition leader Angus Taylor.
He started by saying there are 1,100 people arriving in Australia each day under Labour, which amounts to a new person every 78 seconds.
"Labor is in denial, why were there no cuts to immigration today?" Taylor asked.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke responded:
"If you make cuts too deep, too hard in the immigration system, you trash the Australian economy. That's what happens."
He asked if Taylor had listened to his own backbenchers and farmers, who want backpackers to work in the regions.
But he acknowledged migration needed to be tempered to "give housing a chance to catch up".
— Miles Proust
Key points from Tony Burke's NPC address
If you're just joining us, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has used a National Press Club (NPC) address in Canberra to announce changes to Australia's migration system.
It comes after weeks of heated political debate about migration.
These are the major points from his speech:
- The suite of measures includes removing unlawful non-citizens, cracking down on "visa-hopping" and "rogue migration agents", introducing a ballot system for second- and third-year backpackers, restricting family applicants for most student visas, and prioritising processing for key sectors, such as healthcare, construction and education.
- The measures aim to reduce Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) figure to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28. The NOM in the year to March this year was 292,000.
- Burke addressed "absurd" migration claims, saying Australia was not experiencing "mass migration". He also rubbished claims that the government had been letting in yoga teachers over construction workers.
- He said the housing crisis was not caused by immigration, but immigration could be part of the solution. Construction workers will earn more points under the skilled migration pathway to boost housing construction in Australia.
- He acknowledged visa-hopping was a "genuine problem", with the government to introduce a qualification scale. It means a bachelor's degree student will only be able to move "up the scale" to a master's degree.
- Processing of working holiday visa applications has slowed. Faster processing times will be restored for those in their second or third year who are required to work regionally.
- A "no further stay" provision will be applied to visitor visas, only applying to future visas.
- There will be tougher sanctions for visa overstayers. The government will return to a pre-2015 model in which visa overstayers will be detained. An additional 100 compliance officer roles and 250 beds will be made available. The government will also consider repurposing a former quarantine facility in Melbourne.
- Burke rubbished reports that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese didn't want him to give the speech at the NPC.
- He said One Nation and the Coalition's plans to cut migration would "trash the Australian economy".
— Miles Proust
'It'll send the message that they aren't welcome here'
Young high school students Shubhangi Parihar and Nuri Jung have told SBS News they're worried about the government "targeting" migrants in their city of Perth.
"I think [migrants] offer better community and cultural values, which I think is important in Australia, where immigrants come here so much," Jung told SBS' Christopher Tan.
"I don't know why the government is planning to reduce that, because they were immigrants themselves at one point in time."
She was worried in particular about the loss of Asian food, less representation of people like her, and what sort of message it sent to migrants.
"I think it'll send the message that they aren't welcome here when in reality Australians are pretty welcoming," Jung said.
Her friend questioned the rationale for targeting migrants.
"A lot of them do stay in Australia afterwards, which is good, but a lot of them are just studying so they can get a better job back home," Parihar said.
"I don't see why they are targeting them."
— Alexandra Koster, Christopher Tan
Burke asked how government will win over the public
Burke was asked about how the government expects to win over the public when One Nation and the Coalition have lower migration targets.
One Nation has announced it will reduce temporary migration by 750,000 places over three years.
Last month, Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg said the Coalition would bring the net overseas migration levels under 180,000 people per year on average.
That compares to the federal government's aim of 225,000 by 2027-28.
"Lower levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy. That's what they'll do," Burke said.
"Imagine half of the construction workers who we have to build the houses that we need not coming. Imagine two-thirds of the people who we rely on in aged care or nursing not coming. That's the impact of those policies."
But he acknowledged the concerns held by Australians when they see lines of people waiting to inspect a rental property.
"We have a shortage of homes, and people want to make sure that we guide the immigration system so that we soften our numbers to be able to allow housing to catch up," he said.
"But it would be a complete own goal to say the way we're going to do that is to trash our medical system, trash our aged care system, and not get the construction workers to build the homes that would actually help with the problem."
— Miles Proust
Single Perth international student Rui not concerned about visa changes
On the streets of Perth, international students have shared their perspective with SBS' Western Australian correspondent, Christopher Tan.
International student Rui Lin Zhang, 26, said that the changes may mean students head elsewhere.
"For people with enough money to do international learning, I think they might choose another country, like America or the UK," Lin Zhang said.
But he said he would still pick Australia to study in, despite new rules preventing student visa holders from bringing family members to Australia.
"Some people from other cultures will have family reunions and want to get together," he said.
"But for me, I’m quite fine ... At least for now I'm single, so I'm not quite worried about the new policies."
— Alexandra Koster, Christopher Tan
A tense exchange between Burke and SBS' Anna Henderson
During questions, SBS News' own Anna Henderson asked Burke about migrant communities feeling silence from the government during the migration debate, resulting in a tense exchange.
"Do you acknowledge that while you've been in government, there are points in this debate that have been extremely harmful to migrant communities where Labor was either quiet or, according to those communities, felt there was a silence?" Henderson asked.
Burke pushed back, asking: "Can you give me an example of when I've been silent on that?"
He added that he had spent his "entire political life" standing up against hate speech.
"We've spoken here about mass migration," Henderson responded. "You've today declared that to be absurd.
"The feedback from migrant communities is they haven't felt like the government has had their back to really loudly push back against that.
"So it's not my view. It's the view I'm getting from the community groups who feel that demonisation."
Burke said the "emphatic" speech he had just given proved that wasn't the case.
"The issues of making sure that people, no matter what their their heritage is ... that they are 100 per cent part of the Australian community," he responded.
"It's something that I would be saying on a platform somewhere pretty much every day, and have devoted my political career as much to that," he said, adding that he has contributed more to that cause than any other.
— Alexandra Koster
Burke rubbishes reports PM didn't want him to give speech
Burke was asked if Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who reportedly didn't want Burke to give the speech at the National Press Club, had been convinced to change his mind.
Burke said that report came a day after he'd spoken with Albanese, confirming that he would give the speech at the forum.
"If I were to spend my whole life dealing with stories that have been written that were untrue, that's all I'd spend my time doing," he said.
— Miles Proust
Burke says he 'never leaked against the cabinet'
Burke was asked about reports that the government was considering changes to asylum seeker protection visas, such as changes to the time frames for applying, or the removal of work rights for temporary visa holders whose asylum protection claims have been rejected.
"A lot's been written over the last six weeks, and I can assure people that not one single media drop came from me," he said.
"I've never leaked against the cabinet, and I never will."
He said the government was working with the Opposition and it wanted to prioritise genuine claims.
"I don't think there's much public appetite for people who know they don't have a valid claim, being able to game the system," he said.
"I'm not going to go any deeper than that."
— Miles Proust
'I better say football or I'll get in trouble'
There was also a brief moment of levity as Burke caught himself committing a World Game sin.
Speaking about "disingenuous" asylum protection claims, Burke emphasised that having a protection system for asylum in Australia was critically important.
He then referred to the decision earlier in the year regarding the Iranian women's football team, in which visas were granted for two players.
"There have probably been few issues that I've been involved with where I've had more support and thanks from people on the street than the decision that was taken earlier this year with respect to two elite Iranian soccer players," Burke said, before quickly correcting himself.
"Sorry, I better say footballers or I'll get in trouble."
Visa hopping was then brought up again, with Burke saying there are some exploiting the protection system.
"To give a sense of the gravity of this, if we took the people who apply from countries where more than 85 per cent of the applications fail, that constitutes 80 per cent of our caseload," he said of visa claims under the protection system.
"This is an issue I'd like to be able to deal with ... I want to deal with it in a way that does not, in any way, create problems for the genuine asylum seekers."
— Alexandra Koster
Burke says he's not afraid of using the word 'sovereignty'
Moving into questions, Burke was asked whether he was comfortable with the reforms being compared with former prime minister John Howard's approach.
Howard said at the start of the 2001 federal election campaign: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
Burke said he wasn't afraid of using the word "sovereignty".
"The sovereignty of Australia matters, and people want to know that there's a system," he said.
"What we need to make sure of now as we go to the next layer where people do come on a visa but try to effectively work around the visa system to deliver outcomes that Australia would never intend. And that's what I want us to be able to do."
— Miles Proust
Tougher sanctions for visa overstayers
Burke said the government will impose tougher sanctions on visa overstayers, returning to a scheme in place before 2015.
Before 2015, Burke said visa overstayers would be taken into detention, and within a few weeks, they'd organise their own flight and leave.
"That didn't just affect them. It had a behavioural impact," he said.
"The whole lot of other people who were overstaying thought, 'yeah, it's better that I just get on a plane and leave'."
He said that would not involve "the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries".
The government is also looking at alternative places for detention, including at a former quarantine facility in Melbourne.
He said there will be an additional 100 compliance officers and 250 beds.
"Effectively, what we are going back to doing is simply being able to make sure that if you overstay, you will not be able to say, 'Well, there's no consequences, as if they're ever going to make sure that I leave'," he said.
The code for migration agents will also be changed, with those who encourage claims without merit to be sanctioned and de-registered.
"It's something that should have happened some time ago, and we cannot have people with some sort of official formal status using that official formal status to encourage people to make something which, by any definition, is an unacceptable abuse of the system," Burke said.
He said the reforms were about making sure the system was "working as best as possible for the Australian economy".
— Miles Proust
Changes to student and visitor visas
Burke also addressed new rules targeting visitor visas and student visas.
Visitor visas will also have a "no further stay" provision.
Again, this change will not affect those already in Australia and applies for future visas only.
Burke also addressed student visas more in depth.
He said there are legitimate reasons for why some people may change courses or need to extend their visas, but there is a problem with "progression" in the context of "visa hopping".
"Someone finishes their course and where do they go to next? And one of the classic areas of visa hopping is people finish a course, hop to the next course, hop to the next," he said, also pointing to "illegitimate" educational providers enticing visa holders to stay longer.
To address this, the government will set up what it says is a "qualification scale".
"What we'll be doing is setting a very simple rule: you can go up the qualification scale, but only up the qualification scale," Burke said.
In practicality, that means that at the end of a bachelor degree, those on a visa will only be able to move "up the scale" to a master's degree.
"So, at the end of a bachelor degree, if you want to then do a master's, that's up the scale.
"But to hop around, up and down, to different institutions and claim what is actually just seeking a migration outcome as part of Australia's export of international education will come to an end as a model."
— Alexandra Koster
Changes to points system, backpacker visa processing
Burke said the reforms are split into three parts: who arrives, who stays and who leaves.
Changes will be made to the points test, a scoring system used to rank and select skilled workers for visas, with those with housing trade qualifications receiving the same number of points as a university qualification.
Construction, agriculture, fisheries, resources, and teaching will also be prioritised.
"The fact we are doing that allows us to restore the normal processing speed that we were previously at for primary applications for working holiday-makers," he said.
Working holiday maker visa approvals have slowed, and Burke said faster processing will be restored for those in their second or third year who are required to work regionally.
He said that the remote work requirement does not apply to working holiday-makers from the United Kingdom under a free trade agreement, noting the number of UK backpackers has exploded.
"Just to give you a sense of the pace of the growth, at the time that the free trade agreement was signed, the number of UK backpackers we had here in Australia was in the order of 17,000," he said.
"Now that's a little bit on the low side, so that was the end of the pandemic. But the previous peak had been around 35,000. It's now just shy of 80,000 in terms of numbers of people here in Australia.
"It's a level of growth that means we are just at the moment going to continue to be processing that one slowly."
He said the federal government was having conversations with UK counterparts about it in a "constructive way".
— Miles Proust
International students no longer able to bring family members
The government will be banning new international students from being able to attach family members to their visa.
"We will no longer be allowing the attaching of family members for international students or for graduate visas," Burke said.
But he said those already here with their families would be permitted to stay.
"We're not going to be breaking up families on shore," he said.
"The ones who are already here, that'll stay as is until whatever point they leave Australia, unless they they end up being entitled to a permanent visa.
"But we will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."
— Alexandra Koster
Burke acknowledges visa-hopping is a 'genuine problem'
Tony Burke has acknowledged visa-hopping is a "genuine problem".
But he said people on student visas who then get a graduate visa, start work in an area with a skills shortage, and are sponsored by an employer, were not the problem.
"They get an employer-sponsored temporary work visa in an area of skill shortage, they then apply to the permanent program," he says.
"Once they've been a permanent resident for more than 12 months, given the years that they've already been here, they then become an Australian citizen. That is not visa hopping. That is the system working at its absolute best."
He says the issue is individuals who would never have met the qualifications for permanent residency effectively jump from visa to visa, using the appeals process to stay as long as possible.
"It eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay, because at that point they have Australian citizen children, and at that point they are so integrated into a local community," he says.
— Miles Proust
Housing shortage not caused by immigration, Burke says
Migrants skilled in construction and housing trades will earn more points under the skilled visa format in an effort to boost Australia's housing construction.
Burke also addressed debates claiming migrants were linked with the housing crisis.
"A genuine problem is the concept of what we do with respect to housing," he said.
"Now, I start with this: housing and the housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration, but immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."
He emphasises that immigration is "not putting further pressure on housing", but says that the government needs immigration to "soften enough" so that housing has a chance to "catch up".
Other industries, including agriculture, fisheries, resources and teaching will also be added to the priority list alongside construction.
— Alexandra Koster

Aggrieved party can seek deletion of court clips on socials: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:19:16 UTC

SC Had Earlier Banned Uploads Without Approval From SC Or HCs
SC Had Earlier Banned Uploads Without Approval From SC Or HCs
SC Had Earlier Banned Uploads Without Approval From SC Or HCs
NEW DELHI: In an important clarification on the ban on use of video clips of court proceedings, Supreme Court on Wednesday said if such footage was uploaded on social media, an aggrieved person could approach the authorities under the Information and Technology Act to seek a "takedown" order of the content.This clarification came from a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing a petition filed by an advocate whose arguments on July 1 before one of the SC benches on behalf of his father, accused of jumping bail, went viral on social media.Counsel for the advocate said unauthorised circulation of the proceedings on social media platforms had violated his right to life, liberty, dignity and privacy. "Continuous availability of the impugned videos on social media platforms, even after express judicial orders prohibiting such dissemination, constitutes an ongoing and irreparable injury to the petitioner's fundamental rights," he said.The bench said the SC had passed the ban order on July 24, and the lawyer could approach authorities under the IT Act and seek takedown orders against digital and social media platforms for deleting the alleged offensive content being circulated despite a ban imposed by the top court.
CJI Kant said there was an efficacious remedy available to the advocate and he must avail that. However, he clarified that if any social media or digital platform used footage from livestreaming of court proceedings and either added a narrative or exhibited clips selectively to convey a different meaning, it would be viewed very seriously and may amount to contempt of court.
"If someone adds something to what the court observed or presents the proceedings in such a manner to generate controversy, we will take a very serious view of such acts," the CJI said.The bench advised the lawyer to move the authorities under Section 69A of the IT Act or directly send a legal notice to digital and social media platforms to take down the offensive content. If the intermediaries or authorities did not respond to the request and the grievance remained unresolved, he could file a petition in the SC, it said.Frowning upon edited clips of live-streamed judicial proceedings accompanied by biased commentary flooding social media, the SC on July 24 had banned uploading, sharing and circulation of audiovisual excerpts of court hearings on social media and digital platforms and said any online posting of such clips would require mandatory prior approval from the SC or jurisdictional HCs.

"There's certain moments in our industry where everything is changing, and this is that moment for enterprise," CEO Marc Benioff said at the event.

Meanwhile, in the past three months, Slack, the chat app Salesforce acquired for $27.1 billion in 2021, has emerged as a hub for communicating with AI agents, said Alexa Vignone, the company's president and chief revenue officer.
"I'm not going to use the word 'SaaSpocalypse' anymore," said Miguel Milano, Salesforce's operating chief, at the event. "I hope you don't either, and the market will come to its senses, little by little."

Salesforce spent hundreds of millions of dollars on Anthropic stock, which will likely be worth tens of billions, Benioff told the gathering.
"We'll end up probably selling it," he said, and paying off the company's accelerated share repurchase debt. "So it'll be a good trade for us."

‘People don’t have money’: Syrian fuel hikes deepen economic pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

‘People don’t have money’: Syrian fuel hikes deepen economic pain
Higher diesel and petrol prices are pushing up transport and food costs across an already impoverished Syria.
Damascus, Syria – The fuel price hike hit at midnight on Sunday. By Monday morning, frustration had poured into the streets, sparking open defiance across Syria.
A sudden government decree drove diesel prices up by 40 percent overnight and petrol by 28 percent. For millions of Syrians, the price increase is a direct threat to their survival.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
- list 2 of 3Nations prosper or fail by the institutions they build
- list 3 of 3US set to approve 60,000 heavy bombs for Israel: What that means
Demonstrators quickly gathered in public squares from Aleppo and Idlib in the north to Hama in central Syria and Deraa in the south, burning tyres and blocking key roads – including the main highway between Damascus and Aleppo.
The initial wave of demonstrations has since eased in some areas, but the anger has not disappeared. On Wednesday, protesters in northeastern Syria blocked the M4 highway near Tal Tamr, stranding hundreds of oil tankers. Demonstrators said they would not reopen the route unless the price increases were reversed.
Beyond the protests, a black market for diesel is booming. Syrian security units have started intercepting tankers caught heading to unlicensed refineries to fill up on illegal fuel.
Repeated price increases
The anger stems from the immediate fallout from the government’s decision, which comes on the back of the high international price of oil, largely a result of the consequences of the United States-Israel war on Iran.
The United Nations estimates that nearly 90 percent of Syrians live below the poverty line; any jump in fuel costs instantly drives up the price of transport and basic food.
And Sunday’s hike came on top of repeated increases. Since February, the price of 95-octane petrol has risen by about 86 percent, while diesel has more than doubled. Over the same period, benchmark Brent crude rose by about 44 percent.
It all comes as Syria continues its recovery from a devastating, more than decade-long war, which only ended with the fall of the regime of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. The new government has been attempting to improve the country’s economy, including by successfully working to remove most of the international sanctions that had been placed on the country for years.
But for many Syrians, economic improvements are not coming fast enough.
In Damascus, minibuses – a lifeline for the working class – raised fares immediately from 30 to 45 cents. Drivers say their margins are practically gone. One US dollar is equivalent to about 130 new Syrian pounds.
Adel Ali Meree, a bus driver, worked an eight-hour shift only to see his earnings swallowed by the fuel tank.
“I spent all my money on diesel. I only have four and a half dollars left,” he explained. “At the end of the day, I might earn only $10. I could make this money doing any other kind of work. It’s just not worth it.”
Larger operators face the same grim maths. Bashar Sleiman operates a tour bus that needs 90 litres of diesel daily. With the price hikes, the cost to fill his tank jumped from the equivalent of $84 to $120.
His company hasn’t yet finalised a new pricing structure, but he expects to increase his usual $110-$125 daily rate by at least $15 to cover the increased costs.
“If a tourist comes thinking they will spend $1,500, they will need more,” Sleiman said. “The hotels, food, transportation, and a tour guide will all get more expensive. Traffic has been a bit lighter the last couple of days, but this won’t last. Nobody can afford not to generate an income.”
Feeling the hit
Cross-border routes are also taking a hit. Ahmed Sweid drives a 25-passenger bus for the Shaheen transport company, running between Idlib and Beirut.
A round trip now requires $280 in diesel alone. So far, the company has kept its ticket price at $40, relying on fully booked buses to absorb the financial blow, but operators remain anxious.
At local markets, the crisis is just as obvious. In the Mezzeh neighbourhood of Damascus, produce seller Ahmed Obeid said his delivery freight charges had tripled overnight, jumping from $4 to $12 a load.
“When fuel prices go up, transport costs go up,” Obeid said. “That extra cost is passed on to the consumer. But people don’t have money.”
Damascus officials blame the high cost of securing fuel internationally. The Ministry of Energy says Syria currently produces about 100,000 barrels of crude oil a day, while the domestic market needs roughly 300,000 to 325,000 barrels of oil and petroleum products, leaving the country heavily reliant on imports. It says about 60 percent of Syria’s diesel supply is currently imported.
Syria’s People’s Assembly was set to question Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir over the price increases on Thursday, but on Wednesday said that the session had been postponed until September 20 as the ministry needed more time to prepare.
The government does insist the price hikes are temporary.
But for Syrians dealing with ruined infrastructure and massive inflation, waiting for global markets to stabilise isn’t an option.
For a population just trying to buy groceries, a “temporary” shock is simply too long to survive.

The number of attempts to illegally cross the border from Belarus has sharply decreased in Poland
Kyiv • UNN
Since the beginning of the year, Poland has recorded 472 attempts to illegally cross the border from Belarus, compared with more than 25,000 in 2025. Migration flows have shifted to the borders of Lithuania and Latvia.
Poland has recorded a sharp decrease in the number of attempted illegal border crossings from Belarus — there have been about 472 since the beginning of the year, compared with more than 25,000 during the same period in 2025. This was reported by Polish Ministry of the Interior spokesperson Renata Leoniak during a parliamentary committee meeting, LRT reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
As of September 13, the Polish Border Guard had registered about 472 attempted illegal border crossings. In all cases, the migrants were not allowed to enter the country.
By comparison, during the same period in 2025, the number of such attempts exceeded 25,000.
Migration flows have changed direction
According to Leoniak, only one case was recorded during this period in which a migrant managed to break through the engineering barriers. He was detained. A year earlier, there had been 1,529 such incidents.
The Polish Interior Ministry representative noted that migration flows had shifted to the Lithuanian-Belarusian and Latvian-Belarusian borders. Against this backdrop, Poland reintroduced controls and expanded the buffer zone on the border with Lithuania.
Leoniak also reported an increase in attempts to smuggle cigarettes using weather balloons. According to her, this trend emerged after Minsk introduced a ban on the use of civilian drones.
At the end of August, Warsaw expanded the buffer zone along the border for the seventh time since it was introduced in June 2024. The zone, with strict restrictions and enhanced controls, extends for more than 78 km along the Polish-Belarusian border.

====================================================================================================

Interview: China can set example in balancing AI innovation, regulation -- Saudi expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
07:09:18 CST
08:09:18 KST

RIYADH, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The key challenge in artificial intelligence (AI) governance is to translate principles into practice, Majid Ali AlShehry, acting director-general of the International Center for AI Research and Ethics in Saudi Arabia, said on Wednesday, noting that China can set a global example and help promote international cooperation in balancing AI innovation and regulation.
In an exclusive interview with Xinhua on the sidelines of the fourth UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, AlShehry said there is already a degree of international consensus on the basic principles of AI governance, while some countries have developed their own AI ethics frameworks, regulatory frameworks and guiding principles.
"The challenge now is that we want to move from policies into practice," he said. "We need to move from understanding what the problem is to embedding that compliance into the value chain of building solutions and tools."
AlShehry said China has a vast AI ecosystem spanning infrastructure, data centers, technologies and companies with full-stack capabilities, and therefore can play a significant role in shaping the global AI governance landscape.
China, as a leading nation in AI, could "become an influencer toward the goal of balancing between innovation and regulation," he said, adding that such efforts could help ensure that AI technologies do not go beyond appropriate boundaries while allowing humanity to continue advancing and benefiting from the best technologies.
"I expect China and other countries to work in that direction, and we hope to see some role models coming to this balance from the great nations in AI," he said.
Established in 2023 under the auspices of UNESCO, the Riyadh-based International Center for AI Research and Ethics seeks to build partnerships with universities, research institutions and companies using AI around the world, AlShehry said, adding that it is actively working to establish partnerships with Chinese institutions.
The center is looking to invite Chinese universities to join its newly announced initiative to develop master's degree programs in AI ethics, he said.
Under the initiative, the center will define the key messages and core components of an AI ethics master's degree program, while participating universities will develop their curricula in accordance with their own regulations and educational systems.
"We are building this blueprint in collaboration with international researchers and professors from all over the world," AlShehry said. "Definitely joining this consortium by Chinese universities would add great value to our work."
Commenting on the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai in July, AlShehry said efforts to bring countries together for "truthful discussions" on the future of AI were positive and could help build global consensus on AI governance.
"We are looking to be part of these initiatives in any way possible," he said. ■

U.S. Fed announces 1st interest rate hike in over 3 years as inflation stays sticky

Photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 shows the U.S. Federal Reserve building in Washington, D.C., the United States. The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its target federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent to address persistent inflation, marking its first interest rate hike since July 2023. (Xinhua/Li Rui)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its target federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent to address persistent inflation, marking its first interest rate hike since July 2023.
"Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little," said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in a statement.
In support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, "the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent," the FOMC said.
The committee reaffirmed "its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system."
"Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability," it reiterated.
All 12 FOMC members voted in favor of the rate hike.
In conjunction with the FOMC meeting held on Sept. 15-16, participants also submitted their projections of the most likely outcomes for real GDP growth, the unemployment rate and inflation for each year from 2026 to 2029 and over the longer run.
The Fed's Board members and Federal Reserve Bank presidents projected median U.S. GDP growth of 2.3 percent in 2026, up from the June projection of 2.2 percent. The median unemployment rate was projected at 4.1 percent in 2026, down from the June projection of 4.3 percent.
For 2027, participants raised their GDP growth projection to 2.4 percent from 2.3 percent and lowered their unemployment rate projection to 4.1 percent from 4.3 percent.
As for inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, FOMC participants projected it at 3.7 percent in 2026, up from the June projection of 3.6 percent. The projection for 2027 remained unchanged at 2.3 percent.
The participants defined "appropriate monetary policy" as the future path of policy that best satisfies their interpretation of the statutory mandate to promote maximum employment and price stability.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference after the FOMC meeting. He has said that the risk is that people's inflation expectations become "unanchored," which means people lose faith that inflation may return to normal.
"The Committee's unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis," Warsh said.
Warsh put a very positive spin on the interest rate hike, saying a robust and resilient economy can handle a quarter-point hike.
But he did not indicate whether an aggressive rate-hiking cycle was on the way.
"I'm not in the forward guidance business," he said.
On AI's potential economic impact, Warsh said the Fed has established a task force to study the issue.
Responding to a question about President Donald Trump's calls for interest rate cuts, Warsh said Fed independence is a "two-way street" and that Fed officials "stay in our lane."
In early September, Trump threatened to completely stop trade with countries running trade surpluses with the United States should the Fed fail to cut rates, triggering the Fed independence issue.
Following the Fed's decision to raise interest rates, major U.S. stock indexes turned lower. The 10-year Treasury bond yield rose 2 basis points to 5.012 percent, while the 30-year yield fell 0.5 basis points to 5.357 percent. The U.S. dollar index gained 0.6 percent to 100.3.
Market analysts viewed the unanimous 12-0 vote under Warsh as a hawkish signal, suggesting that policymakers were prepared to implement at least one more rate hike before the end of the year.
Meanwhile, the FOMC participants' updated Summary of Economic Projections indicated that most Fed officials expected the policy rate to rise to a range of 4 percent and 4.25 percent by the end of 2026, as they sought to combat persistent inflation driven by supply shocks and geopolitical pressures.
Financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley, also adopted a more hawkish stance, anticipating further monetary tightening following the Fed's rate hike.
The rate hike would reinforce the Fed's credibility, said Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, in an interview with CNBC. "It is a shift in policy direction."
"I would expect Chair Warsh to keep further hikes on the table while avoiding a commitment to a prolonged tightening cycle," DuBravac said.
Nevertheless, some economists have questioned the fundamental necessity of the hike, arguing that recent increases in core prices stem largely from temporary or supply-side shocks rather than an overheated, demand-driven domestic economy.
The Fed has two more meetings scheduled before the end of 2026, leaving room for further rate hikes if inflation remains elevated. ■

What to know about US Federal Reserve’s first interest rate hike in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:03:37 UTC
08:03:37 KST

What to know about US Federal Reserve’s first interest rate hike in 3 years
The unanimous decision underscores the central bank’s commitment to lowering prices that have remained stubbornly high.
For the first time in more than three years, the United States Federal Reserve has raised interest rates amid mounting inflationary pressures and consumer frustration.
The unanimous decision on Wednesday, supported by all 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point, underscoring the central bank’s commitment to lowering prices.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Oil soars to $109, pushing up chances of US interest rate increase
- list 2 of 3Benchmark US government bond yield hits 19-year peak as oil prices surge
- list 3 of 3US Fed raises interest rates for first time in three years
The Fed’s benchmark rate is now set between 3.75 percent and 4 percent.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters.
Here’s what you need to know:
Why did this happen?
The US Fed has a dual mandate of maximising employment and stabilising prices, maintaining a 2 percent inflation target.
After soaring for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation had finally started to taper closer to target. But over the last several years it has been on the upswing once again and hit 3.4 percent last month.
That comes on the back of tariffs unleashed by President Donald Trump on most trading partners, as well as by the US war in Iran and increased spending on artificial intelligence.
The Fed said Wednesday’s rate increase “will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”.
What impact will this have?
The rate hike has a litany of possible economic and political ramifications.
The increase will hit any US consumer who is paying interest on credit card debt. It will also make it even more expensive for those who hope to borrow for homes, automobiles and other expensive purchases.
When the Fed raises the cost of borrowing it also reduces demand for items, which could impact US businesses and risk the health of the economy.
The rate increase also comes at an inopportune time for Trump and the Republican Party, less than 50 days before the November midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the US Congress.
US consumers have faced years of increasingly higher prices, most recently at the gas pump with the average price for a gallon of petrol hitting $4.36 ($1.15 per litre), up 14 cents in the past week and up from $3.18 a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Voters could opt to vent their frustrations at the ballot box, offering Democrats a chance to seize one – or even both – chambers.
How soon will this translate to higher prices?
US banks looking to borrow money from the Fed will immediately start paying the higher lending rate.
Consumers with credit cards, which generally have variable interest rates that closely follow the prime rate that banks charge their customers, could see their minimum payments increase within a month, as could home owners with variable interest rate mortgages.
What did Trump say?
The decision is a blow for Trump, who has frequently clashed with the Fed over lowering borrowing costs. Trump mounted a pressure campaign against the Fed’s previous chairman, Jerome Powell, over his resistance to doing so.
When Powell’s term ended earlier this year, Trump handpicked his successor, Kevin Warsh, who was placed in the job in May.
At the time, Trump said he would choose someone who supported lower interest rates.
On Sunday during a trip to Ireland, Trump said the US “should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world” after previously threatening to cut off a large section of US trade if rates did not decrease.
On Wednesday, Warsh was asked what his message for Trump was about the rate hike.
“I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he replied.
Nearly three hours after the interest rate decision was announced, Trump lashed out.
“Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “We are “carrying” almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”
Fed members indicated on Wednesday that there would likely be another quarter-point increase this year and those rates would remain unchanged through 2027.
