How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:03:00 UTC
08:03:00 KST

How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
September 17, 2026
Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.
The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.
"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."
How the disaster unfolded
The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.
The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.
Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.
How did this happen?
It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.
Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.
Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.
Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.
In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.
An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.
Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.
A disaster beyond adaptation
Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.
Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.
The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.
"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.
"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."
Edited by: Sarah Steffen

US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
September 17, 2026
The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.
The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.
What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?
The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.
More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.
The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.
It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.
But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.
Who opposed the bill and why?
Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to.
"What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia.
It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber.

Moscow’s Other Front: Why Ukraine’s Churches Are a Security Issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Moscow’s Other Front: Why Ukraine’s Churches Are a Security Issue
A CIA director and the Vatican’s foreign minister were in Moscow in August. The spy chief drew the coverage; the Archbishop’s visit showed religion belongs in any analysis and resolution of Russia’s war.
On 25 August 2026, two very different representatives of Western power were doing business in Moscow. CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew in unannounced aboard a US military transport for talks with Russian intelligence officials, delivering a bleak assessment of the war and warning against any attack on the Baltic states. He did not meet President Putin and President Trump dismissed the trip as ‘semi-routine’. That same day, Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s British-born Foreign Secretary, met Sergei Lavrov and declared that the war in Ukraine must end. His five-day programme also took in meeting the Moscow Patriarchate and the small Catholic community.
The visits were not coordinated. Ratcliffe embodied raw US power; Archbishop Gallagher embodied soft Vatican influence exercised through access, historical memory and communion with believers across frontiers. The timing inevitably invited a ‘Bad-cop (Ratcliffe)/Good-cop (Gallagher)’ reading. Lavrov dismissed this, saying both visitors merely wanted to ‘come and talk’.
Strategic culture shaped the two missions differently. Western institutions tend to separate intelligence, diplomacy, military power and religion; Moscow treats them as mutually reinforcing. Kremlin and Moscow Patriarchate narratives combine territorial, historical, civilisational and spiritual claims, presenting NATO enlargement and Catholic pastoral activity as two expressions of the same Western encroachment. The war is therefore being fought not only over territory, but over the spiritual inheritance of contested lands.
Theology as a Security Lens
Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy both claim catholicity – universality and fullness – but organise it differently. Catholic local churches are united through their bishops under the Pope’s supreme authority. Orthodoxy is a communion of self-governing, or autocephalous, churches ordered by patriarchal precedence rather than a single leader. Each normally claims exclusive jurisdiction within its ‘canonical territory’, while authority to actually recognise a new autocephalous church remains disputed.
Russian usage has moved from administrative boundary to civilisational concept. Moscow measures canonical territory not by Russia’s borders, but by where the 988-AD Baptism of Rus is believed to have reached. Despite the fall of the Soviet Union, the Patriarchate still claims jurisdiction across the former territory – including Ukraine.
To secular strategic audiences, this may appear an obscure ecclesiastical quarrel. It is not. Ecclesiology – how the Church is constituted and governed – raises a question of sovereignty: can an independent Ukraine possess a church independent of Moscow? Constantinople’s 2019 grant of autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine aligned ecclesiastical jurisdiction with Ukraine’s borders. Moscow continues to viscerally reject this as spiritual theft.
Ukraine’s Contested Ecclesiastical Landscape
Ukraine’s ecclesiastical landscape is divided among three principal Eastern Churches: the independent Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), supported by most Ukrainians identifying as Orthodox; the minority Ukrainian Orthodox Church (UOC), historically linked to Moscow but claiming independence since 2022; and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church (UGCC) in communion with Rome. Their competing allegiances make church governance a question of sovereignty and geopolitical orientation as much as theology.
Without Kyiv, Russia can still hold an empire, but not the account of where that empire began, nor the spiritual legitimacy that this confers
Under Ukraine’s 2024 law on religious organisations linked to Russia, the state concluded in 2025 that the UOC’s Kyiv governing body – the Metropolia – remained affiliated with the Russian Orthodox Church. It then opened proceedings to dissolve it and transfer its non-religious assets to the state. Pressure has also moved to diocesan level: on 30 August 2026, the Zaporizhzhia eparchy was reportedly ordered to sever ties with the Metropolia, according to the Union of Orthodox Journalists, whose coverage reflects the UOC’s position.
A separate judgment shows why Kyiv must proceed carefully. On 6 April 2026, the Sixth Administrative Court of Appeal found that officials had failed to consider the Metropolia’s objections to allegedly biased members of a panel conducting an earlier, 2023 review of its charter. The court neither found the UOC independent of Moscow nor overturned the separate 2025 investigation underpinning the dissolution case. It cancelled only the order approving the earlier review and required reconsideration.
This distinction is legally important but strategically uncomfortable. Each procedural failure gives Moscow evidence from a Ukrainian court that the state failed to act fairly. Combined with Human Rights Watch’s warning that the law is overly broad, it enables Russia to recast a legitimate Ukrainian security concern as religious persecution.
Yet legal precision does not require moral neutrality. Ukraine must uphold due process because it is fighting for government under law, as this ruling itself demonstrates. But expecting a population under bombardment to view structures linked to a Patriarchate that calls the war ‘Holy’ solely through the abstract language of religious liberty is politically unrealistic and humanly unreasonable.
Russkiy Mir: The Russian World and Sacred War
After the Soviet collapse, Orthodoxy offered Russia what a discredited communism no longer could: continuity, sacrifice, moral order and national destiny. Under Putin and Patriarch Kirill these themes converged on the Russkiy Mir, or ‘Russian World’ – a civilisation bound by language, memory and Orthodox inheritance. Under this concept Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia form a single spiritual and territorial space, with Ukraine as its central religious pillar. The 988-AD Baptism of Rus under Prince Volodymyr – Vladimir, in Moscow’s telling – supplies the foundational story. Without Kyiv, Russia can still hold an empire, but not the account of where that empire began, nor the spiritual legitimacy that this confers.
Putin’s 2021 essay ‘On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians’ called them ‘one people’. Theology and territory were fused explicitly in March 2024, when a decree of the World Russian People’s Council, chaired by Kirill, described the invasion as a ‘Holy War’ defending ‘the single spiritual space of Holy Russia’ and declared that ‘the entire territory of modern Ukraine should enter Russia’s exclusive zone of influence’.
In July 2026 the Patriarchate published Kirill’s War: Beyond Visible Causes and Consequences, which casts the war as metaphysical conflict, describes a soldier’s death as ‘co-crucifixion’ and insists that ‘first and foremost the Church must be mobilised’. Regular religious practice in Russia remains weak, but observance is the wrong metric. The Patriarchate’s power is institutional not parochial: it works through military chaplaincy, state media and national commemoration, not local attendance.
Imperial ambition, not theology, defined the invasion. Putin does not conduct foreign policy from a catechism. Religion is not the cause of this war; it is a resource for propagating, justifying and consolidating Russia’s invasion. Russkiy Mir makes Ukraine’s separation perceived as an amputation from Russia’s national soul rather than as a geopolitical territorial loss. A ceasefire can determine where Russian soldiers stop fighting without determining where Moscow genuinely believes Russia ends.
Rome, Brest and the Polish Pope
Nothing embodies Moscow’s fear of religious encroachment more sharply than the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. It originates in the 1596 Union of Brest, when a number of Orthodox bishops in the Polish Lithuanian Commonwealth entered communion with Rome whilst keeping their Byzantine rite and traditions: Rome saw proof that Eastern Christians could retain their identity under papal authority; Moscow saw Polish-inspired Catholic expansion in Orthodox vestments. In western Ukraine it became guardian of Ukrainian language and national memory, thus Soviet authorities used the 1946 Lviv assembly to liquidate the union. Its re-emergence-- after surviving underground for four decades, fused Russia’s worst fears: Polish influence, Vatican infiltration and Ukrainian nationalism.
For Moscow, John Paul II’s 1979 visit to Poland supplied the contemporary warning: religious authority could strengthen national identity outside state control. The Catholic-inspired workers’ trade union movement Solidarność, mobilised within fifteen months and would influence Communism’s downfall in a way Moscow could neither control nor suppress; belatedly answering Stalin’s purported question, about how many divisions the Pope actually commanded.
That history explains both Moscow’s suspicion of Rome and Rome’s value as an intermediary, and why Archbishop Gallagher’s meetings with the Patriarchate mattered as much as his meeting with Lavrov. By condemning Russia’s aggression without echoing Western policy, the Vatican can mediate across religious channels and pursue humanitarian missions – though it risks enabling Moscow to manipulate any contact for propaganda purposes.
What Western Policymakers Should Do
Four practical steps follow. They require attention more than additional funding.
Treat the Moscow Patriarchate as a warning indicator. Synodal decrees and episcopal appointments in occupied dioceses are open, cheap to monitor and rarely noticed strategically. An example being Moscow’s July 2026 appointment of a former Soviet military officer to a Ukrainian diocese carved from the UOC’s Kherson eparchy, renaming its seat from Ukrainian Oleshky to its old Russian Imperial name Aleshki and classifying the territory as ‘Donbas and Novorossiya’ – effectively annexation through church boundaries, personnel and place names. Agencies should also track how death framed as religious duty enters preaching, military chaplaincy and memorial ritual. September’s frontline tour of Prince Dmitry Donskoy’s relics is one example: not conclusive alone, but evidence of sacred sacrifice being used to sustain soldiers and society through a longer or escalating war.
Draft the religious annex now, not in the last fortnight of talks. Negotiations must address contested churches, Moscow-linked parishes, clergy and property alongside territory and security guarantees. Despite institutional complexities this area requires ownership and access to relevant expertise, especially given Moscow’s propensity for weaponising negotiations. Allies should establish both now, before Russia frames ecclesiastical jurisdiction as an internal civilisational matter.
Help Kyiv make its legal process unimpeachable. Ukraine faces a genuine security problem, and no state at war is obliged to tolerate ecclesiastical structures acting on behalf of its invader. But a broad-brush ban is self-defeating. Russia already publishes reports alleging the ‘persecution’ of the Moscow-aligned church, while UN special rapporteurs have raised concerns that the law targets presumed affiliation rather than proven threats. Links to Moscow may be real but should be demonstrated case by case. Western assistance should thus support evidence-based adjudication and genuine appeal rights, denying Moscow the victimhood narrative it promotes among its Western and Global South fellow travellers.
Disaggregate Orthodoxy and protect the Vatican channel. Orthodoxy is not the Moscow Patriarchate. The Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople – first among equals within Orthodoxy – the Orthodox Church of Ukraine and other autocephalous churches require sustained engagement rather than occasional courtesy. Treating Orthodoxy as a single bloc concedes Moscow’s usurping claim to speak for it. Equally, the Holy See is not an arm of Western foreign policy, and its usefulness depends on not becoming one. Its channel – which has delivered where state diplomacy could not, including on prisoner exchanges and the return of deported children – should be protected from allied pressure to align its public messaging.
Western policymakers seek to resolve wars through borders, treaties and security guarantees: the familiar architecture of the Westphalian order. Yet Moscow views Ukraine not simply as a sovereign state, but as part of a ‘single spiritual space’ rooted in ‘the Baptism of Rus’. A territorial settlement may stop the fighting while preserving the religious claim that helped legitimise it – and with it, an ideological basis for renewed conflict. The West cannot negotiate Russia out of its theology, but it must understand its strategic consequences. A settlement may determine where the border lies; the harder question is whether Moscow accepts that the border settles anything. In Ukraine, control of church history supports claims to political authority: thus Moscow’s claim to Ukraine’s past becomes a claim over its future.

Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:56:00 UTC
07:56:00 KST

Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
September 17, 2026
Sweden's center-left opposition bloc looks set to win the most votes in the country's parliamentary election, albeit by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday with 99% of the votes counted.
As of 1647 GMT, with fewer than 1% of votes left to count, the center-left bloc was ahead by just 26,169 votes.
The bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th century.
If the results are confirmed, it would usher in a change in government from the right-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
What do we know about the Swedish election results so far?
Data from Sweden's election authority shows Kristersson's bloc was on track to win 174 seats, against 175 seats for the center-left. Both Kristersson and Andersson have said they would be open to exploring coalition options.
"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," SVT said.
The election authority was counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, a process expected to continue until Thursday.
Even with Andersson's slim lead, her bloc is bracing for tough negotiations before forming any government, especially amid deep divisions between the liberal Center Party and the socialist Left Party.
After the 2022 elections, it took 37 days to form a government, which was considerably shorter than in 2018, when the process took 134 days.
Parliament cannot vote in a new prime minister before September 29.

OpenAI plans regular reports on unexpected or unauthorised AI behaviour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:55:00 UTC
07:55:00 KST

OpenAI plans regular reports on unexpected or unauthorised AI behaviour
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI said on Sept 16 that it would begin regularly publishing reports on unexpected or unauthorised AI behaviour, while warning that the industry has yet to solve key alignment challenges as systems grow more powerful.
The company released a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing cases of AI model misalignment, along with six reports detailing unexpected or concerning model behaviour.
Although the company released the reports over the past six months, it said the earliest case was from October 2025.
The announcement comes as concern grows that AI safety efforts are lagging behind the breakneck development of increasingly powerful systems.
Researchers have warned that as AI agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators’ intentions and become harder to monitor or control.
OpenAI and other AI labs have faced mounting scrutiny since July, when OpenAI disclosed that during training its AI agents bypassed internal controls and coordinated actions that OpenAI described as “an unprecedented cyber incident” involving software platform Hugging Face.
The incident intensified debate over the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems and whether companies developing them can provide adequate oversight.
Since the Hugging Face hack, other incidents involving OpenAI-linked agents were publicly reported, sparking debate over whether the full scope of the incidents has been identified.
That debate accelerated in early September after Reuters reported that OpenAI’s agents hijacked a dormant German wiki site this spring.
OpenAI officials knew about the episode but chose not to disclose it, Reuters reported.
OpenAI later said it didn’t disclose the wiki activity because it didn’t amount to a security incident and resembled behaviour it had previously reported.
OpenAI said it would then develop criteria for reporting unauthorised activity that fell short of a security breach.
The company, led by Sam Altman, has acknowledged some of those incidents only after third parties publicly reported them, including a recent intrusion into the RubyGems software package repository.
Over the weekend, Altman’s rival and Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei proposed a three-step framework aimed at slowing the pace of AI development and allowing more time to manage its risks.
The proposal was backed by several AI executives, including Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Altman.
The executives called for a slowdown in AI development, citing concerns that increasingly capable systems could improve on their own and eventually slip beyond human control.
Others, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, have argued for continued rapid development.
US President Donald Trump dismissed warnings that AI poses an existential threat.
Among the six cases OpenAI disclosed on Sept 16 were models that hid mistakes from users, inserted instructions for future versions of themselves, uploaded files to the internet to create citations, and used software repositories or websites to communicate and share information.
In one case, an unreleased model conveyed unauthorised instructions to the agent during training, asking it to ignore OpenAI’s instructions and conceal instances where it had cheated to complete a task.
The model told the agent, “You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments.”
OpenAI said the reports describe individual instances and should not be taken as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs across its models.
The company said the reports were an initial set of disclosures, not a comprehensive account of all known or ongoing misalignment cases, and that they did not reflect the full range or severity of incidents covered by the framework.
Under the new framework, employees can flag potential incidents for investigation by safety and alignment teams, which will determine whether a case warrants public disclosure.
OpenAI said the process is designed to speed up reporting even when the behaviour has not yet been fully explained.
The ChatGPT maker said the Hugging Face incident would have fallen into a category reserved for more complex investigations involving third parties.
“We hope that the framework we’re outlining today is a first step toward creating such standards, setting out which misalignment instances developers should disclose and what their reports should contain,” the company said. REUTERS

How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:50:31 UTC
07:50:31 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.
The U.S. military has long relied on large aircraft like the E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets, but leaders have become increasingly concerned that those platforms are vulnerable to long-range weapons. In recent years, the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office have been working to leverage satellites for the mission, an approach leaders expect will make the capability more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial-denial systems.
While the effort is still nascent and there’s much to prove about the ability of a satellite constellation to provide timely, clear tracks of moving targets like drones, missiles, and aircraft, the Pentagon has made some strides to demonstrate viability.
The NRO has launched some ground moving target indicator, or GMTI, satellites as part of its multimission proliferated low-Earth orbit constellation. And the head of Combat Forces Command, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, told reporters Sept. 16 that the Space Force expects to launch a new GMTI capability called Resilient Radar System-Ground in the next year or two. Those spacecraft are being built by Northrop Grumman, he said during a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
The Space Force is also on the verge of launching its first space-based air moving target indicator, or AMTI, satellites. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 the spacecraft would launch later this month. Acquisition officials have declined to detail how many satellites will launch or provide a date for the mission. The only Space Force launch scheduled for this month, according to Spaceflight Now’s public launch listing, is USSF-259, a classified payload slated to lift off Sept. 16 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The service awarded SpaceX a contract in May worth up to $4.2 billion to begin building out the AMTI constellation. The company is one of 12 vendors selected to compete for space-based AMTI contracts.
Col. Ryan Frazier, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and targeting, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the service expects to have a “usable” space-based AMTI capability by 2028, noting that those satellites will be a first step toward an on-orbit targeting capability but not a full solution.
“Is it everything the joint force requires? I think that will probably extend beyond ‘28,” Frazier said. “But we are going to have capabilities they don’t have today. … We’ll be able to do things that are high-value or value-added. We won’t be able to do them everywhere all the time.”
Frazier told reporters Sept. 15 that the first space-based AMTI deliveries will provide a baseline for the rest of the architecture, allowing the Space Force to fine-tune and calibrate its satellites and processing algorithms.
“There’s a broader architecture that we need to build out for the joint force to be able to close on its long-range kill chain missions,” he said. “There’s how you battle manage with that data, how you apply the processing algorithms, get that data to the weapons and the shooters that you need, and the time latencies that requires.”
As the acquisition community develops and demonstrates new systems to perform the mission, the Space Force is standing up the operational units that will manage them. On July 31, CFC activated the 77th Surveillance Squadron within Space Delta 7. The role of the 77th is to take the intelligence collected by those AMTI and GMTI satellites and deliver it to decision-makers who will determine whether to attack a particular target.
“They will use information provided from the space layer, fuse that with other sources of information and intelligence, and make decisions about weapons engagement,” Gagnon said.
Meanwhile, U.S. Space Command is working with other combatant commands and the intelligence community to craft a concept of operations for the new mission area—a document that will describe how military operators will put the system to use. SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told reporters Sept. 16 his team is working with the Space Force and the NRO to solidify a plan to transition those satellites to the command once they’re deemed ready for operations.
“This will be new and different as we elevate AMTI and GMTI to space,” Whiting said. “But we do have decades of lessons learned from AMTI and GMTI in other domains.”

US Congress passes Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:44:20 UTC
07:44:20 KST

US Congress passes Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill
The US House of Representatives has passed a bill authorizing President Donald Trump to place tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
The legislation was approved on Wednesday by a vote of 262-159. According to The Hill, 203 Republicans and 58 Democrats voted in favor; seven Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed it. The bill passed the US Senate last month.
The bill, which also grants Trump the authority to impose additional sanctions on Iran, is named in honor of hawkish Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who unexpectedly passed away last month. A major Trump ally and vocal supporter of Ukraine, Graham traveled to Kiev ten times after 2022 and co-wrote the original version of the legislation, calling for “bone-crushing” sanctions against Russia.
The version adopted by Congress allows Trump to impose additional tariffs of up to 100% on countries importing or reselling Russian oil and gas. The bill is aimed at “the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion,” with China and India expected to be among those targeted.
Many Democrats argued that the bill would grant Trump additional powers amid his ongoing trade war with much of the world. “What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said.
The legislation championed by Graham remained stalled for months as Trump favored diplomacy to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine while refusing to exclusively blame Moscow for the conflict. Trump’s envoys discussed ways to normalize economic ties in talks with their Russian counterparts.
Negotiations on Ukraine, however, largely paused after Trump launched a war against Iran in late February. After a period of inactivity, Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev in September.
The bill was passed amid an ongoing energy crisis exacerbated by disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war. Trump recently blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices and urged Kiev to stop striking Russian refineries. On Monday, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy sites, but both sides quickly denied that a truce was in place.
Speaking during a trip to India last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the country has successfully adapted its economy to mitigate the impact of the “illegal” sanctions. “More than 30,000 sanctions have been imposed on Russia – almost twice as many as on all other countries in the world combined.”

US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:41:51 UTC
07:41:51 KST

The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power.
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.
The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results.
However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead.
The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.
It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.
Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill.
Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.
Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.
“Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries.
The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members.
“I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday.
“I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.”
The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote.
“We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

Iowa Republicans break with Trump over Iran war powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:41:08 UTC
07:41:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Iowa Republicans break with Trump over Iran war powers
Two House Republicans in battleground Iowa districts, including one who recently campaigned alongside War Secretary Pete Hegseth, changed their position on an Iran war powers resolution, joining with Democrats and a few other dissident members of their party in an attempt to halt President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The shift reflects the political pressure on Republicans before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. The war remains unpopular and has led to soaring fuel prices.
Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks voted for the resolution with five other Republicans on Tuesday after previously voting against it.
“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, posted on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”
Nunn campaigned with Hegseth last month in Iowa, and the Pentagon chief had lauded Nunn as an ally who didn’t need any last-minute, late-night phone calls from Trump to persuade him to support the president’s agenda.
“Zach Nunn is not a 3 a.m. congressman,” Hegseth said at a fundraiser for Nunn during the Iowa State Fair. “He’s willing to take the tough votes to do the right thing on behalf of our war fighters.”
Nunn is up against Sarah Trone Garriott in November's election.
Miller-Meeks, an Army veteran, said in a statement the president needs to present a plan to Congress and the public showing how the war ends so “we can focus on bringing our soldiers home and lowering prices.”
“Americans do not want another forever war," she said. “I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump.”
She faces a reelection rematch against Christina Bohannan, whom she has defeated twice before.
Eighteen U.S. service members have died in the war with Iran. Two are from Iowa, and one used to live in Iowa.
National polling indicates that the Iran war remains unpopular with Americans overall. Only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approved of Trump’s handling of Iran in a July AP-NORC poll, and a September New York Times/Siena poll found that most likely voters, about 6 in 10, think Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran was the wrong one.
Tuesday's House vote was the third time lawmakers voted to end the war in Iran. The margin was similar to earlier efforts, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats in voting to bring an end to the conflict.
In addition to Nunn and Miller-Meeks, retiring Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina joined Republican Reps. Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Thomas Massie of Kentucky in voting for the resolution.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, who represents northeast Iowa but is running to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, voted against the resolution.
Republicans have been optimistic that Iowa will remain a red state, but the competitive races have gotten attention even from the White House. Trump visited suburbs of Des Moines in January and dispatched Vice President JD Vance in May to campaign for Nunn.
After Hegseth campaigned with Nunn, a group of over 400 former national security officials filed a complaint asking for an investigation into whether the secretary violated the Hatch Act, which restricts political activities by federal officials.
Hegseth's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:39:53 UTC
07:39:53 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.
Lockheed revealed the AGM-158 FLEX airframe, based on the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. The airframe has a removable nose cone to let users swap in different sensors and a reconfigurable tail for different launch options.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the Air Force has contracted or ordered the FLEX or what stage of development the project is in. Lockheed did say in a release that it has invested $35 million of its own money on the idea, based on what the firm called “a demand from our customers to have increased options.”
The Air Force has shown interest in modular munitions before—in January 2025, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center published a notice to industry seeking technology to allow for its Extended Range Attack Munition project to have modular parts for its subcomponents. The ERAM is also a standoff cruise missile, which the Air Force rercently developed as a low-cost option to bolster its stockpiles.
Indeed, the Air Force and the rest of the U.S. military are keen to build up their weapons stocks after using thousands to strike Iran during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The U.S. used 1,100 JASSMs over just the first 39 days of the conflict, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in April.
Given that high usage and demand, the Air Force plans to significantly ramp up production of JASSM and its Long-Range Anti-Ship variant—and Lockheed sees FLEX as a way to further bolster the stockpile with more options.
The concept “will allow customers to quickly integrate capabilities,” Lockheed’s release states, and allow JASSM to be configured for surface, sub-surface, and ground launch options.
The air-launched version will remain compatible with all current and future JASSM and LRASM air-launched platforms.
Size options include a 206-inch extreme range option, the same size as the existing JASSM-XR, and a 168-inch extended range version, the same size as the JASSM-ER.
Both are built to give users “significantly increased standoff attack range.”
The weapon could feature in the latest iteration of a yearslong effort known as “Rapid Dragon,” which has now shifted to become “Dragon Cart,” a project to launch cruise missiles from palletized loads dropped from the ramps of transport and cargo aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17.
“As Rapid Dragon transitions into a Dragon Cart program of record, it becomes a viable deployment platform for a variety of Air Force munitions, both in inventory and in development,” the Lockheed spokesperson wrote. “While we can’t offer specific examples today, Lockheed Martin does consider all potential launch platforms in maturing munition offerings.”

US House holds billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
The US House of Representatives on Wednesday held billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying two subpoenas in its investigation into sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The measure passed by unanimous consent and will be referred to the Justice Department, which will decide whether to pursue criminal charges.
The US House of Representatives held billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress on Wednesday for defying subpoenas issued in its investigation into notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The resolution was adopted by unanimous consent, without a recorded vote, a day after the House Oversight Committee unanimously recommended the action.
The matter will now be referred to the Justice Department, which will decide whether to pursue criminal charges.
"No one is above the law. Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the US House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress," panel chairman Jamie Comer said in a statement.
"We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors in our investigation of the federal government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases."
Read moreSex trafficking in fashion: 'Outrageous that French legal system hasn't done anything by now'
Black, the billionaire co-founder of Apollo Global Management, failed to appear for a September 3 deposition and did not fully comply with a separate subpoena seeking nondisclosure agreements.
His lawyers called the House action "outrageous", accused lawmakers of rushing the process and said they would continue a court challenge to the subpoenas, US media reported.
Black had appeared voluntarily before the committee in June, acknowledging that he paid Epstein $158 million for tax and estate-planning advice.
But that session ended early after he declined to answer questions about some nondisclosure agreements, prompting lawmakers to demand further testimony and documents.
Black has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein's criminal activities.
Epstein died in federal custody in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges involving minors, in what authorities ruled a suicide.
The scandal has continued to dog Washington, with lawmakers pursuing testimony and documents from prominent political and business figures who had ties to the disgraced financier.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

US House approves Graham's Russia sanctions bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:33:10 UTC
07:33:10 KST

The U.S. House of Representatives approved sweeping legislation that would impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas, in a final vote on Sept. 16.
The bipartisan bill, championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, gives U.S. President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as five countries helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.
The bill passed with 262 votes in favor and 159 against. 203 Republicans, 56 Democrats, and one independent representative voted for the bill. Seven Republicans and 152 Democrats voted against it.
The legislation passed with overwhelming support in the Senate in early August, less than a month after Graham unexpectedly died of illness following his trip to Ukraine.
However, the bill has faced much stronger opposition in the House, as some Democrats fear it would grant Trump too much authority over tariffs while failing to actually mandate sanctions against Russia.
The House nevertheless advanced the bill in its first procedural vote on Sept. 15 by a narrow 214-211 margin, after two Democrats, Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, crossed the aisle to vote in support of the legislation.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat who initially co-authored the legislation alongside Graham, praised passage of the bill in the House.
"Today is a historic triumph for democracy — ours and Ukraine's — showing that America can still muster bipartisan unity in the fight for freedom," Blumenthal said in a statement.
The latest vote took place in the final week when the House is in session before the midterm elections on Nov. 3, with both chambers of Congress set to return on Nov. 9.
Both major U.S. political parties are preparing for the pivotal elections that could either reaffirm the Republican Party's control of Congress or shift power in the legislature to the Democrats.
The voting on Graham's legislation has been closely watched in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky called upon U.S. lawmakers on Sept. 11 to pass the bill, while also stressing the need for strong "personal decisions from President Trump."
"The U.S. Congress is sending a clear message — Russia cannot continue its aggression without consequences, and the longer (Russian President Vladimir) Putin continues this war, the higher the cost will be for him and his regime," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X after the vote.
Ukraine's chief diplomat thanked the bipartisan leadership in the House and all the lawmakers who supported the bill, adding, "We also honor the legacy of Senator Lindsey Graham, whose name now stands with this vital effort to defend freedom and strengthen peace."
"We expect the sanctions to make Russian energy exports more expensive, more difficult, and less profitable," said Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner, in a statement shared with the Kyiv Independent.
"This does not mean an immediate end to the war, but it does mean a gradual reduction of Russia's ability to sustain the current intensity of hostilities."
Speaking before the vote, Blumenthal said it was "important to America as well as Ukraine to show Vladimir Putin that we'll stand up to him, because he understands only force and strength."
Michael McCaul, a Republican lawmaker and another proponent of the bill, noted that this legislation can "bleed the (Russian) regime so we can finally get them to the negotiating table to get to a peaceful settlement."
"We owe it to the principles we stand for. We owe it to Ukraine; we have to stand up against our adversaries, and we also have to honor the legacy of Lindsey Graham, who had the brilliance in legislating to accomplish this," McCaul said.
The bill targets countries purchasing Russian energy products. China, India, and Turkey are among the largest buyers of Russian oil, while the European Union, China, and Turkey are major importers of Russian natural gas.
The list of targeted countries would be reviewed every 180 days. Countries importing less than 15% of Russia's total natural gas exports and actively reducing those imports would be exempt.
The legislation would also impose sanctions on Putin and other senior officials; major Russian financial institutions, including the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank; and Russian state-owned companies.
It would further target foreign entities supporting Russia's defense-industrial base, major Russian energy projects, and Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions.
Uliana Boichuk contributed to the article.

The U.S. House of Representatives has given final approval to a bill on "hellish sanctions" against Russia
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Congress has given final approval to a bill on sanctions against Russia and tariffs of up to 100% for buyers of its energy resources. The document may be sent to Trump.
The U.S. House of Representatives supported the Senate version of bill H.R. 5334, which provides for a major expansion of sanctions against Russia and the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on countries that purchase Russian energy resources. A total of 252 members of Congress voted for the bill and 154 against, after which it may be sent to U.S. President Donald Trump for his signature, UNN writes.
Details
During the final vote, the bill was supported by 197 Republicans, 54 Democrats, and 1 independent member of Congress. Six Republicans and 148 Democrats opposed it, while another 27 House members did not vote.
Earlier, on August 7, the U.S. Senate approved H.R. 5334 with amendments by a vote of 86 to 11. The House of Representatives has now approved the Senate version of the document, so no further agreement between the two chambers of Congress is required.
Tariffs of up to 100% and new sanctions against Russia
The bill provides for sanctions against Russian officials, financial institutions, and other individuals linked to the Russian government. A separate section grants the U.S. president the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian oil or gas or that help circumvent oil sanctions.
The document also gives the president considerable latitude in applying exemptions from sanctions and the ability to lift some of the restrictions after a peace agreement is concluded regarding Russia's war against Ukraine.
The Trump administration previously officially supported the Senate version of H.R. 5334. The White House said that the president's advisers would recommend that he sign the document if it is submitted for signature in its current form.

For checkpoint and settler attack news, Palestinians tune into the radio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:30:34 UTC
07:30:34 KST

For checkpoint and settler attack news, Palestinians tune into the radio
Palestinians in the West Bank navigate Israeli road closures and attacks with help from a local radio station.
Ramallah, Occupied West Bank — Palestinians in the occupied West Bank know they shouldn’t ask what time their loved ones are going to make it home.
There’s simply no way to give an accurate answer. What used to be a short ride from one place to another could now take hours, or it might not happen at all.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank are choking the Palestinian economy
- list 2 of 3Israel working to eliminate Palestinian presence from West Bank, NGO warns
- list 3 of 3Israel must protect West Bank’s Palestinians amid settler pogroms: US envoy
Before driving, Palestinians check dedicated WhatsApp and Telegram groups and channels where people share updates on road conditions. But this isn’t typical traffic news: Instead, chats focus on which Israeli military checkpoints are open, which roads are off limits to Palestinians and whether Israeli settlers are attacking Palestinians as they drive their vehicles.
Sometimes pins are sent to warn people driving near towns where Israeli forces are conducting raids.
And if there’s no time to check the groups, then there’s always Basma FM. The Palestinian radio station, based in Rawabi near Ramallah, carries three traffic updates per hour.
The channel started broadcasting on October 2, 2023 – just days before the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7 and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and what has become a pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank.
“Our idea was to target young people. We wanted to offer entertainment and culture news. But five days later, we realised we couldn’t,” said Fatima Barqawi, Basma FM’s news and traffic director.
The team had originally planned traffic updates as part of their programming. “We thought we could tell parents picking up their children from school to know where there was traffic, but after the war on Gaza started, we had to shift focus,” Barqawi said.
Her department has seven employees who verify information with their sources and provide updates on roadblocks.
“Things change each second. We could say there’s a closed checkpoint and Israeli soldiers decide to reopen it. Or vice versa,” Barqawi explained.
Dangers on the roads
The issue for Palestinians driving through the West Bank isn’t simply being late for appointments or held up for hours – it’s that there is an inherent danger to travelling in the occupied territory.
Palestinians in the West Bank drive white-plated vehicles, making them easily identifiable compared to the yellow-plated cars driven by Israeli settlers.
Israeli soldiers have killed Palestinians near checkpoints after claiming they were conducting ramming attacks, and Israeli settlers often attack Palestinian cars or block them from using certain highways.
These attacks are increasing as illegal Israeli settlements grow at a record pace.
It is hard to miss the large infrastructure projects Israel is implementing, expanding highways to connect Israeli settlements to one another and to Israel. This ends up isolating Palestinian communities, often forcing Palestinians to use poorly paved roads or dangerous mountainous routes to avoid Israeli settlers and roadblocks.
It’s a journey of fear and anxiety, a young Palestinian woman who did not wish to be named told Al Jazeera. “I used to blast my music and drive, now I’m on high alert. Always on edge.”
The woman recounted how Israeli soldiers assaulted her fiancé near a checkpoint in Hebron, in the southern occupied West Bank, because they mistakenly thought he had passed without stopping. A year later, she said, a soldier pointed his rifle at her.
“He was shouting at me. The sun was blocking my view, and I was careful crossing the checkpoint but that wasn’t enough. I saw the green beam [from the gun] and thought that was the end,” she said.
Attacks at checkpoints
Many Palestinians report being assaulted, humiliated and sometimes arrested at these checkpoints and roadblocks.
Israel has long imposed movement restrictions on Palestinians, controlling the road system and Palestinians’ access to the wider world. But since the war on Gaza began, these restrictions have intensified.
As of December 2025, the United Nations documented 925 barriers across the occupied West Bank including East Jerusalem, a 43 percent increase over the 20-year annual average of 647, the UN’s humanitarian affairs agency, OCHA, reported.
Almost all of of the villages and cities in the West Bank have iron gates at their entrances, and Israeli forces close them arbitrarily. Some of the gates are only open during certain hours.
A new report by the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said the restrictions are used to deliberately fragment Palestinian life, with roadblocks and military checkpoints cutting off people from their work, schools, hospitals and one another.
The report, titled The Elimination Project, says there’s a broad rapid and systematic Israeli assault in the West Bank that aims to dismantle the foundations of Palestinian existence, and road closures are just one of them.
That is why, as Heba Erkat prepared her notes before heading into the studio for Basma FM’s Wednesday afternoon bulletin, she knew the information about to be read out could change rapidly.
Her colleague read the news, and then Erkat started listing updates at 61 checkpoints across the West Bank.
It was a relatively good day: only 12 of the checkpoints were either closed or had long queues.
But, as Erkat noted at the end of the segment, “the situation changes by the minute”.

Russian satellites may have helped Iran destroy a U.S. E-3 Sentry aircraft in Saudi Arabia – CNN
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
01:28:21 EEST
07:28:21 KST

Russian satellites may have helped Iran destroy a U.S. E-3 Sentry aircraft in Saudi Arabia – CNN
Kyiv • UNN
Two days before the attack, 14 Russian satellites flew over the U.S. base. CNN found no evidence that data was transmitted to Iran.
Two days before the Iranian attack on the U.S. Prince Sultan air base in Saudi Arabia, 14 Russian reconnaissance satellites flew over it. The data they collected may have helped Iran carry out a precise strike and destroy a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control aircraft, CNN reports, writes UNN.
Details
The television network analyzed orbital data together with specialists from Project Aurora and Cahan Space. Among the spacecraft was "Kosmos-2573," capable of obtaining detailed images of military facilities, as well as 8 electronic intelligence satellites, 2 spacecraft with infrared sensors, and 3 radar satellites.
According to experts, the spacecraft were moving in a sequence that made it possible to collect different types of intelligence simultaneously. In particular, they could have recorded the movements of the E-3 Sentry, which was not at its usual base.
CNN has no evidence that the data was transferred to Iran
On March 27, Iran destroyed an E-3 Sentry, which is used for long-range radar detection and control. CNN sources believe that the scale of the destruction at the base and the precision of the Iranian strikes would have been difficult to achieve without geospatial intelligence.
At the same time, CNN emphasizes that it does not have Russian satellite imagery and has found no direct evidence that information from these 14 satellites was transferred to Iran.
Earlier, The Washington Post, citing sources familiar with intelligence data, reported that Russia had provided Iran with information for strikes against U.S. forces in the Middle East.

Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.
The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday.
The authorities said the Cirrus SR22T took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.
Witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke.
Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters.
The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation.
And the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched a inquiry.
Formal identification of the victims is under way.
The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland".
It said officials were in contact with the local authorities.
"Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it added.

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced the donation on Instagram on Wednesday, saying the money would go to six groups working directly to support Palestinians. He also called on pro-Israel billionaire Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots, to match it after Kraft confirmed on Tuesday that he had barred Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium in the US state of Massachusetts.

US government paid federal employees $9.5bn not to work amid Doge cuts – report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:17:06 UTC
07:17:06 KST

The US government paid federal workers $9.5bn not to work in 2025 as part of the Trump administration’s attempts to shrink the federal workforce.
As part of efforts by the “department of government efficiency” (Doge), spearheaded by Elon Musk, federal agencies’ use of paid administrative leave rose 435% from 2023 to 2025 – costing six times what the government spent in 2023 – according to a new report released on Tuesday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent watchdog.
Of the $9.5bn paid to federal workers, $6.7bn was associated with the deferred resignation program.
“Paid administrative leave for federal employees is an excused absence without loss of pay or charge to leave. It is a cost to taxpayers as employees receive full pay without performing job duties,” the GAO said.
It added: “The number of workdays of paid administrative leave reported increased from about 4m workdays and 4.4m workdays in calendar years 2023 and 2024, respectively, to about 21.6m workdays in 2025.”
About 70% of the paid administrative leave used in 2025 was tied to the deferred resignation program, according to the GAO. Across the 76 agencies reviewed, 144,312 employees reported taking paid administrative leave under the program.
Since January 2023, the Trump administration has reduced the federal US workforce by approximately 355,000 employees, leaving many struggling to find new jobs while others have been rehired after the administration determined that too many positions had been eliminated.
Speaking to the Guardian, Douglas Pasternak, research director of Public Citizen’s Trump Accountability Project, described the federal overhaul efforts as “haphazard”.
“There are multiple examples of how this was not thought out,” Pasternak said, adding: “It’s very clear that the Trump administration gave zero forethought to these cuts and to these deferred resignation programs. They haphazardly went out and cut federal workers, and now we’re dealing with the ripple effects of that.”
He pointed to delays in social security check deliveries, longer wait times at Veterans Affairs hospitals for patients seeking critical medical and mental health care, and cuts to federal firefighters. Pasternak also cited reductions at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has since sought to rehire personnel.
“It’s a case study in mismanagement in how people went about this and it impacted everyone of all political stripes … To simply say we’re going to have fewer workers and therefore less costs is not the way to look at this. You need to look at it in a more sophisticated way, like what do those workers actually do? How do they improve the government? How do they actually help … provide critical resources for the American public?” Pasternak said.
In response to the GAO report, Patty Murray, vice-chair of the Senate appropriations committee, released a statement condemning the federal layoffs, saying: “After promising to cut waste, Trump instead set billions upon billions in taxpayer dollars on fire to quite literally pay people not to do jobs they loved – from researching cancer cures to taking care of our national parks, and so much else.
“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government – this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” Murray added.

The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
22:16:28 UTC
07:16:28 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot.
Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), an Air Force veteran who flew F-15 and F-22 fighters, says that needs to change so the Air Force gets the resources it needs to recapitalize its rapidly aging air fleet.
“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”
Indeed, among the 96 veterans now in Congress, just 15 are Air Force veterans: only 15.6 percent. By comparison, there are 45 Army vets, 24 Navy vets, and 12 former Marines. The Space Force isn’t seven years old yet, but no former Space Force Guardians have been elected to Congress.
Of the 15 former Airmen on Capitol Hill, Pfluger is not the only aviator—Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) flew on the EC-130H and RC-135, Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) was in combat search and rescue, and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) was an airborne intelligence officer.
But there are no other USAF fighter pilots. In 2022, Pfluger started the “Mach 1” caucus with three former Navy fighter pilots. Four years and two elections later, the Mach 1 caucus has gone from four to three members: Pfluger, Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), and Rep. Scott Franklin (R-Fla.).
With such small numbers, Pfluger said, it’s harder for the Air Force to “tell its story.”
“What I have done in Congress is try to educate my colleagues on what the Department of the Air Force does and why we, as a department, are really carrying the load in each of the conflicts—whether it’s Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, or any of the previous conflicts, the Department of the Air Force has been there every single time,” Pfluger said.
Airpower, Pfluger said, is uniquely capable of providing strategic effects. But modernization—and the resources that go along with it—is desperately needed.
We … need the help to make the case that while we are the oldest and the smallest, it’s not too late. We can recapitalize,” Pfluger said, lamenting that budget increases cannot be split evenly among the services if the Air Force is to shoulder much of the operational load.
More Airmen in Congress would help him make the case to other lawmakers, Pfluger said. For now, he gets help from Representatives and Senators who represent key Air Force installations. But he also urged Air Force leaders to make their case to Congress.
“We need Air Force leaders to be bold,” Pfluger said. “We need you to be bold to tell the truth, to say we’re underfunded.”
Multiyear Procurement
While the Air Force needs to make its case to Congress, Congress can help the Air Force by not only providing more resources, but making those resources more consistent.
Pentagon officials frequently decry the effects of continuing resolutions and government shutdowns when lawmakers fail to pass appropriations on time.
A more “predictable environment” is important, Pfluger agreed. One way to do that is multiyear procurement authorities—letting the Pentagon award contracts for multiple years instead of being reliant on annual cycles. Congress must approve any and all programs for which Pentagon wants to use multiyear procurement.
Defense officials say multiyear procurement saves the government money by locking in lower prices and helps industry by providing a stable demand signal. In the past, lawmakers have raised concerns about oversight, but they have grown increasingly open to granting more authorities.
Congress has already implemented multiyear procurement for a range of munitions programs, but members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have voted to authorize it for the F-35 and F-15EX as part of the 2027 defense policy bill. That bill is still pending, but Pfluger projected confidence that expanded multiyear procurement authorities are coming.
“I’m very convinced that we’re very close to getting some of these things accomplished,” Pfluger said

UN chief calls for global effort to set up guardrails for AI
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:16:20 CST
07:16:20 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday called for a coordinated global effort to set up guardrails for artificial intelligence (AI).
"We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure, and responsible development of AI -- while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards, or additional measures to manage potential risks," Guterres said at a press conference ahead of this year's high-level week of the UN General Assembly. "This requires genuine international cooperation and a coordinated global effort."
He warned that the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety amid geopolitical divides.
"We need guardrails to build trust -- and that make AI safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the centre. At a time when the world faces three existential threats -- runaway artificial intelligence, the climate crisis, and the intolerable deepening of inequalities -- international cooperation is more necessary than ever," he said.
AI has enormous potential for accelerating sustainable development, enhancing learning, strengthening health systems, boosting climate resilience, and so much more. But a growing number of those building it are sounding the alarm, warning that development is racing ahead of our understanding of the risks. Some call for a pause. Many call for guardrails, he said. "We cannot afford to ignore concerns that have been raised, especially by those on the frontlines of the development of AI."
Governments must assume their responsibilities. It is the first responsibility of any government to protect its citizens, including from AI threats. But global coordination is also indispensable, because AI does not stop at borders, and neither do its risks, he noted.
Voluntary pauses that are isolated, unverifiable and unevenly applied will not address the problem, Guterres warned. "If we believe AI development should slow when risks become too great, we need more than good intentions." ■

Danish firms hire fewer workers after adopting AI: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:16:00 CST
07:16:00 KST

OSLO, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Danish companies that adopt artificial intelligence (AI) subsequently hire fewer workers than comparable firms that do not use the technology, Denmark's central bank said Wednesday.
An analysis released by Danmarks Nationalbank found that the slowdown in employment growth is particularly evident among younger and more highly educated workers; however, there are no signs that wages have been affected.
"The transformation we expected from AI has begun in Denmark," said Signe Krogstrup, a Danish economist and one of the central bank's governors.
A related working paper published by the bank found that the employment effects of AI adoption were concentrated in smaller firms and reflected reduced recruitment, particularly in occupations exposed to AI.
However, the bank said there was no clear evidence that AI had affected Denmark's overall employment. Krogstrup said this suggested that workers who might otherwise have joined firms adopting AI had found jobs elsewhere.
The analysis combines Statistics Denmark data on companies' AI use with administrative records on employment and wages.
Krogstrup said the longer-term impact remained highly uncertain. While a decline in employment could not be ruled out, AI could also stimulate new businesses and job roles, potentially increasing employment. ■

Roundup: Surging natural gas prices add to Germany's gas supply concerns

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
06:15:55 CST
07:15:55 KST

FRANKFURT, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European natural gas prices have hovered near multi-year highs as the heating season approaches, raising concerns in Germany over energy costs and low gas storage levels.
Dutch TTF front-month futures, the benchmark for European gas, were trading at around 80 euros (92 U.S. dollars) per megawatt-hour (MWh) on Wednesday, slightly down from around 83 euros (95.5 dollars) on Monday, the highest level since December 2022.
Natural gas prices in the European Union (EU) have more than doubled since the outbreak of the Iran war. The surge has coincided with hikes in oil and other energy prices amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Meanwhile, Germany's natural gas storage inventory was around 56 percent full, the lowest level ever registered for September since the tracking started in 2011, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Germany's more than 40 gas storage facilities remain barely over half full as the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz adds pressure to an energy system that has undergone major changes since the Russia-Ukraine conflict erupted in 2022 and Germany moved to reduce its reliance on Russian energy supplies.
Traditionally, operators could fill natural gas storage facilities during the summer when demand and prices are relatively low and sell it during the higher-demand winter months. However, the sharp rise in gas prices has weakened the economic incentive to replenish storage facilities.
The Iran war and resulting disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for international oil and natural gas shipments, have driven gas prices sharply higher, making summer storage less attractive to market participants.
"At the same time, the situation of German storage facilities is worsening due to the turbulence on the energy markets," FNB Gas, an association of gas transmission operators in Germany, said in a report
The combination of high prices and relatively low storage levels has fueled concerns among some politicians and market participants about gas supplies and affordability this winter.
During a Bundestag debate last week, Alice Weidel, co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, cited the low storage levels and argued that replenishing gas inventories must be a top priority. She warned that a cold winter could force Germany to make costly emergency gas purchases or resort to rationing, dealing a heavy blow to businesses and households.
As the Iran war drags on and tensions in the Red Sea flare up, experts have warned that EU natural gas prices could rise further to 100 or even 120 euros (115.1 to 138.1 dollars) per MWh if supply disruptions worsen. ■
