Putin Declares Children’s Minds a “New Front” as Russia Overhauls Education
Russia has transformed its educational system into a sweeping mechanism for military indoctrination and anti-Western propaganda, effectively rolling back decades of post-Soviet academic autonomy, The Economist reported on September 10.
Labeling the fight for children’s minds as a “new front,” Russian leader Vladimir Putin has mandated a nationwide “federal programme of upbringing” aimed at cultivating militaristic patriotism. This systemic ideological overhaul spans all educational levels, culminating in the formal introduction of state-sponsored patriotic curricula inside Russian kindergartens on September 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The state’s curriculum relies heavily on revising history and embedding combat narratives into daily learning, The Economist reports. Middle and high school teachers are instructed to frame the full-scale invasion of Ukraine as an existential defense of a “multipolar world” while blaming “the collective West” for prolonging the war.
Weekly mandatory classes, titled “Conversations about Important Things,” dedicate significant time to military themes and the “reunification” of occupied territories. Furthermore, Russian educational authorities have aggressively cut social science hours to expand mandated basic military training, drone operation, and standardized history courses crafted by Kremlin propagandists.
To compensate for the absence of a coherent national ideology, the state is heavily promoting militarized youth organizations.
State-sponsored groups like the “Movement of the First” attempt to mimic Soviet-era Pioneers, while the “Yunarmiya” military youth group—which teaches children as young as eight to march in formation—now claims over two million members, The Economist noted.
Concurrently, private military centers founded by combat veterans train children with behavioral issues using strict tactical discipline, drilling them to operate as combat units rather than individuals.
Despite the Kremlin’s efforts, the militarization campaign often breeds apathy and quiet resistance rather than genuine fanaticism, according to The Economist.
Independent reports highlight that many students view the propaganda as a burden, while teachers frequently allow pupils to use ideological class time to complete standard homework.
Educational psychologists observe that this top-down indoctrination is fostering a culture of “doublethink,” where lying and superficial compliance are accepted as a societal norm, ultimately damaging the educational standards and psychological well-being of Russian youth, The Economist wrote.
To enforce this ideological shift and curb growing student apathy, Russian educational authorities have recently started requiring teachers to monitor and report students who resist state narratives. According to updated Ministry of Education guidelines, educators leading the mandatory “Conversations about Important Things” classes must formally track pupils who ask provocative questions or display a “disagreement with value orientations”.
Teachers are instructed to record these incidents in specialized post-lesson assessments, providing school administrators with data to evaluate ideological compliance and strictly enforce the state’s patriotic curriculum.

COVID vaccines no longer free for many Australians from next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Everything you need to know about COVID-19 vaccine changes in Australia
For the past five-and-a-half years, vaccines against SARS‑CoV‑2, the virus that causes COVID-19, have been free for everyone living in Australia.
But that's about to change.
From October 1, only people at highest risk of severe COVID-19 disease will get the jab for free.
What does that mean for Australians more broadly and their access to the jab? And will this lead to more COVID-19 cases?
Who can still get a free COVID-19 vaccine?
From October 1, free COVID-19 vaccines will still be available for:
- Adults 75 and over (two doses per year, about six months apart)
- Adults 65–74 years (one dose per year)
- Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50–74 years (one dose per year)
- Adults aged 18–64 years with severely immunocompromising conditions (one dose per year). This includes people with chronic kidney disease on dialysis and people with leukaemia. If in doubt, have a chat to your doctor.
How much will the COVID-19 vaccine cost?
We don't know yet.
And we may not know until the last week of September, according to Pharmaceutical Society of Australia vaccination ambassador and community pharmacist Julianna Neill.
That's because conversations are still ongoing with manufacturers about what the wholesale price for Australia will be.
"Normally we go from knowing what a private vaccination cost is going to be, and then it becomes free," Ms Neill says.
"We've never really been in this situation before."
Australians typically pay between $25 and $35 for their annual flu jab, but Ms Neill anticipates the COVID-19 vaccine will cost "significantly more".
Why is the COVID-19 vaccine rollout changing?
COVID-19 vaccines, previously funded under the National COVID-19 Vaccine Program, are moving to the National Immunisation Program (NIP) where they will sit alongside respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza vaccines.
"This reflects the shift from an emergency pandemic response to a long-term, routine program focused on protecting people at highest risk of severe illness," a spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing says.
During the pandemic, vaccines were made available at no cost to reach as many people as possible but are now being targeted at those most vulnerable.
Jodie McVernon, director of epidemiology at the Doherty Institute, believes this may make the vaccine more accessible for high-risk groups already rolling up their sleeves for other jabs.
"Including it with the whole package should actually increase coverage by raising awareness, and make it a normal, regular seasonal event," Professor McVernon says.
Will this mean a lower vaccine update?
Potentially.
COVID-19 vaccination rates have been dropping in recent years.
So far this year, 1.7 million people in Australia have received the COVID-19 vaccine, about 6 per cent of the population, compared to 8.9 million people who have had the flu jab.
Loading...
Ms Neill says there may be a slight decline in vaccination rates following the introduction of a fee, as cost can be a barrier.
But instead of looking at Australia's overall vaccination rate, Professor McVernon says it is important to focus on vaccination rates in high-risk groups.
"The main burden of disease for COVID is in the over-75s, we actually see more COVID deaths than flu deaths," she says.
"But not even 40 per cent of people in that age group get the [COVID-19] vaccine."
Will this mean more COVID-19 cases?
It's hard to say.
Over the past few years, the number of reported cases of COVID-19 in Australia has decreased.
But Immunisation Coalition chairman Rod Pearce says many cases are not reported, which means the true number of infections is likely to be much higher.
Dr Pearce says there may be more COVID-19 cases if fewer people are vaccinated and more SARS‑CoV‑2 is circulating.
Professor McVernon says the decline in the number of hospitalisations and deaths over time is a "good indication" the health burden from COVID-19 isn't as significant as it once was.
"We see successive waves year-on-year, and over time, as the population becomes more immune through repeated exposure and vaccination, the infections we see overall are less severe."
Any other health advice?
If you want a COVID-19 booster but you're not eligible for a free jab, now is the time to contact your local clinic as changes won't come in until October 1.
You can find and book a COVID-19 vaccine online, or reach out to your GP or pharmacist for more information.
Even if you aren't in a high-risk group, getting vaccinated can still help protect you against long COVID and limit transmission of the virus if you do get infected, Dr Pearce says.
"Most of it is about having a rapid immune response, because your body is ready to fight the infection as soon as you get it," he says.
Professor McVernon says it is also important to remember basic hygiene principles to help limit transmission, including staying home if you're sick, washing hands frequently and wearing a mask if unwell.

US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:28:29 UTC
03:28:29 KST

The US Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation.
The Fed’s open market committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said on Wednesday. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
After the announcement, Trump said in a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. Trump said the US would make “at least 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year” if it were to stop trading with countries with which it has a deficit.
“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!,” Trump wrote.
Though Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name.
“There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said.
Warsh also declined to answer questions about how Trump would react but reiterated that Fed independence was “a two-way street”.
“We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
New projections showed a majority of officials penciled in another rate hike before the year’s end, with four officials predicting the Fed’s benchmark interest rate would reach a range of 4.25% to 4.5% by the end of the year.
And though estimates on the country’s economic growth and unemployment rate were upbeat, Fed officials believed it would take roughly until 2029 for inflation to reach its 2% goal.
At its last meeting in late July, the open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, the first time in 10 years that so many members shared dissent on a policy decision. Since then, the US and Iran have renewed attacks against each other, driving up the Brent crude benchmark to its highest levels in month.
The war has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.
Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans.
The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025.
At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.
Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.
Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew data.
Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress.
Critics have likened the move to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month.

Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023 in unanimous vote defying Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:25:58 UTC
03:25:58 KST

The Federal Reserve has raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since July 2023, in a unanimous 12-0 vote that puts Chair Kevin Warsh directly at odds with the US president who appointed him.
Kevin Warsh has broken away from US President Donald Trump in his first Fed move, and he has done it with the entire committee behind him.
The Federal Open Market Committee lifted rates on Wednesday after holding them at 3.5% to 3.75% since December, ending a pause that had grown harder to justify as energy costs pushed prices higher.
Not a single member dissented in a unanimous 12-0 vote.
That matters because the pressure ran in both directions as three regional presidents had voted for a hike in July, while the White House spent months demanding cuts.
Nobody voted for either extreme.
At the time of writing, the market reaction to the decision has been fairly muted likely due to the fact that the hike was widely expected.
On the other hand, Trump has already reacted negatively on social media by stating that "interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less [...]".
A statement stripped to the bone
The Fed's communication was as striking as its decision.
The statement ran to three short paragraphs, a fraction of the length markets are used to, with no forward guidance and no hedging.
"Inflation remains elevated," it read, adding that "today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
The word "timelier" carries an implicit admission that the return had been too slow.
Then a sentence the Fed almost never writes: "The Committee will deliver price stability." Not seeks to, not is committed to. Will.
The economic assessment was also confident throughout.
Activity is "expanding at a solid pace", domestic spending "has been resilient", productivity growth is "strong" and capital investment "robust", while job gains "have kept pace with the workforce".
Uncertainty remains elevated, the Fed said, owing partly to "geopolitical developments", its formulation for the Iran war.
By describing an economy in good health, the committee removed the argument that higher rates would damage growth, which is precisely the case US President Donald Trump has been making.
Boxed in by the data
The decision had been building for months.
Three regional Fed presidents dissented in July in favour of an increase, the most in one direction since 2016, and several others said afterwards they were ready to move unless inflation eased which it did not.
The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, ran at 3.7% in both June and July, with core inflation at 3.3%. Before the Iran war sent fuel prices climbing, core stood at 3%.
Consumer prices held at 3.4% in August, but the monthly increase of 0.4% was the sharpest since May, evidence the energy shock is feeding through. Inflation has now been above the 2% target for more than five years.
Warsh had effectively committed himself at Jackson Hole in August, telling the symposium he "would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive" and warning that unless underlying inflation moved to target "clearly and at sufficient speed", the Fed had "work to do".
Markets took him at his word as the CME's FedWatch tool put the probability of a rate hike above 90% before today's decision.
Defying the president who chose him
US President Donald Trump had spent months demanding the opposite, insisting the country should have the lowest interest rates in the world and choosing Warsh partly on the expectation he would deliver them.
Warsh himself said while campaigning for the job that rates could come down.
The treatment of his predecessor sharpened the stakes as Jerome Powell was publicly attacked for moving too slowly, and the US Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into testimony he gave to Congress.
Today's decision could also have a restoring effect on the perceived independence of the Federal Reserve as an institution.
The technical details point to a Fed settling in at the new level.
The interest rate on reserve balances rises to 3.90% from Thursday, the primary credit rate to 4%, and standing repurchase operations will run at 4%. Seven regional reserve banks requested the discount rate increase.
The Fed’s new dot plot shows 12 of 18 officials expect another 0.25% hike by year-end, taking rates to 4.125%, while four see rates reaching 4.375%.
The hawkish signal extends well beyond 2026 as 14 officials see rates ending 2027 above today’s level, while the 2028 median stands at 3.9% versus 3.4% expected.
The longer-run rate also rose to 3.2%, suggesting officials increasingly believe neutral rates have moved higher while economists also expect more to follow.

US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:24:00 UTC
03:24:00 KST

US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
September 16, 2026
The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.
This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair.
"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.
Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation."
"Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.
The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.
Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.
After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should be 1% or lower and that the rates should be cut fast.
"I ... talked to Kevin," Trump said. "And I said you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing."
Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'
Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.
But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing.
"We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision."
"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."
Borrowers will feel some impact
The raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance.
The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.
Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term.
But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.

US Fed raises interest rates for 1st time in over 3 years as inflation remains elevated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:21:42 UTC
03:21:42 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points Wednesday, delivering its first rate hike in more than three years as inflation remained elevated.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) increased the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75%-4% in support of the central bank's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.
The decision was approved unanimously in a 12-0 vote.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed said, adding that the policy action would support a "timelier return" to its 2% inflation target.
"The Committee will deliver price stability," it added.
The latest official data showed US consumer inflation remained well above the central bank's target in August.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% month on month in August, accelerating from a 0.1% increase in July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Annual inflation stood at 3.4%, unchanged from July.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, eased to 2.4% annually from 2.5%, despite accelerating to 0.3% on a monthly basis.
Energy prices jumped 16.3% from a year earlier, including a 27.4% surge in gasoline prices.
The Fed said economic activity continued to expand at a solid pace, while domestic spending remained resilient despite uncertainty that remained elevated partly because of geopolitical developments.
Productivity growth was strong and capital investment remained robust, according to the statement.
The central bank also said job gains had kept pace with growth in the workforce and that the unemployment rate had changed little.
The FOMC said it would continue its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Inside a Palestinian family’s agonizing decision to abandon their home under threat of Israeli settler violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:17:37 UTC
03:17:37 KST

The road to Deir Jarir is a visual prologue to what its people have lived through for the past three years of facing Israel’s military and settler offensive. Arriving from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, the 30-minute minibus journey stretches into a much longer one at the Israeli checkpoint in neighboring Silwad, marking the entrance to the chain of villages east of Ramallah. At the checkpoint, Israeli soldiers stop vehicles for search at varying hours and for changing periods every day, sometimes for half an hour, sometimes for three or four hours.
A long queue of cars waits endlessly for the next chance to move a few feet forward. Once through the checkpoint’s distinctive yellow iron gate, the minibus I’m on passes by the foot of Mount al-Asour, one of the highest points in the West Bank that rises to 1,200 meters above sea level, and where an Israeli military base has sat since the occupation began in 1967. On the slope below the base, mounds of freshly-dug earth and two prefabricated houses mark a newly-installed Israeli settler outpost, positioned directly above Palestinian homes and gardens.
I am heading to Deir Jarir to meet Ali Abu Khdeir, a Palestinian from the town who has experienced Israeli settler violence first-hand, and is still living through its consequences. In the last days of April, he had been forced to leave his family home, built long before he was born by his grandfather. The decision hadn’t come easily, but he felt that he and his family had been left with no choice, given the alternative.
Along the main road into town, a stream of faces flies past the minibus window — portraits of Palestinians killed by the Israeli army or settlers in Deir Jarir since October 2023; there are nine of them, aged between 20 and 55, including one woman. The latest two, Odeh Abu Salha, 55, and Ahmad Abu Makhu, 26, were killed in a single shooting by an Israeli settler on the night of the FIFA World Cup final, last July. They had gone out to confront Israeli settlers stealing sheep from a barn. One settler opened fire at the crowd, and then at the ambulance trying to evacuate the wounded.
For Ali Abu Khdeir, those photographs mark a road he now travels only as a visitor, but it was once the road to the hometown where he had spent his entire life. He now lives in a rented apartment in the neighboring town of Silwad, along with his father, his wife, and four children.
I meet Ali in the middle of Deir Jarir before we get into his car, and he drives off. We’re going to visit his now-abandoned home, but we won’t be able to go inside this time.
As we begin to approach the now sealed-off road to the neighboring village of Kufr Malik, Ali points in the distance.
The house is there, the one his grandfather had built, the one with the large veranda at the edge of town, standing empty.
Ali gazes at his home from a distance for a few seconds. We don’t leave the car. He begins to recall his family’s story.
“My grandfather built the house a few years before the Israeli occupation in 1967,” he said after taking a deep breath.
What happened to Ali’s family in Deir Jarir is part of a documented and accelerating pattern across the eastern villages of the central West Bank. Since October 2023, Israeli settler groups have systematically targeted Palestinian communities along the axis connecting Deir Jarir, Taybeh, Mughayyir, Turmusayya, and Abu Falah, using violence, intimidation, and the seizure of homes to push Palestinians out of villages they have inhabited for centuries.
According to the UN’s humanitarian arm, OCHA, settler attacks and access restrictions have displaced Palestinians across more than 130 communities since January 2023. B’Tselem has documented how the Israeli military routinely escorts settlers during attacks and fails to intervene when Palestinians are targeted. The goal, according to analysts who track the campaign, is territorial — not incidental.
Gradual takeover
“My father and his siblings grew up in it as children,” Abu Khdeir said. “Then they grew up and left, but one of my uncles lived in it with his own family when he got married. Years later, he built his own house and left.” Ali pauses and gazes down, then smiles as if coming back from his memories. “And for the past ten years I have lived in it with my family and my father, until we were forced to leave.”
Deir Jarir is home to some 5,000 Palestinians belonging to nine extended families, with a centuries-old recorded presence on the land and oral traditions linking some of them to pre-Christian times. For most of its history, it was an agricultural village — olive groves and vines in the surrounding hills, wheat and barley in the lower plains.
That economy has changed, but the people of Deir Jarir still work their lands, especially their olive groves east of the town. Since October 2023, those lands have become increasingly inaccessible.
The settlers’ offensive moved in stages. First came attacks at the entrances and edges of the town, including the killing of 30-year-old mother Randa Ajaja on October 12, 2023, shot while driving back home with her family. Then came new outposts on Deir Jarir’s entrances, including the one on the slope of Mount al-Asour, with a road the Israeli army paved specifically to serve settlers. Most recently, settlers began to attack the heart of the town itself.
Since Ali and I spoke at a distance from his house, I later came back on my own to see if I could photograph it up close. This time, I walked the Kufr Malik street alone.
The house is the last one, isolated at the very tip of the street, just under the summit of al-Asour. The recently established settler outpost and Israeli army radars are close by. I’m unsure of how close I can get or how long I’ll be able to stay before I attract the settlers’ attention.
I arrive at the last house before Abu Khdeir’s, some 150 meters away. It is a three-floor building with a porch shaded by a vine tree, and a man in his late fifties standing under it, looking down at the street.
I ask him if it is safe to approach the house. He looks at my camera and asks if I’m a journalist. I confirm, but he takes a longer, more careful look at me, then smiles and declares, “You’re from Taybeh, aren’t you? Come in, let’s have a talk first. I’ll tell you everything you need to know.”
He introduces himself as Muhammad Khamis, Ali Abu Khdeir’s next-door neighbor. He describes the recent series of attacks on Ali’s home in vivid detail. “This part of Deir Jarir, the Kufr Malik road, has become a battlefield with settler groups several times in the past months,” he recalled. “At one point, some 100 settlers attacked at the same time and began to throw rocks at the windows of the houses along the street as the Israeli army watched. The soldiers were stationed at the end of the street and blocked access to the center of the town.”
“If it weren’t for the young men who took to the roofs to defend the houses, the settlers would have entered our bedrooms,” he added.
Khamis takes us around his family’s building, located at the base of al-Asour, below the site where the settlers launched their attacks. “The settlers were here, and there, and they came up to here,” he said, pointing uphill as two little girls followed him shyly.
He recalls further details of the attack from July. “The settlers came from up there in groups, while another group trapped us inside from the street,” he said. “This is why we installed this barbed wire, to prevent settlers in the future from getting close to the houses.” Khamis points to a shining new spiral line of barbed wire stretching some twenty meters from the house.
“The pressure on the Abu Khdeirs was more intense because their house stands alone, and settlers could easily isolate it,” he explained, pointing toward the end of the road, where Ali Abu Khdeir’s house can be seen in the distance.
The settlers’ offensive had begun much earlier than the July attack. Khamis says that when the settlers established the outpost on Mount Asour, “our sense of safety here was lost, especially when they began to bring their livestock to feed on the olive trees.”
“When I confronted them,” he added, “and told them to stay away from our olive trees, one of them told me to leave for Syria, Jordan, or Egypt.” He lets out a sarcastic laugh. “I understood then that harder days were ahead.”
Jamal Jumaa, coordinator of the grassroots Stop The Wall campaign, says the pattern is deliberate.
“The first part of this violent settler campaign after October 7 was expelling rural and Bedouin communities in Area C, but that is largely done,” Jumaa told Mondoweiss. “Now, the settler groups’ strategy is to increase pressure on the villages and towns, taking houses as outposts from which to harass the rest of the community.”
Jumaa says that if the settlers’ strategy succeeds, the next phase will see the gradual takeover of houses at the edges of Palestinian villages, “like we have been seeing in Hebron and Jerusalem for years,” he explains.
This strategy has been reinforced by Israeli government policy. In February, the Israeli government approved the draft bill that would allow Israel to enforce its own law, including on building policy, in areas under the Palestinian Authority’s jurisdiction. The government also revoked a Jordanian-era law that restricted Israeli individuals from purchasing land in the West Bank.
Most recently, in July, a coalition of Israeli settler groups announced a plan to establish 100 settler outposts in Area A, in the heart of Palestinian cities. The plan was endorsed by Israel’s hardline Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, shortly thereafter.
Forced into leaving
For Ali, the takeover of his house followed the same incremental logic. “First, around December 2025, settlers began to roam close to the house, among the fig and almond trees,” Ali recalled during my first trip to Deir Jarir. In late February, the Israeli army demolished the barn Ali had built adjacent to the house, claiming it was located in Area C, the over 60% of the West Bank under full Israeli civil and military control in accordance with the 1993 Oslo Accords. “From that moment on, settlers began to harass us daily.”
“In March and April, settlers attacked the house directly with stones and threatened us,” Ali said. One morning, Ali’s elderly father woke to find a settler sitting on the porch. “That day, I realized that the house wasn’t safe anymore.”
What followed was not a decision so much as a trap: leaving meant risking permanent loss of the house, and staying meant risking the family’s safety. “What I really feared was a fire attack, like the many ones that have happened when settlers set fire to the house in the middle of the night, which I didn’t want to risk,” he recalled.
Finding a solution for his father — for whom the house was not mere property, but the embodiment of his entire family’s legacy — proved to be the hardest part. “The house to him represents his entire life memories,” Ali said. “But he wanted me to leave with my family for the safety of my children.”
Young men from the village offered to take shifts guarding the house while the family was away. But Ali’s father refused to let others be endangered in his place. The family was trapped between several painful choices.
Nakba day
Muhammad Khamis says he was there the night a group of young men came to the Abu Khdeirs’ house to make their offer. “Ali’s father refused emphatically,” Khamis said. “He said he didn’t want anybody to get hurt on account of protecting his own house, but he was clearly disturbed.”
“Ali had begun to look for an apartment to rent, and he had identified one in Taybeh and one in Silwad,” Khamis went on. “It was clear that deep down, he wished that, by some miracle, his family wouldn’t have to leave.”
Khamis sighs before adding in a hushed tone: “We all wished that. Who wouldn’t?”
Khamis describes the days before the Abu Khdeir family’s departure as “tense and sad,” because all the neighbors understood what it meant. “This was only the first part of Deir Jarir that was being expelled, and it made us all even more anxious, forcing us to think through what we would do if faced with the same choice.” Khamis believes this is why Ali decided to leave so swiftly, with as little drama as possible.”
“Finally, my father gave in, because he understood that if he stayed, I would stay,” Ali says. “Up until then, I had only thought of my family’s safety. But when the moment came, the most painful part came with it, all at once: my childhood, my memories, my family’s life here, but I had to keep it all inside, and I pushed on.”
The day they left, Ali and his wife didn’t send the children to school. They loaded their belongings onto a truck, and his father stayed silent throughout. Ali’s wife focused on the children.
That night, in their rented house in Silwad, Ali’s young daughter began to cry when she realized that they weren’t going back home. Her siblings soon followed suit. In the other room, her grandfather dried his tears in silence.
A few days later, Israeli settlers raised an Israeli flag on the rooftop of Abu Khdeir’s house. Residents of Deir Jarir took it down, but the message had already been delivered.
“After the Abu Khdeirs left, settlers came back twice, this time more emboldened, and they’ve gotten closer than they ever have been to the other nearby houses, possibly hoping that others will end up leaving, too,” Khamis recalled.
“After the latest settler attack, I spoke to my neighbor and relative, a school teacher whose house had just been attacked, and he said that he decided to stay, no matter what happens,” Khamis said solemnly. “He was even more determined to stay.”
When I asked what he would do if that came to it, Khamis immediately replied, “The same, of course! I saw what Ali’s family went through, and I’m not leaving. None of us is!”
He turns back to me, raising his finger as if remembering an important detail. “And just because Ali left for now, it doesn’t mean that he gave up on his house!”
I finally decide to approach Ali’s house after Khamis tells me that the settlers are absent. Just a few meters above the street, dry branches scattered along the path towards the house give away that the place is abandoned. The windows are shuttered, but the inside is visible through the glass veranda. Grass has grown, and it’s already dried around the entrance. Just beside the house, a pile of torn-apart corrugated aluminum sheets, bricks, and rebar indicates the location where the sheep barn had stood before the Israeli army demolished it in February.
But the most noticeable thing was the silence, which gave way to a terrifying realization: it gradually dawned on me that I was staring into the face of the same scene that Palestinians have carried with them since the Nakba — the same scene they’ve been struggling to keep from repeating itself. Chills go down my spine, and I remember that I shouldn’t stay much longer. I snap a few photos before hurrying back to the center of Deir Jarir.
That was my only encounter with the Abu Khdeir family’s displacement. But Ali still returns to check on his house and the trees whenever settlers are not around, taking his oldest son with him. He refuses to describe what happened as a permanent loss.
“It is not only about me going back to my house,” he told me during my first visit to Deir Jarir as he drove me back to Silwad. “It’s about why I was forced to leave in the first place. Why did my father have to be expelled from his childhood home at the end of his years? ”
Ali turns the car toward the road leading away from Deir Jarir, away from the familiar. “Why do my children have to remember their expulsion from now on? Why are these violent settlers supported by their government?”
As we leave Deir Jarir, the posters of slain Palestinians are there to see us off, their smiling faces flying past the car window. “Isn’t there anyone who will support and protect us?”
The sun sets to Ali’s left. To his right, the reflected twilight shines off the windows of Israeli settlers’ prefabricated houses, crouched on the slope of Mount al-Asour as they overlook the houses and gardens of Deir Jarir.
Qassam Muaddi

Italy Tests New TESEO MK2/E Anti-Ship Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:17:20 UTC
03:17:20 KST

MBDA has successfully conducted a test launch of the new TESEO MK2/E anti-ship missile for the Italian Navy.
During the test, the missile remained in controlled cruise flight for approximately 20 minutes, allowing it to validate its stated range, MBDA reported.
The successful test paves the way for completion of the development phase and the transition to serial production. The first missile deliveries to the Italian Navy are scheduled for 2028.
Development of the TESEO MK2/E began in 2021 following a contract with Italy’s National Armaments Directorate. In 2025, the parties signed an agreement for its serial production. The new missile is the next-generation member of the TESEO family, also known internationally as OTOMAT.
The weapon is being developed to arm new PPA multipurpose offshore patrol vessels, future DDX destroyers, FREMM-class frigates and Orizzonte-class destroyers. The system will also be integrated with new FREMM EVO frigates, with potential deliveries to international customers.
The missile is equipped with a new radar seeker featuring an active electronically scanned array (AESA).
It can engage both naval and land targets at ranges of more than 350 km. One of the missile’s key advantages is the ability to control its flight in real time via a satellite communications link.

Former director Grigory Sverdlin looks back on how Russia’s Nochlezhka homeless charity built shelters, showers, and laundries while expanding into Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:17:11 UTC
03:17:11 KST

Former director Grigory Sverdlin looks back on how Russia’s Nochlezhka homeless charity built shelters, showers, and laundries while expanding into Moscow — Meduza
Former director Grigory Sverdlin looks back on how Russia’s Nochlezhka homeless charity built shelters, showers, and laundries while expanding into Moscow
Since 1990, the charity Nochlezhka has helped people experiencing homelessness access food, shelter, medical care, psychological support, and legal assistance. Grigory Sverdlin led the organization for more than a decade, from 2011 to 2022. Under his leadership, Nochlezhka launched numerous projects: Neravnodush, a free shower facility; the Counseling Service, which provides legal and social assistance; the Cultural Launderette, where people experiencing homelessness can wash and dry their clothes for free; and a Moscow branch that opened despite threats and harassment from local residents, officials, and even the Rossiya 1 television channel. In his book “Punkt Obogreva” (“Warming Center”), published by Meduza with support from the StraightForward Foundation, Sverdlin recalls the challenges Nochlezhka faced over the years — and how the organization overcame them. We asked him to describe his work at Nochlezhka and show us what it was like.
The Night Bus
“The Night Bus actually ran in the evenings. It was a small minivan with shelving units installed inside, holding 20-liter [5.3-gallon] army thermoses full of soup. Volunteers handed out food day after day, at the same time, at the same stops, so homeless people already knew where and when to show up. The driver was in charge of each run — the only person who did this every workday rather than occasionally, as the volunteers did, earning a small salary for it. It was a Petersburg autumn: cold, dark, and dreary. A huge line, 40 people or so. You could tell many of them had known each other for a long time. I remember being struck by how often people said ‘thank you’ and ‘please’ — far more often than, say, in the Petersburg metro. The Night Bus was clearly a place where they felt safe and were treated like human beings.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“I expected to see people who weren’t very sober and were poorly dressed, mostly elderly. There were plenty of those, but many others showed up too: a smiling teenage boy of about 15; a working-class guy dressed, like me, in a black jacket and jeans; elderly women who knew each other from a nearby building; their pensions weren’t even enough for food, so they took the chance to get a free bowl of hot soup. About a third were people with homes. I really liked that everyone who got in line received food. There was no distinction between people who were homeless and those who weren’t; no need to prove you really needed that bowl of soup and piece of bread. No one waits in a line like that unless they have to. Just asking for help was enough.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“Some trips were especially memorable. Once the wiring burned out and the light in the cab went dead. We had to ladle out soup by feel. And suddenly, almost instantly, an old candelabrum holding about a dozen candles appeared, brought in by one of the clients from who knows where. And all of it — the bus, the soup, the people — turned before our eyes into a Christmas mystery play.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
The Warming Station
“The tent was packed full every day. We opened at eight in the evening, but the line was already forming by seven — people hurried to save a spot, though we ended up letting everyone in anyway. On the coldest nights, we had close to 70 people in a tent meant for 50. It might be crowded, but no one should be left out in the cold. The average winter temperature in Petersburg is minus 11 degrees Celsius [12 degrees Fahrenheit], which because of the city’s humidity, feels another 3–5 degrees colder [about 5–9 degrees Fahrenheit colder]. So staying outside on a winter night is simply life-threatening. We let everyone in: sober or drunk. The only rules were not to drink and not to disturb others trying to rest. It all looked like something out of a Bosch painting: darkness, some grim back alleys along the Obvodny Canal, people wrapped in several layers of clothing and shivering from the cold — that winter the temperature often dropped to minus 20 to 25 degrees Celsius [minus 4 to minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit]. Most visitors were somewhere between 30 and 50 years old, but there were children too, and some very elderly people.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
The Shelter
“Besides the Night Bus and the Heating Point, we had one more project: a shelter. In 2005, the city leased Nochlezhka a building at a reduced rate at the very end of Ligovsky Prospect, beyond the Obvodny Canal. It’s a rough part of the city that has always had a lot of dormitories and flophouses for people who came to Petersburg for work. To be precise, what stood there wasn’t even a building, but its skeleton: no roof, no windows, holes gaping between floors. Renovation took two years, and eventually a shelter for 52 people opened in a space completely unsuited for the purpose.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“The Counseling Service was on the first floor. […] The shelter itself was on the second and third floors — five rooms, each holding eight to 12 people. Four for men and one for women. That roughly matched the ratio among homeless people: there are about four times as many men on the street.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“[We called the biggest room] the Library. Here, shelter residents could read books or sit at a computer to try to find work, get in touch with relatives, or just play solitaire.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
The Counseling Service
“The Counseling Service was a kind of information desk for homeless people: here they got help replacing lost documents and filing requests or complaints with city agencies, and could call home to another city.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“People whose passports had been stolen would come in from time to time, and at the passport office they’d hear: ‘Where were your documents issued? In Rostov? Then go get them replaced there.’ That was completely illegal, but few people knew how to stand up for their rights. Others came who had traveled to Petersburg for work and been cheated by an employer — a very common story. A man works construction, lives in a site trailer, gets some pocket money, and is told: ‘We’ll settle up once the project is done.’ Then three or four months later he hears something like: ‘The contractor paid us less, here’s a couple thousand, now get lost.’ There was no employment contract, and even if there had been, workers like that weren’t prepared to fight for their rights in court. All they wanted was somewhere to spend the night. We bought some of them tickets home. Several dozen people came to the Counseling Service every day.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
The Cultural Launderette
“Nochlezhka isn’t just about restoring documents, finding jobs, or handing out food. It’s also about dignity — maybe, first and foremost, about dignity. People need to be able to feel human, not like outcasts — even if they can’t afford to do laundry. They shouldn’t have to be afraid to walk into a café or go to a job interview because their clothes smell.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“From the very first days, the laundromat was packed with people. Eight professional washing machines provided by Prachka.com churned away, with eight dryers working just as hard. In the first two weeks alone, 274 people came to us. Yes, occasionally older women who weren’t homeless came too. And that was fine — if someone was willing to come do their laundry at a laundromat for homeless people, they clearly needed it. On one of the first days, I witnessed a scene: an elderly man was freezing and clearly didn’t have enough warm clothing. A very poorly dressed young guy walked up to him and gave him his sweater: ‘You need it more; you’ll freeze.’ The man burst into tears.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
Neravnodush
“Then we launched Neravnodush, a place where anyone in need could take a shower for free. Again and again, I was fascinated by the act of creating something from nothing, out of emptiness. An idea would flash through my mind, and then came the hardest part: summoning the will and determination not just to start, but to see it through no matter what it took. And after that, miracles would begin to happen.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“It took us more than four years to open Neravnodush: finding a plot of land, arranging the lease, designing and building the facility after studying similar projects abroad, arranging electricity and water hookups, closing off Novorossiyskaya Street to lay pipe, and so on and so forth.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
The Moscow branch of Nochlezhka
“August 2018. To cut off any path to retreat, I happily posted on social media: ‘It’s official — Nochlezhka’s first project in Moscow will be the Cultural Launderette.’ Sweet summer child. It’s a good thing we can’t see the future. If I’d even suspected what awaited us, I’m not sure I would have had the courage to take that first step.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“For several months, we sent petition after petition and kept showing up at Moscow City Hall, asking the city to give us a space. But we were turned down four times. […] We realized we’d have to start with humanitarian aid, such as a laundromat, rather than with more complex and expensive projects like a rehabilitation shelter and the Counseling Service. […] I had never in my life seen as much hatred as was directed at us in the weeks and months that followed. Our laundromat, which hadn’t even opened yet, was threatened with arson three times, and we lost count of how many times people threatened to report us to Rospotrebnadzor, the sanitary and epidemiological service, the prosecutor’s office, and every other agency imaginable. Almost immediately, a group of activists formed and began campaigning against us.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“Rossiya 1, a Russian national television channel, shot a segment about Nochlezhka in the style of a public denunciation. ‘So-called philanthropists’ and “a strange Petersburg fund,’ the voiceover intoned ominously. ‘How can they put a homeless shelter right in the center of the city?’ the host said incredulously. ‘Especially since in Petersburg itself, Nochlezhka is stuck in a trailer on a vacant lot.’ Despite repeated appeals for people to turn out for the filming, only six showed up to picket Nochlezhka on camera. Even so, they were filmed and presented as ‘large-scale protests by local residents.’ It later turned out that the channel’s deputy director was our neighbor and a fierce opponent of ours.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive
“And finally, in July 2020, two and a half years later: Dasha and I cut the ribbon. The Counselling Service in Moscow is open. And soon a shelter will open in the same building. A full two and a half years. That’s all it took. Just two and a half years, and now Nochlezhka in Moscow has 13 employees, more than 100 volunteers, and the Night Bus feeding 150 to 200 people every evening. Now 20 to 30 people will get help at the Counselling Service every day. Fewer people will be left alone with their troubles. The strange, timeless story of people who didn’t like this world and decided to invent another one for themselves went on.”
Grigory Sverdlin’s archive

UN can offer negotiation platform to Iran, US, but they have to want it — body's chief

UNITED NATIONS, September 16. /TASS/. The United Nations can offer to host negotiations between the United States and Iran, but it's the warring sides that have to decide to talk, Secretary-General of the global organization Antonio Guterres said in response to a TASS reporter’s question.
"We can only organize what people will be willing to do," the UN chief said when asked if he had considered hosting talks between Iranian and US negotiators at the UN General Assembly High-level Week 2026.
Resolving the Middle East crisis without dialogue would be impossible, Guterres emphasized.
The headquarters of the global organization in New York City will host the General Debate of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) with the participation of heads of state and government, as well as foreign ministers, on September 22-26 and September 28. The Russian delegation will be led by Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to address the UNGA session on September 22, while Iran is listed as a speaker on September 23.

Former French culture minister to stand trial on corruption charges, accused of lobbying for Renault-Nissan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:15:32 EEST
03:15:32 KST

Former French culture minister to stand trial on corruption charges, accused of lobbying for Renault-Nissan
Kyiv • UNN
Former French culture minister accused of illegal lobbying for Renault-Nissan. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
A trial has begun in Paris against former French Culture Minister Rachida Dati on corruption charges related to her cooperation with automaker Renault-Nissan, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying: she received €900,000 as a fee for legal services from Renault-Nissan’s Dutch subsidiary while she was a Member of the European Parliament. The court is to determine what exactly the money was paid for.
Dati’s defense rejects all corruption allegations, claiming that she worked "exclusively" as a lawyer for Renault-Nissan’s subsidiary. French prosecutors, however, insist that she was paid to lobby for the automaker’s interests—an activity prohibited for Members of the European Parliament. According to prosecutors, there is no evidence that Dati actually performed legal work.
The investigation into Dati began in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan’s interests between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was a Member of the European Parliament.
Carlos Ghosn, the former head of Renault-Nissan who fell from grace, is also being tried alongside Dati; he will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 on allegations of financial misconduct in another case involving the falsification of data about his personal income for the purpose of personal enrichment. He evaded trial in Japan by fleeing to Lebanon, notably hiding in an audio-equipment box. He denies any wrongdoing both in the Japanese case and in the case involving Dati.
French prosecutors claim that a legal-services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, under which Dati received an annual fee of €300,000, was used to conceal lobbying activities. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan.
Dati, 60, who serves as mayor of Paris’s 7th arrondissement, is one of the best-known figures among French right-wing politicians. She became the first woman of North African and Muslim origin to hold a senior position in the French government when conservative President Nicolas Sarkozy appointed her justice minister. She later returned to the government under President Emmanuel Macron, serving as culture minister.
Dati changed perceptions of a political public figure in France; according to her, growing up in a large family—she was the second of 11 children—in a social-housing neighborhood on the outskirts of the city of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy helped her better understand the French electorate. Earlier this year, she ran for mayor of Paris but lost to Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire.

If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office.
Dati’s lawyers said: "The baseless allegations of influence peddling in the European Parliament are based on an artificial legal construct invented by the prosecution."
In a separate investigation, Dati is accused of receiving nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from energy group GDF Suez while she was a Member of the European Parliament. US President Donald Trump on Wednesday removed Venezuela from a list of countries that Washington said “failed demonstrably” to meet international counternarcotics obligations, citing increased cooperation with the interim government.
“Given the positive advances achieved under the leadership of Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, I have determined that Venezuela should no longer be designated as having failed demonstrably,” Trump said in a document submitted to Congress.

The US said inclusion on the broader list does not necessarily reflect a government’s current counternarcotics efforts or its level of cooperation with Washington.
Countries on the “failed demonstrably” list include Afghanistan, Bolivia, Burma (Myanmar) and Colombia for the previous 12 months.
Washington said continued US assistance to Bolivia, Myanmar and Colombia is vital to its national interests despite their designation.
Under US law, the president is required to notify Congress annually of countries considered major drug transit or illicit drug-producing nations and those deemed to have failed to meet their international counternarcotics obligations.

Village votes to leave U.K. in symbolic protest of plan to house asylum seekers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:14:38 UTC
03:14:38 KST

Tiny English village votes to leave U.K. in symbolic protest over plan to house asylum seekers
Piddington, England — A tiny English village has voted overwhelmingly to leave the United Kingdom in a symbolic referendum triggered by government plans to house more than 1,200 male asylum seekers at a former military site nearby.
Residents of Piddington, a rural village in Oxfordshire, voted 285 to 26 to "secede from the UK and pursue self-determination," with a turnout of nearly 92%. The vote has no legal force.
Piddington has a population of around 350 people. The asylum accommodation plan would house up to 1,256 asylum seekers, more than three times the population of the village, at a former British military base in Bicester, half a mile from Piddington.
The site would operate as a non-detained asylum accommodation, meaning the asylum seekers would be able to come and go. The proposed development would operate for 10 years, the U.K. Home Office said.
Village residents told CBS News they believe there has been insufficient consultation over the plans and raised concerns about safety, crime and the potential impact on their lives.
The referendum was deliberately held on Sept. 15, Battle of Britain Day, commemorating a pivotal day in 1940 during World War II when Britain's Royal Air Force fought off major attacks by Nazi Germany's Luftwaffe. A banner commemorating the anniversary was displayed outside Piddington's village hall during the vote.
The dispute highlights a wider political dilemma for the U.K. government over where asylum seekers should be accommodated. Piddington is a relatively affluent rural community. Historically, asylum seekers have been disproportionately concentrated in poorer parts of Britain, in part because accommodation there has been cheaper.
Reacting to the news of the vote, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC, a CBS News partner, that he understood the village's "strength of feeling."
But he has argued that wealthier communities should shoulder more of the asylum accommodation burden.
"We cannot have a situation where it's only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers," Burnham told GB News.
The government is seeking to reduce its reliance on asylum hotels, the cost of which has become a major political issue, by moving asylum seekers into other spaces, including former military sites.
But, as seen in Piddington, that strategy can create challenges when a large asylum facility is proposed near a small community that has historically accommodated relatively few asylum seekers.
Tim McNally, chairman of Piddington Parish Council and one of the leaders of the campaign against the facility, told CBS News the village deliberately drew inspiration from American history.
"We actually did this referendum … recognizing the United States' 250 years of independence and understanding the strife and struggle they went through to get their self-determination," McNally said.
McNally expressed frustration that no government officials have visited the community or spoken to the residents.
"I'm only 60 miles away [from Parliament], and they can't even be gracious enough to get off their seat and come and see me, or invite me to come and see them," he said.
McNally said the attention the campaign has received reflects wider political discontent.
"The political behavior is of a type that you guys call the swamp," he said, referring to the American political slogan "Drain the swamp." "This is an example of the swamp."
For some residents, concerns center on what the development could mean for everyday life in the village.
"I'm worried about the safety of the children and the women of the village," said Jennifer Owen, who voted to leave the U.K. "The towns won't be the same, they'll be overrun, village will be overrun. It just won't be the same again."
In the neighboring county of Essex, where the government plans to expand an existing asylum accommodation site, Chief Constable Rachel Nolan told the BBC that crime linked to the facility is "very low."
The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics says it does not hold breakdowns of crime by asylum-seeker or migrant status, meaning there is currently no comprehensive national data showing whether asylum seekers are more or less likely to commit crimes than the wider population.
Owen's husband, Herbert Owen, who has lived in the area for 33 years, also voted to leave the U.K. He said he's worried the proposal would have a detrimental impact on house prices.
"What has been the point of working? To pay your mortgage, to pay this in your life, when the government are gonna impose this on you without even talking to you?" he said.
While Piddington remains part of the U.K., organizers of the vote hope the tactic will spread.
McNally said that after publishing a blueprint for the village's campaign, he received more than 500 inquiries from parish and town councillors and residents around the country interested in adopting similar tactics.
The controversy comes as the number of people seeking asylum in Britain remains historically high. Around 100,600 people claimed asylum in the U.K. in 2025, more than twice the number in 2019. Home Office figures show that 41% had arrived by small boat, while 39% had previously entered the country on a visa or other form of legal permission.
Over the past decade, roughly 630,000 people have claimed asylum in the U.K., according to U.K. government figures. Concerns about immigration and asylum seekers consistently rated as one of the top three issues for voters in Britain, according to YouGov polling.

Caine: US Must Prepare for Forces to Be ‘Tracked in Real Time’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:12:00 UTC
03:12:00 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine said the U.S. needs to prepared for future conflicts in which its adversaries will be able to closely track the location of American forces and attack with autonomous systems that use artificial intelligence.
“We have to assume from now on that our formations will be hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum and tracked in real time,” Caine said in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 16.
“And we have to transition the joint force to be prepared to fight and win our future wars by generating and delivering lethality at scale with an agile, optimized, high-low mix of combat capabilities,” he added.
The notion of an increasingly transparent battlefield in which U.S. forces will have few places to hide has been hammered home by the ongoing conflict with Iran. Tehran, the State Department said in May, has used satellite imagery provided by Chinese companies to strike at American forces in the Middle East.
Brig. Gen. Todd Benson, the commander of Space Forces Central, said at the conference that small nations and even subnational groups could also potentially access satellite imagery to track American forces.
“I’ve been coining the term hyper-transparent warfare,” Benson said in a Sept. 15 media roundtable. “Nothing you do today is without being seen. You just can’t hide anymore, and so that’s great for us for our advantage. But you have to assume that any adversary will find some way to access imagery, and so we have to use that, and we have to operate knowing that we can be seen.”
It was a theme Caine underscored as well.
“Future conflicts will demand that we operate without the assumptions of uncontested access, secure rare areas, or uninterrupted or uncontested sustainment,” Caine said. “In the future fight, advantage will go to the side who can see first, who can understand first, decide first, and act first, and along the way be a learning organization”
The chairman noted several ways the U.S. can prepare for future fights.
One way is exploit artificial intelligence and cyber capability, said Caine, who noted the use of AI to enable an unmanned vessel to rescue two U.S. soldiers after an Apache attack helicopter was downed in June near the coast of Oman.
“That capacity did not appear overnight,” said Caine. “What made this possible was a bunch of entrepreneurial Sailors and members of the joint force on watch floors at piers, managing networks of unmanned systems across thousands of miles of water and using AI to turn massive amounts of data into a crisp, clear, perfect maritime picture that allowed us to go grab those two Soldiers in the water.”
Caine said it is also important for commands to empower young Airmen and Guardians to innovate and take risks.
“I need you to be adaptive leaders. The fight will not wait for perfect requirements, perfect processes, or perfect information,” said Caine. “You must always be able to recognize when the old way is no longer sufficient, get close to the problem, and help build a better solution.”
He also stressed the important for industry and the government to cooperate more closely.
“We cannot expect industry to invest in capacity, manufacturing or top talent when we’re moving requirements around, but we have to be able to adapt more quickly. That means sharing risk across government and industry,” he added. “We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time.”

Polish cultural centre named after US soldier who died saving Polish officer
A cultural centre in Oleszno, southern Poland, was named on Wednesday after Staff Sergeant Michael Ollis, a US soldier who was killed in Afghanistan in 2013 while shielding a Polish officer from a suicide bomber.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki attended the dedication ceremony in Oleszno, the home town of the saved Polish officer, retired Captain Karol Cierpica, where he said that the facility serves as a poignant reminder of the core foundations underpinning the Polish-US alliance.
"This alliance, built on shared values and history, has the faces of Michael Ollis and Karol Cierpica here in Oleszno today," Nawrocki said. "Michael Ollis gave his life for his friend, serving with honour, serving his homeland, the United States, and demonstrating the true strength of the Polish-American alliance."
Nawrocki said that the partnership between the two nations spans more than two centuries, forged by historic figures such as Generals Kazimierz Pulaski and Tadeusz Kosciuszko, the American pilots of the Kosciuszko Squadron in 1920, and the Cold War-era cooperation between Pope John Paul II and US President Ronald Reagan. He added that the current presence of US troops on Polish soil provides a "tangible guarantee" of national security.
The insurgent attack occurred on August 28, 2013, at a joint Polish-US forward operating base in Ghazni, Afghanistan, after a truck bomb breached the perimeter wall. During the ensuing firefight, Cierpica, then a lieutenant, was wounded. Staff Sergeant Ollis, 24, stepped between Cierpica and an insurgent, shielding the Polish officer with his own body as the attacker detonated a suicide vest.
"For me, brotherhood simply has a face and a name: Michael Ollis," Cierpica told the ceremony, recalling his late friend's actions and invoking the motto of the US Army's 10th Mountain Division: "Deeds, not words."
The US Consul General in Krakow, Gretchen Cureton, thanked the local community on behalf of Ollis's parents, saying that his name would remain a lasting "symbol of courage, honour, and enduring friendship between Poland and the United States."
In a letter read aloud at the event, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz praised the men, writing that their story represents an "extraordinary brotherhood in arms created not by political declarations or military procedures, but by individuals filled with honour and bravery." “I called on international organizations to provide appropriate assistance to prevent mass deaths,” he added.
Ukrainian officials have continued to call on international organizations to help secure an evacuation corridor for the town and additional humanitarian access, but those efforts have so far produced no tangible results.

CHYBIK + KRISTOF wraps jihlava arena in a jagged red aluminum crown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:10:44 UTC
03:10:44 KST

CHYBIK + KRISTOF’s Jihlava Municipal Arena sits where a much larger building might usually feel difficult to place: directly beside the historic center of the Czech city. The 5,650-seat venue occupies the site of an ice rink that had served Jihlava since the 1950s, keeping hockey in its familiar part of town while opening the grounds to a wider public. The arena now sits between a university and a residential street, with a park close by, giving its unusually large footprint a surprisingly urban setting.
Its shape is immediately recognizable. Red aluminum wraps the elliptical volume, while a jagged triangular crown runs around the roofline. The architects drew the geometry from Jihlava’s Gothic architecture and the hedgehog used as a local symbol. After dark, lighting embedded in the facade responds to what is happening inside, flashing when HC Dukla Jihlava scores and changing for other events.
Much of CHYBIK + KRISTOF’s Jihlava Arena becomes interesting once visitors get closer to the building. Large entrances and expanses of glazing keep the ground level visually connected to its surroundings, while an uninterrupted concourse circles the seating bowl inside. The architects treat this circulation space almost like an indoor public square, giving people somewhere to gather before entering the stands and providing wheelchair users direct access to some of the arena’s strongest sightlines.
The site itself continues to operate as a route through Jihlava. Pedestrians moving between the university and neighboring park can pass beneath an overhanging section of the arena roof, while a new staircase negotiates the six-meter change in level and doubles as stepped seating. Above, a 230-meter running track circles the roof. It is free to use through a booking system, placing another piece of public infrastructure on top of the building even when the arena floor is empty.
exposed structure gives the interior its character
Inside, the architecture stays direct. Prefabricated concrete stands are pigmented in the same deep red as the exterior, while the steel roof trusses remain exposed overhead. The perforated aluminum skin helps bring daylight and air through the envelope, allowing a building of this scale to retain some visual porosity when seen from the street.
The seating bowl is arranged across two tiers for hockey, an unusual decision for an arena of this size. Its standard 5,650-person capacity can grow beyond 7,400 with retractable seating, and concerts can occupy the floor while a curtain closes off the upper tier for a smaller acoustic volume. Even the folding seats take part in the acoustic work: CHYBIK + KRISTOF developed the Highlands chair with David Karásek of Kovostal, molding a geometric pattern into its underside to absorb sound.
the triangular motif moves from facade to graphic identity
The same angular language appears at smaller scales throughout the building. Hand-cast triangular fixtures by Czech glassmaker BOMMA sit within the concrete walls, while graphic designer Lukáš Kijonka translated the facade geometry into the arena’s wayfinding system and custom typeface. The repetition is restrained enough to keep the building from turning into a branding exercise. It simply gives the interiors a visual thread back to the red shell outside.

European Parliament agrees to accelerate issuing permits for defense projects

Ilayda Cakirtekin
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The European Parliament on Wednesday agreed to accelerate issuing permits for defense projects as part of new measures to strengthen the continent's readiness.
The legislative body approved changes to accelerate defense investment and improve the bloc's readiness to address security challenges with a package of proposals under the so-called “Omnibus V” EU simplification measures.
With the changes, the parliament sought to simplify security and defense procurement procedures and EU cooperation on defense contracts.
It agreed to accelerate the approval of permits for defense projects and the export of defense equipment between EU countries. The text was approved by 540 votes in favour, 105 against, with 22 abstentions.
The new rules will introduce an EU-wide default period for permit decisions of 42 working days, while national authorities can extend the time limit by up to 60 days in exceptional circumstances.
The parliament also agreed on measures to remove regulatory obstacles to facilitate and accelerate public procurement in defense and intra-EU transfers of defense-related products.
On defense procurement, lawmakers agreed to raise the threshold for EU procurement rules, extend framework agreements from seven to 10 years, and give member states more flexibility to carry out joint procurement.
The Parliament and Council of the European Union also agreed to consider future measures to simplify the transfer of defense products and strengthen Europe’s defense industry through EU procurement rules.
The new rules also aim to simplify the management and implementation of the European Defence Fund (EDF).
They update and clarify the criteria that defense projects must meet to receive EDF funding, with priority given to projects demonstrating high standards of excellence, quality and efficiency.
The proposals aim to support up to €800 billion ($922 billion) in defense investment over the next four years under the ReArm Europe Plan/Readiness 2030 initiative, helping EU member states and the defense industry respond to growing security challenges.
