Fed hikes rates as US inflation persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:10:30 UTC
03:10:30 KST

Fed hikes rates as US inflation persists
The US Federal Reserve has raised interest rates despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated demands for lower borrowing costs, as stubborn inflation continues to weigh on the world’s largest economy.
The Fed hiked its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4% on Wednesday in a unanimous vote, marking the first increase since 2023 and the first policy change under Chairman Kevin Warsh.
Speaking after the decision, Warsh said inflation was “too high and has been for too long,” while pointing to the resilience of the US economy despite “geopolitical shocks and uncertainty.”
The move had been widely expected. Some 85% of economists surveyed by Reuters after the latest inflation data had forecast a quarter-point increase, while a narrow majority expected at least one more hike by the end of March 2027.
The decision comes after inflation showed renewed signs of pressure. US consumer prices rose 3.4% year-on-year in August and 0.4% from the previous month, with gasoline prices jumping 3.9%, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Price pressures have been fueled in part by higher energy costs linked to the Iran war, while tariffs have also added to inflation concerns. Higher interest rates are intended to slow price growth by making borrowing more expensive, which tends to reduce spending by consumers and businesses.
The Fed has a long-term inflation target of 2%. Warsh said last month that the goal was “firm” and “fixed,” arguing that inflation remained too high and that the central banking system’s main focus should be on prices.
The labor market has remained relatively stable, with unemployment at 4.1% in August and employers adding 162,000 jobs. Growth has slowed, however, with GDP expanding at an annualized rate of 1.5% in the second quarter, down from 2.1% in the first.
The rate increase could make borrowing more expensive for US households already facing higher prices, according to Yung-Shin Kung, chief investment officer at Mast Investments. He said that lower-income consumers could be hit particularly hard, as they face both elevated prices for essentials such as food and housing and higher costs for servicing debt.
Trump repeatedly attacked former Fed Chair Jerome Powell for refusing to deliver the steep rate cuts he sought, calling him a “moron” and a “numbskull.” He nominated Warsh as Powell’s successor in March, with Warsh taking over the Fed in May. The latest decision now puts him at odds with the president.
Lower rates would also cut borrowing costs on the US national debt, which has topped $40 trillion. On Sunday, Trump renewed his pressure on the Fed, saying the US should have “the lowest interest rate in the world” regardless of inflation or other economic data.
Warsh had previously backed higher rates to curb inflation, but shifted toward Trump’s position on lower borrowing costs before taking over the Fed and called for “regime change” at the central bank. Last month, however, he stressed that the Fed must be confident inflation is moving toward its 2% target “clearly and at sufficient speed,” warning that otherwise, “we have work to do.”

It is planned that 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries around the world will attend: 5,000 from Russia and 5,000 from foreign countries. A thousand teenagers aged 14 to 17 will take part in the program. TASS is the general information partner of the event.

How 9/11 hate and Islamophobia targeted Sikh Americans too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:08:56 UTC
03:08:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Balbir Singh Sodhi: 25 years after 9/11, a Sikh family remembers America's first hate crime victim
Rana will always remember the day his brother, Balbir Singh Sodhi, was killed.
He received a call that there was a shooting at his brother's petrol station and assumed there was a robbery. But it wasn't until Rana reached the station that he saw his brother was the only one targeted among those present.
"When I got there and I saw that, it really broke my heart," Rana Singh Sodhi tells The New Arab. "That day, I understood how much hate still exists in American society."
One man saw the colour of Balbir's skin, his beard and turban, assumed he was Muslim and shot him, becoming America's first hate crime victim after 9/11.
Twenty-five years later, the attacks remain etched into the memory of millions. But for Muslims and those mistaken for Muslims, the aftermath also marked the beginning of years of heightened surveillance, discrimination and violence, fuelled by an increasingly hostile anti-Muslim rhetoric.
"My brother's turban, his bracelet, his cloth, is part of American history," Rana tells The New Arab.
"I don't think in the last 25 years, there has been a day when I didn't remember him. I remember him almost every day. We weren't aware that we would be a part of the backlash, that we were going to be targeted," he adds.
"People see the image of Bin Laden, the beard and turban, and then they immediately associate it with us [Sikhs]."
Rana recalls being told to go back to his country by hecklers when he was out shopping once, and another incident where his friend was threatened.
Witnessing the hate and being the target of it, he knew the Sikh community was in trouble.
"At that time, we really felt it. A Sikh person wearing their turban and beard was likely to be targeted in a hate crime," he recalls.
After 9/11, Rana remembered Balbir telling him to stay home, scared he might become a victim, never thinking he himself would go on to become a target.
"Balbir thought that because I was threatened, I had to be very careful," he says.
The incident takes Rana back to the time his family fled India following the events of Operation Blue Star in 1984, when the Indian government targeted members of the Sikh community.
Rana and his family sought refuge in the US, believing it would be a safer place for them, emphasising that he had not experienced any hate before 9/11.
"I didn't have concerns about what I was wearing. I felt I could go out any time, day or night, anywhere," Rana says.
"But 9/11 totally changed my life. It changed the lives of the Sikh community. I discovered that there is a lot of ignorance in American society, and there's a lot of hate towards people of different skin colours and those who look different."
Rana remembers the local community coming together to mourn for Balbir, with hundreds laying flowers at his petrol station in the middle of the night, remembering his kindness.
From giving sweets to children to even giving customers some money to pay for petrol, his kindness and generosity were remembered.
"He had that kind of personality; it amazes me," Rana said.
His family was also shocked after discovering that Balbir had emptied his pockets for a 9/11 fund at a Costco fundraiser an hour before he was killed.
Costco learned of it only after releasing its annual magazine, which revealed Balbir's generosity.
"[Balbir] spoke to one of our brothers when 9/11 happened; he said he wanted to go to New York and help those people. He's that kind of person."
Ten months after his brother's murder, Rana lost another brother in a cab accident. Filled with grief, he decided to channel his emotions into teaching the community not only about the Sikh community but also about spreading love.
"When you lose someone, it's very painful. When you lose someone to hate, it is more painful," he explains.
"Hate is a natural thing. I don't know where it comes from, but when it goes to that level of taking somebody's life, that's crazy. I feel like if my work saves someone's life, then my life is worth it. I'm going to do what I have to do to educate more people, bring peace and love to our community, our nation."
Looking back at Trump's America and the current state of growing hate and racism in the world, Rana speaks of the importance of educating the next generation of young people, reflecting on his children, who have love and respect for all.
"When you give a good education to our young generation, there is no one we hate, and that's the key point," he says.
"I believe it's going to stop one day with help from everyone and education, and if we teach our children, the young generation, how to understand and build respect and love for each other, it will go away."
Anam Alam is a staff writer at The New Arab. She frequently writes about human rights and social issues, including women's rights and sex education

US extends protection for Venezuelan state oil firm bonds until November

Yasin Gungor
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US Treasury Department issued an amended sanctions license Wednesday to extend legal protections shielding bond transactions involving Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) until Nov. 5.
"All transactions related to, the provision of financing for, and other dealings in the Petroleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond that would be prohibited by ... the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations... are authorized" on or after Nov. 5, according to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
The directive replaces and supersedes the previous license, issued Aug. 3, barring creditors from enforcing claims or liquidating collateral tied to the defaulted 2020 8.5% bonds until the November threshold arrives.
The regulatory shield safeguards the Venezuelan state energy company's foreign assets, including a 50.1% controlling equity stake in US-based refining subsidiary Citgo Holding, Inc. that was pledged as collateral for the debt, as Washington navigates political and economic relations with Caracas.
The license renewal unfolds alongside sweeping diplomatic and economic shifts that followed a Jan. 3 US military operation raid in which Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro was captured and transported to the US to face federal charges. Washington subsequently recognized an interim administration headed by Delcy Rodriguez.
Relations shifted further following an August energy pact announced by US President Donald Trump, under which private consortium North American Blue Energy Partners secured concessions in 17 Venezuelan oil fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of proven crude reserves.
The Treasury Department clarified that the newly issued general license does not authorize other activities otherwise barred under broader federal sanctions regulations.

US drops Venezuela from drug list, may remove Colombia, Trump says
BOGOTA – The United States has removed Venezuela from its list of countries which have failed to demonstrably combat illegal drug trafficking for the first time in more than 20 years, US President Donald Trump said in a statement on Sept 16, adding he may consider removing neighbouring Colombia.
Because of his administration’s ouster and arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, cooperation with the country’s interim government, led by Maduro’s former deputy Delcy Rodriguez, is paying dividends, including in the killing of the Tren de Aragua leader known as ‘Nino Guerrero’, Trump said in the presidential determination published by the State Department. Venezuela has been on the failed list since 2005.
“I have determined Venezuela should no longer be designated as having failed demonstrably to fulfill its drug control commitments. I expect to see continued, measurable progress from the interim government in dismantling narcoterrorist groups and stopping drug trafficking through Venezuela,” he said.
“Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere” after the election of President Abelardo De La Espriella, Trump added. “If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status.”
Colombia was designated in 2025 by Trump for failing to combat cocaine production, amid repeated mud-slinging between him and former leftist president Gustavo Petro. Trump endorsed De La Espriella, a former lawyer for people connected to right-wing paramilitaries, who took office in August pledging a security crackdown.
Both countries are still considered by the US to be major transit hubs or major producers, along with Afghanistan, the Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Burma, China, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Jamaica, Laos, Mexico, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Panama and Peru. Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:06:29 UTC
03:06:29 KST

Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.
A review of global research found that for several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions, kidney disease and Parkinson’s, women were less likely to receive the same treatment as men, revealing the extent to which women have significantly unequal care.
Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 38 studies and found that in 33 of them women were less likely to be offered active treatment. Women with myocardial infarction, heart failure or an irregular heart beat were more likely to be given medication, whereas men were more likely to receive a coronary bypass, stent or other surgical treatment. Women were also less likely to be prescribed statins, according to the analysis, which was published in the journal Plos One.
Men with Parkinson’s were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation, while those with liver failure were more likely to receive a transplant than women. Female kidney patients requiring dialysis were less likely to be given permanent access and had to spend longer using a catheter. And women were also less likely to be given opioids for pain management.
For stroke and diabetes, however, there was no significant difference between the sexes in treatment. And women were more likely to be treated for dementia.
The findings come amid growing concern about the gender health gap. In March, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, said women were being let down by “medical misogyny”. The previous Conservative government appointed Lesley Regan as England’s first women’s health ambassador, to help tackle the gender gap.
The analysis concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health. It found that none of the studies identified any guideline recommending different treatment by sex, raising the question of whether unequal care was a factor.
Dr Andrew O’Malley, who co-led the study, said: “For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption.”
He said studies showed doctors more often attributed women’s symptoms to anxiety and made more diagnostic errors with female patients, even when test results were positive.
Dr Miriam Veenhuizen, an honorary lecturer in the School of Medicine at St Andrews, said: “While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was. The same pattern appeared in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care, and it survived statistical adjustment in most studies.”

‘Godfather of AI’ says humanity is ‘losing control’ of the technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:06:19 UTC
03:06:19 KST

‘Godfather of AI’ says humanity is ‘losing control’ of the technology
MONTREAL – The Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, Yoshua Bengio, told AFP that humanity is “losing control” of the technology and that the world needs guardrails similar to nuclear arms controls.
Fears about the dangers of AI have intensified in recent weeks, as workers from major companies have resigned with warnings about potentially existential threats to human life if the pace of technological advancement is not checked.
Bengio is a University of Montreal professor who won the 2018 Turing Award, computing’s Nobel, alongside Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the “godfather of AI”.
For Bengio, “there’s a reason that companies are saying this is going too fast, that we’re losing control”.
“People like me have been expecting this for a long time,” the 62-year-old told AFP on Sept 15, saying security discussions surrounding AI have not been adequately robust.
There was broad-based alarm after OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of AI agents – programmes that can take actions on their own – had carried out an unauthorised breach of the open-source platform Hugging Face in July.
Such autonomous action is the central threat, Bengio said, warning of a situation where AI agents can “get through cybersecurity barriers and enter any company”.
Manipulating human behaviour
In 2025, Bengio founded the non-profit LawZero, aimed at creating a new form of advanced AI that is “designed to be trustworthy and safe”.
LawZero was awarded C$300 million (S$274 million) in funding on Sept 16, split between the governments of Canada and Germany, which have launched several efforts to cooperate on AI.
Speaking to AFP a day before the announcement, Bengio said people need to be aware of the risks ahead.
AI agents may foster “an ability to establish an individual connection and persuade humans to act in ways that suit (AI) but are not necessarily good for all of us”, a capability that could have sweeping consequences for democracies, he said.
Longer-term, “AI might not even need human beings anymore to do real things in the physical world”.
In that scenario, “one extreme could be the destruction of humanity”.
“That’s an extreme,” Bengio acknowledged, but noted that even if a banking system were shut down, “that’s still very, very serious”.
International challenge
The world’s biggest AI companies – OpenAI, Anthropic and Google – have begun working on creating a standards body, a collaboration that seemed to acknowledge the public’s fear that competition between companies and countries might sideline safety.
For Bengio, taming AI’s advance is “an international challenge, a bit like nuclear weapons are an international challenge”.
“So the international community needs to understand the power we are bringing into the world, and that must be managed, must be governed through institutions, treaties and democratic safeguards.”
“Society needs time to put in place what needs to be put in place,” Bengio said.
But political will across key governments appears uneven.
US President Donald Trump on Sept 14 dismissed warnings about the risks of AI as “hoaxes”.
But there is more openness to act in the EU, where European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Sept 16 that she will invite the world’s largest AI labs for talks on “how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was at that speech in Strasbourg, has repeatedly talked about collaborating with the EU on AI safety.
Bengio stressed that all firms must comply with future AI restrictions, particularly US-based companies that have been dominating the sector.
Action is urgent, he said, but voiced optimism that “we can help bring the world to a place that is more aligned with democratic values and values of power sharing”. AFP

MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin has delivered his traditional televised address to the nation ahead of the parliamentary elections.
Voting will take place from September 18-20.
The head of state noted that the large‑scale election campaign is being held amid the special military operation. He said that by participating in the elections, Russians take a responsible civic step that will move the country where they want it to go. According to Putin, every voter’s voice matters — it determines which political forces will represent the people’s interests at all levels.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the head of state.
Importance of election campaign
The large‑scale election campaign in Russia “is being held against the backdrop of the special military operation.”
The election campaign is pivotal: “I consider it important to address you now, when our great country is undergoing a significant, largely decisive election campaign.”
The elections of deputies to the State Duma, as well as to the legislative assemblies and to the heads of a number of regions and municipal authorities, will be held “in strict accordance with the law and within the established timeframes.”
Residents of Donbass and Novorossiya will elect deputies to the State Duma “for the first time since their reunification with Russia.”
Everyone’s voice matters
Every vote counts: “It depends on all of us, on your personal choice, who exactly, which political forces will represent the interests of the people both in the federal parliament and in the regions, and at the local level.”
The most worthy and competent candidates, true patriots of Russia, will win the elections: “Those who will not let us down, those who have proven their devotion to the motherland, their readiness to serve our people, and their willingness to protect the country from any threats.”

Participation in the elections will clearly demonstrate to everyone that behind the military personnel fighting at the front stands a single, cohesive people united by a common history and values: “Your choice and will will again show that behind our fighters are millions of people, that we are a united people, united by common values, historical memory, and love for the motherland.”
The parliamentary elections in Russia will show that no one will be able to split or intimidate the country: “No one will be able to split or intimidate us, to undermine our statehood and socio‑political system.”
Parliamentary elections will be a worthy response to those who dream of weakening Russia or want to deprive it of its sovereignty: “This will be our common response to those who want to weaken Russia, curb its development, deprive us of our sovereignty and the right to determine our own destiny.”
Voting will be everyone’s contribution to the country’s victory: “Participation in elections is our common contribution to Russia’s victory.”
Example for entire country
The courage and loyalty to the fatherland demonstrated by the Russian military personnel serve as an example for the entire country: “I am confident that our soldiers and officers, who are currently engaged in difficult combat work, will take the most active part in the voting. Their courage and loyalty to the fatherland are an example for the entire country.”
Russians now know what their duty is and what their homeland is fighting for: “We know what Russia is fighting for and what the duty of every citizen of the country is.”
Russia’s future victory is being forged now both on the battlefield and by the workers in the rear: “Victory is being forged by our heroes on the battlefield. It is being brought closer by everyone who works honestly for the motherland and understands their responsibility for its future."

US Fed raises interest rates as inflation weighs on economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:03:51 UTC
03:03:51 KST

US Fed raises interest rates for first time in three years
The 25 basis-point hike is the first raise in three years and comes before critical midterm elections in the United States.
The United States Federal Reserve has said it will raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point as inflation, driven by soaring fuel prices amid the US-Iran war, continues to weigh on the economy.
The Fed, which is the central bank of the US, said on Wednesday that it will hike interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent to 4 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate court controversy with Ceuta solidarity shirts
- list 2 of 4Iran war has cost the US $38bn: How will it impact US economy, politics?
- list 3 of 4Poll shows Americans are increasingly alarmed by AI’s ecological footprint
- list 4 of 4UK trade unions back motion to boycott and sanction Israel
It is the first hike in more than three years and comes just weeks before the US midterm elections, despite repeated demands from US President Donald Trump to lower rates.
“Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the Fed said in a statement on Wednesday.
“Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.”
After Wednesday’s hike, Fed officials expect one more rate increase this year, according to their quarterly projections, and expect rates to remain unchanged through next year.
CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecast a 92.3 percent chance of the Fed increasing rates to 3.75 to 4 percent. A week ago, that forecast was a 40 percent chance of a quarter-percent rate increase.
Stress on economy
But in the days since, a slew of data shifted those expectations.
For one, consumer prices jumped in August by 0.4 percent, the highest increase in four months. Trump’s tariffs and capital spending to feed the artificial intelligence boom have also pressed prices.
On an annual basis, prices rose 3.4 percent, matching the increase recorded in July, while the job market remains healthy.
Since then, benchmark crude oil prices have continued to soar as strikes in the US-Israel war on Iran have intensified. Brent crude hovered near $109 per barrel on Tuesday.
The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.36 ($1.15 per litre), up 14 cents in the past week, and up from $4.06 ($1.07 per litre) last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.
Diesel, on the other hand, was at $6.31 ($1.67 per litre), the highest recorded average and roughly double from a year ago. That, in turn, is expected to further stoke prices as diesel is used in trucks to haul everything from fruits and vegetables to steel and cement.
At the same time, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield broke above the psychologically important 5 percent threshold on Tuesday, hitting 5.02 percent, its highest level in 19 years. The yield serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs, including car loans and home mortgages, and is a bellwether for inflation.
“The economy is in an unusual place,” Michael Klein, professor of international economic affairs at Tufts University’s Fletcher School and executive editor of EconoFact, a nonpartisan economic and social policy publication, as unemployment remains at a comfortable level while higher prices continue to stick, sending inflation beyond the Fed’s target of 2 percent.
“There [has been] a lot of pressure on Chairman Warsh to raise interest rates because of inflation coming in high, and that has been compounded by concerns about Trump’s pressure” as the president has continued to demand that interest rates be lowered, Klein said.
“Higher interest rates tend to weaken the economy … but if the market believes that there’s going to be a rate increase, it’s priced in already as prices move on news, so this won’t be news,” Klein said, adding that should help steady yields.
The White House did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the rate increase.
Nearly three hours after the interest rate decision, Trump posted on Truth Social, his social media platform, that “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR. Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment!”
He added, “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” but didn’t mention Warsh directly in the post.
Later on Wednesday, when asked if he still had confidence in Warsh as Fed chair, Trump told reporters that he does.
“I’m relying on Kevin, but he’s got a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people. And the interest rates are too high. They’re not appropriate. I told Kevin, I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter,'” he said.
Trump repeatedly berated Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for not lowering rates. The government even launched a criminal probe into Powell, which he said at the time were “pretexts” to undermine the independence of the Fed.

“Together for Iran” illustration exhibition to open in Tehran
TEHRAN- A group illustration exhibition titled “Together for Iran,” featuring more than 80 works by 64 illustrators from different Iranian cities, will open at Tehran’s Book Garden on Thursday evening.
Organized by Ketabara Group in collaboration with Soore-ye Omid Institute and Book Garden, the exhibition is the outcome of an open call inviting artists to reflect on recent events and the experiences of Iranian people during the war.
The selected works explore themes including homeland, resilience, resistance, courage, social solidarity, the national flag, experiences of war, the future and hope. The artists have also addressed the funeral processions held for the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and the public’s participation in bidding farewell to the country’s heroes and martyrs.
A special section of the exhibition, titled “Angels of Minab,” is dedicated to children and students who lost their lives in the war. Through a human-centered approach that seeks to go beyond geographical boundaries, the section presents artists’ responses to the suffering of children and the devastating consequences of armed conflict.
The Minab tragedy took place in southern Iran during the Ramadan War, when an attack struck a school in the city of Minab, resulting in the deaths of a number of students and teachers. The incident drew widespread attention and prompted artistic and cultural responses commemorating the young victims and reflecting on the impact of war on civilians, particularly children.
In recent months, the memory of the Minab children has also been reflected in exhibitions and other cultural events in Iran and abroad, with artists using visual art as a means of remembrance and as a call for greater attention to the human cost of war.
The organizers of “Together for Iran” also seek to preserve the collection as part of the contemporary visual memory of the country. Alongside images of suffering and loss, the works highlight hope, solidarity and the resilience of Iranian people during difficult times.
A four-day illustration workshop will also be held alongside the exhibition under the supervision of Mahboubeh Khosravi, a professor at Shiraz University and an illustration instructor who has conducted specialized workshops in Iran and other countries. The workshop will provide an opportunity for practical training, artistic exchange and discussion of illustration.
The exhibition will open at 5 p.m. on Thursday at the Negarestan of Tehran’s Book Garden. Artists, students, art and book professionals, and illustration enthusiasts are expected to attend the opening.

Polls: Americans overwhelmingly believe US failed in Iran war, view Trump as ‘dangerous and corrupt’

Instead of rallying behind militaristic posturing, Americans are expressing profound fatigue with endless foreign quagmires designed to serve imperialist and Zionist interests at the expense of ordinary working families.

At Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, photographic evidence confirms a catastrophic direct hit on a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control (AWACS) aircraft, its tail severed and its radar-carrying fuselage gutted by flames. Similar scenes of ruin were documented at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a primary desert staging hub for US ground forces and armored units. The imagery starkly illustrates that conventional US blast fortifications, such as concrete “T-walls,” have proven utterly useless against the kinetic force of modern Iranian aerial operations.

As Iran’s missile forces continue to demonstrate operational adaptation—employing maneuverable warheads, varied trajectories, and precise targeting—the combination of scorched hangars on the ground and dwindling stockpiles in US arsenals confirms that the era of Western military deterrence in the region has reached an irreversible tipping point.

New Canadian rifle shown in Britain for the first time
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:00:51 BST
03:00:51 KST

Colt Canada has given British and European audiences their first sight of the C25 rifle at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the successor to the C7 and C8 family that has served Canadian and allied forces for more than 35 years, the company stated.
The rifle has been selected by the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces, and was developed under the Canadian Modular Assault Rifle project.
Sean Congdon, President and Chief Executive of Colt Canada, said: “We’re really excited to be at this year’s DVD. It marks the start of us telling our story, with C25 as our focus. C25 is not simply about introducing a new rifle. It is our response to how the operational environment is changing and what soldiers need from their weapon system today.
“It builds on decades of experience with the C7/C8 platform, combined with what our customers have told us about the challenges they are facing in the field. As we bring C25 to the UK and other European markets, we’re taking the same approach that has always defined Colt Canada: listening closely to our customers and developing solutions around their operational requirements.”
The reasoning behind the design addresses a problem facing every Western army. Level IV body armour is becoming more common, and according to the company the current 5.56mm cartridge cannot be relied on alone to defeat it, while no settled view has emerged on a next-generation intermediate calibre.
Rather than change the round, Colt Canada has approached the difficulty from the other direction, making the soldier more accurate against the smaller, harder targets that armour leaves exposed, under the fatigue and stress of sustained operations. The company describes the C25 as a precision and human factors programme built around a defined concept of employment. The rifle remains chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO and carries a 13.7 inch chrome-lined, free-floating, cold hammer forged barrel, with a full length top rail on the upper receiver accommodating a range of attachments including the company’s own 1-6x low power variable optic.
The company describes four changes as central to the design, the first being a two-stage trigger intended to deliver a more sensitive, positive break under stress. Optimised barrel geometry reduces disturbance to the projectile, which the company says supports higher practical accuracy across the effective range. Controlled gas redirection at the muzzle decreases sound pressure at the firing position, suppresses flash and reduces felt recoil. The low power variable optic extends the engagement window and reduces the time a soldier spends exposed.
Colt Canada has supplied military customers across Europe since the 1990s, and says approximately 3,000 of its weapon systems are in service with the British Army including the special forces, alongside fleets in the Netherlands, Norway and Denmark.

New psychology research links obsessive celebrity worship to criminal thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:00:18 UTC
03:00:18 KST

New research published in Deviant Behavior indicates that an intense obsession with celebrities tends to go hand in hand with criminal thinking patterns and vulnerable narcissism. The findings provide evidence that the darker sides of celebrity worship are closely tied to a deeply insecure form of self-centeredness and a willingness to justify rule-breaking behavior.
Celebrity worship describes a one-sided, parasocial relationship where an individual becomes intensely attached to a public figure. This behavior exists on a spectrum. On the milder end, people might simply enjoy discussing their favorite actors or musicians with friends for entertainment. On the extreme end, the attachment takes on addictive qualities, leading individuals to obsessively track a celebrity’s life at the expense of their own daily functioning.
Narcissism, a personality trait characterized by an extreme focus on oneself, plays a central role in how these obsessions develop. Psychologists generally divide narcissism into two subtypes: grandiose and vulnerable. People with grandiose narcissism tend to be arrogant, aggressive, and highly self-assured, believing they are superior to others. In contrast, those with vulnerable narcissism suffer from deep insecurities, anxiety, and a constant fear of inadequacy, often reacting to threats with hostility or withdrawal.
Recent explorations of this insecure personality type, such as a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, have found that vulnerable narcissism is consistently rooted in anxious childhood attachment styles. These individuals often struggle to form healthy connections in real life. Because of this social anxiety, people with high levels of vulnerable narcissism seem particularly drawn to idolizing famous figures. A parasocial relationship offers a sense of connection without the fear of real-world rejection.
The relationship between extreme celebrity worship and harmful behavior has been documented for years. A 2007 study provided early evidence that pathological celebrity worshippers exhibit higher rates of criminal tendencies, sometimes showing a willingness to break the law if their idol asked them to. Separately, psychologists have explored how narcissistic traits fuel rule-breaking. A 2021 study demonstrated that distinguishing between grandiose and vulnerable narcissism helps explain the psychological mechanisms that lead people to commit crimes.
More recent work has started connecting these overlapping personality traits. A 2025 study showed that people with vulnerable narcissism are uniquely prone to obsessing over celebrities, while arrogant, grandiose narcissists are not. Building on this progression of research, Joshua L. Williams, a professor and chair of criminal justice and criminology at Georgia Southern University, along with Leanne Confer of the University of Michigan, Flint, and Madeleine Krueger and Lawrence Locker, Jr. of Georgia Southern University, designed a new study to test how these elements interact.
The researchers wanted to see if celebrity worship and the two distinct types of narcissism independently relate to criminal thinking, which includes attitudes that justify illegal acts or ignore the harm caused to victims.
“While some early research, back in 2007, established a basic connection between celebrity worship and personality characteristics associated with criminality, very little empirical work since then explored how celebrity worship relates specifically to criminal thinking patterns,” the researchers told PsyPost. “Furthermore, previous research on personality and crime overwhelmingly focused on grandiose narcissism, leaving a significant gap concerning how vulnerable narcissism relates to both celebrity worship and criminal thinking styles.”
To investigate this, the research team recruited 237 undergraduate students from a large university in the southeastern United States. The participants had an average age of 21, and the group was primarily composed of female students. Through an online survey, the students completed several established psychological questionnaires designed to measure their attitudes and personality traits.
The survey included a measure to assess where participants fell on the spectrum of celebrity worship, from basic entertainment and social interest to intense personal connection and borderline-pathological obsession. To capture narcissistic traits, the researchers used two separate tools: one focused on the confident, superiority-driven traits of grandiose narcissism, and another focused on the defensive, insecure traits of vulnerable narcissism. Finally, the participants answered questions evaluating six categories of criminal thinking, such as a desire for power, a tendency to justify bad behavior, and insensitivity to the impact of crime on others.
When analyzing the data, the researchers found that the two types of narcissism related to celebrity worship in very different ways. As expected from previous research, vulnerable narcissism was reliably associated with higher levels of celebrity worship across the board. The more insecure and anxious participants were, the more intensely they obsessed over their favorite stars. Grandiose narcissism, however, showed no statistical relationship with celebrity worship.
“Furthermore, individuals who struggle with vulnerable narcissism, characterized by anxiety, low self-esteem, and social avoidance, tend to be particularly prone to forming these obsessive parasocial relationships, likely as a maladaptive coping strategy to manage daily distress and identity-development challenges,” the researchers explained.
Both forms of narcissism were linked to criminal thinking, but the patterns diverged. Grandiose narcissism was primarily associated with a desire for power, a sense of personal grandiosity, and a lack of sensitivity to how crimes affect victims. Vulnerable narcissism, on the other hand, predicted a much broader range of antisocial attitudes. It was strongly tied to nearly every category of criminal thinking measured, indicating that the insecurity and hostility characteristic of this trait may foster a widespread acceptance of deviant behavior.
“It was interesting to see that the vulnerable subtype of narcissism continued to be a consistent and strong predictor of celebrity worship, which fits with our previous work,” Williams and his colleagues noted. “However, now we show that the vulnerability associated with that subtype of narcissism, more so than the grandiose subtype, may also be predictive of criminal thinking styles. The consistency of the findings related to vulnerable narcissism underscores its importance to understanding constructs such as celebrity worship and criminal thinking styles in greater detail.”
The data also indicated a strong association between celebrity worship and criminal thinking. The nature of this relationship depended heavily on the intensity of the participant’s obsession. At the lowest level of celebrity engagement, where people simply use celebrities as a topic of social conversation, participants actually showed lower levels of grandiosity and greater sensitivity to the impacts of crime. This suggests that casual, entertainment-focused interest in celebrities is largely harmless and even associated with more pro-social attitudes.
“To prevent misinterpretation, readers should not assume that all forms of celebrity interest are harmful,” the researchers pointed out. “In this study, the entertainment-social level (the lowest level) of celebrity worship was actually predictive of lower criminal thinking and higher social desirability.”
The opposite was true for the more extreme forms of celebrity worship. Participants who scored high in borderline-pathological worship demonstrated a much stronger endorsement of criminal thinking. They were more likely to justify rule-breaking, seek out power and revenge, and disregard the harm caused by illegal actions. Even when the researchers mathematically controlled for both types of narcissism, intense celebrity worship independently predicted these criminal thinking styles.
“Intense, obsessive celebrity worship (the highest levels) is not merely harmless fandom,” they added. “It was only the extreme, obsessive, and borderline-pathological levels of celebrity worship that tended to align with problematic traits and cognitive styles.” Ultimately, the team concluded that “a person’s relationship with celebrities, especially when the relationship is borderline pathological, can be deeply tied to their underlying personality traits and cognitive patterns.”
“Readers should note that the correlations between celebrity worship and criminal thinking styles range from weak to moderate, with the strongest associations emerging at the highest, most obsessive levels of celebrity worship,” the authors said. “In our regression models, the combination of celebrity worship levels and narcissism subtypes accounted for 13% to 30% of the variance across various criminal thinking categories. While these effects demonstrate a meaningful statistical relationship, they also indicate that these psychological traits exist as part of a larger, highly complex web of factors that may influence criminal thinking.”
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data collected at a single point in time, the researchers cannot determine the direction of cause and effect. It is possible that vulnerable narcissism drives people toward celebrity obsession, but it is also possible that extreme parasocial relationships alter how people view themselves and the rules of society.
“Our long-term goal is to transition from cross-sectional designs to longitudinal studies, which would allow us to map out the specific developmental pathways and determine if narcissism drives criminal thinking through celebrity worship,” the researchers said.
The study does have some limitations regarding its sample as well. The participants were entirely composed of college students, a demographic that may not accurately represent the general public or individuals who have actually been involved in the criminal justice system. Future studies tracking these behaviors over time, or examining populations with a history of documented offending, could help clarify how these personality traits and obsessions translate into real-world behavior.
“We also aim to expand our research beyond college students to forensic samples, such as individuals with histories of arrest or incarceration, to see how these cognitive styles translate into actual offending behaviors,” the researchers added. “Finally, we plan to examine how self-control acts as a moderating factor within these relationships.”
The study, “Celebrity Worship, Narcissism, and Criminal Thinking Styles,” was authored by Joshua L. Williams, Leanne Confer, Madeleine Krueger, and Lawrence Locker Jr.

The study’s authors warn that evidence from previous electoral battles between the two parties suggests Labour politicians should dial down direct attacks on the Greens for fear of looking as if they are “kicking a puppy”.
Christabel Cooper, one of the report’s authors, said: “The previous administration [under Keir Starmer] had always banked on the fact that Labour would be able to say to people who vote Green that they would get Nigel Farage as prime minister.
“But in the 40 seats that we have identified, that is no longer the case – the Greens can claim to be the progressives’ party of choice.”
She added that evidence from other elections where the party has gone head to head with Labour suggests that progressives dislike aggressive attacks on the Greens.
“The sorts of people who would consider voting Labour consider attacking the Greens like kicking a puppy. They think, we are all supposed to be nice and liberal, why are we having a go at the Greens?”
The findings, which have been discussed with strategists in No 10 as they look to solidify separate polling gains made in Burnham’s early weeks as prime minister, show Labour faces a difficult task winning back urban progressives who helped the party win the last election.
ThinkLabour’s former chief executive Alison Phillips is now Burnham’s chief of staff, while other alumni of the organisation have senior roles across government.
The research was carried out as Burnham was about to take office in Downing Street, meaning it will not have captured the full effect of the “Burnham bounce”, which has seen Labour gain ground with progressive voters and pull level with Reform UK.
The poll shows that support for the Greens has increased by 12 points in major cities since the general election, while Labour’s vote share has fallen by 20 points, leaving Labour only 4 points ahead in some of its most reliable strongholds.
It found that the move from Labour to the Greens has been more pronounced among voters who are financially struggling, undermining the stereotype of Green voters as affluent liberals.
The report warned that urban voters felt they did not know what Labour’s values were, in part because of some of the counterintuitive measures taken by Starmer in his early days as prime minister, such as cutting winter fuel payments.
It also warns that winning these voters back will mean focusing immigration reforms on tackling small boat crossings rather than wider measures to tackle legal migration.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is bringing in measures to make it harder for legal migrants to achieve settled status, which have proved controversial with Labour MPs and activists.
The report said: “On divisive areas such as immigration, where liberals and social conservatives can agree on some outcomes – reducing small boat crossings, for example – it should primarily focus on these.
“Where its policies appear tough or restrictive, Labour must be able to make a convincing progressive case for them, showing how they solve practical problems rather than simply signalling to the right.”
The researchers also found that attacks on the Greens over foreign policy had the most effect with the voters Labour is trying to win back, in part because they found these more credible than other criticisms.
While urban voters did not like Green policies on legalising drugs – which Labour focused on during the failed campaign to win the Gorton and Denton byelection – they did not view them as a particularly credible threat.
Personal attacks on Polanski, meanwhile, went down badly among those considering voting Green, who viewed criticisms of his CV and his past as a hypnotherapist as especially non-credible.
The Green leader has previously come under fire for telling a journalist in 2013 he could enlarge women’s breasts with hypnotherapy – comments he has since said he regrets.

Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation

Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
September 16, 2026
The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany.
A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate.
The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday.
Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office.
Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period.
What determines the Mass' price?
This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%.
"Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said.
Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades.
Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized.
Festival draws millions
Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds.
The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen.
This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors.
The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival.

New evidence shows that you are only slightly hotter than a T. rex

New evidence shows that you are only slightly hotter than a T. rex
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
If you’ve been to the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, you’ve probably been wowed by the fossilized remains of Thomas, the formidable 34-foot-long Tyrannosaurus rex dominating the Dinosaur Hall.
More than 66 million years after Thomas’ death around the age of 17, the animal is continuing to contribute to science’s understanding of his famous species.
Chemical analysis of one of Thomas’s fossilized teeth has provided the most precise estimate yet of T. rex’s body temperature. The predator was not a cold-blooded creature, but a warm-blooded one with a body temperature probably around 97.3 degrees Fahrenheit, plus or minus 4.5 degrees.
She’s big, she’s green, and she’s L.A.’s newest icon. Meet Gnatalie the dinosaur.
The findings were published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
New analysis techniques developed in recent years have provided strong evidence that theropods like T. rex, velociraptors and other two-legged dinosaurs were endothermic animals like mammals and birds, rather than cold-blooded, or exothermic, like reptiles.
“The significance of this study is the ability to place an unambiguous measurement on the body temperature,” said co-author Robert Eagle, an associate professor at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability. “This is a sort of very direct way of getting at their physiology that’s not been possible before.”
The study looked at bonds between carbon and oxygen isotopes in the fossil. The fewer bonds present, the higher the temperature at which the minerals in the tooth formed.
“The amount of these chemical bonds is basically set 70 million years ago when this tooth first formed in the body of a dinosaur,” Eagle said.
A massive renovation will highlight new science in an L.A. institution
Mapped against the climate of the Cretaceous Period, the T. rex’s likely body temperature would have suited it for life all over what is now North America, a hypothesis born out by the fossil record, Eagle said.
Eagle’s team is conducting further analysis on the tooth, after which it will be returned to the museum’s collection. Museum paleontologists excavated some 70% of Thomas’s fossilized skeleton in the early 2000s, making it one of the most complete T. rex specimens ever found.
“Natural history collections are reservoirs of evidence, often used in ways no one could have predicted when they were first built,” said Luis Chiappe, director of the Dinosaur Institute at the Natural History Museum. “The T. rex teeth we studied were collected decades ago, before the analytical techniques we used were even possible.”

Saudi Arabia Calls Mecca a ‘Red Line’ After Alleged Houthi Drone Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:58:48 UTC
02:58:48 KST

Saudi Arabia on Wednesday accused the Iran-backed Houthis of an attempted attack on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and a site of pilgrimage for Muslims worldwide.
Colonel Turki Al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen, said that the Houthis launched a drone toward Mecca on Tuesday evening, but it was shot down by the Saudi Air Defense Forces before entering the city’s restricted airspace.
“The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line,” said Al-Malki, who warned that the Saudi-led coalition “will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures” against the Houthis.
Riyadh referenced a previous similar incident from July 2017, in which it accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca. The Houthis acknowledged launching a missile from Yemen, but said that it was aiming for the King Fahd air base in Taif.
The Yemeni militia group has denied the allegation, accusing Riyadh of spreading “false accusations” on Wednesday.
“There is no threat from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, and are far from the holy sites,” said Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree via Telegram.
The allegation comes amid a widening regional crisis. Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast are threatening shipping and energy supplies—already disrupted by the conflict in Iran— while drawing growing concern from the U.S. and other Saudi Arabia allies.
The religious stakes: Why Mecca is a ‘red line’
The past month’s escalation is only the latest development amid the wider civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemen government, which has been ongoing since 2014. But a confirmed attack on Mecca would undoubtedly be a turning point.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, whose country signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey last month, called on all parties to exercise restraint. He warned that the conflict was on the “brink of further escalation” and that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only sustainable path to peace.”
At the same time, he condemned the alleged attack.
“There are no words sufficient to express the depth of pain and sorrow we feel toward this unforgivable and shameful deed,” he said Wednesday.
Fawaz Gerges, a professor in international relations at the London School of Economics, questions what the Houthis would have to gain from such an attack. Over 1.7 million Muslims this year performed Hajj, their pilgrimage to Mecca, according to the Saudi government.
“For the Houthis, as a religiously dominant organization, this would be catastrophic for them—to target Mecca,” he tells TIME. “It’s a lose-lose for them.”
Gerges does, however, offer another explanation: “The Houthis are using drones and homemade missiles, so there is a real possibility that the Houthi drone basically misfired.”
In light of Riyadh’s allegation, Gerges assesses that “[Saudi Arabia] is trying to say that the Houthis are not just waging a political and geo-economic war against them, they are trying to target the most sacred religious site in Islam, and that resonates deeply.”
“Both sides are now engaged not only in military hostilities, but also for the hearts and minds of Arabs and Muslims,” he adds.
Houthi advances deepen the Red Sea oil crisis
The Houthis claimed that Saudi aircraft had carried out more than 450 airstrikes this week. The group also claimed, without providing evidence, that it had shot down a Saudi-led coalition F-15 over Yemen.
Houthi strikes, meanwhile, have been largely concentrated along the Yemeni border in the south. They have also made advances in the Red Sea, seizing key sites like Perim Island and the port of Mokha. The captures strengthen their control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—a pivotal shipping lane that could affect global trade and oil prices at a time when they are already under strain.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit lane, remains largely restricted amid continued strikes between the U.S. and Iran. Most recently, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile on Monday.
Amid these regional developments, the price of Brent crude, the global standard for oil, climbed above $100 per barrel earlier this week. The price fell about 3% on Wednesday but remained above $105 a barrel. Experts warn that more strikes between the Saudis and Houthis will only drive up prices further.
“Pressure on global energy is already there, and I think it's just going to get worse,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa program, tells TIME.
Continued fighting this week “is going to start making the West bleed more efficiently over the next few weeks,” he says. “With winter, there will be a lot of need for energy and for heating.”
Pressure grows in Congress to end the Iran war
Amid precarious energy developments in the Middle East, sentiments about ending the Iran conflict seem to be shifting in the U.S. House of Representatives.
In what was its third vote on the matter this summer, three Republican Representatives changed their votes to align with Democrats in favor of a War Powers Resolution to end U.S. military action against Tehran. With a total of seven Republicans voting in favor, the resolution was approved with 220 votes, beating 204 against.
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn of Iowa, and Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina switched their votes in this latest round of considerations. Nunn said that Iran “must be held accountable” but that “with the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization.”
Nunn added: “I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran, and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.”
It is likely the last time the House will bring the matter to a vote ahead of midterm elections this November. But the vote is largely a symbolic gesture, as Trump would likely veto the resolution once it reached his desk.
As pressure builds in Washington to end the war with Iran, the Houthi escalation in Yemen is creating a new regional flashpoint for the U.S.
U.S. warns government personnel away from the Yemeni border
In response to growing security risks, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh prohibited American officials in Saudi Arabia from traveling near the Yemeni border as of Wednesday.
U.S. government employees are not permitted to travel within 20 miles of the border with Yemen, and they require special authorization from the embassy to travel to the regions of Jizan, Asir, and Najran in southern Saudi Arabia.
The embassy also published a travel advisory Tuesday, urging Americans to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia, citing armed conflict, Iranian missile and drone attacks, and renewed threats from the Houthis. Tehran has targeted multiple Gulf states housing U.S. military bases through the conflict, and has threatened U.S. energy assets in the region.
“Armed groups in Yemen have attacked Saudi border towns and other sites in Saudi Arabia with armed drones, missiles, and rockets. People near the border with Yemen are at increased risk. Do not travel to this area for any reason,” the embassy said in its advisory.
TIME has reached out to the White House and State Department regarding the recent developments.
Asked Monday if the Trump Administration was concerned about the recent Houthi advance and capture of Perim Island, Vice President J.D. Vance told reporters: “Concerned, certainly.”
“We’ve been in constant contact with the Emiratis, the Saudis, and others affected in the region. It’s something that the United States Administration is very much on top of,” he continued.
The Vice President added that there has also been direct communication with the Houthis. “We’re going to keep on monitoring it and making sure that America’s best interests are represented,” he said.
President Donald Trump claimed over the weekend that he had spoken with the Iran-backed militia. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with, and we’ll get that straightened out,” he told reporters during a visit to Ireland.
Following a threat from the Houthis to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in July, the U.S. President said, “If something like that happens, we take care of it.”
On Monday, a Houthi spokesperson said that the Strait “is free for navigation for all countries except for Saudi Arabia.”
Could the conflict widen?
Tuesday’s alleged drone attack toward Mecca has prompted international concern over regional escalation.
In light of the joint defense agreement signed between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, Al-Muslimi says that Ankara and Islamabad have greater political latitude to support Riyadh following the contested incident.
“Defending Mecca is going to create legitimacy domestically in their countries if they engage with the Saudis in a war against the Houthis,” says Al-Muslimi.
But Gerges suggests that support from Turkey and Pakistan would be largely ineffective, and therefore unlikely.
“The problem is how could Pakistan and Turkey really provide support since the armies are not integrated,” he says. “The key challenge facing Saudi Arabia is ground forces.”
Gerges notes that Riyadh’s aerial capabilities alone are not enough to inflict necessary damage on the Houthis.
Therefore, diplomacy could be the most viable option.
Gerges says that “the Houthis have proved to be very resilient, very dynamic, very resourceful, very nimble,” throughout the conflict, maintaining significant control in Yemen.
“Taking on the Houthis again in an all-out war, I doubt very much whether there is a viable military option,” he says.

Large drone lands on tank trail in Korean demonstration
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:58:29 BST
02:58:29 KST

A Mojave short take-off and landing aircraft has landed on a rough manoeuvre trail used by South Korean tanks and artillery vehicles during a live-fire range demonstration, taking off again afterwards to continue its mission, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems stated.
The company describes it as the first time a medium altitude, long endurance uncrewed aircraft has conducted flight operations from a simulated battlefield, and carried out the demonstration with Hanwha Aerospace at the Defense Drone Technology Exhibition north of Seoul.
Linden Blue, chief executive of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said: “This demonstration showcased Mojave’s ability to perform tactical missions that are representative of real battlefield requirements and challenges. Whether the user needs contested and austere battlefield operations, ISR, weapons delivery, Air-Launched Effects deployment, troop resupply, counter-UAS, or missions requiring short and unimproved roads for takeoff, our aircraft answer the bell.”
Buhwan Lee, chief executive nominee of Hanwha Aerospace, said: “This demonstration marks an important milestone in delivering tangible results through the partnership between Hanwha and GA-ASI. Going forward, we will work closely with the ROK defense industry to develop unmanned systems designed for future operating environments and expand our presence in global markets.”
The aircraft was configured with dual weapon rails and inert payloads, flying a concept of operations intended to show how short take-off capability improves operational flexibility, survivability and responsiveness. Under the control of pilots at ground control stations, it took off from the conventional runway at the Republic of Korea Army’s 513th Aviation Battalion, flew to the Seungjin Training Field in Pocheon-si to join air operations, landed on the manoeuvre trail, took off again and returned to the battalion.
According to the company, soldiers in an actual combat situation could have refuelled and rearmed the aircraft during its time on the ground at the range, and it states that no other aircraft with Mojave’s endurance, range or payload has that ability.
General Atomics announced in 2025 that it was partnering with Hanwha to co-develop and co-produce short take-off aircraft for a worldwide customer base, including the South Korean Ministry of National Defense, the United States Department of War and other customers. Critical design review for a production Mojave is expected in November, with first flight in 2027.
The demonstrator is due to travel to Changwon for Hanwha’s industry day on 21 September, an event the company says will include a range of South Korean suppliers, many of them contributing to production of the aircraft.
Mojave is a development of the Gray Eagle airframe fitted with an enlarged wing, high-lift devices and a more powerful engine, giving it the ability to operate from strips far shorter than a conventional runway. The aircraft is known in Britain for a trial in November 2023 when it operated from HMS Prince of Wales off the American east coast, the first time an uncrewed aircraft of that size and weight had flown from a Royal Navy carrier.
The appeal of a short field capability rests on where the aircraft can be based. A drone that needs a prepared runway depends on a small number of airfields an opponent can locate and strike, while one that can work from a road or a track can be dispersed, moved and hidden in ways that complicate targeting considerably.
South Korea has been expanding its uncrewed capability, and Hanwha Aerospace has grown into one of the largest defence exporters in Asia, with recent orders from Poland among other customers.

Fossil fuel advertising contracts at all-time high in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
17:58:14 UTC
02:58:14 KST

“It’s that time of the year again,” the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company told Emiratis in a Ramadan advertising campaign. “Where tanks are always full – for night after night of majlis hopping.”
When you think about fossil fuels, you might think of offshore oil platforms flaring gas in rough seas, the US/Iran war or the greenhouse effect heating up the world’s climate. A new report argues, however, that what Big Oil wants you to think about is family, friends and faith instead.
The advertising industry campaign group Clean Creatives went through the records and found that in 2026, the year climate breakdown went so haywire gardeners were growing watermelons in Bristol, there were 1,321 active contracts between the fossil fuel industry and advertising agencies, the most ever recorded.
As the war in Iran intensified global shortages of oil and gas, leading to spiking prices and profits for the oil companies, the fossil fuel industry appears to have invested part of its windfall on its image. Clean Creatives found that 386 fossil fuel companies across 73 countries had engaged 802 advertising and PR agencies to shape their public image and messaging.
Strikingly, business links between the two industries held strong, despite agencies’ claims of environmental responsibility, said the lead researcher, Nayantara Dutta.
“By reading through all of their climate disclosures, what I find most telling this year is this is the first year in our research where advertising agencies are across the board acknowledging climate risk in their annual reports,” she said.
Omnicom was the advertising company that held the most contracts with the fossil fuel industry, with 118 contracts, followed by WPP, with 88. In third place was Publicis, whose 34 fossil fuel industry contracts were no barrier to its being named as one of Time magazine’s most sustainable companies of 2026.
Dutta led a team of four who spent nine months compiling the survey. They painstakingly documented each contract by piecing together information from lobbying databases, creative portfolios and even LinkedIn posts. They quantified the extent of the trade and assessed its storytelling.
Advertising executives were portraying their fossil fuel industry clients as indispensable to our ways of life and economic security, Dutta said.
“The cultural themes we have always seen have continued,” she said. “But there is a global trend of increased economic insecurity and fear-mongering around energy supply and demand, around jobs and around fossil fuels as being essential.”
“Energy security requires all of our energy,” said Equinor, the Norwegian oil company that wants to develop the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea, in a LinkedIn campaign by McCann Relationship Management, an Omnicom agency.
Chevron launched a campaign celebrating the US’s 250th anniversary, announcing it was “the energy that keeps America moving”. “Since 1879, our people have been more than a source of energy. They’ve been a source of progress,” the company claimed in a Facebook ad.
“In the US, UK, and Europe, we’re seeing a lot of nationalism,” Dutta said. “Really connecting the economic prosperity of a country with the fossil fuel industry and its expansion.”
In the global south, on the other hand, fossil fuel firms often tie themselves to family life and cultural events. Pointing to Adnoc’s “unsettling” Ramadan advert, she said: “Basically they position themselves not only as a company that is helping the economy and providing jobs, but as a company who cares about the culture and wellbeing of their people.
“So rather than addressing the political news of what’s happening in the world, they like to focus on the same themes of family and community to show themselves as integral to building that.”
A spokesperson for the Advertising Association told the Guardian: “Fossil fuel advertising represents a very small proportion of overall UK advertising spend. Where such campaigns do run in the UK, they are subject to some of the world’s strictest regulation under the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) and CAP Codes. The rules are clear: ads must not mislead consumers, and companies presenting environmental claims must demonstrate total transparency regarding the full scope of their activity, including distinguishing between renewable and fossil fuel operations.
“The ASA actively monitors and enforces compliance in this space, routinely taking action against claims that fall short. Alongside strict regulatory standards, programs such as Ad Net Zero continue to equip UK agencies and advertisers with the tools to reduce operational emissions, eliminate greenwashing and support the broader transition to a low-carbon economy.”

Russia denounces US naval blockade of Iran as ‘completely unacceptable and illegal’
MOSCOW — Russia has reaffirmed its unwavering strategic partnership with Iran, unequivocally condemning the US naval blockade and the military aggression against the Islamic Republic.
Addressing a press briefing in Moscow, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova delivered a comprehensive critique of Western maritime unilateralism in response to a question regarding Moscow’s stance on Iran’s sovereign right to control the strategic Strait of Hormuz and resist the ongoing American naval blockade.
The background to Zakharova’s remarks is rooted in the dramatic escalation that began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched an unprovoked military campaign against Iran. Following the initial aggression, Washington sought to impose an illegitimate naval blockade in and around the Strait of Hormuz, attempting to sever Iran’s maritime commerce and international logistics.
Zakharova stressed that Moscow’s relationship with Tehran rests on a solid foundation of long-negotiated bilateral agreements, as well as a deep historical tradition tested through times of crisis.
“In the framework of relations with Iran… these relations are shaped based on relevant agreements and arrangements that define our bilateral framework,” Zakharova stated. She acknowledged that while the ratification and implementation process within Iran had taken considerable time, all formal steps were ultimately completed, bringing the foundational agreements into full effect.
Beyond formal treaties, Zakharova emphasized the historical depth of bilateral ties. “We have a long history in our relations with Iran, a history that is far richer, broader, and goes significantly beyond mere existing agreements. Naturally, we also proceed based on the history of our relations, which have been tested across various events and challenges.”
Turning to the crisis in the Persian Gulf, Zakharova reiterated Moscow’s fundamental opposition to the Western coalition’s actions, noting that President Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov have repeatedly articulated this position.
“Regarding our stance on the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, I believe Russia’s position has been clearly stated,” she stressed. “We have explicitly declared, not just once, and not merely at one level, that we are facing direct, unprovoked aggression by the United States and Israel against Iran and its people.”
Zakharova emphasized that Moscow’s assessment is not opportunistic or emotional, but rooted in an objective analysis of facts. “This is not a temporary stance dependent on daily circumstances, nor an emotional view based on personal opinions. It incorporates the complete set of existing facts and factors.”
Widening her critique, the Russian official framed the US blockade against Iran as part of a broader, systemic effort by Western powers to dismantle the international law of the sea in order to impose their own dictated rules upon the global maritime transit.
“The oceans, instead of being governed by legal frameworks and international regulations, is being turned into an arena of catastrophe, piracy, and absolute lawlessness,” Zakharova warned. “This is not limited to the Strait of Hormuz. It reflects the approach of a narrow group of countries, what we call the ‘global minority,’ toward maritime law, or rather, the destruction of maritime law.”
Zakharova accused Western powers of violating the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) in a bid to re-divide the oceans according to their own strategic interests. 
 
 While international waters were previously governed by equal rights and responsibilities under international law, she noted that Western nations now view themselves as “exceptional” and seek to replace established law with a self-serving “rules-based global order.”
“They believe that they themselves should dictate these ‘rules,’ and that only they should determine who must execute them and who should not,” Zakharova added. “This is completely unacceptable and extremely dangerous.”
Addressing the US naval blockade of Iran specifically, Zakharova declared the siege legally invalid and humanely indefensible.
“From a legal perspective, the blockade is fundamentally unacceptable. From the standpoint of humanitarian norms and principles, such an action is equally unacceptable,” she affirmed. “Blockades, illegal sanctions, and any measures designed to disrupt the normal trade, communication, and logistical activities of a sovereign state by another state or group of states are unacceptable and completely illegal.”
Zakharova underscored that only the United Nations Security Council possesses the legal authority to restrict the activities of sovereign nations, noting that no such mandate exists for the US actions in the Persian Gulf.
“The only legal mechanism to restrict the activities of states is UN Security Council sanctions,” Zakharova pointed out. “Has the Security Council authorized or sanctioned what is taking place in the Strait of Hormuz? No. And fundamentally, it could not sanction such actions, as they constitute a blatant and absolute violation of international law.”

“At a time when the world faces three existential threats – runaway artificial intelligence, climate crisis, and the intolerable deepening of inequalities – international cooperation is more necessary than ever.”
