 on Gaza. The late martyr Abu Ubaida, who served as the Palestinian military spokesman, referred to them as “brothers in sincerity.” 
All Palestinian forces have widely praised the military operations carried out by Yemen’s Ansarallah in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as their ballistic missile strikes against various Israeli sites.
They regarded Yemen’s courageous actions as placing strategic pressure on the regime and its allies, while providing genuine support and sacrifice to the Palestinians in Gaza. The Yemeni people, their government, leaders, and infrastructure were subjected to fierce aggression by the U.S. and the Israeli regime.
The assault was aimed at forcing Ansarallah to abandon its geopolitical and military support for Palestine. The Palestinians expressed their solidarity with the Yemeni people, whose sacrifices had become intertwined with those of the Palestinians.
Palestinian resistance forces regard Yemen and Ansarallah as genuine partners in confronting the region’s real enemy: The Zionist regime.

Palestinians and the sense of abandonment

Whoever expects otherwise fails to understand the depth of the suffering inflicted on the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip by every movement, ruler, and institution that abandoned them at the moment when they needed support most.
Moreover, after the genocidal war, Palestinians are no longer capable of indulging anyone with empty courtesies. They have come to understand that maintaining their bonds with the people of sincerity in Yemen, Lebanon, Iran, and Iraq, and with sincere people, figures, and movements around the world, is better for them than placing their hopes in people of slogans.
Those who are lions on the battlefields of sectarian and internal conflicts but ducks when confronting the Israeli regime.

The Palestinian people look with pride and honor upon everyone who confronts the enemies of the Arab/Islamic world and humanity. A regime that has openly declared its objective is to seize Arab lands from the Nile to the Euphrates.

Their role becomes visible only in internal conflicts. They disappear when the Israeli regime is fought. And when they do appear, it is to cast doubt, stab, level accusations, and undermine the anti-Israeli resistance and its supporters, leaving this heroic resistance only more abandoned.

The Israeli security establishment believes that developments in the Red Sea could represent a strategic shift whose repercussions extend beyond the region, particularly amid the U.S. crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the illegal war against Iran.

Poll shows Americans are increasingly alarmed by AI’s ecological footprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:45:04 UTC
01:45:04 KST

Poll shows Americans are increasingly alarmed by AI’s ecological footprint
Over half of Americans fear AI-driven data centers will hike electricity costs and strain water supplies in local areas, according to new poll.
A new survey of adults in the United States finds that more than half worry about artificial intelligence’s environmental impact, up 12 percentage points from last year.
The poll, a joint effort by The Associated Press, the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute, indicated that Americans dread AI’s carbon footprint far more than high-emission giants like meat production and aviation.
Released on Wednesday, data from interviews with 3,424 US adults in August show that 53 per cent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence’s environmental impacts. The increased wariness marks an upward trend from the 41 percent recorded last year.
While Democrats are fuelling much of the rise in eco-awareness, with two-thirds expressing great concern compared to half of independents and 4 in 10 Republicans, greater public anxiety is emerging over how local data centres powering AI and cloud computing could affect nearby communities. According to the survey, most Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centres on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
“We’re undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don’t think there’ll be any putting the milk back in the bottle,” said Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute that collaborated on the survey. “Change is scary, and I think some of that is being reflected here.”
Despite bipartisan pushback, thousands of data centres already span the US, with extensive construction underway to meet escalating demand. The scope includes decades-old conventional facilities alongside massive and newly built hyperscale centres engineered for resource-intensive AI processing. While Virginia and Texas lead the nation in operating facilities, California, Ohio and New York follow behind closely as top digital infrastructure hubs.
United States President Donald Trump has urged communities across the country to embrace the tech facilities, promising that they will bring jobs.
“There’s a lot of water usage by AI data centres that’s taking away from other things like agriculture and farmers and places that really need it, and people who really need it,” Gedeon Kebede, a computer science student and Democrat from Cincinnati, Ohio, told the AP.
While data centres aren’t the US’s largest water gobblers, they still retain water to cool AI chips and computers and can be “nationally modest but potentially locally decisive”, according to Fengqi You, an energy systems professor with Cornell University.
“I think that decisions are being made for the company, not for the community that they’re being built in,” Nancy Antunes, a 60-year-old retired Democrat from Waltham, Massachusetts, told the AP.

Ministry of Defence confirms the death of Major Paul Wilks

Ministry of Defence confirms the death of Major Paul Wilks
It is with great sadness that the Ministry of Defence must confirm the death of Major Paul Wilks, who died in Ukraine on 12 September 2026.
Major Paul Wilks died in a tragic road traffic incident, away from the front lines. He was 40 years old.
Major Wilks was born on 13 November 1985. He commissioned from Sandhurst on 14 April 2012 joining the Intelligence Corps where he remained throughout his career, successfully promoting to the rank of Major. Major Wilks had deployed on multiple operational tours including to Afghanistan. He was recognised for this service with two Operational Service Medals. He was also recently awarded the Long Service and Good Conduct Medal on 7 May 2026.
Major Wilks was an exceptionally bright and professional officer who embodied the best of the UK military. He was a gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him. He was a formidable officer, colleague and friend to all those who knew him.
Above all, Major Wilks was a proud family man and was devoted to his wife and two sons.
His Commanding Officer said:
  It is with profound sadness that we honour the memory of Major Paul Wilks.
Even in high-pressure environments, Paul maintained a sharp sense of humour and a genuine warmth that connected him to everyone in this unit. He was a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with.
He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction. It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice.
Major Wilks represented the finest traditions of UK Defence. It was a privilege to serve alongside him. We will miss him.
His Former Commanding Officer said:
  We are devastated by the loss of Major Paul Wilks.
Paul brought intellect, professionalism and quiet determination to everything he did. He had so much more to give to the Unit, to those under his Command, and to the profession he cared for so deeply.
Yet what marked Paul out most was not just his professional ability, but his humanity. He had that rare and enviable quality of seeing the best in people. He was a consummate professional and a deeply caring Officer, someone who treated mistakes not as failures, but as opportunities to learn and grow. Those he led always came first, whatever the circumstances.
Paul was truly one of the finest leaders and intelligence officers I have had the privilege to work with. A rising star within intelligence, his intellect, compassion, and professionalism were matched by his humility and care for others. He was the best of us.
Chief of Defence Intelligence and Colonel Commandant Intelligence Corps Lieutenant General Matthew Jones said:
  On behalf of the whole Intelligence Corps, we are heartbroken to learn of Major Paul Wilks’ death. Paul was an exceptional leader who was undoubtedly one of the most talented intelligence officers of his generation.
Paul was committed to operational excellence in everything he did. With a selfless and compassionate approach, his primary concern was always his team. He was supremely motivated by developing those around him. Paul possessed a razor-sharp intellect and a steely determination to succeed.
Paul was always calm under pressure, good-humoured even in the most arduous of conditions, shrewd, and decisive. He leaves behind a legacy that will endure within the Intelligence Corps and beyond. The hugely positive example he set will continue to inspire us in the years ahead.
Defence Secretary Rt Hon Wes Streeting MP said:
  Major Wilks served this country with pride and dedication. His loss will be deeply felt by those around him.
The tributes paid by those who worked with Paul illustrate his exceptional talent and ability, underscored by genuine warmth, compassion and a desire to support others.

Risk of 'airport malaria'  in Switzerland deemed very low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:45:00 UTC
01:45:00 KST

Risk of ‘airport malaria’ in Switzerland deemed very low
Despite new cases of malaria in the area around Frankfurt Airport, the Swiss authorities do not see any major risk for Switzerland.
The risk of such infections at Swiss airports is “very low”, the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) told the news agency Keystone-SDA. The recent cases in Frankfurt am Main have not altered the risk assessment for Switzerland, the FOPH added.
Malaria is a notifiable disease in Switzerland. Around 300 cases of malaria are reported in Switzerland each year. Almost without exception, these infections are contracted abroad. However, the FOPH added that there have also been documented cases of so-called “airport malaria” in Switzerland in the past. This occurs when mosquitoes infected with malaria parasites are brought in on aeroplanes from malaria-endemic areas. If they subsequently bite people in the vicinity, they can transmit the disease.
A major outbreak occurred in Geneva in the summer of 1989: five people contracted malaria, even though they had not been to a malaria-endemic area. All lived less than two kilometres from Geneva-Cointrin Airport, as shown by case studies published in 1990.
Residents in Frankfurt fall ill
In Frankfurt am Main, six airport staff members contracted malaria in the summer, two of whom died. On Tuesday evening, it emerged that local residents had also been affected for the first time. The authorities have also classified these two cases as “airport malaria”. Those affected, from the Schwanheim district five kilometres from the airport, had not travelled abroad and did not work at the airport.
The Frankfurt Public Health Authority believes that infected Anopheles mosquitoes from a malaria-endemic area were brought in by aeroplane and subsequently made their way as far as Schwanheim. According to the authorities, the mosquitoes are capable of flying five to ten kilometres. Whether there is a link to the earlier cases is still under investigation.

2027 budget draft envisages UAH 26.3 billion for newly created Minregion
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:43:42 EEST
01:43:42 KST

Ukraine's 2027 state budget draft envisages funding for the Ministry of Communities, Territories and Internally Displaced Persons (Minregion), created in August, at UAH 26.3 billion.
According to draft law No. 16000 on the 2027 state budget, registered September 15, the ministry's public investment projects are allocated UAH 868.7 million, while management and administration is allocated UAH 628 million.
More than UAH 1 billion is planned for social housing construction in 2027, and UAH 151.9 million for the development and implementation of a unified housing information and analytics system.
The draft envisages UAH 11.5 billion in compensation for destroyed housing, UAH 5.4 billion for compensation for destroyed housing under the HOME program, and UAH 3.4 billion for compensation for certain categories of property under the eRecovery program. In addition, UAH 249.6 million is proposed for the "Housing Repair for the Restoration of People's Rights and Opportunities (HOPE)" project.
Under the draft, the charter capital of the State Fund for Youth Housing Construction Support (Derzhmolodzhytlo) is to be increased by UAH 16 million in 2027, with UAH 6.2 million in financial support also to be provided. Meanwhile, UAH 2 million is planned for reducing mortgage costs to provide housing for citizens in need of improved living conditions.
The 2027 budget draft allocates UAH 39.3 million for creating reintegration-related systems and databases, UAH 51.8 million for protecting the rights and freedoms of Ukrainians in the temporarily occupied territories (TOT), and UAH 1.76 billion for reintegration measures for the population of the TOT and social and legal protection for persons deprived of personal freedom as a result of armed aggression against Ukraine.
The draft allocates UAH 680.7 million for the operation of the Energy Efficiency Fund and UAH 117.4 million for energy efficiency projects in public buildings.
The budget draft plans UAH 82.2 million for the development and operation of the national urban planning cadastre. Spending on the operation of the State Inspectorate for Architecture and Urban Planning of Ukraine (DIAM) is planned at UAH 216.4 million for 2027.
In addition, the draft allocates UAH 19.3 billion in subventions to local budgets, down 17.7% from the 2026 budget. Meanwhile, spending on the State Fund for Regional Development remains at last year's level of UAH 2 billion.

CENTCOM Says Hormuz 'Remains Open' As Houthi-Saudi Fighting Threatens Another Key Waterway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

The US military says traffic in the Strait of Hormuz continues to gain momentum amid concerns that escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen threatens another vital artery for global oil supplies in the region.
CENTCOM said in a statement to RFE/RL on September 16 that the strait "remains open for transit." A key artery for global energy supplies, the strategic waterway has been a focal point in the war between the United States and Iran.
"Traffic is flowing and momentum is building despite Iranian attempts to intimidate and harm innocent civilian crews," the statement said.
"In recent months, thousands of commercial ships and nearly one billion barrels of oil have transited through the strait. Iran clearly does not control it. The international waterway remains open for transit," it added.
Commercial traffic through Hormuz has plunged since the Iran war began in February.
Tehran has sought to assert control over navigation through the strait and has attacked commercial vessels, while the United States is enforcing a naval blockade aimed at preventing ships from serving Iranian ports and has also attacked Iran-linked vessels.
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz handled about one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making it one of the world's most important energy chokepoints. Around 125 large commercial vessels a day typically passed through the waterway before the conflict.
Meanwhile, Houthi rebels in Yemen have captured ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea in recent days, threatening the flow of oil through another main shipping artery in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabian warplanes pounded Yemen on September 16 while Houthi fighters launched drones and missiles at Saudi cities as the clashes continue to escalate.
The Houthis have fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week.
An attack attributed to the Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq last week knocked out Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the main route it has used to divert oil exports with the Strait of Hormuz blocked.

During the first phase of operation "Vivaldi," units of the Third Army Corps carried out 36,000 strike missions, including against field fuel depots in Luhansk region, forcing the enemy to disperse its depots into forests and onto Russian territory, which, in turn, slowed down supplies to the front lines, the press service of the Third Army Corps said.
"Systematic strikes on field fuel depots in the Luhansk region were a key factor in the success of operation "Vivaldi." According to Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, the enemy was forced to reroute the supply of fuel and lubricants to Voronezh region, beyond Ukraine's state border," the press service's statement reads, which was received by Interfax-Ukraine agency on Wednesday.
It is noted that thanks to the successful actions of unmanned aerial vehicle units and precision strikes, the enemy was forced to shut down the pipeline through which it had been supplying fuel from Russia to the occupied Luhansk region, after which, with the pipeline out of commission, fuel tankers were forced to travel to Voronezh region. The distance required to evacuate this division's equipment increased by approximately 250 kilometers. The corps achieved this result through regular strikes on enemy field fuel and ammunition depots, communications nodes, command posts, and vehicles carrying fuel and provisions.
It is reported that during Vivaldi operation, the Third Army Corps destroyed enemy logistics in two stages: In the first stage, strike drones isolated a strip up to 50 kilometers from the front line; in the second stage, the zone was expanded to 120 kilometers from the front line. At the same time, the corps' UAVs struck priority targets in key logistical settlements in the occupied territories.
During the first phase of the operation, the Third Corps' drone units carried out 36,000 strike missions.
The corps notes that the reduction in fuel supplies directly to frontline units limits the use of enemy UAVs and electronic warfare systems, which, in turn, increases the effectiveness of high-precision weapons and UAVs within the corps' area of responsibility.

According to the Third Army Corps, Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and the outskirts of Korovy Yar were cleared of enemy infiltration, and Seredne was liberated. Amid a media blackout, the units eliminated pockets of enemy infiltration and cleared 75 square kilometers. Another 10 square kilometers were de-occupied.
Enemy losses at this stage of the operation amounted to approximately 1,500 soldiers, over 12,000 drones, and hundreds of armored vehicles, artillery systems, and motor vehicles. "A devastating blow has been dealt to the combat capability of the Russian Federation's 20th and 25th Armies," the corps said.
At the same time, drone units cut off the enemy's logistics routes. As a result of the corps' strikes, Russian troops were forced to relocate their fuel and lubricant supplies outside Ukraine – to Voronezh region: a pipeline was dismantled and supply depots were moved.
The operation involved the 60th Mechanized Brigade, the 125th Airborne Brigade, the Tank Group of the Third Separate Tank Brigade, the Third Operational-Regimental Brigade and the 25th Operational-Tactical Brigade, as well as attached units – the 66th Mechanized Brigade, the 85th Tank Group of the Eighth Special Operations Regiment, the Artan special unit of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defense, and the 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment "Dozor."
"There is currently a lot of information in open sources suggesting that the ultimate goal of our offensive operations is to reach the banks of the Chorny Zherebets River. But our operation is called "Vivaldi." And as we know, Vivaldi has four seasons. And this is only the first of them. So stay tuned for our official announcements and don't rush to spoil the surprise. 'We will rebuild, again and again': Lebanese chef Husen Fayad tells TNA after Israel destroys guesthouse project
Lebanese chef Husen Fayad remains determined to rebuild in southern Lebanon after an Israeli strike destroyed his new guesthouse project, months after his family-owned hotel and restaurant were also reduced to rubble.
The renowned chef had spent two years building his 'Bouyout Al Moulouk' real-estate project before it was destroyed in an Israeli strike.
"I still see a future for our projects in our south. We will rebuild, again and again," Fayad told The New Arab.
Fayad shared images on his Instagram account, where he has over 4.4 million followers, showing aerial views of the Bouyout Al Moulouk project before and after it was destroyed, with a caption reading: "The war is taking everything."
"I had been building a new project — six villas with a large kitchen — and I wasn’t really worried about it. My dream was to open this project this summer and finally see all the hard work of these past years become a reality," he wrote.
"I didn’t even get the chance to welcome a single guest or visitor. My restaurant is gone, and today my new project is gone too," Fayad wrote on Instagram, where his intricate culinary work had gained traction worldwide.
The project was being built in the southern area of Wadi al-Hujeir, which has been designated a nature reserve since 2010. Like much of Lebanon’s south, the area has been under continued Israeli attack during the nearly three-year-long war on Lebanon.
Israel has razed dozens of towns and villages in the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon. The so-called "Yellow Line," a security zone stretching along the entire border, has seen localities turned to rubble and agricultural land damaged by white phosphorus, preventing hundreds of thousands of residents from returning home.
"I remember every stone as it was being built, every effort we put into making this beautiful place that I never even got the chance to open. Today, it has all been reduced to rubble," Fayad said.
"My heart is hurting, but everything is in God’s hands. No good deed goes to waste," Fayad wrote on another Instagram Story.
Fayad said he wanted Bouyout Al Moulouk, Arabic for 'homes of kings', to showcase Lebanon’s beauty, as he decried the ongoing suffering caused by Israel’s offensive.
"I took photos from the very beginning, watching it being built. I said [to myself], these photos will remain as beautiful memories... Two years of hard work went into building it, and then came the time to open it."
Fayad said the project was intended to show visitors a different side of southern Lebanon.
"My dream was for people to see the beauty of Lebanon and the south. I wish people could see the injustice and pain that is happening there, especially those who live abroad, who know and feel the value of the land," he wrote, adding: "My beloved south, what is happening to you?"
Despite his grief, Fayad told The New Arab he remained optimistic.
"[Despite] going through a lot with this project and putting so much into it - it's not only about financial losses, but also the emotional and moral side of it too, but I still believe in creating projects in our south," he added.
Sympathies poured in on social media, with followers sending messages of love and support.
"What a tragedy. All my support to this valiant young man! I hope he pulls through," one X user wrote.

Malaysia offers to invite Myanmar leader in Rohingya repatriation push
Malaysia has invited Myanmar’s military ruler for a visit to the country in a bid to expedite the repatriation of Rohingya refugees.
Malaysia is offering to invite Myanmar’s military ruler for an official visit to the country in a bid to expedite the repatriation of Rohingya refugees.
Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim made the offer on Wednesday, which, if accepted, would mark another step out of isolation for Myanmar’s military-backed President Min Aung Hlaing.
Min Aung Hlaing, a retired general who seized power in a 2021 coup, has been on a quest for international legitimacy since becoming president in April.
“I invited him to say we can be friends, we can trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them [Rohingya refugees] back,” Malaysia’s president said on a podcast.
Malaysia has been one of the most vocal critics of Myanmar’s former military government and had repeatedly expressed frustration at its refusal to cease hostilities.
“To me, that’s better diplomacy than just shouting angrily at Myanmar. Who’s going to take them? Where do we send them? They don’t even have Myanmar citizenship,” he said, adding that a different approach was needed to resolve the issue.
“We, following ASEAN, don’t want direct relations with Myanmar. So who are we supposed to negotiate with?”
If Myanmar accepts the conditional offer, it would mark Min Aung Hlaing’s fifth visit to an ASEAN member state, after his recent visits to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. He has also visited China, India and Russia.
ASEAN has refused to recognise Myanmar’s election. Since 2021, the body has barred Myanmar’s leaders from its summits.
A civil war in Myanmar has killed an estimated 100,000 people, with the military widely accused of atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya population, which the military has denied.
Malaysia has long been a haven for Rohingya fleeing persecution at home, even though it is not a signatory to the 1951 United Nations Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.
Nevertheless, it hosts more than 126,000 Rohingya from Myanmar.
Prime Minister Anwar announced in July that Myanmar’s military-backed government had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the persecuted Rohingya minority amid rising tensions with local communities in Malaysia.
Malaysia has finalised the first phase of a voluntary repatriation programme that will see at least 1,500 eligible Myanmar refugees return home on September 29, the government said.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) made the comments shortly after the US Department of State on Tuesday told a virtual news conference that the US is opposed to China’s use of diplomatic and military pressure to isolate Taiwan.
Writing in a news release, Lin said Taiwan looks forward to enhancing its cooperation with the US and other partners in Palau as part of a greater drive to help the development of the Pacific region.
Photo: AFP
Taipei is committed to showing its resolve in assisting its friends in the region to bolster their resilience, he said.
US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific Islands Matt Murray told the news conference that the US is creating secure and reliable undersea Internet cables in collaboration with like-minded partners in the Pacific.
The US is working closely with Taiwan, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and the private sector to implement this initiative, he said.
Asked about Washington’s views on China’s role in the region, Murray said that “the US certainly shares concerns with our Pacific Island partners related to China’s malign activities in the Pacific.”
These activities include illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, elite capture and corruption, economic coercion, environmental degradation, and provocations such as the launch of ballistic missiles by Chinese submarines, he said.
“We also obviously are concerned about China’s behavior towards Taiwan when it comes to the Pacific Islands Forum specifically, and we continue to oppose China’s efforts to pressure countries to sever or downgrade ties with Taiwan or Taiwan’s participation in the Pacific Islands Forum,” Murray said.
Asked about Washington’s stance on Taiwan’s place in the forum, Murray said that the US strongly supports the nation’s participation in the organization, as Taiwan has been a development partner of the group since 1992.
“We see Taiwan as a reliable, like-minded and democratic partner that contributes significantly to prosperity and economic development across the Pacific,” he said, adding that “we know that the Taiwan foreign minister had an active schedule while he was on the ground in Palau.”

Groups call for uniform penalties for wage violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

Labor groups yesterday called on the government to adopt uniform penalties for employers that contravene minimum wage laws, saying that wide disparities among local authorities weaken the enforcement of the law.
Taiwan Labour Front Secretary-General Yang Shu-wei (楊書瑋) said some local governments still rely on penalty guidelines under the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) rather than the Minimum Wage Act (最低工資法), while others have no standards for minimum wage contraventions.
Yang described the current system as effectively “23 systems in one country,” referring to Taiwan’s 22 local governments and the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
Photo: CNA
Thresholds for imposing the statutory maximum fine of NT$1 million (US$31,360) range from six to 17 violations across jurisdictions, but rise to 50 or more in ministry-administered industrial parks, which Yang called “absurd and shameful.”
He warned that such disparities could undermine the effectiveness of minimum wage legislation and give noncompliant employers an unfair advantage over those that follow the law.
Yang called on the Ministry of Labor to establish a nationwide standard, under which employers that contravene the law five or more times would face a statutory maximum fine of NT$1 million, regardless of company size.
“Five violations are already a lot, which suggests the employer is deliberately breaking the law,” he said.
Labor authorities last year imposed penalties in 153 cases involving wages below the statutory minimum, with fines totaling NT$3.3 million, labor ministry figures showed.
The six special municipalities accounted for 62.1 percent of the cases, while the support services sector accounted for the largest share by industry, at 33.33 percent.
Yang said the fines averaged only slightly more than NT$20,000 per case.
An employer might think: “If I get caught once, I would be fined NT$20,000, but will they come catch me a second time?” Yang said, adding that such low penalties weaken the deterrent effect of the Minimum Wage Act.
The labor ministry said it is already moving toward a uniform approach to penalties for minimum wage contravention.
The ministry said it recently proposed incorporating Minimum Wage Act contraventions into common principles governing fines for Labor Standards Act violations, and that “all local labor authorities have agreed to cooperate.”
Once the amendment is completed, minimum wage contravention cases nationwide “will be handled according to a uniform set of principles,” it said, adding that it would complete the legal procedures as soon as possible.
Meanwhile, Yang said the monthly minimum wage, currently NT$29,500, should rise beyond NT$30,000 next year and move toward NT$32,000 to NT$33,000, citing Taiwan’s strong economic performance and continued price increases.
The Minimum Wage Review Committee is scheduled to meet on Thursday next week to discuss next year’s minimum wage.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) has said the monthly minimum wage is expected to exceed NT$30,000 next year.

Costs of incompetent governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:36 UTC
01:38:36 KST

Taipei has seen successive incidents involving the shirking of responsibility in recent years.
The first involves city police repeatedly failing to crack down on drug trafficking, only to realize that former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je’s (柯文哲) administration had made public detailed data on all municipal vehicles — including the license plate numbers, makes and models of police vehicles — allowing drug dealers to use artificial intelligence (AI) to cross-reference the data and conduct countersurveillance.
The second involves the controversy over Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) eldest son being selected for a Taipei City Government-funded international student exchange program to study in the US. Taipei City Councilor Chin Huei-chu (秦慧珠) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) slammed the Taipei Department of Education for “living in the Qing Dynasty,” saying that the application forms for the program had not been updated in the past 15 years, causing Chiang to take the blame for a conflict-of-interest scandal.
Although these two controversies appear unrelated, they have given lie to the myth of city governance long touted by the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP). The blame is always placed on a rigid bureaucratic system or lower-level civil servants, while the mayor is portrayed as an innocent victim caught in the crossfire.
Consider the case of the “butt-naked” police surveillance vehicles. Ko blindly pursued “openness and transparency” at the time, disregarding opposition from the police and, with the arrogance of an outsider meddling in a professional field, insisting on publishing confidential vehicle registration data online.
Chiang has been in office for about four years, so he can no longer blame the previous administration. The city government, aware that the data had been copied by organized crime groups, refused to replace the license plates of hundreds of vehicles, citing a “lack of budget.” Detectives risk their lives driving these compromised vehicles. Meanwhile, the city government continues to boast about its ability to provide “fresh milk,” yet claims to be too broke to replace a few potentially life-saving license plates.
Next, consider the so-called “Qing Dynasty” Department of Education. KMT city councilors have defended Chiang by blaming the “poisonous legacy” of previous administrations — while the application form for the exchange program had not been updated in 15 years. This slap lands square in the faces of three consecutive KMT and TPP mayors. The Recusal of Public Servants Due to Conflicts of Interest Act (公職人員利益衝突迴避法) was expanded eight years ago, yet those in charge of legal affairs and ethics have feigned ignorance.
Chiang, who touts his background as a “Silicon Valley lawyer,” is approaching four years in office — yet he has not only failed to identify regulatory blind spots within city government departments, but lacked the political sensitivity to recognize the implications of his son applying for a city government-funded program. Even worse, his administration attempted to double down on the decision.
If a mayor is unwilling to allocate funds for the safety of police officers and cannot even ensure that departmental forms are properly managed, choosing instead to hide behind city councilors’ scapegoating to seek sympathy, is that any different from being a mere figurehead?
From the chaos of the Ko administration to the inaction of the Chiang administration, the pan-blue and white camps have demonstrated the same governing philosophy as former president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) during his time as Taipei mayor: When something goes wrong, blame former Taipei deputy mayor Ou Chin-der (歐晉德). When things go well, it is all thanks to Ma.
They enjoy the prestige and budget of the capital city when times are good, but when mistakes are made, the accumulated failures of the past are to blame. The root cause of Taipei’s stagnation is the incompetence of leaders who refuse to take political responsibility.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Convenience store food in Japan inspired by AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:35 UTC
01:38:35 KST

Fears that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity have dominated global headlines, but in Japan the technology is being used for a sweeter purpose — developing never-before-seen convenience store desserts.
For customers tired of the usual egg sandwiches and rice balls, major chains are turning to AI to develop products, including some unexpected flavors.
Lawson, one of the country’s biggest convenience store operators, yesterday said that it would roll out three new food items, including a pickle-flavored lemon tart and a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yoghurt cream.
Photo: Reuters
The products, to be launched this month in Tokyo and neighboring regions, were created using AI around the theme: “What on earth is this? But it’s delicious.”
“To generate ideas unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends, we used AI during brainstorming, without relying on past sales figures or market data,” the company said in a statement.
Meanwhile, rival FamilyMart said that it fed sales data into AI to help develop a new dessert — a French-style canele pastry made with dough containing sweet potato puree and topped with caramel sauce.
The dessert is to hit shelves nationwide next week, a spokeswoman told reporters, adding that the company had wanted to create something new, but likely to sell.
Like Lawson’s products, AI was used primarily for brainstorming, while human specialists were still involved in product development, the company said.
It is not FamilyMart’s first dessert product that was suggested by AI.
In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment — a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream.
It proved a success, so the company decided to properly pursue AI in product development and plans to launch more of the items in the next few months, the spokeswoman said.
The rapidly advancing capabilities of AI have sparked concern in the past few days.
Researchers have warned of the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems that could evade human control.
Leading US AI labs have called for a coordinated slowdown of their cutting-edge work.

Gaza rescuers yesterday combed through the wreckage of a bombed-out apartment building that collapsed overnight, killing at least 12 people, including five children, and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
The incident highlights the ongoing danger for tens of thousands of Palestinians who live in an estimated 2,000 damaged buildings due to Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.
Rescue workers from the civil defense said that at least 12 people, including five children, were killed and 14 others injured when the seven-story building collapsed.
Photo: AP
Nearly 100 more people were believed to be trapped under the rubble.
A video showed rescue workers trying to pull out two people from under a collapsed wall. Another video circulated on social media showed Gaza’s civil defense spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a little girl, wrapped in a blood-stained scarf, in his hands.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defense service, said at least 10 families lived in the collapsed building and there was still hope of finding survivors.
“We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people,” al-Dahshan said.
Alessandro Mrakic, head of the UN Development Program’s Gaza office, said that people from some UN agencies were taking part in the rescue efforts, which he described as difficult due to the lack of proper machinery.
Egypt’s relief agency was also taking part in rescue efforts.
“The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don’t have the equipment and machinery that is needed. So there are actually people that are digging with their bare hands,” Mrakic said. “We need to prepare” for more deaths.
“There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse. And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter,” he said.

Health coin program to begin next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:35 UTC
01:38:35 KST

The government’s “health coin” program launches next month, but points would not be redeemable until December, as the agency seeks more partners to expand the program’s redemption options, Health Promotion Administration (HPA) Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said yesterday.
The HPA yesterday held its first briefing for businesses interested in joining the program, Shen said.
The briefing would explain how businesses can join the program, who is eligible and what to do to connect to the health coin system, she said, adding that the response from businesses has been enthusiastic.
Photo: CNA
People can start earning the coins by engaging in healthy behaviors starting next month, when the program launches, although they would not be able to redeem points until December, Shen said.
The HPA is expanding the program to offer more choices across different sectors and venues to avoid a situation in which popular rewards run out, she said.
Shen used as an example the sports coin program, where vouchers for PX Mart were quickly redeemed, but vouchers from other convenience store chains were still available.
The health coin program would have multiple partners offering similar rewards, so people are not limited to a single choice, she said.
Items that could be redeemed with the coins have not yet been announced, Shen said, adding that businesses can choose to join in the first or second phase.
After yesterday’s briefing, the HPA would start checking the products and services offered by participating businesses and convene a panel of experts to review them, she said.
The health coin program aims to encourage a cycle of healthy living, so redeemable products and services should promote a healthy lifestyle, Shen said.

Ukrainian NGO official urges support for Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:34 UTC
01:38:34 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine has shown the world that autocracies are willing to use force to change borders, a representative of a Ukrainian non-governmental organization (NGO) said in Taipei yesterday, calling on her country to help strengthen Taiwan.
Liberal Democratic League of Ukraine’s East Asian Office head Mariia Makarovych said at a Taipei forum that Taiwan was one of the first responders after Russia invaded her country in February 2022.
One of the first shipments of humanitarian aid that reached Ukraine was sent by Taiwan, Makarovych said, expressing thanks for the quick response.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
“That’s an example that Taiwan actually believes in Ukraine, while many countries hesitated over whether we would be able to stand against the Russian army or not,” Makarovych said.
“So it’s important to talk not only about how we can continue to support Ukraine, but also how we can share experience, how we can exchange this experience with Ukraine of resistance and our defense,” she said, adding that it is also a relevant topic for Taiwan.
Russia’s war against Ukraine “actually shows a dangerous precedent that autocracies are willing to use force to change borders and to impose their control on other countries and societies,” Makarovych said.
“And that is why Ukraine should support Taiwan, and Ukraine should help Taiwan to be stronger,” she added.
Meanwhile, visiting German parliamentarian Roderich Kiesewetter said at the forum that the outcome of the Russia-Ukraine war would have “direct consequences on all of our lives and also on the future of Taiwan.”
Russia is not only engaged in traditional warfare in Ukraine, but it has also launched a series of hybrid warfare tactics, including state terrorism and cognitive warfare, on countries that support Ukraine, he said.
Furthermore, Moscow has received support from North Korea, Iran and China, Kiesewetter added.
Taiwan knows what is at stake, he said, adding that “if Ukraine is falling or failing, China will have its next target.”
“Therefore, the international community should stand not only with Ukraine, but also with Taiwan,” Kiesewetter said.
Kiesewetter and Makarovych were attendees at the one-day forum in Taipei titled “War, Resilience and Ukraine’s Lessons for Democracies.”
It was organized by the German Institute Taipei and the Liberal Democratic League of Ukraine, an independent, youth-led NGO that lists its mission as to promote liberal democratic values, protect human rights, improve Ukrainian legislation and unite a new generation of civically engaged youth.

The Brazilian Supreme Court engaged in a heated, hours-long debate on Tuesday over how to handle a potential probe into one of its top judges, in an unprecedented public showdown that has eclipsed a presidential election campaign.
The court’s 10 justices were convened by its president, Edson Fachin, to decide whether to open an investigation into Alexandre de Moraes, who has been accused of unsavory ties to a jailed banker involved in a major fraud case.
Fachin opened the session warning that “the country looks to this court. History, too, will look upon this moment.”
Photo: Reuters
However, the six-hour hearing, broadcast live, laid bare divisions, with justices shouting and trading insults as they remained stuck on procedural issues and how to handle internal investigations.
The crisis facing the court is one of many erupting after the arrest last year of banker Daniel Vorcaro for alleged fraud, which unveiled a web of questionable ties that has ensnared judges, lawmakers and even Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, a presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro.
It erupted two weeks ago, when Justice Andre Mendonca, who was appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, unsealed a police report linked to the Vorcaro investigation.
It revealed messages sent by Vorcaro to a number attributed to Moraes, in which the banker sought the justice’s help in the fraud investigation against him.
Moraes is the bete noire of the Bolsonaro family and was briefly sanctioned by US President Donald Trump’s administration over a coup trial against Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence.
Moraes has slammed the move as a bid to frame him for “political and electoral purposes.”
During Tuesday’s session, Moraes accused his rival of being “in the service of a political group that sought to stage a coup d’etat.”
“Liar,” Mendonca said in reply.
In another clash, Gilmar Mendes — an ally of Moraes — provoked Mendonca, who shouted: “Show me some respect.”
One of the questions judges grappled with was whether to unite the case against Moraes with a case questioning whether Mendonca improperly used his powers to investigate Moraes.
However, the hearing ended in a deadlock, with Flavio Dino slamming a “degradation of the court’s image,” securing a postponement that could last until December.
Justice Carmen Lucia, the court’s only female member, expressed her “state of deep dismay and sadness.”
“I am somewhat ashamed that, with less than 20 days to the election, everything revolves around what is happening at the Supreme Court,” she said, asking “forgiveness from the Brazilian people.”
The crisis has dominated the campaign ahead of Oct. 4 elections, expected to be a knife-edge race between Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro.
“No one should remain under a cloud of suspicion. It is important to investigate, and whoever made a mistake must pay the price,” Lula said in an interview on Tuesday.
Moraes has become a near-constant presence in Brazil’s headlines in the past few years, at the center of one major political or judicial battle after another.
“The current president shared his power with Alexandre de Moraes. And in the end, Brazil was left without any president,” Flavio Bolsonaro said in a video on Tuesday.

Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei and Salesforce Inc CEO Marc Benioff said companies have just begun taking advantage of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and need more help to gain the greatest benefits for their businesses.
The power of AI is barely diffused through the economy, with only 5 to 10 percent of the value of the technology being used, Amodei said on Tuesday during an appearance with Benioff at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco.
Implementation of AI at large businesses — like the kind Salesforce mostly serves — remains far away from the futuristic vision professed by executives such as Amodei.
Photo: Bloomberg
Amodei’s comments about AI’s benefits came just a few days after he authored an essay raising the potential risks of the technology and suggesting the pace of development needed to be slowed. Those comments, which were endorsed by executives of rival AI companies such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk have led to discussions by policymakers and within the industry about ways to prevent AI from slipping beyond human control.
Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), CEO of leading AI chipmaker Nvidia Corp, told the Dreamforce audience that “market forces” would regulate the safety of AI.
“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said.
Photo: AFP
There is a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast, Huang added, reiterating a point he has made previously.
“You can definitely have both at the same time,” he said during a conversation with Benioff. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there.”
Companies can decide not to release things that are harmful, Huang said.
“Safety is paramount,” he said. “In a lot of ways, it’s job one. However, safety is an engineering problem.”
If we reach a point when “the company is out of control and the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right,” he said.
Altman, during a conversation later on Tuesday with Benioff at the conference, also said that AI companies can be relied upon to oversee the safe development of the technology.
“I am very confident in our company’s ability — our industry’s ability — to do this safely,” Altman said.
While OpenAI is working with Anthropic and Google’s DeepMind lab to address safety issues, Altman said that AI companies should be able to safely improve AI models on their own.
“I’m disappointed by how it’s been framed,” he said.
Meanwhile, Meta Platforms Inc CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that AI labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe.
“Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice,” Zuckerberg wrote on X on Tuesday.
Some company officials have voiced support for decelerating the pace of AI development and advocated working together to achieve consensus.
Meta decided on its own to slow work on the Muse AI tool, rather than ask peers to also check their own progress first, Zuckerberg wrote.
“Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security,” he wrote. “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

====================================================================================================

The people not worth replacing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:31 UTC
01:38:31 KST

Few ideas have traveled as far as the Great Replacement, which holds that national populations are being deliberately supplanted by immigrants. Coined in France by the writer Renaud Camus, it has furnished the grammar for the advance of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, Viktor Orban’s long reign in Hungary, the Alternative fur Deutschland in Germany, and Donald Trump’s mass-deportation program in the US. It has been cited by mass murderers in Christchurch, El Paso, Hanau and Buffalo.
The idea is easy to understand. It converts a diffuse unease about demographic change into a story with heroes, villains, victims and remedies. It tells believers that they are being pushed aside by identifiable strangers, and that the process can be reversed. It mobilizes voters because it gives fear a face.
That is what makes the uproar over data centers so strange. Three-quarters of Americans say they would oppose the construction of a data center in their community: 83 percent of Democrats, almost 80 percent of independents, and two-thirds of Republicans. State legislatures have introduced a growing number of bills to regulate, delay or block such projects. Governors who courted artificial intelligence (AI) investment have paused new connections to already strained electrical grids. Only Trump still tours the country urging towns to accept what their neighbors are refusing. How can this bipartisan opposition be explained?
Illustration: Mountain People
At first glance, the two fears resemble one another. Both are about the future. Both involve a sense that one’s place in the country is insecure. Both resonate most in the countryside. And both spring from the conviction that immensely consequential decisions are being made elsewhere, by people who do not have to live with the results.
Yet one fear has divided democracies, while the other has united even the most polarized of them. Why should immigration produce rival camps while large, windowless buildings generate something close to a national consensus?
One answer is that the objection to data centers is practical. They consume land, water and immense quantities of electricity. They bring construction work and tax revenue, but few permanent jobs, and their profits flow to distant investors. A deeper answer lies in what the building says. The factory chimney once told a town something reassuring, even as it poisoned the air: You are needed here. The windowless hall says that only the town’s electricity, water and land are needed. It says nothing about the people who live there.
That silence gives the practical objections their force. The data center is the visible infrastructure of an economy that seems to need a community’s resources, but few of its members. The fear it provokes is not primarily a fear of being replaced. It is the fear of not being worth replacing.
Immigration politics is a politics of competition. This is politics of redundancy.
The older fear fueled political division because a fear of replacement needs an identifiable replacer. That replacer is a person, and a person has defenders as well as opponents. When one party says that the migrant is taking your place, the other can point to the migrant’s children in the school play and say: “This, too, is the country’s future.” Defenders can add that strangers are needed to fill the jobs natives would not take, and to pay for the pensions natives expect to collect. One person’s rival is another’s neighbor, employee or child. Immigration arguments, however bitter, remain arguments about membership in a society that still imagines itself to need human beings.
The Great Replacement named an enemy, but it also named a remedy. Deportation flights and a wall are cruel instruments, but they offer reversibility. To fear that strangers would take your job is, at least, to assume that your job would continue to exist. The fear of replacement is the fear of people who still believe they are worth replacing.
Data centers threaten that conviction. They are the most visible infrastructure of an economy that promises, or threatens, to require fewer drivers, clerks, translators, warehouse workers, customer-service representatives and perhaps eventually professionals.
What sort of social order do such buildings portend? The fear they arouse is not of being outnumbered, but of being made useless and unemployable. They foretell an economy in which intelligence is centralized, electricity is consumed on an industrial scale, profits are remote and the connection between a locality’s contribution and its share of the resulting wealth is obscure.
The new threat has no ethnicity and no passport. Nobody can be rounded up for it. There is only a structure at the edge of town, drawing power for a system that does not seem to require the town at all. That is why the fear cannot be confined to right-wing populism, and why the populist who made his career on the older fear is helpless before the new one.
Trump could tell his voters they were being displaced by their inferiors. He cannot tell them that they are not worth replacing. Nor can he tell them who is doing the replacing, because the men doing it stood beside him at his inauguration. The base that believed him about the border does not believe him about the building.
Whom do you deport to bring back a world in which you were needed? A rival can be expelled. No such remedy exists for a job that has become obsolete.
For much of US history, immigration was driven not only by war, persecution and family ties, but by employers’ demands for labor. Farms, factories, railroads, hospitals and households needed more workers. If demand contracts across a widening range of occupations, Trump’s wall might come to seem unnecessary, not because Americans have settled their quarrel over belonging, but because the economy has become less dependent on newcomers and natives alike.
The backlash against data centers is unsettling the old politics without yet settling into a new one. Its unanimity reflects not a country that has overcome polarization, but a threat that resists being sorted by party. A fear with a face can engender parties, counterparties and a program of expulsion. A fear without a face produces moratoria.
Today’s cross-party protest would hold only until people are asked what future they want. Is it merely to build the data center somewhere else?
The Great Replacement was a lie that told its believers their place was worth stealing. The building at the edge of town makes no such promise. It is not coming for your place. It has no use for it.
Stephen Holmes, professor of law at New York University School of Law, is the co-author (with Ivan Krastev) of The Light that Failed: A Reckoning.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Lin welcomed the visit by Jorge Calix, caucus whip of Honduras’ opposition Liberal Party, saying during the meeting that the visit was “a concrete move to show his friendship and support for Taiwan,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Tuesday evening.
The two countries ended formal diplomatic relations in 2023.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
When Taiwan and Honduras were diplomatic allies, they had achieved fruitful results through cooperation in several areas, Lin said.
Taiwan continues to cherish its long-standing friendship with the people of Honduras, the statement cited him as saying.
The government will maintain a “pragmatic and open approach” to the prospect of relations that could “create all kinds of possibilities,” he said.
The statement cited Calix as saying that he sees Taiwan as a model of freedom, democracy and economic development.
Calix said he would be exploring opportunities for cooperation based on the existing foundation.
The ministry did not disclose when the Honduran politician arrived in Taiwan or how long he is staying.
Calix has been serving as a member of the Honduran National Congress since 2014. In early 2022, he briefly served as the disputed president of the Congress.
He is the first Honduran politician to publicly visit Taiwan since the Central American country severed formal diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of Beijing in March 2023, during the tenure of then-Honduran president Xiomara Castro, ending 82 years of formal ties.
Honduran President Nasry Asfura, who took office in January, had pledged during his election campaign to restore ties with Taipei.
Since then, neither Tegucigalpa nor Taipei have spoken publicly about potentially restoring diplomatic ties.

Trade group wants to limit wage hike to 3 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

Taiwan’s minimum wage should not rise more than 3 percent next year to limit the impact of the increase on businesses, particularly traditional industries facing mounting cost pressures, a major business group said yesterday.
Profitable companies should raise employee compensation, but industries struggling with weaker business conditions should receive tax relief and other government support to help offset higher labor costs, Third Wednesday Club chairman Lin Por-fong (林伯豐) said.
Lin’s remarks came ahead of the minimum wage review committee meeting on Thursday next week, when the government is expected to decide on the increase for next year.
Photo: CNA
“A 3 percent increase would be more reasonable considering the impact of inflation,” Lin told reporters on the sidelines of the trade group’s monthly meeting in Taipei.
The government has raised the minimum wage for 10 consecutive years, increasing the monthly rate by a cumulative 47.4 percent and the hourly rate by 63.3 percent, Lin said.
The increases have also pushed up mandatory labor costs, including contributions to the national labor and health insurance programs, Lin said, adding that they account for about 20 percent of personnel expenses.
Higher labor costs are adding to pressure on businesses, particularly traditional industries, even as Taiwan’s economy is forecast to expand 11.05 percent this year on the back of a powerful artificial intelligence (AI) boom, said Lin, who is also chairman of Taiwan Glass Industry Corp (台玻).
The uneven impact of the expansion underscores the challenge for policymakers as AI-related industries benefit from strong global demand, while traditional sectors face higher energy, labor and other costs.
Lin urged the government to continue offering incentives and subsidies to companies that raise wages and share profits with employees, rather than relying solely on across-the-board increases in the minimum wage.
He also called for a cautious approach to monetary policy, saying that Taiwan should take global interest-rate trends into account while avoiding unnecessary changes in borrowing costs.
The central bank’s policy stance has broadly met the expectations of the business community, and it would be better to keep interest rates unchanged for businesses across industries, Lin said.
The central bank is holding its quarterly board meeting today, with investors watching US inflation and the US Federal Reserve’s decision for clues about the outlook for Taiwan’s interest rates.
Lin urged the government to improve energy and talent policies, saying that rapid expansion in AI data centers, advanced semiconductor manufacturing and high-performance computing is driving demand for electricity and skilled workers.
Taiwan also needs to compete more aggressively for international talent rather than focusing on retaining professionals, he said.
Measures could include easing qualification requirements for foreign professionals, streamlining visa and work-permit procedures, and offering tax incentives and better housing support, he added.

Steeplechaser Sable conquers fear of hurdles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

India’s Asian Games steeplechase champion Avinash Sable had no idea if he would compete again after a nasty fall resulted in 14 months on the sidelines and crippling self-doubt.
The 32-year-old won 3,000m steeplechase gold and silver in the 5,000m in Hangzhou, China, three years ago, but sustained a serious knee injury at the Monaco Diamond League meet last year and contemplated retirement when psychological issues complicated his recovery.
“Hurdles scared me,” he told reporters at the Sports Authority of India’s (SAI) Bengaluru center earlier this month.
Photo: Reuters
“I was worried hurdles could get me seriously injured again,” he said. “It felt like I would never be able to return... I had no confidence at all, didn’t know how I would be able to recover.”
Sable is no stranger to hardship, having grown up in a quiet farming community where he ran 6km barefoot to school.
As a teenager he worked in brick kilns and on construction sites with his parents as his family struggled to make ends meet before finding a way out of the grinding poverty by joining the army.
His tough upbringing was no preparation for a long period of inactivity and the slow fight back to fitness after surgery on the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.
“It’s a really dark time for an athlete when workouts that used to be easy make you feel like you don’t know what happened to you,” he said. “I just couldn’t run, my fitness was gone ... at one point I thought my career was over.”
He started running again in November last year, but a shin complaint forced him to stop training again in May.
“My weight had gone up by four to five kilos during the break,” he said. “I couldn’t eat less because it would affect recovery... I think the second injury happened because I tried to push through with extra body weight.”
Sable found reserves of determination and, with the support of fellow athletes and the staff at the SAI’s Bengaluru center, conquered his fears and got back on track again.
“I had missed Commonwealth Games and I didn’t want to miss Asian Games too,” Sable said. “My coaches made me believe that I would get my fitness back ... when I had pain, they motivated me to get through it.”
Sable ran a 5,000m race last month before clocking 8 minutes, 32.39 seconds in a steeplechase in New Delhi on Thursday last week, finishing 18 seconds ahead of the second-placed competitor.
That was still a long way shy of the Asian Games record of 8:19.50 he ran to win gold in Hangzhou, and the Indian national record of 8:09.91 he registered at the Paris Diamond League meet in 2024.
Sable finished 11th in the Olympic steeplechase final in the French capital later that year, won gold at the Asian Championships in May last year, and was aiming for a personal best in Monaco when a rival’s stumble sent him clattering to the deck at the water jump.
Now back in competitive shape after 14 months on the sidelines, Sable aims to defend his Asian Games steeplechase title and hopes to be selected to race in the 5,000m at Aichi-Nagoya.
“The aim is to do better than the last Asian Games,” Sable said. “I want to show everyone who helped me that I can still do well.”

Global power grid to struggle, TrendForce says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Despite rapid growth in data center power demand, global grid capacity has failed to keep pace, market researcher TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) said yesterday.
Global data center power demand is forecast to grow 31 percent to 161 gigawatts (GW) this year from 122.9GW last year, and further increase by more than 30 percent to 211.1GW next year, the Taipei-based researcher said in a statement.
TrendForce attributed the growth to rising power demand from general servers, artificial intelligence servers, other information technology equipment, and non-information technology equipment such as cooling and power supply systems.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
The researcher said grid deliverability was sufficient to meet growing data center power demand through last year, but supply and demand began to diverge this year, with the gap expected to widen markedly after 2028, it said.
By 2030, global data center power demand is forecast to reach 490.7GW, while grid capacity available to data centers would total 222.6GW, it said.
Assuming all other electricity demand is fully met, the gap would still total 268GW, it added.
In the US, where data center deployments are the largest, operators’ self-built power supplies and existing facilities are expected to meet a significant share of demand through 2028, TrendForce said.
This would allow most grid-scheduled projects to be energized on time, it said.
However, grid-delivery delays are expected to become more pronounced from 2028, widening the gap between data center power supply and demand, it added.

Resilience building through democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

In metallurgy, alloys are stronger than pure metals, because adding different-sized atoms to fill into the voids among atoms prevents atomic layers from sliding or breaking. Diversity is strength. However, divergent views might polarize a society to the extent that those would deny a nation the opportunity to continue on its path of prosperity.
The secret of alloys lies in the annealing process of heating and cooling cycles to relax them to the stable atomic structures of minimum energy states.
Primary and general elections may serve as annealing processes in a democratic society by electing candidates with better ideas, greater talents and stronger leadership; by switching from divergent chaos to ordered disciplines; and by forging shared values and common interests into a new culture and even a new identity, leading to greater resilience.
In the 2024 presidential election, opposition parties won a combined majority in the Legislative Yuan. Voters punishing the ruling party is a normal check-and-balance process of alternating stick and carrot cycles, to improve efficiency, cut waste, prosecute corruption and fix unpopular policies. Each election provides people with a chance to steer Taiwan toward a better tomorrow.
However, elections may be compromised by voter intimidation, bribery, disinformation and gerrymandering. External interference will rob a society of healthy development in economy, culture, civility and more. Election flaws directly assault democracy by destroying public trust, weakening institutions and shifting power from the people to self-interested elites.
It is evident that the opposition parties, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party, have thus far have caused the government to idle key projects — defense buildup efforts in particular.
KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) even declared herself Chinese, betraying voters who are troubled by the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) aggressive military posture, and has been assaulting the executive branch and the defense budget.
Moreover, KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) frequently denies that Taiwan is a sovereign country, effectively serving as a CCP propaganda agent.
The KMT’s switch to chaos, which undermines Taiwan’s democracy and freedom, will endanger Taiwan’s security. It calls for a strong condemnation and an imminent correction. Voters must cool this overheated cycle by restraining the opposition parties, and demanding a social and political agenda to help secure Taiwanese sovereignty.
While the November local election does not elect legislators, voters need to send an unambiguous message to opposition parties that they disapprove of extremism and traitorous behaviors.
The elections would allow Taiwanese to review and recalibrate their shared destiny. It would serve as testimony that the corrupt CCP and its cronies in Taiwan would not be allowed to steal elections. We will pass the baton to the future generations of politicians so as to continue our journey for peace, prosperity and progress in the years to come.

Prescription needed for foreign weight loss injections: FDA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:24 UTC
01:38:24 KST

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday reminded the public that GLP-1 receptor agonists require a prescription when brought from abroad.
GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription medications primarily used to treat type 2 diabetes and support weight loss for people with obesity by suppressing appetite.
The amount brought into Taiwan must not exceed the prescription, or be greater than six months’ supply, it said.
Photo: CNA
People carrying the drugs might use the green “Nothing to Declare” channel when entering Taiwan if the amount complies with regulations, but they might still be subject to random inspections, the FDA said.
So far this year, authorities have had 448 cases involving imported GLP-1 drugs, 80 of which were found to be illegal, it said.
A total of NT$2.36 million (US$74,009) in fines were meted out for contraventions, including unauthorized pharmaceutical activities by unlicensed businesses, failure to follow prescribed procedures when dispensing medicines and selling drugs without prescriptions, the FDA said.
The FDA said it is also stepping up online monitoring to combat illegal sale of medicines.
It has asked Meta to remove 1,374 posts advertising the illegal sale of medicines, and asked the Taiwan Network Information Center to block five Web sites suspected of being involved in scams.
The FDA said it has not found any travel agencies arranging overseas trips for people to purchase the drugs, nor has it uncovered any related illegal advertisements.
The agency said it has asked pharmacists to implement risk-control measures, citing 54 adverse-event reports since 2023 involving the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight control.
Reported symptoms include gastrointestinal discomfort, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting and injection-site reactions, the FDA said.
It urged the public not to purchase or self-administer the drugs through unofficial channels, adding that improper use or products from unknown sources could pose health risks.

Will China close the technology gap with the US?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

As the rapid development of artificial intelligence triggers a renewed debate about its risks, the US and China keep racing to develop increasingly powerful models.
The US has outpaced China and other countries in AI model capabilities, research, citations and other areas. China has been rapidly catching up as an AI superpower even as US-led restrictions have blocked China from accessing some of the most advanced technologies, including the cutting-edge chips and the machines to make them.
Experts and recent reports, like one by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, said China has emerged as an AI counterweight to the US and this year appears to be erasing the US lead.
Photo: AP
“The gap between US and Chinese models is narrow and fragile,” said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs.
But both the US and China have also expressed growing concerns over AI. The current debate takes on greater importance ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) expected visit to Washington this month to meet US President Donald Trump, and as experts say the future of AI will depend significantly on what China and the US do and don’t do.
Here’s a quick look at some of the most important Chinese AI models and the concerns in both Washington and Beijing:
Photo: Reuters
MOONSHOT AI
Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI made a splash with the release of Kimi K3, taking Silicon Valley by surprise with capabilities close to US rivals. It was ranked No. 3 globally in model intelligence in July, shortly after its release, behind Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, according to AI benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis. But Kimi K3 now ranks ninth, behind new frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and SpaceXAI, indicating China’s AI lead can be fluid.
AI startup darling DeepSeek was the first to upend global stock markets by proving Chinese AI models are capable of challenging the US lead. The company’s R1 model, released early last year, was more cost-effective than similar US models. In April, DeepSeek previewed its powerful V4 model, saying it has big improvements in knowledge, reasoning and “agentic” capabilities, referring to the ability to plan and execute complex steps autonomously, under limited human guidance.
The powerful GLM-5.2 from startup Z.ai that rolled out in June raised Silicon Valley eyebrows with comparisons to the most advanced Anthropic and OpenAI models. Z.ai then launched GLM-5.3 in August with improved coding and agentic capabilities that pushed it up the global AI model rankings.
In July, China’s Alibaba previewed its Qwen3.8-Max model, which the tech giant said was its most powerful model in the series, challenging Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT.
RISKS TO SECURITY
In China, the head of its state security ministry has warned artificial intelligence poses a range of potential threats to the country, from political and ideological security to cyberattacks, data leaks and even challenges to governance.
In an article published Sunday, Chen Yixin (陳一新) said the technology could threaten China’s political, institutional, and ideological security if used by “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives.”
Some individuals might use AI-generated deepfake audio and video to create “political rumors” on a massive scale, he wrote.
Chen specifically mentioned the capabilities of Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT as examples of how AI could be used to more easily identify and “weaponize” cybersecurity vulnerabilities. He warned certain nations and groups can now “execute complex hacking tasks.”
Top Chinese leaders have said China should accelerate AI development and pursue technological self-reliance. But they also noted the need to control the risks and establish a global framework for AI governance.
CAN US MAINTAIN EDGE?
In the US, Trump and his administration have repeatedly highlighted the importance for the US to maintain its AI edge over China. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump told reporters on Sunday.
The V has accused China’s AI developers of engaging in what it has called “industrial-scale distillation,” in which AI models are trained to copy or imitate the capabilities of more powerful ones. Last week, Anthropic also accused Chinese startups DeepSeek and Moonshot of routing a number of their user requests to its Claude AI models.
In the most comprehensive report by the government to date, the FBI, the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Sept. 8 that Chinese AI developers extracted capabilities from some of the most advanced AI models in the US in “aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities.”
Beijing has rejected that and said distillation is commonly used by many AI companies. It asked the United States to refrain from making “unfounded accusations” and accused the US of pursuing a “monopoly of the AI industry.”
The US allegations “should be read as a contested claim” but not as the explanation for China’s catch-up, said Professor Will Cong of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
The United States has put in a lot of energy controlling the inputs into frontier AI, especially chips, said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis. But now “it may also have to think about the outputs of frontier AI as a form of technology transfer,” she said.
“The US labs spend enormous amounts of compute pushing out the frontier. But Chinese developers can learn from those systems,” said Lee. “And Chinese companies then (can) release very capable open-weight models that spread globally.”
