The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

Dolly Parton’s megawatt smile and big wavy locks are gracing fields across the US and Canada this fall.
Twenty farms have carved large corn mazes to honor the late country music icon, actor and philanthropist, and raise money for her Imagination Library, which provides free books to children.
The Jolene crooner’s death due to cancer on Aug. 25 in Nashville, Tenessee, at age 80 brought an outpouring of tributes. They ranged from a drive to rename the country music capital’s airport in Parton’s honor to a surge in online streams of 9 to 5, Islands in the Stream and her many other hit songs.
Photo: AP
Now she is being immortalized in corn, with the mazes in about a dozen states and two provinces, from Alabama to California and Ohio to Texas. Most also feature a Parton-themed trivia game, photo ops and other offerings.
Brett Herbst, founder of The Maize Inc, a Utah-based consulting company that designed the mazes, called Parton a “true American treasure.”
“Dolly’s impact on the world and her love for farming is immeasurable, and our corn maze tributes now take on new meaning and significance,” Herbst said.
The company said the mazes were in the works months before Parton died and are part of its annual campaign honoring country music’s brightest stars.
Previous honorees included Reba McEntire in 2023, Luke Bryan in 2024 and Lainey Wilson last year.
Parton, who famously grew up poor in rural Tennessee, thanked organizers for supporting her charity before her death.
In a statement provided by The Maize Inc, she encouraged people to “get lost in this year’s country music corn maze for a little fun, laughter and a real good reason to get lost.”
One of the mazes is in an expansive cornfield next to Twins BBQ in Brookfield, Connecticut, about 90km northeast of New York. The likeness of Parton beams skyward, ringed by the words “Dolly” and “An American Treasure” and a series of stars.
Danielle Gallop, who co-owns the business with her husband, said she did not know much about Parton before attending last year’s corn maze convention at Dollywood, the Tennessee theme park Parton co-owned.
However, she came away impressed.
“They told us all about her integrity and how she ran all of her businesses, and how smart and generous and kind and just really ethical and humble” Parton was, “which is all the things that we aspire to be as business owners,” Gallop said.

Taipei’s global financial standing increases: index
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

Taipei has climbed to 42nd place in a global ranking of financial centers released yesterday, up from 73rd two years ago, the Taiwan Stock Exchange Corp (TWSE) said, attributing the rise to the government’s push to develop Taiwan into an Asian asset management hub.
The 40th Global Financial Centres Index placed Taipei 42nd among 139 global financial centers worldwide.
The index assessed financial centers on key policy priorities for the next five years.
Photo: Carlos Garcia Rawlins, Reuters
The latest result showed Taiwan’s continued upward trend, from 73rd in September 2024 to 70th in March last year, 55th in September last year and 51st in March this year in the twice-yearly index compiled by the China Development Institute in Shenzhen, China, and Z/Yen Partners in London.
The latest ranking reflects the rapid transformation of Taiwan’s financial market since the Asian Asset Management Center initiative was launched two years ago, the TWSE said in a statement.
“The improvement reflects growing international recognition of Taiwan’s efforts to open its financial market, promote regulatory innovation, and strengthen global connectivity,” the exchange said.
Since the launch of the initiative, the Financial Supervisory Commission has sought to expand wealth management through deregulation, new business lines, pilot programs and cross-border cooperation, the TWSE said.
Financial institutions have also increased their investment in products, services and talent, helping to strengthen Taiwan’s asset management ecosystem, it said.
Internationally, New York topped the index, followed by London, Hong Kong and Singapore. Shanghai, Tokyo, Seoul, Shenzhen, Dubai and Zurich rounded out the top 10.

CAL, Virgin Atlantic ink codeshare pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:20 UTC
01:38:20 KST

China Airlines (CAL) yesterday announced that it has signed a codeshare agreement with fellow SkyTeam member Virgin Atlantic Airways to facilitate travel for passengers connecting through Europe.
The airline made the announcement at a ceremony marking the 15th anniversary of it joining the SkyTeam.
Under the arrangement, the codeshare service would cover flights from Taipei to London via Incheon International Airport in South Korea. Additional codeshare routes would be introduced at a later stage.
Photo: Huang Ching-yi, Taipei Times
China Airlines president Kevin Chen (陳漢銘) said Virgin Atlantic has an extensive long-haul network in the UK and provides onward connections from London.
The partnership is particularly useful, because it offers more convenient connections and could help attract more European passengers to Taiwan, Chen said.
Meanwhile, passengers traveling from London via Taipei to Australia and New Zealand represent a significant part of the connecting market, with such passengers accounting for nearly 40 percent of traffic, Chen added.
In addition to China Airlines’ new Boeing 787 aircraft, with deliveries starting this year and expected to be completed in 2028, the airline has ordered 15 Airbus A350-1000 passenger aircraft, 15 Boeing 777-9 passenger aircraft and eight Boeing 777-8F freighters, he said.
Deliveries of the new Airbus 350 and Boeing 777 aircraft are scheduled to begin in 2029.
The airline also plans to begin refurbishing its 18 A350-900 aircraft next year to improve service quality and passenger experience.
China Airlines operates 40 and 30 weekly direct flights to North America and Europe respectively.
Connecting passengers account for about 60 percent of traffic on its North American routes and 50 percent on its European routes, Chen said.
The airline operates six direct routes to Europe: Frankfurt, Amsterdam, London, Vienna, Rome and Prague.
For the flight to Prague, the airline offers a connecting bus service between Prague Airport and Dresden, Germany.
Asked about other airlines testing the waters in the Indian market, Chen said China Airlines welcomes the development, but would prefer to focus its limited capacity on markets where it already has strong advantages.
“We recognize India as a significant and rapidly growing passenger and cargo market. However, the airline is constrained by its current fleet capacity,” Chen said, adding that new aircraft deliveries over the next two years would provide additional capacity.
“Until then, we intend to prioritize strengthening existing routes rather than immediately opening numerous new destinations,” he said.
China Airlines said it expects the air freight market to remain strong in the fourth quarter, with cargo capacity already tight and demand being driven by semiconductors, artificial intelligence-related equipment, consumer electronics and other high-value goods.

Notes from Central Taiwan: How the AI industry is reshaping Taiwan’s landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

Focus Taiwan reported on the Kuai Kuai land sale, with a narrative centered on the famed snack factory’s workers. But buried in it was a glimpse of the way Taiwan’s land markets are being relentlessly reshaped by the multiple pressures of sagging traditional industry fortunes and surging AI and related electronics industries.
Kuai Kuai’s owner, the San-ti Group, sold the factory and the land it sits on in Taoyuan’s Zhongli District (中壢). According to Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions Secretary-General Tracy Sun (孫語謙), who was quoted in the piece, rising land prices, especially for industrial land, tempt factory owners to sell off their land to AI and semiconductor firms. Sun suggested San-ti had probably purchased the land intending to sell it in the hot industrial land market.
Industrial land prices are indeed rising, driven by demand from AI. A June report from Sinyi Realty Inc (信義房屋) noted that the hottest industrial land market was in Miaoli County. Several years ago I wrote on attempts to join Miaoli and Hsinchu to form a single municipality in response to the desire of tech firms to reduce the administrative costs of having factories in two separate counties and multiple industrial park managements (“Municipal Independence”, Jan. 3, 2022). This demand will only grow as Miaoli becomes an even more important site of industrial land expansion. Hsinchu City and County now have a combined population exceeding one million, close to the 1.25 million statutory threshold for a special municipality.
Photo: Su Chin-Feng, Taipei Times
The Miaoli experience is being repeated across central Taiwan. Demand for industrial land and commercial office space is booming. An April 2025 report by Colliers International noted rising industrial land prices driven partly by semiconductor and AI-related demand, with industrial expansion increasingly moving south. Demand for industrial land was expanding southward even then.
Recent Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) administrations have been careful to spread the wealth, pushing semiconductors and their associated industries further south. Redistribution from the north to the south has long been a DPP policy goal. Southern expansion also relieves pressure on northern water and electricity systems.
Construction commenced in June on a dedicated semiconductor supply chain park in the southernmost section of the Southern Taiwan Science Park (STSP) in Pingtung County. The STSP stretches across Chiayi, Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) is building advanced packaging fabs in the Chiayi Science Park. National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) Minister Wu Cheng-wen (吳誠文) said the government envisions a vast corridor of semiconductor and associated technology firms in parks extending from Pingtung to Hsinchu, the greatest such collection in the world. Unsurprisingly, the Pingtung portion of the STSP sits within the High Speed Rail (HSR) land allocation for the Pingtung HSR station, on Taiwan Sugar Land, next to the Liukuaicuo Taiwan Rail Station.
Meanwhile, as CommonWealth Magazine noted in another excellent piece last year (“Taiwan’s Machine Tool Makers Struggle to Survive”, Nov. 5, 2025), traditional industry factories are shutting down as competition from the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and the new tariffs of the administration of US President Donald Trump hit them.
“All along the ‘Golden Valley,’ which once supported tens of thousands of families, one roll-up metal door after another is shut tight,” it reported, referring to the dense accumulation of small machinery, metal and sporting goods factories that once spread from Taichung down into Changhua.
This is happening across Taiwan, as the article observed: “older industrial zones in northern Taiwan are also in structural decline.”
Smart young people are studying for jobs in the shiny new semiconductor industry, instead of traditional industries.
Continuing too is agricultural land loss. Taiwan has lost a substantial amount of cultivated land since 1990. Anyone paying attention to the steady conversion of farmland to industrial use, and the large quantities of agricultural land occupied by illegal factories, which always hunger for more land, can understand the objections by local factions and large industrial firms to renewable energy: it drives up agricultural land prices.
A 2023 study in the Journal of Environmental Management (“Solar farm policy and farmland price — A land zoning perspective”, October, 2023) by Chang Hung-hao (張宏浩) and Lin Tzu-chin (林子欽) showed that after the government tightened zoning regulations to prohibit solar panels on farmland under 660 square meters, farmland prices fell by 21.8 percent. They also found that this reduction grew as time passed, and “farmland with higher prices per hectare are most severely affected.”
Land speculators, especially local faction-linked developers and land brokers, probably noticed that land is cheaper when there is no solar power around. Hence, political parties with strong links to local factions attempt to quietly suppress the development of solar power on agricultural land. The domestic economy depends on land and real estate, and a supply of cheap agricultural land is necessary to keep it running. It is also critical to the semiconductor boom.
Researcher Justin Kollar interviewed officials and found that “local governments, enticed by land conversion revenues and industrial prestige, have rezoned agricultural areas at unprecedented speed,” he wrote last year in a must-read paper on semiconductors and land (“Fallowing the fields, feeding the fabs: Territorial restructuring and the political-industrial ecology of high-tech Taiwan”, Environment and Planning E: Nature and Space.
As the semiconductor industry expanded, so did local government rezoning of agricultural land.
Kollar’s work shows how the government quietly prioritizes water development for semiconductors even where it piously says enhanced water facilities are constructed to serve farmers and residents. It is likely that Taiwan is heading towards the same quiet redistribution of electricity as well. The erosion of traditional industries, which are more electricity-intensive per unit of GDP created than semiconductors, has helped ameliorate a possible looming power crisis.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) last month said the government would consider raising its average annual electricity demand growth forecast, originally projected at 2.5 percent annually through 2035 in June, to reflect the high demand scenario.
The world of the future is already being realized as is shown in a case study of farmers experiencing farmland loss in Yunlin County’s Huwei Township (虎尾), which identifies several issues with farmland loss and conversion (“Agricultural Land-Use Transition and Procedural Justice: Evidence from a Systematic Literature Review and a Case Study in Taiwan,” Sustainability, 2026, Vol 18) by Liu Wei-kuang (劉為光) and Shen Yi-wei. The Huwei case takes place in the HSR development corridor (the Yunlin HSR station is nearby).
The farmers and local agricultural experts and officials reported that many farmers did not realize the true value of their land when they sold it to developers. As home prices rose farmers sold their land to pay for houses elsewhere, since they could no longer afford to live in the local community. Sons did not carry on farming, since crop prices were low, water difficult to access and less land was available.
Moreover, some farmers leased land to farm, but the government subsidies for dryland crops, intended to reduce groundwater use, went to land owners rather than farmers. The farmers themselves blamed urban expansion and construction for groundwater overuse, rejecting the narrative that criticizes farmers’ groundwater overuse for subsidence.
This transition is going to take place across the south as the semiconductor industry reorganizes demand for land, power and water. What will the region’s politics look like in a decade?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. The PRC claims most of the South China Sea through its U-shaped 10-dash

A court yesterday ruled that North Korea should pay the South 44.6 billion won (US$32.5 million) for blowing up a joint liaison office between the countries in 2020 as their relations deteriorated following the collapse of nuclear negotiations between Pyongyang and Washington. The ruling by the Seoul Central District Court was symbolic, as the South has no clear way to force the North to pay amid a diplomatic breakdown. The Ministry of Unification, which handles affairs related to North Korea, said it respects the court’s ruling and called for a resumption of inter-Korean diplomacy so that “all issues between the South and North can be resolved through dialogue and cooperation.” North Korean state media did not immediately comment on the ruling. South Korea filed the suit in 2023, describing the North’s detonation of the building in the North Korean border town of Kaesong as an unlawful and violent act that breached previous agreements between the countries and severely damaged “mutual respect and trust.”
CHINA
Major canal opened
A major canal opened yesterday that provides landlocked areas with direct access to the sea, state media said, reducing transport times and costs as the country aims to bolster trade ties with regional neighbors. The 134km Pinglu Canal took four years to build and links Nanning, in the southern manufacturing region of Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin. Goods from the nation’s southwest previously had to be transported to the southern metropolis of Guangzhou to reach the sea, but the new canal cuts the journey by more than 560km, Xinhua news agency reported. The canal also reduces transport costs by 18 to 30 percent, and would generate annual savings of more than 5 billion yuan (US$745 million) in the sector, it said. State broadcaster CCTV broadcast footage of the first barge to pass through the canal and aerial video of ships navigating its calm waters, describing the waterway as “the project of our century.” The canal “opens up the shortest, most economical and most convenient route” to Southeast Asia and will boost economic development, Xinhua said. The new route is particularly important to rural parts of Sichuan, Chongqing and Yunnan, among others, which are less well-connected than more prosperous regions in eastern China.

EDITORIAL: Is the UN worth trying to join?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

Taiwanese-Americans, lawmakers and civic groups marched through Manhattan on Saturday last week in support of Taiwan’s participation in the UN. Marshall Islands Permanent Representative to the UN John Silk joined the demonstration, saying he hoped Taiwan would one day be able to participate in UN meetings as a member, and Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Wang Yi-chuan (王義川) took part while visiting New York City with a delegation.
Taiwanese communities in Vancouver held a “UN for Taiwan” event. The campaign comes as the 81st UN General Assembly gets under way. In Taipei, President William Lai (賴清德) said China was deliberately misinterpreting UN Resolution 2758 to claim sovereignty over Taiwan, adding that the resolution dealt with China’s representation at the UN and did not determine Taiwan’s status.
The campaign raises a broader question: What practical benefits would Taiwan gain from participating in the UN and its affiliated organizations? Taiwan already participates in organizations including the WTO, Asian Development Bank and APEC, but remains excluded from the WHO and others.
At the same time, the campaign raises a larger question about the role of the UN itself. The organization was created to maintain international peace and security. Eight decades later, it remains important to peacekeeping, humanitarian assistance, development and diplomacy, but its effectiveness is frequently hobbled by disagreements among member states, particularly in the UN Security Council.
Does the UN still function as its founders envisioned? How much would a seat or participation change Taiwan’s international position?
The question is important given the limits the organization has faced in dealing with major crises. Taiwan has said that its exclusion from the UN system created problems during the COVID-19 pandemic, saying its early warnings about the outbreak were not incorporated into the international response.
The UN’s record on war and security raises questions about what membership could realistically accomplish. Russia, China and the US are among the five permanent members of the Security Council and possess veto power, yet the council has been unable to prevent or decisively end major conflicts, including the wars in Ukraine and the genocide in Gaza.
For Taiwan, those limitations are particularly significant. China remains its principal military threat, while Beijing’s activities in the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea have contributed to tensions with Japan, the Philippines and other countries in the Indo-Pacific region. Would Taiwan’s admission to the UN improve its ability to deter China, or would Beijing’s permanent seat and veto power simply give it another means of opposing Taiwan’s participation?
Yet, Taiwan has little incentive to abandon the campaign. Giving up its pursuit of international participation could be portrayed as accepting China’s claim that Taiwan is merely part of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) rather than a self-governing political entity entitled to represent its own people.
Does Taiwan actually need UN membership to achieve the goals it associates with international recognition? If those goals include protecting its security, expanding diplomatic relations, participating in international organizations, gaining access to global decisionmaking and establishing wider recognition of its separate political status, could some of those objectives be achieved without becoming a UN member?
Taiwan already participates in some international institutions under various names and arrangements and has extensive unofficial relations with countries that do not recognize it. It could seek greater participation in specialized international organizations, negotiate bilateral and multilateral agreements, and expand unofficial ties with other countries, increasing its international space without resolving the dispute over its status.
What exactly does Taiwan want other countries to recognize? Taiwan operates as a self-governing democracy with its own elected government, military, currency, laws and territory, while the PRC has never governed Taiwan. Its international status remains complicated by the competing positions of Beijing, Taipei and other governments.
Before asking the international community to recognize Taiwan as a nation, Taiwan might have to grapple with what it means by sovereignty itself. Is the goal to maintain the Republic of China framework while seeking greater international recognition, establish recognition of Taiwan as a separate state, or preserve the “status quo” while expanding its participation in international institutions?
Taiwan’s UN campaign is consequently about more than obtaining a seat in New York. It reflects a larger struggle over Taiwan’s international identity, its ability to maintain political space in the face of pressure from Beijing, and whether its goals can be achieved without first resolving the fundamental dispute over its sovereignty.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

As the title suggests, Shuster views a deal between Taiwan and China as an increasingly inevitable alternative to a costly war — one that Taiwan, lacking reliable allies and military capabilities, would eventually be destined to lose. Compass Festival returns to Taichung, but shh ... not too loud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

Two years ago, the music came to an abrupt halt at one of Taiwan’s largest independent music festivals. The problem: a single noise complaint. The DJ’s high-energy tunes had exceeded the allowed sound limit. As per regulation, the performance took a several-minute pause and then continued, this time at a slightly lower decibel.
And then last year, the same event, Compass Taichung International Food and Music Festival, was unexpectedly canceled due to sponsorship issues.
Such are the woes of trying to organize outdoor music festivals these days.
Photo courtesy of Compass Magazine
“It makes it so much harder to put on a festival,” said Courtney Donovan Smith, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, which organizes the annual two-day bash. (Smith is also a columnist for the Taipei Times.)
Undaunted, organizers are trying again as the festival is back this weekend with nearly 20 bands set to take the stage, along with an array of food and beverage vendors. The party kicks off at noon on Saturday and Sunday at Civic Square (市民廣場), the city’s premier outdoor music venue.
“We were really determined to have it this year,” said Douglas Habecker, co-publisher of Compass Magazine. It’s an important event, not just for the musicians and vendors, but also for the people of Taichung, he said. The festival typically attracts upwards of 20,000 people over the course of the weekend.
But with rising costs and more government regulations, organizing these kinds of outdoor festivals has become more burdensome than ever before, Habecker said.
By law, the city’s Environmental Protection Bureau must respond to any noise complaint reported, even if the same person keeps calling. And after 7pm if the decibel level is above 58 as measured from the nearest street, then the music stops, and fines may be levied.
Taichung’s noise regulations are among the strictest in the nation and have become even stricter in recent years, causing frustration not only for organizers and musicians but also for festivalgoers.
“It’s terrible for Taichung and a huge downer for everyone,” Habecker said. “We’re not blasting music irresponsibly.”
While large government-sponsored festivals, such as the Taichung Jazz Festival, are flourishing, the city’s once-thriving music scene, which included numerous small, independent festivals, has all but dried up, Smith and Habecker said.
“It’s become a real headache. It’s like waiting for the Sword of Damocles to drop,” said Habecker, referring to the uncertainty of when officials might appear following a noise complaint.
For some independent festivals, the solution has been to move farther away from residential areas. Tainan May Jam, for example, used a public beach for many years before moving to a scenic area about 20 minutes from downtown.
“There are no noise complaints in the mountains,” said organizer Axel Schuun, whose festival, typically featuring indigenous bands and musicians from Southeast Asia, has attracted thousands of music lovers for the past 25 years.
Sean Scanlan, who organizes multiple music events each year, is sympathetic with those taking on such projects, saying there are “fewer and fewer” independent music festivals in recent years. In addition, he said festivals these days just seem to be attracting fewer people.
“It’s tough out there,” Scanlan said of organizing festivals. “All the red tape sucks.”
Scanlan’s next festival, one that he feels especially close to, will be the Daniel Pearl World Music Day in Taipei early next month.
Back in Taichung, in an effort to help better manage the sound at this year’s Compass Festival, DJs will take over after the live music ends at 7pm each evening.
An additional burden, organizers said, is obtaining enough sponsors to cover the ever rising costs of hosting a festival. Everything from tent and stage rentals to musician fees to insurance and cleanup costs need to be paid for. Between 60 percent to 70 percent of revenue, Habecker estimated, comes from sponsorships.
In past years, Compass Festival relied in part on the financial support of well-known beer brands, including AB InBev, which makes Corona and Budweiser, to help cover the costs. But when Taiwan imposed tariffs of up to 52 percent on imported beer from China, these companies dropped their sponsorship.
Picking up the slack and making this year’s festival financially possible are smaller sponsors, including two local soccer clubs and a luxury hotel, with the addition of long-term supporters, World Gym and Corning Taiwan. Taiwan Beer, Kingfisher and Hellow Brewery have also pledged support.
“In the future, I hope we can find even more sponsors to help keep things going,” Habecker said.
Organizing a festival is tiring and stressful, Smith and Habecker said, but they consider it sort of a public service to the city and residents of Taichung.
“Nothing feels better than when people tell us what a great time they had,” Habecker said. “It energizes us.”
Compass Festival is set to take place rain or shine on Saturday from noon to 9pm and Sunday from noon to 8pm. For the latest updates, check the newly-launched Compass Magazine Line app or the Compass Food and Music Fest 2026 Facebook page.

Phishing cases on rise, CIB says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

Total losses due to fraud declined last month, but reports of phishing rose substantially, with 505 cases and NT$54.51 million (US$1.71 million) in total losses reported, the National Police Agency’s Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) said on Tuesday.
In the same period last year, there were 253 cases and NT$13.05 million of losses due to phishing, data from the CIB’s 165 Anti-Fraud Hotline and online reporting Web site showed.
There were 10,652 telecommunications and Internet fraud cases reported nationwide last month, with losses surpassing NT$4 billion, compared with more than NT$6 billion during the same period last year, it said.
Photo: CNA
Total reports fell by 22.3 percent and losses by 35.1 percent, it added.
The public should be wary of suspicious links and remember to “pause, check and then act,” the CIB said at a campaign event headlined by actor Harry Chang (張懷秋).
Scammers often send e-mails impersonating e-commerce platforms, government agencies, financial services or logistics companies, and lead people to click phishing links with claims of tax refunds, winning lottery invoices or unpaid traffic fines, it said.
Once clicked, the links can allow scammers to steal data, including credit card information, it said.
Recent phishing cases have tended to be fake telecommunications and transportation payment notifications claiming that points or rewards were about to expire or that parking fees had not been paid, it said.
Other common methods include impersonating retailers on online shopping platforms such as Shopee and Momo with claims of abnormal orders, refunds, duplicate orders or membership information update requirements, it said.
Scammers might also falsely advertise themselves as travel or immigration application services such as Thailand’s Digital Arrival Card, the Electronic System for Travel Authorization in the US or the UK’s Electronic Travel Authorization, it added.
Phishing e-mails or URLs usually contain words that are similar to what official channels use, the CIB said, adding that people should close pages that seem suspicious and open official sites via a manual search or by typing the correct URL, or they should contact official customer service to verify claims, it said.
The public should also be on alert for Web sites directing them to speak with online customer service accounts on the Line messaging app and not take directions to use online banking, make ATM transfers, conduct cardless withdrawals or scan QR codes to transfer funds, it said.

The false politics of Western declinism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

As US President Donald Trump plunges the US into another reckless trade war — this time with neighboring Canada, one of its largest trading partners, and a NATO ally — the irony is hard to miss. Despite being the main architect and beneficiary of the multilateral trading system since 1945, the US under Trump has recast itself — at least rhetorically — as the victim of an allegedly unfair economic order.
Trump’s narrative of victimization has long animated the MAGA movement. His triumph, he vowed in his first inaugural address in 2017, would end “this American carnage,” and his return to the White House, he declared eight years later, was the end of US “decline.”
In recent years, that rhetoric has spread to Europe’s Trumpian far right. Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban, whose government adopted “Make Europe Great Again” as the official motto for Hungary’s presidency of the Council of the EU in 2024, praised the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy for recognizing Europe’s “civilizational-scale decline.” Elon Musk has echoed the same message, in newspaper commentaries and in a virtual appearance at a campaign rally for Germany’s Alternative fur Deutschland.
The idea of Western decline is not limited to far-right populists. Presenting his 2024 report on European competitiveness, former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi called for an EU turnaround in order to avoid the “slow agony” of decline. The newly established Rhine Group, led by Draghi and tech billionaire Patrick Collison, frames the stakes in similarly existential terms, albeit without MAGA’s nativist hysteria.
Tellingly, these warnings almost never specify what, exactly, is declining. The term is being used to describe two different phenomena. One is absolute — and easily disproved. Are Americans and Europeans getting poorer in terms of GDP per capita, average income or life expectancy? No. They are richer than ever. The other is relative: Is the West’s share of global output shrinking? Yes, but this has been the case for decades. The populist sleight of hand depends on collapsing the distinction between them.
The West’s declining share of global output can be largely attributed to two trends. The first is convergence: Poorer countries have been catching up. Research by Nobel laureate economist Michael Kremer, Jack Willis and Yang You finds that while real per-capita GDP in poor and rich countries diverged at an annual rate of 0.5 percent from 1985 to 1995, the trend subsequently reversed; GDP growth from 2005 to 2015 converged at an annual rate of 0.7 percent. Second, Western countries are further along in their demographic transitions. A country with a growing workforce can increase its share of global GDP even if no one gets a dollar richer.
Neither trend implies that the West has done something wrong, and neither trend prevents living standards in Western societies from rising. If anything, the opposite is true.
There is one domain in which the West has actually declined: geopolitics. Relative GDP is the currency of international power, and power is much closer to being zero-sum than prosperity is.
Given that much of the world’s economic activity has been concentrated in a handful of Western economies for most of the past two centuries, some loss of relative power was inevitable once the rest of the world began to catch up.
Populists seeking to exploit this shift are helped by genuine domestic grievances. While aggregate living standards across the West have risen, the gains have been unevenly distributed. US median wages, for example, barely moved between the 1970s and the mid-2000s, even as top incomes soared. More recently, post-pandemic increases in wealth and spending have been heavily concentrated among wealthy households.
These dynamics, sometimes described as “K-shaped growth,” point to a real decline in living standards for large segments of the population in the US and other Western countries. That is not the same as a decline of the West as a whole, although it has turned other countries into a convenient culprit for populists seeking to leverage nationalist resentment by exploiting legitimate complaints over the distribution of income and wealth.
How political leaders define “decline” determines the agenda they pursue. If they recognize that relative decline can coexist with rising welfare everywhere, they can accept convergence and seek to establish international rules better suited to a multipolar world economy. That path is slow. It depends on the goodwill of countries the West has spent two centuries dominating, and trust is in short supply these days.
The alternative is to treat GDP as a zero-sum contest. That path, while currently politically expedient, is likely to make almost everyone poorer.
Trump’s tariffs illustrate the second approach. As a tool for maximizing US incomes, they are absurd. But as a tool for maximizing US income relative to Europe’s, they make considerably more sense. At least that is a coherent objective, though not the one Europe thinks it is negotiating over, which helps explain why Europeans have found trade talks with the Trump administration so confounding. If Europe responds to Trump’s bullying tactics in kind, the result would be a standoff that leaves both parties worse off.
Conflating absolute and relative decline is more than just sloppy thinking. Declinist rhetoric nurtures political consent for a zero-sum approach to trade and economic growth. Rejecting the harder but better collaborative path could mean having it forced upon us later, after zero-sum logic has run its course, triggered a major crisis, and forced Western governments back to the negotiating table.
From the Concert of Europe to the Bretton Woods system, new international orders have historically emerged in the wake of catastrophic wars. Waiting for another post-crisis window would be an enormously expensive and painful way to relearn the lesson that playing zero-sum games in a positive-sum world can leave everyone with less.
Carl Johan Dalgaard is professor of economics at the University of Copenhagen and a former chair of the Danish Economic Councils. Mark Medish, a member of the US National Security Council under former president Bill Clinton and a former deputy assistant secretary of the Treasury, is vice Chair of Panterra.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Brewers’ selfless style of ball pays off again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

The best pitcher in baseball on the team with the best record in baseball is not sure how exactly the Milwaukee Brewers keep doing this.
Asked how a team that works on the fringe of baseball’s middle class has turned Champagne celebrations into a September ritual, Jacob Misiorowski shrugged.
“I couldn’t tell you,” the 24-year-old ace said. “You know, I’ve been trying to figure it out all year.”
Photo: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images
The search would continue into next month. The Brewers (94-57) on Tuesday night won their fourth straight National League (NL) Central title, when they rode their flame-throwing star and a couple of timely hits from Luis Lara and Joey Ortiz to a 5-1 victory over Pittsburgh.
When the Atlanta Braves rallied past the Chicago Cubs about 30 minutes later, there was a roar that seeped through the cinderblock walls outside the visitors’ clubhouse at PNC Park. Bottles were popped. Cigars were lit. Beers — Miller Lites, of course — were chugged.
This part of the journey never gets old, not even for Christian Yelich, who has been a fixture during Milwaukee’s run of eight playoff appearances in nine years.
“We’re a good team,” the three-time All-Star and 2018 NL Most Valuable Player said. “This is what we set out to do every season at the beginning of spring training. We just keep playing our game.”
Milwaukee does not overwhelm opponents with power or gaudy stats — outside of Misiorowski’s stream of 161kph-plus fastballs — and instead relies on singles, smart baseball and a selfless approach.
The Brewers gave Pittsburgh a glimpse in the second inning. Jake Bauers led off with a single to right field, advanced to second on a groundout and sprinted to third on a wild pitch. Luis Lara followed with a fly ball to center field deep enough to allow Bauers to dash home.
Just like that, Milwaukee was up 1-0 with the NL Cy Young favorite on the mound. While Misiorowski did not think he had his best stuff on a night he tossed five scoreless innings to drop his ERA to an MLB-best 1.89, it hardly mattered.
“It’s just the boys grinding, them doing their jobs and putting a run across the board,” Misiorowski said. “So that’s all I can ask for.”
A lot of times, it is all he needs. The Brewers do not just, as Ortiz put it, “single you to death.” They largely avoid the mental mistakes that can make all the difference during the 162-game regular season.
The proof came in the fourth when the Pirates put together their only significant rally. Pittsburgh had runners on first and second with one out when Rafael Flores hit a sharp grounder that glanced off Milwaukee third baseman David Hamilton’s glove and rolled into the outfield. Pittsburgh’s Nick Gonzales stayed at third rather than race home after a mix-up with third base coach Tony Beasley.
In the chaos, the Brewers caught Pirates designated hitter Ryan O’Hearn in a rundown between second and third for the second out. Misiorowski got Spencer Horwitz to fly out and end the threat.
It has been like that all year. It has been like that most of the past decade.
“I think we do a really good job of knowing how to win, creating a winning culture and everybody knows, like, every night it’s time to win,” Yelich said.
He believes that culture starts with the ownership group headed by Mark Attanasio and trickles down to general manager Matt Arnold to manager Pat Murphy to a roster whose payroll of about US$140 million is 19th highest in the majors.
The other NL teams that began Tuesday in playoff position — the Los Angeles Dodgers, Atlanta, the Philadelphia Phillies, the San Diego Padres and the Cubs — are all inside the top 10.
Given the Brewers’ success since their renaissance began in 2018, it is hard to paint them as underdogs.
“I wouldn’t say they underestimate us anymore,” Misiorowski said. “I think we’ve gotten to a spot where they kind of see it.”
The Pirates, who are on the cusp of having their playoff drought hit 11 years, certainly have.
“Other teams are definitely looking at what [the Brewers are] doing ... because they haven’t spent the money that the Dodgers have,” Pittsburgh manager Don Kelly said. “Money doesn’t always buy wins or championships. It’s a game that we’re playing. You have to go out there and play good baseball, and the Brewers have done that consistently over the last few years.”

Proposal for monitoring babies with SGA unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

Health officials and doctors yesterday unveiled proposed measures for the long-term monitoring of infants who are “small for gestatational age” (SGA), ahead of Sunday’s Growth Awareness Day.
The Health Promotion Administration (HPA) and Taiwan Society of Neonatology members made the remarks at a seminar in Taipei, saying that small body size in infancy is linked to a failure to thrive, obesity and other disorders later in life.
HPA Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said the government is considering including SGA in the “infant healthbook” to ensure primary care pediatrians are fully informed about the health risks faced by babies.
Photo: CNA
The mechanism allow hospitals and clinics caring for a child to be aware of childhood problems such as SGA, which is crucial for their future health, she said.
Many parents are not aware that infants with SGA must undergo regular check-ups past the age of two, Shen said.
Infants with SGA often make up for their small size in growth spurts, if given good nutrition and care, but the health book could help track those who remain smaller, lighter or shorter than their peers, she said.
Monitoring the growth of such children is essential to making sure that they receive the care they need, in addition to tracking their vaccination status, Shen said.
The measure is in response to calls from the medical community to include SGA in health records, she said.
The HPA is inclined to agree with these suggestions, as many of the metrics used to evaluate SGA infants are the same as those already being recorded in the agency’s primary care pediatrician system, Shen said.
Association chairman president Yang San-nan (楊生湳) said SGA infants often undergo growth spurts at age two or older, but develop low bone density, insulin insensitivity and other conditions in adulthood.
People born as SGA babies must be tracked for disorders linked to these conditions to faciliate preventive care or early treatment, he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:38:02 KST

The politicization and delay of Taiwan’s increased defense spending has raised concerns among Taiwan’s partners, US Representative John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the US and the Chinese Communist Party, said on Tuesday.
Moolenaar released an official statement after meeting with a delegation of Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmakers on Capitol Hill in Washington.
The delegation, led by KMT Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯), discussed Taiwan’s national defense, energy independence and cross-strait policy.
Photo courtesy of US House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the US and the Chinese Communist Party, via CNA
Moolenaar said that, having met with members of the leading parties in Taiwan, they “all share the belief that there is an urgent need to strengthen Taiwan’s defense,” as China’s harassment of Taiwan has grown in recent months, including cyberattacks, intrusions and military exercises.
The KMT-proposed drone budget would increase support for critical drone capabilities, he said, adding that it would be essential for the KMT to “follow through and deliver the resources needed to deliver on Taiwan’s plans to build critical defense capabilities.”
Meanwhile, a statement from the KMT delegation said that they stressed to Moolenaar that the people of Taiwan love and firmly defend their free and democratic way of life, but understand the threat of war as seen in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine, Middle East and Iran conflicts.
The party fully supports the key defense spending necessary to maintain Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities, it said, evidenced by the drone development act and the passage of a special defense budget.
Alongside weapons procurement, critical infrastructure is key to deterrence, and energy security remains one of Taiwan’s most critical vulnerabilities, it said.
The party referenced its proposal to hold a referendum on restarting nuclear power, which could be used to provide a stable supply of electricity during a blockade or crisis.
Speaking on cross-strait issues, the KMT said it places equal emphasis on dialogue and deterrence when dealing with Beijing and seeks to establish stable communication channels to reduce the risk of miscalculation and manage crises.
The KMT said it will continue to deepen cooperation and dialogue with the US Congress in areas including national defense, high-tech supply chain resilience, energy transition, trade and economic affairs, working together towards peace and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region.

Chiayi touts aquaculture, including crocodile meat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

The Chiayi County Agriculture Department yesterday made a pitch for locally raised crocodile meat, touting county aquaculture products as suitable Mid-Autumn Festival barbecue fare.
Chang Chien-cheng (張建成), a section chief in the department’s aquaculture division said in an interview that Chiayi aquaculture products such as oysters, hard clams, whiteleg shrimp, tilapia and eels are low-fat, high in protein and ideal for grilling.
Chiayi has another “special” aquaculture product — crocodile — which is also well-suited for grilling, he said.
Photo courtesy of the Chiayi County Agriculture Department via CNA
Taiwan’s largest concentration of “crocodile,” spectacled caiman, farms is in Yijhu Township (義竹), Chang said.
Chang described crocodile meat as mild in flavor with a firm texture “similar to chicken.”
Restaurants have devised several ways to prepare crocodile, including grilling, deep-frying, boiling, baking and stewing with traditional Chinese medicine ingredients, he said.
The department recommended skinless crocodile leg for grilling, as the dish would stand out in a Mid-Autumn Festival barbecue for its fresh taste and as “a topic of conversation.”
In contrast, skin-on crocodile leg is best used in soups or dishes like “three cup crocodile,” where its taste and texture are similar to giant grouper, it said.
Chang also touted the high quality of Chiayi’s seafood, saying that the oysters and clams are remarkably juicy and release their natural savory flavors with just a brief turn on the grill.
Chiayi’s charcoal-roasted white shrimp offer sweet and tender meat, requiring nothing more than a light sprinkle of salt or pepper to shine, he added.
Taiwanese tilapia features a delicate texture suited for various preparation methods, whether as fillets, chunks, or whole roasted fish, he said, adding that with a squeeze of lemon and a dash of pepper salt, it makes for a nutritious, tasty grilled dish.
People can browse and purchase more than 220 Chiayi aquaculture products by visiting the county’s “Chiayum” Web site (https://www.chiayumfresh.com.tw/), the department said.
Taiwan is to celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday next week.

UN chief Guterres calls for countries fueling Sudan's war to be held accountable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

UN chief Guterres calls for countries fueling Sudan's war to be held accountable
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 16 - United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called on Wednesday for countries providing weapons to the warring parties in Sudan that are used to attack civilians to be held accountable.
"What is happening in Sudan is absolutely horrible. The humanitarian situation in Sudan is devastating. The level of suffering of the Sudanese people is intolerable," Guterres told reporters ahead of the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations in New York next week.
Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
"It is true that the conflict is fueled by a number of countries from the outside," Guterres said. "In my opinion, there should be accountability for the kind of interference in which some countries provide weapons to parties to a conflict when those weapons are used massively to attack civilians."
A U.N. fact-finding mission said earlier this month that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike distant civilian areas with drones. REUTERS

Taiwan shares close higher, but turnover still low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

Taiwanese shares closed higher yesterday, but turnover remained low as investors stayed cautious ahead of a US Federal Reserve policy decision due later in the day, with high expectations of a rate hike.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) closed unchanged at NT$2,380. The stock, which went ex-dividend yesterday, returned to its pre-ex-dividend price within 27 minutes of the market opening.
The quick recovery indicated investor confidence in the outlook for TSMC, a major beneficiary of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, despite investor concern about the possibility of a rate hike by the Fed.
Photo: CNA
The optimism over AI-related demand also supported shares of memory suppliers and some electronic component makers, with Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) rising 5.96 percent and Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電子) gaining 5.96 percent.
The TAIEX ended up 337.41 points, or 0.74 percent, at 45,848.9. However, turnover of NT$643.7 billion (US$20.19 billion) was below the average of NT$689 billion over the previous five sessions, Taiwan Stock Exchange data showed.
“Today’s gains were technical in nature as the TAIEX rebounded from losses in the past few sessions,” Hua Nan Securities Co (華南永昌證券) analyst Kevin Su (蘇俊宏) said.
Over the previous four sessions, the TAIEX had fallen 1,671.87 points, or 3.54 percent.
“But investors showed little interest in chasing prices as many of them awaited the Fed’s decision and signals about its next move,” Su said, adding that investors were focused on comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Fed’s dot plot, which shows policymakers’ projections for interest rates.
There is widespread expectation that the Fed would hike rates for the first time in three years as inflation remains elevated in the US and above the Fed’s 2 percent target.
“Today, financial stocks moved higher on hopes that a rate hike by the Fed will boost their overseas interest income,” Su said.
Cathay Financial Holding Co (國泰金控) gained 2.27 percent and Fubon Financial Holding Co (富邦金控) rose 1.32 percent yesterday.
“Taiwan’s central bank will make its [monetary] decision [on] Thursday afternoon,” Su said. “If the central bank follows its foreign counterparts in raising rates, the TAIEX could be affected.”

SK Hynix mulling making chips in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

South Korea’s SK Hynix Inc is in talks with Intel Corp about a deal that would see it manufacture memory chips on US soil for the first time, three people familiar with the discussions said.
Under one potential scenario, SK Hynix would lease part of Intel’s long-planned chipmaking facility in Ohio, they said. Under another scenario, it could form a venture with Intel and major cloud firms that are keen to lock in memory supplies, two of the people said.
A deal would relieve pressure on Intel, which has been struggling, and mark a big win for US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has been ramping up pressure on chipmakers to build in the US as relentless investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers fuels an acute shortage of memory chips.
Photo: AFP
However, potential opposition from Seoul could be a major hurdle, the sources said.
One of the sources described the talks as exploratory and stressed that no decisions have been made, adding that SK Hynix might consider other ways to structure the deal.
SK Hynix’s product lineup includes DRAM chips used in servers, PCs and smartphones and NAND flash memory chips that provide long-term storage memory. It is also the leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI processing units.
Any agreement to produce advanced memory such as HBM or even DRAM could run into opposition from the South Korean government as those technologies are considered sensitive, said the three sources who declined to be identified as the information is not public.
SK Hynix said in a statement that it is “reviewing various measures, including establishing additional production bases, to strengthen the competitiveness of its memory business,” but “no matters have been determined at this stage.”
Intel declined to comment on what it called speculation, but added that it was continuing with investments in Ohio to ready the site.
Asked about a potential SK Hynix plan to produce chips in the US, South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said any decision would be at the company’s discretion, but if it involved a “national core technology,” it would be subject to a review under the Industrial Technology Protection Act.
The US Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
Manufacturing semiconductors in the US costs much more than in South Korea, the sources said.
Building in the US entails significantly higher labor and construction costs, and much of the semiconductor industry’s supply chain is located within Asia, which also increases US costs, one of them said.
Even so, SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won said in July that the company faces enormous pressure and lobbying from customers and countries to supply more chips.
“I think we need to build a factory in the United States. If possible, I believe we should build it,” he told reporters.

Roberto De Zerbi on Tuesday admitted that Tottenham Hotspur are in a “tough moment” as he apologized for their League Cup exit in a dismal 3-1 defeat against Liverpool.
After a woeful start to the Premier League season, Tottenham’s hopes of a morale-boosting cup run came to a dispiriting end at rain-lashed Anfield. They were swatted aside by Liverpool, with Alexis Mac Allister, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai scoring for the Reds.

Photo: Reuters
De Zerbi’s fourth-bottom team are without a win in their first four league matches, losing twice and drawing twice.
De Zerbi claimed Tottenham have been unlucky this season.
“We have to shoot more times, we have to shoot better, but we are sorry for the result, disappointed, frustrated for the result,” he said.
“I think, unfair, but we have to accept and to be stronger than this unlucky moment,” he said. “I’m honest with myself and I’m honest with you. I think in these five, six games, we have been for sure not lucky with Newcastle, with Everton, even with Nottingham and tonight as well.”
Tottenham’s only win this season has come in the League Cup against second-tier Charlton Athletic.

Making eight changes from last weekend’s draw with Everton was a gamble that backfired for De Zerbi as his side were beaten by an understrength Liverpool line-up.
Former Marseille boss De Zerbi, whose appointment late last season saved Tottenham from relegation, is convinced they are still on the right path.
“We have to understand if we are in the right way or not,” he said. “I think watching the game, the last three games, four games, maybe until minute 60 with Newcastle, I think we are in the right way.”

Book review: Confessions of an ex-Trumper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

The most interesting chapter in Anthony Scaramucci’s All the Wrong Moves is the one where the hedge funder turned podcaster goes to work for Donald Trump. It’s summer 2017, and he’s been given the job of comms director, which he doesn’t know how to do, but he and Trump think it’ll work out because they’re both from New York. Or maybe he took it because he had “Potomac fever,” which afflicts Wall Street financiers who find themselves on the riverfront in Washington DC thinking they know how to run a country just because they’re “full of power and judgmental insight … about to fix everything.”
This appointment lasts only 11 days, not even enough time to be truly tainted by Trump’s first term, though it is enough time for Scaramucci to miss the birth of his son. The account is a mea culpa soup, with the author full of regrets for his hubris, his impulsivity, his “pride, egotism and asinine stupidity,” the fact that, despite the clear-sightedness bestowed by his humble beginnings, he’d come to assume the collective biases of the rich people he hung out with.
But what he doesn’t address is the fact that it was quite plain by then who Donald Trump was. Scaramucci himself identifies the beginning of Trump’s explicit use of racism and the politics of hatred, not in his first taboo-breaking statement that Mexicans were bringing drugs and rapists into the US (2015), but with the Obama birther conspiracy, which had been going on for years. Irrespective of all his pondering as to whether Trump was symptom or cause of a broken US, Scaramucci knew when he joined the White House that he was reporting to a racist, a chancer, an egomaniac and a liar. Bluntly, a person with decent values would not have joined this administration.
That doesn’t invalidate his analysis, but it does flatten it. The US is all about money, he tells us; the founding fathers were actually the investing fathers; anything not obviously a decision motivated by money is the unintended consequence of one. The very United States was “unified — by money,” because that was all Alexander Hamilton was thinking when he created a central bank. The fact that half the English-speaking world could sing the thousand other things Hamilton was thinking in a close harmony hasn’t occurred to the author, who can’t have seen the musical. It makes his potted history of the US a little brutish, and his organizing principle — that the rot started to set in from Clinton onwards, when leaders lost their “moral purpose” — contradictory. If there was never any value higher than money, how can Clinton’s purpose have been any less moral than Franklin D Roosevelt’s?
All of that is just backdrop to the book’s fatal flaw. Scaramucci details the three “catastrophic” errors that have created the US’s current doldrums, and this is all wisdom he came about the hard way, through wrong moves of his own, in the board room, in the situation room, in Trump’s inner circle. These were: privileging China during the globalization era; waging war with no corresponding tax hikes, post 9/11; and bailing out the banks.
It’s hard to disagree with any of it. If the world’s manufacturing all moves to a place where wages are lower, you correspondingly destroy the employment prospects of your own workforce. But these are arguments that were diligently made at the time; by political insurgents from the right, during the 1992 election; by protest movements on the left, in the so-called Battle of Seattle of 1999, and in anti-globalization demonstrations around the world subsequently.
Scaramucci writes that he should have taken this more seriously, they were right, he was wrong, but never reflects on how it came to be. It turns out that without institutional muscle — peculiar for Scaramucci to tell the entire history of his nation’s economy with only the most fleeting mention of Ronald Reagan’s union-busting — mere logic and reason aren’t enough, until it’s too late. He similarly tells the story of the war in Iraq as a cashflow snafu without considering whether anti-imperialists and pacifists might have a point, sometimes, and the story of the 2008 bailouts with only the swiftest nod towards the Occupy movement which, again, was broadly correct in its analysis.
It’s consequently a book of constant catch-up, a man who thought he knew it all, slowly surrendering to more sophisticated analyses when it is too late now anyway: China no longer looks to the US for its place in global markets; American wars are no longer waged with long-term strategic aims if patchy funding streams, but impulsively; and Wall Street no longer calls the shots, techbros do. He nods towards that last reality with a suggestion at the end to break up Silicon Valley monopolies, but never thinks seriously about how far from Kansas the world has actually strayed.
It’s nevertheless quite engaging, and no more or less infuriating than it would be if, say, Alastair Campbell (Scaramucci’s UK opposite number — both coming out with hard-boiled political realism on their Rest Is Politics pods) penned an excoriating critique of the war in Iraq. But it’s hard to choke down an argument whose kernel is “sorry, guys, I just wasn’t listening” from someone still stuck on broadcast.

The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. The Chinese Coast Guard has likewise been ramping up their activities, and the civilian paramilitary People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia has been backing up the navy and coast guard with alarming swarming maneuvers. Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman met in Cairo with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi.
Photo: AP

Neither side gave firm details on any future steps.

The gains have improved the Houthis’ position to seal off the strait to Saudi Arabian shipping, which they have been attacking since late July.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and, from there, to Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil customers in Asia.

He said the jet had been targeted “using a locally made air-to-air missile.”
The spokesman also dismissed Riyadh’s claims that the Houthis had targeted Mecca this week.
“Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,” he said.

Building around US unreliability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

The flurry of new defense agreements signed by Japan suggests Tokyo is attempting to reshape its own security posture. This shift would come in response to China’s geopolitical advances, compounded by the growing unreliability of the US and the associated risks of strategic disengagement.
New security alignments among US allies and partners, which affect various strategic arenas, are increasingly viewed as a reaction to the purported decline of US global leadership during US President Donald Trump’s administration.
The “Mecca Joint Defense Agreement,” signed last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, is seen in a similar light: as an effort by key US allies in the greater Middle East to establish self defense mechanisms against Iran (and Israel) outside the traditional US security umbrella.
However, it remains unlikely that Japan is truly hedging against a future post-US world order dominated by China, even if Tokyo is undoubtedly developing and expanding a complex, multilayered network with allied and like-minded countries.
Japan has deployed fighter aircraft to India for the first time to participate in joint exercises running until Monday next week.
The deployment follows a visit to New Delhi last month by Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi, who agreed with Indian Minister of Defence Rajnath Singh to deepen cooperation through joint drills amid growing security concerns in the Indo-Pacific region.
Similarly, beginning on Tuesday, Japan’s Air Self-Defense Forces is hosting a joint exercise with French forces on Japanese territory. In April, the two countries signed a defense roadmap providing for more joint military training and maneuvers to support regional stability.
In the past few months, Tokyo reinforced bilateral security cooperation with Australia, the Philippines, New Zealand, South Korea and Canada.
All countries that have enhanced military ties with Japan have conducted maritime transits through the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea — where the Philippines is locked in territorial disputes with China — transits that consistently draw indignant reactions from Beijing. These nations are reinforcing military cooperation among themselves, rather than just with Tokyo.
Riho Aizawa, a Japanese Ministry of Defense researcher, does not view Tokyo’s efforts to boost regional defense ties with partners as a hedge against dwindling US engagement. She does not see these initiatives as a response to the Trump administration’s demands for increased military spending.
Rather, in her personal capacity, she told me that “Japan’s growing defense cooperation with these like-minded countries is better understood as part of a longstanding effort to respond to an increasingly severe security environment by maintaining the alliance with America as the cornerstone of its security policy.”
Indeed, Japan’s forces, even in combination with those of its regional partners, might not have the weight to stand against major threats from China without US support.
For instance, Starlink’s use would be vital for Tokyo. Much like its role in supporting Ukraine against Russia’s invasion, the satellite Internet service could keep Japanese and allied forces connected even if ground infrastructure were destroyed by Chinese attacks.
No US Indo-Pacific ally has an operational, fully deployed domestic equivalent to Starlink, although Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are building sovereign low Earth orbit satellite networks for the future.
Europe finds itself in a remarkably similar position, despite its drive to increase defense autonomy from Washington. NATO’s European members would be unable to support Ukraine without US intelligence, satellite and geospatial support.
Japan should build a united front of Indo-Pacific middle powers rather than relying solely on bilateral or trilateral interactions. This should include Taiwan, even though all these actors usually refrain from open cooperation with it.
Even this appears daunting. Just as there are doubts regarding whether NATO’s Article Five on collective defense would trigger an immediate response from member countries — a scenario that many suspect Russian President Vladimir Putin is probing at — it is equally uncertain that solidarity would materialize between Japan and its partners in the event of a crisis with China.
It seems unlikely that India would rush to help Japan if it finds itself embroiled in a conflict with Beijing over Taiwan or the China seas.
At the same time, it is unlikely that Tokyo would swoop to the rescue of India during a possible border conflict between New Delhi and the Chinese.
In the same way, the Mecca deal is already showing its limitations: Despite voicing support, Turkey and Pakistan have so far abstained from direct military intervention against Yemen’s pro-Iran Houthi rebels following the group’s attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, Riyadh is set to receive a US$5.75 billion US arms package, including tank engines and Joint Direct Attack Munitions-Extended Range kits.
Any new security framework developed by Japan, or another US ally, can only complement, rather than replace, the alliance with Washington.
Emanuele Scimia is a journalist and analyst covering foreign affairs and defense issues.

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) yesterday laid out proposed policies to encourage four forms of environmentally friendly commuting in Taipei: walking, taking buses, riding bicycles and using shared electric scooters.
The policies would prioritize commuter safety and convenience, and include proposals to add shared electric scooters to the TPass program and provide 30 minutes for free on the electric YouBike 2.0E during commuter hours, he said at a news conference at the DPP headquarters.
Shen said he would improve pedestrian safety by establishing school commuter zones around all of Taipei’s more than 150 elementary schools within eight years.
Photo: Gan Meng-lin, Taipei Times
Official data showed that the peak period for traffic deaths and injuries in Taipei in 2024 was between 7am and 9am, when students are traveling to school, he said.
The central government recommends defining an area within 150m of a school as a school commuting zone, but the guidelines are advisory and Taipei has only established four this year, he said.
Secondly, Shen said he would enact bus safety reforms, focused on subsidizing bus drivers’ salaries, redesigning driver seats, establishing driver rest stations at major turnaround points and reorganizing bus networks by district.
Thirdly, Shen said he would work to connect, maintain and supplement Taipei’s bicycle network to promote bicycle riding.
After YouBike resumed making the first 30 minutes of rides free, the number of rides increased by 55 percent, surpassing 400 million rides, he said.
Shen proposed providing more crossings over rivers and embankments, including a bicycle bridge across the Keelung River connecting Yingfeng Riverside Park (迎風河濱公園) and Gangqian (港墘) in Neihu District (?湖) to link the riverside cycle route to Neihu Technology Park.
Shen said he would also make the first 30 minutes of YouBike 2.0E electric-assist bicycle rides free during commuter hours and add more bikes at hotspots, while including electric scooters in the TPass program.

Taiwanese book longlisted for National Book Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

The English-language translation of Taiwanese writer Ping Lu’s (平路) To the East of the East (東方之東) has been longlisted for the US’ National Book Award for Translated Literature, marking the second such recognition for a Taiwanese writer after Yang Shuang-zi (楊?子).
Translated by Jeremy Tiang (程異), the novel follows a Taiwanese writer’s trip to Beijing in search of her missing husband and her encounters there, the National Book Foundation said.
The nonprofit announced the longlist on Tuesday.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
To the East of the East was one of 10 titles — originally published in Arabic, Chinese, French, Indonesian, Norwegian, Russian and Spanish — selected from 159 books, the foundation said.
Nine of the longlisted works are novels, while the other is nonfiction, the foundation added.
The foundation said it would announce the finalists on Oct. 6, while the winner would be revealed live at the 77th National Book Awards Ceremony on Nov. 18.
To the East of the East is the first book in the Ping Lu’s “Taiwan Trilogy.” Published in 2011, the novel was followed by Ilha Formosa (婆娑之島) and Passing (夢魂之地). The trilogy was republished in 2024.
In an interview with reporters, Ping Lu, whose real name is Lu Ping (路平), attributed the recognition to Tiang’s translation, saying that he writes well in English and that “my contribution may only be about 10 percent.”
When the book was published in 2011, she had recently returned to Taiwan after working in Hong Kong as director of the Kwang Hwa Information and Culture Center, Taiwan’s cultural office in Hong Kong, the author said.
The novel reflected her circumstances at the time, exploring how a person examines their inner emotions from an outside perspective.
“Sometimes if you go far enough, you can hear the call from within your heart,” she said.
The novel is also about the relationship between an island and the mainland, as well as the betrayal and separation that lead to the realization that one’s ideal life is often linked to the pursuit of freedom, Ping Lu said.
Ping Lu has won several Taiwanese national book awards, such as the National Award for the Arts. Her works have been translated into multiple languages, including English, French, Japanese, Korean and Czech, the foundation said.
Tiang, originally from Singapore, has also translated works by other Taiwanese writers including Su Wei-chen (蘇偉貞), Lo Yi-chin (駱以軍) and Chi Ta-wei (紀大偉).

Chinese minister urges vigilance

Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun (董軍) yesterday urged nations to avoid provocative acts and curb the resurgence of regressive historical trends in remarks likely to be taken as veiled criticism of Japan.
Warning that the world had arrived at a “fragile moment,” Dong called for a fresher, more equal approach to resolving international tension, but offered few specifics or direct criticism of rivals.
“We must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against all latent manifestations of hegemony, militarism and historical revisionism,” he said in an opening speech at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on security.
Photo: Reuters
“We must not turn a blind eye or condone such behavior. By rallying broad-based forces of justice, we must suppress the resurgence of historical dregs and prevent them from exploiting the situation to cause harm,” he said.
Ties between China and Japan soured last year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested that a hypothetical Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response.
